The pattern that matters for exam purposes is the same either way: at/near umbilicus shortly after birth → descends ~1 cm/day → non-palpable by ~day 10–14. · BUBBL-HE — the standard postpartum head-to-toe assessment · Rather than assessing postpartum recovery as a vague overall impression, BUBBL-HE breaks it into seven concrete checkpoints, each targeting a specific system that changes rapidly in the days after birth. · Letter | Focus | Expected finding · B | Breasts | Soft, non-tender; colostrum present · U | Uterus/fundus | Firm, midline, descending ~1 cm/day · B | Bladder | Empty, no distention · B | Bowel | Active bowel sounds · L | Lochia | Rubra → serosa → alba, no foul odor · H | Homan's sign / lower extremities | No calf pain on dorsiflexion (possible DVT if present) · E | Emotional status | Bonding, stable mood (vs. blues/depression) · Note: some instructors teach this as BUBBLE-EL (ending in Episiotomy/perineum + Lower extremities) instead of BUBBL-HE — same core assessment, slightly different letter grouping. Either way, breasts/uterus/bladder/bowel/lochia/perineum-or-Homan's/emotional status all get assessed. · REEDA — perineal/incision assessment · When there's an episiotomy, laceration, or incision to assess, REEDA gives a structured way to describe what you see: R edness, E dema, E cchymosis, D ischarge, A pproximation (are the wound edges closed together, without gaps?). Documenting all five elements every time gives the next nurse a clear baseline to compare against. · Some materials use a similar mnemonic, RETA (Redness, Edema, Tenderness, Approximation) — same idea, one fewer letter. Either way you're checking for infection/healing complications versus a clean, well-approximated repair. · Lochia progression · Lochia is the postpartum vaginal discharge, and its color is meant to progress in one direction only — from blood-heavy to serous to essentially clear — as the uterine lining heals. · Stage | Color | Duration · Rubra | Bright red, small clots | Days 1–3 · Serosa | Pinkish-brown | Days 4–10 · Alba | Yellow/white | Day 11+ (up to 6 weeks) · Lochia going backward (alba back to rubra) or suddenly increasing suggests a uterus that stopped contracting or retained tissue — report it. Saturating a pad in under 15–60 minutes, or foul odor, both warrant provider notification. The 'red zone' danger sign for both mother and newborn is oliguria — urine output <30 mL/hr . · RhoGam (Rho(D) immune globulin) · This connects directly back to the Rh incompatibility pathophysiology covered in the Newborn unit — RhoGam is how that entire hemolysis cascade gets prevented before it can start. · Given to Rh-negative mothers who deliver an Rh-positive infant (indirect Coombs must be negative , meaning she hasn't already formed antibodies) · Administered IM at 28 weeks gestation and again within 72 hours of delivery (also after amniocentesis or other sensitizing events like trauma or miscarriage) · Do NOT give with live-virus vaccines (e.g., rubella given same visit is fine per protocol, but timing/coordination matters) or estrogen-containing meds · Perineal & incision care · Episiotomy/laceration: ice packs (10 min/hr for first 24 hrs), Tucks/hydrocortisone, sitz baths twice daily, keep clean · Episiotomy degrees: 1st = skin only; 2nd = perineal muscles; 3rd = extends into anal sphincter; 4th = through rectal mucosa · Vagina takes 6–10 weeks to regain size/contour · C-section incision: assess bleeding, open to air after first night; pain control per orders

Where all the extra fluid and volume goes · Pregnancy added roughly 45% more blood volume and months of hormonal support to nearly every organ system. All of that has to be reversed in a matter of weeks after delivery, and each system does it a slightly different way. · Cardiovascular · With the uterus and placenta no longer part of the circulatory loop, blood that was flowing through them returns to central circulation, and cardiac output actually increases in the immediate postpartum period before gradually normalizing. The body sheds the extra plasma volume through diuresis (increased urination) and diaphoresis (sweating) — both are expected, sometimes dramatic, and not signs of illness. At the same time, clotting factors remain elevated for weeks after birth, which is protective against hemorrhage but also raises the risk of dangerous clots — this hypercoagulable state doesn't switch off the moment the placenta is delivered. · Gastrointestinal · Constipation is the expected GI complaint, driven by decreased bowel tone from pregnancy, decreased activity during labor, and often genuine fear of pain with a tender perineum. The first postpartum stool is expected around 2–3 days after birth; stool softeners and hydration are the standard preventive approach. · Urinary · Increased bladder capacity combines with decreased sensation to create a real risk of urinary retention that the patient herself may not feel coming. This matters clinically because a distended bladder displaces the uterus , which in turn reduces uterine contraction and increases bleeding — the exact mechanical chain covered in the Involution lesson. · Bladder distention signs: fundus off midline, excessive lochia, small frequent voids ( <150 mL ) — she's overflowing around a full bladder, not actually emptying it. Frequent small voids can look reassuring on a flow sheet if you don't stop to calculate the volume. · Musculoskeletal · Muscle fatigue and aches are common in the first 1–2 days as the body recovers from the physical work of labor. Diastasis recti — a separation of the abdominal rectus muscles that occurred to accommodate the growing uterus — is also common and generally improves gradually with time and targeted core exercises. · Endocrine · As pregnancy hormone levels fall, the body's normal cycle tries to restart — but it doesn't always announce itself with a period first. Ovulation can occur before the return of the first postpartum menstrual period , which is exactly why breastfeeding is not a reliable method of contraception on its own, no matter how frequently the mother is nursing.

What you assess, and who's at risk · A postpartum focused assessment isn't a general check-in — it's a specific list of systems chosen because they're the ones most likely to reveal a developing complication before it becomes an emergency. · Vital signs — watch specifically for orthostatic hypotension, since blood loss and fluid shifts raise fall risk with first ambulation · Fundus — firm, midline, appropriately descending · Lochia — color, amount, odor · Perineum — using REEDA/RETA · Bladder — emptying appropriately, not retaining · Breasts — for engorgement, cracking, or signs of mastitis · Lower extremities — a DVT check (Homan's sign, though a negative Homan's does not fully rule out DVT), edema, deep tendon reflexes · Emotional status — assessed as part of every focused assessment, not an optional add-on, given how common mood changes are in this period · Overlapping risk factors — hemorrhage and infection share a cause · It's not a coincidence that certain risk factors show up on both lists below. Anything that stretches labor out, or puts hands and instruments inside the uterus, raises both risks simultaneously — a stressed, overworked uterus is both more likely to bleed and more likely to become infected. · Hemorrhage risk factors | Infection risk factors · Grand multiparity, prolonged/precipitous labor, retained placenta, operative delivery | Operative delivery, multiple vaginal exams, prolonged ROM (>24h), diabetes · The lists overlap on purpose — anything that stretches labor or puts instruments/hands in the uterus raises both risks at once. When you see a patient flagged for one, it's worth checking whether her history also flags her for the other.

Rubin's phases, blues vs. depression vs. psychosis, and what goes home with her · Rubin's phases — maternal psychological adjustment · Becoming a mother is a psychological transition as much as a physical one, and Rubin described it as unfolding in three predictable phases. Recognizing which phase a patient is in tells you how much teaching she's ready to absorb right now. · Phase | Timing | What it looks like · Taking-In | Day 1–2 | Passive, dependent, focused on own needs (sleep, food); recounts the birth experience repeatedly as she processes it · Taking-Hold | Day 2+ | Active, takes charge of infant care, seeks information, may have self-doubt — the PRIME time for teaching · Letting-Go | Later | Assumes the parenting role; sees the infant as a separate individual; resumes her role as a partner · Taking-Hold is the teaching window — she's motivated and ready to learn, but also vulnerable to feeling like she's failing, so frame teaching supportively, not critically. Trying to teach detailed newborn care during Taking-In, when she's still passive and focused inward, tends to fall flat — she isn't in the headspace to absorb it yet. · Postpartum blues, depression, and psychosis — a spectrum, not one condition · These three terms get used loosely outside of clinical settings, but they describe genuinely different severities that call for different responses. · Postpartum blues affects 70–80% of new mothers, should NOT last longer than 2 weeks , and is not the same thing as postpartum depression or psychosis · The 2-week line is the exam point: mild + resolves within 2 weeks = blues. Persistent, worsening, or beyond 2 weeks = depression → needs referral. · Postpartum psychosis — a psychiatric emergency · Red flags: confusion, disorganized thinking/behavior, hallucinations (e.g., conversations with herself), paranoia, or thoughts of harming self or infant. This is NOT managed like blues — it requires immediate evaluation (ER or emergency psychiatric assessment), not outpatient follow-up or a medication pickup. The distinguishing feature from blues and even from depression is the presence of psychotic symptoms — losing touch with reality — which carries real risk to both mother and infant and cannot wait for a routine appointment. · Discharge — medications to confirm were given · RhoGam (if Rh-negative) · Rubella vaccine (if non-immune — a live vaccine, so timing around future pregnancy matters) · Tdap · Discharge teaching — ACHES · For any patient going home on estrogen-containing contraception, ACHES gives a memorable list of warning signs tied to serious vascular complications. · Letter | Warning sign · A | Abdominal pain · C | Chest pain · H | Headaches (severe) · E | Eye problems (vision changes) · S | Severe leg pain/swelling (calf) · Other signs to report immediately postpartum · Saturating a pad within 1 hour, or pooling of blood under the buttocks · Foul-smelling discharge, fever/chills · Worsening or new perineal/uterine pain · Dyspnea, chest pain · Depression or mood changes affecting relationships/function · Oliguria — urine output <30 mL/hr (the 'red zone' danger sign) · Newborns' & Mothers' Health Protection Act (1995) · Insurance must cover 48-hr stay (vaginal) / 96-hr stay (C-section) · Patient cannot be coerced into early discharge · Postpartum discharge basics · Follow-up visit within first 3 weeks, then again before 12 weeks postpartum · No heavy lifting (nothing heavier than the baby in its carrier) · Resume intercourse 2–4 weeks after birth once bleeding stopped and perineum healed · Lactation suppression (non-breastfeeding): supportive bra x72 hrs, avoid nipple stimulation/warm water, ice packs/cold cabbage leaves for engorgement

Oxytocin, prolactin, colostrum, and getting the latch right · Key hormones — production and delivery are two separate jobs · Hormone/substance | Role · Oxytocin | Causes milk ejection (the 'let-down' reflex) — this is the same hormone responsible for uterine contraction, which is why breastfeeding also supports involution · Prolactin | Stimulates milk production itself · Colostrum | Early, antibody-rich first milk, produced in small quantities before mature milk comes in · Breastfeeding advantages · Enhanced infant immunity · Optimal nutrition · Promotes maternal-infant bonding · Decreases risk of certain infant diseases · Supports maternal uterine involution, since the oxytocin release from nursing helps the uterus contract · Cost-effective · Positioning & technique · Common holds: cradle and football hold · Feed 15–20 minutes per side; begin each feeding on the side last nursed (track with a reminder like a bracelet) · Break the latch by inserting a clean finger into the baby's mouth before removing from breast — never pull the baby off (causes nipple trauma) · For cracked nipples: use lanolin cream and leave nipples open to air after feeding; ensure latch includes the whole areola, rotate/limit time on the sore side · For engorgement: ice packs or chilled cabbage leaves between feedings; warm soaks/shower just before feeding to encourage let-down · Waterproof pads inside the bra trap moisture and cause skin breakdown — not a fix for leaking. Use absorbent breast pads instead. · Newborn hunger cues — read the early signs, not just the cry · Teach parents that crying is actually a LATE sign of hunger — by the time an infant is crying, it's already frustrated and may latch less effectively. Early cues include stretching, eyes opening, yawning, rooting, and sticking the tongue out. Feeding on these earlier cues, rather than waiting for crying, generally produces a calmer feeding session and a better latch. · Nutrition & supplementation · Continue prenatal vitamins; increase hydration and 300–500 kcal/day while breastfeeding · Ensure iron supplementation for exclusively breastfed infants — iron stores deplete around 4 months · Caregivers should watch for foods baby may not tolerate in breast milk (e.g., caffeine, cruciferous vegetables, chocolate) · Mastitis vs. engorgement — tell them apart · Both present with breast discomfort, but the distribution and systemic symptoms point in different directions, and they call for different treatment. ·  | Mastitis | Engorgement · Distribution | Usually UNILATERAL | Typically BILATERAL · Systemic symptoms | Fever, chills, flu-like symptoms | None — localized fullness/discomfort only · Resolves with | Antibiotics + continued feeding/emptying | Feeding or manual expression

Inability to attain/maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse · Erectile dysfunction affects roughly 30 million American men , with prevalence rising sharply with age — about 47% of men over 75 are affected. Understanding the mechanism makes the whole topic click into place: an erection depends on autonomic nerve signaling that triggers arteriolar dilation, which fills the corpus cavernosum with blood. Neurologic dysfunction — from any cause — interrupts that signal, reduces the dilation, and compromises the perfusion needed to sustain an erection. Once you see ED as fundamentally a blood-flow and nerve-signaling problem, the entire risk factor list below stops looking like an arbitrary list of unrelated conditions. · Primary vs. secondary — a distinction based on history, not cause · Type | Definition · Primary | Patient has never achieved a sufficient erection · Secondary | Patient has achieved an erection and completed intercourse successfully in the past, but can no longer do so reliably · Assessment & risk factors — nearly all of them are vascular or neurologic · Detailed health/sexual/psychosocial history, medication list, smoking habits · Physical findings: anxious appearance, signs of depression, reduced body hair, testicular atrophy, penis deformity · Risk factors, almost all traceable back to vascular or nerve damage: overweight, stress, smoking, certain medications, inactivity, obstructive sleep apnea, restless leg syndrome, pelvic injury/surgery, prostate cancer treatment · Diagnostics — each test rules something specific in or out · CBC (rule out infection) · PSA (rule out prostate cancer) · Testosterone (checks for a hormonal contributor) · HgbA1C (uncontrolled diabetes damages both nerves and blood vessels) · Lipid profile (atherosclerosis is a vascular cause of ED) · Blood flow studies/ultrasound and angiography (directly assess the vascular supply itself) · How the workup drives treatment choice · ED treatment isn't one-size-fits-all — it follows directly from what the workup finds. Organic ED (a physical cause identified through the diagnostics above — vascular, neurologic, hormonal) is treated by addressing that underlying cause alongside symptomatic medication. Psychogenic ED (no physical cause found, often tied to performance anxiety or depression) responds better to therapy/counseling than to medication alone. This is exactly why the history and diagnostics come before treatment selection in the first place — treating a hormonal cause with a PDE5 inhibitor alone, for example, misses the actual driver of the problem. · Treatment · PDE5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil — relax smooth muscle and vasodilate, directly addressing the mechanism described above; tadalafil may be safer for patients with cardiac history · Injectable medications, hormone/testosterone replacement (gel absorbs in ~2 hrs — cover the area before contact with others to avoid transferring hormone; patch applied daily to hairless skin, rotating sites) · Mechanical devices: vacuum devices, O-rings, implants — options that work around the vascular/nerve problem rather than treating it directly · Sildenafil (Viagra) — the SATA goldmine · Side effects: priapism (erection >4 hours), headache, and blue-tinted vision (a distinctive visual side effect worth remembering specifically because it's unusual enough to be tested) · Take 30–60 minutes before anticipated intercourse; wait at least 24 hours between doses · Absolute contraindication with any nitrate (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) — risk of cardiovascular collapse · PDE5 inhibitors + nitrates = profound hypotension/cardiac arrest risk — never combine. Both drug classes work by vasodilation, so stacking them doesn't just add their effects, it compounds them into a genuinely dangerous blood pressure drop. Also watch for priapism (erection >4 hours = emergency, seek care immediately).

Amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, PMS/PMDD, endometriosis, and the transition to menopause · Amenorrhea · Amenorrhea is the absence of menstrual periods, and the distinction between primary and secondary matters because it points toward completely different causes. Primary amenorrhea means no menses by age 15 despite otherwise normal growth and development. Secondary amenorrhea means periods that were previously regular have stopped for 3 or more cycles, or 6 months. Whenever a sexually active patient of reproductive age presents with secondary amenorrhea, pregnancy is always the first thing ruled out before any other workup begins — it's the most common cause by far, and treating it as anything else first risks missing an actual pregnancy. · Menstrual bleeding pattern terms · Menorrhagia — excessive or prolonged menstrual bleeding · Metrorrhagia — bleeding between periods, at unexpected times in the cycle · Dysmenorrhea — painful periods, and why they're painful · Dysmenorrhea is caused by excessive prostaglandins , which trigger stronger uterine contractions than necessary and reduce blood flow to the uterine muscle — the same basic mechanism behind other kinds of cramping pain caused by muscle ischemia. Primary and secondary dysmenorrhea are distinguished mainly by timing and cause: ·  | Primary dysmenorrhea | Secondary dysmenorrhea · Cycle type | Occurs in ovulatory cycles | Not limited to ovulatory cycles · Onset | Within about 1 year of menarche | Develops later in life · Pattern over time | Tends to decrease with age | Tends to persist or worsen · Cause | Functional — excess prostaglandins, no structural disease | Pathologic — an underlying condition like endometriosis, fibroids, or ovarian cysts · Dysmenorrhea affects 50–90% of females, with about 10% incapacitated for 1–3 days per cycle — it's genuinely common, not a rare complaint. Early age of menarche is a recognized risk factor. · NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) are first-line — and the timing matters: teach patients to take them BEFORE pain becomes severe, since NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandin production going forward, not by reversing pain that's already underway · Non-pharmacologic measures: heating pad to the lower abdomen, light exercise, increased fluid intake, a low-sodium/low-sugar diet · Supplements sometimes used: ginger, vitamin B1/B6/D3/E · When a patient takes NSAIDs regularly for dysmenorrhea, teach them to watch for and report dark, tarry stools — a sign of GI bleeding from chronic NSAID use, since NSAIDs also reduce the protective prostaglandins that normally shield the stomach lining. · PMS & PMDD · PMS: physical/emotional symptoms occurring 5 days before to 4 days after menses (bloating, irritability, fatigue, food cravings) · PMDD (Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder): a more extreme variant of the same timing pattern, but with severe mood shifts, panic attacks, and depression layered on top of the usual PMS symptoms · Endometriosis · Endometriosis is endometrial-like tissue implanted outside the uterus — on the ovaries, colon, or other abdominal organs. Because this tissue still responds to the menstrual cycle's hormonal signals, it bleeds every month just like the uterine lining does, except this blood has nowhere to go, which is exactly why it produces pelvic pain, painful intercourse (dyspareunia), infertility, and abnormal bleeding. Management focuses on suppressing that monthly cyclical stimulation — hormonal contraceptives to shrink the tissue, other medications, or surgery when needed. · Menopause — definitions and the perimenopausal lead-up · Definition: permanent cessation of menses, confirmed retrospectively after 12 months without a period · Perimenopause = the irregular transition period leading up to it, typically starting around 4 years before the final period, marked by fluctuating hormone levels · Average age: 51 · Estrogen drops by roughly 90%, with downstream effects on breast tissue, skin, bone density, and cardiovascular risk · Why menopause raises cardiovascular risk — the estrogen connection · Estrogen isn't just a reproductive hormone — while present, it actively protects the cardiovascular system by raising HDL and lowering LDL cholesterol, improving vascular elasticity through vasodilation (which also helps keep blood pressure lower), and suppressing pro-inflammatory substances that damage blood vessel walls. When estrogen drops sharply at menopause, all three of those protective effects fade at once, which is exactly why coronary heart disease risk rises in the postmenopausal years. · Treatment · Hormone Replacement Therapy (estrogen most effective, ± progesterone; vaginal estrogen for localized dryness) vs. non-hormonal options (antidepressants for hot flashes, lubricants for dryness) · Osteoporosis prevention: calcium + vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, bone density testing · Comfort measures: dress in layers, use an overhead fan, avoid caffeine/alcohol to reduce hot flash triggers · The Women's Health Initiative study (updated 2002 ) found HT has a complex risk/benefit pattern — appropriate for symptom relief but not supported for chronic disease prevention , and contraindicated after breast cancer, MI, stroke, or blood clot. In other words: HRT treats the symptoms of falling estrogen, but it is not prescribed as a strategy to prevent the cardiovascular risk that falling estrogen also causes.

Diagnosis, treatment ladder, and contraception · Infertility · Definition: no conception after ≥12 months of unprotected intercourse · Affects 1 in 6 couples · Causes split roughly: male 33% / female 33% / unknown 33% — a genuinely even three-way split, which is why both partners are worked up rather than assuming the problem lies with one · Male factor: varicocele is the most common cause ; also heat exposure (hot tubs, tight clothing) can impair sperm production · Ovulation detection: the LH surge occurs 12–36 hours before ovulation, which is the basis for ovulation predictor kits; basal body temperature rises after ovulation has already occurred · The 'Rule of 1 Year' — both menopause (12 months without a period) and infertility (12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception) share this same one-year benchmark. Easy to mix up which direction it points. · Infertility diagnostic workup · Semen analysis is typically done first specifically because it's the least invasive and least expensive test available — it makes sense to rule out or confirm a male factor before moving to more invasive female testing. · Partner | Test | Purpose · Male | Semen analysis | First test performed — non-invasive; checks count/motility · Female | Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) | Radiopaque dye to check tubal patency · Female | Hormonal assays | FSH, LH, progesterone — evaluate ovulation · Female | Transvaginal ultrasound | Visualizes pelvic anatomy and follicular development · Couple | Postcoital test | Evaluates sperm survival in cervical mucus · The infertility treatment ladder — escalating from least to most invasive · Treatment doesn't jump straight to the most advanced option — it escalates step by step, trying the least invasive and least expensive approach first before moving on. · Step | Treatment | What it does · 1 | Clomiphene (Clomid) | Improves the chances of ovulating regularly — first-line for ovulatory dysfunction · 2 | Hormone injections | Improves ovulation chances if Clomid alone isn't successful · 3 | Intrauterine insemination (IUI) | A catheter places sperm directly into the uterus, timed right before ovulation · 4 | In vitro fertilization (IVF) | A multi-step process, typically the last-line option (~35% success rate, can cost thousands out of pocket) · IVF itself unfolds in four distinct steps: hormone injections for several weeks to stimulate the ovaries to mature multiple eggs at once; a minor procedure using a thin needle to retrieve the eggs directly from the ovaries; fertilization of the eggs with sperm in a laboratory dish; and finally, transfer of the resulting embryo(s) into the uterus, where implantation hopefully occurs. · Family planning — method-specific nuances · Method | Mechanism | Key teaching point · Combined OCP | Inhibits ovulation | Increases clot (DVT/PE) risk — contraindicated in smokers over 35 or history of clots; use backup if a dose is missed; report ACHES · IUD (hormonal) | Thins lining, thickens cervical mucus | Risk of perforation/spotting; check the string monthly; contraindicated with current pelvic infection or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding · Depo-Provera (medroxyprogesterone) | Delays ovulation | Risk of decreased BONE DENSITY — counsel on calcium/vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise · Emergency contraception (Plan B) | Delays ovulation | Must be taken within 72 hours; nausea/cycle changes common; contraindicated if already pregnant · NuvaRing | Continuous hormone release | Stays in the vagina 3 weeks, then removed for 1 week to allow menstruation · Diaphragm | Barrier | Must stay in place at least 6 hours after intercourse to be effective · Vasectomy | Blocks sperm transport (vas deferens) | NOT immediately sterile — sperm can remain viable in the reproductive tract for up to 6 months; couples need a backup method until two consecutive negative semen analyses confirm sterility · ACHES — and what each sign can mean · ACHES already appeared in the Postpartum unit as discharge teaching; here it applies to any patient on estrogen-containing contraception long-term. Each letter maps to a specific complication, which is worth knowing rather than treating ACHES as five generic vague symptoms. · Letter | Warning sign | Potential complication · A | Abdominal pain | Liver tumor or gallbladder issues · C | Chest pain | Pulmonary embolism or MI · H | Headaches (severe) | Hypertension or stroke (CVA) · E | Eye problems | Retinal artery thrombosis (vision loss) · S | Severe leg pain | Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) · Hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy, not infection — condoms should still be used with all sexual activity. Best to be off oral contraceptives 1–2 months before attempting to conceive. Antibiotics can reduce OCP effectiveness — backup contraception is needed until the start of the next menstrual period.

Organism categories, curability, and reporting · STIs are caused by organisms from five categories — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and parasites — and which category an infection falls into determines almost everything else about it: whether it's curable, how urgently it needs partner treatment, and what the reporting requirements are. As a rule, bacterial and protozoal/fungal STIs are curable with the right antibiotic or antifungal; viral STIs are not curable , only manageable. · Gonorrhea · Caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacteria), incubation period 2–8 days. In females: purulent urethral/vaginal discharge, a red and edematous urethral meatus, a friable cervix with greenish-yellow discharge, and risk of pelvic inflammatory disease. In males: mucopurulent or purulent urethral discharge and penile edema. Either sex can develop fever, rectal or pharyngeal infection, or arthritis. Gonorrhea frequently co-occurs with chlamydia , which is why treatment covers both. · Treatment: ceftriaxone IM (single dose) , plus doxycycline for presumptive chlamydia coverage in nonpregnant patients. Curable: yes. Report all cases to public health authorities; partners must be notified and treated. · Chlamydia · Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (bacteria). Often asymptomatic, especially in men. In females: cervicitis, urethritis, intermenstrual bleeding, and mucopurulent discharge. In males: dysuria and urethral discharge. · Treatment: doxycycline first-line (azithromycin or levofloxacin as alternatives; azithromycin preferred in pregnancy). Curable: yes. · Syphilis · Caused by Treponema pallidum (bacteria), incubation 3–6 weeks. Progresses through stages if untreated: a painless chancre at the primary stage, then a rash — classically on the palms and soles — at the secondary stage, then a latent period with no symptoms, and finally late-stage neurologic and cardiovascular damage. · Treatment: penicillin G (IM) , the gold-standard treatment. Curable: yes, especially when treated early. Report all cases to public health. · Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: watch for this after giving penicillin for syphilis — a systemic response (fever, hypotension, tachycardia) as spirochetes are killed off and release inflammatory material. It typically lasts about 24 hours and is not a penicillin allergy — don't withhold future penicillin doses because of it. · Genital yeast infection (not classified as an STI, but sexually transmissible) · Caused by Candida (fungus). Presents with vulvar itching, redness, and a thick white ('cottage cheese') discharge. Treatment: antifungals — oral fluconazole or topical agents. Curable: yes. · Bacterial vaginosis (BV) · Caused by an overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and other normal vaginal bacteria. Presents with a gray, thin, fishy-smelling discharge , confirmed on exam by a positive whiff test (an amine/fishy odor released when a sample is mixed with potassium hydroxide). Treatment: metronidazole . Curable: yes. · Trichomoniasis · Caused by Trichomonas vaginalis (a protozoan) — the most common curable STI in the US. Classically presents with a frothy, malodorous, yellow-green discharge and the hallmark 'strawberry cervix' on exam. Treatment: metronidazole (Flagyl) — and partner treatment is essential, since reinfection from an untreated partner is common. · Metronidazole (used for both BV and trichomoniasis) causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — it inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, letting toxic acetaldehyde build up. Symptoms (severe flushing, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension) appear within 10–30 minutes of drinking. Teach patients to avoid all alcohol during treatment and for a period after finishing it. · HPV (Human Papillomavirus) · A virus, and the primary risk factor for cervical cancer. May cause cauliflower-like genital warts, or may be entirely asymptomatic. Treatment: topical medications or cryotherapy to remove visible warts — but this treats the lesions, not the underlying viral infection. Prevention: the Gardasil vaccine . Curable: no. · HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus) · A virus, causing painful vesicles/ulcers and malaise. Treatment: acyclovir (or related antivirals) to control outbreak frequency and severity. Curable: no — antivirals suppress outbreaks, they don't eliminate the virus, and viral shedding (and transmission risk) can occur even without visible lesions. · Quick reference — organism and curability at a glance · Infection | Organism | Curable? · Gonorrhea | Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacteria) | Yes · Chlamydia | Chlamydia trachomatis (bacteria) | Yes · Syphilis | Treponema pallidum (bacteria) | Yes (esp. treated early) · Genital yeast | Candida (fungus) | Yes · Bacterial vaginosis | Gardnerella vaginalis (bacteria) | Yes · Trichomoniasis | Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoa) | Yes · HPV | Papillomavirus (virus) | No · HSV | Herpesvirus hominis (virus) | No · Neonatal transmission (why maternal screening matters) · Gonorrhea/Chlamydia → neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) or pneumonia — this is why erythromycin ophthalmic ointment is given to every newborn shortly after birth ( required by law in all 50 states ) · Chlamydia conjunctivitis may also present with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis features (watch for projectile vomiting, feeding intolerance) · Syphilis crosses the placenta as early as 18 weeks — congenital syphilis causes physical anomalies, CNS damage, and hearing loss · HSV active genital lesions at term → indication for cesarean birth to prevent neonatal transmission · Note: HIV/AIDS is covered later this semester; Hepatitis was covered in NUR 113.

Oxytocin, Cervadil, Cytotec, and Magnesium Sulfate · Oxytocin (Pitocin) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Induce or augment labor (start ~1 milliunit/min, titrate by 1–2 mU every 30–60 min); control postpartum hemorrhage (10–40 units IV) · Mechanism of action | A synthetic version of the natural hormone oxytocin — causes potent, selective stimulation of uterine and mammary smooth muscle. Unlike the natural hormone, it does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier, so it does not trigger the endorphin release that naturally blunts labor pain · Adverse reactions | Uterine tachysystole; fetal distress; water retention/fluid overload (antidiuretic effect); rare but serious: seizures, subarachnoid hemorrhage; postpartum hemorrhage from uterine hypersensitivity/fatigue · Contraindications | Situations where vaginal delivery isn't advised: placenta previa, active genital herpes, fetal malpresentation, severe fetal distress, prior classical uterine incision · Nursing interventions | IV via infusion pump ONLY — never a free-flowing line; monitor contractions, maternal HR/BP, FHR, and blood loss every 15 minutes; monitor I&O for fluid overload; STOP the infusion for tachysystole or non-reassuring FHR · Patient education | Explain that induced contractions may feel more continuous/intense than spontaneous labor, since the drug doesn't trigger the body's natural pain-modulating endorphin response · Oxytocin shows up on both sides of the postpartum hemorrhage story — it's the treatment for uterine atony after delivery, and prolonged exposure to it during labor is itself a listed risk factor for that same atony. An overstimulated uterus can become too fatigued to contract well once the baby is out. · Cervadil (Dinoprostone) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Cervical ripening, given vaginally, for a Bishop score ≤4 · Mechanism of action | A prostaglandin that softens and ripens the cervix, preparing it for induction · Adverse reactions | Uterine tachysystole; non-reassuring FHR · Contraindications | Prior cesarean/classical uterine incision (rupture risk); fetal distress · Nursing interventions | Monitor for tachysystole and non-reassuring FHR; remove the insert if either occurs · Patient education | Explain this is a preparation step before oxytocin, not the induction itself · Cytotec (Misoprostol) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Cervical ripening/induction (vaginal or oral) for Bishop score ≤4; also used for postpartum hemorrhage; more potent than Cervadil · Mechanism of action | A prostaglandin analogue that ripens the cervix and stimulates uterine contraction · Adverse reactions | Uterine tachysystole; uterine rupture (rare but serious) · Contraindications | Prior cesarean section/uterine scar — significantly raises rupture risk · Nursing interventions | Do NOT start oxytocin within 4 hours of the last misoprostol dose; assess for severe abdominal pain or excessive bleeding, which could signal rupture · Patient education | Explain the 4-hour waiting period before any oxytocin, and why (rupture risk from stacking two strong uterine stimulants) · Magnesium Sulfate · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia; also used as a tocolytic to relax the uterus and slow preterm labor · Mechanism of action | A CNS depressant that reduces neuromuscular excitability, preventing the seizures that mark the transition from preeclampsia to eclampsia · Adverse reactions/toxicity | Loss of deep tendon reflexes; respiratory depression (RR <12/min); decreased urine output (oliguria); flushing · Contraindications | Myasthenia gravis; use caution with renal impairment, since magnesium is cleared by the kidneys and toxicity accumulates faster · Nursing interventions | Monitor DTRs, respiratory rate, and urine output regularly; keep calcium gluconate at the bedside as the antidote for toxicity · Patient education | Warn about flushing/warmth sensation with administration; explain the reflex/breathing checks are routine safety monitoring, not a sign something is wrong

Vitamin K, Erythromycin, and Hepatitis B vaccine · These three medications are given to nearly every newborn before discharge, and each one addresses a specific vulnerability the newborn is born with — a clotting factor deficiency, an unprotected exposure during birth, and a vaccine-preventable infection risk. · Vitamin K (Phytonadione) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Prevention of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn); given IM, within about 1 hour of birth · Mechanism of action | Vitamin K is essential for synthesizing clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver. It crosses the placenta poorly, and the newborn gut is sterile (no bacteria yet to help produce it), so every newborn is born with very low vitamin K stores and is at risk for bleeding without supplementation · Adverse reactions | Uncommon: anaphylaxis; bruising/swelling at the injection site; caution in neonates — can increase bilirubin levels · Contraindications | Caution with maternal use of warfarin, phenytoin, or phenobarbital during pregnancy; caution with certain neonatal liver diseases · Nursing interventions | Administer IM in the vastus lateralis using a small needle; consent is required — this is a refusable intervention; monitor the injection site · Patient education | Explain WHY it's given (newborns are born with very low vitamin K and are at risk for serious bleeding) if parents hesitate or refuse; document any refusal · Erythromycin Ophthalmic Ointment · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Prevents ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis) from gonorrhea/chlamydia exposure during birth; applied to the lower conjunctival sac of both eyes shortly after birth · Mechanism of action | A macrolide antibiotic ointment that provides local prophylaxis against the organisms a newborn may have been exposed to passing through the birth canal · Adverse reactions | Temporary blurred vision; mild chemical conjunctivitis (redness) in some infants · Contraindications | Known hypersensitivity to macrolide antibiotics · Nursing interventions | Required by law in all 50 states, regardless of documented maternal STI status; allow bonding/first breastfeeding attempt before applying, since it can blur the newborn's vision · Patient education | Explain this is a universal, legally required prophylaxis — not a sign that anything abnormal was found in the mother's screening · Hepatitis B Vaccine · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | First dose of the hepatitis B vaccine series, typically given IM before hospital discharge · Mechanism of action | Stimulates active immunity against hepatitis B virus before any possible exposure · Adverse reactions | Injection site soreness; low-grade fever (uncommon) · Contraindications | Severe allergic reaction to a prior dose or to a vaccine component · Nursing interventions | Given IM in the vastus lateralis, in a separate site from vitamin K if given close together; if the mother is hepatitis B surface antigen-positive, hepatitis B immune globulin is also given within 12 hours of birth, in a separate thigh; document parental consent · Patient education | Explain the importance of completing the full vaccine series on schedule at follow-up visits

One drug, an entire prevention strategy · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Antenatal prophylaxis for Rh-negative pregnant patients; postpartum prophylaxis if the newborn is Rh-positive; also given after any potential fetal-maternal blood mixing (miscarriage, trauma, amniocentesis, ectopic pregnancy) · Mechanism of action | Suppresses the maternal immune system's ability to recognize and mount an antibody response against Rh-positive fetal red blood cells that have entered her circulation — it neutralizes those cells before her body can build antibodies against them · Adverse reactions | Chills, fever, dizziness, headache, weakness; hypersensitivity reaction; local injection site redness/soreness (expected, since it's a blood product) · Contraindications | Rh-POSITIVE patients (nothing to prevent); patients already sensitized — a positive indirect Coombs test means antibodies already exist and RhoGam can no longer help; immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), due to intravascular hemolysis risk; do not give with live-virus vaccines or estrogen-containing medications · Nursing interventions | Given IM; monitor for hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis for about 20 minutes after administration; monitor ITP patients for at least 8 hours due to higher complication risk; administer slowly in patients with kidney disease · Patient education | Explain that this is prophylaxis for FUTURE pregnancies, not treatment for this one — it prevents her from forming antibodies that would attack a future Rh-positive fetus; report back pain, shaking, chills, fever, discolored urine, or hematuria · The exact timing that makes RhoGam work · Instructor point worth remembering: if BOTH parents are Rh-negative, RhoGam is not needed at all — there's no way the fetus can be Rh-positive, so there's nothing to sensitize against. RhoGam only matters when the mother is Rh-negative and there's a possibility the fetus is Rh-positive (i.e., the father is Rh-positive or unknown). · When | Why · ~28 weeks gestation | Covers the small amount of fetal-maternal blood mixing that can happen silently throughout pregnancy · Within 72 hours of delivery | Covers the much larger blood mixing that happens at birth itself, IF the newborn is confirmed Rh-positive · After any sensitizing event | Miscarriage, amniocentesis, trauma, ectopic pregnancy — any event that could mix fetal and maternal blood outside the routine schedule · The whole drug only works on a very narrow window: it has to be given before the maternal immune system has already recognized Rh-positive cells and started making antibodies. That's exactly why a positive indirect Coombs test is a contraindication rather than a reason to give a bigger dose — once sensitization has happened, RhoGam can no longer prevent what's already occurred.

Opioids, sedatives, and the epidural/spinal review · Opioid analgesics (butorphanol, nalbuphine, meperidine) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | First-stage labor pain management; given IV or IM · Mechanism of action | Opioid agonists/agonist-antagonists that reduce the perception of pain by acting on opioid receptors in the CNS · Adverse reactions | Maternal sedation, nausea/vomiting, respiratory depression; crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression if given too close to delivery · Contraindications | Known opioid dependency (nalbuphine and butorphanol are agonist-antagonists and can precipitate withdrawal in an opioid-dependent patient) · Nursing interventions | Time doses with delivery in mind — avoid giving a dose in the window right before expected birth; have naloxone available; monitor maternal sedation level and respiratory rate · Patient education | Explain the drug will take the edge off pain but won't eliminate it entirely, and that timing near delivery is deliberately managed to protect the newborn · Ondansetron (antiemetic) · Frequently given alongside opioid analgesics, since nausea is one of their most common side effects. It's a serotonin antagonist that blocks the vomiting reflex centrally, rather than treating the stomach directly. · Epidural anesthesia · Category | Detail · Indications | Regional pain relief during labor (stage 1 or 2) · Key adverse reaction | Maternal hypotension → reduced placental perfusion → late decelerations on the FHR strip · Nursing interventions | Bolus IV fluids before placement to help prevent the BP drop; if hypotension occurs, position the patient on her left side , increase IV fluids, and give O2 · Spinal anesthesia · Category | Detail · Indications | Anesthesia for a planned/elective cesarean birth · Key adverse reaction | Post-dural puncture headache; if the block travels too high, it can affect the diaphragm and impair breathing · Nursing interventions | Priority assessment is respiratory effort , not just blood pressure, given the risk of a high block; keep the patient flat if a post-dural headache develops

Sildenafil and hormonal contraceptives · Sildenafil (Viagra) — PDE5 inhibitor · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Erectile dysfunction; 25–50 mg PO, taken 30–60 minutes before anticipated intercourse, no more than once in 24 hours · Mechanism of action | Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and increases blood flow to the corpus cavernosum by inhibiting the enzyme that breaks down cGMP, prolonging the vasodilation needed for an erection · Adverse reactions | Headache, flushing, GI upset, nasal congestion; priapism (erection lasting >4 hours — a urologic emergency); blue-tinted vision , vision loss · Contraindications | Absolute: any nitrate (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) — the combined vasodilation causes severe, potentially fatal hypotension; caution with cardiovascular disease, liver damage, bleeding disorders, active peptic ulcer disease, or existing vision loss · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP and orthostatics; cardiac monitoring especially at treatment initiation or dose changes · Patient education | Never combine with nitrates, under any circumstance; seek immediate care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours; report any vision or hearing changes; tell every provider you take this medication before starting anything new · Combined Oral Contraceptives (estrogen + progestin) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Pregnancy prevention; also used for dysmenorrhea and cycle regulation; taken orally, same time each day · Mechanism of action | Inhibits ovulation and thickens cervical mucus · Adverse reactions | Increased risk of blood clots (DVT/PE); may raise blood glucose in Type 1 diabetics; breakthrough bleeding · Contraindications | Smokers over age 35; history of thromboembolic disease, estrogen-sensitive cancers, or uncontrolled hypertension · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP periodically; encourage monthly self-breast exams; ensure backup contraception is used when starting the method or when antibiotics may reduce its effectiveness · Patient education | Teach ACHES (abdominal pain, chest pain, headaches, eye problems, severe leg pain) as symptoms to report immediately; condoms are still needed for STI prevention; stop 1–2 months before attempting to conceive · Depo-Provera (Medroxyprogesterone) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Injectable contraception, given every 3 months · Mechanism of action | Progestin that delays/inhibits ovulation and thickens cervical mucus · Adverse reactions | Decreased bone density with long-term use — this is the single most distinctive teaching point for this drug; irregular bleeding, weight gain · Contraindications | Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding; known or suspected breast cancer · Nursing interventions | Counsel on calcium and vitamin D intake and weight-bearing exercise to offset bone density loss; track the 3-month injection schedule closely, since this method has no 'missed pill' flexibility · Patient education | Explain the injection schedule must be kept on time; encourage weight-bearing exercise and adequate calcium/vitamin D throughout use

The antibiotics and antivirals behind the STI unit · Ceftriaxone — gonorrhea · Given as a single IM dose. First-line for gonorrhea; often paired with doxycycline to presumptively cover chlamydia, since the two infections frequently co-occur. If a patient has a documented cephalosporin allergy, gentamicin plus azithromycin is the alternative regimen. · Doxycycline — chlamydia · First-line oral treatment for chlamydia. Avoided in pregnancy (tetracyclines affect fetal bone/teeth development), where azithromycin is used instead, with amoxicillin as a backup alternative. · Penicillin G Benzathine — syphilis · The gold-standard treatment for syphilis, given IM. A single dose treats primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis (under 1 year); late latent or late syphilis requires three weekly doses instead of one. For patients with a true penicillin allergy, doxycycline, tetracycline, or IM/IV ceftriaxone are alternatives. · Watch for the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first penicillin dose for syphilis — fever, hypotension, and tachycardia from spirochetes dying off rapidly, typically resolving within 24 hours. This is not a penicillin allergy, and future penicillin doses should not be withheld because of it. · Metronidazole (Flagyl) — trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis · First-line treatment for both trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis, despite these being caused by different organisms (a protozoan and a bacterial overgrowth, respectively). · The single most important teaching point for metronidazole: it causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — flushing, vomiting, tachycardia, and hypotension appearing within 10–30 minutes of drinking, because the drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down a toxic alcohol metabolite. Patients must avoid all alcohol during treatment and for a period afterward. · Acyclovir (and related antivirals) — HSV · Acyclovir, along with valacyclovir and famciclovir, are first-line antivirals for herpes simplex virus. They shorten and reduce the severity of outbreaks and can be used for suppressive therapy to reduce outbreak frequency and transmission risk — but none of them cure the infection, since the virus remains dormant in nerve tissue between outbreaks.

The building blocks every other calculation relies on · Before any drip rate or weight-based dose can be calculated, you need to be fluent in the basic conversions underneath them — pounds to kilograms, and the metric ladder from kilograms down to micrograms. Almost every calculation error in practice traces back to a mistake at this level, not the fancier formula built on top of it. · Basic Dosage Calculation · Formula: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = Amount to administer · Worked example: Order is 500 mg PO; available as 250 mg tablets. (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets . · Worked example 2: Order is 2 mg Lorazepam; available as a 4 mg/mL vial. (2 ÷ 4) × 1 mL = 0.5 mL . · Weight Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Pounds → kilograms | lbs ÷ 2.2 = kg | 154 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg · Kilograms → pounds | kg × 2.2 = lbs | 100 kg × 2.2 = 220 lbs · Almost every weight-based drug calculation in this unit (Dopamine, Heparin, BSA dosing) starts with converting the patient's weight to kilograms — if that first conversion is wrong, every step after it is wrong too, even if the rest of the math is done perfectly. · Metric System Conversions — the 1000 rule · Standard medical units (kg, g, mg, mcg) are each separated from their neighbor by a factor of 1000. · Direction | Rule | Example · Larger → smaller (kg→g, g→mg, mg→mcg) | Multiply by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places right) | 2 g × 1000 = 2000 mg · Smaller → larger (mcg→mg, mg→g, g→kg) | Divide by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places left) | 2500 mcg ÷ 1000 = 2.5 mg · Volume Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Milliliters → liters | mL ÷ 1000 = L | 2500 mL ÷ 1000 = 2.5 L · Liters → milliliters | L × 1000 = mL | 0.5 L × 1000 = 500 mL · Household & Volume Equivalents · Household/Metric | Equivalent · 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL · 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL (or 3 tsp) · 1 ounce (oz) | 30 mL (or 2 tbsp) · 1 cup | 240 mL (8 oz) · 1 quart (approx.) | 1000 mL (1 L) · Two of the formulas in your source material — GTPAL and Naegele's Rule — are OB-specific calculations already covered in depth in the Antepartum unit and the Quick Reference unit. They're genuinely 'math,' but they're taught there with the full clinical reasoning behind them rather than repeated here as a bare formula.

t: IV Flow Rates, Drip Rates & Concentration
x: Getting fluid and medication into the vein at the right speed · These formulas answer one of two questions: how fast should this infusion pump run (mL/hr), or how many drops per minute should a gravity IV be set to (gtt/min) when there's no pump involved? A third formula, concentration, sets up the weight-based drip calculations in the next lesson. · Flow Rate / Infusion Rate (mL/hr) — for infusion pumps · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Total Time (hr) = mL/hr · Worked example: Infuse 1000 mL of Normal Saline over 8 hours. 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr . · Infusion Time — working backward from a known rate · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Flow Rate (mL/hr) = Time (hours) · Worked example: A 1000 mL bag is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How long will it last? 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours . · Drip Rate (gtt/min) — for gravity IV tubing without a pump · There are two equivalent ways to reach the same answer, depending on whether you already know the mL/hr rate or are starting from the total order. · Starting point | Formula · You already know mL/hr | (mL/hr ÷ 60) × Drop Factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min · You're starting from the total order | (Total Volume [mL] × Drop Factor [gtt/mL]) ÷ Time (minutes) = gtt/min · Worked example (method 1): Infuse at 125 mL/hr using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. First, mL/min: 125 ÷ 60 = 2.08 mL/min. Then: 2.08 × 15 = 31.2, rounded to 31 gtt/min . · Worked example (method 2): Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours (480 minutes) with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min — the same answer either way, since both methods describe the same infusion. · IV Push Medication Rate · A common general safety rule for IV push medications is roughly 1 mL per minute unless the drug's specific administration guidelines say otherwise. Worked example: a 10 mL medication is administered over 10 minutes, consistent with the 1 mL/min rule. Pushing too fast is a common cause of adverse drug reactions. · Concentration Calculation — the setup step for weight-based drips · Formula: (Total mg in the bag × 1000) ÷ Total mL in the bag = Concentration (mcg/mL) · Worked example: A bag contains 400 mg of Dopamine in 250 mL of D5W. (400 × 1000) ÷ 250 = 1600 mcg/mL . This concentration number is exactly what feeds into the weight-based infusion formulas in the next lesson.

MAP, CPP, and weight-/unit-based infusions · This lesson groups together the calculations that show up most often in critical care and high-alert medication administration — all of them either measure perfusion pressure directly, or calculate the pump rate for a drug that manipulates that pressure. · MAP — Mean Arterial Pressure · Formula: (Systolic BP + [2 × Diastolic BP]) ÷ 3 = MAP · Worked example: BP is 120/80. (120 + [2 × 80]) ÷ 3 = (120 + 160) ÷ 3 = 93.3 mmHg . · MAP reflects the average pressure driving blood into the organs across the whole cardiac cycle — it's weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more time in diastole than systole. A MAP of roughly 65 mmHg or higher is generally considered necessary to maintain adequate organ perfusion in a critically ill patient. · CPP — Cerebral Perfusion Pressure · Formula: MAP − ICP = CPP · Worked example: MAP is 93, ICP is 15. 93 − 15 = 78 mmHg . · CPP depends directly on MAP — if you already calculated MAP for a patient, you're one subtraction away from CPP. A CPP that drops too low (generally below ~60 mmHg) risks cerebral ischemia, which is why both numbers are tracked together in a patient with a head injury or elevated ICP. · Weight-Based Infusion (mcg/kg/min) — e.g., Dopamine · Formula: (Desired mcg × kg × 60 minutes) ÷ Concentration (mcg/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient, with a concentration of 1600 mcg/mL (from the concentration calculation in the previous lesson). (5 × 80 × 60) ÷ 1600 = 15 mL/hr . · Units-Based Infusion (Units/kg/hr) — e.g., Heparin · Formula: (Units × kg) ÷ Concentration (Units/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 12 Units/kg/hr for a 100 kg patient, with a concentration of 100 Units/mL. (12 × 100) ÷ 100 = 12 mL/hr . · Both weight-based and units-based drips are high-alert medications given by infusion pump only, exactly like oxytocin in the OB units — the shared theme across every high-alert drug in this app is a computerized pump, frequent reassessment, and a clear plan for what triggers stopping or adjusting the rate.

Tracking what goes in, what comes out, and what IV fluids do to cells · Intake and output tracking is really just accounting for fluid — but two categories (ice chips and continuous bladder irrigation) have special rules that are easy to get wrong, and tonicity explains why the choice of IV fluid itself matters beyond just the volume. · What counts as intake · Oral (PO) fluids — water, juice, soda, milk, coffee · Liquid foods — soups, broths, gelatin, sherbet, sorbet, pudding · Ice chips — recorded as half the original volume (200 mL of ice chips = 100 mL intake), since ice chips are mostly air/space between solid pieces · IV fluids — maintenance fluids, boluses, and piggyback medications (like antibiotics) · Tube feedings — formula and water flushes · Irrigation — only counted as intake if the fluid is NOT recovered in the output · What counts as output · Urine — voided, catheterized, or urostomy drainage · Emesis (vomitus) · Liquid stool — diarrhea or colostomy drainage · Wound drainage — from JP drains, Hemovacs, or chest tubes · Suction — gastric (NG) or respiratory · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake of 3000 mL, output of 800 mL. 3000 − 800 = +2200 mL (a positive balance, meaning the patient is retaining more fluid than they're losing). · Continuous Bladder Irrigation — adjusting urine output · Formula: Total Output − Total Irrigation Volume = Actual Urine Output · Worked example: 24-hour total output is 2500 mL; total irrigation fluid instilled was 1500 mL. 2500 − 1500 = 1000 mL actual urine output. Without subtracting the irrigation fluid, you'd wildly overestimate how much urine the patient is actually making. · Insensible Loss · Fluid lost through the skin and lungs that can't be directly measured. Standard estimate: 600–900 mL/day , or roughly 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Worked example: a 70 kg patient: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/hr, or roughly 840 mL/day. · Fluid Weight Calculation · Rule of thumb: a 1 kg weight change equals roughly 1 L of fluid change. Worked example: a patient's weight rises 2 kg over two days — that's roughly a 2 L fluid gain, not necessarily 2 kg of actual tissue. · An output under 30 mL/hr is always reported as a potential emergency — it signals inadequate perfusion to the kidneys. This is the exact same 'red zone' oliguria threshold already flagged in the Postpartum and Newborn units for shock/distress — one number, used across every system in the body. · Tonicity — what different IV fluids do to cells · Type | Solute concentration vs. inside the cell | Effect on the cell | Examples | Clinical use · Hypertonic | Higher outside the cell | Water leaves the cell — it shrinks (plasmolysis) | 3% or 5% NaCl; 10% Dextrose in Water | Cerebral edema, severe hyponatremia · Hypotonic | Lower outside the cell | Water enters the cell — it swells or bursts (cytolysis) | 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline) | Dehydration — pushes water back into cells · Isotonic | Equal inside and outside | No net water movement — equilibrium maintained | 0.9% Normal Saline, Lactated Ringer's, D5W | Routine IV fluid replacement and hydration · A simple way to remember the direction: hyper tonic pulls water OUT of the cell (think 'hyper' = high solute outside, pulling water toward it), while hypo tonic pushes water IN . Isotonic is the 'do no harm' default fluid when you don't want to shift fluid into or out of cells at all.

Calculations that scale a dose to the patient's size · These two calculations both answer a version of the same question — how big is this patient, in a way that's useful for dosing or risk assessment? BMI is a general screening number; BSA is a more precise scaling factor used specifically for drugs where getting the dose right really matters. · BMI — Body Mass Index · System | Formula · Metric | Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]² · Imperial | [Weight (lbs) × 703] ÷ [Height (in)]² · Worked example (metric): Weight 70 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625. Divide weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86 (normal weight range). · Worked example (imperial): Weight 154 lbs, height 69 inches. 154 × 703 = 108,262. Square the height: 69 × 69 = 4,761. Divide: 108,262 ÷ 4,761 = 22.74 — the same result as the metric calculation, just arrived at with different starting units. · BSA — Body Surface Area · BSA approximates a patient's total skin surface area in square meters (m²), and it's used specifically for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, chemotherapy agents, pediatric patients, and burn patients — situations where a small dosing error has an outsized effect. · Formula: BSA = √[(Height in cm × Weight in kg) ÷ 3600] · Fully worked pediatric dosing example · Order: Ceftriaxone 2 mg/m². Patient: 37 lb, 97 cm tall. Supply: 1 mg/mL. · Step 1 — convert weight to kg: 37 lb ÷ 2.2 = 16.8 kg · Step 2 — calculate BSA: √[(97 cm × 16.8 kg) ÷ 3600] = √[1629.6 ÷ 3600] = √0.4527 = 0.67 m² · Step 3 — calculate the dose in mg: 2 mg/m² × 0.67 m² = 1.34 mg · Step 4 — calculate the dose in mL: 1.34 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 1.34 mL to administer · Notice this whole calculation depends on the weight-to-kg conversion from the very first Med Math lesson — get that first step wrong, and every subsequent step (BSA, mg dose, mL dose) inherits the error. This is exactly why that basic conversion lesson exists: it's the foundation everything else in this unit is built on.

Reflection prompts from lecture, with short answers · Short answers to these prompts are provided below, all grounded in content taught elsewhere in this section. · Q: When you think of mental illness, what comes to mind — and are your ideas from TV, movies, or personal experience? · This was an opening reflection prompt with no single correct answer, meant to surface that a lot of common mental-illness imagery comes from media portrayals (often exaggerated or focused on rare violent cases) rather than the much more ordinary, common presentations — depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders — that a nurse actually encounters most often. · Q: What indicates good mental health? · Mental health is framed as a spectrum rather than a binary: the ability to adapt to stressors and cultural norms, with occasional stress or mild distress but no functional impairment, sits at the healthy end. Mental illness only enters the picture once symptoms interfere with daily functioning — it's described as "a disease of exclusion," meaning other causes are ruled out first. · Q: What should the nurse assess for in a depressed client, and what would an appropriate care plan include? · Assessment covers mood/affect congruence, neurovegetative symptoms (sleep, appetite, energy), cognitive symptoms (concentration, guilt, worthlessness), and — always — a direct suicide risk screen. An appropriate care plan starts with safety, then layers in small achievable activities, protected sleep and nutrition, patient involvement in treatment decisions, and combined medication plus psychotherapy. · Q: What are some signs and symptoms of ADHD, and how is it diagnosed? · Inattentive features include distractibility, losing things, and difficulty following through; hyperactive-impulsive features include fidgeting, excessive talking, and acting without considering consequences. Diagnosis is clinical — a structured history from parents, teachers, and the patient documenting the pattern across more than one setting — since there is no lab test or imaging study that diagnoses ADHD. · Q: What nursing interventions and safety precautions are needed for a client with autism spectrum disorder? · Care centers on minimizing unpredictability and sensory overload: consistent routines, advance notice before procedures or transitions, concrete language, and involving caregivers who know the patient's individual sensory sensitivities. Safety-wise, a sensory-overload reaction (covering ears, rocking, distress at loud noise) should be recognized as sensory overload rather than intentional defiance, and addressed by reducing the trigger. · Q: What cardiovascular changes in anorexia nervosa could be life-threatening, and what causes anorexia in the first place? · If malnutrition leads to edema or hypokalemia, ventricular arrhythmias can occur — this is the life-threatening cardiac risk. No single cause of anorexia is known; it's thought to involve a combination of genetic, biological, and environmental factors. · Q: What complications can occur in bulimia nervosa, and which electrolyte imbalances are of concern? · The life-threatening complications are dehydration and electrolyte imbalance from repeated purging — most importantly hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis from the loss of stomach acid and gastric hydrochloric acid, both of which raise the risk of dangerous cardiac arrhythmias. · Q: How do you think a client with binge-eating disorder feels, and what nursing interventions and complications apply? · Patients typically feel significant shame and guilt about their loss of control, often eating alone to hide it. Complications relate to the metabolic consequences of associated weight gain (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease). Nursing interventions include daily achievable goals, patient control over food choices, food journaling, trigger identification, routine weighing, alternative coping strategies, and nonjudgmental, shame-reducing communication. · Q: What are the major elements of PTSD, and what should guide the nursing approach? · The major elements are trauma (re-experiencing via flashbacks/nightmares), emotions (hyperarousal, numbing, exaggerated startle), and guarding (hypervigilance, avoidance). The nursing approach should emphasize a calm, predictable approach, consistency, and awareness that guilt is a common accompanying emotion needing acknowledgment rather than dismissal.

Self-awareness, rapport, and the empathy/sympathy line · Psychiatric nursing runs on a different tool than most of the rest of nursing: the nurse's own self. A dressing change works the same way regardless of who applies it, but a therapeutic relationship only works if the nurse has done the work of understanding their own beliefs, attitudes, values, and even physical stance before walking into the room. A nurse who is uncomfortable with a topic — addiction, self-harm, a particular religion or lifestyle — will unconsciously communicate that discomfort through tone, facial expression, or body language long before they say anything judgmental out loud. That's why self-awareness is listed first: it isn't a soft skill tacked onto the real work, it's the precondition for the real work. · Building rapport: trust, respect, and genuineness · Rapport is the foundation everything else in the relationship is built on, and it rests on three specific qualities. Trust is built through consistency — showing up when you say you will, following through on what you promise, and being honest even when the truth is uncomfortable (for example, telling a patient a procedure will be uncomfortable rather than promising it won't hurt). Respect means treating the patient as a capable adult with the right to make their own decisions whenever safety allows, rather than as a diagnosis to be managed. Genuineness means the nurse's warmth is real, not performed — patients, especially those with conditions like borderline personality disorder that heighten sensitivity to rejection, are often unusually good at detecting insincerity, and a performed rapport tends to backfire. · Empathy vs. sympathy · These two words get used interchangeably in casual speech, but they describe different — and therapeutically unequal — stances. Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone from the outside; it keeps a distance between the nurse's experience and the patient's and can tip into pity, which subtly reinforces the patient's sense of being lesser-than. Empathy is entering into the patient's emotional experience enough to understand it accurately from the inside, while still keeping your own professional footing — you understand why they feel what they feel without drowning in the feeling alongside them. Empathy is the therapeutic goal; sympathy, however well-intentioned, is not. · Transference and countertransference · Transference is when the patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past — often a parent or another authority figure — onto the nurse. A patient who was raised by a harsh, critical father might react to a nurse's ordinary correction with disproportionate anger, because the nurse has momentarily become a stand-in for that father figure. Countertransference is the mirror-image process happening in the nurse: the nurse's own unresolved feelings or past relationships get projected onto the patient, for example a nurse who was raised by an alcoholic parent feeling unusually irritated by or overly protective of a patient with alcohol use disorder. Neither phenomenon means something has gone wrong — they're a normal and expected part of close human interaction — but a nurse who can't recognize when countertransference is happening in themselves is at risk of letting it drive their care decisions instead of the patient's actual needs. · The four phases of the nurse-patient relationship (TRUST) · The therapeutic relationship isn't a single static thing — it moves through four sequential phases, and knowing which phase a relationship is in tells you what work is actually appropriate to do right now. A mnemonic worth holding onto: T rust is built, R apport deepens, work is U ndertaken, S eparation happens, and the relationship T erminates. · Phase | What happens | Nurse's task · 1. Preinteraction | Happens before the nurse ever meets the patient — reviewing the chart, prior notes, and the nurse's own self-awareness of biases or reactions the case might trigger | Prepare: gather background information and examine your own feelings about the upcoming interaction · 2. Orientation (introductory) | The first actual meeting. Roles, expectations, and the boundaries and terms of the relationship (confidentiality, its limits, how long it will last) are established | Introduce yourself and your role, begin building trust, and set the working agreement/contract for the relationship · 3. Working | The bulk of the relationship — the patient explores thoughts, feelings, and problems, and the nurse helps the patient develop coping skills, insight, and problem-solving ability | Facilitate change: this is where most of the actual therapeutic work of the relationship happens · 4. Termination | The planned ending of the relationship — discharge, transfer, or the end of a rotation — which is discussed in advance rather than sprung on the patient | Review progress made, help the patient process feelings about the ending (which can reopen old losses), and ensure a safe handoff or discharge plan · A relationship that skips straight from orientation to termination without a working phase hasn't actually done the therapeutic work — and a termination phase that isn't planned and discussed in advance can feel like abandonment to a patient, especially one with a trauma history around loss. · Theoretical models of behavior (context, not memorization-heavy) · Several theoretical models underpin why psychiatric nursing approaches behavior the way it does. These are lower-yield for direct recall than the four relationship phases above, but recognizing the name-to-idea pairing is still commonly tested. · Model | Key figure(s) | Core idea · Psychoanalytic | Freud | Behavior is driven by unconscious conflict, often rooted in early childhood experience · Interpersonal | Sullivan, Peplau | Personality and behavior develop through relationships with others; anxiety is transmitted interpersonally · Social | Caplan, Szasz | Social and environmental factors (poverty, culture, social support) shape mental health · Existential | Frankl, Perls, May | Distress arises when a person is out of touch with themselves or their environment; focuses on meaning and self-awareness · Nursing | Rogers, Orem, Sister Callista Roy, Peplau | Frames the person as a whole, adapting being in continuous interaction with their environment · Medical | — | Views mental illness through diagnosis and biological/pharmacological treatment, similar to physical disease · Communication | Berne, Bandler, Grindler | Behavior and dysfunction are understood through patterns of verbal and nonverbal communication · Behavioral | Skinner, Wolpe, Eysenck | Behavior is learned and can be unlearned or reshaped through conditioning · Humanistic | Maslow | Behavior is driven by a hierarchy of needs, from basic survival up through self-actualization

Techniques that open a conversation up, techniques that shut it down · Therapeutic communication is not limited to the words a nurse chooses — it includes tone of voice, eye contact, posture, and touch, all of which can either build the relationship or quietly undermine it. A nurse can say all the technically correct words and still communicate poorly if their body language contradicts the message. · A nurse talking with a patient while staring at the computer screen instead of the patient is a concrete example of communication that fails on the nonverbal channel even though nothing wrong was said out loud. A second example: a nurse responding to a patient's substance use disclosure with, "If it were up to me, I would choose not to drink or use drugs," is a failure on the verbal channel — it inserts the nurse's personal judgment into a moment that calls for neutral, nonjudgmental listening. Both are the kind of subtle mistake that's easy to miss but breaks trust immediately. · Part I — techniques that encourage the expression of feelings and ideas · Each of these is a specific, nameable technique — nursing exams test the name, the description, and the ability to recognize a matching example, not just the general idea of "being a good listener." · Technique | What it is | Example · Active listening | Being attentive to what the client is saying, verbally and non-verbally: sit facing the client, open posture, lean toward the client, eye contact, and relax | (nonverbal — posture and attention itself is the technique) · Sharing observations | Making observations by commenting on how the other person looks, sounds, or acts | "You look tired" / "I haven't seen you eating anything today" · Sharing empathy | The ability to understand and accept another person's reality, to accurately perceive feelings, and to communicate understanding | "It must be very frustrating to know what you want and not be able to do it" · Sharing hope | Communicating a "sense of possibility" to others — encouragement when appropriate, and positive feedback | "I believe you will find a way to face your situation, because I have seen your courage in the past" · Sharing humor | Contributes to feelings of togetherness, closeness, and friendliness; promotes positive communication through prevention, perception, and perspective | (used judiciously, matched to the moment) · Sharing feelings | Helping clients express emotions by making observations, acknowledging feelings, giving permission to express "negative" feelings, and modeling healthy anger | (open acknowledgment rather than suppression of the feeling) · Using touch | The most potent form of communication; comfort touch such as holding a hand is especially important for vulnerable clients experiencing severe illness | (holding a hand during a difficult moment) · Silence | Time for the nurse and client to observe one another, sort out feelings, think of how to say things, and consider what has been communicated; the nurse should allow the client to break the silence | (deliberately not filling the pause) · Providing information | Relevant information helps a client make decisions, experience less anxiety, and feel safe and secure | "Susie is getting an echocardiogram right now, which is a test that uses painless sound waves to create a moving picture of her heart structures and valves and should tell us what is causing her murmur" · Clarifying | Restating an unclear or ambiguous message to check whether understanding is accurate, or to better understand it | "I'm not sure I understand what you mean by 'sicker than usual' — what is different now?" · Focusing | Taking notice of a single idea expressed, or even a single word | "On a scale of 0 to 10, tell me the level of the pain you are experiencing in your great toe right now" · Paraphrasing | Restating another's message more briefly, in the nurse's own fresher words, capturing the essential idea | Client: "I can't focus, my mind keeps wandering." Nurse: "You're having difficulty concentrating?" · Asking relevant questions | Seeking information needed for decision-making — one question at a time, fully exploring one topic before moving on; open-ended questions let the client take the conversational lead | "What is your biggest problem at the moment?" / "How has your pain affected your life at home?" · Summarizing | Pulls together information for documentation, gives the client a sense you understand, and brings closure to the interaction | "It is my understanding that your arm pain is a level 1 since you've taken a Vicodin one hour ago... is this correct?" · Self-disclosure | Subjectively true personal experiences intentionally revealed by the nurse to emphasize similarities and differences — used sparingly, and kept relevant, so the client stays the focus | "That happened to me once, too... I went to counseling and it really helped.
