What are your thoughts about seeing a counselor?" · Confrontation | Helping the client become more aware of inconsistencies in feelings, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors — only after trust is established, and done gently, with sensitivity | "You say you've already decided what to do, yet you're still talking a lot about your options" · Part II — non-therapeutic techniques ("blocks" to communication) · Just as important as knowing the techniques that open a conversation up is recognizing the specific, nameable patterns that shut one down — these show up constantly as the "wrong answer" options on nursing exam questions, and the reasoning for why each one fails is testable in its own right. · Block | Why it fails | Example / better alternative · Asking personal questions | Asks about things not relevant to the situation, out of curiosity rather than clinical need | Avoid: "Why aren't you married to Mary?" — Better: "How would you describe your relationship to Mary?" · Giving personal opinions | Takes decision-making away from the client — the problem and the solution belong to the patient, not the nurse | Avoid: "If I were you I'd put your father in a nursing home." — Better: "Let's talk about what options are available to your father." · Changing the subject | Rude, shows a lack of empathy, and signals the nurse doesn't really care what the client is sharing | Avoid: "Let's not talk about your insurance problems, it's time for your walk." · Automatic responses | Generalizations and stereotypes that reflect poor nursing judgment and threaten nurse-client or team relationships | Avoid: "Administration doesn't care about the staff" / "Older adults are always confused." · False reassurance | Offers hope not based on fact or reality; can block conversation and discourage further expression of feelings even though it's meant kindly | Avoid: "Don't worry, everything will be all right." — Better: "It must be difficult not to know what the surgeon will find. What can I do to help?" · Sympathy | Focuses on the nurse's own feelings rather than the client's — a subjective look at another's world that prevents a clear perspective on the issues confronting that person | Avoid: "I'm so sorry about your amputation, it must be terrible to lose a leg." — Better: "The loss of your leg is a major change — how do you think this will affect your life?" · Asking for explanations ("why") | Clients frequently interpret "why" questions as accusations, which can cause resentment, insecurity, and mistrust | Avoid: "Why are you so upset?" — Better: "You seem upset. What's on your mind?" · Approval or disapproval | Imposes the nurse's own values and standards; approving implies only that behavior is acceptable, disapproving implies the client must meet the nurse's standards | Avoid: "You shouldn't even think about assisted suicide, it's just not right." — Better: "I'm surprised you are considering assisted suicide. Tell me more about it..." · Defensive responses | Blocks the nurse from listening uncritically to discover the real reason for a client's anger or dissatisfaction | Avoid: "No one here would intentionally lie to you." — Better: "You believe people have been dishonest with you. It must be hard to trust anyone." · Passive or aggressive responses | Passive responses avoid conflict and reflect sadness, powerlessness, or hopelessness; aggressive responses provoke confrontation and reflect anger or frustration — assertive communication is the professional middle path | Avoid: "Being sick is bad and it's all your fault." · Arguing | Challenging or denying the client's perceptions implies they are lying, misinformed, or uneducated | Avoid: "How can you say you didn't sleep a wink when I heard you snoring all night!" — Better: "You feel like you didn't get any rest at all last night, even though I thought you slept well since I heard you snoring." · What makes communication therapeutic (summary) · It is patient-centered — the goal is to understand the patient's experience, not to share the nurse's opinions or life story · It uses active listening: eye contact, open body language, and reflecting back what the patient said to confirm understanding · It avoids clichés, false reassurance, and judgmental language, all of which shut a conversation down rather than open it up · Touch is used deliberately and only when appropriate — for some patients, especially those with trauma histories or active psychosis, unexpected touch can feel threatening rather than comforting · The therapeutic environment · Nurses are also responsible for structuring the physical and social environment around a psychiatric patient, not just their own conversation with that patient. Three questions guide this: What is the priority? (Safety always outranks comfort or even the treatment plan itself.) What type of environment does this specific situation call for? (A patient in active psychosis needs a low-stimulation environment — dim lighting, few people, minimal noise — while a patient working through grief may need a private space to talk.) What boundaries need to be set and held? (Consistency in boundaries is itself therapeutic; boundaries that shift depending on the nurse or the patient's mood undermine the sense of safety a structured environment is supposed to provide.) · The mental status examination (MSE) · The MSE is an objective, structured snapshot of a patient's cognitive and psychological functioning at a single point in time — think of it as the psychiatric equivalent of a head-to-toe physical assessment. It's repeated over the course of care so the team can compare a patient against their own baseline rather than against a generic norm. · Appearance — grooming, hygiene, dress appropriate to age/weather, eye contact · Attitude/behavior — cooperative vs. guarded, hostile, or agitated · Speech — rate, volume, rhythm, tone (pressured, slowed, slurred, mute) · Motor activity — psychomotor agitation or retardation, tremors, tics, abnormal gait · Mood (the patient's own subjective report, in their words) vs. affect (what the nurse objectively observes) — and whether the two are congruent · Thought process — linear/logical/goal-directed vs. flight of ideas, loose associations, or thought blocking · Thought content — presence or absence of hallucinations, delusions, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation · Orientation — person, place, time, and situation ("oriented x4") · Insight — does the patient recognize they have an illness and need treatment? · Judgment — can the patient make sound, safe decisions about their own care? · Mood vs. affect is a frequent exam trap: mood is what the patient tells you ("I'm good"); affect is what you observe (flat, blunted, labile, or incongruent with the stated mood). A patient who reports feeling "fine" while showing no facial expression at all has a mood/affect incongruence worth documenting. · Putting it together: the nursing implications · In practice, psychiatric nursing care flows through five linked implications: assessment comes first and never stops, because a patient's mental status can shift within a single shift; safety — of both the patient and the environment — is the organizing priority behind every other decision; therapeutic communication is the primary tool used to gather information and build the relationship; structuring the environment to match the clinical situation supports everything else; and medications are layered on top of, not instead of, all of the above. · Three channels of communication and congruence · Communication travels through three simultaneous channels: verbal (the actual words spoken), non-verbal (posture, facial expression, gestures, and appearance), and para-verbal (tone, volume, pitch, and inflection). Congruence is when all three channels convey the same message; when they don't line up — for example, a client saying something positive in a flat or irritated tone — that incongruence is itself a red flag worth documenting, since it often signals unspoken distress or ambivalence the words alone don't capture. · Personal space, boundaries, and cultural factors · Even routine nursing tasks — applying a blood pressure cuff, placing a pulse oximeter, taking a temperature — already invade a patient's personal space before any more invasive care even begins. Every individual has their own boundary threshold, and a nurse attentive to a patient stiffening, pulling away, or growing quiet during a routine task is picking up an early nonverbal cue about where that threshold sits. Touch, eye contact, and family decision-making hierarchy all vary meaningfully by culture and must be actively assessed for each patient rather than assumed from the nurse's own background. · Facilitators vs. barriers, answering the same client statement · Seeing a facilitator and a barrier respond to the identical client statement side by side makes the exam pattern easier to recognize. Client: "Do you think I'm doing the right thing having a bilateral mastectomy?" · Facilitator (therapeutic) | Example phrasing · Offering self | "How about I sit with you and we discuss your thoughts?" · Focusing | "What are your specific thoughts and concerns related to this surgery?" · Seeking clarification | "What led you to your decision?" · Open-ended question | "What options did the provider give you?" · Acknowledging | "This must have been a difficult decision for you." · Presenting reality | "I read in your chart about your risk for breast cancer — was that part of your decision?" · Barrier (non-therapeutic) | Example phrasing · Probing | "Have you really given this a lot of thought?" · Changing the topic | "Has the surgeon discussed your post-op exercises?" · Being defensive | "We provide the best care here." · Agreeing/disagreeing | "I think surgery is a good idea" / "I don't think you should have this surgery" · Stereotyping | "Women your age respond well to this surgery." · Unwarranted reassurance | "I'm sure you made the right decision." · NCLEX pattern to watch for: when an answer option is a quoted statement that opens with something like "Tell me...", it is very often the correct open-ended, therapeutic response. Quoted answer choices are usually testing recognition of a specific communication technique, not just general kindness.

Key terms first, then how to respond safely · Before any specific diagnosis is discussed, psychiatric nursing rests on a shared vocabulary. Psychosis is a state in which a person is detached from reality. Delusions are fixed false beliefs held despite clear evidence against them (believing you are being poisoned by a family member with no supporting evidence). Hallucinations are sensory perceptions with no external stimulus — hearing voices, seeing things, or feeling sensations that aren't there. Auditory hallucinations are the most common type seen in psychiatric care. · Rule out natural causes first · This is one of the most important — and most frequently tested — principles in psychiatric assessment: psychosis is a symptom, not automatically a psychiatric diagnosis. New-onset psychosis in a patient always triggers a workup for medical causes before it's attributed to a primary psychiatric illness. Sleep deprivation, substance intoxication or withdrawal, an infection (especially a UTI in an older adult), a metabolic disturbance, a brain injury, or a high fever can all produce psychotic symptoms. Jumping straight to a psychiatric label without ruling out a treatable medical cause is a patient-safety failure, not just a diagnostic shortcut. · How to care for a patient experiencing psychosis · Positive, nonjudgmental demeanor — your affect sets the tone for the interaction · Do not touch — unexpected touch can be perceived as a threat and provoke a defensive or aggressive response · Empathy — acknowledge the emotion the delusion or hallucination is producing, even though you don't confirm the content itself · Do not argue — you cannot logic a person out of a delusion or a hallucination; arguing only damages trust and rarely changes the belief · Validate feelings, not the psychosis itself — "I can see this is frightening for you" validates the emotion without confirming voices are real · Focus on reality (grounding) — gently redirect attention to real, verifiable things in the room · Distract — a structured activity can reduce the intensity of internal stimuli; a concrete example is inviting the patient to the common room to watch television or engage in a group activity, shifting attention away from internal stimuli toward something shared and observable · Monitor physical needs — psychosis can crowd out a patient's attention to their own food intake, elimination, hydration, and hygiene, so the nurse has to actively track these rather than assuming the patient will report a need · Be aware of command hallucinations — voices instructing the patient to harm themselves or someone else are a safety emergency that overrides all other priorities · When command hallucinations are identified, the response escalates beyond routine monitoring: increase the level of observation (up to continuous one-on-one supervision), remove any means of carrying out the command, notify the treatment team immediately, and reassess whether the current level of restriction (unit privileges, environment) is still safe. Client and staff safety are evaluated together, since a command hallucination instructing harm toward others is as much of an emergency as one instructing self-harm. · "Validate feelings, not psychosis" is the single line worth memorizing from this whole topic: you are always allowed to say "that sounds scary" and never allowed to say "yes, they really are watching you." · A structured way to respond: the empathy model · "Focus on reality" and "validate feelings" are easy to say and hard to do in the moment, so it helps to have a concrete, ordered script for responding to a disturbing delusion or hallucination rather than improvising. The empathy model breaks the response into four steps, moving from acknowledgment to exploration: · 1. Acknowledge what the person has said — you don't need to reinforce the belief to acknowledge it. Use phrases like "You say..." · 2. Acknowledge your own understanding (or lack of it) — rather than stating that what the person believes is untrue, say something like "I can't see that" or "I was told that..." · 3. Try to imagine how the other person might feel — take cues from the person's affect, and check your intuitions tentatively rather than presenting them as certain: "I imagine that I might feel... if I thought... Is that how it is for you?" If you get it wrong, be genuinely interested and ask further open-ended questions rather than abandoning the approach · 4. Explore the feelings and methods of coping — "When you have felt... in the past... what has helped?" Sometimes just acknowledging the feeling is enough; other times, if the feelings are distressing, talking about coping — or what the person can do to cope with the feelings — is the more helpful direction · Worked example: "I have worms eating my brain" · Walking through the four steps against a single concrete delusion shows how they connect into one continuous conversation rather than four separate scripted lines: · Step 1 (acknowledge): "You say you have worms eating your brain." · Step 2 (acknowledge your understanding): "I can't see that, and the tests don't show any worms in your head..." · Step 3 (imagine the feeling): "...I don't know what it's like to think that worms are eating my brain, but I imagine it would feel very uncomfortable... can you tell me what it feels like?" — the patient responds, "It is more than uncomfortable, my head is throbbing." · Step 4 (explore feelings/coping): "Have you had this feeling before? What worked then?" · Notice what never happens across all four steps: the nurse never says the worms are real, and never flatly tells the patient they're wrong either. The whole model is a way of staying honest about reality while still treating the patient's distress as real and worth exploring — which is exactly the balance "validate feelings, not psychosis" is pointing at.

Unconscious strategies the mind uses to manage anxiety · Defense mechanisms are the different ways people handle emotional pain — originally conceived by Sigmund Freud, with much of their further development done by his daughter, Anna Freud. They aren't inherently pathological: defense mechanisms can be healthy or unhealthy depending on the circumstances and how much a person relies on them. Everyone uses some of these at some point, but certain patterns, used rigidly or in place of actually addressing a problem, are hallmarks of specific psychiatric conditions and show up constantly in nursing assessment questions. · ★ marks the 10 mechanisms that appear in your course's own exam study guide — those are the highest-yield, highest-confidence ones to know cold. The rest are still real, correctly-defined defense mechanisms (useful depth and genuinely testable), just not ones confirmed in that specific course document, so don't burn equal study time on all 20 if you're short on time. · Mechanism | What it looks like | Example · ★ Repression | Burying a painful feeling or thought from your awareness, though it may resurface in symbolic form. Sometimes considered a basis of other defense mechanisms | You can't remember your father's funeral · ★ Denial | Not accepting reality because it is too painful | You are arrested for drunk driving several times but don't believe you have a problem with alcohol · ★ Regression | Reverting to an older, less mature way of handling stresses and feelings | You and your roommate have an argument so you stomp off into another room and pout · ★ Projection | Attributing your own unacceptable thoughts or feelings to someone or something else | You get really mad at your husband but scream that he's the one mad at you · ★ Splitting | Everything in the world is seen as all good or all bad, with nothing in between | You think your best friend is absolutely worthless because he forgot a lunch date with you · ★ Displacement | Channeling a feeling or thought from its actual source to something or someone else | When you get mad at your sister, you break your drinking glass by throwing it against the wall · ★ Rationalization | Justifying one's behaviors and motivations by substituting "good," acceptable reasons for these real motivations | "I always study hard for tests and I know a lot of people who cheat so it's not a big deal I cheated this time." · ★ Humor | Focusing on funny aspects of a painful situation | A person's treatment for cancer makes him lose his hair so he makes jokes about being bald · ★ Sublimation | Redirecting unacceptable, instinctual drives into personally and socially acceptable channels | Intense rage redirected in the form of participation in sports such as boxing or football · ★ Suppression | The effort to hide and control unacceptable thoughts or feelings | You are attracted to someone but say that you really don't like the person at all · Reaction formation | Adopting beliefs, attitudes, and feelings contrary to what you really believe | When you say you're not angry when you really are · Compensation | Putting forth extra effort to counterbalance a perceived deficiency, real or imagined, often by excelling or overindulging in another area | A short business owner overcompensates by being unusually aggressive and controlling in business dealings · Identification | Consciously or unconsciously adopting the personality characteristics, attitudes, values, and behavior of someone else — often someone admired — as a way to allay anxiety | A teenager adopts the hairstyle and mannerisms of a favorite celebrity · Introjection | A type of identification in which a person incorporates the traits or values of others into their own personality, without exploring whether those values actually fit them | A child recites the same harsh rules their parent used, now as if they were their own beliefs · Intellectualization | Also called isolation — using excessive, detached reasoning about an event to avoid the uncomfortable feelings connected to it | A person avoids the anxiety of a cancer diagnosis by focusing exclusively on statistics and treatment protocols instead of how they feel about it · Isolation (of affect) | A person blocks the feelings associated with a distressing event or experience, even while discussing the event itself matter-of-factly | A nursing student describes a difficult trauma case in clinical detail without any visible emotional reaction · Fantasy | Creating unrealistic or improbable situations to escape daily pressures, responsibilities, or boredom | Daydreaming excessively about being highly successful while actually feeling unsuccessful · Undoing | Trying to "undo" or make up for harm the person feels they have caused someone else | Saying something hurtful to a friend, then immediately overcompensating with gifts or exaggerated kindness · Acting out | Repeating certain actions or behaviors to ward off anxiety, without weighing the possible consequences of those actions | A patient with unresolved anger repeatedly picks fights on the unit instead of talking about what's bothering them · Withdrawal | Growing emotionally uninvolved by pulling back and becoming passive rather than engaging with a stressor | A patient stops participating in group therapy and avoids conversation after a difficult family visit · Dissociation | Blocking an anxiety-provoking event, or a period of time, from conscious awareness, memory, or perception — leaving the person unable to compartmentalize an uncomfortable experience | A person is found by police unable to explain who they are or where they have been for the past several hours · Two of these are worth flagging for exam purposes because they're easy to confuse with each other: intellectualization/isolation keeps the feeling out of conscious awareness by burying it under detached, over-cognitive reasoning, while rationalization keeps the behavior itself intact by supplying a socially acceptable excuse for it. Intellectualization hides the emotion; rationalization justifies the action. · Splitting deserves special attention because it directly explains a behavior pattern nurses see often on a psychiatric unit: a patient with borderline personality disorder may describe one staff member as "the only nurse who understands me" and another as "completely incompetent" within the same shift — often the same staff member can flip from one category to the other after a single perceived slight. Recognizing this as splitting, rather than reacting personally to being idealized or devalued, is what keeps the care team consistent instead of getting triangulated against each other. · Sublimation is worth distinguishing from suppression and repression because it's the one defense mechanism generally considered healthy and even encouraged: rather than burying or hiding an unacceptable impulse, sublimation actively channels it into something constructive. Directing a patient's anger toward a structured, appropriate outlet (physical activity, art, journaling) is, in effect, coaching them toward sublimation instead of displacement.

t: Suicidal Ideation: Assessment, Safety, and Resources
x: The highest-priority assessment in mental health nursing · Suicide risk assessment is treated as a priority screening item for essentially any patient with a mental illness or a family history of one — not just patients who volunteer the thought. Once suicidal ideation is identified, the entire care plan reorganizes around one word: safety. · Clues and cues · Suicidal ideation doesn't always announce itself directly. Nonverbal signs — giving away prized possessions, a sudden and uncharacteristic sense of calm after a period of severe depression, withdrawing from relationships — can precede a disclosure or an attempt. When a patient does begin to talk about it, that disclosure is a relief to them, not a burden on the nurse: talking openly about suicidal thoughts decreases the patient's isolation and helps them externalize and problem-solve the crisis rather than carrying it alone. This is also why asking directly about suicidal ideation does not "plant the idea" — a persistent myth. Asking a clear, direct question ("Are you having thoughts of ending your life?") opens the door to help rather than creating the risk. · Warning signs · Talking about wanting to die or to kill themselves · Looking for a way to kill themselves, such as searching online or buying a weapon · Talking about feeling hopeless or having no reason to live · Talking about feeling trapped or in unbearable pain · Talking about being a burden to others · Increasing use of alcohol or drugs · Acting anxious or agitated, or behaving recklessly · Sleeping too little or too much · Withdrawing or isolating themselves · Showing rage or talking about seeking revenge · Displaying extreme mood swings · A common and dangerous misconception is that a patient who has attempted suicide before, or who talks about it repeatedly without acting, is "just seeking attention" and therefore lower risk. In reality, patients often attempt suicide multiple times, and a history of threats without a prior completed attempt does not predict that the next disclosure is any less serious. Every disclosure gets the same safety-first response. · Response and resources · When suicidal ideation is identified with any plan or intent, the priority shifts immediately to safety — this can mean continuous observation, removing access to means, and inpatient psychiatric care when outpatient safety cannot be assured. Beyond the immediate crisis, the standard resources a nurse should be ready to connect a patient with include suicide hotlines, crisis centers, mental health apps and licensed mental health professionals, support groups, and simply consistent open communication that keeps the door open for the patient to talk again. · The SAD PERSONS Scale — standardized suicide-risk scoring · SAD PERSONS gives one point for each positive finding, then a score band tells you the disposition: · S ex — male (males more often choose lethal/violent means; females attempt more often but with less lethal means) · A ge — 15–24 or 75+ are the highest-risk age bands · D epression — presence of a depressive disorder · P revious attempts · E thanol/drug use · R ational thinking loss (psychosis, cognitive impairment) · S ocial support lacking · O rganized plan — the more specific and lethal the plan, the higher the risk · N o spouse (single, divorced, widowed, or separated) · S ickness (chronic, debilitating, or terminal illness) · Score | Disposition · 0–2 | No significant problems identified — continue routine monitoring · 3–4 | Close follow-up; consider outpatient referral · 5–6 | Strongly consider hospitalization, voluntary or involuntary, depending on confidence the patient will return for follow-up · 7–10 | Hospitalize, involuntarily if necessary · IS PATH WARM — the other suicide-risk mnemonic worth knowing · A second standardized set of warning signs used alongside SAD PERSONS: I deation, S ubstance use, P urposelessness, A nxiety, T rapped (feeling), H opelessness, W ithdrawal, A nger, R ecklessness, M ood change. · Counterintuitive but high-yield: suicide risk can actually rise as a severe depressive episode starts to lift, not just while it's at its worst. A patient who was too psychomotor-retarded to act on suicidal thoughts may, as energy returns (whether from treatment response or a fresh burst of manic-range energy), now have the physical capability to carry out a plan they already had. Monitor closely through the improvement phase, not just the depths of the episode — this applies to any client recently started on an antidepressant, too.

Four phases, three types, and why every crisis resolves one way or another · A crisis is a sudden stressful event that is perceived as a threat, impacts an individual's problem-solving, and disrupts daily life. All people experience crises during their lives; crises are connected to a precipitating event or series of events, and are interpreted and perceived differently by each individual — a crisis for one person may not be one for another. Crises are typically resolved in a short period of time (1–3 months) and may provide an opportunity for personal growth, or may erode an individual's coping ability with subsequent problems and crises. · How a crisis is experienced · A crisis response is based on the individual's perception of the event, availability of support, and availability of coping strategies. Human responses to crisis include feeling powerless, overwhelmed, and anxious. A person may perceive their coping strategies as inadequate and may become obsessive, solely directed on addressing the crisis, and may experience physical manifestations of anxiety. Hospitalization may be indicated if the client expresses potential to harm self or others. · The four phases of crisis · Phase 1 — exposure to the problem or event, which causes anxiety and the initiation of strategies to cope with additional stress · Phase 2 — current coping mechanisms fail, anxiety increases, impairing functioning · Phase 3 — the person seeks assistance and/or uses all coping resources to resolve the conflict/crisis; resolution may occur · Phase 4 — if unresolved, leads to psychological distress, panic, and disordered thinking; may escalate to risk of harm to self and others · Three types of crises · Adventitious — unexpected stress over which the individual has no control (natural disasters, accidents, violence) · Maturational/developmental — inability to cope with normal developmental stressors (adolescence to adulthood, marriage, childbirth, transitions in aging, retirement) · Situational — unexpected and distressing life events (loss of job, death of a loved one, divorce, unplanned move) · Priority assessments/cues · Plan and/or capacity for harming self or others · Precipitating event, detailed description including when it occurred · Capacity to cope with crises, determine pre-crisis functioning · Physical and emotional status, pre-existing psychiatric issues · Previous experiences with this crisis, coping mechanisms employed · Current coping mechanisms and their effectiveness, use of substances · Existence and adequacy of support systems · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Serum blood alcohol levels and drug/toxicology screens. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Management emphasizes short-term problem identification, mobilization of resources · Focus of management is safety, reducing anxiety, promoting problem-solving, and building support systems · Establish a therapeutic relationship based on acceptance and active listening · Set limits on aggressive, hostile, impulsive, or violent behavior · Clarify the current crisis/problem, explore causes, and compare the nurse's perceptions with the client's · Recognize feelings of anger, resentment, guilt, disappointment · Discuss potential changes and strategies to deal with the crisis, advantages/disadvantages of different coping options, assist the client to select coping strategies · Clarify components of the crisis that cannot be changed and the feelings those evoke · Refer to resources and support systems · Priority medications · No specific medications treat a crisis itself — clients may require medications to manage associated or underlying conditions. · Priority actual & potential complications · Unresolved crisis may lead to anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder · May harm self or others · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Nurses may work with peer-support teams for clients in crisis, including those with personal experience dealing with crisis · Nurses may use crisis intervention skills to help individuals after a disaster, a diagnosis with a life-threatening illness, or significant life change · As clients learn to cope, nurses may be instrumental in fostering new coping mechanisms and ways to deal with future crises · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Ensure that clients and family members are aware of crisis hotlines, crisis centers, and hospital/agency resources focused on crisis intervention · Reinforce personal strengths and effective coping · Notice how directly this maps onto the Suicidal Ideation lesson: a suicide disclosure is very often phase 4 of an unresolved crisis, and the same core toolkit — safety first, a therapeutic and accepting relationship, active listening, and connecting the client to resources — is what both lessons are built around. Crisis intervention is the general framework; suicide risk assessment is its highest-stakes special case. · Aggression: risk factors and the prodromal syndrome · Aggression on a psychiatric unit is associated with substance use disorders, rage, neurocognitive disorders or brain injury, social stressors, frustration, financial strain/poverty, and isolation — but the single strongest predictor of future violence is a past history of violence . Before aggression fully escalates, many clients pass through a prodromal syndrome : early warning behaviors that, if recognized and addressed promptly, give staff a real chance to prevent escalation to actual violence. · Pacing · Yelling · Irritability · Talking to self · Threatening self-harm or harm to others · Poor cooperativeness — refusing to sit for vital signs or paperwork · Clenched fists · Angry facial expression · De-escalation: least invasive first · NCLEX questions about an escalating client almost always reward the least restrictive/invasive option among the answer choices. In roughly increasing intensity: · Reduce environmental stimulation — dim the lights, lower monitor/alarm volume if it's safe to do so · Use a calm voice and a supportive (not irritated or fearful) facial expression · Keep moderate eye contact — not an intense stare, but not avoidant either, and adjusted for cultural context · Use extreme caution with touch — touch can escalate agitation rather than calm it · Avoid "why" questions and accusatory language, which put the client on the defensive · Offer a distraction if appropriate — food, a drink, a walk, a phone call · Attempt a voluntary safety contract with the client if they are organized and cooperative enough to participate · When de-escalation fails: PMAB · PMAB (Prevention and Management of Aggressive Behaviors) is the term for the structured, stepwise agency response once de-escalation alone isn't working: ensure adequate staffing, call security or activate the agency's emergency response, protect other clients on the unit, and only after those measures fail, a manual hold performed by a specially trained individual per agency policy, with sedating medication prepared as the next step. · During and after a manual hold: continuously monitor airway patency and respirations, and treat the client's decreasing struggle as one indicator that de-escalation is occurring. Establish and communicate clear release criteria — such as speaking normally and decreased struggling — before the hold begins, and continue close observation after any sedating medication is given, since these medications take time to reach full effect. · Debriefing after a violent episode · A debriefing after any violent episode is a standard part of the response, not optional: staff review what happened, which interventions were and weren't effective and why, and how to prevent a recurrence. Other clients on the unit who witnessed the event may also need reassurance and support afterward — the event's impact isn't limited to the client and staff directly involved.

t: Legal & Ethical Issues in Psychiatric Care
x: Admission types, patient rights, informed consent, confidentiality, and restraints/seclusion · Psychiatric patients keep every constitutional right any other citizen has — having a mental health disorder is never, by itself, grounds to restrict someone's liberty, and unknowingly violating a patient's rights can carry serious legal consequences for the nurse, the provider, and the facility. This lesson covers the legal framework that shows up constantly on exams: how patients are admitted, what rights they retain once admitted, how consent and confidentiality work, and when restraints/seclusion are legally permitted. · Voluntary vs. involuntary admission · Type | How it happens | Key rights retained · Voluntary admission | The client (or their guardian) seeks admission for care on their own initiative | Free to request discharge/sign out at any time (with provider notification); retains full civil rights · Involuntary admission | Ordered when a person is mentally ill and a danger to self or others, or unable to meet their own basic needs; requires a psychiatrist/PHCP certification, and in most cases a court hearing | Retains the right to informed consent and to refuse treatment (except in an immediate danger situation); can request a hearing to seek release (writ of habeas corpus) · A client on a voluntary hold who is later judged to be a danger to self or others can be converted to involuntary status while legal proceedings are pursued — voluntary admission is not an unconditional guarantee of same-day discharge if new safety concerns emerge. · The psychiatric patient's bill of rights · Right to treatment in the least restrictive setting appropriate to their needs · Right to informed consent, and to refuse treatment (unless a legal exception applies) · Right to confidentiality of their medical/psychiatric information · Right to communicate with people outside the hospital, and to keep personal effects · Right to periodic review of their status and to legal representation · Right to habeas corpus — a hearing to challenge involuntary detention · Right to enter contracts, manage property, marry/divorce, and vote — a psychiatric diagnosis alone does not strip these rights · Confidentiality and HIPAA · All records concerning psychiatric care must be kept confidential unless the patient consents to disclosure — HIPAA is the law, and psychiatric information carries extra sensitivity because of the stigma attached to it. There are four recognized exceptions where disclosure is required even without patient consent: · Suspected child (or vulnerable adult) abuse · Criminal cases/court order · Government requests · When the public has a right to know (for example, a credible, specific threat against an identifiable third party) · A patient telling the nurse their suicidal thoughts "in confidence" is a common exam trap: the nurse cannot promise to keep information confidential when it conflicts with the duty to keep the patient safe. The nurse's duty is to inform the patient up front that anything relevant to safety will be shared with the treatment team — not to make (and then break) a private promise. · Informed consent · Obtaining informed consent is the responsibility of the primary provider, not the nurse — but the nurse plays an essential supporting role: providing relevant information, clarifying questions, and documenting any concerns the patient raises. Before a treatment or procedure proceeds, the patient (or legal guardian) must understand what the treatment is, its risks and benefits, and the available alternatives — and must be able to communicate a choice. If a nurse has doubts about whether a patient truly understands or is competent to consent, the treatment team must be notified before proceeding. · Competency and legal guardianship · A patient is assumed competent unless their thoughts or behavior strongly suggest otherwise — a psychiatric diagnosis by itself does not make someone incompetent. Only a judge can legally declare a person incompetent and appoint a guardian; it is not a clinical decision a nurse or even a psychiatrist can make unilaterally. For a hospitalized minor, a parent or court-appointed guardian must be established at admission; if parents have surrendered responsibility to an institution with proper documentation, the institution may hold that decision-making authority. · Restraints and seclusion · Used only to prevent the patient from injuring themselves or others, and only after less restrictive interventions have failed — never for staff convenience or punishment · Requires an order from a licensed independent practitioner; some states allow emergency application followed promptly by an order · Time-limited, with continuous observation and frequent, scheduled documentation of food, fluids, toileting, circulation, and safety · Discontinued as soon as the patient regains control and can safely agree to remain in control · Governed by facility policy and accrediting-body standards (e.g., The Joint Commission) · Two points reinforce these standards in practice: a manual hold may only be performed by staff who have completed the agency's required specialized training, and a voluntary safety contract negotiated with a cooperative, organized client is itself a least-restrictive alternative worth attempting — and documenting — before any restraint or seclusion order is pursued. · Documentation · Documentation is a legal and ethical duty, not paperwork for its own sake — it is the legal proof of the nature and quality of care provided, supports continuity of care, and confirms that ordered treatments were actually completed. Unclear, incomplete, or subjective documentation can result in denial of reimbursement and creates real liability exposure for the nurse, other providers, and the facility.

t: Treatment Modalities: Milieu, Psychotherapy, Behavior Therapy & ECT
x: Individual, group, family, and environmental therapies — plus the somatic option (ECT) · Medication is only one arm of psychiatric treatment. This lesson maps out the non-pharmacologic treatment modalities that show up across nearly every diagnosis in this section — knowing which therapy fits which situation, and recognizing the vocabulary each one uses, is tested independently of any single disorder. · Milieu therapy · The milieu is the safe physical and social environment in which a patient receives treatment — more than just the physical unit, it's the therapeutic community that staff and patients build together. Safety is always the top priority within the milieu, and every member of the interprofessional team (RN, social worker, recreational/occupational/expressive therapists, psychologist, psychiatrist) contributes to it. Community meetings, activity and social-skills groups, and structured exercise programs are common milieu tools, and staff on psychiatric units often wear street clothes rather than uniforms to make the environment feel less clinical. · Levels of psychotherapy · Level | What it involves | Goal · Supportive | Brief therapy, may extend over years; the therapist reinforces the client's existing coping mechanisms rather than introducing new ones | Help the client express feelings, explore alternatives, and make decisions in a safe environment · Reeducative | A longer, more structured, planned approach — may use short-term techniques like reality therapy, cognitive restructuring, or behavior modification | Teach and practice new, more effective coping skills · Reconstructive | Emotional and cognitive restructuring of the self takes place, aiming for deeper insight | Greater self-understanding, emotional freedom, and development of potential · Individual, group, and family therapy · Individual therapy — one-on-one counseling, short- or long-term, working toward goals the patient and therapist establish together · Group therapy — a psychotherapist guides a group (ideally 4–10 members) with similar concerns; especially useful for addictions, and moves through predictable stages: initial (superficial, members sizing each other up), working (real therapeutic work, established norms/roles), and termination (processing the ending, applying what was learned) · Family therapy — treats the family system, not just the identified patient; useful for childhood/adolescent adjustment issues, marital discord, and abusive family dynamics · Cognitive therapy — targets the negative, distorted thinking patterns ("the future is bleak and hopeless") believed to drive depression; homework assignments (like tracking pleasurable activities) are a hallmark technique · Crisis intervention — short-term, focused on restoring the client to their pre-crisis level of functioning; usually just the client and therapist, may be one session or several over months (see the dedicated Crisis Intervention lesson for the full framework) · Behavior therapy techniques · Behavior therapy assumes maladaptive behavior was learned in response to a trigger, and can be unlearned through the same conditioning principles. Several named techniques fall under this umbrella: · Technique | How it works | Example use · Systematic desensitization | Teach relaxation, then gradually introduce increasing exposure to the feared stimulus | Treatment of choice for phobias — a fear of flying is approached step-by-step from visualization to an actual flight · Implosion therapy (flooding) | Direct, immediate exposure to the feared situation without a gradual buildup or relaxation training first | Contraindicated in fragile patients or those with a medical condition that exposure-induced anxiety could worsen (e.g., cardiac dysrhythmias) · Aversion therapy | Pairs an unwanted stimulus with the habit to be eliminated | Disulfiram (Antabuse) makes a patient violently ill if they drink alcohol · Assertiveness training | Teaches the patient to appropriately stand up for themselves while respecting others' rights | Role-modeling assertive vs. passive-aggressive or aggressive responses · Operant conditioning | Behavior modification through positive or negative reinforcement | Token economy (below) is a direct application · Token economy | Desired behavior is rewarded with tokens the patient exchanges for privileges or objects | Must be applied consistently and promptly to be effective · Thought stopping | The patient learns to interrupt an unwanted thought pattern with a cue word ("stop") and redirect attention | Visualizing an actual stop sign while saying the word · Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) are the two most widely used therapeutic models built on these behavioral principles, and both are referenced repeatedly across the disorder-specific lessons in this section (DBT especially for borderline personality disorder). · Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) — in detail · ECT delivers a brief electrical current through electrodes attached to the temples to induce a controlled, therapeutic seizure. It is not a cure , but it is highly effective and reserved for severe major depression or bipolar depression that hasn't responded to other treatments, especially when rapid symptom relief is needed (active suicidality, catatonia, psychotic depression, or a patient who cannot tolerate medication). Certain patients with schizophrenia may also be candidates. · Before the procedure · Written, signed informed consent is required, with patient/family education that directly addresses myths and fears about ECT — it is a treatment, not a punishment, and is done under anesthesia · Consent must be obtained by the practitioner performing the procedure, and the client retains the right to withdraw consent at any point in the course of treatment, even after signing · The client is kept NPO (nothing by mouth) for at least 6–8 hours before the procedure, exactly as for any other procedure requiring general anesthesia, to reduce aspiration risk · A short-acting general anesthetic is given, followed by a muscle relaxant to minimize outward movement during the seizure · Premedication relaxes the muscles specifically to prevent injury from the seizure activity · An airway or mouth guard is placed to protect the client from biting the tongue · ECT is generally considered a safer alternative to psychotropic medication for severe depression during pregnancy, since it avoids fetal drug exposure · During the procedure · The electrical stimulus is administered and produces a brief seizure lasting about 15–70 seconds. The whole procedure is brief; outward movement is usually only a slight movement of the hands, feet, or a toe because of the premedication. · After the procedure · The client is transported to a recovery area with a blood pressure cuff and oximeter in place, with oxygen, suction, and emergency equipment available · The client typically wakes about 15 minutes after the procedure · Confusion and disorientation are expected for several hours afterward — provide frequent orientation that is brief, distinct, and simple, plus reassurance · The client returns to the nursing unit once oxygen saturation is acceptable, vital signs are stable, and mental status is satisfactory · Expected side effects: confusion, disorientation, and short-term memory loss; also headache, muscle soreness, nausea, and tachycardia. Memory usually recovers fully, though a minority of clients experience memory loss lasting up to 6 months · Safety priority: monitor a client who has recently had ECT — and any client recently started on an antidepressant — closely for suicidal ideation. A sudden increase in energy without a corresponding lift in mood can mean the client now has the physical energy to act on suicidal thoughts they didn't have the energy to act on before · Course and maintenance · The usual course is 6–12 treatments given 2–3 times per week (about 2–5 days apart initially). Maintenance ECT, roughly once a month, may help reduce the relapse rate for a client with recurrent depression. · Detoxification and dual diagnosis · Detox programs provide medically monitored, safer withdrawal from drugs or alcohol than an unsupervised "cold turkey" attempt, with medication used to prevent uncomfortable or life-threatening complications. Dual diagnosis (co-occurring disorders) describes a patient with a psychiatric condition and a substance use disorder together — these patients are less likely to adhere to treatment plans and carry a higher risk of impulsive, violent, or suicidal behavior, which is why an integrated treatment plan addressing both conditions together (not sequentially) is the standard of care.

Six named types, age-specific presentations, and the full antidepressant medication card · Depression is an alteration in mood manifested by sadness, despair, and pessimism that may be chronic or episodic. It's a common psychiatric disorder — lifetime prevalence is roughly 15–17%, making major depressive disorder the single most common mental health diagnosis in the U.S. — twice as common in females than males, with increasing incidence among adolescents and young adults. The median age of onset is around 32.5 years, and more than half of patients who have one episode go on to have at least two more; an untreated episode can last anywhere from a month to a year or longer. It may be linked to socioeconomic wellbeing and seasonal changes. · Six named types · Major depressive disorder (MDD) — symptomatic for at least two weeks, single episode or recurrent; no mania associated; not attributed to substances or a medical condition; transient, mild, moderate, or severe symptoms; may include anxiety and suicidality; may have psychotic or catatonic symptoms with lack of contact with reality · Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — less severe than MDD, no psychotic symptoms; chronic depressed mood and irritability occurring more days than not for at least 2 years in adults, 1 year in children and adolescents · Premenstrual dysphoric disorder — depressed mood, anxiety, mood swings, and disinterest in activities one week prior to menstruation; decreases or discontinues after the menstrual cycle · Substance/medication-induced depressive disorder — related to the effects of a medication, associated with intoxication/withdrawal · Depressive disorder due to another medical condition — infections or inflammatory disease, cancer, neurological, cardiac, or endocrine disorders · Postpartum depression — depressed mood after delivery, more significant than minor "baby blues" sadness; may have psychotic features · Additional DSM-5-TR specifiers · Melancholic features — a distinct, non-reactive depressed mood (unlike ordinary grief) with near-total loss of pleasure, mood that's worse in the morning, early-morning awakening, marked psychomotor agitation or retardation, significant anorexia or weight loss, and excessive guilt · Atypical features — mood reactivity (brightens in response to positive events) plus at least two of: increased appetite/weight gain, hypersomnia, a heavy "leaden paralysis" feeling in the arms or legs, and long-standing sensitivity to interpersonal rejection · Seasonal pattern (seasonal affective disorder, SAD) — episodes that regularly begin and remit at characteristic times of year, classically with fall/winter onset; phototherapy (light therapy) is the treatment of choice · Causes · Family history · Genetics · Neurotransmitter dysfunction · Stress/environment · Medical issues · Medications · Risk factors may be related to genetic, biochemical, and psychosocial influences. Comorbidities include anxiety disorders, substance use, eating disorders, chronic pain, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and borderline personality disorder. · DSM-5-TR criteria for a major depressive episode · Formally, diagnosis requires five or more of the following symptoms nearly every day for the same 2-week period, representing a change from prior functioning, with at least one symptom being depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure: depressed mood most of the day; markedly diminished interest or pleasure in almost all activities; significant unintentional weight change (more than 5% of body weight in a month) or a change in appetite; insomnia or hypersomnia; psychomotor agitation or retardation observable by others (not just a subjective feeling); fatigue or loss of energy; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; diminished ability to concentrate or indecisiveness; and recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation with or without a plan, or a suicide attempt. Symptoms can't be better explained by a mixed episode, a medical condition, a substance, or ordinary bereavement. · Priority assessments/cues · Suicidality — including ideations, plan, and energy level; risk increases in the presence of substance use, recent loss, and past suicide attempts · Mood, feelings, thoughts — anger, hopelessness, worthlessness, pessimism, lack of control; lack of ability to feel pleasure or lack of interest in usual activities (anhedonia); confusion, inability to concentrate, impaired judgment and executive functioning; hallucinations and/or delusions in severe cases · Behavioral symptoms — changes in appetite and bowel habits, insomnia or hypersomnia; level of activity, may be hyperactive or inactive, increased fatigue; lack of attention to hygiene and self-care; slowed, monotone speech; flat, constricted, or blunted affect · Age-related assessments · Age group | What to look for · Infants/toddlers | Feeding problems, lack of play, delays in speech/motor development, aggression · Preschool children | Aggression, auditory hallucinations, phobias · School-age children | Vague physical complaints, poor social skills, aggression, worry, poor self-esteem, lack of play · Adolescents | Anger, aggression, high-risk behaviors, apathy, social withdrawal, sexual acting out, restlessness, substance use · Older adults | Bereavement overload, memory loss, confusion, apathy — may manifest as pseudodementia · Standardized screening tools: the Beck Depression Inventory, the Hamilton Depression Scale, the Geriatric Depression Scale, and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). · A realistic clinical picture: a 36-year-old brought to an occupational health nurse for repeated absenteeism bursts into tears mid-conversation, describing feeling "down all the time," crying spells, days she can't get out of bed, and a 10-lb weight loss over the past few months since her parents died. On exam she's tearful with a flat affect, slumped posture, dry skin, and poor grooming, and describes "constant" fatigue — "I am so tired that I sleep every moment I am not at work" — with vital signs otherwise unremarkable. She denies any intention to hurt herself or others. This combination — anhedonia and low mood tied to a recent loss, neurovegetative symptoms (appetite/weight, sleep, energy), functional impairment (absenteeism), and a direct denial of suicidal intent that still must be documented and reassessed — is the kind of presentation MDD case questions are built around. · Additional diagnostic testing · The dexamethasone suppression test is sometimes used adjunctively: dexamethasone should normally suppress cortisol secretion, and a failure to suppress cortisol is associated with major depression, reflecting hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation. It's a research/adjunct tool rather than a routine primary diagnostic test. · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Serum toxicology — determine substance use · Labs based on physiological needs (hydration/nutritional status, anemia) · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Individualized psychotherapy, group therapy, family therapy, along with medications · Cognitive therapy — replace negative with positive automatic thoughts, consider realistic potential complications, learn new methods to conceptualize and perceive life tasks, recognize and challenge cognitive distortions · Other therapeutic treatments: electroconvulsive therapy , light therapy , and transcranial magnetic stimulation (stimulates nerve cells in the brain) · Suicide precautions — create a safe environment, observe closely, stay with the client, ensure the room and surroundings are cleared of any objects usable for self-harm, determine risk/lethality of ideations, allow for expression of feelings such as anger and guilt, encourage the client to create a safety plan · Build a trusting relationship with an accepting attitude, allow for ventilation of feelings, educate on mood and grief, promote feeling of positive self-worth, provide distraction, physical activity, and outlets for anger and tension · Support hygiene, nutrition, and sleep needs while symptoms are severe · Adjust communication techniques for withdrawn clients — make observations about the environment, use simple concrete language, allow time for the client to respond, avoid platitudes, sit with the client in silence. A concrete example of an observation-based opener: "You're sitting all by yourself, looking sad — is that how you feel?" · Encourage group attendance, maintain assertive and positive communication, engage the client in making decisions and setting realistic goals · Assume an active role in initiating communication rather than waiting for the client to start — a depressed client often lacks the energy or motivation to initiate; speak slowly and allow ample time for a response since the client may think and react sluggishly · Plan activities and higher-demand interactions for whenever the client's energy level naturally peaks during the day · Warm milk and back rubs at bedtime are simple, non-pharmacologic comfort measures that can help with sleep · Priority actual & potential complications · Catatonia, stupor · Physiological impact of neglecting nutritional, sleep, and activity needs · Suicide · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Be aware of the black-box warning on some antidepressants associated with increased rates of suicide in children and adolescents when first starting medications — closely monitor medications for this population · Antidepressants in older adults may interfere with other medications, cause dangerous side effects, or accumulate quickly — lower dosages are recommended · Ensure clients' safety when suicide is a concern — ensure the client is taking medications, not "stockpiling" for overdose, make frequent rounds at irregular times · Many antidepressant medications take 2–4 weeks to take effect and should not be combined or stopped abruptly · Priority medications · Fluoxetine — oral SSRI antidepressant; take in the morning to avoid insomnia; educate the client on signs/symptoms of serotonin syndrome · Duloxetine — oral SNRI antidepressant; may cause orthostatic hypotension, sweating, constipation; also treats anxiety, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and peripheral neuropathy · Bupropion — oral norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) antidepressant; also used for smoking cessation; may decrease seizure threshold; should not "double-up" doses if a dose is missed · Amitriptyline — oral tricyclic antidepressant (TCA); take at night due to sedative effects; watch for anticholinergic side effects and signs of toxicity · Phenelzine — oral MAOI antidepressant; a later agent used if depression is refractory to other treatments; large number of food and drug interactions which may lead to hypertensive crisis (see the Medications unit for the full tyramine/"cheese reaction" detail) · This is the drug-name reference card for the SSRI/SNRI/TCA/MAOI class concepts already covered in the Medications unit — use that lesson for the shared serotonin-syndrome risk and the black-box warning that applies across all four classes, and this one to lock in which specific drug (and route/timing pearl) belongs to depression specifically. · Common drug names by class — the full roster · SSRIs (first-line for most patients — fewer of the disturbing side effects of TCAs/MAOIs): fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), paroxetine (Paxil), citalopram (Celexa), escitalopram (Lexapro), fluvoxamine (Luvox) · SNRIs (often second-line): venlafaxine (Effexor), duloxetine (Cymbalta) · TCAs (older class, effective but a narrow safety margin — overdose can be quickly lethal, and most carry a black-box suicide warning, so they're generally not first-line anymore): amitriptyline (Elavil), imipramine (Tofranil), nortriptyline (Pamelor), desipramine (Norpramin), doxepin (Sinequan), amoxapine (Asendin), trimipramine (Surmontil) · MAOIs (reserved for treatment-refractory depression given the food/drug interaction risk): phenelzine (Nardil), isocarboxazid (Marplan) · Atypical antidepressants (mechanisms less well understood than the classes above; generally second-line): bupropion (Wellbutrin) and mirtazapine (Remeron) · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Referral to support groups, counseling services, mental health clinics, crisis intervention · Encourage adherence to medication regimens, discuss expected outcomes and timing of anticipated effects, do not stop taking medications abruptly · Recognize early signs of worsening depression and notify the health care provider · Ensure family education and support, awareness of the client's risk for suicidality, potential signs of suicidality, means to keep the client safe, and emergency procedures · Safety precautions — the concrete specifics · Remove specific dangerous objects from the client's environment: belts, razors, suspenders, shoelaces, glass, knives, nail files, clippers, and light/electrical cords · Constant (one-on-one) supervision for an acutely suicidal client, with extra vigilance whenever the client is shaving, taking medication, or in the bathroom · Assign the client to a room near the nurses' station to make observation easier · Correct environmental hazards on the unit itself (exposed pipes, windows without safety glass, access to a roof or open balcony) · Watch closely for a sudden lift in energy or mood without a matching improvement in outlook, especially as an episode begins to "lift" or shortly after starting an antidepressant — the client may now have the physical energy to act on a plan they lacked the energy to carry out before · Treatment phases for MDD · Acute phase (roughly 6–12 weeks) — goals are to reduce depressive symptoms and improve functioning; may involve hospitalization and initiation of medication · Continuation phase (roughly 4–9 months) — the effective medication dose is continued; goal is preventing relapse of the current episode · Maintenance phase (1 year or longer, sometimes indefinite) — medication may be continued or gradually phased out; goal is preventing a new depressive episode, especially in a client with a history of recurrent depression

Six named types, the Altman mania scale, and the full mood-stabilizer medication card · Bipolar disorder is a chronic mood disorder manifested with cycles of depression and mania (a persistent elevation in mood, including exaggerated and risk-laden behaviors, hyperactivity, and symptoms of psychosis) or hypomania (distinct but less severe symptoms of mania). Mood is a significant and sustained emotion that impacts a person's perception of the world; affect is the external appearance of that emotional experience. Bipolar disorder impacts about 2.6% of the US population, with 83% of those affected profoundly impacted — it affects all sexes and ages equally, with onset typically between 18–20 (some sources cite an average around 25), and it's often misdiagnosed or undiagnosed. · Affect vocabulary — high-yield therapeutic-communication terms · Affect and mood questions like to test precise vocabulary. Know these distinctions cold, since they show up across every mood and psychotic disorder lesson: · Blunted affect — a severe reduction in the intensity of outward emotional expression · Flat affect — a complete or almost complete absence of outward emotional expression · Constricted affect — a reduction (not a full restriction) in the intensity of outward emotional expression · Inappropriate affect — affect that doesn't match the situation or the content of what's being said (e.g., laughing while discussing a death) · Labile affect — rapid, easily changing affective expression unrelated to external events or stimuli — classic in mania · Six named types · Bipolar I — major depression with mania, the most severe form · Bipolar II — major depression with hypomania, often misdiagnosed as depression alone · Cyclothymic disorder — mild-to-moderate depression with hypomania that disrupts social and occupational functioning · Rapid cycling — at least 4 distinct mood shifts in a 12-month period, associated with higher dysfunction and a poorer prognosis; occurs in about 10–20% of clients with bipolar disorder and is more common in adult females · Substance/medication-induced bipolar disorder — directly caused by drugs during intoxication or withdrawal, or a reaction to other medications such as steroids · Bipolar disorder due to a medical condition — electrolyte imbalance, brain tumor · Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder — in childhood, manifested by severe irritability, temper tantrums, mood swings · Causation is attributed to hereditary, genetic, and physiological (neurotransmitter and neuroanatomical) elements along with stress and trauma. Bipolar disorder is comorbid with ADHD in children. Some patients with bipolar disorder do experience psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and/or delusions) — DSM-5 has a specific specifier, "bipolar disorder with psychotic features," for this presentation. Don't assume psychosis always means schizophrenia. · Episode duration — the DSM-5-TR numbers · Manic episode — abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood plus increased energy, present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization is required to prevent harm) · Hypomanic episode — the same symptom picture as mania but lasting only at least 4 consecutive days, with a definite change in functioning observable by others; unlike mania, it does not cause marked occupational/social impairment or require hospitalization · Cyclothymic disorder — numerous periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that don't meet full episode criteria for mania or major depression, present at least half the time for 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents), with no symptom-free period longer than 2 consecutive months; medical causes of mood alteration (e.g., Cushing disease, stroke, brain tumor, head trauma, drug overdose) must be ruled out first · Mixed features specifier · DSM-5-TR allows a "with mixed features" specifier on either pole: a manic or hypomanic episode that also has at least three concurrent depressive symptoms, or a major depressive episode that also has at least three concurrent manic/hypomanic symptoms. This combination of energy, agitation, and impulsivity together with despair and hopelessness is considered a particularly high-risk presentation for impulsive suicide attempts, since the client can have both the motivation and the physical drive to act at the same time. · The risk-taking of a manic episode has real downstream consequences worth assessing for directly: increased risky sexual behavior raises the risk of STIs and unwanted pregnancy, and impulsive spending/gambling/investing can cause lasting financial harm. And the mood swings themselves carry serious mortality risk — the risk of suicide in bipolar disorder is 20- to 30-fold higher than in the general population, with a suicide attempt able to occur impulsively during either a manic or a depressive episode. Always screen directly, regardless of which pole the client currently presents in. · Priority assessments/cues · Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale — a standardized, 5-item client self-report screening tool; mood, self-confidence, sleep, speech, and level of activity are each scored 0–4, and a total score of 6 or higher suggests clinically significant manic or hypomanic symptoms warranting further evaluation · Signs and symptoms of depression (see the Depression lesson) · Mania, elation, inflated self-esteem, grandiosity, hyperactivity, agitation, distractibility, racing thoughts/flight of ideas, accelerated/forced speech, engagement in high-risk behaviors (substance use, promiscuity/unsafe sexual behaviors, excessive shopping, gambling, investing), irritability, frenzied motor activity, decreased need for sleep, rapid mood swings, lack of hygiene/self-care, weight loss (due to lack of eating), delusions · May have mania behaviors severe enough to impact social and occupational functioning, or hypomania (similar behaviors that do not cause dysfunction), or may begin as cheerful but devolve to irritability and volatility · Assess for danger to self and others, substance use disorder, eating disorders · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Electrolyte levels · Drug and toxicology screens · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Individual or group therapy (self-help or support groups) and cognitive therapy · Psychoeducational-focused family therapy concerning early warning signs and management of manic episodes · Electroconvulsive therapy may be used in severe cases · Consult a dietitian to ensure adequate calories, including finger foods and high-calorie shakes during acute episodes; monitor intake/output and calorie counts · During acute manic episodes: decrease environmental stimuli such as lights and noise; remove dangerous objects, redirect energy to constructive activities when feasible; maintain a calm attitude, set limits on manipulation, and reinforce non-manipulative behaviors; use a team approach to care; support nutrition, sleep, and hygiene needs · Support during depressive episodes (see the Depression lesson) · Priority actual & potential complications · Negative events related to poor decision-making, high-risk behaviors · Physical exhaustion, life-threatening malnutrition · Delirious mania may lead to intensified symptoms that threaten safety of self and others, confused thinking, and stupor · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Maintain calm, consistent care — allow staff to communicate openly and express frustrations to reduce staff splitting and promote consistent limit setting · Treating with antidepressants may trigger a manic episode · Medication non-compliance is a common cause of relapse — the client may enjoy symptoms of hypomania and mania and minimize negative consequences · Priority medications · Lithium carbonate — oral mood stabilizer, effective in about 1/3 of clients; a diuretic effect means monitoring serum sodium and water intake matters (see the Medications unit for the full LITH toxicity mnemonic) · Valproic acid — oral anticonvulsant to stabilize moods; may increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors; may cause sedation, avoid alcohol; cannot be discontinued abruptly · Olanzapine — oral atypical antipsychotic to manage symptoms associated with mania (impulsiveness, agitation, hyperactivity); take at night to enhance sleep; side effects include bloating, swelling, vision changes, poor balance · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Strictly adhere to the medication schedule per the discharge medication instruction sheet · Know and watch for signs and symptoms of toxicity and side effects of each medication · Avoid caffeine to ensure restful sleep · See the follow-up record for scheduled blood draws or medication checks · Attend scheduled therapy sessions to ensure management of acute and chronic signs and symptoms · Lithium: the mnemonic worth memorizing — LITH · Lithium is the classic mood stabilizer for both bipolar disorder and, in some cases, schizophrenia, and its narrow safety margin makes it one of the highest-yield medications in this course. Its most common side effects are weight gain and dry mouth, but the real testable content is toxicity, which the mnemonic LITH organizes cleanly: · L — Levels over 1.5 mEq/L are toxic (therapeutic range is roughly 0.6–1.2) · I — Increase fluid and salt intake, since sodium depletion raises lithium levels; lithium cannot be given to a dehydrated or hyponatremic patient, and diuretics — even caffeine — should be avoided because they promote fluid and sodium loss · T — Toxic signs include excessive urination and thirst, vomiting and diarrhea, tremors, and confusion · H — Hold NSAIDs, which can raise lithium levels to dangerous ranges by reducing renal clearance · Notice the trap NSAIDs and diuretics both set: a patient on lithium who reaches for ibuprofen for a headache, or who starts a diuretic or a high-caffeine habit, can tip into toxicity without changing their lithium dose at all. Medication reconciliation for a lithium patient is really a search for anything that could shift fluid, sodium, or renal clearance. · Other mood stabilizers used alongside or instead of lithium include lamotrigine and divalproex , both of which lack lithium's narrow toxic window but carry their own monitoring requirements (lamotrigine for serious rash, divalproex for liver function and platelets).

Panic, phobias, and generalized worry — the full type breakdown, plus the anxiolytic medication card · Anxiety is a subjective response to stress that impairs functioning in social and work contexts — feelings of dread, impending doom, fear, apprehension, or discomfort, which may or may not be associated with real stressors and may be out of proportion with the stressor. Fear is the cognitive response to a threat; anxiety is the emotional response. Anxiety is a common psychiatric disorder, twice as common in females than males, and can exist across the lifespan. It's attributed to biological, genetic, cognitive, and psychological causative factors, and often exists with comorbidities of depression, substance abuse, and other anxieties. Anxiety disorders are the single most common mental health diagnosis across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood in the U.S. — with treatment, most people recover a full, productive life. · The four levels of anxiety — the single most-tested framework in this lesson · Before memorizing any individual diagnosis, know this progression cold: as anxiety intensity rises, the perceptual field narrows and functioning drops in a predictable, stepwise way. This is exam gold because a case-stem description of behavior ("pacing, screaming, unable to follow directions") should let you name the level without the word "anxiety" ever appearing in the question. · Level | Perceptual field | What it looks like · Mild | Increased — sight and sound are sharper | Everyday tension; can motivate growth, creativity, and learning; restlessness, irritability, mild tension · Moderate | Narrowed — selective inattention begins | Focus is on immediate concerns only; learning and problem-solving still occur, but require effort; physical symptoms (increased heart rate, GI upset, headache, urinary urgency, mild tremors) · Severe | Significantly narrowed — focus on minute/scattered details | Feels like something bad is about to happen; all behavior is aimed at relieving the anxiety; learning and problem-solving are NOT possible; the client needs direction to focus; physical symptoms from sympathetic activation (nausea, dizziness, sleep disturbance, pounding heart, hyperventilation) · Panic | Loss of rational thought/perceptual distortion | Dread and terror with a sense of impending doom; disorganized, can't perceive reality accurately or communicate/function effectively; increased or erratic motor activity (pacing, shouting) or complete withdrawal; if prolonged, can lead to exhaustion and death · Matching the intervention to the level · Mild–moderate: help the client identify the source of anxiety, encourage them to talk about feelings/concerns, identify thoughts and feelings that preceded the onset, encourage problem-solving, encourage gross motor exercise as an outlet · Severe–panic: use a calm manner, remain with the client, minimize environmental stimuli, use clear/simple statements and a low-pitched voice, attend to physical needs first, provide gross motor activity (walk/pace with the nurse rather than trying to talk the client down with complex language) — the immediate priority at this level is always to decrease environmental stimuli and provide a calm, quiet environment · A single line worth memorizing: the immediate nursing action for any client in acute anxiety is to decrease stimuli in the environment and provide a calm, quiet space — before anything else, including trying to talk through the trigger. · Types of anxiety disorders · Panic disorder — sudden feelings of doom, abrupt onset of physical symptoms, not triggered by a specific stressor or situation · Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) — unrealistic, persistent, and excessive worry about many stressors, occurring more days than not for a duration of at least 6 months, with impaired social and occupational functioning · Phobias — persistent, exaggerated, irrational, and intense fear of a situation, object, or activity. Agoraphobia is fear of situations where escape may be difficult or help may not be available (being in a crowd of strangers, traveling in a car or airplane, being on a bridge), often leading to confinement to home. Social anxiety disorder is fear that one might do something embarrassing or be negatively evaluated by others, commonly manifested as fear of public speaking/performance but which can lead to chronic social isolation.
