Other specific phobias include fear of heights, snakes, dogs, and strangers · Obsessive-compulsive disorder — see the OCD lesson · Body dysmorphic disorder — an exaggerated belief that the body is deformed · Trichotillomania — hair-pulling disorder · Hoarding disorder — difficulty discarding and/or excessively acquiring objects regardless of value · Panic disorder — the details · Panic disorder is anxiety in its most severe recurring form: unexpected panic attacks, plus persistent worry between attacks about having another one and about the consequences of the attacks — this in-between worry is itself part of the diagnosis, not just the attacks. A panic attack builds to peak intensity within about 10–15 minutes and rarely lasts longer than 30 minutes , though repeated attacks can recur for hours. Panic attacks can occur as a specifier of another condition (for example, "PTSD with panic attacks") rather than panic disorder itself — the label depends on context, not just the attack. · Roughly 4.7% of the U.S. population experiences panic disorder in their lifetime, twice as common in women, and it's genetically influenced (higher rates in first-degree relatives, higher concordance in identical twins). It's frequently complicated by major depressive disorder, and self-medication with alcohol or antianxiety drugs raises the risk of a co-occurring substance use disorder. Panic attacks and panic disorder both carry an increased risk of suicide attempts and suicidal ideation, especially with a comorbid mood disorder, personality disorder, or alcohol misuse. · Agoraphobia — the details · Agoraphobia is an out-of-proportion fear of being in places or situations where escape might be difficult or embarrassing — open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds, standing in line, or being outside the home alone. It can exist as its own diagnosis or alongside panic disorder, and without treatment it tends to worsen, in extreme cases confining the person to their home entirely. Women are diagnosed more often, and up to a third of people with agoraphobia also have a substance use disorder. · Generalized anxiety disorder — the diagnostic criteria box · GAD has a moderate genetic risk (roughly 30%), closely tied to other anxiety and mood disorders. Diagnosis requires excessive anxiety and worry about several events/activities for more than 6 months, plus at least 3 of the following 6 symptoms, present more days than not: feeling restless or on edge, easily tired, poor attention/concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance (trouble falling or staying asleep). The anxiety must cause significant distress or impaired functioning, without an underlying medical cause, concurrent substance use, or a better explanation from another mental health disorder. · Social anxiety disorder — the FEAR mnemonic · Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) may be limited to performance situations (public speaking, playing music, athletics) or generalized to nearly any social interaction. The hallmark physical response is blushing; other physical signs include profuse sweating, trembling, nausea, and difficulty talking. Onset is typically in childhood/adolescence (median onset: mid-teens), it affects an estimated 3–7% of Americans, and people with social anxiety disorder carry a higher suicide rate than the general population. · Letter | Stands for · F | Fear of an object or a situation · E | Emotional conflict occurring unconsciously · A | Avoidant behavior demonstrated · R | Reacts with severe anxiety · Specific phobia — the details · Specific (simple) phobia is intense, irrational anxiety triggered by a specific object or situation — common enough to affect roughly 7.7–12.5% of the U.S. population over a lifetime, more common in women, with onset varying by the type of phobia. Left untreated, phobias tend to be lifelong (mean duration around 20 years), but exposure-based treatment carries an excellent prognosis. Three mechanisms are thought to explain how a specific phobia develops: direct conditioning (personally experiencing a traumatic event involving the object/situation), vicarious acquisition (watching someone else react fearfully, or witnessing a traumatic event involving the object/situation), and informational transmission (learning to be afraid through what other people or the media say about the object/situation). · Priority assessments/cues · Consider use of standardized anxiety assessment scales · Vital signs for tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension · Signs of vomiting, dyspnea, muscle tension, restlessness, diaphoresis, anxious expression, trembling, hyperventilation, syncope · Symptoms of chest pain or pressure, nausea, palpitations, chills, hot flashes, feelings of choking, dizziness/lightheadedness, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, feeling unsteady, paresthesia, depersonalization, feeling of losing control, fear of dying, "feeling on edge," excessive worry, feelings of powerlessness, lack of control, expressions of doubt about personal capacity, avoiding social events or activities, procrastination, withdrawal from decision-making or anxiety-producing situations, ritualistic behavior, preoccupation with stressor · Manifestations may or may not have a trigger event or stressor · Phobias include anxious response to the feared object, activity, or situation, including panic symptoms, sweating, tachycardia, dyspnea · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Serum toxicology — determine substance use · Labs based on physiological needs (hydration/nutritional status) · Diagnostic tests to rule out physiological etiology (cardiopulmonary disease) · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Support the client in therapies: individual, cognitive, behavioral, along with medication · Explore the client's perceptions of threat, discuss things that can and cannot be changed, explore coping and stress-management strategies, encourage independence and decision-making · Provide structured activity and distractions, replacing behaviors with constructive thoughts and coping mechanisms; controlled systematic desensitization sedation if needed · After the acute episode: explore sources of anxiety, identify triggers, signs of early onset of anxiety, how to cope/de-escalate/avoid escalation · Priority actual & potential complications · Lack of social and occupational functioning, social withdrawal · Inability to meet personal daily needs · Sleep disturbances leading to physical exhaustion · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Anxiety is contagious — nurses have a role in maintaining calm when clients are escalating · De-escalation techniques may be effective in addressing rising anxiety · A variety of therapies, with medications, are often needed to address the complexity and chronicity of anxiety · Non-drug treatment techniques worth naming · Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) — first-line, often paired with medication; includes cognitive restructuring (replacing catastrophic thoughts with realistic ones) and a "worry ledger" (recording worries and the evidence for/against them) · Systematic desensitization — gradual, stepwise exposure to the feared stimulus paired with relaxation training · Implosion therapy (flooding) — direct, repeated exposure to the fear-provoking stimulus without a gradual buildup, often paired with anxiety-provoking imagery · Interoceptive conditioning — deliberately reproducing the physical sensations of a panic attack (e.g., via controlled hyperventilation or running stairs to induce tachycardia) so the client learns the sensation doesn't have to progress to a full attack · Thought-stopping — the client learns to interrupt a negative/anxious thought with a distracting stimulus (snapping a rubber band, an internal "stop" cue) until the thought can be controlled without it · Biofeedback — a device teaches the client to consciously control physiologic responses (heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, perspiration) tied to anxiety · Modeling/assertiveness training — the client observes appropriate behavior in the feared situation and practices standing up for themselves rather than responding passively or aggressively · Priority medications · Benzodiazepines — diazepam (Valium), alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam (Klonopin), chlordiazepoxide (Librium), clorazepate (Tranxene), oxazepam (Serax); oral or nasal for panic symptoms; increased potential for addiction and dependence — short-term or as-needed use only; client may become physically dependent and tolerant, may experience withdrawal symptoms; contraindicated in acute alcohol intoxication and narrow-angle glaucoma; monitor closely after each dose for a possible paradoxical disinhibitory (excitement) effect rather than calming, especially in older adults · Buspirone (Buspar) — oral anti-anxiety drug; takes 10–14 days (up to 3–4 weeks) to be effective, not for as-needed use; causes less sedation and rarely leads to dependence or tolerance the way benzodiazepines do, but still interacts with alcohol as a central nervous system depressant; contraindicated with concurrent MAOI therapy · SSRIs — sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro), fluoxetine (Prozac), fluvoxamine (Luvox), paroxetine (Paxil) — first-line for GAD, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and specific phobia adjuncts; take with food in the morning; therapeutic effect may take up to 4 weeks; never stop abruptly (see the Medications unit for the full class detail and the black-box suicidality warning) · SNRIs — venlafaxine XR (Effexor XR) and duloxetine (Cymbalta) — first-line alongside SSRIs for GAD and panic disorder; monitor blood pressure (can raise it at higher doses) · Beta-blockers — propranolol (Inderal), used off-label specifically for performance-type social anxiety (public speaking, auditions); NOT effective for generalized social anxiety; take the apical pulse for a full minute before administering, and hold for bradycardia · Alpha-2 agonist/ligand adjuncts — gabapentin (Neurontin) and pregabalin (Lyrica), used as first-line adjuncts particularly in social anxiety disorder · Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) — imipramine (Tofranil), clomipramine (Anafranil) — older, second-line option; anticholinergic and cardiac side-effect burden is higher than SSRIs/SNRIs · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Reassure the client that healing is a long process, and there may be times of regression · Encourage clients to maintain therapy and their medication regimen · Counsel clients that most antianxiety agents cause sedation and orthostatic hypotension · Ruling out organic causes and anxiety screening · Cardiac enzyme levels, troponin level, and thyroid studies help rule out organic causes of anxiety-like symptoms (myocardial ischemia, hyperthyroidism) before treating the presentation as a primary anxiety disorder; electrocardiography specifically rules out myocardial ischemia as the cause of chest tightness or palpitations. The USPSTF recommends anxiety screening for adults age 64 and younger — including pregnant and postpartum patients — who don't already have a diagnosed mental health disorder or recognized signs/symptoms of an anxiety disorder; there's no set optimal screening frequency, so clinical judgment about risk factors, comorbidities, and life events guides how often to re-screen. · Additional medication options for treatment-resistant GAD · Antipsychotics — aripiprazole (Abilify) or quetiapine (Seroquel), used as second-line augmentation for GAD that hasn't responded to first-line agents; carry an increased risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (including neuroleptic malignant syndrome and tardive dyskinesia) plus an increased risk of stroke, hypertension, and sudden cardiac death from conduction/electrophysiologic disruption — assess these clients closely and regularly · Hydroxyzine (Vistaril) or gabapentin (Neurontin) — alternatives to a benzodiazepine for short-term treatment of early SSRI-induced insomnia or agitation, specifically favored in a client with a history of substance use · Drug therapy for GAD typically continues for about 12 months once effective; instruct clients to avoid alcohol and limit caffeine intake throughout treatment, and to never discontinue a benzodiazepine abruptly — doing so can trigger life-threatening withdrawal · Therapeutic communication with the anxious client · Open-ended, exploratory responses do more for an anxious client than premature reassurance. "Tell me more about..." invites the client to keep talking instead of shutting the conversation down; reflecting the client's own words back ("You said it feels like something bad is about to happen — tell me more about that") signals that the nurse is listening without minimizing the fear. Avoid jumping straight to reassurance ("You'll be fine") or a closed yes/no question before the client has had a chance to describe what they're actually experiencing.

The obsession–anxiety–compulsion–relief cycle, plus the related-disorder family and medication card · OCD is a group of disorders characterized by obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors. Obsessions are intrusive thoughts that are recurrent and stressful, may be recognized as irrational, but are so powerful and repetitive that they cannot be ignored — a person may try to repress or ignore them, but "giving into" the obsession allows for stress relief. Compulsions are repetitive and ritualistic behaviors or mental acts that individuals feel driven or forced to perform, are completed to reduce the associated anxiety that is generated by the obsession, and a significant dread of a negative event exists if the compulsion cannot be carried out. DSM-5 groups OCD together with a related-disorder family that shares the same obsession/compulsion structure: · Body dysmorphic disorder — fixation on a perceived flaw in appearance (often minimal or unnoticeable to others) with repetitive checking, grooming, reassurance-seeking, or surgery-seeking behavior; onset is usually before age 18, and roughly 70% of clients report a history of teasing or bullying; no medication carries an FDA indication specifically for BDD, but SSRIs are used off-label alongside CBT · Hoarding disorder — persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of actual value, leading to clutter that congests living spaces; distinguished from ordinary collecting by disorganization and lack of pride in the items; frequently comorbid with depression, anxiety, and OCD itself; treated with CBT, motivational interviewing, skills training, and often an SSRI trial · Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and excoriation disorder (skin-picking) — repetitive hair-pulling or skin-picking despite repeated attempts to stop, resulting in noticeable hair loss or skin lesions · Substance/medication-induced obsessive-compulsive and related disorder , and obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition — obsessions, compulsions, or repetitive behaviors that developed during or after substance exposure or a diagnosed medical condition · The OCD cycle · Engaging in compulsive behaviors is stress-relieving, but only temporarily — which is exactly why the cycle repeats. Common compulsions include handwashing, checking, ordering, praying, counting, and repeating words silently, and may be directly related to obsessive thoughts (fear of contamination leading to repeated handwashing). OCD involves obsessions and compulsions that cause social and/or occupational dysfunction, and behaviors take up more than one hour per day. · The four symptom dimensions · OCD presentations cluster into four recognized symptom dimensions, and a client may show features of more than one at once: · Cleaning/contamination — fear of germs or contamination paired with excessive washing or cleaning rituals · Symmetry/counting — need for exactness, evenness, or a "just right" feeling, paired with ordering, arranging, counting, or repeating rituals · Forbidden or taboo thoughts — intrusive aggressive, sexual, or religious thoughts, often paired with mental rituals (silent praying, counting, reviewing) · Harm — fear of causing harm to self or others, paired with checking rituals (locks, stove, that no one was hurt) · OCD is equally common in males and females, affects roughly 2.3% of the general population, and usually begins gradually — adolescence/early adulthood in males, young adulthood in females. It's usually a chronic illness made more complex by a history of trauma, substance use, or a comorbid mood disorder (comorbid depression occurs in 20–60% of clients, and about 30% have a past or current tic disorder). It's associated with changes in the anatomy and physiology of the brain — hyperactivity in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit on imaging — along with serotonin and dopamine signaling abnormalities. In children specifically, a sudden, dramatic onset of OCD symptoms following a streptococcal infection (strep throat, scarlet fever) raises suspicion for PANDAS (pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections) — worth knowing as a pediatric red flag, though it is not the typical adult presentation. Cultural note: culturally prescribed rituals and practices (religious observance, mourning rituals) should not be mistaken for OCD unless they exceed what the person's culture prescribes, occur at times/places judged inappropriate by that culture, or interfere with social functioning. · Priority assessments/cues · Reports of ritualistic or compulsive behavior, obsessive thoughts, inability to meet basic needs or responsibilities · Level of anxiety using standardized scales · Level of anxiety when the client is unable to engage in OCD behaviors · Engaging in alternative coping strategies to replace ritualistic behaviors · Risk for suicide — up to half of clients with OCD report suicidal thoughts at some point; always screen directly, don't assume the ritualistic presentation rules it out · Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) — a self-rating questionnaire to assess severity of symptoms · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · No lab tests diagnose OCD — diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria (time-consuming obsessions/compulsions, more than one hour per day, causing significant distress or impairment, not attributable to a substance or another medical condition). · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Foster a trusting environment, reassure clients that they are safe, use open-ended questions · Stay with the client when in a panic or highly anxious · Use brief messages, stay calm, describe agency routines · Encourage slow, deep abdominal breaths · Decrease environmental stimuli · Manage hyperventilation — instruct the client to take several breaths in a paper bag, use sedation as needed · Explore sources of anxiety once the "attack" has subsided · Identify triggers or early onset of anxiety, how to deal with these including deep breathing, imagery, prayer, meditation, or exercise · Ensure basic needs (food, rest, hygiene) are met first — compulsive rituals routinely crowd these out · Do not interrupt a compulsive behavior unless it is unsafe — allow time for the ritual, but set limits on behaviors that would interfere with the client's physical well-being or safety · Implement a structured schedule of simple activities, games, or tasks that distracts from and limits time available for rituals; establish a written contract with the client to gradually decrease the frequency of compulsive behaviors and reinforce nonritualistic behavior · For specific OCD behaviors, consider use of controlled systematic desensitization (gradual exposure to stimuli) or implosion therapy (flooding with stimuli) · Exposure and response prevention (ERP) — the behavioral treatment of choice: the client is gradually exposed to the feared obsession-triggering stimulus while being coached to resist performing the compulsion. Used alone as first-line for mild-to-moderate OCD, combined with medication for moderate-to-severe OCD; effective in roughly half of mild-to-moderate clients · Explore coping strategies and anxiety-management methods to replace ritualistic behavior · The COPING mnemonic for nursing care · C oncerns and feelings discussed · O ffer a structured routine that allows time for rituals · P ractice thought-stopping skills · I nitiate a behavioral contract to decrease rituals and reward nonritualistic behavior · N urture effective problem-solving · G et the patient to perform relaxation techniques · Priority actual & potential complications · Substance use/abuse as self-medication · Generalized anxiety disorder · Major depressive disorder, risk for suicide · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Times of stress, such as illness or trauma, may cause a client to revert to OCD behaviors, requiring the nurse to assist with coping mechanisms or refer to psychiatric consultation or counseling · Provide methods to deal with stress including progressive muscle relaxation, yoga, exercise, music, meditation, imagery, prayer, or affirmations · Priority medications · SSRIs have been the first-line pharmacologic treatment for OCD for more than 30 years and are often dosed higher than for depression; five carry an FDA indication specifically for OCD — fluoxetine (Prozac), fluvoxamine (Luvox), paroxetine (Paxil), sertraline (Zoloft) , and the tricyclic clomipramine (Anafranil) ; side effects of the SSRIs include sleep disturbance, headache, and restlessness · Clomipramine — oral tricyclic antidepressant; may lower seizure threshold; side effects include orthostatic hypotension, sedation, sexual dysfunction · SNRIs and other TCAs are also used, generally as second-line or augmentation options when SSRIs alone are insufficient · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Assist in recognizing and averting rising anxiety levels that lead to OCD behaviors · Reinforce healthy coping mechanisms to replace ritualistic behavior · Teach the client and family about the nature of the illness, management of illness, and the need for ongoing counseling · DSM-5-TR insight specifiers · An OCD diagnosis carries an insight specifier, which matters clinically because it describes how believable the obsession feels to the client: good or fair insight (the client recognizes the OCD beliefs are probably or definitely not true), poor insight (the client thinks the OCD beliefs are probably true), and absent insight/delusional beliefs (the client is completely convinced the OCD beliefs are true). A specifier of "with poor" or "absent" insight does not by itself mean the client has a psychotic disorder — it describes conviction about the obsession, not a break from reality overall. · Delegating care for a client with OCD · When delegating to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP): encourage the client to participate in deciding the sequence of care delivery, allow ritualistic behaviors to run their course as needed, communicate with the client calmly even when the repetitive behavior is frustrating or delaying care, and maintain a safe, caring environment — do not rush the client through rituals or insist they abandon them just to stay on a fixed schedule

PTSD vs. acute stress disorder vs. adjustment disorder, and the full medication card · Trauma occurs in response to an extremely stressful and distressing experience that leads to emotional shock and incurs significant and long-lasting psychological effects. A trauma response may arise from child abuse and neglect, sexual violence, accidents, injuries, prolonged illness, or exposure to natural disasters, war, or poverty. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a stress response to a triggering event that is outside usual human experience and of significant magnitude, with diagnosis based on severity of symptoms, persistence of more than a month, and significant impact on social or occupational functioning. · PTSD vs. acute stress disorder vs. adjustment disorder · Acute stress disorder — symptoms similar to PTSD, but resolution occurs within one month: recurrent memories, distressing dreams, intense reactions, depression, dissociative symptoms, avoidance behaviors, hypervigilance or hyperarousal · Adjustment disorder — the triggering event is not as severe (such as failure, rejection, or divorce); the disorder is usually resolved within six months of the stressor, manifested as stress reactions to routine daily events, alterations in mood, difficulty coping, or altered relationships; ability to work and engage in social activities is retained; mood changes include tearfulness, feelings of hopelessness, nervousness, worry, restlessness; a history of conduct disorders — truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, fighting — may be present · Adjustment disorders, as well as PTSD, may occur across the lifespan · Individual response to trauma is influenced by the severity and scope of the event and the individual's ego-strength, temperament, coping resources, perception of the event, and previous experiences with stress. Symptoms may occur immediately post-trauma or may be delayed, and emotional reactions may include guilt, anger, and aggression. Based on history (or family observations), a client may exhibit a pattern of difficulty accepting change or ineffective coping skills. · Priority assessments/cues · General — standardized tools to assess levels of depression and anxiety; risk for harm to self or others; elicit history from family and others as needed; substance use and abuse as a means to numb emotional response; nature of the triggering event, client's role in the event, timeframe of event, and any current effects of the event · PTSD-specific — impact of trauma on self-care, relationships, work engagement in activities; determine event causing symptoms, client's role in event, current factors related to event; intrusive memories, dissociative reactions (flashbacks), nightmares, sleep disturbances; high level of anxiety or arousal (hypervigilance); avoidance behaviors of experiences or stimuli (noises, reminders of event); comorbid mood or substance use disorders; support systems, other coping mechanisms · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Serum alcohol levels and drug toxicology screens. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Encourage safety-related behaviors and provide precautions as needed · Create a non-threatening environment with consistent caregivers · Ensure a therapeutic, trusting relationship · Stay with the client during flashbacks, nightmares, and intrusive memories · Encourage communication about experiences and emotions at the client's pace · Explore coping mechanisms and support systems — discuss coping mechanisms that were effective before the trauma · Address the client's feelings of guilt or self-blame · Promote healthy grieving (see the Grief priority exemplar) · Allow for expression of pent-up anger, guilt, and frustration, including physical exercise, walking, work, and creative expression (artwork, poetry) · Use role-play to act out stressful situations and potential responses · Refer to trauma-informed therapy, including cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure therapy, group and family therapy, self-help groups, crisis intervention, and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (allows the client to process traumatic events while focusing on external stimuli) · Consider the impact of trauma on victims and the need for increased awareness and resources in the community, advocating for clients with these experiences as they work through their trauma · Priority actual & potential complications · Suicide, harm to self or others · Debilitating social and/or occupational dysfunction · Substance use disorder · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Need for trauma-informed care — nurses must recognize the prevalence of trauma-related incidents and identify signs/symptoms in clients to avoid retraumatizing · Some clients experience a variety of traumas in their lives, and nurses should employ sensitive and astute assessments to ensure clients receive needed assistance · Priority medications · Paroxetine — oral SSRI antidepressant; may take 1–4 weeks to be effective · Amitriptyline — oral tricyclic antidepressant · Carbamazepine — oral anticonvulsant; reduces intrusive thoughts and flashbacks · Cannabinoids — oral; may help to calm the client, control symptoms, and stimulate appetite; clients with PTSD may have low endogenous cannabinoid levels · Prazosin — oral antihypertensive used to manage recurrent nightmares · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Educate the family on the nature of traumatic responses, methods of intervention, and ongoing supports · Community resources to provide support, including self-help groups, peer counseling, education, and protective respite care · Reinforce past coping mechanisms that have proven effective · Provide teaching about relaxation techniques and anxiety-reducing strategies · DSM-5-TR symptom clusters · PTSD diagnosis requires symptoms from four clusters, all persisting more than one month: intrusion (recurrent distressing memories, nightmares, flashbacks, and intense physiological reactivity to reminders of the trauma); avoidance (avoiding thoughts, feelings, people, places, or conversations associated with the trauma); negative alterations in cognition and mood (persistent negative beliefs about self or others, distorted self-blame, detachment from others, and an inability to feel positive emotions); and alterations in arousal and reactivity (irritability or angry outbursts, hypervigilance, an exaggerated startle response, sleep disturbance, and poor concentration). A client's flat refusal to discuss the traumatic event at all is itself a classic avoidance symptom, not just reluctance to talk. · Trauma-focused therapies, named · Prolonged exposure therapy — repeated, gradual, guided recounting of the traumatic memory (in imagination and in real-life avoided situations) until it no longer triggers overwhelming distress · Cognitive processing therapy (CPT) — a structured cognitive-behavioral variant that targets the client's distorted beliefs about the trauma (self-blame, safety, trust) through written accounts and guided questioning · Responding to trauma disclosure — a therapeutic communication example · When a client discloses fear or avoidance tied to trauma — for example, a sexual assault survivor stating, "I am going to be afraid to go out by myself again, especially at night" — the priority is open-ended exploration, not premature reassurance. "Tell me more about being afraid to go out at night" invites the client to keep talking; jumping straight to "You'll be fine" or "You must resume your normal activities as soon as possible" shuts the conversation down and can feel dismissive. The same principle applies to any client minimizing or refusing to discuss a traumatic event — stay curious and unhurried rather than pushing for details or offering false reassurance. · A combat veteran with new-onset PTSD may present with irritability, sudden anger over minor things, sleep disturbance, frequent nightmares, restlessness, episodes of "zoning out" (dissociation), increased alcohol use, decreased appetite, low energy, and statements reflecting hopelessness or worthlessness ("I don't deserve a happy life") — often with grossly normal vital signs. Any statement suggesting hopelessness should trigger a direct suicide risk screen even when the client denies current ideation.

The full spectrum of psychotic disorders, four symptom clusters, and the complete medication card · Schizophrenia spectrum disorders are a spectrum of disorders with a variety of etiological factors (biological, psychological, and environmental), with a wide variety of treatments that must be tailored to the individual and their symptoms. They're characterized by thoughts and experiences not grounded in reality, disorganized thoughts, speech, or behaviors, and difficulty with daily activities and relationships. This spectrum includes schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders — delusional disorders, psychotic disorder induced by a medical condition/medication/substance use, brief psychotic disorder, and schizophreniform disorder. · The rest of the psychotic-disorder spectrum · Delusional disorders — clients have delusions (fixed, false beliefs) without bizarre behaviors, and are not severe enough to impair functioning: erotomanic (belief that high-status people are in love with them), grandiose (delusions of grand status, personal worth, and talents), jealous (perseverating that a sexual partner is unfaithful), persecutory (belief that they are being mistreated or spied on), somatic (delusions that the body is changing or diseased), reference (belief that ordinary events, objects, or other people's behavior have special personal meaning directed at them), nihilistic (belief that a catastrophe is about to occur), control (belief that an outside force, group, or person controls their thoughts, feelings, or behavior — including thought withdrawal , belief that thoughts are being removed, and thought insertion , belief that outside thoughts are being placed in their mind). Unlike schizophrenia, day-to-day functioning and cognition often stay intact outside the delusion itself — the presentation can look almost unremarkable except for the fixed false belief · Schizoaffective disorder — a combination of schizophrenia's psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and/or delusions, disorganized thinking) together with a mood episode (depression or mania) in the same illness; prognosis tends to fall between schizophrenia and a mood disorder alone, and treatment combines an antipsychotic with an antidepressant or mood stabilizer depending on the mood component · Psychotic disorder induced by medical condition, medication, or substance use · Brief psychotic disorder — sudden onset of psychotic symptoms lasting less than one month, with return to previous level of functioning · Schizophreniform disorder — symptoms of schizophrenia accompanying an episode of major depression and/or mania, not associated with substance use or another medical condition · Schizophrenia affects about 1% of the population; onset is in late adolescence and early adulthood, and may begin in childhood. It's a progressive disease with exacerbations and a chronic course, with phases including premorbid, prodromal, active (psychotic/acute schizophrenic episodes), and residual. Suicide is highly prevalent — one-third of clients have suicidal ideations, and 10% die from suicide. · Genetics and the dopamine hypothesis · Schizophrenia runs strongly in families: in monozygotic (identical) twins, the concordance rate is 40–50% — if one twin develops it, the other has roughly a 50% chance — versus only 10–15% in dizygotic (fraternal) twins, confirming a substantial genetic component layered on top of environmental triggers (prenatal infection, birth complications, malnutrition before birth). The leading biochemical explanation is the dopamine hypothesis : hyperactivity of dopamine in the brain's limbic regions produces positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, agitation), while hypoactivity of dopamine in the prefrontal cortex produces negative symptoms (flattened affect, anhedonia, executive-function deficits). This single hypothesis explains why antipsychotics — which block dopamine — are much better at controlling positive symptoms than negative ones. · Onset by age and sex · The first psychotic episode typically occurs earlier in males (18–25 years) than in females (25–35 years). Late-onset schizophrenia (LOS) refers to onset after age 40, and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis (VLOSLP) refers to onset after age 60 — both are more common in women, and medications in this older population are typically dosed more conservatively to reduce the risk of falls, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and confusion. · Disease course and phases · The illness moves through four phases: the prodromal phase (months to years before the first hospitalization, marked by withdrawal, peculiar behavior, and declining hygiene/functioning), the acute phase (florid psychotic symptoms, often triggered by a stressful event, frequently requiring hospitalization), stabilization (symptoms begin to diminish, often supported by outpatient or partial hospitalization), and the residual phase (positive symptoms mostly resolve, but negative symptoms like blunted affect and impaired role functioning may become more pronounced). The overall course is classified as mild (adherent to treatment, only 1–2 major relapses by age 45), moderate (inconsistent adherence, several relapses, symptoms persisting between relapses), or severe/unstable (nonadherent, frequent relapses, significant ADL impairment) — adherence to the drug regimen is the single biggest driver of which course a given patient follows. · Psychosis vs. schizophrenia — the key distinction · This distinction is tested constantly because the two terms are so often confused. Psychosis is an episode of detachment from reality — it is a symptom that can be caused by sleep deprivation, substance use, another mental illness, or a medical condition, and it can be temporary. Schizophrenia is a specific, chronic mental illness for which psychotic symptoms (delusions and hallucinations) are only two of the possible diagnostic features, alongside disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms — and the diagnosis requires the six-month duration criterion. In short: every case of schizophrenia involves psychotic-type symptoms, but not every episode of psychosis is schizophrenia. · The DSM-5-TR two-symptom rule — and its one-symptom exception · Diagnosis formally requires two or more of the following, present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period: delusions, prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms. There's a notable exception worth knowing: only one of these symptoms is required if the delusions are bizarre (no possibility of being true), or if the hallucinations consist of a single voice issuing a running commentary on the client's behavior, or two or more voices conversing with each other — these three specific presentations are considered so characteristic of schizophrenia that they count double. · The four symptom clusters · Cluster | What it includes · Positive symptoms | Delusions; hallucinations (distorted sensory perceptions); disorganized speech, including echolalia (echoing a previous word), incoherence, neologisms (new language), loose associations, "word salad" (speech or topics that do not make sense); disorganized behavior, including hyperactivity, hostility, agitation, catatonia, waxy flexibility, posturing, pacing, rocking, abnormal eye movement — symptoms that add something abnormal to experience · Negative symptoms | Lack of speech, intonation, or gesturing; anhedonia, apathy, asociality, alogia, avolition (inability to move or initiate activity); poor hygiene, lack of self-care — symptoms that take something away from normal functioning · Cognitive symptoms | Disorganized speech (a sign of disorganized thinking); concrete thinking (inability to think abstractly); anosognosia (the client does not believe they are ill); impairments possible in short-term memory, attention, information processing, and/or executive functioning · Affective symptoms | Mood labile or incongruent with circumstances; flat or blunted affect, inappropriate or bizarre affect · "Positive" and "negative" here don't mean good and bad — they describe whether the symptom adds an abnormal experience (positive) or removes a normal one (negative). Negative, cognitive, and affective symptoms are the most difficult to treat, and may not respond to medication — this matters clinically because antipsychotic medications are generally far more effective against positive symptoms, which is why a well-medicated patient can still struggle significantly with motivation and social withdrawal even once hallucinations are controlled. Symptoms affect social functioning, relationships, quality of life, and the ability to perform ADLs and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). · Speech and thought vocabulary — the exam-favorite word list · ★ marks terms that show up directly in this section's own symptom-cluster breakdowns for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder — confirmed course-exemplar content, not just this glossary. · Term | Meaning · ★ Flight of ideas | Rapid, continuous flow of speech that jumps from topic to topic, with some thread of connection that's hard to follow — classically a manic-state finding as well · ★ Word salad (schizophasia) | Illogical, random word groupings with no discernible meaning · ★ Neologisms | Made-up words that have meaning only to the client · ★ Loose associations | Haphazard, illogical shifting from one topic to another with no logical connection between them · ★ Echolalia | Pathological, parrot-like repetition of another person's words or phrases · ★ Pressured speech | Speech that feels forced out rapidly, as if the words can't come fast enough · ★ Waxy flexibility | A limb or the body stays in whatever position it's placed, as if made of wax · ★ Anosognosia | The client lacks awareness or insight that they are ill at all — distinct from simple denial · ★ Anhedonia | Loss of interest or pleasure in activities that were previously enjoyable — a core negative symptom · ★ Avolition | Lack of motivation or drive to initiate and follow through on goal-directed activity — a core negative symptom · ★ Alogia | Poverty of speech — reduced speech output or content, speaking little even when prompted · ★ Apathy | Lack of feeling, emotion, interest, or concern · ★ Asociality | Lack of interest in, or withdrawal from, social relationships and interaction · ★ Catatonia | Marked psychomotor disturbance — ranges from stupor/immobility to excessive, purposeless motor activity · ★ Posturing | Voluntarily assuming and holding an inappropriate or bizarre body position for an extended time · ★ Incoherence | Speech that is disorganized and largely incomprehensible, lacking a logical connection between words or phrases · ★ Clang association | Rhyming or sound-alike words strung together with no logical connection ("It's the rain, train, pain") · ★ Tangentiality | Wandering off in a new direction before ever reaching or completing the original point · Echopraxia | Pathological repetition/mimicking of another person's movements · Thought blocking | Sudden interruption/cessation of a thought mid-sentence, followed by an unrelated new thought · Circumstantiality | Getting caught up in excessive, unnecessary detail before finally getting to the point · Confabulation | Filling a memory gap with a fabricated but believed-true detail, to preserve self-esteem — classically seen in Korsakoff psychosis · Perseveration | Persistent repetition of the same word or idea in response to different questions · Mutism | Absence of verbal speech altogether · Religiosity | Excessive, often disorganized preoccupation with religious ideas · Verbigeration | Purposeless, stereotyped repetition of words or phrases · Magical thinking | Belief that one's own thoughts or wishes can control other people or outside events · Thought broadcasting | A Schneiderian first-rank delusion: the belief that one's own thoughts are audible to others or are being transmitted/broadcast outward, distinct from thought withdrawal or thought insertion · Priority assessments/cues · Client history helps determine progression of symptoms: frequency and severity of psychotic episodes, current medications and level of compliance, suicidal ideation and previous attempts, comorbid illnesses including physical illnesses, substance use, anxiety, and depression, and learning and support needs. · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Complete blood count (CBC) — neutropenia · Metabolic panel — physical conditions · Serum alcohol levels and drug toxicology screens · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · General management includes medications with therapy (individual, group, family, behavioral, assertive community) to enhance social skills and self-care; acute phase focuses on client safety until medications manage signs and symptoms; stabilized phase focuses on client/family education needs and ensuring effectiveness of medications; maintenance phase focuses on adherence to medications and preventing relapse · Interventions for self-directed violence — frequent, irregularly timed observations, suicide precautions, one-on-one supervision, no harmful objects in environment, investigate for suicidal ideations or plans, develop a no-suicide contract if appropriate · Interventions for other-directed violence — low stimulus environment, promote communication, increased supervision, de-escalation, distraction, use seclusion and restraints only as a last resort · Interventions for hallucinations — assess content, but do not reinforce perceptions (state inability to see, hear, or sense what the client is experiencing, use words such as "the voices" to differentiate them from reality), avoid touch, focus on client emotions or needs, distract/engage in activities, promote reality testing by providing evidence to discredit hallucinations, discuss association between stress and hallucinations, teach clients to use voice dismissal (verbally counter hallucinations) · Interventions for delusions — assess content, promote trusting relationships with consistent caregivers, avoid touch, avoid whispering or laughing around the client (may suspect it is about them), orient to surroundings, promote reality testing but do not argue, focus on underlying needs, provide packaged or home foods if the client is suspicious of agency foods (client may also suspect foods from home) · Interventions for relationships — encourage hygiene, promote self-care, develop a toileting schedule, encourage independence and decision-making as appropriate · Worked example: therapeutic responses to hallucinations and delusions · The general rule — validate the feeling, never the content — becomes easier to apply with concrete phrasing. In each case, the nurse acknowledges that the sensation or belief is real to the client , states their own perception honestly without arguing, and keeps the client's safety and trust intact: · Client: "The voices tell me you are trying to kill me." Nurse: "I know the voices are telling you that, but I do not believe that, and I have your best interest in mind — I am trying to keep you safe." · Client: "I believe I am being poisoned." Nurse: "You are not being poisoned, although I know that belief feels very real to you." (A concrete follow-up intervention: offer food in sealed, unopened containers the client can open themselves, so they can see for themselves that it hasn't been tampered with.) · Client: "I have bugs crawling all over my body." Nurse: "I'm standing right here, and I don't see any bugs on your body, although I know you feel them. Let's go to the day room for a while." — pairing a calm reality statement with a distraction/redirection · Client: "I smell a fire, I know you said there isn't one, but I smell it." Nurse: "We've checked — the fire alarms and sprinklers aren't going off, and I don't smell a fire, although I know that sensation is real to you." · Client: "I stopped taking my medications because they're poison." Nurse: "The medications are actually meant to help you feel better, although I understand that belief feels real to you right now." · Two response patterns to avoid: don't argue or try to logically disprove the hallucination/delusion, and don't pretend to see or hear what the client describes just to smooth over the conversation — both damage trust. Also avoid questions that could reinforce the belief that the voices are an external, independent presence (for example, asking a client whether the voice "sounds like" a specific deceased relative feeds the idea that the voice is a real outside entity rather than a symptom). · Medication administration specifics · Confirm the medication is actually swallowed and not being "cheeked" (held in the cheek to spit out later) — a common way a nonadherent or suspicious client appears to be taking medication without actually doing so · Obtain a baseline white blood cell count and a baseline blood pressure before starting clozapine specifically, in addition to the ongoing neutropenia/myocarditis monitoring already covered above · Physical and mental status findings on assessment · Beyond the symptom clusters above, a few specific findings show up on exam and history: decreased emotional expression or social awkwardness, unusually long pauses before answering questions, right-left confusion, and an inability to identify objects by touch or numbers traced on the skin. A disturbed wake-sleep cycle and declining academic, social, and interpersonal functioning are also common findings in the history leading up to diagnosis. · Priority actual & potential complications · Total social withdrawal and lack of participation in society · Depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, substance use disorder · Side effects of medications — metabolic disorders, neurological damage · Frequent relapses associated with poor outcomes, leading to longer hospitalizations, higher costs, and greater disruptions to family and personal life · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Be vigilant for clients who may be at risk for self- or other-directed harm · Evaluate and treat for extrapyramidal symptoms — treatment may include changing the psychotropic medication, reducing the dose, or adding an anticholinergic agent · Ensure a holistic, family approach to prevent caregiver role strain, abuse, neglect, and abandonment · Priority medications · Chlorpromazine — oral typical antipsychotic; risk for extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonic reaction, akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), sedation, gynecomastia, metabolic syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome · Risperidone — oral atypical antipsychotic; encourage water or hard candy for dry mouth, may cause nausea and vomiting; risk for metabolic side effects, seizures, sexual dysfunction · Clozapine — oral atypical antipsychotic; monitor for neutropenia and myocarditis; risk for metabolic side effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic toxicity · Benztropine/diphenhydramine — oral anticholinergics to decrease extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS); increased anticholinergic effects: sedation, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Schizophrenia is chronic — importance of compliance with medications and therapy to reduce relapses and prolong functionality · Smoking increases metabolism of antipsychotic drugs — refrain from smoking or adjust dosage accordingly · Caution with activities, operating equipment, or work tasks due to orthostatic hypotension and sedation · Maintain stable weight, sleep schedule, and stress-reduction activities · Photosensitivity — importance of sunscreen · Managing hallucinations and delusions by reducing stress and stimulation, using activities or other stimuli to distract or compete with sensory experiences, reality testing techniques, talking with a trusted friend or family member · Support gr

Typical vs. atypical, and the emergency you can't miss · Antipsychotic medications fall into two broad categories that differ in both their symptom coverage and their side effect profile. · Typical (conventional/first-generation) antipsychotics · Typical antipsychotics work by blocking postsynaptic dopamine receptors and are effective primarily against positive symptoms. Because of their side-effect burden, they've generally been replaced by atypicals as first-line therapy over the past decade, though a patient already stable and tolerating one may be kept on it. Their signature adverse effect is extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) — caused by dopamine blockade in motor pathways rather than just the limbic system: · Dystonia — prolonged, repetitive muscle contractions causing twisting or jerking movements, especially of the face, tongue, neck, and back, including abnormal/involuntary upward eye deviation and laryngeal spasm that can cause respiratory distress; occurs in about 5% of clients within days of starting a typical antipsychotic — the earliest-appearing EPS · Parkinsonism (drug-induced) — bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, shuffling gait, stooped posture, flat/masked facies, tremors, and drooling; may emerge anywhere from 1 week to several months after starting the drug · Akathisia — subjective restlessness, an inability to sit or stand still, and pacing/rocking; occurs in about 20% of clients taking typical antipsychotics, also early in the course of treatment · EPS is treated with benztropine or diphenhydramine , both anticholinergic medications that counteract the movement side effects. High-potency typicals (haloperidol) carry the highest EPS risk; low-potency agents (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) are more sedating/anticholinergic and more likely to cause orthostatic hypotension, but carry less EPS risk. Examples: chlorpromazine, fluphenazine, haloperidol (Haldol), loxapine, molindone, perphenazine, pimozide, thioridazine, thiothixene, trifluoperazine. · Tardive dyskinesia · A distinct, delayed-onset movement disorder from long-term antipsychotic use (typical or atypical): repetitive, involuntary, purposeless movements — grimacing, rapid eye blinking, tongue protrusion/rolling/smacking, lip puckering/sucking/chewing motions, and rapid movements of the hands, arms, legs, and trunk. It develops later in treatment than the other EPS types — in roughly 20–30% of clients who've taken typical antipsychotics for more than a year — and tends to be more severe in older adults and more prevalent among clients who smoke (smoking speeds metabolism of the medication). Symptoms may resolve or may become permanent even after the drug is stopped, which is why early recognition matters. · Management options beyond switching agents or lowering the dose include adding a benzodiazepine (helps akathisia, dystonia, and TD), a beta blocker (akathisia and TD), or a calcium channel blocker (TD); emerging options studied for TD specifically include vitamin E, clozapine, tetrabenazine (also used in Huntington disease), and amantadine. · Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics · Atypical antipsychotics cover both positive and negative symptoms (the "+/-") by combining dopamine blockade with increased serotonin activity, and as a class produce far fewer EPS/motor side effects and little to no prolactin elevation. Many atypical antipsychotic generic names end in "-pine" or "-done," a pattern that's useful for quickly recognizing the drug class on an exam or a medication list. Examples: aripiprazole (Abilify), asenapine (Saphris), brexpiprazole (Rexulti), cariprazine (Vraylar), clozapine (Clozaril), iloperidone (Fanapt), lurasidone (Latuda), olanzapine (Zyprexa), paliperidone (Invega), quetiapine (Seroquel), risperidone (Risperdal), ziprasidone (Geodon). · One atypical agent deserves a specific safety flag: clozapine can cause agranulocytosis — a dangerous drop in white blood cells (and neutrophils specifically) — which is why patients on clozapine require regular WBC/ANC monitoring throughout treatment; caught early, it's usually reversible. Clozapine also carries rare risk of cardiomyopathy and myocarditis, and should be used with extreme caution in older adults with dementia-related psychosis due to cardiovascular risk. Across the atypical class as a whole, the tradeoff for fewer motor side effects is metabolic syndrome — dyslipidemia, weight gain/obesity, hypertension, and hyperglycemia/new-onset diabetes — so baseline and ongoing metabolic monitoring (weight, glucose, lipids) is standard of care. · Long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotics · Several antipsychotics are available as long-acting injectable (LAI/depot) formulations given intramuscularly on a biweekly-to-monthly schedule, including aripiprazole, fluphenazine, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone (both 4-week and 12-week versions), and risperidone. The clinical advantage is medication adherence: a patient who struggles to take a daily pill, or who has a history of stopping medication once symptoms improve, maintains steadier drug levels with an LAI, which helps prevent relapse, rehospitalization, and the difficult-course trajectory that comes with inconsistent treatment. · Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) · NMS is a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic medications, marked by high fever, confusion, extremely rigid muscles, and altered consciousness (progressing to seizures if untreated) — it can occur hours to months after starting the drug or increasing the dose. Risk rises in clients who are agitated, fatigued, or dehydrated at the time they receive an antipsychotic. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate discontinuation of the antipsychotic and supportive medical treatment — recognizing the fever-plus-rigidity pattern quickly is what separates a good outcome from a fatal one. · NMS is classically remembered by four cardinal signs : hyperthermia (high fever), rigidity (extreme muscle rigidity), autonomic instability (tachycardia/dysrhythmias, blood pressure swings, diaphoresis), and altered mental status . Additional findings can include seizures and rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown). Left untreated, NMS can progress to renal failure, respiratory failure, or coma. Management: stop the antipsychotic immediately, apply a cooling/hypothermia blanket and aggressive IV hydration, and give supportive medications such as dantrolene (a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant), benzodiazepines, and antipyretics. · Memory jogger for antipsychotic/schizophrenia treatment goals overall: PRESSURE — Psychiatric medications administered properly and monitored, Realistic perceptions and self-expectations developed, Environmental situations managed effectively, Safety needs addressed, Self-care performed adequately, Use of community resources on an ongoing basis, Relationships developed and sustained, Establishment and maintenance of family involvement in care.

Three categories, ten types — where borderline and antisocial fit in the bigger picture · A personality disorder is the deviation of individual traits or characteristics from cultural norms or mores that is inflexible, impairs functioning, and contributes to dysfunctional behaviors. Causation is multifactorial, with both physiological and psychological influences. DSM-5 recognizes 10 types, officially grouped into three named clusters — know the cluster names themselves, since exam questions often test "which cluster" rather than the specific diagnosis. Personality disorders affect an estimated 12% of the U.S. population; some (antisocial, borderline) tend to soften in intensity by middle age, while others (obsessive-compulsive, schizotypal) tend to become more pronounced with age. · Cluster | Behavior pattern | Types · Cluster A | Odd or eccentric | Paranoid (pervasive distrust/suspicion of others' motives), schizoid (detached, indifferent to relationships, restricted emotional expression), schizotypal (odd thinking/speech, magical thinking, eccentricity — shares some features with schizophrenia but is a distinct diagnosis) · Cluster B | Emotional, dramatic, erratic | Antisocial (disregard for rights of others, deceit, lack of remorse), borderline (unstable relationships/mood/self-image, impulsivity, fear of abandonment), histrionic (excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, seductive/theatrical), narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy) · Cluster C | Anxious or fearful | Avoidant (social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to criticism), dependent (excessive need to be taken care of, difficulty making independent decisions), obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (perfectionism, rigidity, preoccupation with control and rules — distinct from OCD itself: no true obsessions/compulsions, and the person often sees the traits as correct rather than distressing) · General DSM-5 diagnostic criteria (applies across all 10 types) · Every personality disorder is diagnosed against the same general framework, then further distinguished by disorder-specific criteria: an enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates markedly from the person's culture, showing up in two or more of cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, or impulse control; the pattern is inflexible and pervasive across personal and social situations; it causes clinically significant distress or impairment; it's stable, long-standing, and traceable back to adolescence or early adulthood; and it isn't better explained by another mental disorder or by the physiologic effects of a substance or medical condition. In other words: patterns, not moments — a personality disorder doesn't develop overnight and isn't diagnosed off a single interaction. · Priority assessments/cues (shared across personality disorders) · Impaired social relationships, changes in cognition and affect, poor impulse control, emotional dysregulation · Symptoms must be significant enough to impair functioning to meet the diagnostic threshold — individuals may manifest some characteristics of personality disorders at some point in their lives without meeting that bar · Poor impulse control often manifests as acting out to manage internal pain — physical/verbal attacks, self-injurious behavior, manipulation, substance misuse, promiscuity, and suicide attempts · Impaired judgment, impaired reality testing (often with projection of the person's own feelings onto others), impaired self-perception, and an impaired stimulus barrier (poor attention span, excessive response to noise/light, agitation) · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Tests to determine underlying physiological conditions — a genuine personality change can be the first sign of a neurologic, endocrine, or other medical illness (a frontal lobe tumor, for example), so this must be ruled out before attributing the presentation to a personality disorder · Serum toxicology if drugs or alcohol are suspected — intoxication can mimic personality-disorder features · General nursing interventions (apply across the personality-disorder family) · Maintain safety against self-destructive behaviors; ensure the whole care team responds consistently to acting-out behavior so the client can't play one staff member's response against another's · Allow the client to make choices and be as independent as possible; encourage discussing feelings rather than acting them out, and consider a feelings journal · Discuss expectations, responsibilities, and the consequences that follow specific behaviors; make clear that harm to self, others, or property is unacceptable · Develop a written safety or behavioral contract with the client · Identify and name splitting behavior directly when it occurs · Encourage participation in group activities and praise nonmanipulative behavior; set and maintain limits to reduce manipulative behavior; remove the client from group situations where attention-seeking behavior is escalating · Provide realistic praise for positive behaviors in social situations · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Nurses may encounter clients with personality disorders in any clinical setting, not only psychiatric units · Management of clients with personality disorders may pose significant challenges to health care professionals · Personality disorders are often chronic, characterized by exacerbations and remissions · Common treatment modalities across the personality-disorder family · No medications are FDA-approved to treat a personality disorder itself; drug therapy targets specific symptoms rather than the diagnosis. Across the 10 types, the medication classes that come up most are antidepressants (for depressive/anxious symptoms), anxiolytics (for acute anxiety), antipsychotics (for transient distortions in thinking, often in low doses), and mood stabilizers (for irritability and impulsivity). Therapy is the mainstay of treatment; the disorder-specific lessons that follow name the psychotherapy approaches most associated with each diagnosis, but psychoanalytic/psychodynamic, group, cognitive, and behavioral therapies are all used across the cluster depending on the individual client. · The next two lessons work through the two Cluster B disorders most heavily tested — borderline personality disorder, organized around fear of abandonment, and antisocial personality disorder, organized around disregard for the rights of others — with their own specific assessments, interventions, and medication use.

Fear of abandonment as the organizing feature, plus the full care plan · Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is organized around one central, driving fear: fear of abandonment . Much of the behavior that looks confusing or contradictory from the outside — intense, unstable relationships, rapid swings between idealizing and devaluing the same person, impulsivity, and self-harming behavior — makes more sense once it's understood as an attempt (often unsuccessful and self-defeating) to manage that underlying fear. · Priority assessments/cues · Mood swings, a perpetual state of crisis, impulsivity · Depression, anger, acting out, agitation · Inability to be alone, unstable relationships · Splitting (all good/all bad), clinging/distancing behaviors · Self-destructive behaviors (substance abuse, overspending, self-harm, unsafe sexual behaviors) · Splitting, revisited · BPD is the disorder most classically associated with the defense mechanism of splitting, covered earlier in this section: seeing people as entirely good or entirely bad, with a single perceived slight capable of flipping someone from one category to the other. On an inpatient unit, this frequently shows up as a patient idealizing one staff member while devaluing another, which can fracture team consistency if the team isn't aware of the pattern and doesn't communicate about it. Splitting is understood as a primitive defense against the intolerable idea that the same person can be both loving and disappointing at once — collapsing that ambiguity into all-good or all-bad protects the client from the anxiety of holding both at the same time. · Epidemiology, causes, and risk factors · BPD occurs predominantly in females (up to 75% of diagnosed cases) and frequently coexists with other personality disorders, which can delay accurate diagnosis · Prevalence is roughly 10% in outpatient psychiatric populations and 20% in inpatient psychiatric populations — far higher than the general-population rate · Cause is largely unknown but is thought to be a combination of genetic factors, traumatic life experiences, and changes in the brain areas governing emotional regulation, impulsivity, and aggression · Key risk factors: a history of childhood physical, emotional, or sexual abuse and neglect, and having a parent diagnosed with a personality disorder · Physiologic theory points to frontal lobe dysfunction as a contributor to the impulsivity, cognitive inflexibility, poor self-monitoring, and perseveration seen in BPD · Nearly 6% of people with BPD die by suicide — the single most important complication to screen for · DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria · Diagnosis requires five or more of the following nine criteria: frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment; a pattern of unstable and intense relationships; unstable self-image or sense of identity; impulsivity in at least two potentially self-damaging areas (overspending, sex, substance use, reckless driving, binge eating); recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or threats, or self-mutilating behavior; wide mood swings — irritability or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days; chronic feelings of emptiness; inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger (frequent temper displays, constant anger, recurrent physical fights); and transient, stress-related paranoia or dissociation/loss of contact with reality. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Provide frequent and irregular client observations · Reinforce independence, decrease manipulation, rotate staff · Ensure a safe environment, remove objects that could harm self or others, establish a no-harm contract · Provide appropriate routes to ventilate anger and emotions, set limits on behavior · Explore sources of anger, potential for grief, explore fears · Ensure participation in counseling, reinforce counseling principles · Encourage appropriate ventilation of anger · During acute escalation, use medication, staff show of strength, and restraints as indicated · Set clear expectations with an attitude of acceptance, encourage and reward positive behaviors, ensure the client is aware of consequences of behavior violations · Promote development of personal insights · Ensure participation in counseling and the plan of care · Priority actual & potential complications · Harm to self or others · Poor social functioning, weak or lacking social relationships · Priority medications · No medications are FDA-approved to treat personality disorders — psychotropic medications may be used off-label to treat symptoms for mood stabilization. · Olanzapine — oral or intramuscular antipsychotic, antimanic agent to address mania; may become physically dependent and tolerant, with withdrawal if abruptly withdrawn · Fluoxetine — oral SSRI antidepressant · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Importance of ongoing adherence to medication and therapy/counseling — personality disorders are often chronic, characterized by exacerbations and remissions. · Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) · DBT is the psychotherapy most specifically developed for and studied in BPD, alongside other options such as cognitive behavior therapy, mentalization-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy. DBT combines individual therapy with skills-group training built around four skill modules: · Mindfulness — building the capacity to observe and describe one's own thoughts, emotions, and sensations nonjudgmentally, in the present moment, rather than being swept along by them · Distress tolerance — skills for getting through a crisis without making it worse (impulsive self-harm, substance use), when the situation can't be changed in the moment · Emotion regulation — identifying and naming emotions accurately and reducing vulnerability to intense mood swings · Interpersonal effectiveness — asking for what one needs, setting boundaries, and maintaining relationships and self-respect while doing so · Managing self-harm and parasuicidal behavior · Treat every episode of self-harm or suicidal gesture as clinically significant rather than dismissing it as purely attention-seeking — intent and lethality still have to be assessed each time · Institute safety precautions to prevent injury, and collaboratively develop a written safety plan that lists specific coping strategies and sources of support the client can use before acting on the urge · Assess and document scarring or physical findings from prior self-mutilation as part of the physical exam · Monitor anxiety level, use of coping strategies, impulsivity, and suicidal ideation on an ongoing basis, not only at admission · Respond matter-of-factly and consistently rather than with visible alarm or excessive reassurance, which can inadvertently reinforce the behavior as a way to obtain attention or care · Boundary- and limit-setting specifics · Establish clear boundaries at the outset of care and maintain them without exception — boundaries that shift erode trust and can be experienced by the client as further evidence of instability · State expectations and the consequences of violating them concretely and in advance, rather than reactively in the moment of a violation · Keep a clear treatment alliance between staff and client, and stay well-integrated with other services (therapist, case manager, prescriber) through a multidisciplinary approach — communicate and review the plan of care across services specifically to prevent manipulation and splitting · Nursing approach · Consistency across the entire care team is the single most protective nursing behavior with BPD: consistent limits, consistent responses to manipulative or testing behavior, and a team that communicates with each other so the patient can't (even unintentionally) play one staff member's interpretation against another's.

Charm on the surface, disregard for laws and norms underneath · Antisocial personality disorder sits in the same "emotionally charged" category as BPD, but the organizing feature is different: rather than fear of abandonment, it's a profound disregard for the rights of others, paired paradoxically with a surface charm that can make the underlying pattern easy to miss at first meeting. · Priority assessments/cues · Rage, anger, violence — may appear charming, cooperative · Poor at delaying gratification, deceitful, manipulative · Poor coping, replicating negative behaviors · Criminal behaviors, disregard for laws and norms · Profound lack of empathy, inability to feel guilt or remorse · Conduct disorder as a childhood precursor · Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18, but a diagnostic requirement behind it looks backward into childhood: evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. Conduct disorder involves a repetitive pattern of violating the basic rights of others or age-appropriate social norms — aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations (truancy, running away). A documented childhood or adolescent history along these lines is part of why a thorough history, not just the current presentation, matters for this diagnosis. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Reduce environmental stimuli, provide frequent and irregular observation of clients, ensure a safe environment · The same general de-escalation, limit-setting, and counseling-participation principles covered for personality disorders overall (see the Personality Disorders overview lesson) apply here as well · Managing manipulation and lack of remorse · Maintain firm, consistent limits stated in concrete, matter-of-fact terms, and follow through on stated consequences every time — inconsistency is what manipulation is designed to find and exploit · Avoid power struggles and debating the rules; state the limit once, calmly, and disengage rather than arguing the client's counterarguments point by point · Confront manipulative or deceitful behavior directly and without judgmental language, using specific observed behavior rather than character attacks · Do not rely on the client's expressed remorse or promises as evidence of behavior change — evaluate change by observed, sustained behavior over time instead · Keep the whole care team communicating so the client cannot play one staff member's response against another's (the same principle that prevents splitting in BPD applies here to manipulation) · Priority actual & potential complications · Harm to self or others · Altercations with law enforcement, incarceration · Legal and forensic context · Because disregard for laws and the rights of others is core to the diagnosis, clients with antisocial personality disorder are overrepresented in the criminal justice system, and nurses may encounter them in forensic or correctional psychiatric settings as well as general inpatient units. Maintaining a therapeutic, nonjudgmental stance while still holding firm boundaries is a documented challenge in these settings, since the same charm that complicates recognition on a general unit can also complicate the therapeutic relationship in a secure or forensic setting. · Priority medications · Lorazepam — oral, intramuscular, or intravenous benzodiazepine antianxiety agent to manage acute anxiety and distress; high potential for addiction and tolerance · Priority teaching/discharge needs · As with other personality disorders, importance of ongoing adherence to medication and therapy/counseling, and awareness that the disorder is often chronic with exacerbations and remissions. · The charming-but-manipulative presentation is what makes antisocial personality disorder genuinely risky to miss: a patient can be cooperative and likable with staff while showing a documented pattern of deceit, exploitation, and disregard for others outside the room — the profound lack of empathy and remorse is the feature to weigh, not the moment-to-moment charm.

Why addiction is a disease, not a choice — plus the standardized screening tools · Substance use disorder is the continued pathological use of a substance despite negative consequences — from impaired self-control, social and occupational functioning, to dangerous behaviors and physical side effects. Addiction describes the cycle of abuse, dependence, withdrawal, and relapse that often accompanies use of psychoactive substances or behaviors that activate the brain's reward or pleasure centers. Repeated substance use physically rewires the brain's dopamine reward pathway , so that the substance (or the associated cues) triggers dopamine release the way a natural reward normally would, while everyday sources of pleasure become comparatively less rewarding. This rewiring is a large part of why addiction is not simply a choice a person can reason their way out of once it's established, even though choices contributed to the initial use. There is also a documented familial and genetic component — a family history of addiction raises an individual's own risk independent of environment, alongside environmental and cultural etiological factors. · Key vocabulary: intoxication, tolerance, withdrawal · Intoxication is a state of euphoria, exhilaration, lethargy, or stupor that occurs due to substance ingestion, and may have physical and emotional dimensions. Tolerance occurs when greater amounts of a substance are needed to produce intoxication. Withdrawal describes the physical and emotional symptoms that occur after addictive substances are discontinued abruptly; symptoms vary depending on the substance used and may be life-threatening if not properly managed — client intake of the substance may need to be maintained rather than allowed to become intoxicated, specifically to prevent withdrawal symptoms. The breadth of symptoms depends on the substance used, the amount used, and the duration of usage. · Behavioral (process) addiction · Behavioral addiction results from uncontrollable patterns of behavior that continue despite adverse effects to financial status, relationships, or other functioning. Gambling addiction is the only behavioral addiction currently recognized in the DSM-5, though future editions may include shopping, sexual activity, gaming, or social media use.
