Behavioral addictions stimulate the same reward/pleasure pathways of the brain without the physiological effects of intoxication — withdrawal symptoms from a behavioral addiction are psychological rather than physical. · Standardized screening tools · CAGE — asking whether the client has ever felt a need to C ut down drinking, felt A nnoyed by others criticizing their drinking, felt G uilty about their drinking, or ever needed an E ye-opener drink in the morning (may be modified for substances other than alcohol) · Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test · Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST) · Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar) — covered in the Alcohol lesson · Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) — covered in the Opioids lesson · Stages: use, intoxication, withdrawal · Addiction is understood as a disease that moves through stages of use , intoxication , and withdrawal , each with its own clinical presentation and its own nursing priorities — assessing which stage a patient is in changes what the nurse watches for and how urgently they need to act, since withdrawal from some substances (alcohol and benzodiazepines in particular) can be medically dangerous or fatal, while withdrawal from others (opioids) is miserable but rarely life-threatening on its own. Potential for dual diagnosis with mental health disorders is common, so comorbid psychological disorders (mood disorders, PTSD, schizophrenia) are part of every substance use assessment. · The use-to-addiction spectrum · Beyond the use/intoxication/withdrawal stages above, it helps to think of substance involvement as a spectrum of increasing severity: use (intermittent, without adverse consequences) progresses to abuse (variable frequency, with some adverse consequences), which can progress to physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms occur on cessation, dose reduction, or antagonist administration) and/or psychological dependence (a subjective, felt need to keep using for the positive effects or to avoid negative ones). Addiction sits at the far end of this spectrum — a primary, chronic, neurobiological disease marked by loss of control and compulsive use despite ongoing harm, distinct from dependence alone. · Why the brain keeps seeking the substance · Chronic, prolonged stress alters the body's corticotropin-releasing factor and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis , and this alteration itself contributes to substance-seeking behavior — the brain undergoes adaptive changes as it tries to restore homeostasis, which is part of the neurobiological basis for why the reward-pathway rewiring described above is so difficult to reverse through willpower alone. · Screening tool score cutoffs worth memorizing · AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test) — a score greater than 8 indicates unhealthy alcohol use · CRAFFT — used specifically with adolescents and young adults; 2 or more affirmative answers suggests an alcohol use disorder · Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test, brief version — a score of 3 or higher suggests alcoholism · CAGE — 2 affirmative answers suggest an alcohol problem (see above) · Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST) — any score greater than 0 indicates a drug use disorder

CIWA-Ar, the legal BAL threshold, a five-phase withdrawal timeline, and disulfiram/naltrexone · Alcohol is the most commonly encountered substance in clinical practice, and its complications span nearly every organ system when use is chronic and heavy — peripheral neuropathy, alcoholic myopathy, alcoholic cardiomyopathy, esophagitis, gastritis, pancreatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and sexual dysfunction. · Severity grading — DSM-5's four symptom clusters · Alcohol use disorder is graded by how many symptoms are present across four clusters: impaired control (taking more than intended, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, excess time spent obtaining/using/recovering, intense craving), social impairment (failing role obligations, continuing use despite recurring problems, giving up activities), risky use (using in physically hazardous situations, continuing despite known harm), and pharmacologic dynamics (tolerance, withdrawal). 2–3 symptoms present = mild AUD; 4–5 = moderate; 6 or more = severe. · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Blood alcohol level — intoxication occurs between 100 and 200 mg/dL (long-term alcohol abuse may result in high blood alcohol levels without signs of intoxication, since tolerance shifts the dose-response curve) · Breathalyzer — in most states, 0.08% is the legal intoxication threshold while driving · Serum toxicology levels — detect other substances · Metabolic panel — nutritional deficits, organ dysfunction · Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar) — the standardized scoring tool used to objectively grade withdrawal severity and titrate symptom-triggered medication dosing; scored at regular intervals throughout the withdrawal course, not just once on admission · Major complications of alcohol addiction · Wernicke's encephalopathy / Korsakoff's psychosis — a thiamine (B1) deficiency-driven neurologic disorder causing confusion, ataxia, memory loss, lethargy, and stupor · Peripheral neuropathy, alcoholic myopathy, alcoholic cardiomyopathy, esophagitis, gastritis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, cirrhosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, sexual dysfunction · Fetal alcohol syndrome — for pregnant patients, alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause lasting physical and cognitive impairment (craniofacial abnormalities, developmental delays, learning disabilities, organ dysfunction) — no amount of alcohol has been established as safe during pregnancy, and nurses need to instruct pregnant clients to abstain · Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) · For sedatives/hypnotics/opioids taken concurrently — respiratory depression, cough suppression · For stimulants taken concurrently — myocardial infarction, cardiac dysrhythmias · Hospital complications — patients admitted for unrelated reasons who are also alcohol-dependent are at risk for unrecognized withdrawal during the hospital stay itself, which is why alcohol use history is a standard admission screening question · The alcohol withdrawal timeline · Alcohol withdrawal unfolds in a recognizable, time-based progression, and recognizing where a patient is on this timeline changes the urgency of the nursing response: · Timeframe | What to expect · ~6 hours | Anxiety, insomnia, possible seizures can begin · 12–24 hours | Auditory and visual hallucinations · 24–48 hours | Withdrawal symptoms intensify: shaking, heavy sweating · 48–72 hours | Delirium tremens (DTs): very high heart rate, elevated body temperature, seizures — this is the most dangerous window · 72+ hours | Illusions, racing heartbeat, high blood pressure, continued perspiration, high fever can persist · Delirium tremens is the single most dangerous point on this entire timeline — the combination of severe autonomic instability (heart rate, temperature, blood pressure) and seizure risk makes the 48–72 hour window the period of highest mortality risk in untreated alcohol withdrawal, which is exactly why patients with a heavy drinking history are monitored closely rather than simply left to "detox" unsupervised. The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar) is the standardized tool used to score withdrawal severity and titrate treatment along this exact timeline. · Priority interventions during withdrawal · Monitor vital signs and neurological status, reorient as needed · Remove potentially harmful objects from the environment, minimize stimulation · Seizure precautions, determine the need for restraints or security devices · One-on-one supervision as appropriate · Medications to control symptoms, intravenous fluids and electrolytes, vitamins · Maintain hygiene · Medications specific to alcohol use disorder · Disulfiram — oral alcohol deterrent; generates unpleasant symptoms (nausea/vomiting, dyspnea, confusion, headache) if alcohol is ingested, with severity based on the amount of alcohol and individual sensitivity; should not be started until after 24 hours of alcohol abstinence; instruct the client about alcohol hidden in selected over-the-counter medications and other substances · Naltrexone — oral opiate antagonist that blocks the effects of narcotics; treats both alcohol and heroin addiction · Vitamin supplementation — oral folic acid, thiamine, and multivitamins with long-term alcohol use, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy and correct nutritional deficits · Acute withdrawal management — the fuller medication picture · IV glucose and fluids containing thiamine and B-complex vitamins — corrects nutritional deficiencies and supports glucose metabolism; give thiamine before the glucose load whenever possible, since IV glucose given to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy · Furosemide (Lasix) — eases overhydration · Magnesium sulfate — reduces CNS irritability · Benzodiazepines (Ativan) — long-acting agents such as diazepam or short-acting agents such as lorazepam are the mainstay for controlling withdrawal; anticonvulsants, antiemetics, or antidiarrheals are added as needed for specific symptoms · Antipsychotics — used to control hyperactivity and psychosis if present · A withdrawal-specific physical exam cue · A patient describing a sensation of bugs crawling on the skin (formication) is a classic, testable physical exam cue for alcohol withdrawal specifically — worth recognizing alongside the tremor, diaphoresis, and hallucinations already covered on the timeline above.

t: Opioid Use Disorder, Withdrawal & Body Effects
x: Timeline, symptoms, and system-by-system impact · Opioid withdrawal follows a more predictable, dose-and-half-life-driven timeline than alcohol withdrawal, and while it is intensely uncomfortable, it is rarely life-threatening on its own the way alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal can be. · Opioid withdrawal timeline · Symptoms begin 6–12 hours after the last dose for short-acting opioids, or up to 30 hours after the last dose for long-acting opioids. Symptoms typically peak around 72 hours and include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, diarrhea, goosebumps, irritability or depressed mood, weakness, anxiety, insomnia, tachycardia, hypertension, and intense drug cravings — dependent-substance-specific symptoms are tracked with the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) , the opioid-specific counterpart to the alcohol-focused CIWA-Ar. · Nutritional support during opioid treatment · Nutritional support and a dietitian consult are part of the treatment plan, with protein limited and dietary sodium decreased if liver impairment exists from concurrent alcohol or hepatitis exposure, small frequent meals and non-irritating food provided if gastritis or esophagitis exists, and thiamine supplementation as indicated. · Effects of opioids on the body · System | Effect · Brain | Heavy use can cause sedation · Heart | Heart lining can become infected from contaminated heroin or crushed pills used intravenously · Blood | IV injection of heroin or crushed pills can cause veins to collapse · Lungs | Respiratory depression from slowed breathing — potentially fatal, and the primary mechanism of opioid overdose death · Digestive system | Slowing of GI motility results in significant constipation · Liver | Shared, infected needles can transmit hepatitis · Nervous system | Chronic use can increase sensitivity to pain over time · Immune system | Increased vulnerability to infection from reduced immune response · Respiratory depression is the line item that matters most in an emergency: it's the mechanism behind fatal opioid overdose, and it's exactly what naloxone (Narcan) is designed to reverse. · Physical exam cues that point to opioids specifically · Constricted (pinpoint) pupils — opiate use or withdrawal · Lacrimation (excess tearing) — opiate withdrawal · Rhinorrhea — opiate withdrawal (also seen with cocaine abuse) · Drooping eyelids — opiates or other CNS depressants · By contrast, dilated pupils point away from opioids and toward hallucinogens or amphetamines — a useful exam-cue contrast when the substance involved isn't yet known · A limit on what naloxone can do · It's worth stating plainly in the opioid context: naloxone reverses opioids only . It has no pharmacologic activity of its own beyond displacing opioids from their receptors, so it will not reverse respiratory depression caused by benzodiazepines or other sedatives. And because naloxone's duration of action can be shorter than that of the opioid it's reversing — especially with long-acting or high-potency opioids — a patient can slip back into respiratory depression after an initial response, which is why repeat dosing and continued monitoring, not a single dose and discharge, is the expectation.

Why abrupt discontinuation is dangerous · Benzodiazepines are highly effective for acute anxiety and seizure control, but they are also highly addictive, and abrupt discontinuation after regular use carries real medical risk — most seriously, seizures , including grand mal seizures. Benzodiazepines potentiate GABA, producing sedation, muscle relaxation, anti-anxiety, and anticonvulsant effects; the same class of drug acts as a hypnotic at high doses, an anxiolytic at moderate doses, and a sedative at low doses. Half-life ranges widely by agent, from about 4 to 20 hours. · Common benzodiazepine drug names · alprazolam (Xanax), chlordiazepoxide (Librium), clonazepam (Klonopin), diazepam (Valium), flurazepam (Dalmane), lorazepam (Ativan), midazolam (Versed), oxazepam (Serax), temazepam (Restoril), triazolam (Halcion). · Symptoms of benzodiazepine withdrawal · Grand mal seizures · Aches and pains · Abnormal body sensations · Delirium or detachment from reality · Muscle spasms · Anxiety and panic attacks · Insomnia · Nausea · Depression · This symptom list overlaps closely with alcohol withdrawal, which makes sense physiologically — both alcohol and benzodiazepines act on the same GABA neurotransmitter system, which is exactly why benzodiazepines are used medically to treat alcohol withdrawal (a controlled, tapered substitution rather than an abrupt stop), and why benzodiazepine withdrawal itself must also be tapered rather than stopped cold. · Withdrawal timeline and taper strategy · Withdrawal symptoms typically begin 1–4 days after the last dose — sooner with a shorter-acting agent, later with a longer-acting one — and can persist for weeks to months (occasionally a year or longer) in a minority of patients. The standard approach for a patient withdrawing from long-term, high-dose use is substitution and taper : a rapid-onset agent such as IV lorazepam or diazepam is given first to control acute symptoms, the patient is then switched to an equivalent dose of a long-acting oral agent (milder withdrawal profile), and that agent is tapered slowly — typically over 2–6 months . For milder withdrawal, non-cross-dependent anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine (Tegretol) or valproate (Depakote) have also been used successfully. · Flumazenil — use with caution · Flumazenil (Romazicon) , a GABA antagonist given IV, is the only specific benzodiazepine antidote and rapidly reverses sedation and respiratory depression. It's generally reserved for severe poisoning, however, because in a patient with chronic benzodiazepine dependence it can precipitate acute withdrawal and seizures — the same trade-off nurses anticipate with naloxone in opioid overdose. · Physical exam cues tied to benzodiazepines as a CNS depressant · Nystagmus — a classic exam finding in intoxication with CNS depressants (including benzodiazepines) or PCP · Drooping eyelids — seen with CNS depressant intoxication, including benzodiazepines, as well as with opiates

Two commonly under-covered substances on this course's own misuse ranking — withdrawal, complications, and cessation medications · Nicotine misuse · Nicotine withdrawal can last a month or longer, and cravings themselves may persist for six or more months after the last use — this is longer than most patients expect, and is worth setting realistic expectations around during teaching. · Nicotine withdrawal symptoms · Irritability and anxiety · Difficulty concentrating · Increased appetite and weight gain · Insomnia and restlessness · Depressed or dysphoric mood · Intense cravings for nicotine · FDA-approved smoking cessation medications · Non-nicotine medications — bupropion (Zyban) and varenicline (Chantix) · Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) — gum, transdermal patch, nasal spray, lozenges, inhaler; these deliver nicotine without the other harmful combustion byproducts in smoke, to ease withdrawal while the behavioral habit is broken separately · Behavioral interventions and nursing care · Remove environmental cues (cigarettes, lighters, ashtrays) from the home/immediate environment · Help the client develop healthier coping strategies and alternatives to the smoking habit itself, not just the nicotine craving · Build trigger awareness and enlist social support · Adjunctive measures — support groups, 12-step programs, biofeedback · Nursing interventions — assess readiness/motivation to quit before pushing cessation resources; administer NRT or prescribed cessation medication as ordered; monitor for withdrawal symptoms and for medication side effects (bupropion lowers seizure threshold; varenicline carries a neuropsychiatric-symptom warning); provide consistent encouragement and nonjudgmental support, since relapse is common and is part of the quitting process, not a failure to document punitively · Cannabis misuse · Cannabis contains two main active components with very different effects: THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is the psychoactive component responsible for the "high" and carries the addiction potential; CBD (cannabidiol) is non-psychoactive. Cannabis (medically or otherwise) is used to treat glaucoma, chronic pain, and epilepsy — this legitimate medical use is part of why assessing recreational vs. therapeutic use matters clinically. · Cannabis withdrawal · THC can remain detectable in the system for up to 30 days after last use in regular users, which is far longer than most other substances and is worth knowing for both withdrawal-timeline and drug-screening questions. Withdrawal symptoms include restlessness, irritability, decreased appetite, and sleep difficulties. · Cannabis misuse — complications · Short-term memory and learning impairment — the most commonly cited cognitive complication · Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome — cyclic, severe nausea and vomiting in chronic heavy users, classically relieved (temporarily) by hot showers · Respiratory irritation/chronic bronchitis symptoms — from smoked forms specifically, similar to tobacco smoke exposure · Increased psychosis risk in individuals with a predisposition to psychotic disorders · Dependence and amotivational features with heavy, sustained use · Cannabis intoxication — assessment findings · Wild/erratic behavior — hallucinations, impaired cognition, paranoia, spontaneous laughter · Euphoria · Elevated heart rate (tachycardia) · Distorted sense of time and self-perception · Decreased muscle tone, dry mouth · Treatment for acute cannabis intoxication is primarily supportive: a calm, low-stimulation environment, reassurance and reorientation (especially for paranoia or perceptual disturbance), monitoring vital signs, and treating specific symptoms (an antiemetic for nausea, benzodiazepines for severe agitation) as needed — there is no reversal agent, unlike naloxone for opioids or flumazenil for benzodiazepines.

t: Medical Treatment of Substance Use Disorders
x: Stabilization, substitution therapy, and aftercare · Regardless of which substance is involved, medical treatment of substance use disorders follows a similar overall structure. · Assessment of immediate medical issues — identifying and addressing any acute, life-threatening complications first · Tapered use under medical supervision — for substances where abrupt stopping is dangerous (alcohol, benzodiazepines) · Vitamin and fluid replacement — correcting nutritional deficiencies (such as thiamine, to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) and dehydration · Substitution therapy — using a longer-acting, more controllable medication to manage withdrawal: benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal, and suboxone or methadone for opioid withdrawal · Naloxone (Narcan) — reverses opioid overdose, but pushes the patient into abrupt, immediate withdrawal, so administering it is a trade-off between saving a life and causing acute withdrawal symptoms · Aftercare — individual ongoing counseling and group therapy, referrals to self-help, addiction therapy, and counseling services, encouraging support group participation, and addressing family/home situations that may support or undermine recovery · The nurse-client relationship and motivational interviewing · Develop a nurse-client relationship that conveys an attitude of acceptance, discouraging manipulation, rationalization, denial, and projection. Address misconceptions about substance use with objective facts, and teach about the impact of substances on the body. Motivational interviewing is the specific technique used to let the client set goals for their own personal recovery, identify assets that support goal attainment, assess personal strengths to facilitate change, determine obstacles to change, and develop strategies for goal attainment — the emphasis throughout is on the client's own motivation rather than the nurse's prescription for what recovery should look like. · Additional reversal and deterrent agents · Naltrexone — oral opiate antagonist that blocks the effects of narcotics; treats both alcohol and heroin addiction; for alcohol use disorder it can be given orally daily or as a monthly injection, and if the client is also using opioids, those must be stopped 7–10 days before starting naltrexone to avoid precipitating withdrawal — acamprosate (Campral) is the alternative for a client who still needs pain control with opioids · Flumazenil — intravenous antidote to benzodiazepine overdose · Methadone — oral or intravenous; prevents withdrawal in clients addicted to opioids, part of a comprehensive cessation program · Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) — sublingual tablet or film (once or twice daily) or a monthly injection; buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist that suppresses cravings and withdrawal without producing the same level of euphoria as a full agonist, and combining it with psychosocial treatment significantly reduces relapse risk · Disulfiram — oral alcohol deterrent (see the Alcohol lesson for the full detail) · Naloxone — administration specifics · Naloxone (Narcan) is an opioid antagonist that works by displacing opioids from their CNS receptors. It can be given intranasally, IV, IM, or subcutaneously, repeated every 2–3 minutes as needed — it works fast, rapidly reversing CNS/respiratory depression and increasing respiratory rate within 1–2 minutes. Because many opioids (especially potent synthetic forms like fentanyl) last longer in the body than a single dose of naloxone, a patient who appears to be revived can relapse back into respiratory depression once the naloxone wears off — this is why continued monitoring of respiratory rate and depth after reversal is essential, not optional, and why today's more potent forms of heroin/fentanyl may require multiple naloxone doses to fully reverse an overdose. · Naloxone deserves special attention here: it is a genuine, immediate life-saver in an opioid overdose, but nurses should anticipate that the patient will emerge from it in acute, unpleasant withdrawal — this is an expected trade-off, not a sign anything went wrong with the reversal. Flumazenil plays the same reversal role for benzodiazepine overdose specifically, and should not be confused with naloxone's opioid-specific mechanism — giving naloxone for a pure benzodiazepine overdose, or flumazenil for a pure opioid overdose, does nothing for the actual cause of the respiratory depression. · General nursing approach during withdrawal and treatment · Maintain a nonjudgmental approach throughout every interaction, regardless of the substance or the circumstances that led to admission · Seizure precautions for any patient at risk (alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal in particular) · Suicide precautions as appropriate, given how commonly substance use disorders co-occur with depression and suicidality · A calm environment with minimized stimuli — overstimulation can worsen agitation and autonomic symptoms during withdrawal · Small, frequent meals with fresh fruits and vegetables to help rebuild nutritional status · Help the patient build a safety plan with concrete coping strategies for cravings and triggers, not just a plan for the inpatient stay · Set clear limits around manipulative behavior, paired with positive reinforcement for progress — consistency among staff matters here just as it does in other conditions where manipulation is a coping pattern · Why early, effective treatment matters — the complications of untreated chronic substance use · Chronic substance use disorders carry a long list of possible complications that make early identification and treatment a genuine safety issue, not just a quality-of-life one: cardiac or respiratory arrest, intracranial hemorrhage, AIDS, subacute bacterial endocarditis, hepatitis, cirrhosis, septicemia, pulmonary emboli, malnutrition, depression with suicide risk, and psychosis . Framing treatment this way — as prevention of these downstream complications, not just cessation of use — can also help make the case to a resistant or ambivalent patient. · A medication not yet covered: cocaine withdrawal · For cocaine withdrawal specifically, amantadine or bromocriptine may be used to ease symptoms — worth knowing alongside the alcohol-, benzodiazepine-, and opioid-specific agents already covered in this unit, since cocaine withdrawal management looks different from all three.

BMI thresholds, refeeding syndrome, and the deadliest mortality rate in psychiatry · Anorexia nervosa involves fear of obesity, a distorted body image, preoccupation with food, and refusal to eat, with a perception of being overweight despite being emaciated. It may or may not be accompanied by a loss of appetite, and features reduced food intake/fasting, extensive exercising, self-induced vomiting, or use of laxatives or diuretics. It has a higher incidence in Western cultures with societal pressures on appearance and weight, primarily affects females ages 12–30 years (male incidence may be underestimated), and is associated with complex physiological, environmental, familial, and psychodynamic factors. · Anorexia nervosa carries a mortality rate of roughly 10–20% — the highest of any psychiatric disorder. Death results from either the medical complications of starvation (most often cardiac) or from suicide, which is why aggressive medical monitoring and psychiatric safety assessment both matter from the first encounter, not just after the patient is medically stable. · Two subtypes · Restricting type — weight loss is achieved through not eating and increased exercise · Binge-eating/purging type — the person periodically eats a large amount of food and then self-induces vomiting or otherwise purges, similar in behavior to bulimia but occurring alongside the significantly low body weight that defines anorexia · Priority assessments/cues · Weight and BMI — weight may be less than 85% of normal weight; BMI less than 17, and less than 15 is considered extreme · Eating pattern — restricted amount and/or timing of eating, may also include binging and purging · Physical assessment — lanugo (downy-like body hair), peripheral edema from low serum protein levels, amenorrhea, emaciated appearance, muscle/bone loss, constipation, cold extremities, bradycardia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension · Depression, anxiety, guilt, self-blame, preoccupation with appearance, distorted perceptions of body and appearance, stressors, secrecy, boredom, low self-esteem, history of trauma or relationship dysfunction · Use standardized screening tests including the Eating Disorders Inventory, Body Attitude Test, Eating Attitudes Test, or Diagnostic Survey for Eating Disorders · HUNGER — the key features of anorexia nervosa · A memory jogger for the core clinical picture: H ates the way their body looks; U nrealistic image of their body (distorted body image); N ever satisfied with weight loss (never "thin enough"); G rossly reduced food intake; E xcessive exercise; R efusal to maintain a healthy/normal body weight. · SCOFF — a five-item screening questionnaire · A quick screening tool for eating disorders (two or more "yes" answers suggests further evaluation is needed): do you make yourself S ick because you feel uncomfortably full? Do you worry you've lost C ontrol over how much you eat? Have you recently lost more than O ne stone (about 14 lb) in a 3-month period? Do you believe yourself to be F at when others say you are too thin? Would you say that F ood dominates your life? · Prevalence, onset, and genetics · Onset of anorexia is often associated with a stressful life event, most commonly in adolescence. Researchers suspect an interplay of genetic, biological, behavioral, environmental, family, and psychosocial factors — first-degree relatives of someone with anorexia have an increased incidence of the disorder, supporting a genetic component alongside the well-documented sociocultural pressure toward thinness. · Prognosis · Outcomes for anorexia roughly follow a "rule of thirds": about one-third of patients recover fully, one-third improve but remain subthreshold (some lingering symptoms), and one-third go on to a chronic, unremitting course. This is the worst long-term prognosis of any eating disorder, which tracks with its having the highest psychiatric mortality rate. · CUES — patient/family teaching topics · A memory jogger for what to cover in teaching: C auses of eating disorders; U nderstanding how to overcome power struggles and issues of separation and autonomy; E ffects of the eating disorder on physical and mental health; S ymptoms of eating disorders and signs of relapse. · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Complete blood count (CBC) — elevated hematocrit (dehydration), low hemoglobin (anemia) · Urine specific gravity — elevated (dehydration) · Metabolic panel — abnormal electrolytes, glucose, protein · Electrocardiogram (ECG) — ST segment and T wave changes associated with electrolyte changes · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Hospitalization indicated in cases of malnutrition, dehydration with electrolyte disturbances, bradycardia, cardiac dysrhythmias, hypotension, hypothermia · Address nutritional needs — if taking food by mouth, work with a dietitian to slowly increase calories; small, frequent feedings; encourage a diet high in fiber, low in sodium and caffeine · Establish weight gain goals, weigh daily, use behavior modification strategies (privileges and consequences); monitor intake and output · Contract for set mealtimes, stay with the client during and after meals, look for stashed or discarded food · If refusing food by mouth or if condition deteriorates, may require nasogastric feedings · Address emotional needs — explore feelings of inadequacy, coping mechanisms, underlying fears, family issues, feelings of control or lack of control; discuss body image and credibility of distorted perceptions; examine areas of personal self-worth other than appearance; refer for individual, group, or family therapy; determine risk for suicide · Specific numeric hospitalization criteria · Beyond the general indications above, textbooks give concrete admission thresholds nursing exams like to test: weight loss ≥15% of expected body weight or BMI <16; heart rate ≤50 beats/min; systolic blood pressure ≤90 mmHg; core body temperature ≤97°F (36.1°C); and significant electrolyte disturbance. Any of these findings in a patient with an eating disorder should prompt urgent medical evaluation for inpatient stabilization, not outpatient management. · Nursing technique during refeeding — five named strategies · Person to person — maintain one-on-one supervision during meals and for 1–3 hours afterward to ensure compliance and prevent covert vomiting; remember that for a hospitalized patient with AN, food is considered a medication ; give a limited time to complete each meal (such as 30 minutes); food choices are made in conjunction with a dietitian; allow the patient control over nonfood-related activities in the therapeutic environment · Liquidation strategy — during an acute anorexic episode, nutritionally complete liquids are sometimes more acceptable than solid food because they don't require the patient to select foods, which patients with AN commonly find difficult; if tube feeding becomes necessary, explain the measures and address the patient's fears, but limit discussion about the food itself · Pound by pound — weigh the patient daily (after voiding, before breakfast) on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing; monitor closely beforehand, since patients may hide objects in clothing or drink large amounts of fluid to falsely inflate their weight; anticipate a weight gain of about 1–3 lb/week · Defusing fat fears — if edema or bloating occurs after resuming normal eating, reassure the patient this is temporary so they don't fear they're "getting fat" and stop complying; encourage the patient to recognize and assert feelings freely so they learn that expressing true feelings won't cause them to lose control or love; explain how improved nutrition reverses the effects of starvation; advise family members to avoid discussing food with the patient · Preservation tactics — recognize that patients with AN use exercise, food preoccupation, ritualism, and even manipulation as ways to preserve the only sense of control they feel they have; maintain contact with outpatient treatment teams to promote a smooth transition after discharge; involve family therapy focused on communication strategies, since families often carry heavy guilt that should not be reinforced by assigning blame — patients and families are not responsible for causing the illness, but all are responsible for participating in treatment and recovery · A sample plan-of-care order set · An example inpatient care plan for anorexia illustrates how concrete these interventions get in practice: daily weights with a new client gown provided by the nurse; obtain weight immediately upon waking, limiting water intake prior to weighing; goals focused on weight gained, not food eaten; supervise all meals, watch for hiding food; encourage solid food, limit fluids during meals; support mealtime normalization and interactions; limit meals to 30 minutes followed by 30 minutes of supervised rest; escort to the restroom or limit restroom use after meals; maintain boundaries, limit manipulation, communicate clear rewards and consequences; allow the client more meal choices, portions, and control as the client progresses; maintain a positive therapeutic relationship. · Priority actual & potential complications · Malnutrition/emaciation · Electrolyte disturbances · Cardiac dysrhythmias · Heart disease, diabetes, and other consequences of obesity and renal failure (in binge-eating comorbidities) · Refeeding syndrome · The life-threatening cardiovascular risk · The most dangerous complication of anorexia is cardiac, and it traces back to the malnutrition itself: if malnutrition leads to edema or hypokalemia (low potassium), ventricular arrhythmias can occur. This is why electrolyte monitoring, especially potassium, and cardiac monitoring are standard parts of caring for a patient with anorexia — the danger isn't only the visible weight loss, it's the invisible electrolyte and cardiac instability underneath it. · Refeeding syndrome · Aggressive, rapid refeeding may cause refeeding syndrome in clients after prolonged periods of undernutrition — a dangerous shift of fluids and electrolytes (especially phosphate) as the body suddenly has carbohydrates to metabolize again. This is exactly why nutritional rehabilitation for anorexia starts slowly and is built up gradually under dietitian guidance rather than restoring full caloric intake all at once. · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Nurses may be instrumental in building relationships with clients, ensuring that manipulative behaviors are limited · Focus on healthy eating to meet body needs, consequences of over- or under-eating · Nurses may play a key role in assessing and assisting clients and families to address issues such as control, coping, stress, and healthy communication · Priority medications · Fluoxetine — oral SSRI antidepressant to assist with depression, bulimia (may decrease carbohydrate cravings), and anorexia; may take 1–2 weeks to take effect, may increase risk of suicide especially in adolescents; used in conjunction with counseling/therapy. There is no medication FDA-approved specifically to treat anorexia itself — low-dose olanzapine is sometimes used off-label after weight restoration has begun, to ease the ruminative anxiety around food and weight that persists even once weight is closer to normal. · Evidence-based psychotherapy · The same family of therapies is used across all three eating disorders: CBT-E (enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy, tailored specifically for eating disorders), interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) , and Maudsley/family-based therapy (FBT) , which is especially emphasized for adolescents with anorexia and actively involves the family in renourishing the patient at home rather than treating the family as a bystander. · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Provide client and family with education about the chronic nature of eating disorders and overall management of illness · Assist the client and family to recognize the complexity of emotional and physical issues · Refer to community organizations for all forms of eating disorders — support groups and websites such as the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Related Eating Disorders and the National Eating Disorders Association provide education and support · Monitor internet and social media use, especially in adolescents — some websites and blogs perpetuate the myth that extreme thinness or disordered eating is a legitimate lifestyle choice and can actively undermine recovery · BMI-based severity scale (adults) · Severity | BMI · Mild | ≥17 · Moderate | 16–16.99 · Severe | 15–15.99 · Extreme | <15 · Starvation physiology — why the body responds the way it does · Decreased calorie intake depletes fat and protein stores, producing hypoglycemia , vitamin deficiencies , release of endogenous opioids , excess cortisol , and suppressed thyroid function . Loss of the fat needed as a lipid substrate for estrogen production drives the estrogen deficiency behind amenorrhea , and as the body is forced to use fat for energy, ketoacidosis can result. Anorexia affects females roughly 10 times more often than males, and its mortality rate is higher than that of any other psychiatric disorder — suicide accounts for about 25% of deaths in anorexia, underscoring why a psychiatric safety assessment belongs alongside the medical workup. · Additional physical exam findings · Lanugo — fine, downy hair on the face/body, a compensatory response to loss of insulating subcutaneous fat · Bradycardia, hypotension, and hypothermia as the body downshifts metabolically to conserve energy · Calluses or abrasions on the knuckles — classically taught as a sign of self-induced vomiting (Russell sign), most relevant in the binge-eating/purging subtype · Painless enlargement of the salivary glands · Peripheral edema from low serum protein · Refeeding syndrome — expanded safety detail · Refeeding syndrome describes the metabolic disturbances that occur as nutrition is restored after prolonged undernutrition. Risk correlates with both the degree of prior weight loss and the speed of refeeding, and is greatest during the first 2 weeks of treatment . Watch closely for hypophosphatemia , hypokalemia , hypomagnesemia , and volume overload with edema — this is exactly why nutritional rehabilitation is built up gradually rather than restoring full caloric intake all at once. · Hospitalization criteria — additional cited thresholds · Other references add further concrete admission triggers to know for exams: weight <75% of expected, or a rapid loss of ≥15% of body mass; bradycardia ≤40 bpm; systolic BP <90 mmHg; core temperature ≤97°F (36.5°C); symptomatic hypoglycemia <60 mg/dL; serum potassium <3 mEq/L; serum phosphorus <2 mg/dL; severe dehydration; or suicidal ideation. Any of these warrants urgent inpatient stabilization. · 1-on-1 meal supervision and weight-gain medication · Supervise the patient one-on-one during meals and for a full hour afterward to prevent self-induced vomiting, and evaluate for medication hoarding as part of that same supervision. Negotiate food intake and set weekly (not just daily) weight-gain goals with the patient, and involve them in care decisions wherever possible — this builds a sense of control that counters the loss of control driving the illness. Note that olanzapine is used specifically as an adjunctive therapy to promote weight gain in anorexia, not as a first-line or stand-alone treatment. · DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria · Persistent restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight · Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, despite being at a significantly low weight · Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight · Illustrative case: an adolescent athlete's presentation · Bethany Cole, a 16-year-old female, is admitted at 94 lb (42.6 kg), BMI 15.6 — meeting the severe category on the BMI scale above — after fainting during PE class, her third ED visit in 6 months for this issue. Her mother reports Bethany refuses to eat and that they "argue constantly about food and meals"; the family was referred to an eating disorder center but Bethany refused to go. Bethany minimizes the problem: "I'm just not hungry, I'm fine, I do well in school...I'm on the track team. I just don't need a lot of food, and I need to keep my weight down for track. I haven't had my period in a few months, but that's just because I'm active. I do wish I wasn't always constipated, though. My belly gets huge and hard." On exam she is pale, anxious, and tearful, with dry mucous membranes, cool skin, fine lanugo on the shoulders and upper arms, and agitated pacing. Vitals — T 97.8°F (36.6°C), HR 66, RR 11, BP 88/58, SpO2 99% on room air — show the classic starvation-adaptation pattern of bradycardia, hypotension, and a low-normal respiratory rate. The case is a compact illustration of several exam-favorite cues at once: minimization/denial of illness severity, exercise-driven restriction rationalized as athletic performance, amenorrhea, constipation from dehydration and poor intake, and lanugo as compensatory thermoregulation.

The binge–purge cycle, its comorbidities, and its electrolyte consequences · Bulimia nervosa involves episodic, uncontrolled, rapid, compulsive eating of large quantities of food over a short period of time, followed by attempts to rid the body of calories through purging (self-induced vomiting, inappropriate use of laxatives/diuretics) or other compensatory behaviors (vigorous exercise, prolonged fasting). It's most common in females during late adolescence/early adulthood. Unlike anorexia, body weight in bulimia is often normal or even above normal, which can make the disorder easier to conceal — patients often go to great lengths to hide the binge-purge cycle from family and providers alike. · RIDS BODY — the clinical features of bulimia · A memory jogger, since not everyone with bulimia purges: R ecurrent binge-eating episodes; I ntense exercise; D iuretic, laxative, and enema use; S elf-induced vomiting; B ody image distortion; O rdinary eating alternating with episodes of binge-purge cycles; D epression and anxiety disorders may be present; Y o-yo effect of tension relief and pleasure experienced with bingeing, followed by guilt and depression after purging. · Myth busters · Myth: all patients with eating disorders are either very thin or very overweight. Reality: a patient with bulimia may have a weight within the normal range — this is exactly what makes the disorder so easy to miss on a routine visit · Myth: open conflict and verbal fighting are common among families of adolescents with eating disorders. Reality: conflict avoidance , not open conflict, is the more typical family pattern · Prevalence, onset, and genetics · Bulimia is more common than anorexia and carries a better prognosis. It usually begins in late adolescence or young adulthood, affects both sexes at roughly a 10:1 female-to-male ratio (though the true proportion of affected males may be underestimated, possibly as high as 20%), and about 1–3% of the population meets full diagnostic criteria, with up to 5–15% showing some symptoms — likely an underestimate, since many patients successfully hide their symptoms. Researchers have proposed genetic links at chromosomes 1, 3, and 10p. · Prognosis · The prognosis for bulimia is more favorable than anorexia, with 50–70% recovery rates, though about half of those who recover may relapse. Unlike anorexia, there's an increased probability of eventual recovery from bulimia even after 10 years of illness. · Comorbidities across eating disorders · Eating disorders as a group commonly co-occur with anxiety disorders (such as phobias and obsessive-compulsive disorder), trauma-related disorders (such as PTSD), substance use disorders , and depressive disorders (bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, borderline personality disorder). Patients with bulimia specifically also carry an elevated risk of suicide and self-harm relative to the general population, which means a psychiatric safety assessment — not just a nutritional and electrolyte workup — is a standard part of the initial evaluation. · Signs, symptoms, and behavioral findings · Preoccupation with body shape and weight, alongside a self-evaluation that is unduly influenced by body shape and weight · Evidence of binge eating: disappearance of large amounts of food, hoarding food, eating in secret · Evidence of purging behavior: frequent trips to the bathroom after meals, running water to mask vomiting sounds, laxative or diuretic wrappers · Russell's sign — calluses or scarring on the knuckles or back of the hand from self-induced vomiting · Dental enamel erosion and increased dental caries from repeated stomach acid exposure · Parotid gland swelling ("chipmunk cheeks") · Menstrual irregularities · Fluctuating weight that is often normal or above normal, unlike the low body weight seen in anorexia · Life-threatening medical complications · The complications of bulimia center on dehydration and the electrolyte imbalances that result from repeated purging — most importantly hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis from the loss of stomach acid and gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting (laxative overuse instead tends to produce metabolic acidosis, from reduced sodium bicarbonate). Just as in anorexia, low potassium raises the risk of dangerous cardiac arrhythmias and ECG changes, which is why electrolyte panels are a standard, recurring part of monitoring a patient with bulimia, not a one-time admission lab. Other complications include esophageal erosion, ulcers, tears, and bleeding; tooth and gum erosion and dental caries; GERD; edema; and toxicity from substances like ipecac used to induce vomiting, which is associated with severe cardiac disease. · Hospitalization · If binge eating and purging have caused serious physical harm, hospitalization provides around-the-clock observation of all eating and elimination (urinating, bowel movements, and vomiting). As symptoms stabilize, the patient gradually resumes control over their own eating. · Treatment: medication · Fluoxetine (Prozac) , an SSRI, is the medication most associated with treating bulimia nervosa and is the only FDA-approved medication for this indication. As with any antidepressant, the nurse must monitor for the black-box warning of increased suicidal ideation , particularly in adolescents and young adults and especially in the first weeks of therapy or after a dose change — this matters even more here given the baseline elevated suicide risk in this population. · Evidence-based psychotherapy · The same therapies effective for anorexia show effectiveness for bulimia: CBT-E , interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) , and Maudsley/family-based therapy (FBT) and other family therapy approaches. Treatment addresses the issues that cause the behavior, not just the behavior itself, and typically combines individual, group, and family therapy with nutritional counseling. · Nursing interventions · Establish a behavioral contract with the patient that specifies expected food amounts and types to be consumed at meals · Provide supervision during and for 1–2 hours after meals to prevent purging — this window covers the period when the urge to purge is highest; set a clear time limit for each meal and provide a pleasant, relaxed eating environment · Discourage fasting or restrictive food intake, since this can itself trigger a binge episode · Encourage journaling (a food diary documenting time of eating, food eaten, mood, life events, and binge urges/behaviors) to identify triggers such as hunger from inadequate intake, emotional distress, or an automatic conditioning response · Provide assertiveness training to help the patient gain control over their behavior and achieve a realistic, positive self-image · Encourage the patient to discuss stressful issues — achievement, independence, socialization, sexuality, family problems, and control — rather than managing them through the binge-purge cycle · Assess passive and active suicide potential and risk for self-harm · Monitor electrolytes and cardiac status routinely throughout treatment, not just on admission · Recognize this is often a long haul — treatment may need to continue for years to prevent relapse — and refer to support groups such as Overeaters Anonymous · Bulimia vs. binge-eating disorder — the key differentiator · The defining line between the two disorders is the compensatory behavior : bulimia nervosa is a binge plus an inappropriate compensatory behavior — purging, laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise — to prevent weight gain. Binge-eating disorder is a binge without any compensatory behavior. This single distinction is what separates the two diagnoses and explains why bulimia often presents with a normal-to-overweight body habitus while its medical complications center on purging trauma rather than on obesity. · DSM-5-TR severity specifier · Diagnosis requires binge eating with compensatory behavior occurring, on average, at least once a week for 3 months. Severity is then graded by the average number of compensatory episodes per week: Mild 1–3, Moderate 4–7, Severe 8–13, Extreme 14 or more. · Bupropion is contraindicated — a critical safety alert · Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with a current or past eating disorder , including bulimia, because it increases seizure risk specifically in this population. This is a distinct point from the fluoxetine black-box suicidality warning above — two separate medication safety issues to keep straight for this population. · Additional medications · Besides fluoxetine as the only SSRI FDA-approved specifically for bulimia, sertraline , fluvoxamine , and escitalopram are used as second-line alternatives. Ondansetron may be added to help prevent vomiting, and psyllium can help prevent constipation during withdrawal from chronic laxative use. · Purge-specific complications beyond the esophagus · Repeated purging can also produce Barrett esophagus , gastric dilation or rupture , parotid gland hypertrophy , rectal prolapse , and pancreatitis — a mechanical and chemical trauma profile that is distinct from the starvation-based complications of anorexia.

Binging without the compensatory behaviors · Binge-eating disorder involves recurrent eating of large amounts of food without compensatory behaviors — the person usually eats alone and may feel guilty or depressed after an episode. It's more common in females than males, most common in adults ages 46–55, and related to problems with impulse control/addiction. As a result, individuals with binge-eating disorder are often overweight or obese — binge eating causes substantial weight gain, and obesity, with a BMI that begins as normal and then increases — and the psychological experience is typically one of significant shame, guilt, and distress about the loss of control, often eating alone specifically to hide the behavior. · Physical assessment findings · Signs of metabolic syndrome, abdominal distention, and gastrointestinal dysfunction are the physical assessment findings that distinguish binge-eating disorder from the malnutrition-driven findings seen in anorexia and bulimia. Insomnia is also common, and body weight ranges from normal to obesity (BMI >30). · Prevalence, onset, and genetics · Binge-eating disorder is the most common eating disorder in the United States — up to 3.5% of females and 2% of males will experience it at some point in their lives, with average onset in young adulthood, slightly later than for anorexia or bulimia. It affects women somewhat more than men. Heritability is estimated at 41–57%, and brain chemistry changes are seen as with the other eating disorders; stressful life events increase risk. Long-term outcomes are slightly more favorable than for the other eating disorders. · Diagnosis · Diagnosis often includes a neuropsychological evaluation in addition to the clinical history, since binge-eating disorder is a psychiatric condition and the evaluation helps characterize the cognitive and emotional drivers of the binge pattern, not just the eating behavior itself. · Complications · Because there's no purging to cause the electrolyte disturbances seen in bulimia, the complications of binge-eating disorder overlap heavily with those of clinical obesity: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, gallbladder disease, musculoskeletal problems, and obstructive sleep apnea — alongside the significant psychological burden of the disorder itself, including higher risk for suicide and self-harm compared to those without the disorder. Common comorbidities include anxiety disorders, mood disorders, and substance use disorders. · Treatment: two priorities · Treatment is framed around two sequential priorities. The first and immediate priority is to interrupt the binge-eating pattern itself — through therapy (cognitive behavioral therapy in particular) and, where appropriate, medication. Only once the binge pattern is under control does the second priority — facilitating weight loss, if appropriate for the patient — become the focus. Leading with weight loss before the binge pattern is addressed tends to backfire, since dieting pressure is itself a common binge trigger. · Treatment: medication · SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine) and SNRIs (e.g., venlafaxine/Effexor) are used to target the underlying mood and anxiety drivers of binge eating · Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) , a stimulant, is FDA-approved specifically for moderate-to-severe binge-eating disorder in adults · Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) agonists are also used, targeting appetite regulation and satiety · Nursing interventions · Help the patient set daily, achievable goals rather than large, all-or-nothing changes · Give the patient control over their own food choices rather than imposing a rigid diet, to reduce the sense of restriction that can trigger binges · Encourage food journaling to build awareness of intake and patterns · Help the patient identify triggers for binge episodes (emotional, situational, or social) · Encourage routine weighing as a neutral data point rather than a source of shame · Teach alternative coping strategies to replace binge eating as a response to stress or negative emotion · Refer to support resources such as Overeaters Anonymous and eating-disorder-specific organizations for ongoing peer support · Use nonjudgmental, shame-reducing communication throughout — shame is often what drives the secrecy that keeps the binge cycle going · Comparing the three eating disorders at a glance · Feature | Anorexia | Bulimia | Binge-eating disorder · Weight/BMI | ↓ weight, BMI <18.5 | Normal to overweight, BMI 18.5–30 | Tends toward overweight/obese · Vital signs | ↓ BP, ↓ HR (worsened by dehydration/electrolyte imbalance) | Usually near normal unless purging is severe | Usually normal; metabolic syndrome findings instead · Compensatory behavior | Refuses to eat; typically does NOT purge | Purges after bingeing (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics) | No compensatory behavior after a binge · Hallmark findings | Amenorrhea, lanugo, ↓ subcutaneous tissue → hypothermia, constipation from dehydration | Teeth erosion, bad breath, parotid swelling, Russell sign | Abdominal distention, GI dysfunction, insomnia · Core fear/driver | Intense fear of gaining weight | Binge–purge cycle tied to body image | Binging triggered by depression, shame, or self-hatred · Treatment emphasis | Increase weight slowly (2–3 lb/week), monitor exercise | Monitor during and after meals for purging | Interrupt the binge pattern first, weight loss second · The emotional-eating trigger cycle · Binging in binge-eating disorder is frequently triggered by depression, shame, or self-hatred — the person eats in response to the emotion, feels worse (more shame and guilt) as a result of the binge, and that worsened emotional state feeds the next episode. Breaking this cycle is a core reason therapy targets the emotional trigger itself, not just the eating behavior. · Refeeding syndrome as a shared risk across eating disorders · Refeeding syndrome is not unique to anorexia — it is a risk whenever nutrition is reintroduced to any malnourished client, across eating disorders. The nutritional rehabilitation must be done slowly regardless of which eating disorder is being treated. · Universal treatment principles for all eating disorders · Teach coping skills to replace the disordered eating behavior · Maintain trust with the client throughout treatment · Make the client part of the decision-making and plan of care · Use therapy — group, individual, or family — as a core treatment component regardless of which eating disorder is involved

Signs, drug-holiday logic, and the full stimulant/non-stimulant medication picture · ADHD is characterized by behaviors of inattention and/or hyperactivity with impulsivity, ranging from mild to severe. Hyperactivity is increased psychomotor activity that may or may not be purposeful — rapid physical movements and verbal activity, and may include being highly distractible. Impulsivity is acting without reflection or thought to consequences, an inability to resist acting. The disorder is present across more than one setting (school and home, for example) rather than confined to a single environment — symptoms must be present before age 12 and occur in two or more settings (home, school, with others) to meet diagnostic criteria. · Three DSM-5-TR presentations · ADHD is diagnosed as one of three presentations, and a client's presentation can change over time: Combined (meets criteria for both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity), Predominantly Inattentive , and Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive . DSM-5-TR criteria require 6 or more symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity for children age 16 and younger, but only 5 or more for adolescents age 17 and older and adults — symptoms must have been present for at least 6 months, with several symptoms evident before age 12, and present in two or more settings. · Causes and risk factors · The underlying cause of ADHD isn't fully understood, but it has a strong genetic component — twin studies estimate heritability around 76% — and brain imaging shows structural differences that may relate to functional impairment. On average, 8–11% of school-age children have ADHD, roughly 6.1 million children in the U.S. Suspected risk factors include genetics, environmental toxin exposure (such as lead) at a young age, maternal use of drugs/alcohol/cigarettes or exposure to environmental poisons during pregnancy, prematurity or low birth weight, and brain injury. · Adult ADHD · ADHD is frequently comorbid with anxiety disorders, mood disorders, and substance use disorders. In adults, ADHD affects those of all sexes at roughly equal rates — a sharp contrast to childhood diagnosis, which is skewed heavily male — underscoring that ADHD is not simply a childhood condition many outgrow. · Pathophysiology · Proposed mechanisms include possible alterations in dopamine gene alleles and dopamine transmission. Prenatal hypoxia or hypotension may selectively damage frontal lobe neurons, which is one theory linking perinatal complications to later ADHD risk. · Why boys are diagnosed more often · ADHD affects both sexes, but males are diagnosed more often — this doesn't necessarily mean more males actually have ADHD, just that they're more likely to be identified. One leading theory: males more often present with disruptive, hyperactive behavior that prompts earlier intervention, while females more often present with inattentive symptoms that are less disruptive and easier to overlook. · How presentation shifts with age · Caregivers often report the child was very active even as a toddler, with hyperactivity and inattention becoming more visible in early elementary school. By adolescence, the outward, visible signs of hyperactivity often diminish and turn inward — showing up instead as a subjective sense of restlessness, annoyance, and impatience rather than obvious physical hyperactivity. Adolescents with ADHD frequently experience emotional dysregulation that negatively affects peer relationships, and those with prominent inattentive symptoms tend to struggle academically and socially. · Priority assessments/cues · Requires observation of the child in a variety of settings, and a history from family, teachers, and caregivers · Standardized psychiatric testing methods · Ability to perform age-appropriate tasks, complete activities, and stay with activities until completed · Ability to engage in difficult tasks, length of attention span, ability to cooperate, ability to tolerate frustration, level of distractibility · Ability to form relationships with peers, siblings, and classmates · Difficulty with organization and time management, often loses objects, forgetful · Level of activity, including fidgeting with hands/fingers, squirming in seat, or engaging in risky or dangerous behaviors · Ability to hear and listen to others, observe for excessive talking or frequently using interruption to dominate conversation · Impact on relationships with parents, siblings, teachers, and peers · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · There is no single lab test or imaging study that diagnoses ADHD — diagnosis is clinical, requiring a complete medical and neurologic exam plus hearing/vision screening. Diagnostic tests instead target potential comorbidities (sleep disorders) and are used to rule out other medication or psychological causes : anxiety, depression, conduct disorder, developmental disorders, thyroid dysfunction, brain injury, and substance use disorder. A lead level may be drawn given lead exposure's link to ADHD risk. Standardized behavior rating scales (such as the Vanderbilt Assessment Scale) completed by parents and teachers are exceptionally helpful, and a psychiatric evaluation assessing intellectual ability, academic achievement, and possible learning disorders rounds out the workup — speech/language evaluation is added when indicated. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Ensure safety related to high levels of physical activity without cognitive controls · Create a safe, consistent environment for learning and play, considering distractibility and impulsivity · Focus on reinforcing coping skills and impulse control, improving social relationships, caregiver and family dynamics · Set realistic goals for success and provide clear, concrete instructions · Encourage a highly nutritious diet, eat early in day to avoid impact of anorexia related to medications, limit sugar and caffeine · Reinforce the need for family/individual therapy along with medication management · Form trusting relationships and ensure consistent caregivers; convey acceptance, positive regard, provide positive feedback · Behavior plan with logical consequences for engagement in high-risk behaviors · Expose to group learning and play as tolerated · Monitor for insomnia related to stimulant medications, and monitor for substance use · Priority actual & potential complications · Potential exists for misdiagnosis and incorrect treatment · Exacerbation of behavioral issues due to mismanagement · Increased rate of traffic accidents · Priapism — specifically associated with methylphenidate · Suicidal ideation · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Early diagnosis increases effectiveness of interventions · Ensure families understand the need for therapy along with medications · Encourage frequent monitoring to ensure revisions in plan of care as children grow and change · Nurses must be sensitive to and capable of working with clients with ADHD across the lifespan · Priority medications · Dextroamphetamine/amphetamine, methylphenidate — oral stimulants to calm hyperactivity and increase attentiveness; high risk of dependence; appetite depressants — give early in day and monitor for weight loss; monitor blood pressure and avoid over-the-counter medications; may disturb sleep, so give in the morning or at least 6 hours before bedtime (14 hours for extended-release); may cause growth retardation, so clients are encouraged to take "drug holidays" to allow for growth during summer or breaks from school · Methylphenidate transdermal patch — apply to the hip approximately 2 hours before the intended effect is needed, and remove 9 hours later; timing the patch is a frequently tested administration detail · Atomoxetine — oral non-stimulant, effective in clients with comorbid anxiety; monitor for increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and liver enzymes; use with caution in clients with comorbid depression, and monitor for increased suicidal ideation · Viloxazine — a newer oral non-stimulant option, alongside atomoxetine, for clients who cannot tolerate or should avoid stimulants · Guanfacine — oral non-stimulant (alpha-2 agonist); an option when stimulants are poorly tolerated or contraindicated; monitor for hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, and sedation rather than the cardiac-stimulant profile seen with methylphenidate/amphetamines — never discontinue abruptly, since stopping suddenly can cause rebound hypertension · Bupropion — oral antidepressant used to manage mood swings, may be used in place of stimulants for adults with ADHD; may cause headache, sedation, and dizziness · Tricyclic antidepressants (desipramine, nortriptyline) — alternatives to stimulants in select clients, carrying the same anticholinergic and cardiotoxicity concerns as TCAs used for depression · Methylphenidate and the other stimulants work by blocking the re-uptake of dopamine at the synapse — with the stimulant on board, dopamine accumulates in the synaptic cleft instead of being pulled back into the pre-synaptic terminal, which is the mechanism behind improved attentiveness and calmer, less impulsive behavior. It's worth naming out loud for a patient or family who assumes a stimulant should make hyperactivity worse, not better — this is the "paradoxical effect" : a CNS stimulant calms hyperactive behavior in ADHD because of how it shifts dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex. · Why symptoms are more visible at school or work · ADHD symptoms are often MORE pronounced in structured, demanding environments — school or work — and less noticeable at home, where expectations and structure are looser. This is a major reason ADHD can go undiagnosed until adolescence or adulthood: a child may function well enough at home that no one suspects ADHD until the structured demands of a classroom (or, later, a job) expose the inattention or impulsivity. · CNS stimulant side effects — full picture · Anorexia · Growth retardation in children · Insomnia · Tachycardia and palpitations · Dry mouth · Potential for tolerance and dependence with chronic use · Rare risk of stroke/CVA · Memory jogger for the major treatment components of ADHD: PEPS — Psychotherapy, Education, Pharmacology, Strengths (build on the child's individual strengths, not just manage the deficits). · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Reinforce the importance of ongoing care, behavioral surveillance, and collaboration with school/workplace, family, and health care providers — ADHD management is a long-term, multi-setting partnership rather than a medication prescribed once and left alone. The child may benefit from an individualized educational plan (IEP) built with special-education services to support identified vulnerabilities (untimed tests, repeated or reviewed instructions, tutoring). Teach caregivers that hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the need to urinate can all trigger or worsen hyperactive behavior, that a healthy meal/snack plan matters because poor nutrition can exacerbate symptoms, and that stimulant medications should never be stopped abruptly. · Give stimulant medications EARLY in the day to avoid insomnia · Encourage a large, protein-rich breakfast — appetite drops as the day goes on, so front-loading nutrition helps offset anorexia and growth retardation · Discuss provider-guided "drug holidays" during summer or school breaks to allow catch-up growth · Taper the medication rather than stopping abruptly, given the potential for tolerance and withdrawal · Avoid alcohol and other CNS stimulants, including excess caffeine

A spectrum with frequent overlapping conditions, and two controversial antipsychotics · Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a varied set of neurodevelopmental syndromes characterized by a wide range of communication impairments, social withdrawal, and repetitive/unusual physical behaviors, which cause significant social impairment. ASD includes conditions previously diagnosed separately as autism, childhood disintegrative disorder, pervasive developmental disorder, and Asperger's disorder — all now grouped under the spectrum. It may be associated with other conditions such as epilepsy, genetic disorders (Rett syndrome), and intellectual disabilities. · ASD is more common in males and in those born before 26 weeks of gestation, with increased risk within families — the disorder occurs roughly four to five times more frequently in boys than girls, and about 1 in 59 children in the U.S. is diagnosed with ASD. Girls without obvious intellectual impairment or language delay may go unrecognized longer, since their presentation is easier to miss. It's diagnosed early in childhood — most children are diagnosed by ages 2–3, and signs may manifest as early as six months — and chronic symptoms persist into adulthood. Etiology is unknown, but is thought to involve genetic/chromosomal predisposition, environmental factors and exposures, and perinatal influences; brain scans in children with ASD show differences in brain shape and structure. There's no single definitive diagnostic tool — the interprofessional team (psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and others) rules out other conditions first (hearing loss, speech problems, neurologic disorders, intellectual development disorder) before arriving at the diagnosis. · Three severity levels · Severity for ASD is staged by how much support the person needs, based on the degree of impairment in social communication and the restrictiveness/repetitiveness of behaviors: Level 1 requires support, Level 2 requires substantial support, and Level 3 requires very substantial support. This staging is what tells the care team how much scaffolding — not just what type of intervention — a given patient needs. · Level | What it looks like · 1 — Requires support | Noticeable difficulty with social interaction; inflexible behavior may hamper independence; with appropriate support in place, impairments may not be readily noticed · 2 — Requires substantial support | Significant impairment in both verbal and nonverbal social communication; marked distress when routines or expectations change · 3 — Requires very substantial support | Severe impairment in social communication; minimal response to social overtures from others; great distress with change, and impairment interferes with functioning in all contexts · Epidemiology · ASD is approximately four times more common in males and carries a heavy psychiatric comorbidity burden — about 70% of individuals with ASD have another mental disorder, and about 40% have two additional mental disorders. · Vaccine safety — a common misconception to correct: no scientific link has been established between immunizations, including thimerosal-containing vaccines, and autism. Nurses should be prepared to address this myth directly and calmly with families, pointing them toward the actual evidence rather than dismissing the concern. · Developmental red flags (screening cues by age) · No or limited eye contact by 6 months · Failure to babble, point, or reach by 12 months · Failure to say single words by 16 months · Failure to say two-word phrases by 24 months · Persistent preference for solitude, or marked resistance to routine changes, at any age · Loss of previously acquired language or social skills at any age — this regression pattern (normal development until roughly age 2, then rapid loss of skills) is a well-documented ASD presentation, distinct from a steady early delay · Common screening instruments include the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised (M-CHAT-R) — a short parent questionnaire for 18-month-olds — the Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ), and the Screening Tool for Autism in 2-Year-Olds (STAT), which uses direct observation of play, motor imitation, and joint attention. No single screening tool is diagnostic on its own; a positive screen prompts referral for the full interprofessional evaluation. · Pathophysiology and risk factors · ASD is thought to arise from CNS defects, possibly from prenatal complications or genetic factors, with cellular abnormalities identified in the frontal and temporal lobes and the cerebellum. Possible dysfunction of serotonin, neuropeptides, oxytocin, and vasopressin has also been implicated. Risk factors include having a sibling with autism, advanced parental age, low birth weight, fetal valproate exposure, and prenatal infections or teratogen exposure. During periods of significant stress, a patient with ASD may exhibit catatonic phenomena or an undifferentiated psychotic state. · Priority assessments/cues · Based on placement on the spectrum and level of functionality, amount of support needed · Screen for intellectual disability and age-appropriate development (accelerated, delayed, or normal) · Social and relational difficulties, including decreased interest in others, capacity to imitate others, demonstration and receipt of affection, attachment, imaginative activity, ability to empathize and process feelings of others, ability to play with others, ability to create and sustain friendships · Verbal and/or non-verbal communication difficulties, including eye contact, using and interpreting facial expressions and gestures, ability to hold a reciprocal conversation; may demonstrate echolalia, idiosyncratic utterances, or monotone speech · Physical activities and interests, including over- or under-reaction to stimuli (especially sounds), irritability, compulsivity, fascination with certain objects, need for consistent routine and surroundings, repetitive verbalizations, repetitive body movements (clapping, banging, rocking), self-injurious behaviors · Altered family dynamics and strain on relationships with caregivers and siblings · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Developmental tests — delays in language and social skills · Hearing and vision tests — potential deficits · Diagnostic tests — potential comorbidities such as epilepsy · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Ensure safety related to high levels of physical activity without cognitive control · Create a safe, consistent environment for learning and play · Provide familiar foods, objects, and routines · Support the client's interactions with others, set goals for success, and provide clear, concrete instructions · Form trusting relationships that convey acceptance; reinforce positive behaviors such as eye contact, socially acceptable behaviors, appropriate use of touch, and communication · Only touch clients when they appear receptive — follow the client's cues · Expose to group learning and play as tolerated · Ensure a consistent, limited number of caregivers · Encourage self-care and capitalize on individual, personal strengths to meet goals · Avoid placing excessive demands on the client, and use simple, concrete, literal language — the client is likely to interpret words concretely · Maintain a regular, predictable daily routine with consistent times for waking, dressing, eating, school, and bed;
