if the routine must change, prepare the client for the change in advance · Use a picture board or visual schedule, especially for visual learners, to help make transitions easier · Teach caregivers to recognize triggers and early behavioral cues (increased hand-flapping, irritability) that precede a tantrum or self-injurious episode, and intervene before it escalates · For self-injurious behavior, use protective measures such as helmets or padding rather than punishment — punishment can worsen self-injurious behavior · Make the home safer with locks and gates so the client cannot wander unsupervised · Prepare the client for changes by explaining them BEFORE they happen — predictability reduces distress · Help the family build strong one-on-one relationships with the client · Reinforce the client's individual strengths rather than focusing only on deficits · Priority actual & potential complications · Potential exists for misdiagnosis and incorrect treatment · Assumption of lower cognitive function related to communication impairment · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Early diagnosis increases effectiveness of interventions · Provide support with symptoms of self-injury, aggression, hyperactivity, and impulsivity · Be aware of savants who may excel in music, art, puzzles/patterning, design, or memory · Children and adults with autism may seek health care related to other physical needs/diagnoses — nurses need to be sensitive to and capable of working with clients with autism across the lifespan · Priority medications · Risperidone — oral antipsychotic; controversial use for irritability in children ages 5–15 years; assess for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, and hyperglycemia/diabetes mellitus · Aripiprazole — oral antipsychotic; controversial use for irritability in children ages 6–17 years; may cause sedation, fatigue, weight gain, drooling, and tremoring · Ziprasidone — short-term antipsychotic option specifically for aggression · Atomoxetine or methylphenidate — used when comorbid ADHD symptoms are present alongside ASD · Fluvoxamine (SSRI) — may reduce ritualistic behavior and improve language and mood · Both antipsychotics used in ASD are considered controversial for the same reason: they're prescribed off-label for the behavioral symptom of irritability rather than for autism itself, and they carry the full antipsychotic side-effect burden (EPS, NMS, metabolic derangement) in a pediatric population — which is exactly why the age ranges, and the specific monitoring for each drug, are worth locking in separately rather than lumping "antipsychotic for autism" into one fact.

Sudden and reversible vs. gradual and permanent — the single highest-yield bedside distinction in this unit · Delirium , dementia , and depression can all present with confusion, memory complaints, or altered behavior — which is exactly why they get confused for each other at the bedside. The fastest way to tell them apart is onset and course: delirium arrives suddenly and is usually reversible, dementia creeps in gradually and is usually permanent, and depression can mimic either one but leaves memory largely intact underneath the low mood. · Delirium vs. Dementia vs. Depression — full comparison · Feature | Delirium | Dementia | Depression · Onset | Sudden — often traceable to a single event (surgery, ICU stay, trauma, infection) | Slow, gradual, insidious | Gradual or sudden; may be reactive or chronic · Duration/reversibility | Days to weeks — generally REVERSIBLE once the cause is treated | Progressive, chronic — generally IRREVERSIBLE | Highly variable — treatable · Awareness | Impaired, fluctuating, not permanent | Deteriorates progressively as disease advances | Usually aware/intact, but may be selective or narrowed by mood · Attention | Severely impaired, poor focus — often driven by hallucinations or disorganized thought | Relatively preserved early, affected late | Distorted — may struggle to attend to anything outside the depressed mood · Memory | Short-term memory loss can appear early and acutely | Often the FIRST sign, worsens progressively ("did I take my medication?") | Usually INTACT — pseudodementia can mimic memory loss, but true memory is preserved · Hallucinations | Common, especially visual/sensory — contributes to agitation | May occur LATE in the disease, often visual | Possible, but typically AUDITORY if present · Sleep | Disturbed, disorganized | Disturbed, day-night reversal common (Sundowner's syndrome) | Variable — hypersomnia or insomnia, often worse in early morning · Thought pattern | Disorganized, jumps from topic to topic | Impoverished/limited insight; may confabulate or use compensatory strategies (writing things down) | May be organized but empty/lacking substance, or perseverate on one or two themes · Sundowner's syndrome — in dementia, confusion, wandering, and agitation characteristically worsen as evening approaches. It's a dementia-specific pattern worth naming separately from delirium's generally around-the-clock fluctuation. · Three vignettes — same complaint, three different diagnoses · Mr. Jason Millar, 71 , is postoperative day 6 from a total bowel resection. He is disoriented, agitated, pulling at his IV lines, and believes the hospital carts rolling by are trains he's late for. This is classic delirium : sudden onset tied directly to a recent surgery/hospitalization, with hallucination-driven, disorganized behavior. · Mrs. Viola Schmidt, 71 , lives in assisted living and has grown increasingly confused over the past 6 months. She recently wandered off her unit, and her family is now considering a transfer to a memory-care unit. This is classic dementia : an insidious, progressive pattern with a concrete safety consequence (wandering). · Mrs. Angela Petrie, 71 , attends a senior center and reports feeling sad, saying her life feels "useless"; she admits to past suicidal ideation with no current intent. Depression in older adults can mimic cognitive impairment — a pattern called pseudodementia — and must always be screened for rather than assumed to be dementia. (Full depression content lives in the Mood Disorders unit; this is a cross-reference, not a duplicate.) · NCLEX case in focus: postoperative delirium · Graham Rice, 63 , was admitted after a motor vehicle accident with traumatic brain injury and evacuation of an intracranial hematoma. He was extubated on day 7 and is now progressively disoriented, agitated, restless, and combative, hallucinating that people are touching him or his equipment; his blood pressure has been elevated above his baseline throughout. His family is confused and concerned about his slow recovery and behavior, and he becomes agitated trying to communicate his needs. This is postoperative/post-TBI delirium in the ICU/stepdown setting — a highly testable pattern. New-onset agitation plus hallucinations plus a fluctuating level of consciousness in a recent postoperative or neuro patient should make you think delirium first — not "dementia" (too gradual for this timeline) and not "new psychosis" (there is an obvious acute medical driver). · Delirium — risk factors and manifestations · Risk factors: hospitalization, ICU stay, polypharmacy, old age, stroke, surgery, use of restraints · Always secondary to an underlying medical condition — infection, electrolyte imbalance, substance use/withdrawal, and more — there is ALWAYS a cause to find and treat · Manifestations: disorganization, impaired memory, anxiety/agitation, delusional thinking; level of arousal ranges from lethargic to hypervigilant · Orientation to time and place is typically lost first and is the most common orientation deficit · Symptoms are often worse at night · Delirium is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY. It requires prompt diagnosis and treatment of the underlying cause — the confusion itself is a symptom, not the diagnosis. · Alzheimer's disease — risk factors · Genetics/family history in an immediate family member · Head injury or traumatic brain injury · Advanced age — risk is highest after age 65 · Cardiovascular disease and unhealthy lifestyle factors: inactivity, poor diet, high cholesterol, obesity, diabetes · Alzheimer's disease — staging · Stage | What it looks like · Mild/early | Not noticeable to others; memory lapses, misplacing things, difficulty focusing; client can still accomplish their own ADLs · Moderate/middle | Increasing forgetfulness and short-term memory loss; PERSONALITY CHANGES; client gets lost or wanders; unable to complete own ADLs/self-care; may become incontinent · Severe/late | Needs full assistance with ALL ADLs; progressively loses physical skills such as walking, eating, and swallowing; may ultimately result in coma or death · Alzheimer's disease — priority interventions · Safety first — prevent physical harm, and avoid restraints whenever possible · Attend to physical needs — hygiene, food, water, sleep · Anti-anxiety or antipsychotic medications may be needed as ordered for severe agitation or distress · Alzheimer's disease — communication · Speak slowly · Give one direction at a time · Avoid complex or open-ended questions — ask simple, direct questions instead · Face the client directly when speaking · Cholinesterase inhibitors — donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine · Generic donepezil (Aricept) , galantamine (Razadyne) , and rivastigmine (Exelon) are used in the early and moderate stages of dementia/Alzheimer's disease to improve quality of life — they do NOT cure the underlying disease. This class is also sometimes used in Parkinson's disease. Alzheimer's pathophysiology involves degeneration of cholinergic neurons (decreased acetylcholine) along with plaque and tangle buildup; cholinesterase inhibitors work by inhibiting the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, which increases acetylcholine availability at the synapse and improves cognitive function or slows memory deterioration. · Rivastigmine is highly hepatically metabolized and should be used cautiously, with limited dosing, in liver disease — it can accumulate with hepatic impairment · Side effects across this class: orthostatic hypotension, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia · Best taken WITH FOOD to reduce GI side effects · Keep the vocabulary straight: dementia is the general umbrella term for a group of symptoms/decline in cognitive function; Alzheimer's disease is one specific disease that can cause a major neurocognitive disorder — the terms are not interchangeable. And remember the reversibility rule that ties this whole lesson together: delirium is REVERSIBLE if treated promptly; Alzheimer's and other major neurocognitive disorders are generally IRREVERSIBLE.

When psychological stress shows up as physical illness — and why the symptoms are real to the client either way · Somatization is psychological stress that presents through physical manifestations that cannot be explained by any identifiable pathology or diagnosis. Somatic symptom and related disorders cover a spectrum of presentations, but they share one nursing principle above all others: the symptoms feel completely real to the client, even when no organic cause is found, and the nurse's job is to validate that experience rather than dismiss it. · Somatic Symptom Disorder · Client is consumed by physical symptoms to the point they disrupt daily life · Seeks medical help from multiple providers/facilities — a "doctor shopping" pattern · Pattern of remission and exacerbation over time · May over-medicate with analgesics and antianxiety medications · Direct relationship between stress and symptoms — increased stress leads to increased somatic symptoms · Assessment tool · The PHQ-15 (Patient Health Questionnaire-15) is used to identify 15 of the most common somatic symptoms and screen for somatic symptom disorder. · Nursing considerations — Somatic Symptom Disorder · SAFETY is a priority — assess for symptoms or thoughts of self-harm or suicide · Understand that the somatic symptoms feel REAL to the client even though no organic pathology is found — validate the client's experience rather than dismissing it · Help the client verbalize feelings, while limiting the amount of time spent discussing the somatic symptoms themselves, to avoid reinforcing the symptom focus · Assess coping mechanisms and educate on alternative, healthier coping strategies · Conversion Disorder · Conversion disorder involves the sudden onset of neurological manifestations and physical symptoms WITHOUT a known neurological diagnosis. Symptoms can be related to a psychological conflict or need that is beyond the client's conscious control — they are NOT intentionally produced or faked. · Type | Manifestations · Motor | Paralysis, pseudoseizures · Sensory | Blindness, deafness, sensations of burning or tingling, inability to smell or speak · Pseudocyesis — signs and symptoms of pregnancy without the presence of an actual fetus. It may occur in a client who strongly desires to become pregnant, and it's a good example of how deeply a conversion presentation can mimic an organic condition. · Nursing considerations — Conversion Disorder · Ensure safety · Gain trust and rapport with the client · Assess coping mechanisms and educate on alternative ways of coping · Assess stress-management methods · Encourage therapy — individual, group, or support groups · Medications for conversion disorder may include antidepressants or anxiolytics, targeting the underlying anxiety or mood component rather than the physical symptom itself. · Nursing considerations for PTSD — relaxation techniques, anxiety-reduction strategies, support groups, and antidepressants — overlap substantially with somatic-disorder care. See the PTSD lesson in the Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders unit for the full content; it isn't duplicated here.

What this section is building toward · After completing this module, you will be able to: · Utilize elements of clinical decision making for patients with selected concepts and alterations. · Integrate health promotion, specialized modalities and pharmacological agents for patients with selected health concepts and alterations. · Distinguish clinical manifestations and diagnostic findings for patients with selected health concepts and alterations. · Prioritize nursing interventions for selected health concepts and alterations, while recognizing scope of practice for the practical and registered nurse. · Analyze foundational concepts and emergent care. · Apply relevant informatics related to selected health concepts/alterations.

The course blueprint for Immune, Inflammation & Cellular Regulation · Exemplars · Inflammation — Hypersensitivity reaction (allergies); Diffuse connective tissue diseases (Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus); Osteoarthritis; Gout · Immune — HIV Infection / AIDS · Cellular Regulation — Cancer · Medication classes to know · ART (antiretroviral therapy) for HIV/AIDS — no individual drugs to memorize, but the therapy category as a whole, and the distinction between PrEP and PEP · DMARDs (disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs) · Corticosteroids · Antihistamines · NSAIDs · Chemotherapy — the general drug class, not individual agents · Filgrastim · Epoetin alfa · Allopurinol · Colchicine

t: Immunity Types & the Cells That Carry It Out
x: Four kinds of immunity, and which cell does what · Before the specific inflammatory and autoimmune conditions in this section make sense, it helps to have the underlying immune vocabulary straight — both how immunity is acquired and which cell lineages are doing the work. · Four types of immunity · Type | How it's acquired · Natural active | The body is exposed to a pathogen and produces its own antibodies in response (having and recovering from an actual infection) · Natural passive | Antibodies are transferred from one person to another naturally, without the receiving person's own immune system producing them (maternal antibodies crossing the placenta or passing through breast milk) · Artificial active | The body produces its own antibodies in response to a deliberately administered antigen (a vaccine) · Artificial passive | Premade antibodies are administered directly (an immunoglobulin injection), giving immediate but temporary protection since the person's own immune system never had to build the response · "Active" always means the person's own immune system is doing the antibody manufacturing (whether triggered by natural infection or a vaccine); "passive" always means the antibodies came from somewhere else and the protection fades once those borrowed antibodies degrade. · Where immune cells come from · All immune cells trace back to a single stem cell in the bone marrow, which branches into two major lines. The lymphoid line produces lymphocytes: B cells (which mature into antibody-producing plasma cells and long-lived memory cells), T cells (which branch further into helper T, cytotoxic T, and suppressor/regulatory T cells), and natural killer cells. The myeloid line produces granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells) along with monocytes, which themselves mature into macrophages and dendritic cells. · Three functional categories · Category | Cells | What they do · Phagocytic | Neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils | Engulf and destroy pathogens directly — the immune system's cleanup crew · Humoral | B cells, plasma cells, and the antibody classes IgA, IgM, IgG, IgE, IgD, plus memory cells | Antibody-based immunity: a B cell that encounters an antigen differentiates into an antibody-producing plasma cell and a long-lived memory cell that allows a faster response on re-exposure · Cell-mediated | Helper T (CD4) cells, suppressor/regulatory T cells, cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells | Direct cell-to-cell immune action: helper T cells coordinate the broader immune response, cytotoxic T cells and NK cells kill infected or abnormal cells directly, and suppressor/regulatory T cells dial the response back down once the threat has passed · Phagocyte-by-phagocyte: role and what goes wrong · Cell | Role | What happens when it's abnormal · Neutrophil | The first responder — smaller than a macrophage, it rapidly phagocytizes bacteria and fungi at the site of an acute infection | Neutropenia sharply raises the risk of rapid, severe bacterial infection and sepsis — the basis for neutropenic precautions · Macrophage | The larger, longer-acting phagocyte — clears cellular debris and secretes cytokines that recruit more immune cells to the site | Dysfunction impairs wound healing and pathogen clearance, and is part of the mechanism behind granulomatous diseases such as tuberculosis · Monocyte | Circulates in the bloodstream before migrating into tissue, where it matures into a macrophage or dendritic cell — essentially the macrophage's immature, circulating form | Abnormal counts (monocytopenia or monocytosis) alter the body's ability to replenish tissue macrophages during chronic inflammation or infection · Eosinophil | Releases toxic granules to destroy multicellular parasites (helminths) and participates in allergic reactions | Overactivity drives chronic tissue damage and airway hypersensitivity, as in asthma or hypereosinophilic syndrome · Basophil | Releases histamine and heparin into the bloodstream during systemic allergic reactions and inflammation | Over-activation causes the systemic vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and fluid shifts of anaphylaxis · CD4 is the marker worth remembering on sight: helper T cells are also called CD4 cells, and CD4 count is exactly what's tracked to stage HIV/AIDS progression later in this section — the same cell type shows up again as the one HIV specifically targets and destroys. · T-cell and NK subtypes — what goes wrong · Cell | Role | What happens when it's abnormal · Helper T (CD4) | Coordinates the immune response by releasing cytokines that activate macrophages, B cells, and cytotoxic T cells — it doesn't kill anything directly, it flags and directs | HIV destroys CD4 cells, paralyzing both cell-mediated and humoral immunity and opening the door to opportunistic infections (covered in depth later in this section) · Suppressor/regulatory T | Suppresses an overactive immune response and maintains self-tolerance once a threat has passed | Loss of suppression lets T cells attack healthy self-tissue — the mechanism behind autoimmune disease broadly, and specifically IPEX syndrome · Cytotoxic T (CD8) | Directly kills infected host cells and tumor cells using perforin and granzymes | Deficits allow unchecked viral replication and raise cancer risk · Natural killer (NK) cell | Destroys virus-infected or malignant cells that lack MHC Class I markers, without needing any prior exposure to the antigen | Dysfunction is linked to familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — uncontrolled immune activation and severe organ damage · The five immunoglobulin classes · Class | % of total Ig | Key role | What happens when it's abnormal · IgG | 75% | In serum and tissue; the major player in bloodborne and tissue infections; activates complement; the only class that crosses the placenta | Hypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG) causes recurrent bacterial infections; excessive antibody targeted at self-tissue drives tissue-specific autoimmune disease · IgA | 15% | In secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk, mucus); protects the respiratory/GI/GU tracts and passes to a nursing infant for protection | IgA deficiency leads to recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections · IgM | 10% | Mostly intravascular; the first immunoglobulin produced in a new infection; activates complement | Hyper-IgM syndrome — an inability to switch from IgM to IgG/IgA — leads to severe, recurrent infections · IgD | 0.2% | Small serum amounts; functions as an antigen receptor on naive B-cell membranes to assist B-cell maturation | Minimal clinical impact alone; alterations can affect initial B-cell activation efficiency · IgE | 0.004% | Drives allergic and hypersensitivity reactions (the antibody behind Type I reactions in the next lesson); also fights parasitic infections | Elevated levels drive Type I hypersensitivity — atopic dermatitis, asthma, anaphylaxis · Medications ending in "-mab" are monoclonal antibodies — lab-made versions of a B-cell antibody, engineered to target one specific protein, inflammatory cytokine, or tumor marker. Belimumab (for SLE) and the biologic DMARDs used in RA, both covered later in this section, follow this same naming pattern. · Complement — the amplification system behind antibody binding · Complement is a group of circulating plasma proteins, made in the liver, that activate in a cascade once an antibody binds its antigen. Antibody-antigen binding alone doesn't destroy an invader — it also takes complement activation, arrival of killer T cells, or recruitment of macrophages. Complement can be triggered through three pathways (classic — antibody-triggered; lectin — a plasma protein binding microbial sugars; alternative — direct activation on a microbial surface) and, once active, increases blood vessel permeability, attracts phagocytes to the site, and can directly lyse cells. This is highly useful but a double-edged sword: chronic or inappropriate complement activation is part of the mechanism behind many autoimmune diseases and chronic inflammation. · Factors that affect immune function — what the health history screens for · Age (immunosenescence) — aging brings impaired B- and T-lymphocyte function, decreased antibody production, reduced phagocytic response, and a failing ability to distinguish self from non-self — the net effect is more infections, more cancer, more autoimmune disease, and often blunted or absent classic signs/symptoms of infection and inflammation in an older adult · Nutrition — protein depletion causes lymphoid tissue atrophy, reduced antibody response, fewer circulating T cells, and impaired phagocytosis; specific micronutrient deficiencies (zinc in particular) are also linked to impaired immune function · Gender/hormones — estrogen tends to enhance immunity while androgens tend to be immunosuppressive, which helps explain why autoimmune diseases are more common in females · Genetics — a number of immunodeficiency and autoimmune disorders have known or suspected genetic/inheritance patterns, so a three-generation family history (both maternal and paternal sides) is part of a thorough immune assessment · Assessing for immune dysfunction, by system · A focused immune assessment watches for cues across every system: respiratory (rate changes, cough, wheezing/crackles/rhonchi, rhinitis, bronchospasm), cardiovascular (hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, vasculitis, anemia), gastrointestinal (hepatosplenomegaly, colitis, vomiting, diarrhea), genitourinary (frequency/burning, hematuria, discharge), musculoskeletal (joint mobility, edema, pain), skin (rashes, lesions, dermatitis, hematomas/purpura, edema/urticaria), and neurosensory (cognitive dysfunction, hearing/vision changes, headaches, ataxia, tetany). The health history itself also screens broadly: nutritional status, infection and immunization history, allergies, known autoimmune/neoplastic/chronic disease, surgeries, medications, and blood transfusions.

Four types, one timeline each, how each reaction actually presents, and the full medication lineup · A hypersensitivity reaction is an undesirable reaction associated with an immune response acting against foreign antigens or an organism's own tissue — sometimes a genuine threat overreacted to, and sometimes a harmless substance (a food, a medication, pollen, latex) mistakenly treated as dangerous. There are four classically described types, and each has its own mediator, onset timeline, and hallmark example. · Type | Mediator | Onset | Example · Type I | IgE-mediated (mast cell degranulation) | Within 1 hour | Anaphylaxis · Type II | IgG or IgM cytotoxic | Hours to days | Hemolytic anemia, hemolytic transfusion reaction, Goodpasture's syndrome · Type III | Immune complex-mediated (with complement activation) | 1–3 weeks | Serum sickness, SLE · Type IV | T-cell-mediated (cytokine-driven, not antibody-driven) | Days to weeks | Contact rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome · Type I is the one to recognize fastest in practice: it's IgE-driven, it happens within minutes to an hour of exposure, and it's the mechanism behind everything from a mosquito bite reaction to a full anaphylactic emergency — the same mechanism, just different severity and extent. Type IV stands out mechanistically, since it's driven by T cells and cytokines rather than antibodies at all, which is why it has the slowest onset of the four. · How Type I reactions actually present · Localized anaphylactic reaction — a pale, edematous wheal on the skin that contains fluid and is surrounded by a red flare; the classic example is a mosquito bite · Systemic anaphylactic reaction — starts as edema and pruritus at the exposure site, then progresses to bronchiole constriction, airway obstruction, and shock — this is the life-threatening version and a medical emergency requiring rapid, advanced care · Atopic reactions — a family of chronic, allergen-driven presentations rather than a single acute event (broken out below) · Anaphylaxis severity — a staged progression · The faster the onset after exposure, the more severe the reaction tends to be — and prior reaction severity does not predict how severe the next exposure's reaction will be. Mild reactions bring peripheral tingling, warmth, fullness in the mouth/throat, nasal congestion, periorbital swelling, and tearing, usually within the first 2 hours of exposure. Moderate reactions add flushing, anxiety, itching, and — more seriously — bronchospasm and airway/laryngeal edema with dyspnea, cough, and wheezing. Severe reactions (anaphylactic shock) progress rapidly to laryngeal edema, severe dyspnea, cyanosis, and hypotension, plus dysphagia, abdominal cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, and seizures — cardiac arrest and coma can follow. · Common causes of anaphylaxis · Foods — peanuts, tree nuts (walnuts, pecans, cashews, almonds), shellfish (shrimp, lobster, crab), fish, milk, eggs, soy, wheat · Medications — antibiotics (especially penicillin and sulfa drugs), allopurinol, radiocontrast agents, anesthetic agents (lidocaine, procaine), vaccines, hormones (insulin, vasopressin, ACTH), aspirin, NSAIDs — antibiotics and radiocontrast agents cause the most serious anaphylactic reactions , and penicillin is the most common medication trigger overall (about 10% of the population reports a penicillin allergy, though less than 5% have a clinically significant IgE- or T-cell-mediated allergy) · Other pharmaceutical/biologic agents — animal serums (tetanus antitoxin, snake venom antitoxin, rabies antitoxin), antigens used in skin testing · Insect stings — bees, wasps, hornets, yellow jackets, ants (including fire ants) — the Hymenoptera family causes the most common serious sting-related allergic reactions · Latex — medical and nonmedical products containing latex · A closely related but distinct entity is an anaphylactoid reaction — it looks like anaphylaxis and is treated the same way, but it's triggered by non-IgE-mediated mast cell/basophil degranulation (from medications, food, exercise, or cytotoxic transfusions) rather than a true allergic mechanism. It's rarely fatal, but the nurse's response to it is identical to true anaphylaxis. · The atopic reactions · Reaction | Presentation · Hay fever | Sneezing, nasal drainage, swelling of the nasal mucosa that can obstruct the airway, itching around the eyes and throat, excessive tearing · Asthma reaction | Wheezing, chest tightness, thick sputum production, dyspnea · Atopic dermatitis | Edematous skin lesions that contain vesicles · Angioedema | Swelling starts in the face and progresses to other parts of the body; lesions the client describes as itching, burning, or stinging · Urticaria (hives) | Raised, edematous, pink areas on the body that the client describes as itching · Type II and beyond · A Type II hypersensitivity reaction shows up clinically as kidney injury, pulmonary hemorrhage (Goodpasture's syndrome), and hemolytic blood transfusion reactions — antibodies attacking cells or tissue directly, rather than forming circulating complexes the way Type III does (the mechanism behind SLE, covered in its own lesson). A reaction can also occur in response to immunotherapy itself once allergen injections have been initiated, which is exactly why immunotherapy sessions include a monitored observation period after each injection. · Next Gen-style scenario worth knowing: a client sustains a hemolytic blood reaction from incorrect blood administration. This is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction — think ABO/Rh incompatibility. Expected cues include fever, chills, low back pain, flank pain, hypotension, tachycardia, and hemoglobinuria; the nurse's first action is always to stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV line open with normal saline, and notify the provider — then send the remaining blood/tubing back to the blood bank per policy. The whole scenario is also a teaching moment on prevention: the two-nurse patient/blood product verification check at the bedside exists specifically to prevent this reaction. · Diagnosing an allergy: skin testing · Patch test — the allergen is placed on a patch applied to the skin; the reaction is delayed because the patch must be worn for 48–72 hours · Scratch or prick test — the allergen is placed on the skin and a pricking device allows it to enter; a reaction appears in 5–10 minutes · Intradermal test — the allergen is injected under the skin; a reaction appears in about 10 minutes · A wheal-and-flare response to any of these tests indicates a positive reaction · Other diagnostic cues: sputum, nasal, and bronchial secretions showing eosinophils; a pulmonary function test showing deteriorated functioning; a CBC with white blood cell differential pointing toward immunodeficiency; and elevated total serum IgE, which supports the diagnosis since most allergic reactions are IgE-mediated. Before skin testing , antihistamines and corticosteroids (including OTC allergy medications) must be stopped 48–96 hours beforehand since they suppress skin test reactivity and would produce a false negative; testing is never performed during active bronchospasm, and emergency equipment must be on hand in case the test itself triggers a reaction. · Priority nursing interventions · Ensure all allergies are documented on the health record — medications, food, latex, and anything else · Use latex-free gloves and supplies for any client with a latex allergy · Provide prescribed pre-treatments as indicated before selected procedures, medications, or treatments · Administer antihistamines, decongestants, anti-itch medications, corticosteroids, and leukotriene receptor antagonists as ordered · Treat skin rashes and manage anaphylactic shock as needed · For immunotherapy: rotate injection sites, and observe the client for 20–30 minutes after each injection to catch any adverse reaction · Never leave a client alone during allergy skin testing — some clients are highly sensitive and can develop an anaphylactic reaction to the test itself · Be aware that hypersensitivity responses can intensify with repeated exposure to the same allergen, not just the first one · During an active anaphylactic reaction: assess airway, breathing, and vital signs first; notify the rapid response team/provider promptly; give epinephrine (1:1000 dilution, subcutaneous, upper extremity or thigh, may be followed by a continuous IV infusion) — antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and should never be substituted for epinephrine; give supplemental oxygen and IV fluids (normal saline, volume expanders, vasopressors) to support hemodynamics; older adults and those with hypertension, arteriopathy, or ischemic heart disease are at higher risk for adverse effects from epinephrine · After epinephrine, transport/observe the patient in an ED-level setting — a biphasic ("rebound") reaction can occur 4–8 hours after the initial reaction, and longer observation is warranted for anyone who ingested the allergen, needed more than one epinephrine dose, had hypotension or pharyngeal edema, or has a history of asthma · For insect-sting allergy, venom immunotherapy is used as a control measure (not a cure) to reduce systemic reaction risk; for penicillin or insulin allergy in a patient who needs the drug, desensitization (controlled anaphylaxis with gradual mediator release) may be used — patients must avoid lapses in therapy afterward, since a gap can let the allergic reaction reappear · Priority complications · Anaphylactic shock · Soft tissue angioedema · Comorbidity with asthma and sinusitis · Priority medications · Diphenhydramine — oral/IV antihistamine for urticaria and allergic rhinitis; given together with famotidine (an H2 receptor blocker) and IV methylprednisolone for an emergent allergic reaction; causes drowsiness · Pramoxine/calamine — topical antipruritic lotion; do not use on broken skin · Epinephrine — subcutaneous, IM, or IV; a sympathomimetic drug for anaphylaxis that causes bronchodilation and stimulates heart rate; don't use if the solution is cloudy or contains particles; available in self-injector pens for clients at risk for allergic/anaphylactic reactions · Pseudoephedrine — oral/nasal decongestant for allergic rhinitis; should not be used more than 2–3 days to avoid rebound congestion (some agents may be used long-term depending on the specific drug) · Montelukast, zafirlukast — oral leukotriene receptor antagonists that block leukotriene-driven airway edema, bronchoconstriction, and mucus production · Ketotifen, olopatadine, azelastine, cromolyn — nasal, oral, or inhaled (depending on the agent) mast cell stabilizers that inhibit the release of histamine and leukotriene to treat allergic rhinitis · Flonase, Beconase, Nasocort, Rhinocort — nasal corticosteroids to treat allergic rhinitis; may be used long-term without rebound congestion risk, depending on the specific agent · Immunotherapy — subcutaneous, titrated amounts of allergen; takes 1–2 years to reach maximum effect, with injections given at a clinic or provider's office; a home-based sublingual alternative exists, administered until hyposensitivity is achieved; used when usual drug therapy is ineffective or the client cannot avoid the allergen · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Avoid the allergen; observe for signs and symptoms of a hypersensitivity reaction · How to administer prescribed medications, including nasal sprays · The potential for a delayed reaction to immunotherapy injections, and what to do if a reaction occurs · Seek medical assistance at the first sign of anaphylaxis · Report all allergies at every health care visit, including latex · Using an epinephrine auto-injector · Patient education on the auto-injector follows three steps worth walking through explicitly, since a patient or caregiver may need to do this under extreme stress: slide the device out of its carrying case, pull off the blue safety cap (never put a thumb over the orange needle end while doing this), and push the orange needle end firmly against the outer thigh until it clicks, holding it in place for the several seconds specified on the device before removing it.

A multisystem autoimmune disease with a signature facial rash — and a genuinely long medication list · Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, progressive autoimmune disease that causes failure of major organ systems — the immune system attacks the body's own tissue, and because there's no single target organ, its symptom list looks scattered until it's organized by system. · Epidemiology, pathophysiology, and triggers · SLE occurs 4–12 times more often in females than males. The disease starts when the immune system mistakenly recognizes components of the cell's nucleus as a foreign antigen; B cells overproduce antibodies with help from cytokines such as B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) , and the resulting antigen-antibody immune complexes get trapped in capillaries of visceral organs and destroy host cells — this is the mechanism behind most SLE clinical manifestations. Given the strong female predominance, estrogen and X-linked genetic factors are thought to play a role. Exogenous/environmental triggers include cigarette smoke, alcohol, ultraviolet light (sunlight and fluorescent bulbs), certain medications (hydralazine, minocycline, procainamide — the classic drug-induced lupus triggers), viral infections, emotional or physical stress (surgery, pregnancy), and occupational silica dust exposure. · Neuropsychiatric SLE · Central nervous system involvement in SLE spans the full range of neurologic disease: psychosis, cognitive impairment, seizures, peripheral and cranial neuropathies, transverse myelitis, and stroke. These often present subtly, as changes in behavior or cognitive ability, which is why the nurse specifically asks the patient and family about behavioral changes, not just physical symptoms. · Priority assessments/cues · Vital signs for fever · Cough, difficulty breathing, cardiac dysrhythmias · Polyarthralgia (pain in many joints) and stiffness in the morning · Excessive fatigue, weight loss · Redness to the face with a "butterfly" rash over the cheeks and bridge of the nose, and a scaly rash to the face and upper torso, erythema of the palms · Feeling of malaise, weakness, and anorexia · Ulcers of the mouth and nose, balding, lesions on the scalp · Seizures, disordered thinking, impaired memory, peripheral neuropathy, photosensitivity · Symptoms of SLE, by system · System | Findings · Skin & hair | Photosensitivity, butterfly rash, alopecia · Mental | Cognitive dysfunction, psychosis, seizures, fever · Lungs | Pleuritic chest pain, inflammation, pneumonia, pleuritis · Heart | Pleuritic chest pain, heart murmur · Kidneys | Inflammation, failure · Joints & muscle | Swollen joints, arthritis · Blood | Lab abnormalities, blood clots, anemia · Mouth | Ulcers · The butterfly rash is the single most recognizable clinical clue for SLE, but it's neither universal (not every SLE patient has it) nor exclusive to SLE — it's a strong pointer, not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion. SLE is also the classic example of a Type III hypersensitivity reaction (covered in the previous lesson): circulating immune complexes deposit in tissue throughout the body and trigger complement-mediated inflammation, which is exactly why the damage shows up in so many organs rather than one localized site. · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Antinuclear antibody (ANA) — positive in more than 99% of clients with SLE, giving it exceptional sensitivity (though not specificity — see the hook below) · Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) — antibody against DNA that is highly specific to SLE and helps differentiate it from drug-induced lupus · Antiphospholipid antibodies (ALPs) — positive in about 30% of clients with SLE; this is the lab value that explains the blood-clot risk in the table above, and why warfarin shows up in the medication list below · Anti-Smith antibody (Sm) — a specific nuclear protein antibody, positive in about 30% of clients with SLE · C-reactive protein (CRP) — elevated; used to determine disease status and therapy effectiveness · Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) — elevated; used the same way, to track disease status and therapy effectiveness · Complete blood count (CBC) and coagulation studies — thrombocytopenia, anemia, leukocytosis or leukopenia, and impaired clotting · ANA is positive in SLE about 97% of the time, but it's also positive in up to 30% of clients with rheumatoid arthritis — so a positive ANA alone doesn't distinguish the two. The anti-Smith antibody and antiphospholipid antibodies are more specific to SLE, while rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (covered in the RA lesson) point toward RA. · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Provide meticulous skin care; apply creams and ointments for skin rash as indicated · Give medications to manage pain and decrease the inflammatory response · Perform client care activities with built-in rest periods, due to fatigue · Oxygen therapy as indicated · Measure intake and output if the client is receiving corticosteroids (fluid retention risk) · Ensure safety with memory deficits, personality changes, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, weakness, or paresthesia · Diet high in iron, protein, folic acid, and vitamins if there's no contraindication — kidney disease would rule out a high-protein diet — and help maintain appropriate weight · Provide emotional support and a supportive environment for the client to verbalize feelings · Priority actual & potential complications · Complications of SLE can affect every system: stroke, seizures, memory impairment, myocardial infarction, dysrhythmias, pericarditis, heart failure, pleurisy, dyspnea, kidney failure, severe arthralgia, impaired mobility, and paralysis. Anxiety, depression, and psychosis are also common while a client is dealing with a life-altering, chronic illness. · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · SLE is a multisystem disorder, so the focus of care spans all body systems — it may cause hypertension, arrhythmias, nephritis, pericarditis, anemia, and coronary artery disease · Monitor clients for depression from managing the many systemic complications SLE presents, and make appropriate referrals · Decreased secretion of saliva and tears ( Sjögren's syndrome ) can occur, causing dry eyes, photosensitivity, and dry mouth · Attend to the psychosocial needs of both the client and family · Priority medications · Indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac — oral NSAIDs for arthralgia and arthritis; most significant adverse effect is GI bleeding · Hydroxychloroquine — oral antimalarial drug to treat fatigue, joint pain, and skin disorders; recommended eye exam every 6–12 months, since it causes retinopathy · Dapsone — oral antileprosy drug used to manage urticaria, oral ulcers, and chronic symptoms; used if the client cannot tolerate hydroxychloroquine · Methylprednisolone — IV/oral corticosteroid to treat severe skin disorders; tapering doses may manage polyarthritis flare-ups; high doses are effective but should be limited due to side effects · Methotrexate — oral/IV steroid-sparing immunosuppressant, considered a standard treatment used as an alternative to corticosteroids; monitor CBC for hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression · Tacrolimus, pimecrolimus — topical calcineurin inhibitors/immunosuppressants used instead of corticosteroids to manage skin rashes · Azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolic acid — oral/IV immunosuppressants used to treat severe organ involvement with SLE (most frequently lupus nephritis); prevents the need for long-term corticosteroid therapy; contraindicated in pregnancy along with methotrexate · Warfarin — oral/IV anticoagulant to prevent blood clotting/DVTs (the clinical answer to that positive antiphospholipid antibody result); monitor INR · Belimumab — IV monoclonal antibody specifically for SLE; binds and inactivates BLyS, preventing it from stimulating B cells to make antibodies against the body's own nuclei; live vaccines are contraindicated for 30 days before starting this medication · Rituximab — an additional monoclonal antibody used for its immune-modulating effect in SLE · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Identify and avoid triggers for SLE · Avoid sun or ultraviolet light exposure, or protect with sunscreen and appropriate clothing — sun/UV exposure can trigger a flare · Use fragrance-free soap for skin care; avoid perfumed or harsh emollients · Medication therapy, rationale, administration, and side effects · Meal planning for optimal nutrition — consult a dietitian as needed, especially given the increased cardiovascular disease risk (hypertension, atherosclerosis) associated with SLE · Smoking cessation , including e-cigarettes/ENDS — smoking worsens kidney function, inhibits liver function (which can blunt the effectiveness of medications like hydroxychloroquine), and raises the risk of osteoporosis, skin disease, and (in SLE specifically) lung cancer and other rare cancers · Bone health monitoring — long-term corticosteroid use raises osteoporosis/fracture risk, so get a baseline bone mineral density test at diagnosis and before starting steroids, then every 2 years; encourage daily calcium and vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise · Watch for signs of infection given corticosteroid-related immunosuppression, especially in acutely ill patients · Information for SLE support groups and community resources

A mechanical, wear-and-tear joint disease — and how it differs from the autoimmune process in the next lesson · Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive disorder marked by destruction of the articular cartilage of the joints — a mechanical, degenerative process rather than the autoimmune process behind rheumatoid arthritis (RA), covered in the next lesson. · Priority assessments/cues · Joint pain that is aggravated by activity, alleviated by rest · Difficulty moving from sitting to standing, or joint stiffness after being in one position for extended periods · Difficulty completing daily activities due to joint pain · Heberden's nodes or Bouchard's nodes — redness, swelling, or bony outgrowths around the finger joints caused by osteophyte formation · Asymmetry of affected extremities — OA is generally unilateral · Crepitation in the joint; cartilage particles in the joint cavity · Knees may be bowlegged or knock-kneed · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · CT scan, MRI, bone scan — arthritic changes to joints · X-rays — stage the degree of damage to joints · Synovial fluid analysis — differentiates OA from other types of arthritis; synovial fluid is normal with OA (compare to RA, where WBC count is elevated and viscosity is decreased) · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Administer drug therapy as prescribed · Assist with completion of activities of daily living (ADLs) · Immobilize the affected joint with a brace or splint during the acute phase of inflammation · Range-of-motion exercises; physical and occupational therapy consults · Bed cradle to keep pressure from bed linens off the client's affected feet · Moist heat to help with stiffness; ensure rest · Priority actual & potential complications · Physical immobility and disability · Sleep disturbance and social isolation · Gout and bone death (osteonecrosis) · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · OA can be debilitating in advanced stages, impacting all functionality of the client's life. · Priority medications · Ibuprofen — oral NSAID and analgesic; watch for gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding · Capsaicin cream — topical analgesic that blocks the pain impulse; available by prescription and over the counter · Cortisone — intra-articular corticosteroid to decrease joint inflammation and swelling; further intervention is needed after 4 injections if pain and swelling are not relieved · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Heat for joint pain, cold compresses for active inflammation · End exercise and rest if pain starts in the affected joint · Take pain medications as prescribed · Wear splints on the affected joint as prescribed · Use assistive devices to help with immobility · Weight loss to minimize stress on the joints · Modify the home environment for safety · Provide support and resources when arthritic changes require additional assistance with ADLs and mobility · OA vs. RA at a glance · Feature | Osteoarthritis | Rheumatoid Arthritis · Underlying process | Degenerative — loss of articular cartilage, bone ends rub together | Autoimmune — swollen, inflamed synovial membrane, erosion of bone · Joint pattern | Asymmetrical | Symmetrical · Morning stiffness | Lasts less than 30 minutes | Lasts more than 30 minutes · Symptoms | Pain and stiffness in movement | Pain, stiffness, and inflammation · The 30-minute stiffness cutoff and symmetrical-vs-asymmetrical pattern are the two fastest bedside discriminators — see the Rheumatoid Arthritis lesson for the full autoimmune picture, deformities, labs, and the much longer RA medication list.

A chronic systemic autoimmune disease — deformities, specific antibodies, and the longest medication list in this section · Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic immune disease characterized by inflammation and destruction of connective tissue and membranes within the synovial joints — a fundamentally different process from the mechanical wear-and-tear of osteoarthritis (OA), covered in the previous lesson. · Epidemiology and risk factors · RA is an autoimmune disease of unknown origin, with females affected about 3 times more often than males. Onset can occur at any age but is most common between the third and sixth decades of life, and incidence increases with age. Identified risk factors include family history, environmental influences (diet, geographic location), nulliparity, and the modifiable factors of smoking and obesity — an elevated BMI increases the risk of RA and shortens the time to onset, an association strongest in women and smokers; obesity also worsens disease-related outcomes and lowers the likelihood of achieving remission. · Pathophysiology — how the joint gets destroyed · An autoimmune reaction occurs in the synovial tissue: antigens are presented to T lymphocytes, triggering proliferation of T and B cells. B cells (plasma cells) produce antibodies that combine with antigens to form immune complexes, which deposit in synovial tissue and trigger inflammation. The RA synovium breaks down collagen, causing edema and proliferation of the synovial membrane. In chronic inflammation, this doesn't resolve — instead, pannus forms (a proliferation of new synovial tissue infiltrated with inflammatory cells), which destroys cartilage and erodes bone, producing loss of articular surfaces and joint motion. Muscle fibers degenerate, and tendon/ligament elasticity is lost. The same inflammatory process is also implicated in atherosclerosis (RA interferes with production of protective HDL cholesterol) and in neuropathies/paresthesias from synovial inflammation compressing adjacent nerves. · ACR/EULAR classification criteria · The American College of Rheumatology and European League Against Rheumatism established a point-based scoring system for diagnosing RA: a total score of 6 or greater is required. Points are assigned for joint involvement (number and size of joints affected), serology (low- or high-positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP), abnormal acute phase reactants (ESR or CRP), and symptom duration greater than 6 weeks. This applies to patients with at least one joint showing synovitis not explained by another disease. · Priority assessments/cues · Vital signs for elevated temperature — low-grade with inflammation, fever with infection · Severity and duration of morning pain, usually lasting 30 minutes or more , and may last throughout the day · Joint pain, warmth, swelling, stiffness, tenderness to touch, limited range of motion, deformity, nodules at joints, and muscle atrophy · Excessive fatigue, weight loss, anorexia · Difficulty grasping objects, due to extensor and flexor tendon involvement in the wrist · Decreased secretion of saliva and tears ( Sjögren's syndrome ), causing dry eyes, photosensitivity, and dry mouth · Psychosocial needs of the client and family · The deformities of RA · Swan neck deformity — the middle joint of the finger is extended (bent back) more than normal, and the end joint is flexed (bent down) · Boutonnière deformity — the finger permanently bends down at the middle joint while the end joint bends backward · Ulnar drift — swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints (the knuckles at the base of the fingers) causes the fingers to become displaced toward the little finger · Hallux valgus (bunion) — lateral deviation of the hallux (great toe) on the first metatarsal · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · White blood cell count (WBC) in synovial fluid — elevated, with decreased viscosity · C-reactive protein (CRP) — elevated, showing active inflammation · Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) — elevated, showing active inflammation · Rheumatoid factor (RF) — positive in up to 90% of clients with RA · Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) — positive in over 80% of clients with RA · Antinuclear antibody (ANA) — positive in up to 30% of clients with RA (also positive in SLE — see that lesson's lab hook for how to tell the two apart) · X-ray — erosion and narrowing of joint space, bony growths, and osteoporosis · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Assist with activities and provide rest periods, being mindful of morning stiffness · Provide range-of-motion exercises to maintain joint function · Avoid weight bearing on inflamed extremities · Use splints on affected extremities to prevent contractures · Cold and heat applications to joints as indicated · Medication as prescribed, to manage pain and decrease the inflammatory response · Provide optimal nutrition to compensate for appetite loss due to pain and fatigue · Provide meticulous skin care · Measure intake and output — corticosteroids may cause fluid retention · Provide emotional support and a therapeutic environment to verbalize feelings · Consult physical and occupational therapy as indicated · Priority actual & potential complications · Scleritis, Sjögren's syndrome (decreased tears/saliva) · Pericarditis, myocarditis, pleural effusion, pneumothorax · Physical immobility due to deformities · Cardiovascular disease — up to 40% of RA deaths trace to cardiovascular disease, driven by elevated lipids, chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, or abnormal homocysteine levels · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · Clients with long-standing RA may develop Felty syndrome — low WBC and splenomegaly, raising infection risk · RA is common in older adults, who may be on several medications already — polypharmacy issues should be considered · DMARDs — the two families, and where they fit in the treatment sequence · Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) can suppress the autoimmune response, alter disease progression, and halt further tissue damage — unlike NSAIDs, they can actually slow or stop bone loss and destruction, which is why treatment starts with a DMARD within the first 3 months of diagnosis rather than waiting. Nonbiologic DMARDs (methotrexate is the preferred first agent, alongside leflunomide, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine) reduce proinflammatory cytokines and increase anti-inflammatory ones. Biologic DMARDs are engineered to target a specific inflammatory mediator — TNF-alpha, B cells, T cells, IL-1, or IL-6 — and tend to work faster with less radiologic progression, but are reserved for moderate-to-severe RA that hasn't responded adequately to nonbiologic DMARDs because of cost and shorter track record. A newer class, JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib), bind Janus kinase enzymes to block cytokine production, and are used after initial DMARD therapy has failed. Before starting biologic therapy, screen for latent TB (tuberculin skin test) and hepatitis B/C, since immunosuppression can reactivate these infections. · Priority medications · Aspirin — oral NSAID to decrease pain and inflammation; most significant adverse effect is GI bleeding; monitor serum salicylate levels for toxicity if dosage exceeds 3,600 mg daily · Celecoxib — oral COX-2 inhibitor to decrease pain and inflammation; fewer GI side effects than traditional NSAIDs, though the risk still exists — NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors relieve symptoms only and do not prevent erosions or alter disease progression · Hydroxychloroquine — oral antimalarial drug to treat fatigue and joint inflammation; recommended eye exam every 6–12 months, since it causes retinopathy · Leflunomide, sulfasalazine — oral antirheumatic drugs; leflunomide blocks immune cell overproduction and is teratogenic — should not be administered unless pregnancy is ruled out; sulfasalazine decreases pain and inflammation and may prevent damage to joints · Hydrocortisone, prednisone — intra-articular/oral corticosteroids to manage acute RA flare-ups, or as a short-term "bridge" while waiting for slower-acting DMARDs like methotrexate to take effect (roughly 6 weeks); not recommended long-term due to side effects, and weight gain is a leading reason patients stop taking them · Methotrexate — oral/IV steroid-sparing immunosuppressant used as an alternative to corticosteroids; monitor CBC for hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression · Tofacitinib, baricitinib — oral JAK inhibitors that interfere with Janus kinase enzymes that cause joint inflammation; used after initial DMARD therapy fails · Adalimumab — a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor that decreases immune and inflammatory response, used for clients who have not responded to other antirheumatic drugs; given as a subcutaneous biologic injection · Anakinra — subcutaneous interleukin-1 receptor antagonist that blocks the inflammatory response; used for clients who have not responded to, or cannot tolerate, other antirheumatic drugs · Opioid analgesics are generally avoided in RA given the potential for continuing need for pain relief in a chronic disease; low-dose antidepressants (amitriptyline, paroxetine, sertraline) may be used short-term for sleep and mood · Nonpharmacologic management and surgery · Heat (warm baths/showers, moist compresses, paraffin dips for small joints — maximum benefit within 20 minutes) relieves pain, stiffness, and spasm; therapeutic exercise is more comfortable and effective after heat application · Splints and braces rest acutely inflamed joints and limit motion; canes, crutches, and walkers offload painful weight-bearing joints · Physical and occupational therapy for range-of-motion, muscle-strengthening, pacing activities, and work simplification · Reconstructive surgery (synovectomy, tenorrhaphy, arthrodesis, joint replacement) is used when pain isn't relieved by conservative measures and independence is threatened; surgery is avoided during exacerbations · A Mediterranean-style diet may reduce RA disease activity; smoking cessation should always be discussed given the RA-smoking-BMI risk relationship above · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Long-term expectations of the disease · Medication administration and side effects · Protection of small joints — avoid repetitive movements, use the strongest joints for tasks, modify activities to decrease stress on joints · Modifications that may be needed to the home, and assistive devices to maintain a safe environment · Potential for corticosteroid therapy to cause weight gain — counsel on a weight loss program and a tolerable exercise regimen that minimizes overexertion · Aquatic exercises in warm water, cold and heat therapy to relieve stiffness, muscle spasms, and pain · RA support groups and community resources, including the Arthritis Foundation

Crystal-induced arthritis — one joint, one classic presentation, and a treat-the-flare vs. lower-the-baseline medication split · Gout is a metabolic form of inflammatory arthritis caused by hyperuricemia — chronically elevated serum uric acid. When uric acid concentration exceeds what the blood can keep dissolved, it precipitates out as needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals that deposit in and around joints, triggering an intense inflammatory response. Unlike RA (autoimmune) or OA (mechanical wear), gout is fundamentally a problem of purine/uric acid metabolism and excretion. · Where the uric acid comes from · Uric acid is the breakdown product of purines — compounds found in the body's own cells and in certain foods. Hyperuricemia develops from overproduction (the body makes too much uric acid), underexcretion (the kidneys don't clear it efficiently enough — the more common mechanism), or both. Hyperuricemia alone does not equal gout: many people run a high uric acid level and never develop a flare, and an acute attack can occur even with a uric acid level that momentarily reads normal, so the diagnosis rests on the clinical presentation and joint fluid findings, not the lab number alone. · Classic presentation — podagra · The hallmark presentation is podagra : sudden, severe pain, swelling, warmth, and redness at the base of the great toe (the first metatarsophalangeal joint), often starting overnight and waking the client from sleep. The pain is often so severe that even the weight of a bedsheet is intolerable. Other joints can be affected — ankle, knee, wrist, fingers — but the great toe is the single most classic and most frequently tested location. A single joint (monoarticular) is typical of an acute attack; chronic, untreated gout can eventually become polyarticular. · The four stages of gout · Stage | What's happening · Asymptomatic hyperuricemia | Elevated serum uric acid with no symptoms yet — most people in this stage never progress further · Acute gouty arthritis (a flare) | Sudden-onset, intensely painful monoarticular inflammation — classically podagra — triggered by crystal deposition · Intercritical period | The symptom-free interval between flares; crystals may still be silently depositing even though the joint feels normal · Chronic tophaceous gout | Long-standing, poorly controlled disease leads to tophi — visible, firm deposits of urate crystals in soft tissue (classically the ear helix, fingers, and around joints) — plus joint damage and deformity · Common triggers for a flare · Diet — purine-rich foods: red meat, organ meats, shellfish; high-fructose corn syrup · Alcohol — beer in particular, both a purine source and a driver of underexcretion · Dehydration — concentrates uric acid and impairs renal clearance · Certain medications — thiazide and loop diuretics reduce uric acid excretion; low-dose aspirin has a similar effect · Rapid changes in uric acid level — including starting urate-lowering therapy itself, which can paradoxically trigger a flare in the first weeks (this is why colchicine or an NSAID is often co-prescribed as flare prophylaxis when allopurinol is first started) · Obesity, trauma/surgery, and acute illness · Priority diagnostics · Joint (synovial) fluid aspiration and analysis — the gold standard: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals under polarized light confirm gout, and fluid is also sent for culture to rule out septic arthritis, which can mimic gout's presentation and is a true emergency if missed · Serum uric acid — supportive but not diagnostic alone, since it can be normal during an acute flare and elevated in people who never develop gout · X-ray — may show "punched-out" bony erosions in longstanding disease; often normal early in the disease course · 24-hour urine uric acid — helps distinguish overproduction from underexcretion, which can guide medication choice · Exam trap worth knowing: pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, CPPD) looks clinically similar to gout — sudden monoarticular joint pain and swelling — but is caused by a different crystal (calcium pyrophosphate, not urate) that is rhomboid-shaped and positively birefringent, and more often affects the knee rather than the great toe. The two are told apart by joint aspiration, not by symptoms alone. · Medications — treat the flare vs. lower the baseline · Gout medications split cleanly into two jobs that are easy to mix up on an exam: calming an active flare right now, versus lowering uric acid long-term to prevent future flares and tophi. Starting a urate-lowering drug during an active flare is generally avoided — it's started once the flare has resolved, and typically with flare-prophylaxis medication overlapping the first few weeks. · Colchicine — the classic acute-flare medication; most effective when started within the first 12–24 hours of an attack; the most common dose-limiting side effects are GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), and it has a narrow therapeutic window with serious toxicity (including bone marrow suppression) in overdose or with renal/hepatic impairment — also used at a lower dose for flare prophylaxis when starting allopurinol · NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen, ibuprofen) — first-line for an acute flare in clients who can tolerate them; avoid in significant renal impairment, active GI bleeding, or in a client already on an anticoagulant · Corticosteroids (oral prednisone, or intra-articular injection) — an alternative for an acute flare when NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated or not tolerated, particularly useful when only one or two joints are involved (intra-articular) or in an older adult with multiple comorbidities · Allopurinol — the first-line urate-lowering medication for chronic/long-term management; a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production; start at a low dose and titrate up to the target uric acid level; requires renal dose adjustment, and carries a rare but serious hypersensitivity/Stevens-Johnson risk, especially in clients of Southeast Asian descent carrying the HLA-B*5801 allele · Febuxostat — an alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor for clients who can't tolerate allopurinol; carries a boxed warning for increased cardiovascular death risk compared to allopurinol · Probenecid — a uricosuric agent that increases renal excretion of uric acid instead of reducing production; less commonly used, and ineffective in significant renal impairment; requires adequate fluid intake to prevent uric acid kidney stones · Priority nursing interventions · During an acute flare: rest and elevate the affected joint, avoid weight-bearing on it, apply ice (not heat — heat worsens acute inflammatory joint pain), and administer prescribed medication promptly since early treatment shortens the flare · Encourage generous fluid intake (2–3 L/day if not otherwise restricted) to promote uric acid excretion and reduce kidney stone risk · Dietary teaching — limit purine-rich foods (organ meats, red meat, shellfish) and alcohol (especially beer); limit high-fructose corn syrup; low-fat dairy and vitamin C may be protective · Teach that urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol/febuxostat) is a long-term, ongoing commitment aimed at the uric acid level itself, not a rescue medication for an active flare — stopping it once a client feels better lets uric acid climb back up · Monitor renal function, since kidney disease both raises gout risk (impaired excretion) and limits some medication choices · Never start allopurinol during an acute flare — treat the flare first, then start urate-lowering therapy once it resolves, typically with colchicine or an NSAID overlapping the first weeks as flare prophylaxis

CD4 destruction, the full assessment and lab picture, and the ART/PrEP/PEP distinction · HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is a retrovirus that damages the immune system, making the host susceptible to infections that would otherwise be prevented by the body's immune response. It specifically targets and destroys CD4 (helper T) cells — the same cell type introduced earlier in this section as the coordinator of the broader cell-mediated immune response. · There is currently no cure for HIV: the virus establishes hidden reservoirs in the body that ART cannot reach or eliminate, and viral levels rebound quickly if treatment is stopped. This is the underlying reason ART is a lifelong, daily therapy rather than a fixed-length course — it's not that ART "isn't working" once a client feels well, it's that stopping it lets a reservoir that was never actually cleared start replicating again. · HIV infection vs. AIDS · HIV infection describes the presence of the virus, which can exist for years without progressing further, especially with treatment. Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is severe immunodeficiency and susceptibility to malignancies and infections resulting from untreated HIV — the advanced stage, diagnosed once CD4 count falls below a defined threshold or the client develops a defined AIDS-defining opportunistic illness. · CD4 staging, stage by stage · Stage | CD4+ T cells/µL | CD4+ % · Stage 0 | — | — · Stage 1 | ≥ 500 | ≥ 26% · Stage 2 | 200–499 | 14–25% · Stage 3 (AIDS) | < 200 | < 14% · If a stage 3–defining opportunistic illness has been diagnosed, the client is classified as stage 3 (AIDS) regardless of CD4 count . That list of stage-3-defining illnesses is long, but the highest-yield ones to recognize are: Candida of the bronchi/trachea/lungs or esophagus, invasive cervical cancer, disseminated or extrapulmonary coccidioidomycosis or cryptococcosis, chronic intestinal cryptosporidiosis (>1 month), CMV disease or CMV retinitis with vision loss, HIV encephalopathy, chronic herpes simplex ulcers (>1 month), disseminated/extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, Kaposi sarcoma, Burkitt/immunoblastic/primary brain lymphoma, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex or M. tuberculosis , Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, recurrent Salmonella septicemia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, and HIV wasting syndrome. · Transmission · HIV is transmitted through contact with infected blood, seminal fluid, vaginal secretions, amniotic fluid, and breast milk — not through casual contact . Higher viral concentration in the fluid raises transmission risk. Mother-to-child transmission can occur in utero, at delivery, or through breastfeeding, though most perinatal transmission happens during labor and delivery, which is why zidovudine is dosed as above around that window. A client who takes ART as prescribed throughout pregnancy and delivery, and whose infant receives HIV medicine for 2–6 weeks after birth, can bring the risk of transmitting HIV to the baby to less than 1% ; the current U.S. recommendation supports shared decision-making between the client and provider about infant feeding, since even an undetectable viral load does not bring breastfeeding transmission risk to zero. Risk factors include sharing injection drug equipment, condomless sex with an infected partner (either gender), and (historically) receiving contaminated blood products or organ transplants — donated blood has been tested for HIV antibodies and the p24 antigen since 1999, making transfusion-related transmission now extremely rare. · Priority assessments/cues · Nausea, headache, malaise, swollen lymph nodes, sore throat, fever, joint pain, rash (typically 2–3 weeks after infection), and signs of opportunistic infections · Pericardial friction rubs or murmurs, dyspnea, tachypnea, wheezing, cough · Memory loss, slurred speech, tremors, agitation, seizures, paralysis, papilledema, eye exudate · Candida patches, blisters, and other lesions in the mouth; white lesions on the sides of the tongue; white patches in the throat; tooth decay, gingivitis, vomiting, diarrhea, rectal lesions · Pallor, cyanosis of tissues, alopecia, poor skin turgor, lesions and other skin eruptions, bruises on mucous membranes · Lesions and discharge from the genitals, excoriation of the perineum · Diagnostic criteria of HIV progression to AIDS · Priority laboratory tests/diagnostic cues · Rapid HIV screening test — if positive, followed by a confirmatory blood test · In-home HIV testing — self-administered, with confidential results · P24 antigen assay — measures the amount of HIV viral core protein in the blood · CD4 T-cell count — monitors progression of HIV; normal is 800–1,200 cells/mm³ , and it decreases as the disease progresses · Viral load — higher viral loads indicate disease progression; the treatment goal is an undetectable viral load · Complete blood count (CBC) — pancytopenia · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Provide antiretroviral therapy (ART); monitor for and treat side effects; monitor viral load and CD4 T-cell count · Provide adequate oxygenation if the client has pneumonia · Provide gentle care, since the client may be emaciated and experiencing pain and discomfort from muscle wasting; provide gentle skin care and protect bony prominences · Priority actual & potential complications · Opportunistic infections, progression of HIV to AIDS · Social isolation, depression, coma · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · The prognosis and potential quality of life associated with HIV has improved such that life expectancy for a client with HIV who receives treatment is similar to a client without HIV · ART interacts with many over-the-counter drugs and alternative therapies — clients should seek advice from their health care provider before adding anything · Priority medications (antiretroviral therapy, by class) · Nevirapine, delavirdine, efavirenz — oral non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), block HIV cell replication · Zidovudine, lamivudine, abacavir sulfate — oral/IV nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), block HIV cell replication; zidovudine given in pregnancy is dosed orally until labor, then administered IV until the umbilical cord is clamped, to prevent vertical transmission · Indinavir — oral protease inhibitor, blocks protease and slows HIV growth · Enfuvirtide, maraviroc — subcutaneous entry/fusion inhibitors, prevent viral replication · Raltegravir, dolutegravir — oral integrase inhibitors, limit viral DNA from entering the host cell · Fixed-dose combination drugs — oral; more than one drug combined in a single tablet, slows HIV growth · Priority teaching/discharge needs · Preventative measures, alternate safe sexual activities · Slowing or preventing progression of HIV to AIDS · Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) drug therapy (tenofovir and emtricitabine) for contacts/partners at ongoing risk · Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is indicated for workplace, episodic, or emergency exposure (condom rupture, sexual assault, use of infected needles); prevention of exposure is key, with careful use of condoms and PrEP for those at risk · Importance of vaccinations and other measures to reduce the risk of opportunistic infections — but live vaccines (such as MMR or varicella) require caution and are generally avoided in significant immunosuppression, the same live-vaccine principle that applies to any immunocompromised client elsewhere in this section; vaccines in general are also most effective when CD4 count is above 200 cells/mm³ · There is currently no vaccine that prevents HIV infection — prevention still rests on ART/U=U, PrEP, PEP, and condom use, not immunization · Meal planning for optimal nutrition; consult a dietitian · Community resources and support (for example, needle/syringe exchange programs) · PrEP vs. PEP — the timing distinction ·  | When it's used | Duration · PrEP | Ongoing, daily use by an HIV-negative person at ongoing risk, taken before any exposure occurs | Ongoing, daily, for as long as risk continues · PEP | Started as soon as possible after a specific known or suspected exposure — must begin within 72 hours to be effective | A defined course, typically about 28 days · The 72-hour window for PEP is the single most testable fact in this pairing: PEP started even one day late is far less likely to prevent seroconversion, which is why any needlestick or high-risk exposure is treated as a time-sensitive occupational health emergency, not something to schedule for the next routine appointment. For a health care worker with a needlestick involving HIV-infected blood, the actual occupational infection risk is low (about 0.3%) — but PEP (a 3-drug regimen) is still started immediately rather than waiting to see. · PrEP specifically combines tenofovir + emtricitabine in a single daily pill for an HIV-negative person at ongoing risk; HIV status is rechecked every 3 months while on PrEP. A person taking ART as prescribed who achieves and maintains an undetectable viral load has effectively no risk of transmitting HIV through sex ("undetectable = untransmittable") — but since PrEP and ART don't protect against other STIs, condom use is still recommended alongside them. Consistent, correct condom use remains the only effective method (besides abstinence) to reduce sexual transmission risk; nonlatex condoms protect against pregnancy for a client with a latex allergy but do not protect against HIV transmission the way latex condoms do. · Nursing considerations · Standard precautions (not special isolation) are sufficient for routine care of a patient with HIV/AIDS, since transmission requires direct contact with specific body fluids rather than airborne or casual spread.
