As CD4 counts fall, nursing priorities shift toward infection prevention (protecting a patient with limited immune reserve from the nurse, other patients, and the environment, rather than the reverse), nutritional support, and psychosocial support given the stigma many patients with HIV continue to experience. · Infection-prevention teaching for the immunocompromised patient · Beyond ART adherence, patients with significant immune deficiency (from HIV/AIDS or other causes) need concrete self-care teaching to reduce infection risk: meticulous hand hygiene, total-body hygiene and foot care, skin integrity with emollients for dry/chafed skin, good oral hygiene and regular dental checkups, avoiding people with active infections or recent vaccinations and avoiding crowds, deep breathing/incentive spirometry every 4 hours while awake if mobility is restricted, avoiding raw fruits/vegetables and undercooked food and refrigerating leftovers immediately, avoiding cleaning birdcages or litter boxes and, when possible, gardening/soil exposure, frequent disinfecting of kitchen and bathroom surfaces, and avoiding alcohol, tobacco, and unprescribed medications. The patient and caregiver should also know the signs of infection to report immediately — fever, chills, new cough, breathing problems, white oral patches, swollen glands, persistent GI symptoms, changes in urination, red/swollen/draining wounds, and severe fatigue.

Benign vs. malignant, primary vs. secondary symptoms, and the three treatment pillars · Cancer is, at its core, a disorder of cellular regulation: normal cells follow built-in controls on when to divide and when to stop, and cancer arises when a cell line escapes those controls and proliferates unchecked, eventually forming a tumor. · Immune surveillance is the standing defense against this happening: cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells routinely detect and destroy abnormal cells before they become an established tumor, and B cells can mark abnormal, "non-self" cells — cancer cells included — as targets for attack. Cancer isn't just uncontrolled cell division; it's also a failure of this surveillance system to catch and eliminate that division early, which is part of why an immunocompromised patient (from HIV/AIDS, chronic immunosuppressant therapy, or advanced age) carries a higher cancer risk. · Benign vs. malignant tumors · Not every tumor is cancer. A benign tumor grows locally, stays within a defined capsule, does not invade surrounding tissue, and does not spread (metastasize) to distant sites — it can still cause problems by compressing nearby structures as it grows, but it is not cancer in the malignant sense. A malignant tumor invades surrounding tissue directly, lacks a well-defined capsule, and has the capacity to metastasize — spread to distant organs via the bloodstream or lymphatic system — which is the single feature that makes malignancy so much more dangerous than a benign growth of similar size. · Benign vs. malignant, side by side · Characteristic | Benign | Malignant · Cells | Well-differentiated, resemble the tissue of origin | Undifferentiated, may bear little resemblance to the tissue of origin · Mode of growth | Expansion; does not infiltrate surrounding tissue; usually encapsulated | Grows at the periphery and invades/infiltrates surrounding tissue · Rate of growth | Usually slow | Variable — the more anaplastic (undifferentiated) the tumor, the faster it grows · Metastasis | Does not metastasize | Gains access to blood/lymphatic channels and metastasizes to distant sites or across body cavities · General effects | Usually localized, unless it compresses a vital structure | Often causes generalized effects — anemia, weakness, systemic inflammation, weight loss, cancer-associated cachexia syndrome (CACS) · Tissue destruction | Not usual, unless it interferes with blood flow | Common, as the tumor outgrows its blood supply or produces cell-damaging substances · Ability to cause death | Not usual, unless location interferes with vital function | Will eventually cause death unless growth is controlled · Grading and staging — how a cancer's severity gets a common language · Grading is the pathologic classification of tumor cells — how much they resemble (or don't) the tissue they came from. Grade I is well-differentiated (closely resembles the tissue of origin, better prognosis); Grade IV is poorly differentiated/undifferentiated (barely resembles the tissue of origin, more aggressive, worse prognosis, less responsive to treatment). Staging describes tumor size, local invasion, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis, most commonly with the TNM system : T (extent of the primary tumor, Tis = carcinoma in situ, T1–T4 = increasing size/local extent), N (regional lymph node involvement, N0 = none, N1–N3 = increasing involvement), and M (distant metastasis, M0 = none, M1 = present). These T/N/M values combine into an overall anatomic stage group (I–IV, increasing severity) that guides treatment decisions and prognosis. · Cancer prevention and detection · Primary prevention reduces risk before disease develops — health promotion (weight management, physical activity, limiting high-calorie foods) and vaccination against infections linked to cancer (the HPV vaccine against cervical and head/neck cancers; the hepatitis B vaccine against liver cancer). Secondary prevention is screening and early detection in people who don't yet have symptoms — mammography, colonoscopy, Pap tests, and similar screening tools — aimed at catching precancerous lesions or early-stage disease, when treatment is simpler and outcomes are better. · Priority actual & potential complications — oncologic emergencies · Certain complications of cancer or its treatment are true emergencies requiring immediate recognition: · Emergency | Recognize it by | First-line management · Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) | Progressive dyspnea, facial/neck/arm edema, distended neck and chest wall veins, cough, hoarseness; most often from lung cancer or lymphoma compressing the SVC | Radiation or chemo to shrink the mass; elevate the head/upper body (semi-Fowler, never fully supine); avoid upper-extremity venipuncture and BP checks; avoid tight clothing/jewelry on the affected side · Spinal cord compression | Local/radicular back or neck pain worsened by movement, coughing, or Valsalva; motor weakness progressing toward paralysis; bladder/bowel dysfunction — an emergency because delay risks permanent paralysis | Corticosteroids to reduce cord edema, radiation or surgical decompression; keep the patient still/positioned per spine precautions until stabilized; assess neuro status frequently · Hypercalcemia | Fatigue, weakness, confusion, nausea/vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, arrhythmias; serum calcium >10.4 mg/dL | IV hydration followed by diuretics (forced diuresis); bisphosphonates for longer-term control; treat the underlying malignancy · Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) | Follows rapid cell death from chemo/radiation, especially in leukemia/lymphoma; produces hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia (→ hypocalcemia), and hyperuricemia; watch for arrhythmias, seizures, and acute kidney injury | Aggressive IV hydration started 24–48h before cytotoxic therapy; allopurinol or rasburicase to control uric acid; treat hyperkalemia (cation-exchange resin, or insulin/dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly); hemodialysis if refractory · Palliative and hospice care — the distinction that matters · Palliative care is an interdisciplinary approach to symptom management and psychosocial/spiritual support for anyone with a serious, life-limiting illness — it can start at diagnosis, run alongside curative or disease-directed treatment, and continue into bereavement support for the family; it is not only for the dying. Hospice is a specific type of palliative care focused on comfort at the end of life: enrolling in hospice means the patient has chosen to forgo disease-directed (curative) therapy in favor of comfort-focused care. The Medicare Hospice Benefit (Medicare Part A) covers interdisciplinary palliative care and services for patients with a terminal illness and a life expectancy of less than 6 months. Palliative sedation — controlled, monitored use of sedatives/nonopioids to reduce consciousness for otherwise-refractory pain or symptoms — is intended to relieve intractable suffering, not to hasten death. · Primary vs. secondary symptoms · Cancer symptoms are usefully split into two categories. Primary symptoms come directly from the tumor itself — a mass effect from local growth, pain from compression of nearby structures, or bleeding and obstruction when a tumor is in a hollow organ or vessel. Secondary symptoms come from the body's broader systemic response to the cancer rather than the tumor's local presence — fatigue, unintended weight loss, anemia, and the metabolic and immune effects sometimes described as cancer cachexia. Recognizing which category a symptom falls into matters because it shapes the workup: a primary symptom points toward the tumor's location, while a cluster of secondary symptoms can be the first sign of a cancer that hasn't caused any localized symptoms yet. · Treatment: the three pillars · Modality | Options | Key nursing concerns · Surgery | Debulking (removing as much tumor as possible without full cure intent), curative resection, hormone-producing tissue removal, palliative surgery, and reconstructive surgery | Post-operative recovery and body image concerns, especially after disfiguring or organ-removing procedures · Chemotherapy | Administered through a variety of routes; a Port-a-Cath is commonly placed for reliable, repeated IV access, and many chemotherapy agents are vesicants (capable of causing severe tissue damage if they leak outside the vein), which makes secure venous access and careful administration a patient-safety priority | Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), bone marrow suppression (with resulting infection and bleeding risk), anorexia, alopecia, family planning/fertility concerns, and risk of future secondary cancers · Radiation | Internal (brachytherapy, where a radioactive source is placed inside or next to the tumor) or external beam radiation (with skin markers used to precisely and consistently target the same site each session) | Radiation precautions, skin damage at the treatment site, mucosal damage (especially with head/neck or GI-tract radiation), long-term tissue damage, and risk of future secondary cancers · Bone marrow suppression from chemotherapy deserves a specific callout because it cascades into the two supportive medications named in this section's blueprint: filgrastim , a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor that boosts neutrophil production to reduce infection risk during chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, and epoetin alfa , a synthetic erythropoietin that stimulates red blood cell production to manage chemotherapy-induced anemia. Both medications treat a downstream consequence of bone marrow suppression rather than the cancer itself. · The Port-a-Cath · A Port-a-Cath is a small, surgically implanted reservoir placed under the skin (commonly on the upper chest) with a catheter that threads into a large central vein. It's accessed through the skin with a specialized non-coring needle (through the septum), which lets a patient receive repeated chemotherapy infusions, blood draws, or other IV therapy over months without needing a new peripheral IV every time — a particularly important feature given how many chemotherapy agents are vesicants that would be dangerous to infuse through a fragile, easily infiltrated peripheral line.

Four classes, one shared risk (serotonin syndrome), and a black-box warning that applies to all of them · Antidepressants are grouped by which neurotransmitter(s) they act on and, for the older classes, by the specific safety problem that makes them second- or third-line today. All four classes carry the same FDA black-box warning: increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults up to age 24, especially in the first weeks of therapy or after a dose change — this is the single highest-yield antidepressant fact across every class. · SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) — first-line · Examples: fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), paroxetine (Paxil), citalopram (Celexa), escitalopram (Lexapro). SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin at the synapse, increasing its availability. They're first-line because their side-effect profile is the most tolerable of the four classes. · Common side effects — nausea, sexual dysfunction, insomnia or drowsiness, weight changes · Onset — full therapeutic effect takes 4–6 weeks; patients need to know this so they don't stop early believing the drug "isn't working" · Never stop abruptly — taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, flu-like symptoms, "brain zaps", irritability) · Key exam fact — fluoxetine is the SSRI most associated with treating bulimia nervosa and is FDA-approved for that indication · SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) · Examples: venlafaxine (Effexor), duloxetine (Cymbalta). Act like SSRIs but also block norepinephrine reuptake, which can help with comorbid chronic pain and tends to produce a more "activating" effect. Same suicide-risk warning, same abrupt-discontinuation risk, plus a tendency to raise blood pressure at higher doses (monitor BP). · TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants) — older, higher-risk · Examples: amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine. Effective, but largely replaced by SSRIs/SNRIs because of a much narrower safety margin. · Anticholinergic side effects — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation · Cardiotoxicity — the defining danger: TCA overdose can cause fatal cardiac dysrhythmias, so a baseline EKG is often obtained and TCAs are prescribed cautiously (small quantities at a time) in patients with active suicidal ideation · Orthostatic hypotension — fall risk, especially in older adults · MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors) — last-line, dietary restriction · Examples: phenelzine, tranylcypromine. Block the enzyme that breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Reserved for treatment-resistant depression because of two serious interaction risks. · Tyramine ("cheese") reaction — aged cheese, cured/processed meats, red wine, and fermented foods can trigger a hypertensive crisis in a patient on an MAOI, because tyramine normally gets broken down by the same enzyme the drug is blocking · Serotonin syndrome risk — combining an MAOI with any other serotonergic drug (SSRI, SNRI, triptans, even St. John's Wort) can be life-threatening; a washout period is required when switching between an MAOI and an SSRI · Serotonin syndrome — the cross-class emergency · Any combination of serotonergic agents can trigger serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia/clonus, diaphoresis, and tachycardia . It's a medical emergency — stop the offending agent(s) and provide supportive care. Recognize the pattern (fever + neuromuscular hyperactivity + autonomic instability) and distinguish it from NMS (antipsychotics, rigidity, and a slower onset) covered in the antipsychotics lesson. · Additional exam-relevant details · SSRIs/SNRIs are typically dosed in the morning since they can cause insomnia — a practical detail that often trips up dosing-schedule questions · Avoid combining an SSRI/SNRI with St. John's Wort (serotonin syndrome risk) and limit grapefruit juice intake · The most common reason for antidepressant non-adherence is often sexual dysfunction (anorgasmia, impotence) — usually manageable, but worth asking about directly since clients rarely volunteer it · In older adults, the greatest antidepressant-related risk to monitor for is hyponatremia — check sodium periodically, especially early in treatment · TCAs also lower the seizure threshold and can cause a withdrawal reaction if stopped abruptly — taper rather than discontinue suddenly · Antidepressants are prescribed for indications beyond depression, including severe anxiety, obesity, bulimia, smoking cessation, alcoholism, bipolar disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder · Some atypical antipsychotics (notably aripiprazole ) are used adjunctively alongside an antidepressant to manage treatment-resistant major depressive disorder — a cross-topic fact worth remembering · The black-box suicide warning has a clinical mechanism worth understanding, not just memorizing: as a depressive episode starts to lift, a client can regain enough energy and organization to act on suicidal thoughts that were present all along but that severe psychomotor slowing had prevented them from acting on. This is why close suicide-risk monitoring matters most in the earliest weeks of treatment or right after a dose change — not only at the point of diagnosis.

Lithium's narrow safety margin, plus the anticonvulsants borrowed for bipolar disorder · Mood stabilizers are the backbone of bipolar disorder treatment, used to prevent both manic and depressive poles rather than treating a single episode type. · Lithium — the classic mood stabilizer · Lithium has one of the narrowest therapeutic windows of any commonly used psychiatric drug (therapeutic level roughly 0.6–1.2 mEq/L), which is why it is one of the highest-yield medications in this entire course. Common, expected side effects are weight gain and dry mouth — the real testable content is toxicity. · LITH mnemonic | Toxicity sign · L | L ethargy / confusion · I | I ncreased urination (early) progressing to renal impairment · T | T remor (coarse, worsening from fine baseline tremor) · H | H ypotension / cardiac dysrhythmias · The trap: NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, dehydration, a low-sodium diet, and excessive caffeine can all push lithium levels toward toxicity without the patient's lithium dose changing at all. Medication reconciliation for a lithium patient is really a search for anything that shifts fluid, sodium, or renal clearance — ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs are the two most commonly tested interacting drug classes. · Monitoring — regular serum lithium levels, renal function, thyroid function (lithium can cause hypothyroidism), and steady sodium/fluid intake · Patient teaching — maintain consistent daily fluid and sodium intake; don't start or stop an NSAID or diuretic without telling the prescriber; hold the dose and call the provider for any early toxicity sign (GI upset, coarse tremor, confusion) · Anticonvulsants used as mood stabilizers · Several antiepileptic drugs are also first-line or adjunct options for bipolar disorder, especially when lithium is contraindicated or not tolerated. · Valproic acid / divalproex (Depakote) — monitor liver function and platelet counts; teratogenic (avoid in pregnancy) · Carbamazepine (Tegretol) — risk of agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia; monitor CBC · Lamotrigine (Lamictal) — must be titrated slowly; rapid titration raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, a life-threatening rash · Lithium — additional mechanism and practical details · Lithium works by modulating neurotransmitter release and intracellular signaling to calm mania, though it is not effective for every client with bipolar disorder. Because lithium is administered as a sodium salt , it is one of the few medications that requires a consistently high sodium and fluid intake — a low-sodium diet or dehydration concentrates lithium in the body and pushes levels toward toxicity, so a sodium-restricted diet started for an unrelated reason (like a new cardiac diagnosis) is a genuine hidden danger for a client on lithium. Lithium is teratogenic and should be used cautiously in clients with thyroid disease. · Additional expected side effects beyond weight gain and dry mouth: polyuria, thirst, edema, metallic taste, bloating · Response typically takes 1–2 weeks to lift bipolar symptoms, with frequent monitoring especially early in treatment; suicide risk should always be assessed alongside mood · When lithium isn't effective or tolerated, anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine) or haloperidol may be used as alternatives · A unique adherence challenge in bipolar treatment: some clients miss the energy, productivity, and euphoria of a manic episode and stop taking their mood stabilizer voluntarily once they start feeling "leveled out." Building the client's own insight into this pattern — rather than only reciting side effects — is a key nursing intervention for long-term adherence. · Anticonvulsant mood stabilizers — additional risks · Valproate/divalproex also carries risk of pancreatitis in addition to hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity · Lamotrigine's Stevens-Johnson Syndrome risk typically starts with flu-like symptoms before progressing to a painful, peeling rash — teach clients to report any new rash immediately rather than waiting to see if it worsens

The specific drug names on the blueprint, plus what treats the movement side effects · This lesson is the drug-name reference card for the typical-vs-atypical concepts already covered in the Psychotic Disorders unit — use that lesson for the pathophysiology (EPS, NMS, clozapine/agranulocytosis) and this one to lock in which brand name goes with which generic name. · Atypical antipsychotics (second-generation) — named on the blueprint · Brand name | Generic name · Abilify | Aripiprazole · Zyprexa | Olanzapine · Seroquel | Quetiapine · Risperdal | Risperidone · Geodon | Ziprasidone · Clozaril | Clozapine (agranulocytosis risk — requires regular WBC monitoring) · Notice the pattern from the earlier lesson: most of these generic names end in -pine or -done/-idone — a fast way to recognize an atypical antipsychotic on a medication list you haven't memorized. · Typical antipsychotics (first-generation) · Haloperidol (Haldol) is the classic example — effective against positive symptoms, but with the highest EPS risk of any class. · Brand name | Generic name · Haldol | Haloperidol · Thorazine | Chlorpromazine · Prolixin | Fluphenazine · Mellaril | Thioridazine · Stelazine | Trifluoperazine · Navane | Thiothixene · Treating EPS: benztropine · Benztropine (Cogentin) is an anticholinergic medication used specifically to treat or prevent extrapyramidal symptoms (tremor, rigidity, akathisia, acute dystonia) caused by antipsychotics. Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) , also anticholinergic, is an alternative for the same purpose, particularly for acute dystonic reactions. Both work by restoring the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in motor pathways that antipsychotics disrupt — specifically, benztropine is thought to block central cholinergic receptors in the basal ganglia. · Anticholinergic side effects to watch for with benztropine itself — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation (the classic anticholinergic picture); watch especially closely in older adults and debilitated clients, who are more sensitive to these effects and to toxic psychosis (confusion, disorientation, memory impairment, visual hallucinations) · Acute dystonia is an emergency-adjacent event — sudden muscle spasm (often neck/throat/eyes) that is frightening but treatable; IM/IV benztropine or diphenhydramine typically resolves it quickly, with IM/IV onset around 15 minutes versus about 1 hour PO · Not for tardive dyskinesia — benztropine is specifically not recommended for tardive dyskinesia; at certain doses it produces atropine-like toxicity that can actually aggravate TD symptoms rather than treat them · Never stop abruptly — benztropine is tapered down gradually rather than discontinued all at once · Heat caution — benztropine can reduce sweating (anhidrosis), so clients should limit hot-weather activity to avoid overheating/heat stroke · Look-alike/sound-alike alert — don't confuse benztropine with bromocriptine, a different drug entirely · Additive anticholinergic risk — combining benztropine with amantadine, haloperidol, phenothiazines, or tricyclic antidepressants can cause additive anticholinergic effects (confusion, hallucinations, GI effects, fever, heat intolerance)

Fast-acting and dependence-prone vs. slow-onset and non-habit-forming · Anxiolytic treatment splits into two philosophies: benzodiazepines, which work almost immediately but carry real dependence and withdrawal risk, and buspirone, which takes weeks to work but carries essentially no dependence risk. Choosing between them (or combining them short-term) is a recurring clinical decision. · Benzodiazepines — the blueprint list · Brand name | Generic name · Valium | Diazepam · Klonopin | Clonazepam · Ativan | Lorazepam · Xanax | Alprazolam · Versed | Midazolam · Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of GABA (the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter), producing rapid anxiolytic, sedative, muscle-relaxant, and anticonvulsant effects. This is exactly why they're also first-line for alcohol withdrawal (covered in the Substance Use unit) — cross-tolerance with alcohol at the GABA receptor. · Common side effects — sedation, dizziness, ataxia (fall risk, especially in older adults) · Dependence/withdrawal — physical dependence develops with regular use; abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use can cause seizures, making these drugs dangerous to stop "cold turkey" — always taper · Respiratory depression — the danger multiplies when combined with other CNS depressants (opioids, alcohol); this combination is a leading cause of overdose death · Versed (midazolam) stands apart from the others on this list — it's primarily used for procedural sedation and anesthesia induction rather than outpatient anxiety management · Buspirone — the non-benzodiazepine option · Buspirone is a non-habit-forming anxiolytic that does not act on GABA and carries no dependence or withdrawal risk, but it takes 2–4 weeks for full effect and does nothing for an acute panic attack in the moment — it's a maintenance drug, not a rescue drug. This is the direct trade-off nurses need to teach patients: benzodiazepines work now but carry dependence risk; buspirone is safer long-term but won't help today. · Additional indications and precautions · Beyond anxiety, benzodiazepines are also used for acute alcohol withdrawal, skeletal muscle spasms, preoperative sedation, and seizures/status epilepticus. They are not intended for long-term use — tolerance and dependence develop with regular use, which is exactly why any benzodiazepine must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly. · Black-box warning: benzodiazepines are used with extreme caution in clients with suicidal ideation — the same mechanism as antidepressants: raising a depressed client's energy level can give them the physical capability to act on a suicide plan even before their mood has fully lifted · Contraindicated with alcohol; less effective when combined with high caffeine or nicotine intake · Teratogenic — use caution in clients who are or may become pregnant · Reduce the dose in older adults, who accumulate and excrete these medications more slowly · Buspirone — additional details · Because buspirone doesn't cause CNS depression and carries no addiction potential, it's often the better choice for a client with a substance use disorder history. It generally produces fewer side effects than a benzodiazepine, but grapefruit and grapefruit juice should be restricted while taking it. · A subtle but testable behavioral sign that an anxiolytic or antipsychotic is working: improved hygiene and grooming, and appropriate dress, often show up before the client can verbally describe feeling less anxious — mood and cognitive organization improving enough to reinvest in self-care is itself a positive clinical sign.

The mainstay ADHD treatment, plus the safety monitoring that goes with it · Stimulant medications are first-line pharmacologic treatment for ADHD, working by increasing dopamine and norepinephrine availability in the prefrontal cortex — the paradox being that a stimulant improves focus and reduces impulsivity in ADHD rather than worsening hyperactivity. This paradoxical calming effect comes from stimulating dopamine and norepinephrine release while blocking their reuptake, which improves the signaling deficits underlying ADHD's inattention and impulsivity. Methylphenidate is also indicated for narcolepsy, and is classified as a Schedule II controlled substance — amphetamine-like, with high abuse and dependence potential. · Common agents · Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) · Amphetamine/dextroamphetamine salts (Adderall) · Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) — a prodrug, which gives it a lower abuse potential than immediate-release stimulants · Monitoring and side effects · Cardiovascular — stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure; a baseline cardiac history/EKG is prudent before starting, and ongoing vital sign monitoring continues through treatment · Growth suppression — appetite suppression can affect growth velocity in children; height and weight are tracked at routine visits · Insomnia — dosing earlier in the day helps; a common reason for a late-afternoon "add-on" low dose to be avoided · Controlled substance — most stimulants are Schedule II, meaning strict prescribing rules and a real misuse/diversion potential that requires patient and caregiver education · Full adverse effect profile — anorexia, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, agitation, diuresis, tachycardia, palpitations, dry mouth, growth retardation in children, rare stroke/CVA, and tolerance/dependence with chronic use · Medication is typically combined with behavioral therapy and structured environmental supports (covered in the ADHD lesson) rather than used as a stand-alone treatment. · Nursing and patient teaching · Administer stimulant doses early in the day to avoid insomnia · Encourage a large, protein-rich breakfast to offset appetite suppression, since anorexia tends to worsen as the day goes on · Discuss provider-guided "drug holidays" during school breaks to allow catch-up growth in children · Taper rather than abruptly discontinue, given the potential for tolerance and withdrawal · Avoid alcohol and other CNS stimulants · For the methylphenidate transdermal patch: apply 2 hours before the needed effect, remove 9 hours later, and titrate the dose weekly as needed

Mechanism, administration, and the re-sedation trap · Naloxone (Narcan) is an opioid antagonist that rapidly displaces opioids from receptor sites, reversing respiratory depression in an opioid overdose. It is the definitive answer whenever a scenario describes an unresponsive patient with pinpoint pupils and a slow, shallow respiratory rate after opioid exposure. · Key facts · Onset — works within 2–5 minutes, whether given IV, IM, intranasally, or via auto-injector, which is why it's the community-distributed, layperson-administered antidote for suspected overdose · Duration is shorter than most opioids — naloxone's effect can wear off before a long-acting opioid (like methadone or extended-release oxycodone) has cleared, so the patient can slip back into respiratory depression after the naloxone wears off; repeat dosing and close monitoring are required, not a single dose and discharge · Precipitates withdrawal — in an opioid-dependent patient, naloxone can trigger acute, uncomfortable (though not typically life-threatening) opioid withdrawal symptoms — this is expected and is a sign the drug worked, not a paradoxical reaction · No effect on non-opioid overdoses — naloxone won't reverse respiratory depression from benzodiazepines or other sedatives; the diagnosis has to actually be opioid-related for it to help · Dosing and routes · Adult dosing is typically 0.4–2 mg IV, IM, or subcutaneously , repeated every 2–3 minutes if there's no response. The intranasal spray formulation (Narcan) comes as a single-dose device and can be repeated in alternating nostrils every 2–3 minutes. · Onset by route · Route | Onset · IV | 1–2 minutes · IM or subcutaneous | 2–5 minutes · Intranasal | 8–13 minutes · Cardiac risk on abrupt reversal · Because naloxone is displacing opioids so quickly, abrupt reversal can trigger ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, or cardiac arrest — cardiovascular status needs close monitoring after any dose, and this risk is specifically emphasized for postoperative reversal of opioid effects, not just street-overdose scenarios. · Look-alike/sound-alike alerts · Don't confuse naloxone with naltrexone (used for ongoing maintenance therapy, not emergency reversal), Lanoxin , or nalbuphine · Don't confuse the brand name Narcan with Marcaine · Neonatal risk · Precipitated opioid withdrawal from naloxone can be life-threatening in neonates under 4 weeks old — watch for excessive crying, hyperreflexia, and seizures in this population specifically, not just the adult withdrawal picture (nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, tachycardia, CNS excitement, increased blood pressure). · Patient and family teaching · Give naloxone immediately for a suspected opioid overdose — don't wait to be certain · Seek emergency help immediately after giving the first dose · Give additional doses every 2–3 minutes if there's no response, while waiting for EMS to arrive

t: NSAIDs, DMARDs, Corticosteroids, Antihistamines & Gout Meds
x: The consolidated drug-name reference card for RA, OA, SLE, gout, and hypersensitivity — full detail lives in each condition's own lesson · NSAIDs — symptom control, not disease-modifying · Examples: ibuprofen (OA), aspirin, celecoxib — a COX-2 inhibitor (RA), indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac (SLE). NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, reducing prostaglandin production and, with it, pain, fever, and inflammation. They relieve symptoms in OA, RA, and SLE alike, but don't alter the underlying disease process. · GI risk — prostaglandins normally protect the gastric lining, so NSAIDs raise the risk of gastric ulcers and GI bleeding — the most significant adverse effect across the NSAID class · Aspirin-specific — monitor serum salicylate levels for toxicity if the daily dose exceeds 3,600 mg · Renal risk — reduced renal blood flow, especially in older adults, with dehydration, or with concurrent ACE inhibitor/diuretic use · Key interaction to remember — NSAIDs reduce renal clearance of lithium, pushing lithium toward toxicity (see the Mental Health Medications unit) · DMARDs — traditional/non-biologic (disease-modifying) · Examples: methotrexate (RA and SLE), hydroxychloroquine (RA and SLE), leflunomide and sulfasalazine (RA). Unlike NSAIDs, DMARDs slow or halt joint/organ damage rather than just controlling symptoms. · Methotrexate — oral/IV steroid-sparing immunosuppressant, used as an alternative to corticosteroids in both RA and SLE; monitor CBC for hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression · Hydroxychloroquine — oral antimalarial, treats fatigue and joint inflammation (RA) or fatigue, joint pain, and skin disorders (SLE); requires an eye exam every 6–12 months due to retinopathy risk · Leflunomide — blocks immune cell overproduction; teratogenic — rule out pregnancy before starting · Sulfasalazine — decreases pain and inflammation, may prevent joint damage · DMARDs — targeted/biologic agents (RA) · Tofacitinib, baricitinib — oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors that interfere with the enzymes driving joint inflammation; used after initial DMARD therapy fails · Adalimumab — a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor that decreases immune/inflammatory response; used when other antirheumatics haven't worked · Anakinra — subcutaneous interleukin-1 receptor antagonist; used when other antirheumatics haven't worked or can't be tolerated · Belimumab (SLE) — IV monoclonal antibody that binds and inactivates BLyS, halting the B-cell antibody production that drives lupus; live vaccines are contraindicated for 30 days before starting it · Rituximab (SLE) — an additional monoclonal antibody used for its immune-modulating effect when belimumab or standard therapy isn't enough · Corticosteroids · Hydrocortisone, prednisone — intra-articular/oral, for acute RA flare-ups; low doses are typically bridged in until DMARDs take effect · Methylprednisolone — IV/oral, for severe SLE skin disorders and tapering-dose management of polyarthritis flares · Cortisone — intra-articular, for OA joint inflammation/swelling; if pain/swelling isn't relieved after 4 injections, further intervention is needed · Other immunosuppressants (severe SLE organ involvement) · Azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolic acid — oral/IV; treat severe organ involvement (most often lupus nephritis), prevent the need for long-term corticosteroids; along with methotrexate, these are contraindicated in pregnancy · Tacrolimus, pimecrolimus — topical calcineurin inhibitors, used instead of corticosteroids for SLE skin rashes · Dapsone — oral antileprosy drug, an option for urticaria/oral ulcers/chronic SLE symptoms when hydroxychloroquine isn't tolerated · Warfarin — anticoagulant for the clotting risk that comes with positive antiphospholipid antibodies in SLE; monitor INR · Gout medications · Colchicine — the classic acute-flare drug, most effective within 12–24 hours of onset; dose-limiting GI side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); narrow therapeutic window; also used at a lower dose as flare prophylaxis when starting allopurinol · Allopurinol — first-line long-term urate-lowering therapy; a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production; requires renal dose adjustment; never started during an active flare · Febuxostat — alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor when allopurinol isn't tolerated; boxed warning for increased cardiovascular death risk versus allopurinol · Probenecid — a uricosuric that increases renal excretion of uric acid instead of reducing production; needs adequate fluid intake to avoid kidney stones; ineffective in significant renal impairment · NSAIDs and corticosteroids (both already listed above) are also standard acute-flare options for gout · Antihistamines & allergy-specific drug classes · Diphenhydramine (first-generation, sedating) — urticaria and allergic rhinitis; loratadine/cetirizine/fexofenadine (second-generation, non-sedating) block H1 receptors without crossing the blood-brain barrier as readily · Pseudoephedrine — decongestant; limit to 2–3 days to avoid rebound congestion · Montelukast, zafirlukast — leukotriene receptor antagonists · Ketotifen, olopatadine, azelastine, cromolyn — mast cell stabilizers · Flonase, Beconase, Nasocort, Rhinocort — nasal corticosteroids · Epinephrine — the reversal agent for anaphylaxis itself (see the Hypersensitivity Reactions lesson for full detail) · The shared risk to remember · Every DMARD and immunosuppressant on this list shares the same core risk: immunosuppression , meaning increased infection risk. These patients need monitoring for signs of infection and are generally advised against live vaccines while on therapy — this is the one nursing consideration that applies no matter which specific agent is on the medication administration record. Before starting a biologic DMARD specifically, screen for latent TB (tuberculin skin test) and hepatitis B/C, since immunosuppression can reactivate these infections.

t: ART for HIV/AIDS: PrEP vs. PEP
x: One therapy category, and the timing distinction that shows up on every exam · ART as ongoing treatment · ART combines multiple antiretroviral drug classes (reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, and others) to suppress HIV viral replication as much as possible, ideally to an undetectable viral load. ART doesn't cure HIV, but it allows CD4 counts to recover and dramatically reduces both disease progression and transmission risk. It's taken daily, indefinitely, and adherence is the single most important nursing teaching point — inconsistent dosing allows the virus to develop drug resistance. · PrEP vs. PEP — the timing distinction ·  | When it's used | Purpose · PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) | Taken ongoing, before any potential exposure, by an HIV-negative person at ongoing risk | Prevents infection from ever taking hold if exposure occurs · PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) | Started within 72 hours after a specific known or suspected exposure (needlestick, unprotected sex, assault) | A short course (about 28 days) to prevent the exposure from becoming an established infection · The fastest way to keep these straight: PrEP is proactive and ongoing; PEP is reactive and time-limited , with a hard 72-hour window that makes it a genuine time-sensitive nursing priority — a patient presenting after a needlestick or sexual assault needs PEP initiated as soon as possible, not "whenever it's convenient."

Targeting two specific chemo side effects — low neutrophils and low red cells · Chemotherapy, as a general drug class, works by targeting rapidly dividing cells — which is why it kills cancer cells but also damages other fast-turnover tissues, including bone marrow. Two supportive medications exist specifically to counteract chemotherapy's effect on two different blood cell lines. · Filgrastim (Neupogen) — for neutropenia · Filgrastim is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that stimulates the bone marrow to produce more neutrophils. It's given when chemotherapy has caused (or is expected to cause) dangerously low neutrophil counts, since neutropenia leaves a patient highly vulnerable to infection with too few white cells available to fight it. · Nursing priority — neutropenic precautions: monitor temperature closely (fever in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency, since the usual signs of infection/inflammation may be blunted), reverse/protective isolation as ordered, meticulous hand hygiene, avoid fresh flowers/raw produce per facility policy · Side effect — bone pain is common as the marrow ramps up production · Caring for the immunocompromised client — hospital vs. home · In the hospital | At home · Neutropenic precautions / reverse isolation; private room, positive-pressure preferred, door closed | Strict handwashing for the patient and family — before eating and after using the restroom · Strict staff hand hygiene before and after every patient contact | Disinfect countertops, handles, and kitchen items frequently · Administer filgrastim (G-CSF) if ordered to stimulate WBC production | No raw meat, raw fish/sushi, or unwashed raw produce — no uncooked food at all · No visitors with a recent live vaccine, active illness, or cold symptoms | No live vaccines; avoid close contact with anyone recently given a live-virus vaccine · No live plants or flowers — standing water and soil carry fungal spore risk | Avoid gardening, soil exposure, and cut flowers left in standing water · Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures/venipunctures; universal precautions | Avoid large crowds, enclosed spaces, and anyone currently ill · PPE (protective garments, chemo gloves) during cytotoxic drug administration | Use an electric razor, not a blade, and handle knives/scissors carefully · Restrict young child visitors — higher viral exposure rates | Never share personal hygiene items — toothbrushes, razors, towels · Confirm non-live immunizations are up to date per protocol | Daily cleaning; routine laundering of linens/clothes; clean air filters · Limit portals of entry — minimize lines, catheters, and invasive tubing | Avoid pet waste, litter boxes, and bird cages · Daily CHG wipes, sterile technique, and routine site checks for any invasive line; weekly sterile dressing changes for a central line | Thorough oral care with a soft toothbrush; gentle skin and nail care · Turn/Cough/Deep-Breathe (TCDB) plus incentive spirometry to prevent pneumonia | Adequate vitamin C, vitamin D, and protein intake; no unpasteurized dairy · Watch for confusion or lethargy — often the first sign of infection in an older adult | Monitor temperature daily; report any elevation immediately · Infection alert — temperature >99°F (37.2°C): immediate pan-cultures (blood, urine, sputum) before starting scheduled antibiotics | Practice safe sex (condoms); avoid contact with body fluids; avoid uncovered standing water/drinks · For an immunocompromised or neutropenic patient, use the lower, more conservative threshold: a temperature greater than 99°F (37.2°C) is enough to trigger immediate pan-cultures and prompt antibiotics, since a neutropenic patient's usual fever response can be blunted and a true infection may not mount a classic high fever. The ≥100.0°F (37.8°C) combined with an ANC below 500/mm³ threshold describes the general, non-immunocompromised definition of a fever — for this patient population, act on the lower number. · Epoetin alfa (Epogen, Procrit) — for anemia · Epoetin alfa is a synthetic erythropoietin that stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells. It's used for chemotherapy-induced (or chronic kidney disease-related) anemia to reduce fatigue and transfusion needs. · Monitoring — hemoglobin/hematocrit trends, blood pressure (can cause or worsen hypertension), and iron stores (adequate iron is needed for the drug to work) · Boxed warning — increased risk of thromboembolic events (DVT, stroke, MI) and, in cancer patients, a possible increased risk of tumor progression/recurrence in some studies — used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed · The clean way to keep these two apart: filgrastim → neutrophils → infection risk; epoetin alfa → red blood cells → anemia/fatigue. They treat two different chemotherapy complications and are never substitutes for each other.

The building blocks every other calculation relies on · Before any drip rate or weight-based dose can be calculated, you need to be fluent in the basic conversions underneath them — pounds to kilograms, and the metric ladder from kilograms down to micrograms. Almost every calculation error in practice traces back to a mistake at this level, not the fancier formula built on top of it. · Basic Dosage Calculation · Formula: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = Amount to administer · Worked example: Order is 500 mg PO; available as 250 mg tablets. (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets . · Worked example 2: Order is 2 mg lorazepam; available as a 4 mg/mL vial. (2 ÷ 4) × 1 mL = 0.5 mL . · Weight Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Pounds → kilograms | lbs ÷ 2.2 = kg | 154 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg · Kilograms → pounds | kg × 2.2 = lbs | 100 kg × 2.2 = 220 lbs · Almost every weight-based drug calculation in this unit starts with converting the patient's weight to kilograms — if that first conversion is wrong, every step after it is wrong too, even if the rest of the math is done perfectly. This matters directly in this module for weight-based pediatric dosing (ADHD/ASD medications) and for BSA-based chemotherapy dosing. · Metric System Conversions — the 1000 rule · Standard medical units (kg, g, mg, mcg) are each separated from their neighbor by a factor of 1000. · Direction | Rule | Example · Larger → smaller (kg→g, g→mg, mg→mcg) | Multiply by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places right) | 2 g × 1000 = 2000 mg · Smaller → larger (mcg→mg, mg→g, g→kg) | Divide by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places left) | 2500 mcg ÷ 1000 = 2.5 mg · Volume Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Milliliters → liters | mL ÷ 1000 = L | 2500 mL ÷ 1000 = 2.5 L · Liters → milliliters | L × 1000 = mL | 0.5 L × 1000 = 500 mL · Household & Volume Equivalents · Household/Metric | Equivalent · 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL · 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL (or 3 tsp) · 1 ounce (oz) | 30 mL (or 2 tbsp) · 1 cup | 240 mL (8 oz) · 1 quart (approx.) | 1000 mL (1 L)

t: IV Flow Rates, Drip Rates & Concentration
x: Getting fluid and medication into the vein at the right speed · These formulas answer one of two questions: how fast should this infusion pump run (mL/hr), or how many drops per minute should a gravity IV be set to (gtt/min) when there's no pump involved? A third formula, concentration, sets up weight-based drip calculations. · Flow Rate / Infusion Rate (mL/hr) — for infusion pumps · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Total Time (hr) = mL/hr · Worked example: Infuse 1000 mL of Normal Saline over 8 hours. 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr . · Infusion Time — working backward from a known rate · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Flow Rate (mL/hr) = Time (hours) · Worked example: A 1000 mL bag is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How long will it last? 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours . · Drip Rate (gtt/min) — for gravity IV tubing without a pump · There are two equivalent ways to reach the same answer, depending on whether you already know the mL/hr rate or are starting from the total order. · Starting point | Formula · You already know mL/hr | (mL/hr ÷ 60) × Drop Factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min · You're starting from the total order | (Total Volume [mL] × Drop Factor [gtt/mL]) ÷ Time (minutes) = gtt/min · Worked example (method 1): Infuse at 125 mL/hr using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. First, mL/min: 125 ÷ 60 = 2.08 mL/min. Then: 2.08 × 15 = 31.2, rounded to 31 gtt/min . · Worked example (method 2): Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours (480 minutes) with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min — the same answer either way. · IV Push Medication Rate · A common general safety rule for IV push medications is roughly 1 mL per minute unless the drug's specific administration guidelines say otherwise. Worked example: a 10 mL medication is administered over 10 minutes, consistent with the 1 mL/min rule. Pushing too fast is a common cause of adverse drug reactions — relevant here for IV push benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam for agitation/status epilepticus) and IV antihistamines. · Concentration Calculation — the setup step for weight-based drips · Formula: (Total mg in the bag × 1000) ÷ Total mL in the bag = Concentration (mcg/mL) · Worked example: A bag contains 400 mg of a drug in 250 mL of D5W. (400 × 1000) ÷ 250 = 1600 mcg/mL .

MAP, CPP, and weight-/unit-based infusions · This lesson groups together the calculations that show up most often in critical care and high-alert medication administration — all of them either measure perfusion pressure directly, or calculate the pump rate for a drug that manipulates that pressure. Relevant here for a client in delirium tremens, an oncology patient in septic shock, or any client on a high-alert IV drip. · MAP — Mean Arterial Pressure · Formula: (Systolic BP + [2 × Diastolic BP]) ÷ 3 = MAP · Worked example: BP is 120/80. (120 + [2 × 80]) ÷ 3 = (120 + 160) ÷ 3 = 93.3 mmHg . · MAP reflects the average pressure driving blood into the organs across the whole cardiac cycle — it's weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more time in diastole than systole. A MAP of roughly 65 mmHg or higher is generally considered necessary to maintain adequate organ perfusion in a critically ill patient. · CPP — Cerebral Perfusion Pressure · Formula: MAP − ICP = CPP · Worked example: MAP is 93, ICP is 15. 93 − 15 = 78 mmHg . · CPP depends directly on MAP — if you already calculated MAP for a patient, you're one subtraction away from CPP. A CPP that drops too low (generally below ~60 mmHg) risks cerebral ischemia, which is why both numbers are tracked together in a patient with a head injury or elevated ICP. · Weight-Based Infusion (mcg/kg/min) · Formula: (Desired mcg × kg × 60 minutes) ÷ Concentration (mcg/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient, with a concentration of 1600 mcg/mL (from the concentration calculation in the previous lesson). (5 × 80 × 60) ÷ 1600 = 15 mL/hr . · Units-Based Infusion (Units/kg/hr) — e.g., Heparin · Formula: (Units × kg) ÷ Concentration (Units/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 12 Units/kg/hr for a 100 kg patient, with a concentration of 100 Units/mL. (12 × 100) ÷ 100 = 12 mL/hr . · Both weight-based and units-based drips are high-alert medications given by infusion pump only — the shared theme across every high-alert drug is a computerized pump, frequent reassessment, and a clear plan for what triggers stopping or adjusting the rate.

Tracking what goes in, what comes out, and what IV fluids do to cells · Intake and output tracking is really just accounting for fluid — but a couple of categories have special rules that are easy to get wrong, and tonicity explains why the choice of IV fluid itself matters beyond just the volume. This is directly relevant to fluid management in cancer/chemotherapy patients, HIV/AIDS patients with diarrhea or wasting, and any client receiving IV psychiatric medications. · What counts as intake · Oral (PO) fluids — water, juice, soda, milk, coffee · Liquid foods — soups, broths, gelatin, sherbet, sorbet, pudding · Ice chips — recorded as half the original volume (200 mL of ice chips = 100 mL intake), since ice chips are mostly air/space between solid pieces · IV fluids — maintenance fluids, boluses, and piggyback medications (like antibiotics) · Tube feedings — formula and water flushes (relevant for a client with anorexia nervosa on enteral nutritional rehabilitation) · What counts as output · Urine — voided, catheterized, or urostomy drainage · Emesis (vomitus) — relevant for a client with bulimia or chemotherapy-induced nausea · Liquid stool — diarrhea or colostomy drainage · Wound drainage — from JP drains, Hemovacs, or chest tubes · Suction — gastric (NG) or respiratory · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake of 3000 mL, output of 800 mL. 3000 − 800 = +2200 mL (a positive balance, meaning the patient is retaining more fluid than they're losing). · Insensible Loss · Fluid lost through the skin and lungs that can't be directly measured. Standard estimate: 600–900 mL/day , or roughly 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Worked example: a 70 kg patient: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/hr, or roughly 840 mL/day. · Fluid Weight Calculation · Rule of thumb: a 1 kg weight change equals roughly 1 L of fluid change. Worked example: a patient's weight rises 2 kg over two days — that's roughly a 2 L fluid gain, not necessarily 2 kg of actual tissue. · An output under 30 mL/hr is always reported as a potential emergency — it signals inadequate perfusion to the kidneys. · Tonicity — what different IV fluids do to cells · Type | Solute concentration vs. inside the cell | Effect on the cell | Examples | Clinical use · Hypertonic | Higher outside the cell | Water leaves the cell — it shrinks (plasmolysis) | 3% or 5% NaCl; 10% Dextrose in Water | Cerebral edema, severe hyponatremia · Hypotonic | Lower outside the cell | Water enters the cell — it swells or bursts (cytolysis) | 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline) | Dehydration — pushes water back into cells · Isotonic | Equal inside and outside | No net water movement — equilibrium maintained | 0.9% Normal Saline, Lactated Ringer's, D5W | Routine IV fluid replacement and hydration · A simple way to remember the direction: hyper tonic pulls water OUT of the cell (think 'hyper' = high solute outside, pulling water toward it), while hypo tonic pushes water IN . Isotonic is the 'do no harm' default fluid.

Calculations that scale a dose — or a diagnosis — to the patient's size · These two calculations both answer a version of the same question — how big is this patient, in a way that's useful for dosing or risk assessment? BMI is a general screening number used constantly in this module's eating-disorder content; BSA is a more precise scaling factor used specifically for chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · BMI — Body Mass Index · System | Formula · Metric | Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]² · Imperial | [Weight (lbs) × 703] ÷ [Height (in)]² · Worked example (metric): Weight 70 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625. Divide weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86 (normal weight range). · Worked example (imperial): Weight 154 lbs, height 69 inches. 154 × 703 = 108,262. Square the height: 69 × 69 = 4,761. Divide: 108,262 ÷ 4,761 = 22.74 — the same result as the metric calculation, just arrived at with different starting units. · This is exactly the calculation behind the BMI thresholds in the Anorexia Nervosa lesson: a BMI under 17 is a diagnostic marker of the disorder, and under 15 is considered extreme/life-threatening. Knowing how to compute BMI from a height and weight given in a case stem — not just recognize the threshold — is testable on its own. · BSA — Body Surface Area · BSA approximates a patient's total skin surface area in square meters (m²), and it's used specifically for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, chemotherapy agents, pediatric patients, and burn patients — situations where a small dosing error has an outsized effect. This is the calculation behind chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · Formula: BSA = √[(Height in cm × Weight in kg) ÷ 3600] · Fully worked pediatric dosing example · Order: a chemotherapy agent at 2 mg/m². Patient: 37 lb, 97 cm tall. Supply: 1 mg/mL. · Step 1 — convert weight to kg: 37 lb ÷ 2.2 = 16.8 kg · Step 2 — calculate BSA: √[(97 cm × 16.8 kg) ÷ 3600] = √[1629.6 ÷ 3600] = √0.4527 = 0.67 m² · Step 3 — calculate the dose in mg: 2 mg/m² × 0.67 m² = 1.34 mg · Step 4 — calculate the dose in mL: 1.34 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 1.34 mL to administer · Notice this whole calculation depends on the weight-to-kg conversion from the first Med Math lesson — get that first step wrong, and every subsequent step (BSA, mg dose, mL dose) inherits the error.

How long symptoms must last, and at what age they typically start · This lesson is a pure cheat sheet — the numbers behind the mechanisms already explained across the Mental Health units. Use it for rapid-fire review, not first-time learning; if a number here doesn't ring a bell, go back to the full lesson it came from. · Duration/diagnostic-criteria numbers · Condition | Duration/criterion · Major depressive disorder | Symptoms nearly every day for ≥2 weeks · Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) | ≥2 years in adults, ≥1 year in children/adolescents · Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) | Symptoms in the final week before menses, improving within a few days after onset, minimal/absent in the week postmenses, for most cycles in the past year · Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) | A seasonal pattern (typically fall/winter onset) for ≥2 consecutive years · Generalized anxiety disorder | Excessive worry more days than not for ≥6 months, plus ≥3 of 6 associated symptoms · Panic disorder | Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + ≥1 month of persistent worry about additional attacks or maladaptive behavior change · PTSD | Symptoms present for >1 month (before 1 month, it's acute stress disorder) · OCD | Time-consuming obsessions/compulsions — more than 1 hour per day, causing significant distress/impairment · Brief psychotic disorder | Psychotic symptoms lasting <1 month, with return to baseline · Schizophreniform disorder | Symptoms of schizophrenia lasting 1–6 months · Schizophrenia | Two or more characteristic symptoms persisting >6 months · Delusional disorder | ≥1 month of delusions without other psychotic symptoms · Borderline personality disorder | ≥5 of 9 DSM-5 criteria, pattern present since early adulthood, across multiple contexts · ADHD | Several symptoms present before age 12, in ≥2 settings · Autism spectrum disorder | Most children diagnosed by ages 2–3; signs possible as early as 6 months · Anorexia/bulimia nervosa (binge-purge cycle, BN) | Binge eating + compensatory behavior ≥1×/week for ≥3 months · Binge-eating disorder | Binge episodes ≥1×/week for ≥3 months, without regular compensatory behavior · Onset-age numbers · Fact | Value · Schizophrenia — first episode, males | 18–25 years · Schizophrenia — first episode, females | 25–35 years · Late-onset schizophrenia (LOS) | Onset after age 40 · Very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis (VLOSLP) | Onset after age 60 · Bipolar disorder — typical age of onset | Late teens to early 20s (average ~25) · Borderline personality disorder — symptoms typically first apparent | Adolescence/early adulthood · Antidepressant black-box suicidality warning — age range | Increased suicidality risk up to age 24 · Binge-eating disorder — most common age range | 46–55 years · Anorexia nervosa — peak onset age range | Adolescence, ~13–18 years · Delirium — most common in | Older adults (>65) and the critically ill/hospitalized · Anxiety-disorder numbers · Fact | Value · Panic attack — time to peak intensity | 10–15 minutes · Panic attack — typical maximum duration | Rarely longer than 30 minutes · GAD — prevalence (U.S.) | ~5% of the general population · GAD diagnostic criteria | ≥6 months worry + ≥3 of 6 symptoms (restless, easily tired, poor concentration, irritable, muscle tension, sleep disturbance)

hold for vomiting/diarrhea/N-V, dehydration, or low-sodium diet — all raise lithium levels; encourage steady daily sodium/fluid intake, not restriction · Valproic acid (Depakote) | 50–125 mcg/mL | >125 mcg/mL | Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity) and platelets/CBC; Role | What happens when it's abnormal · Neutrophil | The first responder — smaller than a macrophage, it rapidly phagocytizes bacteria and fungi at the site of an acute infection | Neutropenia sharply raises the risk of rapid, severe bacterial infection and sepsis — the basis for neutropenic precautions · Macrophage | The larger, longer-acting phagocyte — clears cellular debris and secretes cytokines that recruit more immune cells to the site | Dysfunction impairs wound healing and pathogen clearance, and is part of the mechanism behind granulomatous diseases such as tuberculosis · Monocyte | Circulates in the bloodstream before migrating into tissue, where it matures into a macrophage or dendritic cell — essentially the macrophage's immature, circulating form | Abnormal counts (monocytopenia or monocytosis) alter the body's ability to replenish tissue macrophages during chronic inflammation or infection · Eosinophil | Releases toxic granules to destroy multicellular parasites (helminths) and participates in allergic reactions | Overactivity drives chronic tissue damage and airway hypersensitivity, as in asthma or hypereosinophilic syndrome · Basophil | Releases histamine and heparin into the bloodstream during systemic allergic reactions and inflammation | Over-activation causes the systemic vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and fluid shifts of anaphylaxis · T-cell and NK subtypes — what goes wrong · Cell | Role | What happens when it's abnormal · Helper T (CD4) | Coordinates the immune response by releasing cytokines that activate macrophages, B cells, and cytotoxic T cells — it doesn't kill anything directly, it flags and directs | HIV destroys CD4 cells, paralyzing both cell-mediated and humoral immunity and opening the door to opportunistic infections · Suppressor/regulatory T | Suppresses an overactive immune response and maintains self-tolerance once a threat has passed | Loss of suppression lets T cells attack healthy self-tissue — the mechanism behind autoimmune disease broadly, and specifically IPEX syndrome · Cytotoxic T (CD8) | Directly kills infected host cells and tumor cells using perforin and granzymes | Deficits allow unchecked viral replication and raise cancer risk · Natural killer (NK) cell | Destroys virus-infected or malignant cells that lack MHC Class I markers, without needing any prior exposure to the antigen | Dysfunction is linked to familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — uncontrolled immune activation and severe organ damage · The five immunoglobulin classes · Class | % of total Ig | Key role | What happens when it's abnormal · IgG | 75% | In serum and tissue; the major player in bloodborne and tissue infections; activates complement; the only class that crosses the placenta | Hypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG) causes recurrent bacterial infections; excessive antibody targeted at self-tissue drives tissue-specific autoimmune disease · IgA | 15% | In secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk, mucus); protects the respiratory/GI/GU tracts and passes to a nursing infant for protection | IgA deficiency leads to recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections · IgM | 10% | Mostly intravascular; the first immunoglobulin produced in a new infection; activates complement | Hyper-IgM syndrome — an inability to switch from IgM to IgG/IgA — leads to severe, recurrent infections · IgD | 0.2% | Small serum amounts; functions as an antigen receptor on naive B-cell membranes to assist B-cell maturation | Minimal clinical impact alone; alterations can affect initial B-cell activation efficiency · IgE | 0.004% | Drives allergic and hypersensitivity reactions; also fights parasitic infections | Elevated levels drive Type I hypersensitivity — atopic dermatitis, asthma, anaphylaxis · Medications ending in "-mab" are monoclonal antibodies — lab-made versions of a B-cell antibody, engineered to target one specific protein, inflammatory cytokine, or tumor marker (belimumab for SLE, and the biologic DMARDs used in RA, are both examples). · Care of a Client with Immunocompromise · In the hospital | At home · Neutropenic precautions / reverse isolation; private room, positive-pressure preferred, door closed | Strict handwashing for the patient and family — before eating and after using the restroom · Strict staff hand hygiene before and after every patient contact | Disinfect countertops, handles, and kitchen items frequently · Administer filgrastim (G-CSF) if ordered to stimulate WBC production | No raw meat, raw fish/sushi, or unwashed raw produce — no uncooked food at all · No visitors with a recent live vaccine, active illness, or cold symptoms | No live vaccines; avoid close contact with anyone recently given a live-virus vaccine · No live plants or flowers — standing water and soil carry fungal spore risk | Avoid gardening, soil exposure, and cut flowers left in standing water · Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures/venipunctures; universal precautions | Avoid large crowds, enclosed spaces, and anyone currently ill · PPE (protective garments, chemo gloves) during cytotoxic drug administration | Use an electric razor, not a blade, and handle knives/scissors carefully · Restrict young child visitors — higher viral exposure rates | Never share personal hygiene items — toothbrushes, razors, towels · Confirm non-live (37.2°C): immediate pan-cultures (blood, urine, sputum) before starting scheduled antibiotics | Practice safe sex (condoms); avoid contact with body fluids; avoid uncovered standing water/drinks · For Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing — built from Sky's handwritten class notes, defense mechanisms handout, mental health concepts slide deck, bipolar and GAD study sheets, and exam review · Part 1 · Foundational Concepts · 1.1 Mental Health as a Continuum · Mental illness interferes with everyday life — an extended period where the person is not performing daily tasks. · Marked by a lack of coping and exists on a continuum. · Disease of exclusion — all other illnesses must be ruled out first. · Why it matters — a diagnosis does not necessarily mean permanent mental illness. Once someone has a mental illness, it is still possible to return to healthy well-being. · 1.2 Disease of Exclusion · You must rule out every other possible cause before attributing symptoms to a mental illness. · Category | Conditions that can mimic mental illness · Physiologic | Stroke · Brain tumor · Brain injury · Hepatic encephalopathy · Hypoxia · Hormone imbalance · Infectious / Metabolic | UTIs (especially in older adults) · Thyroid disorder · Situational | Stress · Grief · Lack of sleep · 1.3 Key Psychiatric Terms · Psychosis — a break away from reality. · Delusions — strongly held beliefs/thoughts not rooted in reality; related to psychosis, including erotomania (delusion that someone else is in love with them, even with evidence to the contrary), grandeur (false beliefs about one's own power, wealth, talents, or other traits), and paranoid delusions (false beliefs of being threatened or mistreated, even with little or no reason). · Hallucinations — sensory delusions (any sense). · Why it matters — natural causes must always be ruled out first. Example: a patient who believes bugs are all over them should still be physically checked for bugs. · Part 2 · The Nurse's Role · 2.1 Therapeutic Use of Self · Requires self-awareness of beliefs, biases, and other thoughts that could cause the nurse to give unfair or unsafe care. · "Set your views aside" — don't impose your own beliefs on the patient. · 2.2 Establishing Rapport · Built on three things: Trust, Respect, Genuineness. · 2.3 Empathy vs. Sympathy · Empathy | Sympathy · Connects with the PATIENT'S feelings — "understands feelings" | Focuses on the NURSE'S feelings — feeling pity · Example: "How do you think losing your leg will affect your life?" | Example: "I am so sorry about your amputation." · Do NOT share personal experiences | "At least..." statements — generally not therapeutic · 2.4 Transference vs. Countertransference · Transference — similar to projection; occurs on behalf of the PATIENT when they transfer feelings about a situation or person onto the staff. · Countertransference — happens on behalf of the NURSE, who "matches energy" instead of stepping away from the situation. · 2.5 Therapeutic Environment & Restraints · Priority is SAFETY — a full assessment for the safety of both patient and staff. · Use the LEAST restrictive environment unless it is no longer safe — then move to the next level of restriction. · Chemical or physical restraints are the LAST resort, though certain steps can be skipped depending on severity. · Chemical restraints must be monitored every 15 minutes. · Physical restraints must be monitored every 2 hours. · It is appropriate to set boundaries with patients no matter the illness. · 2.6 Responding to Disturbing Beliefs — An Empathy Model · When a patient voices a delusion (e.g., "I have worms eating my brain"), don't argue and don't reinforce the belief: · Step | What to do | Example · 1. Acknowledge what they said | Use phrases like "You say..." — you don't need to reinforce the belief. | "You say you have worms eating your brain." · 2. Acknowledge your understanding | "I can't see that..." or "I was told that..." — never call the belief untrue outright. | "I can't see that, and the tests don't show any worms." · 3. Imagine how they might feel | Be tentative, not certain. If you get it wrong, ask more open-ended questions. | "I imagine that would feel very uncomfortable — can you tell me what it feels like?" · 4. Explore feelings & coping | Sometimes just acknowledging the feeling is enough. | "Have you had this feeling before? What worked then?" · 2.7 Nursing Implications — General Framework · Assessment — safety first (patient & environment) · Therapeutic communication · Structure the environment for the situation · Medications · Part 3 · Suicidal Ideation & Safety · PRIORITY assessment for everyone with a mental illness or family history — always think safety first. · Get the patient to tell you their specific plan; develop a safety plan. · Pay close attention to nonverbal cues (giving away possessions, sudden calm after depression, saying goodbyes). · Multiple attempts and repeated threats should always be taken seriously. · National Suicide & Crisis Lifeline — call or text 988 for immediate support. If you are personally struggling with thoughts of suicide or self-harm, please reach out. · Part 4 · Mood Disorders · 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) · Pathophysiology: imbalance of neurotransmitters — serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine. · Clinical manifestations · Persistent sadness, hopelessness, or irritability · Fatigue, difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite · Psychomotor agitation or retardation · Suicidal ideation · Priority interventions · Assess for suicide risk (develop a safety plan if needed) · Encourage therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) · Educate about medication adherence and side effects · Non-pharmacological therapy: exercise, healthy diet, self-care, sleep, support groups, getting outside · Why it matters — high suicide risk, especially as energy returns roughly 2 weeks into antidepressant treatment. · 4.2 Bipolar Disorder — Overview · An affective disorder with severe mood swings, ranging from hyperactivity to depression. · Type | Definition · Bipolar I | At least ONE manic episode — often with mood swings — or hypomania plus major depression · Bipolar II | At least one hypomanic episode PLUS one major depressive episode · Cyclothymia | Mild hypomania and depressive symptoms not meeting the major criteria for bipolar disorder · Bipolar NOS | Symptoms don't fit into any of the other categories · 4.3 Cyclothymic Disorder · Chronic mood disturbance lasting 2+ years in adults (1+ year in children/adolescents). · Symptoms occur 50% of the time and are never absent for 2+ months. · Mild hypomania and depressive symptoms — not severe enough for major depression or bipolar disorder. · Medical causes (endocrinopathies, brain disorders, drug overdose, etc.) must be ruled out. · 4.4 Bipolar — Pathophysiology, Incidence & Complications · Mechanisms unclear: genetic (autosomal dominant), neurotransmitter imbalances (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine). · Risk factors: family history, substance abuse, life stressors (death, divorce), high-income countries, stress. · Affects 5.7 million Americans annually. · Median onset at age 25, but can occur from childhood to the 50s. · Complications: emotional/social consequences (exhaustion, poor performance, relationship issues); risk of suicide and substance abuse. · 4.5 Bipolar — Assessment & DSM-5-TR Criteria · Depressive Symptoms | Manic Symptoms · Depressed mood, slowed speech, lethargy | Excessive activity, impulsive actions · Weight/appetite changes | Delusions, grandiosity, flight of ideas · Suicidal thoughts | Rapid speech, racing thoughts · Loss of interest in activities (anhedonia) | Inflated self-esteem, doesn't sleep · History: sleeping/eating disturbances, poor judgment, high sex drive, poor concentration. · DSM-5-TR Criteria — Bipolar I: manic episode for 1+ week, with at least 3 symptoms (e.g., grandiosity, decreased sleep, impulsivity). Bipolar II: hypomanic episode lasting 4+ days AND a major depressive episode. · Diagnostic tests: no specific lab or imaging studies — clinical and psychological exams are used. · 4.6 Bipolar — Treatment, Nursing Care & Discharge · Treatment · General: therapy (group, individual, CBT), inpatient care for severe cases; ECT for treatment-resistant cases. · Mood stabilizers: Lithium, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, valproate) · Antipsychotics: Aripiprazole, Olanzapine · Antidepressants: Fluoxetine, Citalopram · Benzodiazepines: for anxiety (e.g., Clonazepam) · Nursing considerations · Safety — develop safety plans, monitor suicidal thoughts, assist with hygiene and nutrition · Mania — reduce overstimulation, set limits, provide diversional activities · Depression — encourage activity, limit decision-making, assess suicidal ideation · Patient teaching · Importance of medication (lithium carbonate) adherence and hydration · Side effects (lithium toxicity, antipsychotic side effects), tapering antidepressants · Discharge planning · Ensure understanding of diagnosis, medications, and follow-up · Provide a safety plan and support resources · Confirm proper medication management post-discharge · Part 5 · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders · General interventions: decrease stimuli, keep the patient calm, use grounding techniques. · 5.1 Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) — Overview · Persistent feelings of apprehension, dread, or uneasiness. · A reaction to perceived internal threats with uncontrollable worry lasting at least 6 months. · Interferes with normal functioning and narrows perception. · Pathophysiology: neurotransmitter aberration — GABA, serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, cholecystokinin. · Cause: unknown. · Risk factors · Family history of anxiety disorder · Stressful life events · Childhood physical/emotional abuse · More common in females · Incidence · Prevalence 0.2%–4.3% globally; coexists with major depression and other anxiety disorders. · Common in primary care settings; rarely occurs before adolescence. · Complications: impaired social/occupational functioning, substance abuse, suicidal behaviors. · 5.2 GAD — Assessment & Diagnosis · History · Muscle aches, headaches, difficulty relaxing · Apprehension, fear, anger, irritability · Difficulty concentrating, eating, sleeping; insomnia, fatigue, memory loss · Physical findings · Trembling, shortness of breath, tachycardia, elevated BP, sweating · DSM-5-TR Criteria for Diagnosis — excessive worry occurring most days for at least 6 months. Difficulty controlling worry, associated with 3+ of: restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbances. Impairs social, occupational, and daily activities — and is NOT due to substances or another mental condition. · Diagnostic tests: cardiac enzymes/troponin and EKG rule out organic causes (myocardial ischemia); psychiatric evaluation confirms the diagnosis. · 5.3 GAD — Treatment & Nursing Care · Therapies: cognitive-behavioral, psychodynamic, emotional regulation, mindfulness. · Line | Medications · First-line | SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) · Alternatives | TCAs (imipramine), benzodiazepines (short-term only), buspirone · Second-line | Antipsychotics (aripiprazole, quetiapine) for treatment-resistant cases · Warning — benzodiazepines: caution with dependence and withdrawal risks. Type | Description | Examples · Positive | Symptoms present that shouldn't be | Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, concrete thinking, speech alterations · Negative | Normal functions that attention, problem-solving | Impaired memory, poor attention, executive dysfunction, poor insight (anosognosia) · Examples in practice — Positive: a patient believes they are being followed by
