Immunity, Inflammation & Cellular Regulation — built from Sky's handwritten class notes, slide deck, exemplar review sheets, and lecture summaries · Part 1 · Types of Immunity · Type | Definition | Duration · Natural Active | Exposure — your own immune system fights and remembers | Lifelong · Natural Passive | Transfers from mom to baby | Short-term · Artificial Active | Vaccine | Depends · Artificial Passive | Exposed, then treated with immunoglobulin | Time-specific · 1.1 Examples & Lifespan · Natural Active: acquired through direct exposure to a pathogen — the body develops its own antibodies and memory cells. Example: contracting chickenpox, leading to lifelong immunity. Generally lifelong, though immune system efficiency decreases with age. · Artificial Active: acquired through vaccination — the body is exposed to an attenuated or inactivated pathogen to stimulate an immune response. Example: the varicella vaccine for those who haven't had chickenpox. Generally lifelong, but boosters may be needed as immunity wanes with age (e.g., the flu vaccine, due to viral mutations). · Natural Passive: transferred antibodies from mother to baby. Example: placental antibodies, breastfeeding. Temporary — hence the recommendation for prolonged breastfeeding. · Artificial Passive: direct administration of antibodies to an individual. Example: giving antibodies to prevent HIV after exposure, or healthy antibodies for autoimmune diseases. Temporary. · What helps vs. hurts natural immunity — Factors that improve effectiveness: nutrition, hygiene, genetics, outdoor activity (Vitamin D), and adequate sleep. Factors that decrease effectiveness: stress, close quarters, autoimmune disorders, and certain medications (e.g., steroids, chemotherapy). · Part 2 · Leukocytes (Immune Cells) · Phagocytic | Humoral | Cell-Mediated · Neutrophil | B-Cells | T-Cells · Macrophage | Plasma cell | Helper T (CD4) · Monocyte | IgA | Suppressor T · Eosinophil | IgM | Cytotoxic T · Basophil | IgG | Natural Killer cell · — | IgE | — · — | IgD | — · — | Memory cell | — · 2.1 Humoral vs. Cell-Mediated · Humoral: B cell → differentiates into an antibody-producing plasma cell and a memory cell. · Cell-Mediated: Helper T (CD4) coordinates the response; Cytotoxic T, Suppressor T, and Natural Killer cells carry it out. HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4 cells (see Part 8). · 2.2 Where Immune Cells Come From · All immune cells originate from stem cells, which differentiate based on genetic signals and chemical messengers — for example, erythropoietin drives red blood cell production, while interferons and tumor necrosis factor drive white blood cell production. · 2.3 Phagocytic Cells — "Eat Invaders" · Neutrophils: first responders to bacterial infection; the most abundant white blood cell. Short lifespan — their death after engulfing bacteria forms purulent drainage. Low neutrophil counts require neutropenic precautions. · Macrophages: larger phagocytic cells ("big Pac-Mans") that eat larger germs; live longer than neutrophils; secrete chemicals that signal for more white blood cell production. · Monocytes: circulate in the blood and mature into macrophages once in tissue ("teenager macrophages"). · Eosinophils & Basophils: primarily involved in allergic reactions and defense against parasites; secrete histamine, causing allergy symptoms (itchiness, runny nose, redness, inflammation). · 2.4 Lymphocytes — Specific Immunity · B Cells & Antibody Types · Upon encountering an antigen, B cells divide into two types: antibodies (plasma cells) that directly attack the invader, and memory cells that remember the invader for a faster, stronger response on future exposure. · Antibody (Ig) | Description · IgA | Primarily found in breast milk; less significant in adult immune systems · IgG | Most common antibody (~70% of total); prolific, crucial for long-term immunity; used in treating autoimmune diseases · IgM | First-responder antibody — divides fastest · IgD | Function not fully understood; initiates immune responses (a "helper bee") · IgE | Involved in allergic reactions, along with eosinophils and basophils · T Cells · Helper T Cells (CD4): the immune system's "informants" or "security guards" — they don't directly kill, but identify self vs. non-self (foreign invaders, cancer cells) and flag abnormal cells for destruction by other immune cells. Targeted by HIV, leading to profound immunosuppression (Part 8). · Natural Killer (NK) Cells: kill abnormal cells without needing specific instructions; the body produces relatively few of these. · Cytotoxic T Cells: the "dive bombers" — kill cells tagged by Helper T cells by poking holes in them and inducing apoptosis (programmed cell death). · Suppressor T Cells: the "go home" cells — regulate and stop immune responses once a threat is cleared. Dysfunction can lead to autoimmune disease. · Monoclonal antibodies — the "-mab" drugs. Many newer medications, with generic names ending in "-mab" (e.g., adalimumab, infliximab, belimumab, rituximab — see Parts 6 and 7), target these specific immune cells to modulate the immune response rather than suppressing it broadly. · Part 3 · Nursing Care for the Immunocompromised Patient · 3.1 Hospital Care · Infection control: limit sick visitors, private rooms, dedicated equipment, masks. · Environmental control: avoid fresh plants/flowers, especially for neutropenic patients. · Early intervention: pan cultures (blood, sputum, urine) before starting antibiotics if infection is suspected. · Catheter management: remove Foley catheters ASAP due to UTI risk. Strict insertion criteria (surgery, urinary retention after a bladder scan/straight cath trial, strict I&O in critical illness, end-of-life care). Avoid Foleys for incontinence — use PureWicks instead. · Skin integrity: regular skin checks, meticulous wound care — gauze dressings changed every 24 hours; central line/PICC dressings changed weekly (antimicrobial patch); sacral dressings changed as needed (every few days). · Monitoring: watch for subtle signs of infection — e.g., delirium in older adults. · Food/drink safety: no raw food, clean water, no open containers, no sharing drinks. · 3.2 Home Care (Patient Education) · Hygiene: good oral hygiene, short nails, frequent handwashing. · Environmental: avoid animal waste, keep pets healthy, change air filters, avoid dust. · Lifestyle: get vitamin D (sunshine), monitor temperature, avoid stasis — stay active. · Food safety: safe food handling/preparation, good nutrition, clean dishes/utensils. · Travel: avoid countries with outbreaks/natural disasters; avoid international travel if possible. · Vaccinations: avoid live vaccines. · Healthcare access: use telehealth/home health to avoid crowded clinics. · Medication awareness: discuss potential immunosuppressant OTC medications with a doctor. · General health: maintain a healthy lifestyle — sleep, stress management. · Part 4 · Hypersensitivity Reactions & Allergies · A hypersensitivity reaction is an undesirable reaction from an immune response acting against foreign antigens or the body's own tissue — sometimes a genuine threat overreacted to, sometimes a harmless substance (food, medication, pollen, latex) mistakenly treated as dangerous. · 4.1 The Four Types · Type | Mediator | Onset | Example · Type I | IgE-mediated (mast cell degranulation) | Within 1 hour | Anaphylaxis · Type II | IgG or IgM cytotoxic | Hours to days | Hemolytic anemia, hemolytic transfusion reaction, Goodpasture's syndrome · Type III | Immune complex-mediated (with complement activation) | 1–3 weeks | Serum sickness, SLE · Type IV | T-cell-mediated (cytokine-driven, not antibody-driven) | Days to weeks | Contact rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome · Why it matters — Type I is IgE-driven and happens within minutes to an hour — it's the mechanism behind everything from a mosquito bite reaction to full anaphylaxis, just different severity/extent. Type IV is driven by T cells and cytokines rather than antibodies at all, which is why it has the slowest onset of the four ("T-cells take time"). · 4.2 How Type I Reactions Present · Localized anaphylactic reaction: a pale, edematous wheal on the skin containing fluid and surrounded by a red flare — classic example is a mosquito bite. · Systemic anaphylactic reaction: starts as edema and pruritus at the exposure site, then progresses to bronchiole constriction, airway obstruction, and shock — a life-threatening emergency requiring rapid, advanced care. · Atopic reactions: a family of chronic, allergen-driven presentations rather than a single acute event (see table below). · The atopic reactions · Reaction | Presentation · Hay fever | Sneezing, nasal drainage, swelling of the nasal mucosa (can obstruct airway), itching around eyes/throat, excessive tearing · Asthma reaction | Wheezing, chest tightness, thick sputum production, dyspnea · Atopic dermatitis | Edematous skin lesions containing vesicles · Angioedema | Swelling starts in the face and progresses to other body parts; lesions described as itching, burning, or stinging · Urticaria (hives) | Raised, edematous, pink areas on the body described as itching · 4.3 Anaphylaxis Severity — a Staged Progression · The faster the onset after exposure, the more severe the reaction tends to be — and prior reaction severity does NOT predict how severe the next exposure's reaction will be. · Mild (usually within first 2 hrs): peripheral tingling, warmth, fullness in mouth/throat, nasal congestion, periorbital swelling, tearing. · Moderate: adds flushing, anxiety, itching — plus bronchospasm and airway/laryngeal edema with dyspnea, cough, wheezing. · Severe (anaphylactic shock): laryngeal edema, severe dyspnea, cyanosis, hypotension, dysphagia, abdominal cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, seizures — cardiac arrest and coma can follow. · 4.4 Common Causes of Anaphylaxis · Foods: peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, eggs, soy, wheat. · Medications: antibiotics (especially penicillin & sulfa), allopurinol, radiocontrast agents, anesthetics (lidocaine, procaine), vaccines, hormones (insulin, vasopressin, ACTH), aspirin, NSAIDs — antibiotics and radiocontrast agents cause the most serious reactions; penicillin is the most common trigger overall (~10% report an allergy, <5% have a clinically significant IgE/T-cell allergy). · Other agents: animal serums (tetanus antitoxin, snake/rabies antitoxin), antigens used in skin testing. · Insect stings: bees, wasps, hornets, yellow jackets, ants (incl. fire ants) — Hymenoptera causes the most common serious sting reactions. · Latex: medical and nonmedical latex-containing products. · Anaphylactoid reaction — looks the same, different mechanism. Triggered by non-IgE-mediated mast cell/basophil degranulation (medications, food, exercise, cytotoxic transfusions) rather than a true allergic mechanism. Rarely fatal, but the nurse's response is identical to true anaphylaxis. · 4.5 Type II and Beyond · Type II reactions show up clinically as kidney injury, pulmonary hemorrhage (Goodpasture's syndrome), hemolytic blood transfusion reactions, and organ transplant rejection (now rare, thanks to modern screening) — antibodies (cytotoxic T cells, IgG, IgM) attack the body's own cells directly, rather than forming circulating complexes the way Type III does (the mechanism behind SLE, Part 7). A reaction can also occur once allergen immunotherapy injections have started, which is why sessions include a monitored observation period afterward. · Next Gen-style scenario — know this cold. A client sustains a hemolytic blood reaction from incorrect blood administration — this is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction (think ABO/Rh incompatibility). Expected cues: fever, chills, low back pain, flank pain, hypotension, tachycardia, hemoglobinuria. First action: stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV line open with normal saline, notify the provider — then return the remaining blood/tubing to the blood bank per policy. Prevention: the two-nurse patient/blood product verification check at the bedside exists specifically to prevent this reaction. · 4.6 Common Allergens & Allergy Treatment Options · Common allergens: nuts (not just peanuts), penicillin (many reported penicillin allergies may not be clinically true allergies), sulfa drugs. · Exposure therapy: introducing small, consistent amounts of an allergen to train an IgG response instead of an IgE response. · Allergy shots: administered in-office due to anaphylaxis risk; patient is monitored for 30 minutes afterward. · Over-the-counter options: antihistamines such as Claritin and Allegra. · 4.7 Diagnosing an Allergy — Skin Testing · Patch test: allergen placed on a patch applied to the skin; delayed reaction — patch worn 48–72 hours. · Scratch/prick test: allergen placed on skin, pricking device allows entry; reaction appears in 5–10 minutes. · Intradermal test: allergen injected under the skin; reaction appears in about 10 minutes. · A wheal-and-flare response to any of these tests indicates a positive reaction. · Other diagnostic cues: sputum/nasal/bronchial secretions showing eosinophils; pulmonary function test showing deteriorated function; CBC with WBC differential pointing toward immunodeficiency; elevated total serum IgE (supports diagnosis since most allergic reactions are IgE-mediated). · Before skin testing — stop antihistamines and corticosteroids (including OTC allergy meds) 48–96 hours beforehand — they suppress skin test reactivity and cause a false negative. Never test during active bronchospasm. Emergency equipment must be on hand in case the test itself triggers a reaction. · 4.8 Priority Nursing Interventions · Ensure all allergies (medications, food, latex, etc.) are documented on the health record. · Use latex-free gloves/supplies for any client with a latex allergy. · Provide prescribed pre-treatments before selected procedures/medications/treatments. · Administer antihistamines, decongestants, anti-itch meds, corticosteroids, and leukotriene receptor antagonists as ordered. · Treat skin rashes and manage anaphylactic shock as needed. · For immunotherapy: rotate injection sites; observe the client 20–30 minutes after each injection. · Never leave a client alone during allergy skin testing — some clients are highly sensitive and can develop anaphylaxis to the test itself. · Hypersensitivity responses can intensify with repeated exposure to the same allergen, not just the first one. · During an active anaphylactic reaction — assess airway, breathing, and vital signs first; notify the rapid response team/provider promptly. Epinephrine (1:1000 dilution, subcutaneous, upper extremity or thigh, may be followed by continuous IV infusion) — antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and should NEVER be substituted for epinephrine. Give supplemental oxygen and IV fluids (normal saline, volume expanders, vasopressors) to support hemodynamics. Older adults and those with hypertension, arteriopathy, or ischemic heart disease are at higher risk for adverse effects from epinephrine. After epinephrine, transport/observe in an ED-level setting — a biphasic ("rebound") reaction can occur 4–8 hours later. Extend observation for anyone who ingested the allergen, needed more than one epi dose, had hypotension/pharyngeal edema, or has a history of asthma. · Venom immunotherapy: used as a control measure (not a cure) for insect-sting allergy to reduce systemic reaction risk. · Desensitization: for penicillin or insulin allergy in a patient who needs the drug — controlled anaphylaxis with gradual mediator release. Patients must avoid lapses in therapy afterward, or the allergic reaction can reappear. · 4.9 Priority Complications · Anaphylactic shock · Soft tissue angioedema · Comorbidity with asthma and sinusitis · 4.10 Priority Medications · Medication | Key Points · Diphenhydramine | Oral/IV antihistamine for urticaria & allergic rhinitis; given with famotidine (H2 blocker) and IV methylprednisolone for an emergent allergic reaction; causes drowsiness · Pramoxine / calamine | Topical antipruritic lotion; do not use on broken skin · Epinephrine | SubQ, IM, or IV sympathomimetic for anaphylaxis — causes bronchodilation, ↑ heart rate; don't use if solution is cloudy/has particles; available as self-injector pens · Pseudoephedrine | Oral/nasal decongestant for allergic rhinitis; do not use more than 2–3 days (rebound congestion risk) · Montelukast, zafirlukast | Oral leukotriene receptor antagonists — block leukotriene-driven airway edema, bronchoconstriction, mucus production · Ketotifen, olopatadine, azelastine, cromolyn | Nasal/oral/inhaled mast cell stabilizers — inhibit histamine & leukotriene release for allergic rhinitis · Flonase, Beconase, Nasocort, Rhinocort | Nasal corticosteroids for allergic rhinitis; may be used long-term without rebound congestion, depending on agent · Immunotherapy | SubQ titrated allergen doses; 1–2 years to max effect; clinic-administered (sublingual home option exists); used when drug therapy is ineffective or the allergen can't be avoided · 4.11 Priority Teaching / Discharge Needs · Avoid the allergen; observe for S/Sx of a hypersensitivity reaction. · How to administer prescribed medications, including nasal sprays. · Potential for a delayed reaction to immunotherapy injections, and what to do if one occurs. · Seek medical assistance at the first sign of anaphylaxis. · Report all allergies at every health care visit, including latex. · 4.12 Using an Epinephrine Auto-Injector · Slide the device out of its carrying case. · Pull off the blue safety cap — never put a thumb over the orange needle end while doing this. · Push the orange needle end firmly against the outer thigh until it clicks; hold firmly in place (even through clothes, avoiding seams) for the seconds specified on the device before removing it. · "Blue to the sky, orange to the thigh" — after administration, immediately call 911 / seek medical attention — do not treat the auto-injector as the end of care. A second dose can be given after 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist; auto-injectors come in a pack of two for this reason. Why medical attention is still needed: epinephrine's half-life is short, while the allergen's effect can be prolonged — this can lead to a rebound (biphasic) reaction. Epinephrine also significantly increases heart rate. Storage: keep the auto-injector easily accessible and check expiration dates regularly, replacing it when expired. That said, an expired EpiPen is still better than none in an emergency — it only loses potency, it doesn't become harmful. Do not hesitate to use it at the first sign of a severe allergic reaction. · Part 5 · Osteoarthritis (OA) · A mechanical, wear-and-tear joint disease marked by destruction of articular cartilage — a degenerative process, distinct from the autoimmune process behind RA (Part 6). · 5.1 Priority Assessments / Cues · Joint pain aggravated by activity, alleviated by rest. · Difficulty moving from sitting to standing; joint stiffness after prolonged positioning. · Difficulty completing daily activities due to joint pain. · Heberden's nodes or Bouchard's nodes — redness, swelling, or bony outgrowths around finger joints from osteophyte formation. · Asymmetry of affected extremities — OA is generally unilateral. · Crepitation in the joint; cartilage particles in the joint cavity. · Knees may be bowlegged or knock-kneed. · 5.2 Priority Labs / Diagnostics · CT scan, MRI, bone scan — arthritic changes to joints. · X-rays — stage the degree of joint damage. · Synovial fluid analysis — normal with OA (compare to RA: elevated WBC, decreased viscosity). · 5.3 Priority Interventions · Administer drug therapy as prescribed. · Assist with ADLs. · Immobilize the affected joint with a brace/splint during acute inflammation. · Range-of-motion exercises; PT/OT consults. · Bed cradle to keep linens off affected feet. · Moist heat for stiffness; ensure rest. · 5.4 Compl

GFR, oliguria, anuria, azotemia, uremia — and what aging does to the kidney · The kidneys' elimination job is to filter the blood, pull out metabolic wastes and excess water and electrolytes, and hold on to what the body needs. Almost every renal disorder in this module is ultimately a story about that filter failing — too little blood reaching it, the filter itself being damaged, or the outflow being blocked — so the vocabulary for measuring how well it's working comes first. · Key terms · Term | Definition | What it tells the nurse · Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) | The volume of water filtered out of the plasma per unit of time — normal is 100–120 mL/min | The single best overall measure of kidney function; it falls as kidney disease progresses and is used to stage chronic kidney disease · Oliguria | Less than 500 mL of urine in 24 hours | The kidneys are not producing enough urine to clear the day's wastes — fluid, potassium, and nitrogenous wastes start to accumulate · Anuria | Less than 50 mL of urine in 24 hours | Essentially no urine output — a severe finding that needs immediate provider notification · Azotemia | A rise in BUN, creatinine, uric acid, and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood | A lab finding — wastes are building up, whether or not the patient has symptoms yet · Hematuria | Blood in the urine | Glomerular damage (glomerulonephritis), stones, infection, trauma, cyst rupture, or bleeding after a biopsy · Proteinuria | Protein in the urine | The glomeruli are leaking — a hallmark of kidney damage and of nephrotic syndrome · Hyperproteinemia | An excess of protein in the blood | Not the same as proteinuria — don't mix up blood vs. urine · Bacteremia | Bacteria in the blood | An infection (e.g., pyelonephritis) has spread beyond the urinary tract — watch for urosepsis · Uremia | Azotemia with symptoms — hyperkalemia, edema, anemia, and other systemic effects | A clinical syndrome — the waste buildup is now affecting other body systems · Uremia = an excess of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood (with symptoms). Azotemia = the concentration of nitrogenous wastes in the blood. The -uria terms are in the urine (hematuria, proteinuria); the -emia terms are in the blood (hyperproteinemia, bacteremia). · Azotemia vs. uremia is a lab-vs-symptoms distinction: azotemia is the numbers going up; uremia is the patient showing the effects. A patient can be azotemic without being uremic, but not uremic without being azotemic. · Labs used alongside these terms · BUN (blood urea nitrogen) — typical adult range about 10–20 mg/dL; rises with kidney failure but is also raised by dehydration, GI bleeding, high protein intake, and catabolism, so it's less specific than creatinine · Serum creatinine — typical adult range about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL; a byproduct of muscle metabolism that is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys, making it the more specific marker of kidney function. It rises only after roughly half of kidney function is lost , so a "slightly high" creatinine is significant · BUN-to-creatinine ratio — normally about 10:1 to 20:1; a ratio above 20:1 points toward a prerenal cause such as dehydration, because BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine when perfusion is low · Urine output — the minimum acceptable adult output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (roughly 30 mL/hr); falling below this for several hours is an early cue of kidney injury · Urine specific gravity — normal about 1.005–1.030; concentrated (high) urine suggests the kidney is trying to conserve water, as in dehydration; a urine fixed near 1.010 suggests the tubules have lost their ability to concentrate or dilute · Collecting urine specimens · Urinalysis: first morning voiding if possible, clean container; note menstruation on the requisition · Culture and sensitivity: clean-catch midstream specimen in a sterile container (or straight catheter if the client can't); collect before antibiotics ; send to the lab immediately · 24-hour urine / creatinine clearance: at the start time, have the client void and discard that urine; collect all urine for 24 hours, keep it on ice or refrigerated; at the end, have the client void and add that final urine. If a void is missed, the test usually must restart · Contrast studies: check allergies and kidney function (BUN, creatinine) beforehand; afterward encourage fluids (unless restricted) and monitor urine output — contrast is nephrotoxic, especially in older or dehydrated clients · Gerontologic considerations · Aging changes the kidney and bladder in predictable ways, and each one shifts how the nurse interprets findings in an older adult: · GFR decreases with age — medications cleared by the kidneys (many antibiotics, digoxin, metformin, low-molecular-weight heparins) accumulate more easily and often need dose adjustment · Structural and functional changes — the kidney loses mass and nephrons, and the ability to concentrate urine declines, so older adults dehydrate more easily and more quickly · Sclerosis of the glomerulus and renal vessels — the same hardening process that underlies nephrosclerosis, accelerated by long-standing hypertension and atherosclerosis · Bladder constriction — decreased bladder capacity and tone lead to frequency, urgency, nocturia, and incomplete emptying · BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) — in older men, prostate enlargement can obstruct urine outflow and cause postrenal kidney injury · Urinary incontinence — common with aging, but never assumed to be "normal"; it raises the risk of skin breakdown, falls (rushing to the bathroom), and social isolation · Serum creatinine can look deceptively "normal" in a frail older adult. Creatinine comes from muscle, so someone with low muscle mass produces less of it — a creatinine of 1.1 in a frail 89-year-old may actually reflect a markedly reduced GFR.

Post-biopsy bleeding watch, and the dietary side of stone prevention · Renal biopsy — before the procedure · Verify informed consent · Baseline vital signs and coagulation studies — report abnormal results before the biopsy · NPO as prescribed · During the procedure the client lies prone with a pillow under the abdomen · Renal biopsy — post-procedure care · The kidneys are highly vascular, so the primary red flag after a renal biopsy is hemorrhage . Apply pressure to the site (about 30 minutes or as prescribed), then keep the client on strict bed rest, supine (often with a back roll for pressure), for 2 to 6 hours . Encourage fluids (about 1,500–2,000 mL as prescribed), check under the client for bleeding, and teach the client to avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for 1–2 weeks and to report fever or hematuria after the first 24 hours. · Watch for | Red flags · Vital signs | Hypotension and tachycardia · Pain | Intense, aching pain in the flank or back · Urine | Gross or microscopic hematuria — pink-tinged urine is common at first, but bright red blood or clots are emergency signals · Biopsy site | Visible bleeding, or blood soaking through to the skin under the client's back · Labs | Decreasing hemoglobin and hematocrit · Infection | Temperature above 100°F (37.8°C) · After a nephrectomy, the flank incision sits just under the diaphragm, so altered breathing pattern and risk for ineffective airway clearance are common problems. Aim to keep SpO₂ at 90% or higher and the lungs clear of adventitious sounds; monitor I&O for a urine output above 30 mL/hour ; control pain well enough to allow movement, deep breathing, and rest. Blood-tinged drainage from the JP drain is expected in the early postoperative period. · Kidney stones (urolithiasis) — dietary prevention · Depending on the stone type, avoid high-oxalate foods — spinach, rhubarb, chocolate · …and high-purine foods — sardines, organ meats · Stones are also a postrenal cause of AKI when they obstruct urine flow — relieved by lithotripsy, surgery, or a urinary catheter

Normal values, who compensates for whom, and acute (uncompensated) vs. chronic (compensated) · Arterial blood gas (ABG) interpretation belongs in the Elimination module because the kidneys are one of the body's two acid–base regulators. When the kidneys fail, they can no longer excrete acid or make bicarbonate, so metabolic acidosis is an expected finding in renal failure — and the lungs will try to make up for it. · Normal values · Value | Normal range | What it represents · pH | 7.35–7.45 (absolute normal is 7.40 ) | Below 7.35 = acidosis; above 7.45 = alkalosis · PaCO 2 | 35–45 mmHg | The acid — controlled by the lungs (respiratory). Because CO 2 is an acid, the ends of its range are reversed: above 45 = acidotic , below 35 = alkalotic · HCO 3 | 22–26 mEq/L | The base — controlled by the kidneys (metabolic). Below 22 = acidotic , above 26 = alkalotic · PaO 2 | 80–100 mmHg | Oxygenation. Low = hypoxemia ; high = usually oxygen therapy · SaO 2 | 95–100% | Oxygen saturation. Low = hypoxemia · The body always tries to compensate to get back to 7.40 . Carbon dioxide and bicarbonate will fluctuate to make this happen. · Who compensates, and how fast · System | Controls | Speed | How it compensates · Lungs (respiratory) | CO 2 (acid) | Fast — within minutes to hours | Breathe fast to blow off CO 2 (raises pH); breathe slow to retain CO 2 (lowers pH) · Kidneys (metabolic) | HCO 3 (base) | Slow — may take days | Make more HCO 3 (raises pH); make less HCO 3 (lowers pH) · Kussmaul respirations — deep, rapid breathing — in a patient with renal failure or DKA are the lungs compensating for metabolic acidosis by blowing off CO 2 . In a renal patient, expect the pH to be low (below 7.35). That breathing pattern is a cue, not the primary problem. · Uncompensated, partially compensated, fully compensated ·  | Uncompensated (acute) | Partially compensated | Fully compensated (chronic) · pH | Abnormal | Still abnormal | Normal (7.35–7.45) · CO 2 and HCO 3 | Only one is abnormal; the other is normal (or close to it) | All three values are abnormal | Both are abnormal · Why | One system is causing the problem, and the other hasn't started fixing it yet | The opposing system has started to help, but hasn't finished | The opposing system has pushed the pH back into range, but is working hard to hold it there · Pattern tables · Uncompensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ Low (acid) | ↑ High (acid) | Normal · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ High (alk) | ↓ Low (alk) | Normal · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ Low (acid) | Normal | ↓ Low (acid) · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ High (alk) | Normal | ↑ High (alk) · Partially compensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ Low | ↑ High (cause) | ↑ High (fixing) · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ High | ↓ Low (cause) | ↓ Low (fixing) · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ Low | ↓ Low (fixing) | ↓ Low (cause) · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ High | ↑ High (fixing) | ↑ High (cause) · Fully compensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | Normal (low side, 7.35–7.39) | ↑ High | ↑ High · Respiratory alkalosis | Normal (high side, 7.41–7.45) | ↓ Low | ↓ Low · Metabolic acidosis | Normal (low side, 7.35–7.39) | ↓ Low | ↓ Low · Metabolic alkalosis | Normal (high side, 7.41–7.45) | ↑ High | ↑ High · Worked example of partial compensation: pH 7.31 (acid), CO 2 50 (acid), HCO 3 28 (base). The pH is still abnormal, and all three values are abnormal. High CO 2 matches the acidosis, so this is respiratory acidosis — and the kidneys are partially compensating by raising HCO 3 . · Reading a compensated gas — finding the "problem child" · Look at which end of the scale the pH is closer to. Below 7.40 = the underlying problem is acidosis ; above 7.40 = the underlying problem is alkalosis · You will never have a compensated problem with a pH right smack in the middle — it will always lean toward one end or the other · In a compensation situation, HCO 3 and CO 2 will both be high or both be low together · Too much base (high HCO 3 ) or too little acid (low CO 2 ) = alkalosis · Too much acid (high CO 2 ) or too little base (low HCO 3 ) = acidosis · Whichever value matches the direction of the pH is the problem child (the cause); the other value is the compensation · Step-by-step method · Step 1 — pH: acidosis (<7.35), alkalosis (>7.45), or normal? If normal, note whether it leans below or above 7.40 · Step 2 — CO 2 : is it high (acid excess), low (acid deficit), or normal? · Step 3 — HCO 3 : is it high (base excess), low (base deficit), or normal? · Step 4 — match: which value explains the pH direction? That names the disorder — respiratory if CO 2 , metabolic if HCO 3 · Step 5 — compensation: if the other value is normal = uncompensated; if all three are abnormal = partially compensated; if both are abnormal and pH is normal = fully compensated · ROME: R espiratory O pposite (pH and CO 2 move in opposite directions — pH down, CO 2 up in respiratory acidosis), M etabolic E qual (pH and HCO 3 move in the same direction — pH down, HCO 3 down in metabolic acidosis). · Causes and priority treatment for each imbalance · Imbalance | The problem | Common causes | Priority treatment · Respiratory acidosis (CO 2 ↑) | Lungs are retaining CO 2 (hypoventilation) | COPD, asthma, opioid overdose , pneumonia, oversedation | Improve ventilation — oxygen, incentive spirometry, naloxone (Narcan) if opioid-induced, BiPAP or intubation · Respiratory alkalosis (CO 2 ↓) | Lungs are blowing off CO 2 (hyperventilation) | Anxiety/panic attack, pain, fever, high altitude | Slow the breathing — paper bag breathing, treat pain and anxiety · Metabolic acidosis (HCO 3 ↓) | Kidneys losing bicarbonate or retaining acid | Renal failure (AKI/CKD) , severe diarrhea, DKA (ketones) | Fix the cause — dialysis (renal), insulin (DKA), antidiarrheals · Metabolic alkalosis (HCO 3 ↑) | Stomach losing acid | Vomiting, NG suctioning, antacid overuse | Stop the loss — antiemetics, stop suctioning, replace electrolytes (K⁺) · Acidosis and potassium travel together. In acidosis, hydrogen ions move into cells and potassium moves out into the blood — so a patient in renal failure with metabolic acidosis is doubly at risk for hyperkalemia. Correcting the acidosis (for example, with sodium bicarbonate) pushes potassium back into cells.

Prerenal, intrarenal, postrenal — and the oliguric and diuretic phases · Acute kidney injury (AKI), still often called acute renal failure, is a sudden loss of kidney function over hours to days. BUN and creatinine rise, urine output usually falls, and fluid, electrolytes, and acid–base balance all start to drift. The key difference from chronic kidney disease is that AKI is potentially reversible if the cause is found and treated quickly. · The three categories of cause · Category | Where the problem is | Common causes | Priority treatment | Key clue · Prerenal | Before the kidney — a perfusion/flow problem | Hypovolemia: dehydration, hemorrhage, burns. Low cardiac output: heart failure, shock. Also sepsis, poor oral intake | Restore perfusion — fluids, blood products, or vasopressors | BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1; concentrated urine (high specific gravity). Reversible if perfusion is restored quickly · Intrarenal | Inside the kidney — direct tissue damage | Nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, contrast dye, gentamicin, vancomycin. Glomerulonephritis. Prolonged ischemia (acute tubular necrosis) | Remove the toxin/cause — restrict fluids if oliguric; dialysis if severe | Urine specific gravity fixed near 1.010; casts on urinalysis. Untreated prerenal injury can progress to intrarenal · Postrenal | After the kidney — obstruction/blockage | Renal calculi (stones), BPH (enlarged prostate), tumors, a kinked or blocked catheter | Relieve the obstruction — surgery, lithotripsy, or a Foley catheter | Bladder distention or hydronephrosis on ultrasound; output may stop abruptly · Before calling a patient anuric, rule out the easy postrenal cause: any sudden, complete stop in urine flow in a client with a Foley should prompt the nurse to inspect, flush, or change the catheter , and a client without one gets a bladder scan. A distended bladder means the kidneys are making urine that just can't get out. · How the labs tell the three types apart · Value | Prerenal | Intrarenal (ATN) | Postrenal · Urine volume | Oliguria | Anuria, oliguria, or non-oliguric | May alternate between anuria and polyuria · Urine specific gravity | Increased (above 1.020) — the kidney is concentrating urine to save water | About 1.010 (fixed) — tubules can't concentrate | Varies · Urine sodium | Low (below 20 mEq/L) — the kidney is holding sodium | High (above 40 mEq/L) — damaged tubules can't hold sodium | Varies · Urine sediment | Normal, few casts | Muddy-brown granular casts , tubular epithelial cells | Normal; may show crystals (stones) · BUN:creatinine | Above 20:1 | 10:1–15:1 (both rise together) | 10:1–15:1 · Prerenal AKI and ischemic ATN are a continuum — if low perfusion isn't corrected quickly, tubular cells die and restoring blood flow no longer fixes the problem. A fluid bolus that improves urine output is both treatment and proof that the cause was prerenal. Note that raising BP with vasoconstrictors (e.g., norepinephrine) doesn't guarantee better kidney perfusion — urine output is the better gauge. · Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity typically starts 5–10 days into therapy — monitor peak and trough levels and creatinine. Contrast-induced AKI appears within 3–5 days of contrast and is usually non-oliguric and reversible; nephrotoxic drugs are ideally stopped 24 hours before contrast. · Postobstructive diuresis: after an obstruction is relieved (e.g., a catheter placed for BPH), output can exceed 3 L/day . This is potentially life-threatening — monitor closely for dehydration, electrolyte loss, and hypovolemic shock, and replace fluids and electrolytes. · Phases of AKI · Phase | Key signs & symptoms | Critical labs & risks | Nursing priority · Initiation (onset) | The initial insult — hours to days | Rising creatinine begins | Recognize the cause early; x: How AKI and CKD affect each system, and what the nurse monitors and does · AKI and CKD share most of the same complications. Management starts with treating the primary cause, then supporting each body system the failing kidney affects. · Fluid balance · AKI: prompt fluid replacement matched to the loss (blood for hemorrhage, crystalloids for dehydration) when the cause is prerenal; in a sustained oliguric state, fluid is limited to the previous day's output plus about 500–800 mL · CKD: fluid and sodium restriction; fluid limited to about 500 mL plus the previous day's urine output. Diuretics work until GFR falls very low (about 10–15), after which dialysis is needed · Loop diuretics are used short-term for volume overload; high-dose IV furosemide is infused no faster than 4 mg/min (ototoxicity) · Spread the fluid allowance over 24 hours, with periodic sips and ice chips to ease thirst; frequent mouth care · Cardiovascular · Hypertension — from sodium/water retention and renin–angiotensin activation; managed with fluid/sodium restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives, dialysis. Target BP in CKD is generally below 130/80 · Hyperkalemia ECG progression: about 6–7 mEq/L — tall, peaked T waves, prolonged PR, ST depression; about 8–9 — P waves disappear; about 10–11 — QRS widens toward a sine-wave pattern, then ventricular fibrillation or standstill. Muscle weakness typically starts in the legs and ascends · Clients with long-standing high potassium tolerate it better than those whose potassium rises suddenly — always read the potassium with the ECG · Uremic pericarditis (mainly stage 5 CKD): sharp chest pain that is relieved by sitting forward and worse with deep breathing, fever, and a pericardial friction rub . Treated with aggressive (often daily) dialysis with low or no heparin · Cardiac tamponade — distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, narrowed pulse pressure, pulsus paradoxus, decreased LOC — is an emergency requiring pericardiocentesis · Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in CKD — statins are recommended for CKD clients 50 and older · Pulmonary · Pulmonary edema — dyspnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum , tachypnea, tachycardia, low SpO₂. Managed with fluid and sodium restriction, diuretics if the kidneys can respond, HOB elevation, and often emergent dialysis or intubation · Also pleural effusion, uremic pleuritis/pneumonitis, and pulmonary infections — teach coughing and deep breathing; incentive spirometer · Gastrointestinal · GI bleeding is a potentially life-threatening complication — check vomit and stool for blood; monitor H&H and signs of volume loss; H2 blockers or PPIs · Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, metallic taste, uremic fetor — good oral hygiene, antiemetics, adequate dialysis · Constipation (from fluid restriction, inactivity, iron, and phosphate binders) — bulk and stool softeners; avoid magnesium-containing cathartics (magnesium citrate) and phosphate (Fleet) enemas · Neuromuscular · Sleep disturbances, difficulty concentrating, short-term memory loss, lethargy, muscle irritability · Restless leg syndrome and burning feet syndrome (paresthesias and numbness of the soles and lower legs) — teach protection from heat and injury · Rising BUN can cause cerebral edema → seizures, projectile vomiting, coma — seizure precautions · Teach in short, frequent sessions with reinforcement, and include family — uremia impairs concentration and memory · Hematologic · Bleeding tendency — uremia impairs platelet function; monitor platelets and coagulation studies; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin when possible; soft toothbrush. Heparin during dialysis can cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), which requires stopping heparin · Immune impairment — infection is a major cause of death. Uremic clients have a lower baseline temperature , so any rise above baseline is significant . Hand hygiene; remove invasive catheters as soon as possible · Anemia — mainly from erythropoietin deficiency (plus shortened RBC survival — about 70 days instead of 120 — and blood loss). Treated with ESAs (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin), iron, vitamins, and transfusion for profound anemia, since ESAs take weeks to work · Oral iron is poorly absorbed when taken with phosphate binders, antacids, H2 blockers, or PPIs — separate the timing. IV iron works better but can cause allergic reactions · Drug elimination · Many drugs are excreted by the kidneys — doses and intervals are adjusted to GFR (which may change daily in AKI) · Monitor therapeutic drug levels · Know which drugs are removed by dialysis so they're timed after treatment · Skeletal — renal bone disease · High phosphorus + low calcium + low active vitamin D → rising PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) → calcium and phosphate pulled from bone · When the calcium × phosphorus product exceeds about 55 , calcium-phosphate crystals deposit in soft tissue ( metastatic calcifications ) — blood vessels, heart valves, lungs, joints, skin, and eyes ("red eye") · Complications: bone pain, fractures, spontaneous tendon rupture, proximal muscle weakness, pruritus · Phosphate binders: calcium acetate (PhosLo), calcium carbonate (Tums), sevelamer (Renagel/Renvela) and lanthanum (calcium-free — preferred when calcium is high), iron-based binders (ferric citrate). Aluminum binders are rarely used because of aluminum toxicity (bone and nervous system) · Active vitamin D (calcitriol, paricalcitol) suppresses PTH — watch for hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia · Calcimimetics (cinacalcet, etelcalcetide) lower PTH — risk of hypocalcemia ; cinacalcet can cause nausea/vomiting · Parathyroidectomy for refractory cases · Integumentary · Itching in chronic renal failure: bathe in tepid water — hot water strips more oil from the skin and increases dryness and itching. Use moisturizing lotions and creams without perfume , avoid scratching, and keep nails trimmed. · Dry skin (xerosis), pruritus , pallor, bruising, yellow or darkened pigmentation, hair loss, nail changes ("half-and-half" nails) · Uremic frost — white powdery urate crystals on the skin, seen only with severe, untreated uremia · Keep skin clean and moisturized (superfatted or lanolin-based soap, emollients), trim fingernails, antihistamines for itching, turn every 2 hours · Nutrition · Restrict fluid, sodium, potassium, and phosphorus; supplement iron, vitamins, and calcium as ordered · High-calorie diet with most calories from carbohydrates and fats, to prevent catabolism · Adequate protein, at least half of high biological value (e.g., eggs, meat); protein restriction must never cause malnutrition — in AKI, protein restriction isn't recommended · Monitor weight, albumin, prealbumin, total protein, H&H; dietitian consult; small, frequent feedings · Psychosocial · Fear, anxiety, powerlessness, body image changes, disrupted family roles · Thorough teaching, active involvement of client and family, adequate rest, explore feelings, social services and clergy as appropriate

t: Fluid & Electrolyte Concepts in Renal Failure
x: Potassium, phosphorus, calcium, sodium, magnesium, and fluid volume — and how each is treated · Most of the life-threatening problems in renal failure are fluid and electrolyte problems. The kidney normally excretes potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, acid, and excess water — so when it fails, all of these build up, while calcium falls. · The renal failure electrolyte pattern at a glance · Electrolyte | Typical range | Direction in renal failure | Why · Potassium (K⁺) | 3.5–5.5 mEq/L (many references: 3.5–5.0) | ↑ High (above 5.5) | Kidneys can't excrete it; acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells · Phosphorus | About 2.5–4.5 mg/dL | ↑ High (above 4.5) | Kidneys can't excrete it; dialysis removes only a small amount · Calcium (Ca²⁺) | About 8.5–10.5 mg/dL | ↓ Low (below 8.5) | Inverse relationship with phosphorus, plus the kidney can't activate vitamin D, so less calcium is absorbed from the gut · Magnesium (Mg²⁺) | About 1.5–2.5 mEq/L | ↑ High (above 2.5) | Kidneys can't excrete it — worsened by Mg-containing antacids and laxatives · Sodium (Na⁺) | 135–145 mEq/L | Variable — often ↓ low (dilutional) with fluid overload | Water retained in excess of sodium dilutes it; dehydration concentrates it · Bicarbonate (HCO₃) | 22–26 mEq/L | ↓ Low (metabolic acidosis) | Kidneys can't excrete acid or regenerate bicarbonate · Hyperkalemia — the most immediately dangerous · Heart rate pattern: as potassium climbs, the heart gets more irritable — tachycardia first , then it crashes to bradycardia and asystole at critical levels. A slowing heart rate in hyperkalemia is not improvement; it can be the step before arrest · Cues: muscle weakness, paresthesias, fatigue, abdominal cramping/diarrhea, bradycardia, and ECG changes — tall peaked T waves , flattened or absent P waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS , progressing to ventricular fibrillation or asystole · Priority action: place the patient on a cardiac monitor and notify the provider · Rising BUN and creatinine predict a high potassium (not the other way around) — when the BUN/creatinine climb, the first electrolyte to check is potassium, because it kills first · Goal | Treatment | How it works | Nursing points · 1. Protect the heart | Calcium gluconate IV | Stabilizes the cardiac cell membrane | Works within minutes but does not lower K⁺ — it buys time. Cardiac monitoring during administration ·  | Calcium chloride IV | Same job as gluconate — stabilizes the heart | About 3 times more concentrated than calcium gluconate and works faster; doses may be repeated (e.g., every 30 minutes) in critical hyperkalemia · 2. Shift K⁺ into cells | Regular insulin IV + D50 (50% dextrose) | Insulin drives K⁺ into cells; dextrose prevents hypoglycemia | Regular insulin (the only insulin given IV) — about 10 units IV, not subQ — given together with D50. D5 or D10 isn't enough to cover the insulin. Monitor blood glucose closely for hours afterward ·  | Sodium bicarbonate IV | Corrects acidosis, which pushes K⁺ back into cells | Most useful when metabolic acidosis is present ·  | Albuterol (nebulized) | Beta-2 stimulation shifts K⁺ into cells | Monitor for tachycardia · 3. Remove K⁺ from the body | Sodium polystyrene sulfonate with sorbitol, patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma) | Bind K⁺ in the GI tract so it's eliminated in stool | Slower onset — not a stand-alone emergency treatment ·  | Loop diuretics | Increase renal K⁺ excretion | Only useful if the kidneys still produce urine ·  | Hemodialysis | Removes K⁺ directly from the blood | The definitive treatment in ESRD or when other measures fail · Shifting is temporary — insulin, bicarbonate, and albuterol only move potassium into cells, and it drifts back out within hours. Only binders, diuretics, and dialysis actually remove it from the body. · Before giving sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), assess bowel sounds . If the gut isn't moving, the potassium can't leave the body, and the drug can cause intestinal necrosis. · Hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia — the pair · Phosphorus and calcium have an inverse relationship : as phosphorus rises, calcium falls · High phosphorus cues: itching (pruritus), calcium-phosphate deposits in soft tissue, blood vessels, heart, and lungs; weak, brittle bones over time · Chvostek = cheek (tap in front of the ear → facial twitch); Trousseau = tourniquet (BP cuff → hand/carpal spasm). If you see Chvostek's and aren't sure of the diagnosis, the client needs calcium · Progression: paresthesias (fingers, toes, lips) first → Chvostek/Trousseau → cramps, weakness, tetany → seizures, bronchospasm, QT prolongation and dysrhythmias → coma. The gap between tingling and life-threatening is small — replace calcium urgently · Mental status: the client is usually alert and oriented — but terrified , fully aware their body is spasming and they can't control it. Altered mental status and coma come late · Low calcium cues: numbness and tingling around the mouth and fingers, muscle cramps, tetany, positive Chvostek's sign (facial twitch when the facial nerve is tapped) and Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm with a BP cuff inflated), hyperactive reflexes, seizures, prolonged QT · Safety: positive Trousseau's or Chvostek's sign means a high risk of seizures and laryngeal spasm — implement seizure precautions · Treatment: low-phosphorus diet, phosphate binders with the first bite of every meal , active vitamin D (calcitriol) to improve calcium absorption, calcium supplements, IV calcium gluconate for symptomatic hypocalcemia, dialysis · Because of the inverse relationship, treating the high phosphorus first helps the calcium rise · The calcium–phosphorus see-saw: when phosphorus rises, calcium drops, and the body steals calcium from the bones to balance the blood — secondary hyperparathyroidism and "renal bone disease" (renal osteodystrophy) · In renal failure the kidneys fail to excrete most electrolytes and fail to activate vitamin D — producing the trio of high phosphorus, low calcium, and bone disease · Magnesium imbalances · Magnesium is mainly an intracellular electrolyte (about 60% is in bone) that controls neuromuscular and cardiac irritability and helps the body make parathyroid hormone — so it's tied to calcium and potassium. The kidneys are the main route of excretion, which is why kidney failure is the most common cause of hypermagnesemia . Course range: about 1.5–2.5 mEq/L (some references use 1.3–2.1 mEq/L). Because about 30% of magnesium is bound to albumin, check the albumin with the magnesium — a low albumin makes the total magnesium read low. ·  | Hypermagnesemia (high) | Hypomagnesemia (low) · Effect on nerves & muscles | Depresses — blocks neuromuscular transmission | Irritates — nerves and muscles become hyperexcitable · Renal causes | Kidney failure (most common); magnesium-containing antacids and laxatives (Milk of Magnesia, magnesium citrate); magnesium-rich dialysate; magnesium sulfate infusions; untreated DKA; older age; adrenal insufficiency | Hemodialysis; loop and thiazide diuretics ; aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin), cisplatin, cyclosporine, amphotericin B; glomerulonephritis and pyelonephritis (impaired reabsorption); diarrhea, NG suction, alcohol use disorder, PPIs · Cues | Flushing and warmth, hypotension, nausea/vomiting, diminished or absent DTRs , weakness progressing to flaccid paralysis, drowsiness/lethargy, slow, shallow respirations , bradycardia , heart block, cardiac arrest | Hyperactive DTRs , tremors, twitching, tetany , + Chvostek and Trousseau (with low calcium), seizures, confusion, dysphagia, laryngeal stridor, tachycardia, dysrhythmias (torsades de pointes, V-tach, A-fib), digoxin toxicity · ECG | Prolonged PR, widened QRS, tall T waves | Prolonged PR and QT, widened QRS, ST depression, flattened T waves, prominent U waves · Treatment | Stop all magnesium products; IV/oral fluids and a loop diuretic if the kidneys work; IV calcium gluconate (the antagonist) in an emergency; dialysis with magnesium-free dialysate in renal failure; ventilation or pacing if needed | Magnesium-rich diet and oral supplements for mild cases; IV magnesium sulfate for severe cases (assess renal function first) · Nursing | Frequent VS (hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression); DTRs and muscle strength; continuous cardiac monitoring; monitor BUN/creatinine and urine output; flag the chart "No magnesium products" ; calcium gluconate and resuscitation equipment ready | Seizure precautions; check swallowing before oral intake; cardiac monitoring when below about 1 mEq/L; monitor K⁺ and Ca²⁺ (they fall together); watch for digoxin toxicity · Hypermagnesemia — symptoms climb with the level · Serum magnesium (about) | Signs & symptoms · 3 mEq/L | Feeling of warmth, flushing, mild hypotension, nausea and vomiting · 4 mEq/L | Facial paresthesia, diminished DTRs , muscle weakness, drowsiness · 5 mEq/L | ECG changes, bradycardia, worsening hypotension · 7 mEq/L | Loss of DTRs — an absent patellar reflex is reported immediately · 8 mEq/L | Respiratory compromise, heart block · 12 mEq/L | Flaccid paralysis, coma · 15 mEq/L | Respiratory arrest · 20 mEq/L | Cardiac arrest · RENAL = hypermagnesemia, because poor renal excretion is the main cause: R eflexes decreased (weakness, paralysis), E CG changes (bradycardia) and hypotension, N ausea and vomiting, A ppearance flushed, L ethargy (drowsiness, coma). For low magnesium, think STARVED : S eizures, T etany, A norexia and arrhythmias, R apid heart rate, V omiting, E motional lability, D TRs increased. · IV magnesium sulfate safety · Infusion pump only — no faster than 150 mg/minute ; a rapid bolus can cause cardiac arrest · Check VS and DTRs; watch for hypotension and respiratory distress (signs of excess) about every 15 minutes · Monitor urine output before, during, and after — notify the provider if output is less than 100 mL in 4 hours (magnesium is excreted by the kidneys) · Continuous cardiac monitoring; keep calcium gluconate at the bedside · Always write out "magnesium sulfate" — MgSO₄ is easily confused with MSO₄ (morphine sulfate) · Sodium imbalances · Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal 135–145 mEq/L ) — it controls where water goes. "Think sodium, think water": sodium problems are really water-balance problems, and their signs are mainly neurologic because water moves into or out of brain cells. Renal failure causes both: the kidney can't excrete water (dilutional hyponatremia) or sodium (sodium and water retention, hypertension). ·  | Hyponatremia (below 135 mEq/L) | Hypernatremia (above 145 mEq/L) · What's happening | Too much water for the sodium — cells swell (cerebral edema) | Too little water for the sodium — cells shrink · Types / causes | Hypovolemic (sodium lost more than water): vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, burns, adrenal insufficiency. Hypervolemic (water gained more than sodium): heart failure, liver failure, nephrotic syndrome , excess hypotonic IV fluids. Isovolemic (dilutional): kidney failure , SIADH , hypothyroidism | Water loss: fever, burns, vomiting/diarrhea, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis, older adults with an impaired thirst response, clients who can't drink. Sodium gain: sodium bicarbonate, sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) , hypertonic saline, tube feedings, corticosteroids · Cues | Headache, irritability, confusion, lethargy, muscle twitching, weakness, abdominal cramps, nausea/vomiting (often starting around 115–120 mEq/L); stupor, seizures, coma near 110 mEq/L. Hypovolemic: poor turgor, orthostatic hypotension, weak rapid pulse. Hypervolemic: edema, hypertension, weight gain, bounding pulse | Intense thirst , restlessness/agitation, low-grade fever, flushed skin, twitching, hyperreflexia, confusion → seizures, coma. Water loss: dry mucous membranes, oliguria, orthostatic hypotension. Sodium gain: hypertension, bounding pulse, dyspnea · Treatment | Fluid restriction (primary treatment for dilutional; about 1 L/day in SIADH); isotonic saline if hypovolemic; 3% saline only for severe, symptomatic cases (below 120) in the ICU — slowly, no more than about 1–2 mEq/L per hour (no more than 25 mEq/L in 48 hours) to avoid brain injury | Treat the cause; replace water gradually over about 48 hours (D5W, then ½ NS) — correcting too fast shifts water into brain cells ( cerebral edema ); restrict sodium · Nursing | Neuro checks; daily weights; strict I&O; post fluid restriction signs; seizure precautions; infusion pump for any saline | Neuro checks; daily weights; strict I&O; mark cups and give a target intake per shift; mouth care; seizure precautions; infusion pump · SALT = hypernatremia: S kin flushed, A gitation, L ow-grade fever, T hirst. Whichever direction the sodium is off, correct it slowly . · Sodium and fluid volume ·  | Fluid volume excess (overload) | Fluid volume deficit (dehydration) · When seen | Oliguric AKI, CKD/ESRD, missed dialysis, nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis | Prerenal AKI, diuretic phase of AKI, poor intake, vomiting/diarrhea, over-diuresis · Cues | Weight gain, edema, crackles, dyspnea, JVD, bounding pulses , hypertension, low SpO₂ | Weight loss, tachycardia, hypotension, weak/thready pulses , dry mucous membranes, poor turgor, concentrated urine, confusion (older adults) · Sodium | Often low (dilutional hyponatremia) | Often high (hypernatremia) when water is lost in excess of sodium · Hematocrit | Low (diluted) | High ( hemoconcentration ) · Priority actions | High Fowler's, oxygen, fluid and sodium restriction, loop diuretics (if still making urine), dialysis | Isotonic IV fluids; correct hypernatremia slowly to avoid cerebral edema; monitor for overload in older/cardiac patients · Weight is the most accurate indicator of fluid gain or loss in an acutely ill client. Get an accurate daily weight — same time, same scale, same clothing — and record it. A 1-kg (about 2.2-lb) change equals about 1,000 mL of fluid. · The hematocrit vs. hemoglobin dilution trick: hematocrit is a percentage of the blood that is cells, so added water drops it; hemoglobin is an absolute amount and stays more stable. A falling hematocrit with a stable hemoglobin = fluid gain . If both fall together, think bleeding. · Dilutional hyponatremia: the sodium is low because of too much water, not sodium loss — remove the water, don't add salt · Fluid restriction counts every source: PO fluids, maintenance IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and the fluid IV medications are mixed in · Watch for overcorrection: dialysis and diuretics can push the client into fluid volume deficit — hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness after a dialysis run or a dose of furosemide. Daily weights and BP catch it · Ascites: the fluid wave test — hand on the middle of the abdomen (or the side if obese), tap gently on the other side; a positive test is a fluid wave felt across the abdomen. A fluid-filled abdomen feels squishy, not hard, and percusses dull (air is tympanic) · Orthopnea: can't breathe lying flat — ask how many pillows the client sleeps on. An S3 gallop means the ventricle is being overfilled · Hyponatremia and hypernatremia both show up as neurologic changes — confusion, lethargy, seizures — because sodium shifts pull water into or out of brain cells. That's also why correcting either one too fast is dangerous. · Metabolic acidosis in renal failure · Kidneys can't excrete hydrogen ions or regenerate bicarbonate → low HCO 3 , low pH · Cues: Kussmaul respirations (compensation), headache, confusion, lethargy, nausea, hyperkalemia · Treatment: oral sodium bicarbonate in CKD; IV bicarbonate for severe acidosis (pH below 7.35); dialysis · The metabolic acidosis of chronic renal failure is often asymptomatic ; when it causes symptoms, it is reduced with sodium bicarbonate supplements or dialysis · Class poster review — fluid volume overload · Signs & symptoms | Interventions · Neuro: headache, altered mental status, neuro changes/ seizures from ↑ ICP, fatigue, ↓ appetite Respiratory: pulmonary edema, dyspnea/shortness of breath, orthopnea , crackles/wheezing, wet cough, pink frothy sputum , ↑ RR, ↓ O₂ sat Cardiovascular: hypertension, tachycardia, S3 heart sound , murmur, bounding pulse , JVD, cool/clammy skin Fluid: fluid retention, pitting edema, anasarca , weeping skin, third spacing, ascites , rapid weight gain Labs: hyponatremia (dilutional), low H&H (dilution), ↑ BUN/creatinine; severe electrolyte dilution can lead to seizures and death | Raise the HOB ; administer/titrate O₂ as needed Strict I&O charting ; daily weights Restrict intake — fluid and sodium; limit IV fluids ; renal/low-sodium diet Turn every 2 hours; elevate extremities Bed rest until stable, then activity as tolerated Neuro checks; seizure monitoring/precautions PRN; fall-risk precautions Diuretics — furosemide (Lasix) ; monitor K⁺ Encourage voiding; incentive spirometer Albumin for third spacing (pulls fluid back into the vessels; needs kidney function or dialysis to remove it) Mannitol — less commonly used in kidney failure (more common for increased ICP/cerebral edema); it first pulls fluid into the bloodstream, so without working kidneys (or dialysis) it can worsen pulmonary edema and heart failure Dialysis · Incentive spirometry and suctioning don't remove pulmonary edema. IS helps prevent atelectasis and pneumonia in a client on bed rest, but it doesn't move fluid out of the alveoli — and suctioning edema fluid is "like trying to catch bubbles." What actually removes the fluid: raising the HOB and O₂ for the breathing, then diuretics and dialysis . · Class poster review — hyperkalemia · Signs & symptoms | Interventions · Cardiac: dysrhythmias, peaked T waves , widened QRS , irregular heart rate and rhythm, PVCs, tachycardia or bradycardia , ↓ BP, V-tach Neuromuscular: muscle weakness, muscle irritability, paresthesia, fatigue GI: abdominal cramps, GI issues Acid–base: metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul respirations Severe: seizures, coma, death | Cardiac monitoring (ECG) Calcium gluconate FIRST — protect the heart IV regular insulin + 50% glucose — monitor blood sugar Sodium bicarbonate; albuterol Kayexalate / Lokelma Non-potassium-sparing diuretic ( furosemide ); NO spironolactone Monitor I&O and BUN/creatinine Limit K⁺ in the diet; no salt substitutes Seizure precautions; safety/fall precautions Dialysis (last resort) · Class poster review — hypocalcemia / hyperphosphatemia · Signs & symptoms | Interventions · Hypocalcemia: tetany , tingling fingers, numbness around the mouth, muscle cramps, pain/aches, + Chvostek , + Trousseau , laryngeal and bronchospasm , dysrhythmias, prolonged ST and QT, tachycardia, seizures, altered mental status Hypocalcemia (this semester's board): paresthesia, muscle weakness, dysrhythmias, QT prolongation , bronchospasm, respiratory distress, coma, cardiac arrest Hyperphosphatemia: weak bones/osteoporosis, low bone density, ↑ fracture risk, joint pain, fatigue, hypotension, severe pruritus /skin rash, dry scaly skin, brittle nails | Heart monitor IV calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride); t: Dialysis Types: Hemodialysis, Peritoneal Dialysis & CRRT
x: How each one works, access types and care, and the complications to watch for · Dialysis takes over the kidneys' filtering job by moving wastes, excess electrolytes, and water across a semipermeable membrane. It relies on three principles: diffusion (solutes move from higher to lower concentration — urea, creatinine, and potassium move out of the blood), osmosis (water moves toward the higher solute concentration), and ultrafiltration (water is pushed out by a pressure gradient). The three types differ in where the membrane is and how often they run. · When is dialysis needed? — AEIOU ·  | Indication · A | Acidosis — metabolic acidosis not controlled by bicarbonate · E | Electrolytes — severe hyperkalemia (or hyperphosphatemia) refractory to medical treatment · I | Intoxication — dialyzable drug or toxin overdose (e.g., salicylates, lithium) · O | Overload — symptomatic fluid overload/pulmonary edema not responding to diuretics · U | Uremia — uremic complications such as pericarditis or encephalopathy; also anuria · Comparing the three types ·  | Hemodialysis (HD) | Peritoneal dialysis (PD) | Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) · Membrane | Artificial membrane in an external dialyzer (the "artificial kidney") | The patient's own peritoneum acts as the semipermeable membrane | Artificial filter, run continuously at the bedside · Access | AV fistula, AV graft, or a temporary central venous dialysis catheter | Tenckhoff catheter surgically placed into the peritoneal cavity | Large-bore central venous dialysis catheter · Schedule | Usually 3 times a week, about 3–4 hours per session, at a center | Daily — manual exchanges several times a day (CAPD) or overnight by a machine (APD, cycler) | 24 hours a day in the ICU · Best for | Rapid removal of fluid, K⁺, and wastes; most ESRD patients | Patients who want independence at home; those who can't tolerate rapid fluid shifts | Hemodynamically unstable ICU patients who can't tolerate the rapid shifts of HD · Diet | More restrictive — K⁺, phosphorus, sodium, and fluid build up between treatments | More liberal — K⁺ is removed daily; phosphorus still limited; higher protein because protein is lost into the dialysate | Managed by the ICU team · Hemodialysis access types · Access | What it is | Timing | Key points · AV fistula | Surgical connection of an artery directly to a vein (usually in the forearm), so the vein enlarges and thickens | Needs about 1–3 months to mature before use (ideally created months before dialysis starts) | Preferred access — longest-lasting, lowest infection and clotting risk. Over years the vein can become visibly enlarged and bulging · AV graft | A synthetic tube tunneled under the skin connecting an artery to a vein | Usable in about 2–3 weeks | For patients whose vessels are not suitable for a fistula; higher risk of clotting and infection than a fistula · Vascath (temporary central catheter) | Temporary, non-tunneled, double-lumen catheter | Usable immediately — for acute needs (AKI) | High infection risk; not permanent. Strict sterile dressing changes; do not use for fluids or meds · Permacath (tunneled catheter) | Tunneled, long-term catheter under the skin | Usable immediately; lasts longer than a Vascath | Risk of clotting and infection. Monitor the exit site for redness; maintain the heparin lock · The AV fistula is the gold standard — lowest infection and clotting risk — but takes months to mature. The graft is a good option for clients with poor veins but has a higher risk of clotting (thrombosis), infection, aneurysm, and stenosis. · More access details · Dialysis catheters: placement in the upper chest is confirmed by x-ray before first use; the lumens are filled with concentrated heparin, so don't inject IV fluids or meds into them and don't unclamp unless preparing for dialysis (blood will fill the lumen and clot). The red lumen is "arterial" (blood to the machine) and the blue lumen is "venous" (blood back to the client). Temporary catheters are generally used for up to about 3–4 weeks. After removal, apply pressure and check the site for several hours — dialysis catheters are large and bleed more · AV fistula: ideally created months before dialysis is expected to start; after healing, the client exercises the arm (e.g., squeezing a ball) to help it mature. Check patency more often when the client is hypotensive (low BP promotes clotting). For post-dialysis needle-site bleeding, apply just enough pressure to stop the bleeding without occluding the vessel · AV graft: avoid puncturing a new graft for about 2–4 weeks while tissue grows into it · Vein preservation: in clients who may need a fistula someday, avoid PICC lines and subclavian catheters (they cause central vein stenosis) and protect the nondominant arm's veins · Fistula teaching: wash the site daily with antibacterial soap and before dialysis; don't pick scabs; check for redness, warmth, or a pimple-like spot; feel for the thrill several times a day and report any change; ask staff to rotate needle sites · Caring for an AV fistula or graft · Palpate for a thrill (a buzzing vibration) and auscultate for a bruit (a whooshing sound) every shift — their presence means the access is patent; absence means possible clotting and must be reported immediately · No blood pressures, venipunctures, IVs, or injections in the access arm · No tight clothing, jewelry, or restraints on the access arm; don't carry heavy objects with it or sleep on it · Post a sign or band identifying the access limb · Assess for infection — redness, warmth, drainage, fever · Check distal circulation — a pale, cold hand (with pain or numbness) can signal steal syndrome (the access diverts too much arterial blood from the hand) — a red flag, along with an absent thrill or bruit · After dialysis, apply gentle pressure to needle sites to control bleeding (heparin is used during the treatment) · Nursing care before and after hemodialysis · Before: weigh the patient (1 kg = 1 L), take vital signs, check labs, assess the access, and hold antihypertensives and water-soluble vitamins (and other drugs removed by dialysis, such as some antibiotics) until after treatment, per orders · After: weigh again (weight loss reflects fluid removed), take vital signs, assess for bleeding at the access and for hypotension, and watch for disequilibrium syndrome · CRRT nursing care · A slower, 24/7 form of dialysis — gentle on blood pressure, so it's used for hemodynamically unstable ICU clients who can't tolerate the rapid fluid shifts of hemodialysis · Requires close (often 1:1) ICU nursing care · Vital signs hourly for hemodynamic shifts · Check the filter for clotting — early sign is a falling ultrafiltration rate; then rising venous pressure and dark blood lines · Frequent electrolyte monitoring (at least twice daily) to prevent rapid imbalances; daily weights · An hourly fluid-balance goal is set; the nurse totals all intake and output each hour and adjusts replacement fluid to meet it · Blood leak alarm — blood in the ultrafiltrate means the filter has ruptured; gross blood = don't return the circuit blood to the client · Hypothermia — blood cools outside the body; use a blood warmer or warming blanket (hypothermia can also mask fever) · Hold ACE inhibitors before CRRT as ordered (risk of severe hypotension or reaction) · During and after hemodialysis · Vital signs before, during, and after dialysis — a slight temperature rise is expected from warming of the blood, but a persistent elevation suggests infection; watch for any precipitous drop in BP · Monitor for bleeding — heparin is used during dialysis to prevent clotting (reversed with protamine); watch platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia · BP and pulse at least every 30 minutes during acute hemodialysis; keep the access visible at all times (a disconnected line can cause rapid blood loss); discourage eating during treatment (can trigger hypotension and nausea) · Draw post-dialysis labs at least 2–3 hours after treatment — values drawn immediately afterward are falsely low while solutes re-equilibrate · Dry weight — the weight at which the client has no fluid excess or deficit — guides how much fluid to remove · Monitor for fluid overload before dialysis and for hypovolemia after · A client with a femoral catheter should sit up at less than a 45-degree angle and not lean forward, to avoid occlusion or kinking · Monitor the graft/fistula for clotting — inability to feel a thrill or hear a bruit, or client complaints of arm discomfort and paresthesia · The thrill feels like a "purring"; the bruit sounds like rushing water ("like a washing machine") · Complications of hemodialysis · Hypotension — from rapid removal of blood volume; the most common complication · Nausea, vomiting, chest pain, visual changes · Muscle cramps — from rapid fluid and electrolyte shifts (and low-sodium dialysis solution) · Steal syndrome — pain distal to the access site, poor capillary refill, paresthesia · Insertion/access site bleeding, hematoma, or infection · Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome — urea is removed from the blood faster than from the brain, pulling water into brain cells → headache, nausea/vomiting, restlessness, confusion, seizures. Highest risk in first treatments or after a long gap with a very high BUN; prevented with shorter sessions (e.g., 1–2 hours on 3–4 consecutive days) · Hypotension is treated with a normal saline bolus (about 100–200 mL) and slowing fluid removal; antihypertensives are often held 4–6 hours before dialysis and sedatives avoided. Muscle cramps are treated by lowering the ultrafiltration rate and giving a saline bolus · Dysrhythmias and angina in clients with heart disease — slow the fluid removal · Bleeding — from heparin used during treatment · Infection — especially with central catheters · Air embolism — rare but serious · Peritoneal dialysis — how an exchange works · Fill: warmed dialysate (dextrose solution) flows in by gravity through the Tenckhoff catheter · Dwell: it stays in the peritoneal cavity for a prescribed time while wastes and water move across the peritoneum by diffusion and osmosis (the dextrose pulls water out) · Drain: the bag is lowered below the abdomen and the fluid drains out by gravity, carrying wastes and excess water · CAPD (continuous ambulatory PD) — manual exchanges about 4 times a day; APD (automated PD) — a cycler machine performs exchanges overnight · CCPD (continuous cyclic PD — cycler exchanges overnight with a long daytime dwell) gives the client more independence during the day, but the risk of peritonitis is greater · Peritoneal dialysis nursing care · Before starting: baseline vital signs and weight; have the client empty the bladder (if still making urine); assess the abdomen and catheter site · Warm dialysate to body temperature in a commercial warmer — never a microwave (uneven heating can burn the peritoneum) · Strict aseptic technique for every connection. The infusion clamp is opened during inflow and clamped after ; when the dwell is done, the drain clamp is opened and fluid drains by gravity into the drainage bag · Typical exchange: fill by gravity over about 5–10 minutes, dwell about 30–45 minutes (acute) or hours (CAPD), drain by gravity in no more than about 20 minutes. Dextrose strengths are 1.5%, 2.5%, or 4.25% — higher concentrations pull off more fluid · If drainage is short by 500 mL or more after several exchanges, evaluate for fluid retention (abdominal distention, fullness, weight gain) · Clear fluid leaking around the catheter can be confirmed as dialysate with a glucose test strip (positive because of the dextrose) · Hypokalemia is common (dialysate usually has no potassium) — KCl may be added; insulin may be added for hyperglycemia · PD is contraindicated with existing peritonitis, recent or extensive abdominal surgery, or abdominal adhesions; in cardiac arrest, the abdomen is drained immediately · Strict aseptic technique with every connection; mask during exchanges; daily catheter exit-site care · Outflow (effluent) should be clear, straw-colored / pale yellow . Blood-tinged outflow is expected in the first few exchanges after catheter placement · Outflow color guide: clear straw-colored = normal; cloudy = peritonitis; bloody after the first few exchanges = vascular complication; brown = bowel perforation; urine-colored = bladder perforation — report anything other than clear · Don't let the dwell run longer than prescribed (more glucose absorbed → hyperglycemia). If outflow is less than inflow, the difference has been absorbed and is counted as intake · Abdominal cramping is common during inflow in the first few exchanges (warm dialysate helps). After catheter placement, smaller volumes are used for about 1–2 weeks while the cuffs heal in, to prevent leaking · Catheter cuffs are made of Dacron polyester. As tissue grows into them they stabilize the catheter , prevent dialysate from leaking , and provide a barrier against microorganisms · Cloudy outflow = peritonitis until proven otherwise — along with fever, abdominal pain, rebound tenderness, and a rigid, board-like abdomen ; send a sample for culture and notify the provider · Poor (sluggish) outflow: the main cause is a full colon — prevent constipation with fiber and stool softeners. Also check for kinks and closed clamps, keep the bag below the abdomen, and reposition the client side to side (or elevate the HOB, gently massage the abdomen); fibrin clots may need heparin added to the dialysate as ordered · Shortness of breath during the dwell means the fluid may be pushing on the diaphragm — drain the fluid immediately · Intake and output math for dialysis · True urine output = total output − the amount of dialysate/irrigant instilled · Ultrafiltration (fluid removed) = dialysate drained out − dialysate put in. Example: 2,000 mL in, 2,500 mL out → 500 mL of fluid removed · Outflow should equal or exceed inflow; if less drains out than went in, the client is retaining fluid · Complications of peritoneal dialysis · Peritonitis — the most serious; cloudy outflow, abdominal pain, fever · Exit-site or tunnel infection · Hyperglycemia and weight gain from dextrose absorbed from the dialysate · Hernias and back pain from the weight of the dialysate (orthopedic binders may help back pain) · Pneumonia and atelectasis from pressure on the diaphragm during the dwell · Ongoing protein loss and malnutrition — monitor nutritional status · The two access-patency checks are paired senses: you feel a thrill and hear a bruit. For PD, the eyes do the work — any cloudy bag is peritonitis until proven otherwise.

t: The Renal Diet: Potassium, Phosphorus & Sodium
x: From the GU diet handout — what to limit, why, and the "double jeopardy" foods · Why potassium matters · Potassium is a mineral found in most foods. It helps with muscle movement, keeps the nervous system healthy, and helps balance the amount of water in the body. The kidneys control the blood potassium level, so in kidney disease it can build up to high levels — hyperkalemia — which can be dangerous for the heart. · Why phosphorus matters · Phosphorus helps build strong bones and teeth and helps convert food into energy. Kidneys normally release extra phosphorus into the urine; kidney disease prevents this, and the buildup causes problems for the bones and heart. · Hemodialysis diet · Potassium is limited because it builds up between dialysis treatments, causing weakness, muscle cramps, tiredness, irregular heartbeat, and even heart attack · Potassium is found mostly in fruits, vegetables, and dairy products . Eating a large amount of a low-potassium food can still add up to a dangerous level · Most foods contain some potassium — meat, poultry, bread, pasta.
