Butter, margarine, and oils are the only potassium-free foods · Phosphorus is limited because hemodialysis removes only a small amount. Without diet limits and phosphorus binders, levels climb — causing itching, weak and brittle bones, and calcium deposits in blood vessels and organs including the heart and lungs · Phosphorus is highest in high-protein foods, dairy, nuts, seeds, dried beans and peas, chocolate, colas, and whole-grain foods · Peritoneal dialysis diet · Because PD is performed daily , the diet is a little more liberal · Potassium is usually removed well through PD, so most PD patients keep a normal or even low potassium — those with low levels may be told to eat potassium-rich foods such as tomatoes, orange juice, and bananas · Phosphorus is not removed well during PD, so PD patients still need to limit phosphorus · Double jeopardy foods — high in both potassium and phosphorus · Most high-potassium foods come from plants (fruits and vegetables). High-protein foods such as meats, along with dried beans and peas, tend to be high in phosphorus. Foods high in both — dairy, nuts, seeds, chocolate, and some whole-grain foods — are best avoided or used in very small amounts. · Double jeopardy food | Kidney-friendly alternative · Cheese | Vegan rella cheese, low-fat cottage cheese, a sprinkle of parmesan (very small amounts of extra-sharp cheese for maximum flavor) · Chocolate | Desserts made with lemon or apple, white cake, rice-crispy treats · Cream soup | Broth-based soups with pureed vegetables, or soups made with acceptable milk substitutes · Dried beans and peas | Green beans, wax beans · Ice cream | Sorbet, sherbet, popsicles · Milk | Almond milk, Rice Dream original, unenriched rice beverage · Nuts | Low-salt snack foods — pretzels, tortilla chips, popcorn, crackers, Sun Chips · Peanut butter | Low-fat cream cheese, jam, or fruit spread · Phosphorus targets · CKD stages 3 and 4: keep phosphorus between 2.7 and 4.6 mg/dL · Dialysis patients: keep phosphorus between 3.0 and 5.5 mg/dL · Seven ways to help control phosphorus levels · 1. Reduce phosphorus intake — eat foods low in phosphorus · 2. Take phosphorus binders — taken with meals and snacks ; they act like sponges that soak up phosphorus in the stomach so it passes through the GI tract instead of entering the bloodstream. A low-phosphorus diet is still necessary for binders to work well · 3. Take vitamin D — an active form called calcitriol helps balance calcium and phosphorus. Active vitamin D cannot be taken if calcium or phosphorus levels are too high , because it increases the risk of deposits in soft tissues such as arteries, lungs, eyes, and skin · 4. Take a calcimimetic medicine — helps lower parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcium, and possibly phosphorus to keep bones healthier · 5. Stay on dialysis the entire time — dialysis removes some phosphorus; staying for the full treatment time gives the best results · 6. Start a provider-approved exercise program — builds strength and, in some cases, bone · 7. Parathyroid surgery — in some cases, removing part of the parathyroid glands prevents long-term PTH release that weakens bone and calcifies tissues · Patients should tell their provider and dietitian about all medicines and supplements, because some contain phosphorus · Shopping for a low-phosphorus diet · Shop the outer perimeter of the grocery store (fresh foods); avoid the middle aisles, where shelf-stable boxed foods use phosphorus as a preservative · Dark sodas use phosphorus for color — clear sodas are lower · Milk and dairy are avoided even though the client's calcium is low — the phosphorus in them drives calcium down further. "Drink more milk to raise your calcium" is a wrong answer · Fresh vegetables are generally acceptable (watch the high-potassium ones) · Cheap, shelf-stable food is the easiest to get, so cost can be a real barrier — assess barriers and refer to a dietitian or social work rather than just re-teaching the diet · Kidney-friendly snacks · Fruit: apples, grapes, tangerines, strawberries; dried cranberries or blueberries; fruit cups with peaches, pears, pineapple, mandarin oranges, or mixed fruit · Low- or no-sodium microwave popcorn · Low-sodium crackers, pita chips, or unsalted pretzels · A small can or pouch of tuna or chicken with individual mayonnaise packets · Kidney-friendly nutrition bars or supplements that meet these guidelines: protein 15 g or more , potassium 200 mg or less , phosphorus 150 mg or less , sodium 300 mg or less · Stocking a kidney-friendly kitchen (key tips) · Compare brands — sodium and potassium levels vary significantly · Choose low-sodium broths, stocks, and condiments; fresh vegetables or no-salt-added frozen/canned (drain and rinse canned vegetables) · Use only 1/4 of the tomato sauce and canned tomatoes a recipe calls for, to limit potassium and sodium · Rinse canned fish or chicken; limit canned goods in general · Avoid baking and pancake mixes with added salt and baking powder · Use sweet pickles instead of dill pickles · Check cereals for sodium; oatmeal has more phosphorus but may be okay 1–2 times a week if phosphorus is well controlled · Check vinegars (seasoned rice vinegar has added salt), and avoid store-bought sauces and gravies · Choose homemade soups — some canned soups contain more than 800 mg sodium per serving · Don't trade sodium for potassium — some salt substitutes replace salt with potassium chloride · Limit nuts, seeds, and chocolate — high in potassium and phosphorus · Renal diet quick table (CKD & ESRD) · Nutrient | High — avoid/limit | Lower — safer choices | Why / nurse tip · Potassium | Bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach, tomatoes, avocados | Apples, berries, grapes, green beans, cabbage | Avoid salt substitutes (potassium chloride). The kidneys can't excrete it; high K⁺ leads to lethal dysrhythmias · Phosphorus | Dairy (milk, cheese, yogurt), nuts, dark colas, whole grains | Rice milk, sorbet, clear sodas, white bread/rice | "Double jeopardy" foods like chocolate and dairy are high in both K⁺ and phosphorus. High phosphorus pulls calcium from bones · Sodium | Canned soups, processed meats, pickled foods, soy sauce | Fresh herbs, lemon juice, no-salt-added canned vegetables | Rinse canned fish or vegetables to remove salt. Sodium causes water retention, HTN, and edema · Protein | Excessive meat, poultry, or eggs (pre-dialysis CKD) | Small portions of high-biological-value protein (egg whites) | Limit protein before dialysis; once on dialysis, protein may be increased to replace losses · Fluid | Anything liquid at room temperature counts — water, ice, Jell-O, ice cream | Measured amounts | Prevents fluid volume overload. Use small cups; suck on hard candy or chew gum for thirst · Renal rule of thumb: if it's "healthy" elsewhere, it's often dangerous in renal disease — bananas, spinach, oranges, and whole grains are all restricted because of their potassium and phosphorus. · Phosphate binders: "If you skip the meal, skip the pill." They only work when there is food in the stomach to bind to — so they're taken with the first bite of every meal. · The salt-substitute trap is a classic exam item: a patient with kidney disease who switches to a salt substitute to lower sodium may be adding potassium chloride — exactly what the kidneys can't get rid of.

An immune reaction in the glomeruli — often after a recent strep infection · Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli , the kidney's filtering capillaries. In the classic acute form, antigen–antibody complexes from a recent streptococcal infection (often strep throat, typically about 2–3 weeks earlier) lodge in the glomeruli, causing inflammation and a decreased glomerular filtration rate . This is an immune reaction to the infection — not bacteria infecting the kidney itself. · Glomerulonephritis vs. pyelonephritis: glomerulonephritis is an immune problem (antibody complexes after strep), so antibiotics alone don't fix the kidney. Pyelonephritis is an infection of the kidney itself, so antibiotics are the treatment. · Primary presenting features of acute glomerulonephritis: hematuria, edema, azotemia (excess nitrogenous wastes in the blood), and proteinuria. · Causes beyond strep: acute glomerulonephritis is also associated with varicella zoster virus, hepatitis B, and Epstein-Barr virus . · Priority assessments/cues · Recent strep infection — ask about a sore throat or skin infection in the past few weeks · Headache · Elevated blood pressure — from sodium and water retention · Facial / periorbital edema — often most noticeable in the morning · Lethargy · Low-grade fever · Weight gain (from edema) · Urine: proteinuria, hematuria, oliguria, dysuria ; urine may be dark, tea- or cola-colored from blood · Signs of fluid overload — crackles, dyspnea, JVD · Priority laboratory/diagnostic cues · Urinalysis — hematuria with RBC casts, proteinuria (mild to moderate), increased specific gravity · Elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer — evidence of a recent strep infection · Elevated BUN and creatinine; decreased GFR · Decreased serum complement levels · Elevated ESR (inflammation) · Kidney biopsy may be done to confirm the type · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Rest during the acute phase, until urine clears and BP normalizes · Monitor BP closely; give antihypertensives as ordered · Sodium and fluid restriction ; daily weights; strict I&O · Loop diuretics for edema and fluid overload · Antibiotics if a strep infection is still present (treats the infection, not the kidney inflammation) · Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants for some forms (such as rapidly progressive disease) to suppress the immune reaction · Protein restricted if azotemia is significant; adequate calories · Teach the patient to report decreased urine output, increasing edema, or headache; teach the importance of treating future strep infections fully · Priority actual & potential complications · Hypertensive encephalopathy — severe headache or neuro changes = emergency · Heart failure and pulmonary edema from fluid overload · Acute kidney injury · Progression to chronic glomerulonephritis and CKD · The Nephritic vs. Nephrotic slide also names Berger's disease (IgA nephropathy) as the most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis — an immune condition in which IgA antibody deposits in the glomeruli, often producing hematuria after an upper respiratory infection.

Bacterial infection of the kidney — acute illness, and scarring when it becomes chronic · Pyelonephritis is not a simple UTI — it is a bacterial infection of the renal pelvis, tubules, and interstitial tissue of the kidney. It usually starts as a lower urinary tract infection that ascends from the bladder up the ureters. E. coli is the most common organism. The lecture image contrasts a normal kidney with a pyelonephritic kidney showing inflammation, pus, scarring, and atrophy of the cortex . · Risk factors · Lower UTI that isn't treated or treated fully · Urinary obstruction or stasis — stones, BPH, tumors · Vesicoureteral reflux (urine flowing backward from the bladder into the ureters) · Indwelling urinary catheters and instrumentation · Pregnancy · Diabetes and immunosuppression · Female anatomy (shorter urethra) · Acute vs. chronic ·  | Acute pyelonephritis | Chronic pyelonephritis · What it is | An active kidney infection | Repeated or persistent infections causing scarring and loss of kidney tissue · Cues | Fever and chills, flank pain , costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness , nausea/vomiting, malaise, plus lower UTI symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency); cloudy, foul-smelling urine | Often few symptoms until late — fatigue, headache, hypertension, poor appetite, polyuria and nocturia (the kidney loses concentrating ability) · Outcome | Usually resolves with antibiotics | Scarring, atrophy, and progression to CKD · Priority laboratory/diagnostic cues · Urinalysis — WBCs (pyuria), WBC casts (confirm the infection is in the kidney, not just the bladder), bacteria, positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase, possibly hematuria · Urine culture and sensitivity — collect before starting antibiotics · CBC — leukocytosis · Blood cultures if urosepsis is suspected · Imaging (ultrasound or CT) to look for obstruction or abscess · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · IV antibiotics as ordered, then oral — often about 2 weeks total. Teach the patient to finish the entire course even when feeling better, to clear the infection and prevent kidney scarring · Follow-up urine culture to confirm the infection is cleared · High fluid intake — 2–3 L/day unless contraindicated — to flush bacteria; IV fluids until the client can tolerate oral fluids · Collect a clean-catch urine sample (teach the correct technique to prevent contamination); use sterile technique if a catheter must be inserted · Analgesics and antipyretics for flank pain and fever; warm, moist heat to the flank · Re-culture the urine after antibiotics are completed (about 2 weeks after the course ends) to confirm resolution; a relapse may need antibiotics for up to 6 weeks · Measure I&O carefully and check the temperature every 4 hours in the hospitalized client · Monitor for signs of urosepsis — hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, high fever · Teach UTI prevention: void frequently and after intercourse, wipe front to back, avoid holding urine, report early UTI symptoms · Priority actual & potential complications · Urosepsis , septicemia, and septic shock · Renal abscess · Chronic pyelonephritis with scarring — leading to hypertension, renal calculi, and end-stage kidney disease · AKI and progression to CKD, dialysis, or transplant · Priority hypotheses for nursing care · In older adults, a common cause of pyelonephritis is catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) — avoid unnecessary catheters · UTIs may be life-threatening in infants and older adults — rapid progression to sepsis · Older adults may present with new confusion or agitation rather than classic urinary symptoms · Priority medications (antibiotics) · Ampicillin — broad-spectrum; oral, IM, or IV · Vancomycin (IV) — often combined with gentamicin or tobramycin; monitor drug levels (trough about 10–20 mcg/mL). Infusing too quickly causes red man syndrome (itching and flushing of the head, face, neck, and upper torso) · Gentamicin, tobramycin (aminoglycosides) — nephrotoxic and ototoxic; monitor levels and kidney function · Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (oral) — may be switched to once culture results are back; check for sulfa allergy · Ciprofloxacin (oral, IV) — risk of tendonitis or tendon rupture (primarily the Achilles tendon) · NSAIDs for mild pain — the most significant adverse effect is GI bleeding

A leaky glomerulus — massive proteinuria, low albumin, severe edema, high lipids · In nephrotic syndrome, damage to the glomerulus makes it abnormally permeable to protein — the lecture's "leaky glomerulus lets protein out." Large amounts of protein, mainly albumin, spill into the urine. The loss of albumin lowers the blood's oncotic pressure, fluid leaks into the tissues, and severe edema follows. The liver responds to low protein by making more lipoproteins, so cholesterol rises. · The four hallmark findings · Massive proteinuria — more than 3.5 g/day (heavy urinary protein loss) · Hypoalbuminemia · Severe edema — periorbital, peripheral, and generalized (anasarca), plus ascites · Hyperlipidemia — high LDL cholesterol · Urine appears foamy or frothy from the protein · Causes · Primary glomerular disease (such as minimal change disease — the most common cause in children) · Diabetes (diabetic nephropathy) · Systemic lupus erythematosus · Chronic glomerulonephritis · Multiple myeloma · Renal vein thrombosis · Other systemic diseases, infections, and certain drugs · Priority assessments/cues · Edema — location and degree; daily weight and abdominal girth · Urine — foamy appearance, output · Signs of infection — immunoglobulins are lost in the urine, so infection risk rises · Signs of blood clots — DVT (unilateral leg swelling, pain), pulmonary embolism, renal vein thrombosis · Skin integrity over edematous areas · Respiratory status if ascites or pleural effusion develops · Priority laboratory/diagnostic cues · 24-hour urine protein greater than 3.5 g · Low serum albumin and total protein · Elevated cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides · BUN and creatinine — may be normal early, rising as disease progresses · Kidney biopsy to identify the underlying cause · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Corticosteroids (prednisone) and other immunosuppressants to reduce proteinuria, depending on the cause · ACE inhibitors or ARBs to lower glomerular pressure and reduce protein loss · Loop diuretics for edema · Statins for hyperlipidemia; anticoagulants if clots develop or risk is high · Diet: low sodium , low saturated fat, and moderate — not high — protein · Meticulous skin care; reposition often; elevate edematous extremities · Infection prevention — hand hygiene, avoid sick contacts, vaccinations as ordered · Encourage mobility to reduce clot risk · Priority actual & potential complications · Thromboembolism — clotting proteins are lost in the urine, making the blood hypercoagulable · Infection · Accelerated atherosclerosis · Acute kidney injury and progression to CKD · Nephritic vs. nephrotic syndrome · These are often confused. Remember: Nephritic = blood/HTN ; Nephrotic = protein/edema . Neph r-I-tic = I nflammation; neph r-O-tic = O verflowing protein. · Feature | Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic) | Nephrotic syndrome · Primary cause | Post-infectious — often strep throat about 2–3 weeks earlier; Berger's disease (IgA nephropathy) is the most common cause of primary glomerulonephritis | Glomerular damage causing massive "leaking" — e.g., minimal change disease, diabetic nephropathy · Key symptom | Cola-colored (smoky) urine (hematuria); oliguria | Massive edema (anasarca/periorbital) · Urinalysis | RBCs, mild protein | Massive proteinuria (more than 3.5 g/day); foamy urine · Blood pressure | Hypertension is common | Normal or low (fluid shifts out of the vessels) · Key lab | Positive ASO titer (strep antibodies); rising BUN/creatinine | Hypoalbuminemia (low blood protein) and hyperlipidemia · Nursing priority | Manage BP, fluid restriction, antibiotics (if strep is active) | Skin care (edema), infection prevention (loss of immunoglobulins), corticosteroids · The Nephritic vs. Nephrotic cartoon: the nephritic side shows an inflamed glomerulus with a BP cuff (HTN), dripping urine (oliguria), and cola-colored urine (hematuria); the nephrotic side shows a swollen patient (peripheral edema), protein in the urine sample (massive proteinuria), and blood full of fat globules (hyperlipidemia) with too little albumin.

Hardening of the renal arteries — the kidney damage of long-standing hypertension · Nephrosclerosis is hardening of the renal arteries . The lecture image shows plaque building up where the renal arteries leave the aorta, narrowing the renal artery . As the vessels thicken and narrow, blood flow to the kidney falls, the tissue becomes ischemic, and nephrons are gradually lost. It is typically caused by prolonged, uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes (type 1 or 2), along with atherosclerosis, and it's a major cause of CKD. It's a "silent killer": BUN and creatinine rise with minimal symptoms at first. · A two-way street with hypertension · High blood pressure damages the renal arterioles, and the damaged, underperfused kidney then activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, which raises blood pressure further. Each problem worsens the other, which is why blood pressure control is the core of management. · Two forms ·  | Benign nephrosclerosis | Accelerated (malignant) nephrosclerosis · Associated with | Long-standing, often moderate hypertension; aging; atherosclerosis | Severely elevated blood pressure (hypertensive emergency) · Course | Slow and gradual; often no symptoms early | Rapid — kidney function can decline over weeks · Cues | Hypertension, mild proteinuria, slowly rising BUN and creatinine | Severe hypertension, headache, visual changes (hypertensive retinopathy), rapidly rising BUN and creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria · Priority assessments/cues · Blood pressure trends · Kidney function labs over time — BUN, creatinine, GFR · Urine — protein, blood · Risk factors — hypertension, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia, older age · Vision changes and headache (malignant form) · Signs of CKD as it progresses · Priority interventions/collaborative actions · Aggressive blood pressure control is the primary intervention — the only way to slow progression to ESRD. ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) are often preferred because they also protect the kidney and reduce proteinuria; beta blockers are also used · Lifestyle: sodium restriction, weight management, exercise, smoking cessation , limit alcohol · Lipid control (statins) and glucose control · Monitor kidney function regularly · Teach medication adherence — uncontrolled BP drives progression · As function declines, CKD management and eventually dialysis or transplant · Priority actual & potential complications · Progression to CKD and ESRD · Hypertensive emergency (malignant form) · Cardiovascular disease — heart attack and stroke share the same vascular process

An inherited disorder — fluid-filled cysts crowd out the nephrons · Polycystic kidney disease is a genetic disorder in which numerous fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidneys, enlarging them and destroying the nephrons. There's no cure — it progresses to CKD and kidney failure . It's the most common inherited cause of kidney failure. · Types ·  | Autosomal dominant (ADPKD — "adult") | Autosomal recessive (ARPKD — "infantile") · How common | Most common form (about 90%) | Rare (about 10%) · Inheritance | One affected parent can pass it on | Both parents are carriers but unaffected · Onset | Often no symptoms until about age 30–40; progresses to end-stage kidney disease | Begins in utero or the first months of life; often fatal in infancy · Cysts can also form in the liver and pancreas , and clients are at risk for brain (cerebral) aneurysms and cardiovascular problems. · Priority cues · Flank, lumbar, or abdominal pain — worse with activity, relieved by lying down; increasing abdominal fullness and girth · Palpable, enlarged kidneys / abdominal masses · Hypertension (often an early finding) — the finding the nurse is most likely to assess; it is present in about 75% of clients at diagnosis · Hematuria (cyst rupture), proteinuria, pyuria · Recurrent UTIs , fever and chills (infected cysts); kidney stones · Signs of progressing CKD — rising BUN/creatinine, the fluid and electrolyte problems of renal failure · A family history of kidney disease · Diagnostics · Renal ultrasound — the preferred test to see the cysts · Genetic testing if imaging is unclear; family history · Urinalysis, BUN/creatinine, GFR · Priority interventions · Control blood pressure (antihypertensives) to slow the decline · Pain management — avoid NSAIDs and aspirin (bleeding risk and they're nephrotoxic); dry heat to the flank or abdomen for comfort · Monitor for gross hematuria (cyst rupture) — bed rest if a cyst ruptures · Prevent and treat UTIs ; antibiotics for infected cysts · Adequate fluids; in early disease some clients lose sodium rather than retain it, so sodium and water may be encouraged as prescribed · Prevent constipation (enlarged kidneys press on the colon) — fiber, fluids, activity · Tolvaptan may be prescribed to slow the loss of kidney function — watch for polyuria/thirst and liver injury · Percutaneous drainage of a cyst for obstruction or abscess · Prepare for dialysis or transplant as the kidneys fail · Genetic counseling for the client and family; psychosocial support · PKD is the one renal exemplar you can inherit. Think big kidneys + family history + hypertension + flank pain and hematuria — and remember it ends in the same place as every other exemplar: CKD, with fluid overload, high potassium, high phosphorus, and low calcium.

t: Impaired Vision: Helping a Client Adjust
x: Communication, safety, and the environment for a client who can't see well · Every sensory station asked the same first question: determine two ways the nurse can help a client adjust to life with this alteration. Many of those strategies are shared across all types of vision loss, so they're collected here; each disorder's own lesson adds what's specific to it. · Communicating with a client who has impaired vision · Announce yourself by name and role when entering the room, and say when you are leaving · Speak in a normal tone — vision loss is not hearing loss, so there's no need to raise your voice · Explain what you are doing before you touch the client or start a procedure · Describe the surroundings and who else is in the room · Use the clock method to describe a meal tray ("your coffee is at 2 o'clock, the potatoes are at 6 o'clock") · Offer large-print or audio materials, and read important documents aloud · Safety and the environment · Orient the client to the room — bathroom, call light, bed controls, furniture · Keep belongings and furniture in the same place ; don't rearrange without telling the client · Keep pathways clear of clutter, cords, and spills; keep doors fully open or fully closed · Keep the call light and personal items within reach · Provide good lighting while reducing glare · Use high-contrast colors (for example, a dark plate on a light tray, colored tape on step edges) · Sighted guide technique: offer your arm; the client holds it just above your elbow and walks about a half step (one step) behind you while you keep your arm close to your body so the client can feel the direction of movement; describe steps, curbs, and doorways as you approach them · Cane for the blind: straight, white with a red tip; held in the dominant hand a few inches off the floor and swept across the path where the next step will land · Let the client touch objects in the room to learn the layout; use a focal point for orientation; talking clocks, radios, or a Braille watch · Assess fall risk and implement fall precautions · Supporting independence · Low-vision aids — magnifiers, large-print items, talking watches and devices, screen readers · Referral to low-vision services, occupational therapy, and community resources · Encourage the client to do as much as possible independently · Allow time to grieve — vision loss changes driving, reading, work, and independence; watch for depression and social isolation · Legal blindness is defined as central visual acuity of 20/200 or less in the better eye with correction, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less.

A cloudy lens — gradual, painless blurring treated with surgery · A cataract is an opacity (clouding) of the lens . Light can't pass clearly through a cloudy lens, so vision becomes blurred — the lecture's side-by-side image shows the whole scene softly blurred and hazy compared with normal vision. On inspection, the pupil may look cloudy, white, or gray instead of black. · Risk factors · Aging (the most common) · UV light exposure · Smoking · Diabetes · Long-term corticosteroid use · Eye trauma · Family history · Priority assessments/cues · Painless , gradual blurred, cloudy, or hazy vision — blurred vision and decreased color perception are early signs ; diplopia, reduced acuity, absent red reflex , and a white pupil are late signs · Glare and sensitivity to bright light; difficulty driving at night; halos around lights · Colors appear faded or yellowed (abnormal color perception); double vision (diplopia) · Redness and pain in the eye (more prominent in age-related cataracts) · Frequent changes in eyeglass prescription · Cloudy/white pupil; decreased red reflex · Knowledge of the surgical procedure and ability to follow post-op instructions · Diagnostics · Visual acuity test — vision impairment · Slit lamp exam — cataract on the lens · Glare testing — vision loss · Pupil dilation test — extent of the cataract's impact on vision · Treatment: cataract surgery · Surgery is the only cure. The clouded lens is removed (usually by phacoemulsification — ultrasound breaks up the lens) and replaced with an intraocular lens (IOL) implant. It's usually done as an outpatient procedure under local anesthesia, one eye at a time. Dilating drops are given before surgery. · Pre-op care · Teach what to expect from surgery and post-op care · Administer mydriatic (dilating) eye drops as prescribed · Decrease lighting after the mydriatic is given (photophobia) · Post-op care and home teaching · Maintain eye coverage with a patch as prescribed; analgesics as needed · Position off the operative side (back or non-operative side), head of bed elevated about 30–45 degrees ; place belongings on the non-operative side; side rails and assist with ambulation (depth perception is decreased with a patch) · Eye drops are usually needed several times a day for 2–4 weeks ; wipe drainage with a sterile wet cotton ball from the inner to the outer canthus · Avoid lifting more than about 5 lb , bending, straining, coughing, sneezing, and rapid movements · Mild itching and discomfort for a few days are normal; decreased vision, severe pain, increased redness, or discharge are not · Wear the eye shield at night (and as directed) to prevent rubbing or pressure on the eye · Visual acuity may not return for 1–2 weeks after surgery · Wear sunglasses outdoors · Avoid activities that raise intraocular pressure : bending at the waist, heavy lifting, straining (prevent constipation), vigorous coughing, sneezing, or vomiting · Don't rub or press on the eye · Sleep on the back or on the non-operative side · Instill prescribed drops correctly — antibiotic, corticosteroid, and/or NSAID drops — with hand hygiene first · Avoid swimming and eye makeup for the period directed · Report immediately: sudden or increasing eye pain, decreased vision, increased redness or drainage, flashes of light, floaters, or a curtain over the vision (possible retinal detachment) · Emergency potential? · Cataracts themselves are not an emergency — they develop slowly. The emergencies are post-operative: infection, bleeding, increased intraocular pressure, dislocation of the implanted lens , and retinal detachment. · Helping the client adjust · Use bright lighting while reducing glare; avoid night driving until treated · Cataracts in older adults may cost independence (driving, reading) — be supportive and give information on ways to stay independent

Increased intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve — peripheral vision goes first · Glaucoma is a group of conditions in which increased intraocular pressure (IOP) damages the optic nerve. Normally, aqueous humor is produced and drained at a balanced rate; when drainage is blocked, pressure builds. Glaucoma is called the "quiet thief of sight" . The damage causes loss of peripheral vision first — the lecture image shows a clear center surrounded by darkness (" tunnel vision "). Vision lost to glaucoma cannot be restored ; treatment only prevents further loss. · Normal IOP is about 10–21 mmHg . IOP varies through the day and is usually highest in the morning, so the time of measurement is documented. Early signs of glaucoma are diminished accommodation and rising IOP; because central vision is spared, gradual peripheral loss can go unnoticed. Contact tonometry uses a topical anesthetic — the client must not rub the numbed eye afterward. · Open-angle vs. angle-closure ·  | Primary open-angle glaucoma | Acute angle-closure glaucoma · What happens | Drainage through the trabecular meshwork gradually becomes less efficient | The iris bulges forward and suddenly blocks the drainage angle · Onset | Slow, gradual, usually both eyes | Sudden · Symptoms | Painless , often no symptoms until significant peripheral vision is lost; difficulty adjusting to darkness; halos | Severe eye pain , headache, nausea and vomiting , blurred vision, halos around lights , red eye, cloudy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil · Urgency | Chronic — lifelong management | Medical emergency — can cause permanent blindness within hours to days · Diagnosis · Tonometry — elevated IOP · Visual acuity test and perimetry (visual field testing) — maps peripheral vision loss · Slit lamp exam — fixed pupil and flat anterior chamber angle in angle-closure; normal angle in open-angle · Gonioscopy — examines the drainage angle · Ophthalmoscopy — a deeper, wider optic disc (cupping) in open-angle glaucoma · Other cues: diminished accommodation; the client's understanding of the condition and ability to follow a lifelong treatment regimen. · Treatment and medications · Lifelong eye drops — the mainstay for open-angle glaucoma: · Beta blockers (timolol) — decrease production of aqueous humor · Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost) — increase outflow of aqueous humor; given once daily at bedtime · Other classes: alpha-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, miotics (pilocarpine — constricts the pupil to open the drainage angle) · Laser trabeculoplasty or surgery (trabeculectomy, drainage devices) when drops aren't enough · Acute angle-closure glaucoma — emergency care · Notify the provider immediately — the goal is to lower IOP fast · Medications as ordered: miotic drops (pilocarpine), topical beta blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide), and an IV osmotic diuretic (mannitol) to pull fluid out of the eye · Treat pain and nausea/vomiting — vomiting raises IOP further · Laser peripheral iridotomy or surgical iridectomy once pressure is lowered, to create a permanent drainage opening · Post-op: eye patch, analgesics, position off the operative side with HOB 30–40 degrees, assist with ambulation, prevent bending and coughing · No atropine — never give drugs that dilate the pupil (mydriatics and anticholinergics) to a client with glaucoma; dilation blocks outflow and spikes IOP · Detached retina is painless ; acute angle-closure glaucoma is extremely painful . Both are emergencies — pain is the cue that tells them apart. · Helping the client adjust · Teach that the drops must be used every day for life , even with no symptoms — skipping doses lets pressure rise silently · Teach correct drop technique, including punctal occlusion (pressing on the inner corner of the eye) to avoid systemic effects, and waiting 5–10 minutes between different drops · Teach the client to scan by turning the head, since peripheral vision is lost; remove fall hazards · Open-angle glaucoma is treated with medications to control, not cure , the condition · Avoid lifting and actions that increase eye pressure — lifting restricted to 5 lb · Encourage regular eye exams, and screening for family members · Wear a medical alert ID ; tell all providers about the glaucoma before new medications are prescribed (avoid atropine-containing products)

Central vision loss — the peripheral vision stays · Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is deterioration of the macula , the central part of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed central vision. The lecture image shows the center of the picture blurred and darkened while the edges remain visible — the opposite pattern from glaucoma. · Dry vs. wet AMD ·  | Dry (atrophic) AMD | Wet (exudative / neovascular) AMD · What happens | Gradual thinning of the macula with yellow deposits called drusen | Abnormal new blood vessels grow under the retina and leak blood and fluid · Frequency | Most cases | Fewer cases, but responsible for most severe vision loss · Course | Slow, gradual | Rapid — vision can drop over days to weeks · Treatment | No cure; AREDS2 vitamin/mineral supplements (vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) may slow progression; stop smoking | Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections (such as ranibizumab, aflibercept) to stop abnormal vessel growth; photodynamic or laser therapy · Risk factors · Age · Smoking (the most important modifiable risk) · Family history · Hypertension and cardiovascular disease · Light-colored eyes, UV exposure · Priority assessments/cues · Blurred or dark spot in the center of vision · Straight lines appear wavy or distorted · Difficulty reading (words blurred), recognizing faces, and doing close work · Floaters or spots in the field of vision — scotomas · Needing brighter light to work · Diagnostics · Amsler grid — the client looks at a grid of straight lines; distorted or missing areas indicate macular damage · Ophthalmoscopy — drusen deposits · Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — anatomy of the retina and macula; also used to assess response to treatment · Fundus photography and angiography — clarifies extent and whether AMD is wet or dry · Helping the client adjust · Teach daily home monitoring with the Amsler grid — a sudden change can mean dry AMD has converted to wet AMD and needs prompt treatment · Low-vision aids: electronic hand-held magnifiers, electronic readers, image zooming, large print, bright task lighting, audio books · Assist with intravitreal injections; monitor afterward for eye irritation, photosensitivity, and eye pain · After photodynamic therapy (a light-activated drug plus laser destroys abnormal vessels), keep all skin covered and avoid intense light and sunlight for 5 days — sunlight activates the drug and causes burns · Teach the client to use peripheral vision by looking slightly to the side of an object (eccentric viewing) · Stop smoking; protect eyes from UV light; eat leafy greens · Driving safety evaluation; safety at home · Emergency potential? · AMD isn't usually an emergency, but a sudden change in central vision or the Amsler grid should be reported promptly, because wet AMD responds best to early treatment.

Flashes, floaters, and a curtain over the vision — a surgical emergency · A retinal detachment is a separation of the retina from the underlying layer (the choroid) that supplies it with oxygen and nutrients. Without that supply, the detached retina stops working. The lecture image shows a wedge of the visual field blacked out — the area served by the detached portion. It is painless and a medical emergency : vision can be saved only if the retina is reattached quickly. · Risk factors · Aging · Severe nearsightedness (myopia) · Eye trauma · Previous eye surgery (including cataract surgery) · Diabetic retinopathy · Family history or previous detachment in the other eye · Priority assessments/cues · Sudden floaters (spots or cobwebs in the vision) · Flashes of light (photopsia) · A curtain, veil, or shadow moving across part of the visual field · No pain · Emergency care · Notify the provider/ophthalmologist immediately — see a specialist ASAP · Immediate bed rest ; keep the client quiet · Cover BOTH eyes (eye patches) to minimize eye movement until surgery — both eyes move together · Position as ordered (often so the detached area is dependent) · Avoid activities that raise IOP; prepare for surgery · Surgical repair · Laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy — seals retinal tears · Scleral buckle — a silicone band placed around the eye pushes the wall of the eye against the retina · Pneumatic retinopexy — a gas bubble is injected into the eye to press the retina back into place · Vitrectomy — the vitreous gel is removed and replaced with gas, air, or silicone oil · Post-op care and home teaching · Speak to the client before approaching (both eyes may be patched); avoid jerky head movements · Prevent nausea and vomiting and restlessness (they raise IOP and can cause hemorrhage); encourage deep breathing but avoid coughing · Sudden, sharp eye pain → notify the provider · Limit reading for about 3–5 weeks; dark glasses during the day and an eye patch/shield at night · Keep follow-up appointments — detachment can recur or occur in the other eye · Positioning is critical after a gas bubble — the client may need to keep the head in a specific position (sometimes face-down) for days so the bubble presses on the right spot · With a gas bubble in the eye: no air travel, no high altitudes , and no nitrous oxide anesthesia until the bubble is absorbed — the gas expands and can dangerously raise IOP · Avoid bending, heavy lifting, straining, and rubbing the eye · Instill drops as ordered; wear the eye shield as directed · Report increased pain, decreased vision, new floaters or flashes, or nausea

Loss of half the visual field — usually after a stroke · Hemianopsia is blindness in half of the visual field . The lecture image shows the right half of the picture completely blocked out. The most common form, homonymous hemianopsia , affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes and results from damage to the visual pathway in the brain — most often a stroke , but also tumors or head injury. The eyes themselves are healthy; the brain can't process that half of what they see. · Hemianopsia is a neurological problem, not an eye problem: a "disconnect" in the visual pathway interrupts signals from the retina to the brain, so the brain can't stitch together a full image. Causes include stroke (the leading cause of permanent visual field defects), traumatic brain injury, tumors pressing on the optic chiasm or occipital lobe, and CNS infections. Unlike macular degeneration, the central point of focus often stays sharp — the "panorama" is cut in half. · Types · Type | Characteristics · Homonymous hemianopsia | Loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes (e.g., both left halves) · Bitemporal hemianopsia | Loss of the outer (peripheral) halves of the visual field in both eyes — often from pressure on the optic chiasm · Quadrantanopia | Loss of one-quarter of the visual field rather than a full half · The visual field loss is on the same side as the paralysis , which is the side opposite the brain lesion. A client with a right-sided brain stroke typically has left-sided weakness and loses the left half of the visual field. · Priority assessments/cues · Bumping into furniture or doorframes on the "blind" side · Reading difficulty — "losing" the beginning or end of a sentence on a page · Eating only half the food on the plate · Difficulty driving and navigating crowded spaces · Not noticing people or objects on the affected side · The client may be unaware of the deficit, especially with neglect · New-onset hemianopsia with other stroke signs is a stroke emergency — activate the stroke protocol · Helping the client adjust · In the acute phase, approach and place items on the unaffected side — call light, water, phone, tray · Teach scanning : turn the head toward the affected side to bring that half of the environment into view · As rehabilitation progresses, gradually encourage attention to the affected side (for example, rotate the meal tray, place some items on the affected side) · Fall precautions; keep the environment uncluttered · Remind the client and family that the client cannot see objects on the affected side; driving is usually not safe · Occupational therapy and vision rehabilitation · Treatment and management · Stage | Management · Early diagnosis | Neurological imaging (MRI/CT) and formal visual field testing (perimetry) · Vision restoration | Vision restorative therapy to stimulate neural plasticity · Compensatory training | Saccadic scanning training — teaching the eyes to glance quickly toward the blind side · Optical aids | Prisms fitted to eyeglasses to shift images from the blind field into the seeing field · The vision loss may be permanent, but scanning techniques can significantly improve quality of life. Safety first: clients have a high risk of falls and accidents because they are unaware of objects in the blind spot. · Emergency potential? · No — hemianopsia is a chronic, post-stroke deficit and isn't treated with an emergency procedure. Its sudden onset , however, signals a stroke, which is a time-critical emergency.

Damage to the retina's small blood vessels from high glucose or high pressure · Retinopathy is a general term for damage to the retina. While macular degeneration specifically targets the macula, retinopathy usually involves broader damage to the retinal blood vessels. It is primarily vascular : persistent high blood sugar or high blood pressure damages the small vessels, causing leakage of fluid or lipids, ischemia , neovascularization (fragile new vessels prone to bleeding, much like wet AMD), and eventually fibrotic scarring or retinal detachment. · Other forms include retinopathy of prematurity (abnormal vessel growth in some premature infants). The two main adult forms connect directly to this module's renal content: diabetic retinopathy shares the same microvascular damage as diabetic kidney disease, and hypertensive retinopathy shares the same vascular process as nephrosclerosis. · Diabetic retinopathy · Stage | What happens · Nonproliferative | High glucose weakens capillary walls → microaneurysms, small hemorrhages, and leaking fluid. Leakage into the macula causes macular edema and blurred central vision · Proliferative | The ischemic retina grows fragile new blood vessels (neovascularization) that can bleed into the vitreous and cause scar tissue that pulls the retina off — retinal detachment · Cues: early stages are often asymptomatic . Later: floaters (spots or dark cobweb-like strings), fluctuating vision that changes day to day with blood sugar, dark or empty "patchy" areas (rather than the consistent central blur of AMD), impaired color vision, and sudden vision loss (vitreous hemorrhage or detachment) · Annual dilated eye exam for clients with diabetes — because early stages have no symptoms, exams are essential for detection · Stage | Management · Prevention / early stage | Strict control of blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol; smoking cessation · Advanced proliferative | Panretinal photocoagulation (laser) to shrink abnormal blood vessels · Macular edema | Intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF agents (e.g., aflibercept) · Severe bleeding | Vitrectomy — surgery to remove the blood-stained vitreous gel · Hypertensive retinopathy · Chronic high blood pressure narrows and hardens retinal arterioles — the classic finding is "silver wiring" of the arteries · Severe or malignant hypertension can cause retinal hemorrhages and swelling of the optic disc — visual changes and headache in a client with very high BP are a hypertensive emergency cue · Treatment: blood pressure control · Helping the client adjust · Emphasize glucose and BP control as the way to protect remaining vision · Low-vision aids; adaptive devices for diabetes self-care (talking glucometers, large-print or preset insulin pens) as vision declines · Teach to report sudden vision loss, a shower of floaters, or a curtain over the vision — possible hemorrhage or detachment

t: Eye Emergencies, Eye Injuries & Eye Surgery
x: Penetrating trauma, chemical exposure, other emergencies, and post-op care and home teaching · Penetrating trauma care · Do not remove the penetrating object · Stabilize the object and cover the eye with a rigid shield (such as a paper cup or metal shield) — no pressure on the eye · Cover the unaffected eye too, since both eyes move together (sympathetic movement) — movement of the good eye moves the injured eye · Keep the client calm, head of bed elevated; no bending over and no lying flat (can move the object); no pressure on the eye · X-ray or CT of the orbit is used — MRI is contraindicated (a metal object could move) · Keep NPO in anticipation of surgery; give antiemetics as ordered — vomiting raises IOP · Do not irrigate or apply medication; tetanus status; transport for emergency ophthalmology care · Exposure (chemical) trauma care · Irrigate immediately — this comes before anything else, including a full history · Use copious water or normal saline for at least 15 minutes , continuing until the eye's pH is neutral (about 7.0–7.4, checked with pH paper); document visual acuity once irrigation is underway · Irrigate from the inner canthus to the outer canthus , so contaminated fluid runs away from the other eye · Remove contact lenses if they don't come out with irrigation · Alkali burns (lye, cleaning products, cement) are generally more damaging than acids because they penetrate deeper · Then: pain control, visual acuity, and ophthalmology evaluation · Other eye emergencies · Emergency | Cues | Care · Acute angle-closure glaucoma | Severe eye pain, headache, N/V, halos, red eye | Lower IOP immediately — miotics, osmotic diuretic (mannitol), laser iridotomy · Retinal detachment | Painless flashes, floaters, curtain over vision | Limit activity, notify immediately, surgical repair · Blunt trauma / hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber) | Visible blood in front of the iris, pain, blurred vision | Semi-Fowler's (HOB 30–45 degrees), rest, avoid sudden eye movements for 3–5 days, eye shield/patch, cycloplegic drops as ordered, avoid aspirin/NSAIDs; usually resolves in 5–7 days · Contusion ("black eye") | Bruising, pain, photophobia, edema, diplopia | Ice immediately ; thorough eye exam · Foreign body (superficial) | Pain, tearing, feeling of something in the eye | Don't rub; irrigate. A visible particle on the lower lid can be lifted with a saline-moistened cotton-tipped applicator (have the client look up while the lower lid is pulled down). Embedded objects are removed by the provider · Orbital fracture | Swelling, double vision, limited eye movement | Ice, head elevation, no nose blowing · Central retinal artery occlusion | Sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye | Emergency — immediate ophthalmology care · Eye surgery — which disorders? · Cataract — lens removal with intraocular lens implant · Glaucoma — laser trabeculoplasty, laser iridotomy, trabeculectomy · Detached retina — scleral buckle, pneumatic retinopexy, vitrectomy, laser/cryotherapy · Diabetic retinopathy / wet AMD — laser photocoagulation, intravitreal injections, vitrectomy · Penetrating trauma — surgical repair · General post-op care · Protect the eye — shield as directed, especially at night · Avoid increased IOP: no bending at the waist, heavy lifting, straining, or forceful coughing/sneezing; treat nausea and prevent constipation · Position as ordered (back or non-operative side; specific head positioning after a gas bubble) · Pain control; sudden sharp or increasing pain may signal hemorrhage or increased IOP and must be reported · Safety — depth perception is altered; fall precautions · Teaching for home care · Hand hygiene before touching the eye or instilling drops · Eye drop technique: tilt the head back, pull down the lower lid, and instill into the conjunctival sac (not directly on the cornea); never let the dropper tip touch the eye or lashes; close the eye gently (don't squeeze); and apply punctal occlusion — press the inner canthus for 1–2 minutes (at least 60 seconds) to prevent systemic absorption · Wait 5–10 minutes between different eye drops to prevent "washing out" the first medication; instill drops before ointments · Don't rub the eye; wear the shield and sunglasses as directed · Avoid swimming, eye makeup, and dusty environments for the directed period · Keep follow-up appointments · Report: increased pain, decreased vision, increased redness, swelling or drainage, fever, flashes, floaters, or a curtain over the vision

t: Hearing Loss & Communicating with the Hearing Impaired
x: Conductive vs. sensorineural, ototoxic drugs, and communication techniques · Conductive vs. sensorineural hearing loss · Feature | Conductive | Sensorineural · Location | Outer or middle ear | Inner ear (cochlea) or cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear) · Pathophysiology | Sound waves are mechanically blocked from reaching the inner ear | The sensory fibers or the nerve that transmits sound to the brain are damaged · Common causes | Obstruction: cerumen (wax) impaction , foreign bodies. Infection: otitis media . Structural: otosclerosis (bone hardening), tympanic membrane perforation | Aging: presbycusis . Ototoxic medications . Trauma: prolonged loud noise. Disease: Ménière's disease, acoustic neuroma · Reversibility | Often reversible — remove the wax, treat the infection | Usually permanent and progressive · Weber test (tuning fork on the top of the head) | Sound is louder in the affected (bad) ear | Sound is louder in the unaffected (good) ear · Rinne test (bone vs. air conduction) | Bone conduction ≥ air conduction (abnormal) | Air conduction > bone conduction (normal pattern, just reduced time) · Treatment | Remove the obstruction, antibiotics, hearing aids (amplification works well) | Cochlear implants (bypass damaged hair cells); hearing aids are less effective because they just make distorted sound louder · Mixed hearing loss combines both types. · Ototoxic medications to know · Because sensorineural loss is often permanent, watch for drugs that damage CN VIII: · Aminoglycoside antibiotics — gentamicin, tobramycin; also vancomycin · Loop diuretics — especially IV furosemide (push slowly!) or high doses (connects to the diuretics on this module's blueprint) · High-dose aspirin (tinnitus is an early toxicity sign) · Chemotherapy — cisplatin · Cues of ototoxicity: tinnitus , feeling of fullness, hearing loss, vertigo — report promptly; risk is higher with kidney impairment because the drugs accumulate · Cues of hearing loss · Onset of symptoms; history of ear infections, ear injuries, prolonged exposure to loud noise · Tinnitus — among the first signs of hearing loss · Turning the head to one side to hear, favoring one ear · Not responding unless looking directly at the speaker's lips · Asking people to repeat themselves; inappropriate responses to questions · Changes in volume and tone of voice in conversation · Progressively turning up the volume on the TV or radio · Withdrawal from large or social gatherings; impact on quality of life · Presbycusis (age-related) is gradual and bilateral; clients often say they can hear but can't understand the words, or that people are mumbling. Teach clients never to insert cotton-tipped applicators into the ear canal (trauma, perforation). Ear irrigation for cerumen is contraindicated with a known or suspected perforated eardrum or otitis media; the solution is warmed to body temperature to prevent vertigo and nausea. · Diagnostics · Tuning fork tests (Weber, Rinne) — determine the type of hearing loss (conductive vs. sensorineural) · Audiometry — degree of hearing loss and how best to treat it · Whisper test — whether the client can hear spoken words from a certain distance · Some older adults with presbycusis believe hearing loss is just part of aging and simply accept it — present all options for assistive devices and techniques. Complications of unaddressed hearing loss include complete hearing loss and social isolation . There are no specific medications to treat hearing impairment. · Communication with the hearing impaired · Get the client's attention first — a light touch or a wave — before you start speaking · Face the client directly at eye level and maintain eye contact , with light on your face (not behind you) so lips and expressions can be seen for lip-reading · Reduce background noise — turn off the TV, close the door · Speak clearly at a normal rate, slightly louder if needed, but don't shout — shouting distorts sound; use a lower pitch · Don't cover your mouth, chew gum, or turn away while talking · If the client doesn't understand, rephrase rather than repeat the same words · Use written notes, pictures, gestures, and whiteboards; confirm understanding with teach-back · Speak toward the better (unaffected) ear, standing close to the client · Make sure your nonverbal expression matches your words · Support the client with hearing aids, cochlear implant surgery, and other augmented-hearing options · Use a qualified sign language interpreter for clients who use sign language — not family members for medical information · Flag the chart and the call-light system so all staff know about the hearing loss · Communicating with people who are deaf or have severe hearing loss · Situation | What the nurse does · Every client | Ask how the person prefers to communicate — don't assume writing, gestures, or another method is best. If the person uses sign language, use a professional interpreter (the best means of accurate communication) · Hard of hearing, speech difficult to understand | Give full attention — look and listen, don't do another task while listening. Start with conversation where you can anticipate the replies to get used to the speech pattern. Use context to fill in details. Don't pretend to understand — if in doubt, have the person write the message , then repeat it in speech. Written material at about a third-grade level · Hard of hearing, speech reads (lip reads) | Lip reading alone is limited — even skilled lip readers catch less than 30% of spoken words. Face the person directly with your face well lit (not silhouetted against a window); nothing in or over your mouth. Tell them the topic first so they can use context. Speak slowly and distinctly , pausing more often. Check that important instructions were fully understood · Mouth covered or out of sight (mask, x-ray, MRI, colonoscopy, dark rooms) | The client can't read lips, see a signer, or read in the dark — write or communicate instructions another way before and during the procedure · Providers are legally obligated to make accommodations for effective communication — certified interpreters are essential for clients who communicate through sign language. · Hearing aid care · Hearing aids work well for conductive loss but have limited value for sensorineural loss — they make sound louder, not clearer, and amplify background noise · Teach new users to begin slowly, wear the aid for short periods at first, and keep the volume at the lowest effective level to prevent squealing (feedback) · Turn the aid off before removing it; keep extra batteries · Check that the aid is in, turned on, and the battery works before communicating · Remove at night and when bathing or showering; store in a labeled, dry case · Turn off or open the battery door when not in use · Clean with a soft, dry cloth; keep away from water, heat, and hair spray · Keep the ear canal free of wax buildup · Ear surgery post-op teaching (myringotomy, mastoidectomy, stapedectomy) · Sneeze and cough with the mouth open ; avoid forceful coughing · Avoid blowing the nose — if necessary, one side at a time with the mouth open · Avoid straining, drinking through a straw, rapid head movements, bending, and air travel as instructed · Keep the ear dry — no showering or getting the head wet for about a week as prescribed; a cotton ball with petroleum jelly can protect the ear · Hearing is usually worse at first because of packing and swelling (improvement after stapedectomy can take weeks) · Move the head slowly; assist with ambulation (vertigo); avoid people with colds · Report excessive drainage, fever, facial weakness, or severe vertigo · All of these prevent pressure changes in the middle ear that could dislodge the graft or prosthesis

Vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss from inner-ear disorders — safety first · Ménière's disease and labyrinthitis are disorders of the inner ear that affect balance and cause dizziness. In Ménière's disease , a buildup of fluid (endolymphatic hydrops ) distends and can rupture the labyrinth, causing episodic attacks and a sensorineural hearing loss that can become permanent. Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear (labyrinth) that affects the vestibular nerve. · Priority assessments/cues · The Ménière's triad: vertigo (intense, even when lying down), tinnitus , and hearing loss — usually unilateral , on the affected side · A feeling of fullness in the ear · Nausea and vomiting; lack of balance · Nystagmus, difficulty focusing vision · Headaches, which may be severe · Spatial disorientation — a feeling of spinning in space or being pulled to the ground · Symptoms lasting hours or days · Diagnostics · Audiometry — determines hearing loss · Vestibular testing — isolates the cause · Electronystagmography (ENG) — reduced balance response in one ear with Ménière's · Glycerol test — audiograms after an oral dose of glycerol; hearing and speech discrimination improve with Ménière's · EEG — rules out other causes (labyrinthitis) · 1. Acute vertigo attack (the "spinning" phase) · Priority #1: safety / fall prevention — the client is at high fall risk. Bed wheels locked, side rails up, bed in the low position; do not let the client walk alone ; bedside commode and call bell within reach · Environment: bed rest in a quiet, darkened room . Avoid bright or flickering lights (no TV) and sudden head movements, which worsen vertigo · Teach the client to move the head slowly · Medications: antiemetics for nausea/vomiting and antivertiginous drugs such as meclizine (Antivert) to sedate the vestibular system; monitor for adverse effects · 2. Maintenance (preventing future attacks) · Low-sodium diet (1,000–2,000 mg/day) to reduce endolymphatic fluid retention · Avoid triggers that alter fluid balance: caffeine, alcohol, and MSG ; fluid restriction may be prescribed; stop smoking · During attacks avoid watching TV — flickering light worsens symptoms · Vestibular rehabilitation as prescribed; hearing loss becomes permanent as attacks become more frequent · Diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide may be prescribed to reduce fluid pressure in the ear · Change positions slowly; avoid jerking and quick head motions · Remove fall hazards from the home; smoking cessation; avoid allergens · Labyrinthitis: diet low in processed foods; vestibular exercises · Priority medications · Medication | Route | Purpose · Diphenhydramine | PO, IV | Antihistamine to decrease sensations (both conditions) · Lorazepam | PO, IV | Benzodiazepine to decrease sensations (both conditions) · Meclizine | PO | Antihistamine to treat vertigo (both conditions) · Prochlorperazine | PO, IV | Antiemetic for nausea and vomiting (both conditions) · Hydrochlorothiazide | PO | Diuretic to reduce inner-ear fluid (Ménière's) · Prednisone | PO | Corticosteroid to control swelling (labyrinthitis); taper — never stop abruptly (adrenal insufficiency/withdrawal) · Surgery · Options include endolymphatic sac decompression with shunt placement, vestibular nerve section, or labyrinthectomy · Post-op: monitor the neurological system; assess dressing/packing for bleeding and infection; medications for vertigo and nausea; bedside commode; call bell in reach; don't let the client ambulate alone; speak to the client on the nonoperative side · Nursing process: care of the patient with vertigo · Nursing diagnosis | Goal | Key nursing interventions · Risk for fall-related injury — impaired balance, gait disturbance, vertigo | Free of physical trauma from imbalance and falls | Assess attacks (onset, duration, frequency, hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness); check for nystagmus and a positive Romberg; assess vision and proprioception for ADLs; reinforce vestibular/balance therapy; give or teach antivertiginous/vestibular sedative meds; have the client sit down and restrict activity when dizzy ; pillow on each side of the head to limit movement; help identify the aura (ear fullness/pressure) so meds can be taken before an attack; keep eyes open and stare straight ahead when lying down with vertigo; remove home hazards/use assistive devices · Risk for negative quality of life — unpredictability of vertigo | Modifies lifestyle to decrease disability; maximum control and independence | Identify strengths and roles that can still be fulfilled; teach about vertigo and what to expect; include family in rehab; let the client make decisions and take on more of their own care · Risk for hypovolemia — increased fluid output, altered intake, medications | Normal fluid and electrolyte balance | Monitor I&O (emesis, liquid stools, urine, diaphoresis) and electrolytes; assess for dehydration (orthostatic BP, pulse, skin turgor, mucous membranes, LOC); oral fluids as tolerated; discourage caffeine (a vestibular stimulant); antiemetics as prescribed · Anxiety — threat of, or change in, health status and disabling effects of vertigo | Less or no anxiety | Assess anxiety and past coping skills; teach about vertigo and its treatment; let the client discuss concerns about attacks; teach stress management (stress can worsen attacks) or refer; comfort measures; avoid stress-producing activities · Self-care deficits (feeding, hygiene, dressing, toileting) — labyrinth dysfunction and vertigo | Able to care for self | Antiemetics/sedatives to relieve nausea, vomiting, and vertigo; encourage self-care during vertigo-free periods ; review the diet ( sodium restriction helps inner-ear fluid balance) and offer fluids · Risk for powerlessness — illness regimen and helplessness from vertigo/balance disturbance | Increased sense of control over life and activities | Assess needs, values, and readiness; let the client express feelings about self and illness; identify coping behaviors that worked before · Complications · Hearing loss · Loss of balance, fall risk · Social isolation · Meningitis (with labyrinthitis)

When the brain can't produce or understand language · Aphasia is a loss of the ability to use or understand language, caused by damage to the language centers of the brain — most often a stroke affecting the left hemisphere (the dominant hemisphere for language in most people), but also brain tumors and head injury. Aphasia affects language, not intelligence. · The three types · Type | Brain area | What the client can and can't do | Communication strategies · Expressive (Broca's, nonfluent) | Frontal lobe (Broca's area) | Understands what is said but has great difficulty producing speech or writing; speech is slow, halting, with short phrases. Clients are usually aware of the problem and frustrated | Ask yes/no questions ; give plenty of time; use picture/communication boards, gestures, and writing; don't finish sentences for the client · Receptive (Wernicke's, fluent) | Temporal lobe (Wernicke's area) | Speech flows easily but may make little sense ; the client can't understand spoken or written language and may be unaware of errors | Use gestures, demonstration, and pictures ; short, simple sentences; one-step instructions; point to objects · Global | Extensive damage to both language areas | Severe impairment of both understanding and expression | Rely heavily on nonverbal communication — gestures, facial expression, touch, pictures; establish a simple yes/no system · Broca's = B roken speech (knows what to say, can't get it out). Wernicke's = W ord salad (speech flows, but meaning doesn't get in or out). · Aphasia vs. dysarthria: aphasia is a language problem in the brain. Dysarthria is a motor problem — weak or uncoordinated muscles of the mouth, tongue, and throat cause slurred speech, but the client understands language and chooses words normally. A client with dysarthria may also have swallowing problems, so assess swallowing before giving anything by mouth. · General nursing interventions for aphasia · Speak slowly and clearly in a normal tone — don't shout and don't talk down to the client · Face the client; reduce distractions and background noise · Use short, simple sentences and ask one question at a time · Allow time to respond; don't rush or interrupt · Use communication boards, pictures, gestures, and writing as appropriate for the type · Praise efforts; acknowledge frustration · Don't pretend to understand when you don't · Involve family in learning the strategies that work · Refer to a speech-language pathologist (SLP) · Keep the call light within reach and make sure the client has a reliable way to signal needs

Furosemide, Spironolactone, and Mannitol · Furosemide (Lasix) — Loop Diuretic · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO/IV, daily or BID. Renal failure with fluid volume overload/edema , pulmonary edema, edema in glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome, hyperkalemia (while the kidneys still make urine). Still works at a low GFR. High-dose IV furosemide is infused no faster than 4 mg/min (ototoxicity). Related loops: bumetanide, torsemide · Mechanism of action | Inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the ascending loop of Henle — the most potent class of diuretics. Water follows the sodium out, and potassium is lost with it · Adverse reactions | Hypokalemia ; ototoxicity (tinnitus, hearing loss — worse with rapid IV push, high doses, kidney impairment, or other ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides); dehydration/hypovolemia and orthostatic hypotension ; hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia; hyperglycemia; hyperuricemia (gout); metabolic alkalosis · Contraindications | Anuria ; sulfonamide (sulfa) allergy — furosemide and bumetanide are sulfonamide derivatives · Nursing interventions | Monitor K⁺ levels and BP (including orthostatic), daily weight, I&O, lung sounds, and edema; give IV doses slowly; hypokalemia raises the risk of digoxin toxicity ; loop diuretics can raise lithium levels; report new ringing in the ears · Patient education | Eat potassium-rich foods (unless the client has renal failure with hyperkalemia); rise slowly ; take it in the morning to avoid nocturia; report tinnitus, muscle weakness, or dizziness · Spironolactone (Aldactone) — Potassium-Sparing Diuretic · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, daily. Renal/fluid management: edema without potassium depletion ; heart failure; hyperaldosteronism; often combined with a loop or thiazide diuretic. Related drugs: eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene · Mechanism of action | Blocks aldosterone in the distal tubule — sodium and water are excreted while potassium is retained · Adverse reactions | Hyperkalemia ; gynecomastia; menstrual changes · Contraindications | Hyperkalemia (K⁺ above 5.0) ; severe renal failure · Nursing interventions | Monitor potassium and the ECG for dysrhythmias ; use cautiously with ACE inhibitors and ARBs (they also raise potassium); no potassium supplements · Patient education | Avoid salt substitutes — they're made of potassium chloride; don't overdo high-potassium foods; report muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat · Mannitol (Osmitrol) — Osmotic Diuretic · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV, emergent. Acute angle-closure glaucoma — rapidly reduces intraocular pressure; also pulls fluid from the brain (increased ICP) · Mechanism of action | Increases the osmotic pressure of the plasma and filtrate, pulling fluid out of the tissues (eye, brain) into the blood, where it's excreted by the kidneys · Adverse reactions | Tachycardia; pulmonary edema and fluid overload (it pulls fluid into the bloodstream before it's excreted); electrolyte shifts; dehydration · Contraindications | Active intracranial bleed ; severe dehydration; use caution with anuria and severe heart failure · Nursing interventions | Must use a filter needle — mannitol crystallizes, especially at low temperatures; inspect for crystals. Key lab: serum osmolality . Monitor neuro status, I&O, electrolytes, and lung sounds for crackles ; watch for heart failure · Patient education | Explain the increase in urination; report shortness of breath, chest tightness, or new swelling · Loop = Lose potassium. Potassium-sparing = Keep potassium. With hyperkalemia and fluid overload, the loop is the diuretic you reach for — the potassium-sparing is the one you avoid.

Phosphorus binders, Calcium gluconate, Vitamin D, and the potassium binders · Phosphorus (Phosphate) Binders — Calcium Acetate (PhosLo), Sevelamer (Renvela/Renagel), Lanthanum · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, with meals (and snacks). CKD/ESRD — lowers phosphorus and prevents secondary hyperparathyroidism. Calcium-based: calcium acetate (PhosLo). Non-calcium: sevelamer (used when calcium is already high), lanthanum. Sevelamer dose per meal = total daily dose ÷ number of meals the client actually eats . Calcium carbonate (Tums) is mainly a calcium supplement , not the binder of choice · Mechanism of action | Binds dietary phosphate in the GI tract so it's excreted in stool instead of absorbed — a "sponge" for phosphorus · Adverse reactions | Constipation, nausea, diarrhea, GI upset; hypercalcemia with calcium-based binders · Contraindications | Hypophosphatemia; bowel obstruction · Nursing interventions | Give with the first bite of every meal — if the client doesn't eat, don't give it; separate from other oral meds as directed (binders can bind other drugs); lanthanum must be chewed thoroughly; monitor phosphorus and calcium · Patient education | "Skip the meal, skip the pill." A low-phosphorus diet is still needed for binders to work; tell the provider and dietitian about all supplements — some contain phosphorus · Calcium Gluconate (IV) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV, emergent. Hyperkalemia — cardiac protection in renal failure; symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures); hypermagnesemia · Mechanism of action | Antagonizes the effect of high potassium on cardiac membrane excitability — it stabilizes the heart but does not lower potassium · Adverse reactions | Bradycardia , hypotension, syncope, dysrhythmias (especially with rapid administration); extravasation → tissue necrosis ; hypercalcemia · Contraindications | Hypercalcemia; digitalis (digoxin) toxicity — calcium increases the risk of digoxin toxicity · Nursing interventions | Requires cardiac monitoring ; give slowly ; stop the infusion if bradycardia occurs ; confirm IV patency; do not mix with sodium bicarbonate (forms a precipitate); monitor serum calcium and ECG · Patient education | Explain the heart monitor; report burning or pain at the IV site, dizziness, or palpitations · Calcium gluconate buys time — it protects the heart within minutes, but the potassium is still high. Insulin + dextrose (shift), then binders, diuretics, or dialysis (remove) have to follow. · Vitamin D Analogs — Calcitriol (active); Cholecalciferol (D3) / Ergocalciferol (D2) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, daily. Renal bone disease — compensates for the failing kidney's inability to activate vitamin D. Calcitriol is the active form; D3 and D2 are nutritional (inactive) forms used to replace low stores · Mechanism of action | Increases intestinal absorption of calcium ; calcitriol also suppresses parathyroid hormone · Adverse reactions | Hypercalcemia — fatigue, weakness, constipation, nausea, confusion; headache; dry mouth · Contraindications | Hypercalcemia; vitamin D toxicity. Active vitamin D cannot be taken if calcium or phosphorus is too high — it raises the risk of calcium–phosphorus deposits in arteries, lungs, eyes, and skin · Nursing interventions | Monitor calcium and phosphorus closely — they're inversely related. Cholecalciferol (D3) is the form commonly given to kidney clients in the hospital · Patient education | Report symptoms of high calcium (constipation, nausea, weakness, confusion); keep all lab appointments · Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate with Sorbitol (Kayexalate) — Cation Exchange Resin · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO or PR (retention enema — hold 30–60 minutes), daily. Hyperkalemia — fecal excretion of potassium. Acts over hours, so it isn't a stand-alone emergency treatment · Mechanism of action | Exchanges sodium for potassium in the intestines; sorbitol causes diarrhea to speed elimination · Adverse reactions | Constipation, fecal impaction, gastric irritation; diarrhea; intestinal necrosis ; sodium retention and hypernatremia; hypokalemia · Contraindications | Bowel obstruction ; paralytic ileus · Nursing interventions | Assess bowel sounds first — if the gut isn't moving, potassium can't leave the body and the drug can cause necrosis; monitor potassium, sodium, and for fluid overload · Patient education | Expect loose stools; report severe abdominal pain, bloating, or no bowel movement · Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) is used to lower the potassium level seen in acute renal failure — it pulls potassium out through the stool. · Patiromer (Veltassa) — Potassium Binder · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, daily, with food. Chronic renal failure — long-term K⁺ management . Delayed onset (hours to days) — not for emergency use · Mechanism of action | A non-absorbed polymer that binds K⁺ (in exchange for calcium) in the GI tract so it's excreted in stool · Adverse reactions | Hypomagnesemia ; constipation; hypokalemia · Contraindications | Severe constipation; bowel obstruction · Nursing interventions | Give at least 3 hours apart from other oral medications; monitor potassium and magnesium · Patient education | Mix the powder with water and take with food; keep the 3-hour spacing from other meds; report constipation · Sodium Zirconium Cyclosilicate (Lokelma) — Potassium Binder · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO. Hyperkalemia — the fastest-acting binder (onset about 1 hour) · Mechanism of action | Traps potassium in exchange for sodium and hydrogen throughout the GI tract · Adverse reactions | Edema and fluid overload (it contains sodium); hypokalemia · Contraindications | Hypersensitivity; use caution with heart failure or other conditions that require sodium restriction · Nursing interventions | Oral only — mix immediately before giving; causes less diarrhea than Kayexalate. Monitor potassium for hypokalemia; watch for edema and weight gain; separate some oral meds by 2 hours · Patient education | Mix the powder with water right before taking — it settles and separates — then drink it all right away; report swelling or rapid weight gain · All three potassium binders work in the gut and need time. An acute hyperkalemia with ECG changes still gets calcium gluconate first (protect the heart) and insulin + dextrose (shift K⁺ into cells) while the binders and dialysis remove it.

t: Epoetin Alfa, Corticosteroids, Acetylcysteine & Sodium Bicarbonate
x: The rest of the renal medication list · Epoetin Alfa (Epogen, Procrit) — Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agent · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | SubQ or IV, 1–3 times weekly (IV during hemodialysis is common). Anemia of renal failure — replaces the erythropoietin the failing kidneys no longer make · Mechanism of action | Stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow · Adverse reactions | Hypertension ; seizures; thromboembolic events (stroke, MI, clotting of the dialysis access — black box warning); headache · Contraindications | Uncontrolled hypertension · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP and Hgb ; hold if Hgb is above about 10–11 g/dL (stroke risk) and notify the provider; check iron levels; don't shake the vial · Patient education | Iron supplements may be needed for it to work; the hemoglobin rises gradually over weeks; report headache, chest pain, or swelling/pain in a leg · Corticosteroids — Prednisone, Methylprednisolone (Prednisolone Acetate Eye Drops) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO/IV, daily, then taper . Nephritis/glomerulonephritis — reduces kidney inflammation; nephrotic syndrome (especially minimal change disease); kidney transplant rejection. Eye drops reduce inflammation after cataract and retinal surgery · Mechanism of action | Suppresses inflammation and the immune response · Adverse reactions | Hyperglycemia ; weight gain; infection risk (and masking of infection signs); sodium and fluid retention (edema, HTN); hypokalemia; osteoporosis; GI ulcers; mood changes; delayed wound healing; adrenal suppression.
