Long-term eye drops can raise IOP and promote cataracts · Contraindications | Systemic fungal infections · Nursing interventions | Monitor blood glucose , BP, weight, electrolytes, and for signs of infection; give oral doses in the morning with food · Patient education | Never stop abruptly — taper to avoid adrenal crisis; wash hands often and avoid sick contacts; report fever or signs of infection · Acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) — Mucolytic / Renal Protectant · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO/IV, prior to scans with contrast (sometimes after as well), alongside IV hydration. Contrast protection — prevents AKI during imaging. Other uses: acetaminophen overdose antidote; inhaled mucolytic · Mechanism of action | An antioxidant that scavenges free radicals · Adverse reactions | Nausea, vomiting; bronchospasm (caution in asthma); IV can cause an anaphylactoid reaction (rash, flushing) · Contraindications | Hypersensitivity · Nursing interventions | Dilute the PO dose in juice or cola to mask the "rotten egg" (sulfur) smell; confirm it's given before the contrast study; monitor creatinine and urine output afterward · Patient education | Explain it protects the kidneys from the contrast dye; the smell and taste are expected; drink fluids as instructed · Sodium Bicarbonate — Alkalinizer · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO/IV, PRN per ABG. Metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.35) in renal failure — oral daily for CKD, IV for severe acidosis; IV in hyperkalemia with acidosis (shifts K⁺ into cells) · Mechanism of action | Buffers excess hydrogen ions in the blood · Adverse reactions | Metabolic alkalosis ; sodium and fluid overload (hypernatremia) (edema, HTN, heart failure); hypokalemia (K⁺ shifts into cells); gas and bloating with oral forms · Contraindications | Respiratory alkalosis ; severe edema · Nursing interventions | Monitor ABGs and serum sodium , bicarbonate, potassium, and fluid status; don't mix IV bicarbonate with calcium (precipitate) · Patient education | Separate oral bicarbonate from other oral meds (it changes stomach pH); report swelling or shortness of breath

Timolol, Latanoprost, Pilocarpine, Dorzolamide, and Atropine · Timolol (Timoptic) — Beta Blocker Eye Drops · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Eye drops, BID (once or twice daily). Glaucoma maintenance — lowers intraocular pressure (IOP). Related: betaxolol (cardioselective — safer for the lungs), levobunolol · Mechanism of action | Decreases production of aqueous humor · Adverse reactions | Local stinging, burning, blurred vision. Absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal duct → bradycardia , hypotension, bronchospasm , fatigue; can mask hypoglycemia; can worsen heart failure · Contraindications | Asthma/COPD ; bradycardia ; heart block ; caution in heart failure and diabetes · Nursing interventions | Check apical pulse and BP before giving — usually hold and contact the provider if the pulse is 60 or less or systolic BP is below 90 (get parameters); apply punctal occlusion (press the inner canthus) for 1–2 minutes to prevent systemic absorption; additive effect with oral beta blockers · Patient education | Use the drops for life — glaucoma has no symptoms until vision is lost; apply punctal occlusion after every dose; report shortness of breath, dizziness, or a slow pulse; tell every provider about the drops · Latanoprost (Xalatan) — Prostaglandin Analog Eye Drops · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Eye drops, nightly (once daily at bedtime — using it more often can make it less effective). Glaucoma — lowers IOP. Related: bimatoprost, travoprost · Mechanism of action | Increases outflow of aqueous humor · Adverse reactions | Permanent darkening of the iris (brown, especially in hazel/green eyes); eyelash growth (longer, thicker, darker); eye redness; darkening of the eyelid skin. Systemic effects are minimal · Contraindications | Pregnancy (relative); eye inflammation · Nursing interventions | Refrigerate unopened bottles as directed; remove contact lenses before instilling and wait about 15 minutes to reinsert; punctal occlusion · Patient education | It may permanently change eye color (especially noticeable if only one eye is treated); use it at bedtime ; don't use extra doses · Timolol turns off the faucet (less aqueous made); latanoprost opens the drain (more aqueous out). Either way, pressure falls. · Pilocarpine — Miotic (Cholinergic) Eye Drops · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Eye drops. Glaucoma , including emergency angle-closure glaucoma. Related cholinergic: carbachol · Mechanism of action | Constricts the pupil (miosis), contracting the iris sphincter so the trabecular meshwork opens and aqueous flows out · Adverse reactions | Poor night vision / dim vision in low light (the pupil can't dilate in the dark); systemic: bradycardia, bronchospasm, increased salivation, sweating · Contraindications | Conditions where pupil constriction is undesirable (e.g., acute eye inflammation); caution with asthma and cardiac disease · Nursing interventions | Punctal occlusion; fall precautions in dim lighting; monitor HR · Patient education | Avoid driving at night ; use good lighting at home · Dorzolamide (drops) / Acetazolamide (PO/IV) — Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Eye drops (dorzolamide); PO/IV (acetazolamide). Glaucoma · Mechanism of action | Decreases production of aqueous humor · Adverse reactions | Paresthesias of fingers, toes, and face; polyuria; hypokalemia ; renal calculi; photosensitivity; lethargy · Contraindications | Sulfa (sulfonamide) allergy · Nursing interventions | Assess for sulfa allergy before giving; monitor potassium; increase fluids unless contraindicated · Patient education | Remove contact lenses before use; wait 15 minutes to reinsert; report tingling or muscle weakness · Atropine / Tropicamide — Mydriatics & Cycloplegics · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Eye drops. Dilate the pupil for eye exams or surgery (tropicamide also paralyzes the ciliary muscle); cycloplegic drops after some eye injuries · Mechanism of action | Blocks the muscles that constrict the pupil (dilation) and focus the lens (cycloplegia) · Adverse reactions | Blurred vision, photophobia. Atropine toxicity: dry mouth, tachycardia, fever, urinary retention, confusion · Contraindications | Never give to clients with glaucoma — dilation blocks outflow and spikes IOP · Nursing interventions | Confirm there's no glaucoma history; arrange for a driver after the exam · Patient education | Wear sunglasses ; vision will be blurred and light-sensitive; don't drive for 24 hours unless told otherwise · Other Eye Medications to Know · Medication | Purpose | Critical safety & nursing tips · Mannitol (IV osmotic diuretic) | Rapidly pulls fluid from the eye into the blood — emergency angle-closure glaucoma | Filter needle (crystallizes at low temperatures); watch for fluid overload and pulmonary edema (crackles). Full card in the Diuretics lesson · Adrenergic agonists (dipivefrin, brimonidine) | Decrease production of aqueous humor (glaucoma) | Local irritation; monitor BP · Anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, pegaptanib) | Intravitreal injection — inhibit abnormal blood vessel growth; slow vision loss in wet AMD | Monitor for eye pain, redness, vision change, discharge (endophthalmitis); increased IOP · Ketorolac ophthalmic | NSAID drops — reduce inflammation and pain (post-op) | Local burning/stinging · Post-op drops after cataract surgery | Antibiotic, corticosteroid, and NSAID drops | Hand hygiene, correct technique, follow the schedule. Long-term corticosteroid drops can raise IOP, cause cataracts, and mask infection · General Administration "Golden Rules" · Wait time: 5–10 minutes between different eye drops to prevent "washing out" the first one · Asepsis: never let the dropper tip touch the eye, lashes, or any surface · Position: tilt the head back, pull down the lower lid, and instill into the conjunctival sac — not directly on the cornea · Punctal occlusion: press the inner canthus for 1–2 minutes (at least 60 seconds) after instilling to prevent systemic absorption · Instill drops before ointments ; apply ointment in a thin ribbon along the lower conjunctival sac from inner to outer canthus, ideally at bedtime (it blurs vision) · Soft contact lenses can absorb some eye medications; preservatives can discolor lenses

The building blocks every other calculation relies on · Before any drip rate or weight-based dose can be calculated, you need to be fluent in the basic conversions underneath them — pounds to kilograms, and the metric ladder from kilograms down to micrograms. Almost every calculation error in practice traces back to a mistake at this level, not the fancier formula built on top of it. · Basic Dosage Calculation · Formula: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = Amount to administer · Worked example: Order is 500 mg PO; available as 250 mg tablets. (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets . · Worked example 2: Order is 2 mg lorazepam; available as a 4 mg/mL vial. (2 ÷ 4) × 1 mL = 0.5 mL . · Weight Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Pounds → kilograms | lbs ÷ 2.2 = kg | 154 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg · Kilograms → pounds | kg × 2.2 = lbs | 100 kg × 2.2 = 220 lbs · Almost every weight-based drug calculation in this unit starts with converting the patient's weight to kilograms — if that first conversion is wrong, every step after it is wrong too, even if the rest of the math is done perfectly. This matters directly in this module for weight-based pediatric dosing (ADHD/ASD medications) and for BSA-based chemotherapy dosing. · Metric System Conversions — the 1000 rule · Standard medical units (kg, g, mg, mcg) are each separated from their neighbor by a factor of 1000. · Direction | Rule | Example · Larger → smaller (kg→g, g→mg, mg→mcg) | Multiply by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places right) | 2 g × 1000 = 2000 mg · Smaller → larger (mcg→mg, mg→g, g→kg) | Divide by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places left) | 2500 mcg ÷ 1000 = 2.5 mg · Volume Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Milliliters → liters | mL ÷ 1000 = L | 2500 mL ÷ 1000 = 2.5 L · Liters → milliliters | L × 1000 = mL | 0.5 L × 1000 = 500 mL · Household & Volume Equivalents · Household/Metric | Equivalent · 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL · 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL (or 3 tsp) · 1 ounce (oz) | 30 mL (or 2 tbsp) · 1 cup | 240 mL (8 oz) · 1 quart (approx.) | 1000 mL (1 L)

t: IV Flow Rates, Drip Rates & Concentration
x: Getting fluid and medication into the vein at the right speed · These formulas answer one of two questions: how fast should this infusion pump run (mL/hr), or how many drops per minute should a gravity IV be set to (gtt/min) when there's no pump involved? A third formula, concentration, sets up weight-based drip calculations. · Flow Rate / Infusion Rate (mL/hr) — for infusion pumps · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Total Time (hr) = mL/hr · Worked example: Infuse 1000 mL of Normal Saline over 8 hours. 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr . · Infusion Time — working backward from a known rate · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Flow Rate (mL/hr) = Time (hours) · Worked example: A 1000 mL bag is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How long will it last? 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours . · Drip Rate (gtt/min) — for gravity IV tubing without a pump · There are two equivalent ways to reach the same answer, depending on whether you already know the mL/hr rate or are starting from the total order. · Starting point | Formula · You already know mL/hr | (mL/hr ÷ 60) × Drop Factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min · You're starting from the total order | (Total Volume [mL] × Drop Factor [gtt/mL]) ÷ Time (minutes) = gtt/min · Worked example (method 1): Infuse at 125 mL/hr using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. First, mL/min: 125 ÷ 60 = 2.08 mL/min. Then: 2.08 × 15 = 31.2, rounded to 31 gtt/min . · Worked example (method 2): Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours (480 minutes) with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min — the same answer either way. · IV Push Medication Rate · A common general safety rule for IV push medications is roughly 1 mL per minute unless the drug's specific administration guidelines say otherwise. Worked example: a 10 mL medication is administered over 10 minutes, consistent with the 1 mL/min rule. Pushing too fast is a common cause of adverse drug reactions — relevant here for IV push benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam for agitation/status epilepticus) and IV antihistamines. · Concentration Calculation — the setup step for weight-based drips · Formula: (Total mg in the bag × 1000) ÷ Total mL in the bag = Concentration (mcg/mL) · Worked example: A bag contains 400 mg of a drug in 250 mL of D5W. (400 × 1000) ÷ 250 = 1600 mcg/mL .

MAP, CPP, and weight-/unit-based infusions · This lesson groups together the calculations that show up most often in critical care and high-alert medication administration — all of them either measure perfusion pressure directly, or calculate the pump rate for a drug that manipulates that pressure. Relevant here for a client in delirium tremens, an oncology patient in septic shock, or any client on a high-alert IV drip. · MAP — Mean Arterial Pressure · Formula: (Systolic BP + [2 × Diastolic BP]) ÷ 3 = MAP · Worked example: BP is 120/80. (120 + [2 × 80]) ÷ 3 = (120 + 160) ÷ 3 = 93.3 mmHg . · MAP reflects the average pressure driving blood into the organs across the whole cardiac cycle — it's weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more time in diastole than systole. A MAP of roughly 65 mmHg or higher is generally considered necessary to maintain adequate organ perfusion in a critically ill patient. · CPP — Cerebral Perfusion Pressure · Formula: MAP − ICP = CPP · Worked example: MAP is 93, ICP is 15. 93 − 15 = 78 mmHg . · CPP depends directly on MAP — if you already calculated MAP for a patient, you're one subtraction away from CPP. A CPP that drops too low (generally below ~60 mmHg) risks cerebral ischemia, which is why both numbers are tracked together in a patient with a head injury or elevated ICP. · Weight-Based Infusion (mcg/kg/min) · Formula: (Desired mcg × kg × 60 minutes) ÷ Concentration (mcg/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient, with a concentration of 1600 mcg/mL (from the concentration calculation in the previous lesson). (5 × 80 × 60) ÷ 1600 = 15 mL/hr . · Units-Based Infusion (Units/kg/hr) — e.g., Heparin · Formula: (Units × kg) ÷ Concentration (Units/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 12 Units/kg/hr for a 100 kg patient, with a concentration of 100 Units/mL. (12 × 100) ÷ 100 = 12 mL/hr . · Both weight-based and units-based drips are high-alert medications given by infusion pump only — the shared theme across every high-alert drug is a computerized pump, frequent reassessment, and a clear plan for what triggers stopping or adjusting the rate.

Tracking what goes in, what comes out, and what IV fluids do to cells · Intake and output tracking is really just accounting for fluid — but a couple of categories have special rules that are easy to get wrong, and tonicity explains why the choice of IV fluid itself matters beyond just the volume. This is directly relevant to fluid management in cancer/chemotherapy patients, HIV/AIDS patients with diarrhea or wasting, and any client receiving IV psychiatric medications. · What counts as intake · Oral (PO) fluids — water, juice, soda, milk, coffee · Liquid foods — soups, broths, gelatin, sherbet, sorbet, pudding · Ice chips — recorded as half the original volume (200 mL of ice chips = 100 mL intake), since ice chips are mostly air/space between solid pieces · IV fluids — maintenance fluids, boluses, and piggyback medications (like antibiotics) · Tube feedings — formula and water flushes (relevant for a client with anorexia nervosa on enteral nutritional rehabilitation) · What counts as output · Urine — voided, catheterized, or urostomy drainage · Emesis (vomitus) — relevant for a client with bulimia or chemotherapy-induced nausea · Liquid stool — diarrhea or colostomy drainage · Wound drainage — from JP drains, Hemovacs, or chest tubes · Suction — gastric (NG) or respiratory · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake of 3000 mL, output of 800 mL. 3000 − 800 = +2200 mL (a positive balance, meaning the patient is retaining more fluid than they're losing). · Insensible Loss · Fluid lost through the skin and lungs that can't be directly measured. Standard estimate: 600–900 mL/day , or roughly 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Worked example: a 70 kg patient: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/hr, or roughly 840 mL/day. · Fluid Weight Calculation · Rule of thumb: a 1 kg weight change equals roughly 1 L of fluid change. Worked example: a patient's weight rises 2 kg over two days — that's roughly a 2 L fluid gain, not necessarily 2 kg of actual tissue. · An output under 30 mL/hr is always reported as a potential emergency — it signals inadequate perfusion to the kidneys. · Tonicity — what different IV fluids do to cells · Type | Solute concentration vs. inside the cell | Effect on the cell | Examples | Clinical use · Hypertonic | Higher outside the cell | Water leaves the cell — it shrinks (plasmolysis) | 3% or 5% NaCl; 10% Dextrose in Water | Cerebral edema, severe hyponatremia · Hypotonic | Lower outside the cell | Water enters the cell — it swells or bursts (cytolysis) | 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline) | Dehydration — pushes water back into cells · Isotonic | Equal inside and outside | No net water movement — equilibrium maintained | 0.9% Normal Saline, Lactated Ringer's, D5W | Routine IV fluid replacement and hydration · A simple way to remember the direction: hyper tonic pulls water OUT of the cell (think 'hyper' = high solute outside, pulling water toward it), while hypo tonic pushes water IN . Isotonic is the 'do no harm' default fluid.

Calculations that scale a dose — or a diagnosis — to the patient's size · These two calculations both answer a version of the same question — how big is this patient, in a way that's useful for dosing or risk assessment? BMI is a general screening number used constantly in this module's eating-disorder content; BSA is a more precise scaling factor used specifically for chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · BMI — Body Mass Index · System | Formula · Metric | Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]² · Imperial | [Weight (lbs) × 703] ÷ [Height (in)]² · Worked example (metric): Weight 70 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625. Divide weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86 (normal weight range). · Worked example (imperial): Weight 154 lbs, height 69 inches. 154 × 703 = 108,262. Square the height: 69 × 69 = 4,761. Divide: 108,262 ÷ 4,761 = 22.74 — the same result as the metric calculation, just arrived at with different starting units. · This is exactly the calculation behind the BMI thresholds in the Anorexia Nervosa lesson: a BMI under 17 is a diagnostic marker of the disorder, and under 15 is considered extreme/life-threatening. Knowing how to compute BMI from a height and weight given in a case stem — not just recognize the threshold — is testable on its own. · BSA — Body Surface Area · BSA approximates a patient's total skin surface area in square meters (m²), and it's used specifically for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, chemotherapy agents, pediatric patients, and burn patients — situations where a small dosing error has an outsized effect. This is the calculation behind chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · Formula: BSA = √[(Height in cm × Weight in kg) ÷ 3600] · Fully worked pediatric dosing example · Order: a chemotherapy agent at 2 mg/m². Patient: 37 lb, 97 cm tall. Supply: 1 mg/mL. · Step 1 — convert weight to kg: 37 lb ÷ 2.2 = 16.8 kg · Step 2 — calculate BSA: √[(97 cm × 16.8 kg) ÷ 3600] = √[1629.6 ÷ 3600] = √0.4527 = 0.67 m² · Step 3 — calculate the dose in mg: 2 mg/m² × 0.67 m² = 1.34 mg · Step 4 — calculate the dose in mL: 1.34 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 1.34 mL to administer · Notice this whole calculation depends on the weight-to-kg conversion from the first Med Math lesson — get that first step wrong, and every subsequent step (BSA, mg dose, mL dose) inherits the error.

t: Renal Math: Urine Output, Fluid Restriction & Daily Weights
x: The calculations behind the AKI, CKD, and fluid-balance lessons · Hourly Urine Output (mL/kg/hr) · Formula: Urine output (mL) ÷ Hours ÷ Weight (kg) = mL/kg/hr. The minimum acceptable adult output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (roughly 30 mL/hr). · Minimum for a given client: Weight (kg) × 0.5 = minimum mL/hr. A 70 kg client needs at least 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr . · Worked example: An 80 kg client voids 200 mL over 8 hours. 200 ÷ 8 = 25 mL/hr; 25 ÷ 80 = 0.31 mL/kg/hr — below 0.5, so it's reported as an early warning of AKI. · 24-Hour Output — naming the problem · 24-hour urine output | Term · Less than 400–500 mL | Oliguria (the oliguric phase of AKI: below 400 mL/day) · Less than 50 mL | Anuria · 4–5 L/day | Diuretic phase of AKI — watch for fluid volume deficit · More than 3 L/day after an obstruction is relieved | Postobstructive diuresis · Fluid Restriction · Formula: Previous 24-hour urine output + about 500–600 mL (insensible losses) = Fluid allowance for the next 24 hours. (Some references use 500–800 mL.) · Worked example: A client in the oliguric phase put out 350 mL of urine yesterday. 350 + 500 = 850 mL to 350 + 600 = 950 mL — a fluid allowance of about 850–950 mL for today. · The fluid allowance is spread across all 24 hours — with sips, ice chips, and frequent mouth care for thirst — and it has to include the fluid used to take medications. · Daily Weights — 1 kg = 1 L · Rule: a 1 kg weight change equals about 1 L of fluid (about 2.2 lb per liter). Weigh at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing. · Worked example: Yesterday 72.0 kg; today 74.5 kg. 74.5 − 72.0 = 2.5 kg = about 2.5 L of retained fluid . · Worked example (pounds): A weight gain of 4.4 lb ÷ 2.2 = 2 kg = about 2 L of fluid. · BUN:Creatinine Ratio · Formula: BUN ÷ Creatinine. Normal is about 10:1 to 20:1; above 20:1 points toward a prerenal cause (dehydration, low perfusion). · BUN | Creatinine | Ratio | Points toward · 48 mg/dL | 1.2 mg/dL | 48 ÷ 1.2 = 40:1 | Prerenal — BUN rising out of proportion (dehydration) · 80 mg/dL | 8.0 mg/dL | 80 ÷ 8 = 10:1 | Intrarenal or postrenal — both rising together · Phosphate Binder Dose per Meal (Sevelamer) · Formula: Total daily dose ÷ Number of meals the client actually eats = Dose per meal · Worked example: Sevelamer 4,800 mg/day. Three meals a day: 4,800 ÷ 3 = 1,600 mg with each meal . The same client skips breakfast and eats 2 meals: 4,800 ÷ 2 = 2,400 mg with each meal . · The number of meals comes from the client's eating pattern, not a standard schedule — fewer meals means a bigger dose with each meal. And no meal, no binder. · Maximum-Rate Problems · Formula: Dose (mg) ÷ Maximum rate (mg/min) = Minimum time (minutes) · Worked example: High-dose IV furosemide is infused no faster than 4 mg/min (ototoxicity). For a 120 mg dose: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes minimum . · Rapid IV furosemide is what causes the tinnitus and hearing loss — if the math says 30 minutes, it never goes in faster, even when the client is fluid overloaded. · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake: PO 600 mL + IV 900 mL + ice chips 200 mL (counts as 100 mL) = 1,600 mL. Output: urine 450 mL + emesis 150 mL = 600 mL. 1,600 − 600 = +1,000 mL — a positive balance (fluid retention).

t: Dialysis Fluid Math: Hemodialysis, PD & CRRT
x: How much fluid came off — and how to count it · Hemodialysis — Fluid Removal Goal · Formula: Pre-dialysis weight − Dry (target) weight = Fluid to remove (1 kg = 1 L) · Worked example: Pre-dialysis weight 78.4 kg; dry weight 76.0 kg. 78.4 − 76.0 = 2.4 kg = about 2.4 L to remove. The post-dialysis weight confirms how much actually came off. · Peritoneal Dialysis — Net Ultrafiltration · Formula: Outflow (drained) − Inflow (instilled) = Net fluid removed. A negative result means the client absorbed (retained) dialysate. · Inflow | Outflow | Result | Meaning · 2,000 mL | 2,500 mL | +500 mL | 500 mL removed — recorded as output · 2,000 mL | 1,800 mL | −200 mL | 200 mL retained — counts toward intake; check for kinks, constipation, and position · Multiple exchanges: add the net result of each one. Exchanges of +300, +150, and −100 mL = +350 mL net removed. If drainage is short by 500 mL or more over several exchanges, evaluate for fluid retention and notify the provider. · PD outflow is not urine. Record the client's true urine output separately from the dialysate drained. · CRRT — Hourly Fluid Balance · The nurse totals all intake and output every hour and adjusts to meet the ordered hourly balance goal. · Formula: Hourly net fluid removal needed = Hourly intake (IV fluids, meds, feedings, replacement fluid) + Desired hourly fluid loss · Worked example: The goal is a net loss of 100 mL/hr. This hour the client receives IV fluid 50 mL + tube feeding 60 mL + IV meds 40 mL = 150 mL. To achieve −100 mL, the machine must remove 150 + 100 = 250 mL of fluid from the client this hour.

x: Normal values and the arrow patterns for all four imbalances · ABG values · Test | Normal | ↓ Value | ↑ Value · pH | 7.35–7.45 | Acidosis | Alkalosis · PaCO₂ | 35–45 mmHg | Alkalosis | Acidosis · HCO₃⁻ | 22–26 mEq/L | Acidosis | Alkalosis · PaO₂ | 80–100 mmHg | Hypoxemia | O₂ therapy · SaO₂ | 95–100% | Hypoxemia | — · PaCO₂ is the one that runs backward: CO₂ is an acid, so a high PaCO₂ means acidosis and a low PaCO₂ means alkalosis . pH and HCO₃⁻ read the same direction as the imbalance. · Uncompensated (acute) — only one system is off · System | ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Lungs | Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | Normal · Lungs | Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | Normal · Kidneys | Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | Normal | ↓ · Kidneys | Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | Normal | ↑ · Partially compensated — pH still abnormal, the other system has started to move · ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ · Fully compensated (chronic) — pH back in range, both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ abnormal · ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Respiratory acidosis | Normal (7.35–7.39, acid side) | ↑ | ↑ · Respiratory alkalosis | Normal (7.41–7.45, alkaline side) | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic acidosis | Normal (7.35–7.39, acid side) | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic alkalosis | Normal (7.41–7.45, alkaline side) | ↑ | ↑ · Same arrows, different pH. The PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ arrows look identical in partial and full compensation — the pH is what tells them apart. Abnormal pH = partial; normal pH = full. Acute = uncompensated (pH abnormal, only one value off); chronic = compensated (pH normal, both values off). To name the original problem in full compensation, look at which side of 7.40 the pH leans toward. · ROME: R espiratory O pposite — pH and PaCO₂ arrows point in opposite directions. M etabolic E qual — pH and HCO₃⁻ arrows point in the same direction.

t: Dialysis Chart: Access Types & Dialysis Types
x: The dialysis assignment — description, pros, cons, and nursing care for each access and each modality · Dialysis requires reliable vascular or peritoneal access to remove waste products and excess fluid. The access types — Vascath, Permacath, AV graft, AV fistula, and Tenckhoff catheter — differ in design, longevity, infection risk, and which dialysis type they support. · Dialysis access types · Access | Brief description | Pros | Cons | Nursing care for this access · Vascath | A temporary, non-tunneled, double-lumen central venous catheter inserted into a large vein (internal jugular, femoral, or subclavian) | • Can be used immediately • Suitable for short-term/emergency dialysis (AKI) • Inserted quickly at the bedside | • Highest infection risk • Not for long-term use • Risk of thrombosis and central vein stenosis | • Strict aseptic dressing changes • Monitor for infection • Maintain patency (lock per protocol) • Do not use for IV fluids, meds, or blood draws · Permacath | A tunneled , cuffed central venous catheter designed for longer-term use | • Can be used immediately • Lasts longer than a Vascath • Tunnel and cuff give lower infection risk than a Vascath • Bridge while a fistula or graft matures | • Still a higher infection risk than a fistula or graft • Clotting and catheter malfunction | • Regular sterile catheter/dressing care • Monitor the exit site for redness, drainage • Maintain the heparin lock • Monitor for infection and thrombosis • Dialysis staff use only · AV graft | A synthetic tube tunneled under the skin connecting an artery to a vein | • Usable sooner than a fistula (about 2–3 weeks ) • Option when the client's veins aren't suitable for a fistula | • Higher clotting (thrombosis) and infection risk than a fistula • May need repeated interventions to stay open | • Palpate thrill , auscultate bruit every shift • No BP, IVs, or blood draws on that arm • Monitor for infection and clotting • Teach access-arm care · AV fistula | A surgical connection of the client's own artery and vein, creating a durable access point | • Gold standard — best long-term access • Lowest infection and clotting rates • Longest-lasting | • Takes about 1–3 months to mature before use • Not suitable for every client (vessel quality) | • Palpate thrill , auscultate bruit every shift • No BP, IVs, or blood draws on that arm • No tight clothing/jewelry, heavy carrying, or sleeping on the arm • Watch for steal syndrome (pale, cold hand) · Tenckhoff catheter | A catheter surgically placed into the peritoneal cavity for peritoneal dialysis | • Allows home-based dialysis • Avoids vascular access • An alternative to hemodialysis | • Risk of peritonitis • Requires client training and adherence | • Strict aseptic technique for all connections/exchanges; mask • Daily exit-site care • Outflow should be clear; cloudy = infection • Monitor for fever and abdominal pain · Dialysis types · Dialysis type | Brief description | Access that can be used | Pros | Cons · Hemodialysis | Blood is filtered through a machine (artificial kidney) outside the body — usually about 3–4 hours, 3 times a week | Vascath, Permacath, AV graft, AV fistula | • Rapid, effective removal of wastes, fluid, and potassium • In-center, or at home with training | • Requires vascular access • Infection and clotting risk • Rapid fluid shifts → hypotension, cramps, disequilibrium syndrome • Strict schedule and diet; time-consuming · CRRT (continuous renal replacement therapy) | A slower, continuous (24/7) form of blood filtration used in the ICU | Temporary dialysis catheter (Vascath); a tunneled catheter may also be used | • Gentle on BP — suited to hemodynamically unstable clients • Continuous, steady fluid and solute removal | • ICU only; requires specialized equipment and close (often 1:1) nursing • Filter clotting; frequent electrolyte monitoring • Client is immobilized at the bedside · Peritoneal dialysis | Dialysate is instilled into the abdomen, and the peritoneal membrane acts as the filter (fill, dwell, drain) | Tenckhoff catheter | • Daily, gradual dialysis with steadier fluid balance • Done at home; more independence • Avoids vascular access • More liberal diet (especially potassium) | • Risk of peritonitis • Requires client/caregiver training and adherence • Glucose absorption (hyperglycemia, weight gain), protein loss, hernia risk · Key insights · Vascular access types differ mainly in how long they last , their infection risk , and whether the client's vessels are suitable · AV fistulas are the preferred long-term access because of low complication rates and durability, but they need time to mature and suitable veins · Vascaths are essential for immediate dialysis but carry the highest infection and clotting risk · Permacaths bridge short- and long-term use; tunneling reduces infection risk · AV grafts are the alternative when a fistula isn't feasible, with higher complication risk · The Tenckhoff catheter enables home peritoneal dialysis without vascular access but demands strict infection control · CRRT is chosen for critically ill, unstable clients because it is gentle and continuous; it is not a home therapy · Nursing care across all access types · Infection prevention is paramount — strict aseptic technique, regular monitoring, client education · Check patency: thrill and bruit for fistulas and grafts · Teach limb protection, hygiene, and signs of complications · Catheter care: dressing changes, locking/flushing protocols, surveillance for clotting or infection · Peritoneal dialysis: make sure the client can perform sterile exchanges and recognizes early signs of peritonitis · CRRT: hourly vital signs, filter checks, and frequent electrolytes

t: Clinical Judgment Activity: Marie vs. Frank
x: Two patients with the same BUN and creatinine — and opposite fluid problems · This NurseThink activity compares two patients with identical BUN (80) and creatinine (3.96) whose presentations point in opposite directions. The patient charts are in the case tabs of this lesson's quiz. The worked answers below follow the activity's four clinical judgment steps. · The two patients ·  | Marie Hunter, 89 | Frank Woods, 56 · Setting | Admitted from SNF — altered mental status, gradual decline over a week, poor intake | ED — shortness of breath and fatigue for 2 weeks · History | GERD, cataracts, right-sided stroke 5 years ago (no residual effects), pacemaker for 3rd-degree heart block; Eliquis and Protonix daily; sulfa allergy | Diabetes, HTN, ESRD on dialysis for 10 years , CHF, COPD. Missed dialysis — wife has been sick and unable to drive him, no other support · Assessment | Lethargic, confused, follows minimal commands; lungs clear; 1+ pulses; no edema; no urine output, no bladder distention | A&O x4; crackles ; bounding pulses , 2+ lower-extremity edema; + thrill and bruit in left AV fistula; small amount of urine · Vitals | T 99.5, HR 115, RR 14, BP 105/62, SpO₂ 95% | T 98, HR 115, RR 32 , BP 178/94 , SpO₂ 84% · Labs | Na 156 , K 4.7, glucose 70, BUN 80, Cr 3.96, WBC 10.6, HCT 49 , Hgb 12, Plt 200 | Na 130 , K 6.7 , glucose 214, BUN 80, Cr 3.96, WBC 8.4, HCT 29, Hgb 8 , Plt 215 · 1. Recognizing cues · Most concerning assessment / highest priority: For Marie, the combination of altered mental status, no urine output, tachycardia with a soft BP, and weak (1+) pulses — she is volume depleted and not perfusing her kidneys. For Frank, the SpO₂ of 84% with RR 32 and crackles is the highest priority (airway/breathing), immediately followed by the potassium of 6.7 , which can cause a fatal dysrhythmia at any moment. · Interpreting the labs: · Lab | Marie | Frank · Sodium | 156 — hypernatremia : water lost/not taken in, so sodium is concentrated | 130 — dilutional hyponatremia : retained water dilutes sodium · Potassium | 4.7 — normal | 6.7 — critical hyperkalemia ; kidneys can't excrete it and he's missed dialysis · BUN / creatinine | 80 / 3.96 — azotemia; ratio about 20:1, consistent with a prerenal (perfusion) cause | 80 / 3.96 — azotemia from ESRD with no dialysis to clear wastes · HCT / Hgb | 49 / 12 — HCT elevated = hemoconcentration from dehydration | 29 / 8 — anemia of CKD (no erythropoietin), made to look worse by dilution · Glucose | 70 — low-normal; poor intake | 214 — hyperglycemia; diabetic · WBC | 10.6 — upper-normal; with a low-grade temp, keep infection on the radar as a cause of decline | 8.4 — normal · 2. Analyzing cues — what's going on? · Marie: prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration/hypovolemia (a week of poor intake in a frail older adult), with hypernatremia causing her altered mental status. No bladder distention argues against a postrenal cause · Frank: ESRD with missed dialysis → fluid volume excess with pulmonary edema, critical hyperkalemia, dilutional hyponatremia, and uremic fatigue. The root cause is social — no transportation to dialysis · 3. Prioritizing hypotheses and generating solutions ·  | Marie | Frank · Priority treatment | IV fluid replacement to restore renal perfusion, correcting sodium slowly | Breathing and the heart first: high Fowler's, oxygen, cardiac monitor, emergency hyperkalemia treatment (calcium gluconate, insulin + dextrose, K⁺ binder), then emergent hemodialysis to remove both fluid and potassium · Nursing care | Strict I&O and hourly urine output; daily weight; lung sounds and vitals frequently (watch for overload — age, pacemaker/cardiac history); serial sodium, BUN, creatinine; neuro checks; fall, aspiration, and skin-breakdown precautions; bleeding precautions (Eliquis); goals-of-care discussion with the family | Continuous cardiac monitoring; frequent respiratory assessment and SpO₂; fluid and sodium restriction; protect the AV fistula arm (no BP/IV/lab draws) and confirm thrill and bruit; monitor glucose after insulin; strict I&O and weights; social work / case management referral for dialysis transportation · 4. Evaluating outcomes ·  | Marie | Frank · Expected outcomes | Urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr; HR and BP normalizing; sodium trending down gradually; BUN/creatinine improving; mental status returning to baseline | SpO₂ above 92%, RR and lung sounds improving; K⁺ back to 3.5–5.5 with no dysrhythmias; BP down and weight back to dry weight; a transportation plan in place so he doesn't miss dialysis again · Potential complications of treatment | Fluid overload /pulmonary edema from resuscitation in an 89-year-old with cardiac history; cerebral edema if sodium is corrected too fast; progression to intrarenal injury (ATN) if perfusion isn't restored; bleeding and fall injuries on Eliquis | Dysrhythmia or cardiac arrest before potassium is controlled; hypoglycemia after IV insulin; dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (very high BUN after a long gap); hypotension and cramping from rapid fluid removal; respiratory failure needing intubation · Venn diagram — Marie, Frank, and the overlap · Marie only | Both | Frank only · Fluid volume deficit ; hypernatremia; hemoconcentration (HCT 49); low-normal BP; weak pulses; clear lungs; altered mental status; prerenal AKI (potentially reversible); sulfa allergy; on an anticoagulant | BUN 80, creatinine 3.96 ; HR 115; hypoactive bowel sounds; kidney failure driving a fluid and electrolyte crisis; need for close I&O, weights, and lab trending; full code | Fluid volume excess ; dilutional hyponatremia; hyperkalemia ; anemia; hypertension; bounding pulses; crackles and hypoxemia; ESRD (irreversible); AV fistula; social barrier to care · Same kidney numbers, opposite fluid problems. The BUN and creatinine confirm that the kidneys aren't clearing waste — but the vital signs, lung sounds, pulses, sodium, and hematocrit are what tell you which direction the fluid has gone, and that decides whether the patient gets fluids or fluid removal. · Marie's sulfa allergy matters for this module: furosemide and bumetanide are sulfonamide-derived loop diuretics. If she becomes fluid overloaded from resuscitation, flag the allergy before a loop diuretic is given.

(Hint: A-W-E-T-B-E-D) · Acid–base balance · Water balance · Electrolytes — K⁺, Ca²⁺, phosphorus · Toxin removal — BUN and creatinine · Blood pressure (renin) / bicarb · Erythropoietin — RBC production · D — activates vitamin D · 1.2 Define the following: · GFR: volume of plasma filtered per minute; normal ~100–120 mL/min; decreases with age · Oliguria: < 500 mL urine in 24 hrs (instructor slide); hourly red flag < 30 mL/hr · Anuria: < 50 mL urine in 24 hrs · Azotemia: rise in BUN, creatinine, uric acid — lab finding only · Uremia: azotemia WITH symptoms (hyperkalemia, edema, anemia, confusion, itching) · 1.3 Which lab is the best indicator of kidney function? Why is BUN less reliable? · Creatinine. BUN is affected by the liver, hydration, protein intake, and GI bleeding — not just the kidneys. · 1.4 Normal Lab Values: · Lab | Normal Value | Significance in kidney disease · Creatinine | 0.6–1.2 mg/dL | ↑ — best indicator of kidney function · BUN | 10–20 mg/dL | ↑ — azotemia · BUN:Cr ratio | 10–20:1 | > 20:1 suggests dehydration/prerenal · Potassium | 3.5–5.0 mEq/L | ↑ — dysrhythmias, cardiac arrest · Phosphorus | ~2.5–4.5 mg/dL (dialysis goal 3.0–5.5) | ↑ — itching, bone disease, calcifications · Calcium | ~8.5–10.5 mg/dL | ↓ — tetany, laryngospasm · Hemoglobin | ~12–16 (F) / 14–18 (M) g/dL | ↓ — anemia from ↓ erythropoietin · pH / HCO₃⁻ | 7.35–7.45 / 22–26 | ↓ — metabolic acidosis · 1.5 What four things should NOT be found in urine? · Protein · RBCs (blood) · Ketones · Glucose · 1.6 List four gerontologic changes in the urinary system. Is metabolic acidosis a normal age-related change? · ↓ GFR · Sclerosis of glomerulus and vessels · Bladder constriction/decreased capacity → frequency · BPH (men) and urinary incontinence · No — metabolic acidosis is NOT age-related; look for a cause. · 1.7 What does a renal angiography show vs. a renal ultrasound? How does each one compensate? · Lungs — fast (minutes to hours): breathe fast to blow off CO₂, slow to retain CO₂. · Kidneys — slow (days): make more or less HCO₃⁻. · 2.3 Define: · Uncompensated: pH abnormal, only one of CO₂/HCO₃⁻ abnormal · Partially compensated: pH abnormal, both CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ abnormal · Fully compensated: pH normal (leans toward one side of 7.40), both CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ abnormal · 2.4 Interpret each ABG (imbalance + compensation): · pH | CO₂ | HCO₃⁻ | Interpretation · 7.22 | 72 | 23 | Respiratory acidosis, uncompensated · 7.30 | 42 | 6 | Metabolic acidosis, uncompensated · 7.50 | 25 | 23 | Respiratory alkalosis, uncompensated · 7.48 | 41 | 35 | Metabolic alkalosis, uncompensated · 7.37 | 72 | 36 | Respiratory acidosis, fully compensated · 7.38 | 15 | 6 | Metabolic acidosis, fully compensated · 7.42 | 25 | 18 | Respiratory alkalosis, fully compensated · 7.43 | 50 | 35 | Metabolic alkalosis, fully compensated · 7.25 | 38 | 15 | Metabolic acidosis, uncompensated · 7.30 | 55 | 30 | Respiratory acidosis, partially compensated · 7.36 | 30 | 16 | Metabolic acidosis, fully compensated · 7.52 | 48 | 38 | Metabolic alkalosis, partially compensated · 2.5 What acid–base imbalance is expected in CKD? Why? How is it treated? · Metabolic acidosis (usually compensated) — kidneys can't excrete acid or make bicarb. Treat with sodium bicarbonate and dialysis. Acidosis also raises K⁺. · Part 3 · Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) · 3.1 Complete the chart: ·  | Prerenal | Intrarenal | Postrenal · Definition | ↓ perfusion to kidneys (before) | Damage in the kidney itself | Obstruction of urine outflow (after) · Causes | Dehydration, hemorrhage/trauma, ↓ cardiac output (MI, HF), burns, vomiting/diarrhea, sepsis | Nephrotoxic meds (NSAIDs, "-mycins," chemo, contrast dye), glomerulonephritis/infection, rhabdo, HTN & DM | Stones, BPH/prostate, UTI → retention, clots, tumors, poorly draining Foley · Prevention / Treatment | Strict I&O, stop bleeding & replace, correct low BP, fluids | Peak & trough (~3rd dose), treat disease, hydrate + bicarb/acetylcysteine for dye | Foley care, urinary education, treat prostate (TURP → bladder irrigation) · 3.2 Which two medication classes reduce blood flow into the kidney and should be watched in at-risk patients? When are peak and trough levels drawn? · NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. Peak & trough are usually drawn around the 3rd dose of nephrotoxic antibiotics (aminoglycosides, vancomycin). · 3.3 Phases of AKI: · Phase | Length | What happens | Nursing actions · Onset / Initiation | Time of injury | Triggering event | Treat the cause · Oliguric | 1–7 days | ↓ UOP, azotemia, hyperkalemia, FVO, metabolic acidosis | Strict I&O, daily weights, EKG, K⁺ labs, fluid restriction, low-protein diet, dialysis if needed · Diuretic | 1–3 weeks | Large amounts of dilute urine | Watch for dehydration (FVD) and hypokalemia · Recovery | 3–12 months | Function slowly returns | Avoid nephrotoxins — kidneys stay sensitive; some develop CKD · 3.4 Which phase is most dangerous and why? Also warm solution with dry heat (never microwave). · Part 7 · Renal Diet · 7.1 What should the patient on dialysis be taught about the following? How would you explain this as the nurse? · a. u: NUR 113 Review: Hypertension & Peripheral Vascular Disease
x: The silent killer — categories, accurate readings, lifestyle, first-line drugs, and crises · What hypertension is · Hypertension (HTN) is a sustained elevation of blood pressure. BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance, so anything that raises blood volume, heart output, or vessel constriction (sympathetic overactivity, RAAS activation, kidneys holding sodium and water, stiff arteries) can raise BP. The goal of treatment is to prevent target organ damage — it is controlled, not cured . · HTN is called the "silent killer" because it usually has no symptoms — many people have it for years without knowing. When symptoms do appear (headache — often occipital on waking — dizziness, blurred vision, nosebleeds, chest pain, SOB), they usually mean damage to blood vessels and organs has already started . · Why this matters in Module 4: years of high pressure drive CAD, heart failure, and stroke . The heart pumps against higher pressure → LVH → HF; damaged arteries → plaque → angina/MI and ischemic stroke. · Primary vs. secondary · Type | What it means | Examples / clues · Primary (essential) | No identifiable cause — most adults with HTN; a mix of genetics and lifestyle | Develops gradually with age and risk factors · Secondary | High BP from an identifiable cause — treat the cause and BP improves | Chronic kidney disease , renal artery stenosis, polycystic kidney disease, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's syndrome, pheochromocytoma, thyroid or parathyroid disease, coarctation of the aorta, obstructive sleep apnea , preeclampsia, drugs ( NSAIDs , corticosteroids, oral contraceptives, decongestants, alcohol, cocaine, amphetamines). Suspect it with abrupt onset, onset before age 30, or HTN resistant to 3 or more drugs · Risk factors · Nonmodifiable: advancing age, family history, African American heritage, sex (men higher risk until about 64; women higher at 65 and older) · Modifiable: overweight/obesity, high-sodium diet and low intake of potassium, vegetables, and fiber, sedentary lifestyle, tobacco/nicotine (including e-cigarettes and secondhand smoke), excess alcohol (more than 2 drinks/day for men, more than 1 for women), stress, high cholesterol · Conditions: diabetes, chronic kidney disease, sleep apnea, pregnancy/preeclampsia · Blood pressure categories (2017 ACC/AHA) · Category | Systolic (mm Hg) | and/or | Diastolic (mm Hg) · Normal | below 120 | and | below 80 · Elevated | 120–129 | and | below 80 · Stage 1 HTN | 130–139 | or | 80–89 · Stage 2 HTN | 140 or higher | or | 90 or higher · Hypertensive crisis | above 180 | and/or | above 120 · If the systolic and diastolic fall in different categories, use the higher category (e.g., 124/86 = stage 1). Diagnosis is based on the average of 2 or more readings on 2 or more occasions . Isolated systolic hypertension (high SBP, normal DBP) is the most common form in older adults because the big arteries stiffen. · " Elevated " (120–129 with a diastolic below 80) replaced the old "prehypertension" — it is treated with lifestyle changes, not medication . The old 140/90 cutoff for diagnosing HTN is no longer used. · Getting an accurate reading · No caffeine, smoking, eating, or exercise for 30 minutes before; empty the bladder · Sit quietly for 5 minutes : back supported, feet flat on the floor, legs uncrossed, arm supported at heart level ; no talking during the reading · Right-size the cuff — bladder width at least 40% of the arm's circumference. A cuff that is too small reads falsely HIGH ; too large reads falsely low · First visit: measure both arms and use the arm with the higher reading from then on (arms normally differ by no more than 5 mm Hg) · Take 2 readings 1–2 minutes apart and average them; document the arm and the position · Before starting drugs, get lying, sitting, and standing BPs; report a drop of 10 mm Hg or more (orthostatic hypotension) · Home or ambulatory monitoring helps catch white coat HTN (high only in the clinic) and masked HTN (normal in the clinic, high at home) · Target organ damage (complications) · Organ | What high BP does | What you may find · Heart | Works against high pressure → left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) ; speeds atherosclerosis | CAD (angina, MI), heart failure , dysrhythmias; S4 heart sound; LVH on ECG/echo · Brain | Damaged, narrowed, or ruptured cerebral vessels | TIA, stroke (mostly ischemic; also intracerebral hemorrhage) — vision or speech changes, weakness, dizziness, sudden fall · Kidneys | Damaged glomerular vessels | Chronic kidney disease — ↑ BUN and creatinine, protein in the urine, nocturia · Eyes | Retinal vessel damage | Retinopathy — hemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots, papilledema; blurred vision, spots, blindness · Peripheral vessels | Accelerated atherosclerosis | Peripheral arterial disease — weak or absent pulses, claudication; aortic aneurysm/dissection · Retinal vessel damage seen on an eye exam suggests similar damage elsewhere in the vascular system. · Diagnostics · BUN and creatinine — kidney damage · Urinalysis — protein (albuminuria) or blood = kidney damage; glucose = diabetes · Electrolytes — sodium, potassium (a low K⁺ can point to hyperaldosteronism), calcium · Fasting glucose and a lipid panel — other cardiovascular risk factors · 12-lead ECG — LVH or ischemia; echocardiogram confirms LVH; chest X-ray may show an enlarged heart · Thyroid tests and other studies if a secondary cause is suspected · Lifestyle first — for every stage · Lifestyle change is the first step at every stage and continues even when drugs are added. Elevated BP is treated with lifestyle alone (recheck in 3–6 months). · Weight loss if overweight — one of the most effective changes · DASH diet — high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy; low in saturated fat, cholesterol, and sugar · Sodium: the standard DASH diet allows no more than 2,300 mg/day ; with hypertension the goal is below 1,500 mg/day (follow the ordered limit). Avoid canned, processed, cured, and fast foods; season with herbs, spices, lemon, or vinegar — taste buds adjust to less salt in 2–3 months · Potassium-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach, beans) help lower BP — unless the client has kidney disease or takes a drug that holds potassium ( ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic ) · Limit alcohol — no more than 2 drinks/day for men, 1 for women · Exercise — aerobic activity at least 30 minutes most days (about 150 minutes/week) · Stop all nicotine — cigarettes, e-cigarettes, chewing tobacco; manage stress; treat sleep apnea · DASH food group | Servings (2,000-calorie plan) | Serving examples · Whole grains | 6–8 per day | 1 slice bread; 1 oz dry cereal; ½ cup cooked rice or pasta · Vegetables | 4–5 per day | 1 cup leafy greens; ½ cup cooked vegetables (choose low-sodium canned) · Fruits | 4–5 per day | 1 medium fruit; ½ cup fresh, frozen, or canned (no added sugar) · Low-fat or fat-free dairy | 2–3 per day | 1 cup milk or yogurt; 1.5 oz cheese · Lean meat, poultry, fish | 6 or fewer 1-oz servings per day | 1 oz cooked meat or fish; 1 egg — less red meat · Fats and oils | 2–3 per day | 1 tsp vegetable oil or soft margarine · Nuts, seeds, legumes | 4–5 per week | ⅓ cup nuts; 2 tbsp nut butter; ½ cup cooked beans · Sweets | fewer than 5 per week | 1 tbsp sugar or jelly · Drug therapy · Drugs are added for stage 2 , and for stage 1 in clients with cardiovascular disease or high cardiovascular risk. The goal for all adults is below 130/80 . Start low; if BP isn't at goal, the dose is increased and a second drug from a different class is added. A once-daily pill or a combination pill helps adherence. · First-line classes: thiazide diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone), calcium channel blocker (amlodipine), ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) or ARB (losartan) · Chronic kidney disease → ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is favored — it slows kidney damage · African American clients without HF or CKD → start with a thiazide or CCB · Beta blockers are used when there is another reason for them (CAD, HF, rate control) · Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB (hyperkalemia, kidney injury, hypotension) · ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy · Resistant HTN = not at goal despite 3 drugs from different classes (one a diuretic) — first check adherence and cost, then look for a secondary cause · Hydrochlorothiazide, Chlorthalidone, Indapamide, Metolazone — Thiazide Diuretics · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO once daily in the morning (if a second dose is ordered, give it in the early afternoon — no later than about 6 p.m.); with or without food. The full BP-lowering effect can take several weeks · Mechanism of action | Blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule → water follows → ↓ blood volume and ↓ BP. check with the provider or pharmacist before OTC drugs; diabetics check glucose more often; report joint pain (gout) or eye pain/vision changes · Thiazide labs go DOWN for sodium and potassium ("hypo-K, hypo-Na") but UP for G lucose, U ric acid, and C alcium — "they raise the GUC." · Side effects by class · Class | Examples | Watch for | Key teaching · Thiazide diuretic | hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone | Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, gout, photosensitivity, orthostatic hypotension | Morning dose; potassium-rich foods; sunscreen; rise slowly · ACE inhibitor ("-pril") | lisinopril, enalapril, captopril | Dry cough , angioedema (even after years), hyperkalemia , first-dose hypotension, ↓ kidney function | Report face/lip/tongue swelling (911); Bring the BP down slowly — dropping it too fast starves the brain, heart, and kidneys that have adapted to high pressure (stroke, MI, kidney injury). · Teaching and adherence · HTN is lifelong and usually silent — keep taking the medicine even when you feel fine ; never stop suddenly (rebound hypertension). Keep an extra supply when traveling (carry-on bag) · Report side effects instead of quitting — another drug can usually be found · Home BP monitoring : upper-arm automatic cuff, correct technique, keep a written log, bring the log and the machine to visits · Rise slowly (sit on the edge of the bed first); report dizziness or low readings — fall risk, especially in older adults ("start low, go slow") · Avoid OTC decongestants and cold/sinus products (vasoconstrictors) and NSAIDs (raise BP and hold fluid) — check with the provider or pharmacist before any OTC drug · Follow the DASH/low-sodium plan, stay active, limit alcohol, stop nicotine, and keep follow-up appointments; report vision changes, chest pain, SOB, swelling, or neuro changes

u: NUR 113 Review: Hypertension & Peripheral Vascular Disease
x: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) — side by side · Two different plumbing problems · Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is narrowing of the arteries to the legs, almost always from atherosclerosis — oxygen-rich blood can't get down to the tissues, so they become ischemic . Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) is a problem with the veins : stretched, leaky valves (often after a DVT) let blood pool in the lower legs instead of returning up to the heart, causing venous hypertension, edema, and skin breakdown. · Arterial = Away from the heart — blood can't get DOWN: dangle the legs . Venous = blood can't get back UP: elevate the legs . · Atherosclerosis — the cause of PAD · Atherosclerosis is a buildup of lipids, calcium, and fibrous tissue ( plaque ) on the inner lining of large and medium arteries. It is a whole-body disease : a client with PAD very likely has plaque in the coronary and carotid arteries too, so PAD is a marker for CAD and stroke risk . As an artery slowly narrows, small collateral vessels enlarge to route blood around the blockage — exercise helps them grow. · The side-by-side comparison · Feature | ARTERIAL (PAD) | VENOUS (CVI) · Problem | Blood can't get to the tissue (ischemia) | Blood can't get back to the heart (pooling) · Pain | Intermittent claudication — cramping/aching in the calf, thigh, or buttock with walking, relieved by rest ; later rest pain in the foot/toes, worse at night and with elevation, relieved by dangling | Aching, heaviness , fullness; worse at the end of the day or after standing; relieved by elevation · Pulses | Decreased or absent ; bruits may be heard | Normal (may be hard to feel through edema) · Color | Pale on elevation ; dependent rubor (dusky red/cyanotic when dangling) | Brownish discoloration (hemosiderin staining) around the ankles and lower legs · Temperature | Cool | Warm · Skin, hair, nails | Thin, shiny, dry skin ; hair loss on the legs and toes; thick, brittle toenails ; muscle atrophy; delayed capillary refill | Stasis dermatitis — dry, itchy, scaly, cracking skin; thick, hardened (fibrosed) skin over time; dilated superficial veins · Edema | Absent or minimal | Present — ankle/lower-leg edema, worse in the evening · Ulcer location | Toes (tips, between toes), pressure points of the feet , heel, lateral ankle | Medial malleolus (inner ankle) — the " gaiter area " of the lower leg · Ulcer appearance | Small, round, deep ("punched out"); pale base; little drainage; may have black eschar/gangrene | Large, shallow , irregular edges; red , beefy base; heavy drainage · Ulcer pain | Very painful | Less painful (aching) · Positioning | Keep legs dependent or level — dangle , recliner, feet on the floor; don't elevate | Elevate legs above the heart ; avoid dangling · Compression | Avoid — compression cuts off what little arterial flow there is | Use graduated compression stockings/wraps · PAD: risk factors and diagnosis · Smoking/nicotine is the most important modifiable risk factor — nicotine causes vasoconstriction and vasospasm, carbon monoxide steals oxygen from hemoglobin, and platelets clump more. E-cigarettes and chewing tobacco count · Diabetes — earlier, faster, and more below-the-knee disease; higher amputation risk · Hypertension and hyperlipidemia ; also sedentary lifestyle, obesity, stress, increasing age, family history · Ankle-brachial index (ABI) : ankle systolic BP ÷ brachial (arm) systolic BP, measured with a Doppler. Normally the ankle pressure is about the same as or higher than the arm (ABI about 1.0); an ABI below 0.90 indicates PAD — the lower the number, the worse the disease · Doppler (hand-held, more sensitive than palpation for weak pulses) and duplex ultrasound ; treadmill testing for claudication; angiography before a procedure · Always compare both legs : pulses, color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation · PAD nursing care · Walking program: walk to the point of pain , rest until the pain goes away , then walk again . This builds collateral circulation and increases walking distance over time. A supervised exercise program is ideal · Position: legs neutral or dependent — raise the head of the bed, use a recliner, or sit with the feet on the floor · Keep warm, avoid cold (cold = vasoconstriction): warm socks, layers, warm room · Never apply heating pads, hot-water bottles, or hot soaks to ischemic legs or feet — heat raises tissue O₂ demand the narrowed artery can't meet, and decreased sensation means burns go unnoticed. Test bath water. (Heat to the abdomen is safer and causes reflex vasodilation in the legs.) · Avoid constriction: no tight socks, garters, knee-highs, or tight shoelaces; don't cross the legs · Stop all nicotine ; manage stress (sympathetic stimulation constricts vessels); low-fat diet and weight loss · Foot care: inspect feet daily (use a mirror); wash with mild soap and lukewarm water and pat dry ; lotion for dry skin but not between the toes ; clean, loose cotton socks; always wear well-fitting shoes or slippers — never barefoot; trim nails straight across (podiatrist if vision is poor or diabetic); report any blister, cut, or color change right away · After a revascularization (angioplasty, stent, bypass graft): check pulses/Doppler, color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation, and movement and compare with the other leg; a pulse that disappears = possible graft occlusion → notify the surgeon immediately · Cilostazol — Phosphodiesterase III Inhibitor (for claudication) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, usually 100 mg twice daily , taken at least 30 minutes before or 2 hours after breakfast and dinner . Intermittent claudication from PAD — improves pain-free and maximum walking distance . Improvement takes weeks — often 2–6 weeks, sometimes up to 12; if there's no improvement after about 3 months, it is usually stopped · Mechanism of action | Inhibits phosphodiesterase III → direct vasodilator and inhibits platelet aggregation · Adverse reactions | Headache (most common), diarrhea , palpitations /tachycardia, dizziness, peripheral edema; ↑ bleeding risk when combined with other antiplatelets or anticoagulants · Contraindications | Boxed warning: contraindicated in heart failure of ANY severity (drugs in this class shorten survival in HF); active bleeding or bleeding disorders; caution with CAD (may worsen angina) and severe kidney or liver impairment · Nursing interventions | Screen for any history of heart failure before the first dose ; monitor HR, BP, new cardiac symptoms, and for bleeding; periodic CBC (platelets, WBC); assess walking distance and pain to evaluate the effect; dose is lowered with some interacting drugs (e.g., diltiazem, omeprazole) · Patient education | Keep taking it — it can take several weeks to notice better walking ; take it on an empty stomach (before breakfast and dinner); avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice (raises the drug level); stop smoking (smoking lowers the drug's effect, and nicotine constricts vessels); keep doing the walking program; may cause dizziness — be careful driving until you know how it affects you; report palpitations, chest pain, swelling or SOB, or unusual bleeding · Cilostazol and the heart: "No HF, no grapefruit." It's a boxed warning — any heart failure, even mild, rules it out. · Other PAD drugs: antiplatelets — aspirin or clopidogrel — are recommended for symptomatic PAD to prevent MI and stroke (watch for GI upset/bleeding). Statins are first-line for PAD: they stabilize plaque, lower cardiovascular risk, and can increase walking distance (report muscle pain or dark urine). · Niacin (Vitamin B3, Nicotinic Acid) — Lipid-Lowering Agent · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO (immediate- or extended-release; some products at bedtime). Lowers LDL and triglycerides and raises HDL ; also treats niacin deficiency. Started low and increased slowly — if it's stopped, it may need to be restarted at a low dose · Mechanism of action | A B vitamin that, in large doses, reduces the liver's production of LDL and VLDL (triglyceride-carrying) particles and raises HDL · Adverse reactions | Flushing (warmth, redness, tingling of the face and upper body — the most common reason people stop it), itching, GI upset; liver toxicity (↑ liver enzymes, jaundice, dark urine); hyperglycemia ; gout attacks (↑ uric acid); rarely rhabdomyolysis when combined with a statin · Contraindications | Active liver disease or unexplained ↑ liver enzymes, active peptic ulcer disease, bleeding problems; caution with diabetes, gout, heavy alcohol use, and older adults · Nursing interventions | Baseline and periodic liver enzymes , glucose (closely in diabetics), uric acid, and lipid panel; aspirin about 30 minutes before the dose may be ordered to reduce flushing; separate from bile-acid binders (cholestyramine, colestipol) by 4 hours; with a statin, ask about muscle pain · Patient education | Take it with food ; avoid alcohol, hot drinks, and spicy foods around the dose (worsen flushing); flushing is expected and usually lessens over time; if flushing wakes you at night, get up slowly (dizziness); swallow extended-release tablets whole — don't crush or chew; diabetics check glucose more often; report yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, joint pain, or muscle pain/weakness; don't switch brands or forms without the provider · Niacin = the "hot flash" vitamin. Prevent the flush: aspirin 30 minutes before (if ordered), take it with food, no hot drinks or alcohol . Watch the L-G-G : L iver enzymes, G lucose, G out. · Chronic venous insufficiency care · Elevate the legs above the heart often — at least 15–20 minutes, four times a day; raise the foot of the bed about 6 inches at night · Graduated compression stockings (stronger compression than anti-embolism/TED hose): put them on in the morning before getting out of bed or after the legs have been elevated (veins emptiest); smooth, never rolled or bunched at the top (a rolled stocking becomes a tourniquet); remove at night and inspect the skin. Not for clients with severe PAD · Avoid prolonged sitting or standing ; walk and do leg exercises (ankle pumps, calf raises) — the calf muscle pump pushes blood up · Don't cross the legs or sit with the legs dangling (pressure behind the knee); avoid tight garments that leave marks · Skin care: keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized; protect the legs from bumps and scratches; report any new skin breakdown — ulcers heal slowly and recur often · Weight loss if overweight · Leg ulcer care · Identify the cause first — arterial or venous determines the positioning and whether compression is safe . Check pulses (and ABI) before any compression is applied · Cleanse gently with normal saline or a mild cleanser and lukewarm water; keep the wound bed moist and the surrounding skin protected; débridement removes dead tissue · Venous ulcers: compression (stockings, wraps, Unna boot) plus elevation — the key to healing · Arterial ulcers: no compression ; protect from pressure (heel protectors, bed cradle to keep sheets off the feet); referral for revascularization · Watch for infection (redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, odor) — systemic antibiotics based on culture · No heating pads or hot soaks ; diet high in protein, vitamins A and C, iron, and zinc for healing · Acute arterial occlusion — the 6 P's · A sudden blockage — usually an embolus from a clot in the heart ( A-fib , MI, HF) or a thrombus on top of plaque — cuts off blood flow to the limb. This is an EMERGENCY : there are only about 4–6 hours to restore flow before tissue dies. · P | What you find · Pain | Sudden, severe, unrelieved · Pallor | Pale, mottled limb below the blockage · Pulselessness | No pulse below the blockage · Paresthesia | Numbness, tingling, loss of sensation · Paralysis | Loss of movement — the most advanced (latest) P · Poikilothermia | Limb is cold — takes on the temperature of the room · Notify the provider immediately. Expect IV heparin right away (prevents the clot from growing and new emboli) and an emergency embolectomy or other procedure to restore flow. Keep the limb level and protected — no elevation, no heat, no massage — and reassess the 6 P's frequently. · A client with A-fib who suddenly has a cold, pale, pulseless, numb leg has an arterial embolus until proven otherwise — the same clot that can cause a stroke can lodge in a leg.

Layers, chambers, valves, coronaries, the cardiac cycle and the conduction system · Every perfusion problem comes down to one of four things: the pump fails (HF, dysrhythmias), the pipes narrow (CAD, stroke), clots block flow (DVT/PE), or there is not enough blood to carry oxygen (anemia). It all builds on how a normal heart moves blood. · Layers of the heart · Layer | What it is | Why it matters · Pericardium | Two-layer sac around the heart (visceral layer on the heart, tough parietal layer outside) with about 20 mL of lubricating fluid between them | Reduces friction as the heart beats; anchors the heart in the mediastinum · Epicardium | Outer layer of the heart wall | The coronary arteries run on the surface of the heart · Myocardium | Middle, muscle layer — does the pumping | The layer damaged by ischemia/MI; troponin leaks out of these cells · Endocardium | Smooth inner lining of the chambers and valves | Lines everything blood touches · Chambers · Right atrium — receives deoxygenated blood from the body (superior and inferior vena cava) and from the heart itself (coronary sinus). · Right ventricle — pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery (a low-pressure system). The pulmonary artery is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood. · Left atrium — receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins. · Left ventricle — pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body through the aorta. It is the thickest, most muscular chamber (2–3 times the right ventricle) because it must push against the high pressure of the systemic circulation. · Atria have thin walls (they only push blood a short way into the ventricles); ventricles have thick walls. · Valves and heart sounds · Valves keep blood moving in one direction . They open and close in response to pressure changes in the chambers. · Valve | Between | Type | Closure makes · Tricuspid (3 leaflets) | Right atrium → right ventricle | Atrioventricular (AV) | S1 (“lub”) · Mitral / bicuspid (2 leaflets) | Left atrium → left ventricle | Atrioventricular (AV) | S1 (“lub”) · Pulmonic | Right ventricle → pulmonary artery | Semilunar | S2 (“dub”) · Aortic | Left ventricle → aorta | Semilunar | S2 (“dub”) · S1 = AV valves close as the ventricles start to contract → marks the start of systole ; loudest at the apex (5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line — the PMI). · S2 = semilunar valves close as the ventricles relax → marks the start of diastole . · Papillary muscles and chordae tendineae hold the AV valve leaflets shut during contraction so blood does not flow backward (regurgitation) into the atria. · A murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow through a valve that is narrowed or leaking. An extra sound (S3) can be heard in heart failure. · “Try before you buy”: tri cuspid on the right comes before the bi cuspid (mitral) on the left. Lub = AV valves close (systole starts); dub = semilunar valves close (diastole starts). · Blood flow through the heart, step by step · 1. Body → superior and inferior vena cava · 2. → right atrium · 3. → tricuspid valve → right ventricle · 4. → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery · 5. → lungs (blood picks up O₂ and drops off CO₂) · 6. → pulmonary veins → left atrium · 7. → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle · 8. → aortic valve → aorta → rest of the body · Right side = to the lungs; left side = to the body. When the left side fails, blood backs up into the Lungs ; when the right side fails, blood backs up into the Rest of the body. · Coronary arteries · The heart muscle gets its own blood supply from the coronary arteries , which branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve. Unlike every other artery, the coronaries fill during DIASTOLE — when the aortic valve snaps shut, blood falls back against it and flows into the coronary openings while the heart muscle is relaxed. · Artery | Supplies (mainly) · Right coronary artery (RCA) | Right atrium, right ventricle, and the inferior (bottom) wall of the left ventricle; its posterior descending branch supplies the posterior wall. In most people it also feeds the SA and AV nodes. · Left main coronary artery | Short trunk that splits into the LAD and the circumflex — a blockage here cuts off a huge area of the left ventricle. · Left anterior descending (LAD) | Front (anterior) wall of the left ventricle and most of the septum — the main pumping muscle. · Circumflex | Wraps around to the lateral (side) wall of the left ventricle and the left atrium. · Clinical tie: a fast heart rate shortens diastole, so the coronaries have less time to fill. That is why tachycardia can cause chest pain and ischemia , especially in a patient with CAD — and why beta blockers (which slow the rate) protect the heart. · Coronaries fill in diastole: fast heart = short diastole = hungry heart muscle. · The cardiac cycle · Phase | What happens · Diastole (relaxation / filling) | All chambers relaxed; AV valves open, semilunar valves closed; ventricles fill; coronary arteries fill. Normally the longest part of the cycle. · Atrial systole (“atrial kick”) | Near the end of diastole the SA node fires, the atria contract and top off the ventricles with the last portion of blood (roughly 15–25% more). · Ventricular systole (contraction / ejection) | Ventricular pressure rises → AV valves close (S1) → semilunar valves open → blood is ejected into the pulmonary artery and aorta. When pressure falls, the semilunar valves close (S2) and diastole begins again. · Clinical tie: in atrial fibrillation the atria quiver instead of contracting, so the atrial kick is lost → less filling → lower stroke volume and cardiac output. The blood that sits in the quivering atria can pool and clot. · Conduction system overview · The heart makes its own electrical impulses — the brain does not tell it to beat. The impulse normally travels: · SA node (right atrium) — the heart's natural pacemaker → impulse spreads across both atria → atria contract ( P wave ). · AV node — the gatekeeper; briefly delays the impulse so the ventricles can finish filling (part of the PR interval ). · Bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricles contract ( QRS complex ). · Ventricles recover/reset ( T wave = ventricular repolarization). Atrial repolarization is hidden inside the QRS. · Pacemaker site | Intrinsic rate (bpm) | When it takes over · SA node | 60–100 | Normal pacemaker · AV node / junction | 40–60 | Backup if the SA node fails · Purkinje fibers / ventricles | 20–40 | Last resort if both higher pacemakers fail · Heart rate is also adjusted by the nervous system: the sympathetic system (beta-1 receptors, catecholamines, excess thyroid hormone) speeds it up; the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) slows it down. Atropine works by blocking the vagal slowing. · The farther down the pathway the pacemaker, the slower the rate: SA 60–100 → AV 40–60 → ventricles 20–40.

What makes the pump move blood — and how meds change it · Cardiac output · Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate (HR) × stroke volume (SV). It is the amount of blood one ventricle pumps out per minute — normally about 4–8 L/min at rest. If either HR or SV drops (and the other cannot make up for it), cardiac output falls and tissues are under-perfused. · Stroke volume = the amount of blood pumped out of the ventricle with each beat. · Stroke volume is set by three things: preload, afterload, and contractility . · Heart rate helps only up to a point: a very fast rate leaves too little time to fill (and to fill the coronaries), so SV and CO actually drop . A very slow rate pumps too few times per minute. · Ejection fraction (EF) · EF = the percentage of the blood in the left ventricle at the end of filling that is pumped out with each beat. Normal EF is 50–70%. It is a measure of how well the ventricle squeezes (contractility) and is measured by echocardiogram . An EF below 50% = reduced pumping = HFrEF (systolic heart failure). · Preload — the VOLUME · Preload = the volume of blood returning to the heart (into the right atrium ) that fills the ventricle by the end of diastole and stretches the muscle fibers. Preload deals with volume. · Starling's law (Frank–Starling): within limits, the more the muscle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts and the bigger the stroke volume — like a rubber band. Stretch it too far (an overfilled, failing heart) and it stops snapping back. · ↓ preload: diuretics, venodilators (nitrates), blood loss, dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea, diaphoresis). · ↑ preload: hypervolemia — IV fluids, blood transfusion, fluid retention; regurgitation of the cardiac valves (blood leaks backward through a valve that doesn't close and refills the chamber). · Afterload — the PRESSURE · Afterload = the resistance (pressure) the ventricle must push against to eject blood. · Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) = resistance to flow in the systemic circulation — the afterload of the left ventricle. Think: systemic BP. · Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) = resistance created by the pulmonary circulation — the afterload of the right ventricle. · Afterload and stroke volume move in opposite directions: vasoconstriction/hypertension ↑ afterload → ↓ SV and ↑ workload; vasodilation ↓ afterload → ↑ SV. · ↓ afterload: BP medications and vasodilators (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, nitrates, CCBs like amlodipine). · Preload = volume. Afterload = pressure. Too much volume? Take it off (diuretics). Too much pressure? Open the pipes (BP meds/vasodilators). · Contractility and compliance · Contractility = the force of the heart muscle's squeeze, independent of how full it is. ↑ by the sympathetic system/catecholamines and some drugs (digoxin, dopamine, dobutamine); ↓ by hypoxemia, acidosis, damaged muscle (MI), and beta blockers. · Compliance = how easily the ventricle (or a vessel) stretches to accept volume. A thick, stiff ventricle has low compliance — it can't fill well (HFpEF, “diastolic — thick”). Stiff, hardened arteries also have low compliance and raise BP. · Effects of preload and afterload on the heart · Change | Common causes | Stroke volume | Ventricular work | Myocardial O₂ requirement · ↑ Preload | ↑ fluid volume (hypervolemia), valve regurgitation, vasoconstriction | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ · ↓ Preload | Hypovolemia, vasodilation | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ · ↑ Afterload | Hypertension, hypovolemia*, vasoconstriction | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ · ↓ Afterload | Vasodilation | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ · *Hypovolemia → the body vasoconstricts to compensate → increased afterload. · Tying it to the meds · Medication | Main hemodynamic effect | Why it helps · Nitroglycerin | ↓ preload and ↓ afterload (dilates veins and arteries) | Less volume returning and less pressure to push against → ↓ cardiac workload and O₂ demand → relieves angina · Diuretics (e.g., furosemide) | ↓ preload | Remove excess fluid volume (heart failure, fluid overload) · ACE inhibitors / ARBs | ↓ afterload | Dilate arteries and lower BP so the left ventricle pushes against less resistance · Beta blockers | ↓ HR and ↓ contractility | Lower O₂ demand, lengthen diastole for coronary filling, reduce dysrhythmia risk · Digoxin (HF add-on) | ↑ contractility, ↓ HR | Stronger squeeze for a failing pump · Vocabulary review · Term | Meaning · Afterload | Resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood (the pressure) · Arteriosclerosis | Hardening and loss of elasticity of the arteries · Atherosclerosis | Fatty deposits (plaque) building up on the inner walls of arteries — the type of arteriosclerosis behind CAD and ischemic stroke · Cardiac output | HR × SV; the amount of blood pumped per minute · Compliance | Ability of the ventricle or vessel to stretch and expand with volume · Contractility | Force of the heart muscle's contraction · Ejection fraction | Percentage of the ventricle's end-diastolic volume pumped out per beat;
