normal 50–70% · Heart murmur | Abnormal sound from turbulent blood flow, usually from a narrowed or leaking valve or a defect · Ischemic | Lacking adequate blood supply (and therefore oxygen) to a tissue · Preload | Volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole (the stretch) · Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) | Resistance to flow out of the right ventricle created by the pulmonary circulation · Stroke volume | Amount of blood pumped out of the ventricle with each beat · Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) | Resistance to flow in the systemic circulation (the left ventricle's afterload) · Anything that makes the heart work harder (↑ HR, ↑ preload, ↑ afterload, ↑ contractility) also raises its O₂ demand — dangerous for a heart with narrowed coronaries.

Troponin, BNP, lipids, coags, electrolytes — and reading the heart from 12 views · Sort cardiac testing by the problem: Pump = CHF (BNP, echo/EF) · Perfusion = CAD (troponin, CK-MB, lipids, stress test, cath) · Electrical = EKG (12-lead, telemetry). · Cardiac biomarkers — is heart muscle damaged? · When heart muscle cells are starved of oxygen long enough to be injured, they leak proteins into the blood. These biomarkers plus the 12-lead ECG and the assessment are how heart damage is identified. · Lab | What it tells you | Key nursing points · Troponin | Gold standard for heart muscle damage; comes from the myocardium | Normally about 0 (undetectable); above 1 is significant . First lab priority for chest pain. Drawn on arrival and repeated serially (about every 6 h × 2). Rise is delayed , so one normal value does not rule out MI; stays elevated for days. · CK-MB | Cardiac-muscle fraction of the enzyme creatine kinase | Drawn with troponin; supports the diagnosis of heart muscle injury. · Myoglobin | Oxygen-binding protein in skeletal and cardiac muscle | Rises early but is not cardiac-specific — any muscle injury (trauma, rhabdomyolysis) raises it. Not the priority lab. · BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) | Released by the ventricles when they are stretched by volume/pressure | Below 100 pg/mL = normal; above 100 = heart failure — the higher, the worse. Useful to diagnose and track HF. High-sensitivity (HS) BNP: above 400 = abnormal. · Troponin is the T ruth-teller for heart damage — but it's a slow talker. Draw it on arrival and draw it again. · Lipid panel — risk for CAD · Test | Goal | Notes · Total cholesterol | Below 200 mg/dL |  · LDL (“bad” — deposits plaque) | Below 100 mg/dL with CAD (below 130 otherwise) | Lowered with statins, diet, exercise · HDL (“good” — carries cholesterol away to the liver) | Above 40–60 mg/dL — higher is better | Raised by exercise, quitting smoking · Triglycerides | Below 150 mg/dL | Raised by diabetes, alcohol, obesity; drawn after a 12-hour fast · L DL = L ousy (keep it Low). H DL = H appy (keep it High). · Coagulation studies — for anticoagulated patients · Test | Monitors | Remember · PTT / aPTT | Heparin | “Two t's make an H” — p tt → heparin. Antidote: protamine sulfate. · PT / INR | Warfarin | INR goal 2–3 for most anticoagulated patients (a patient not on warfarin is about 1). Antidote: vitamin K. · Coags (plus a CBC with hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets) are also drawn as baselines before invasive procedures such as cardiac cath. · BMP vs CMP and the electrolytes that matter · Panel | Includes | Cardiac use · BMP (basic metabolic panel) | Sodium, potassium, chloride, CO₂, BUN, creatinine, glucose, calcium | Electrolytes for dysrhythmia risk; kidney function before contrast dye and with ACE inhibitors/diuretics · CMP (comprehensive) | Everything in the BMP plus liver tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, protein) | Liver function — e.g., monitoring patients on statins or amiodarone · Potassium (K⁺) 3.5–5.5 mEq/L. Too low or too high → dangerous dysrhythmias. Watch K⁺ with diuretics (loop diuretics waste it; potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise it). · Magnesium (Mg²⁺) is not part of a BMP or CMP — it is ordered separately. Low magnesium → ventricular dysrhythmias, including torsades de pointes (treated with magnesium). · Electrolyte imbalance is one of the first causes to look for (and fix) with any new dysrhythmia. · Hemoglobin & hematocrit — low values (anemia, bleeding) mean less O₂ delivered to the heart and tissues; watch them closely on anticoagulants and thrombolytics. · The 12-lead ECG · Ten electrodes record the heart's electrical activity from 12 different views (leads) at the same time, so it can show damage all around the heart. · Electrode placement: 4 limb electrodes (RA, LA, RL, LL) + 6 chest electrodes V1–V6 across the chest — V1 and V2 at the 4th intercostal space on either side of the sternum, V3 between V2 and V4, V4 at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line , V5 at the anterior axillary line, and V6 at the left midaxillary line . · Used to find ischemia, injury, or infarction (ST-segment changes), dysrhythmias, conduction problems, enlarged chambers, and electrolyte effects. · For chest pain, the 12-lead ECG is obtained within 10 minutes of arrival/onset — along with assessment and a troponin. · Also get a 12-lead for any new rhythm change or when a patient becomes symptomatic of decreased cardiac output. ·  | 12-lead ECG | Continuous monitoring / telemetry · What | A snapshot from 12 views | Continuous recording from 1–2 leads, shown at the bedside or a central station · Best for | Diagnosing ischemia/MI and where it is | Catching rhythm changes as they happen in patients at risk for dysrhythmias · Teaching | Lie still, breathe normally | The monitor does not detect chest pain or shortness of breath — report new symptoms right away · Artifact — false readings · Artifact is interference that makes the tracing look abnormal when the heart is not. Always assess the patient, not the monitor — a patient talking to you with a strong pulse is not in V-fib. · Cause | Fix · Sweaty/oily skin | Dry the skin before placing electrodes · Hair under the electrode | Clip (or shave) the area · Dried-out electrode gel | Replace the electrodes · Loose or disconnected lead | Reattach / check connections · Movement, shivering, deep breaths, patient handling the wires | Have the patient rest still; warm the shivering patient; secure the wires · Monitor alarm → look at the patient first. Responsive with a pulse = probably artifact. Unresponsive = real emergency.

What each test shows — and the nursing care before and after · Which test answers which question? · Test | Question it answers | Invasive? · Stress test | How does the heart do when it has to work harder? (ischemia that only shows up with demand) | No (an IV for the medication version) · Echocardiogram (transthoracic — also called transcutaneous) | How well does it pump and fill? EF, valves, wall thickness, clots | No — ultrasound on the chest · TEE (transesophageal echo) | Clearer pictures — especially clots in the atria (before cardioversion) | Yes — probe down the esophagus with sedation · Cardiac cath / coronary angiogram | Are the coronary arteries blocked? Where? Can it be opened now? | Yes — catheter through an artery with contrast dye · Cardiac stress test · Healthy coronary arteries dilate when demand goes up; narrowed ones cannot, so ischemia often appears only under “stress.” The heart is stressed by exercise (treadmill — most common) or by medication for patients who cannot walk or exercise enough: dipyridamole or adenosine (vasodilators) or dobutamine (makes the heart work harder). Some tachycardia during the test is expected. · Before | During | After · Informed consent; explain the test NPO for several hours No caffeine/tobacco (caffeine blocks the vasodilator drugs) Hold beta blockers (and other rate-slowing drugs) as ordered — they keep the HR from rising Baseline vitals, heart and lung sounds, ECG Walking shoes, comfortable clothes Crash cart available | Continuous ECG, BP, and symptom monitoring Compare to baseline vitals | Monitor until vitals and assessment return to baseline (about 10–15 minutes) A positive (abnormal) result usually leads to cardiac cath · STOP the stress test if the patient develops any of these: · Chest pain · Dysrhythmia (abnormal rhythm) · Shortness of breath · Pallor · Diaphoresis · BP too high or too low · O₂ saturation below 90% · Stress test stop signs: pain, rhythm, breath, pale, sweaty, BP, sat below 90. · Echocardiogram and TEE · An echo is an ultrasound of the heart . It shows the ejection fraction (the go-to test for heart failure), valves opening and closing, wall thickness (thick and stiff vs stretched and boggy), overall contraction, and clots . · Transthoracic (also called transcutaneous ) echo — probe on the skin of the chest; noninvasive, no sedation, no special aftercare; pictures are less clear because sound passes through ribs and lung. · Transesophageal echo (TEE) — probe passed down the esophagus, right behind the heart, for much clearer pictures. · TEE before cardioversion: a clot sitting in the atria (A-fib, A-flutter) could be shocked loose → left ventricle → aorta → the brain = stroke . TEE checks for clots first. · Pre-TEE | Post-TEE · Informed consent NPO Remove dentures /retainers Conscious (moderate) sedation; throat numbed with a topical anesthetic | NPO until the throat numbness wears off and the gag reflex returns (aspiration risk) Then start clear liquids and advance as tolerated Monitor vitals, sedation level, and breathing Mild sore throat is expected · TEE = a tube down the throat → check the gag reflex before anything by mouth. · Cardiac catheterization (coronary angiogram) · A catheter is threaded through an artery (wrist/radial or groin/femoral) to the heart, and contrast dye is injected to show the coronary arteries and how the heart is perfused. During the same procedure the cardiologist can open blocked vessels and place stents . It is ordered after a positive stress test or when angina is unstable. Wrist access has fewer complications than the groin. Heparin and other blood thinners are given during the procedure, so bleeding is the big post-procedure risk. · Pre-cath | Post-cath · NPO after midnight Informed consent Ask about contrast (iodine) allergy — premedication may be ordered Check kidney function (BUN, creatinine) — dye is hard on the kidneys; acetylcysteine and bicarbonate/IV fluids protect the kidneys as ordered Hold anticoagulants as ordered ; baseline coags and CBC Baseline vitals and distal pulses (mark them) | Vitals q15 min × 1 h, q30 min × 1 h, then hourly Every check: insertion site (bleeding, hematoma), distal pulses, color, temperature, sensation — compare to the other extremity Groin: lie flat with the leg straight for several hours (how long depends on how the artery was closed); HOB no higher than 30° Hold pressure about 10 minutes after the sheath is removed Fluids to flush the dye; I&O; watch creatinine Report chest pain right away; help the patient the first time up · Post-cath complications to catch · Finding | Means | Action · Swelling/firm lump at the site, bleeding | Hematoma / bleeding | Apply firm pressure above the site — never massage it; notify the provider · One-sided severe back or flank pain + ↓ BP + ↑ HR | Retroperitoneal bleed — the artery was punctured through the back wall and blood is pooling behind the abdomen | Emergency — notify the provider immediately; CT confirms · Cool, pale, numb, or pulseless extremity | Arterial occlusion (clot) below the site | Notify the provider immediately · Rising creatinine, low urine output | Contrast-induced kidney injury | Fluids as ordered; monitor I&O and labs · Not part of post-cath care: checking the gag reflex (that's TEE). Not part of pre-cath care: lying flat for 6 hours (that's after the cath).

Causes, signs, and the care plan you'll use for dysrhythmias, HF — and anemia · Decreased cardiac output means the heart is not pumping enough blood to meet the body's needs. Dysrhythmias, heart failure, CAD, and anemia can all end here, and the goal of treating any dysrhythmia is to optimize cardiac output . · Causes · Problem | Examples | How CO drops · Rate too slow | Symptomatic sinus bradycardia, heart block; causes such as drug overdose (beta blockers, CCBs), electrolyte imbalance, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, hypoxia | Too few beats per minute (CO = HR × SV) · Rate too fast | SVT, A-fib with rapid rate, sinus tach from fever, pain, anxiety, dehydration, hemorrhage, sepsis, hyperthyroidism | No time to fill (↓ SV) and less coronary filling · Pump failure | Heart failure, MI/ischemia, valve problems | Weak or stiff muscle → ↓ SV · Loss of atrial kick | A-fib, A-flutter | Less ventricular filling → ↓ SV · Not enough volume | Hypovolemia — hemorrhage, dehydration, vomiting/diarrhea | ↓ preload → ↓ SV · Not enough oxygen carriers | Anemia | Tissues get less O₂ even when the heart pumps; the heart speeds up to compensate · Signs and symptoms — and why · When output falls, the body compensates (↑ HR, ↑ RR, vasoconstriction) and shunts blood to the brain, heart, and lungs and away from the skin, gut, and kidneys. The signs follow that logic. · Finding | Why it happens · ↑ Heart rate | Compensation — the heart tries to raise CO by beating faster · ↓ Blood pressure | Less blood being pushed into the arteries · Weak, thready peripheral pulses ; poor capillary refill | Low volume reaching the periphery; vasoconstriction · Cold, clammy, pale skin (on darker skin check gums/mucous membranes); diaphoresis | Blood shunted away from the skin; sympathetic response · ↑ Respiratory rate , shortness of breath | Compensation for poor tissue perfusion; fluid backing up into the lungs in HF · Low SpO₂ (may be normal at first) | Impaired gas exchange/perfusion — a normal sat early does not mean the patient is fine · Nausea/vomiting | Blood shunted away from the GI tract · ↓ Urine output | Less blood to the kidneys → prerenal acute kidney injury risk · Confusion → dizziness → syncope | Less blood to the brain; confusion/disorientation often comes first · Chest pain, fatigue , activity intolerance, lightheadedness | Heart muscle and tissues not getting enough O₂ · Cyanosis | Too little oxygenated blood reaching the tissues · Dependent edema (lower extremities) | A weak pump lets fluid back up and pool in the lowest parts of the body · Low output looks like shock in slow motion : fast heart, low BP, cold clammy skin, little urine, foggy brain. · Priority: assess first · Symptomatic of decreased CO → treat . Asymptomatic → monitor . Some patients live at an out-of-range baseline (an athlete with a HR of 50, chronic A-fib) without symptoms. · Look for and treat the cause first (bleeding, dehydration, hypoxia, electrolytes, fever, pain, medications) — meds second . · Some patients need long-term maintenance therapy (e.g., rate control and anticoagulation for A-fib). · Decreased cardiac output care plan · Intervention | Rationale · I&O ; keep the patient hydrated unless contraindicated (e.g., fluid overload) | Track kidney perfusion; restore volume (preload) if the patient is dry · Bedrest while acute , then increase activity as tolerated; change positions and rise from bed or chair slowly | Lowers O₂ demand and fall risk from dizziness/syncope · Cluster care with periods of rest ; calm environment | Saves the patient's energy and lowers O₂ demand · Fall precautions | Dizziness, lightheadedness, and syncope raise fall risk · Telemetry and a 12-lead ECG (the 12-lead sees the entire heart) | Identify the rhythm, ischemia, or injury behind the low output · Labs and diagnostics as ordered | Find the cause (troponin, BNP, electrolytes, H&H, coags) · O₂ PRN | Support tissue oxygenation when SpO₂ drops · Positioning: HOB up if BP is okay; if BP is low, flat with knees up / legs elevated (Trendelenburg is no longer indicated) | Moves blood pooled in the legs back into the central circulation · Goal: SBP above 90, MAP 65 or higher | Minimum pressure for adequate organ perfusion · Treat the cause and the symptoms | Fixing the cause fixes the output · NPO for certain tests (e.g., TEE) and when N/V or a procedure is planned | Aspiration risk; procedure prep · Avoid Valsalva if the HR is low (no straining/bearing down — stool softeners as ordered). The Valsalva maneuver = bearing down against a closed airway, like straining to have a bowel movement | Bearing down stimulates the vagus nerve → drops HR and BP. The same reflex can be used on purpose : the nurse may have the patient bear down when the BP is really high , and as a vagal maneuver to slow a fast rhythm such as stable SVT. · MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3. Example: BP 84/48 → (84 + 96) ÷ 3 = 60 → below 65 = organs are under-perfused. · When to call the provider · SBP below 90 or MAP below 65 · New or worsening confusion, dizziness, or syncope · Urine output below about 30 mL/hr · New chest pain, new dysrhythmia, or a HR that is very slow or very fast with symptoms · Falling SpO₂ or increasing shortness of breath despite O₂ · Cold, mottled extremities or weakening pulses · The same plan works for anemia · Anemia means too few RBCs (or too little hemoglobin) to carry O₂, so the patient looks just like someone with decreased cardiac output — fatigue, weakness, pallor, cold, dizziness, SOB, tachycardia, low BP. This care plan is the core of anemia nursing care , plus activities spaced out with rest periods, fall precautions, diet, and supplements. · Cause first, meds second. Symptomatic → treat; asymptomatic → monitor. Keep the SBP above 90 and the MAP at 65 or higher.

Graph paper, waves, the 6 questions, and artifact · The graph paper · Every rhythm strip is printed on the same grid, so time can be measured by counting boxes. Little box = 0.04 seconds. Big box (5 little boxes) = 0.20 seconds. Five big boxes = 1 second, so 30 big boxes = a 6-second strip — the standard length used for rhythm checks. · Unit | Time | Why it matters · 1 little box | 0.04 s | Measures PR and QRS precisely · 1 big box (5 little) | 0.20 s | Normal PR is less than one big box; a normal QRS fits well inside one · 5 big boxes | 1 second | Marked at the top of many strips · 30 big boxes | 6 seconds | Standard strip — count QRS × 10 for HR · Waves and intervals — what each one means · The ECG records electrical activity. The mechanical squeeze follows the electricity, which is why you always confirm a rhythm with a pulse and an assessment. · Part | Electrical event | Normal · P wave | SA node fires → atrial depolarization (atria contract) | Upright, rounded, one before every QRS · PR interval | Start of P to start of QRS: impulse travels through the atria and is briefly held at the AV node | 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 little boxes; less than one big box) · QRS complex | Ventricular depolarization (ventricles contract); atrial repolarization is hidden inside it | 0.06–0.10 s , narrow; 0.12 s or more = wide · ST segment | End of QRS to start of T: ventricles beginning to recover | Flat, at the baseline; elevation or depression can mean ischemia/injury · T wave | Ventricular repolarization (resetting/recovery) | Upright, rounded, after every QRS · ST-segment elevation — STEMI · When the ST segment is raised above the baseline , think ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) — heart muscle is being injured right now. The underlying rhythm may look normal, so always look at the ST segment, not just the rate and P waves. · Emergency — stay with the patient, assess chest pain and vitals, notify the provider immediately · 12-lead ECG to confirm; troponin · MONA /medications per protocol · Reperfusion: thrombolytic or cardiac cath (management detail is NUR 211) · ST up = heart muscle hurting. A "normal-looking" rhythm with a raised ST segment is still an emergency. · The 6 questions — ask them in order, every time · 1. Rate? Count the QRS complexes in the 6-second strip × 10. · 2. Regular? Is the distance from R to R the same across the strip? (Measure with calipers or mark a paper edge.) · 3. P wave? Is there one upright P before every QRS? If yes, the rhythm starts in the SA node and you may use the word “sinus.” · 4. QRS complex? Present after every P? Narrow (0.06–0.10 s, fits inside a big box)? · 5. T wave? Present after every QRS? · 6. PR interval? 0.12–0.20 s (less than one big box) and the same every beat? · “A P for every QRS” = sinus. If every answer is “yes/normal,” it's normal sinus rhythm. If only the rate is off, it's sinus brady or sinus tach. If the P waves or baseline are the problem → atrial rhythm. If the QRS is the problem → ventricular rhythm. · Calculating heart rate · Use the 6-second method : count every QRS complex in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10. Example: 8 QRS complexes × 10 = 80 bpm . This works for regular and irregular rhythms, so it is the go-to method for A-fib. · Intrinsic pacemakers — the backup system · The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker. If it fails, a lower site takes over at a slower built-in rate. The lower the pacemaker site, the slower and less reliable the rhythm. · Pacemaker site | Intrinsic rate | What you see · SA node | 60–100 | Normal P before each narrow QRS · AV node / junction | 40–60 | Narrow QRS, P absent, inverted, or hidden · Ventricles (Purkinje fibers) | 20–40 | Wide, bizarre QRS, no P · Normal values to memorize · Heart rate: 60–100 (below 60 = brady, above 100 = tachy) · PR interval: 0.12–0.20 s · QRS: 0.06–0.10 s ; 0.12 s or more = wide (ventricular origin or abnormal conduction) · Rhythm: regular R-to-R · Pause · A pause is a gap on the strip where an expected beat is missing — for example, the pause after a PVC, or a sinus pause when the SA node briefly fails to fire. Short pauses may cause no symptoms; long pauses drop cardiac output and can cause dizziness or syncope → assess the patient and report them. · Lead placement basics · Most bedside monitors use a 3- or 5-lead system. A 12-lead ECG uses 10 electrodes to look at the heart from 12 angles at once — it is ordered to look for ischemia or damage all around the heart (for example, with chest pain). · Electrode (5-lead) | Placement · White | Right upper chest, 2nd intercostal space (below the clavicle) · Black | Left upper chest, 2nd intercostal space (below the clavicle) · Green | Right lower chest/abdomen · Red | Left lower chest/abdomen · Brown | Chest lead — often V1 (4th intercostal space, right of the sternum) · “White on the right, smoke over fire.” White goes upper right; black (smoke) sits above red (fire) on the left; “snow over grass” — white above green on the right; and chocolate (brown) goes close to the heart. · Artifact — a false reading · Artifact is distorted, extra squiggles on the monitor that do not come from the heart. It can look like V-fib or V-tach. Always look at the patient, not the monitor — a patient talking to you with a strong pulse is not in V-fib. · Cause | Fix · Sweaty/oily skin | Dry the skin (wash with soap and water); apply new electrodes · Chest hair | Clip (or shave) the area so the electrode lies flat · Dried-out electrode gel | Replace the electrodes · Loose or disconnected lead | Reattach/secure the lead and wire · Movement, shivering, tremors, big deep breaths, patient handling the wires | Reposition, warm the patient, ask them to lie still; recheck the strip · Monitor alarm for “V-fib”? Check the patient first — responsive and has a pulse = look for artifact. Unresponsive and pulseless = it's real; call for help and start CPR.

NSR, sinus brady, sinus tach — everything normal except (maybe) the rate · The sinus family · All three sinus rhythms start in the SA node, so all three have a P wave before every QRS , a normal PR, a narrow QRS, and a T after every QRS. The only thing that changes is the rate. · Rule | NSR | Sinus bradycardia | Sinus tachycardia · Rate | 60–100 | Below 60 | Above 100 (usually 100–150) · Regular? | Yes | Yes | Yes · P wave | One before every QRS | One before every QRS | One before every QRS (may run into the T at fast rates) · PR interval | 0.12–0.20 s | 0.12–0.20 s | 0.12–0.20 s · QRS | Narrow, 0.06–0.10 s | Narrow | Narrow · T wave | After every QRS | After every QRS | After every QRS · Sinus bradycardia · Causes — some are normal, some are dangerous: · Expected/benign: well-conditioned athletes, sleep · Medications: beta blockers, calcium channel blockers (diltiazem), digoxin, amiodarone · Vagal stimulation: vomiting, bearing down/straining (Valsalva), suctioning, severe pain · Low metabolic states: hypothermia, hypothyroidism · Hypoxia — a common cause of unstable, symptomatic bradycardia · Heart disease: MI (especially inferior wall), SA node dysfunction · Overdose (for example beta blocker, CCB, or opioid), increased intracranial pressure, electrolyte imbalance · Sinus tachycardia · Sinus tach is almost always the body responding to something . Find the trigger: · Pain, anxiety, fear, stress · Fever /hyperthermia, infection, sepsis · Low volume: dehydration, hemorrhage, hypovolemic shock · Anemia and hypoxia (heart speeds up to deliver more O₂) · Hyperthyroidism · Stimulants: caffeine, nicotine, cocaine/amphetamines; medications such as atropine or epinephrine · Heart failure, exercise, electrolyte imbalance · Sinus tach is a symptom, not a disease . Treat the cause: pain → analgesic, fever → antipyretic, hemorrhage/dehydration → fluids or blood, anxiety → reassurance. Slowing the heart with a drug while the patient is bleeding removes their compensation. · Is the patient symptomatic? (signs of decreased cardiac output) · A rate that is too slow means less blood pumped each minute. A rate that is too fast shortens filling time, so each beat pumps less. Either way, watch for decreased cardiac output : · ↓ BP, dizziness, syncope, confusion/change in mental status (often first) · Chest pain/angina, shortness of breath, ↑ RR · Weak, thready pulses; poor cap refill; cool, clammy, pale skin; diaphoresis · ↓ urine output; nausea/vomiting · Low SpO₂ (may be normal at first) · Treatment · Rhythm | Asymptomatic | Symptomatic · NSR | No treatment | — · Sinus brady | Monitor (an athlete with HR 50 and no symptoms needs nothing) | Treat the cause (hold the beta blocker as ordered, warm the patient, give O₂ for hypoxia, stop vagal stimulation); if HR typically below 50 with symptoms → atropine 1 mg IV push q3–5 min, max 3 mg → if ineffective, transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine (5–20 mcg/kg/min) or epinephrine (2–10 mcg/min) drip → transvenous pacing/expert consult · Sinus tach | Treat the cause ; monitor | Treat the cause (fluids, blood, analgesia, antipyretic, O₂, treat infection/thyroid); rate-control drugs are not the first answer · Atropine = brady drug. IV push, short-acting, blocks the vagus nerve's slowing effect so the SA node speeds up. Dopamine and epinephrine drips are vasopressors — titrated, large vein/central line, vesicants.

SVT, A-fib, A-flutter — a problem with the P waves or baseline · The big picture · Atrial rhythms are a problem with the P waves or the baseline . The QRS is usually narrow , because the ventricles still conduct normally. These rhythms are more stable than ventricular rhythms — many people live with them for years — but they can drop cardiac output and cause clots. Because there is no normal P before every QRS, you cannot use the word “sinus.” · Atrial rhythms: “you can live with these.” Ventricular rhythms: the ones that can kill. Rule of thumb — narrow QRS = above the ventricles = usually more stable. · Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) · Rate 150–250 ; regular · P waves not seen — typically lost in the T waves once the rate reaches about 160; PR not measurable · Narrow QRS; T waves present · Often starts and stops suddenly (paroxysmal) · Triggers: caffeine, stimulants, stress, fatigue, hyperthyroidism, hypoxia, heart disease · S/S: palpitations, racing heart, anxiety, dizziness, chest pain, SOB; ↓ CO because the ventricles don't have time to fill · Atrial fibrillation (A-fib) · Hundreds of chaotic impulses make the atria quiver instead of contract . The AV node lets some through at random, so the ventricular rhythm is irregularly irregular . Rate may be controlled (60–100) or fast (above 100, called A-fib with rapid ventricular response, RVR). · A-fib “gold standard”: irregular + no discernible P waves + fibrillating (wavy) baseline + narrow QRS. · Lost atrial kick: the atria normally top off the ventricles before each beat; without it, cardiac output drops (worse with a fast rate). · Clots/stroke: blood pools in the quivering atria → clots form → can travel to the brain. A-fib is a major cause of embolic stroke. · Causes/risk: hypertension, CAD/MI, heart failure, valve disease, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, older age, after cardiac surgery, sleep apnea. · Common in HF; many patients live with chronic A-fib on maintenance meds. · Atrial flutter (A-flutter) · Sawtooth flutter waves instead of P waves; one irritable spot fires rapidly (atrial rate about 250–400) · Ventricular rhythm regular or irregular depending on how many flutter waves conduct (2:1, 3:1, 4:1) · Narrow QRS; PR not measurable · “Sister of A-fib”: atria don't fully contract → pooling → clot risk ; treated much like A-fib · Comparing the three · Feature | SVT | A-fib | A-flutter · Rate | 150–250 | Varies — controlled 60–100 or RVR above 100 | Varies — depends on the conduction ratio · Regular? | Regular | Irregularly irregular | Often regular; can be irregular · P waves | Hidden in T waves | None — wavy fibrillating baseline | None — sawtooth flutter waves · QRS | Narrow | Narrow | Narrow · Main danger | ↓ CO from fast rate | ↓ CO (lost atrial kick) + clots/stroke | ↓ CO + clots/stroke · First-line approach (stable) | Vagal maneuver → adenosine | Rate control + anticoagulation | Rate control + anticoagulation · Treatment · Always start with the patient: symptomatic or not? Look for and treat the cause (caffeine, hypoxia, thyroid, electrolytes, dehydration). Unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, acute HF) → synchronized cardioversion . · Rhythm | Stable patient | Unstable patient · SVT | 1. Vagal maneuver (bear down as if having a bowel movement) 2. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push + 20 mL NS flush; may repeat with 12 mg 3. Beta blocker or CCB (diltiazem) | Synchronized cardioversion · A-fib / A-flutter | Rate control: beta blocker (metoprolol) or CCB (diltiazem) Rhythm control: amiodarone Anticoagulation: heparin, warfarin (INR 2–3), or a DOAC Elective cardioversion after TEE | Synchronized cardioversion · Adenosine: “reboots” the heart — brief asystole for a few seconds is expected; crash cart and provider at the bedside; give through an antecubital or central line; push fast and flush (very short half-life). · A-fib longer than 48 hours (or unknown) → anticoagulate first and/or do a TEE to rule out an atrial clot before cardioversion — a shock can knock a clot loose → aorta → brain = stroke. · Maintenance therapy is common: long-term rate control and anticoagulation; bleeding precautions and teaching. · A-fib = think anticoagulant. Before any cardioversion of A-fib/flutter ask: “How long? Anticoagulated? TEE done?”

A problem with the QRS — recognize them and know which ones kill · The big picture · Ventricular rhythms are a problem with the QRS . When an impulse starts in the ventricles it spreads slowly, cell to cell, so the QRS is wide (0.12 s or more) and bizarre with no P wave in front. These rhythms are lethal or potentially lethal . The goal is to recognize them and know the big-picture response; detailed code management comes later, in Medical Emergencies. · PVCs — premature ventricular contractions · A PVC is an early, wide, bizarre beat with no P wave, usually followed by a pause. The patient may feel a “skipped beat.” Name the underlying rhythm first, then the PVCs (for example, “NSR with unifocal PVCs”). Causes include caffeine, stress, nicotine, hypoxia, low K⁺ or Mg²⁺ , MI/ischemia, heart failure, and digoxin toxicity. · Type | What you see | Concern level · Unifocal | All PVCs the same shape | Occasional ones can be normal (caffeine, stress); watch frequency · Multifocal | PVCs of different shapes | Concerning — more irritable ventricles · Couplet | 2 PVCs in a row | Dangerous — potentially lethal · Run (3 or more in a row) | 3+ PVCs back-to-back | = a run of V-tach ; potentially lethal · R on T | PVC falls on the T wave | Potentially lethal — can trigger V-tach/V-fib · PVCs getting more frequent, multifocal, paired, or landing on the T = irritable ventricles. Check the patient, check K⁺ and Mg²⁺, check O₂, and notify the provider. · Ventricular tachycardia (V-tach, VT) · Rate usually 100–200 ; regular; wide, bizarre QRS ; no visible P waves; no measurable PR · Causes: MI/ischemia, inflammation, trauma, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte imbalance (K⁺, Mg²⁺) · VT with a pulse: the patient may be awake but often has signs of ↓ CO — potentially lethal ; can deteriorate at any moment · Pulseless VT: no cardiac output — lethal ; treated like V-fib (CPR + defibrillation) · Torsades de pointes · “Twisting of the points.” A polymorphic VT linked to a prolonged QT interval and low magnesium (also low K⁺; QT-prolonging drugs). It quickly becomes pulseless. Big-picture treatment: IV magnesium . · Torsades = Twisted = magnesium. Think “Mg twists it back.” · Ventricular fibrillation (V-fib, VF) · The ventricles quiver instead of pumping: no pulse, no BP, no cardiac output ; the patient is unresponsive. Most common rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest. Lethal — immediate CPR and defibrillation . · Asystole · “Flatline”: no electrical activity, no pulse — lethal · Check the patient (a loose lead also gives a flat line) and confirm in a second lead · Not shockable — CPR and epinephrine ; look for a reversible cause · Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) · The monitor shows organized electrical activity — the strip can look like a near-normal rhythm — but the patient has NO pulse . The electricity is there, but the heart isn't pumping, so there is no cardiac output. · Lethal — the patient is unresponsive and pulseless even though the monitor looks organized · Not shockable — CPR + epinephrine (same as asystole) · Treat the cause — look for what stopped the pump (for example, severe blood loss, hypoxia, electrolyte problems) · PEA = the monitor lies. A rhythm on the screen means nothing without a pulse — always check the patient. · Big-picture response to a lethal rhythm · Check the patient — responsive? breathing? pulse? · Call for help — call the code, get the crash cart/defibrillator · Start CPR if there is no pulse · Shock or not? V-fib and pulseless VT = shockable → defibrillate . Asystole and PEA = not shockable → CPR + epinephrine · When in doubt, give epinephrine ; torsades → magnesium · Lethal vs non-lethal — every rhythm at a glance · Category | Rhythms | Response · Lethal (no cardiac output) | V-fib , pulseless V-tach , asystole , PEA ; torsades (quickly becomes pulseless) | Check pulse → call code → CPR → defibrillate if shockable (VF, pulseless VT) → epinephrine (asystole and PEA are not shockable); torsades → magnesium · Potentially lethal (can turn lethal fast) | V-tach with a pulse , R on T , runs of PVCs (3+), couplets , multifocal PVCs; heart block with ↓ CO | Assess, notify provider immediately, stay with the patient, crash cart nearby; unstable VT with a pulse → synchronized cardioversion · Non-lethal — treat if symptomatic | Sinus brady, sinus tach, SVT, A-fib, A-flutter; occasional unifocal PVCs | Assess for ↓ CO; treat the cause; meds; synchronized cardioversion or pacing if unstable · Emergency (heart muscle injury, any rhythm) | STEMI — ST-segment elevation | Notify immediately, 12-lead ECG, MONA/meds per protocol → thrombolytic or cath (NUR 211) · Normal | Normal sinus rhythm | None · Dying rhythm | Agonal rhythm | Often DNR / comfort care; if full code → treat as pulseless · Not a rhythm | Artifact | Assess the patient; fix the leads/skin · Lethal = no cardiac output. Your first move is never the monitor — it's the patient and the pulse .

Spot the spike, understand the block, recognize a dying heart · Pacemakers — what they are for · A pacemaker sends an electrical impulse to make the heart beat when its own system is too slow . Pacemakers are for bradycardia (including heart block). On the strip each impulse shows as a spike — a thin, straight up-and-down line. · Reading the spike · Type | Where the spike is | What follows · Atrial paced | Spike before the P wave | P wave, then the patient's own narrow QRS · Ventricular paced | Spike before the QRS | Wide QRS ; no P wave after the spike · Dual / AV paced | Two spikes : one before the P, one before the QRS | P wave, then wide QRS · Every spike should be followed by a wave (P or QRS) — that means the pacer captured . · A spike with nothing after it = possible malfunction → assess the patient and notify the provider (troubleshooting is NUR 211). · A spike should never land on the T wave — that creates an R on T risk (V-tach/V-fib). · Spike → P = atrial. Spike → wide QRS = ventricular. Two spikes = dual. Spike on a T = danger. · Temporary vs permanent · Type | How | When · Transcutaneous (temporary) | Large pads on the chest (front and back); machine set to a rate, output turned up until each spike captures a beat; painful — sedation/analgesia | Emergency for symptomatic bradycardia when atropine fails · Transvenous (temporary) | Pacing wire threaded through a vein into the right heart (cath lab/bedside) | Bridge until the cause resolves or a permanent device is placed · Permanent | Implanted generator under the skin of the upper chest; leads threaded through a vein into the right atrium and/or right ventricle | Chronic bradycardia/heart block; works on demand — fires only when the heart's own rate drops below the set rate · Heart block — basic understanding · A problem with the PR interval — the impulse is delayed or blocked at the AV node · PR may be long (more than one big box, 0.20 s) or QRS complexes are dropped · Key clue: more P waves than QRS complexes · Fewer ventricular beats → bradycardia and ↓ cardiac output (dizziness, syncope, hypotension, confusion) · Avoid beta blockers and calcium channel blockers — they slow AV conduction further; in general give these drugs slowly, because they can cause a block · Symptomatic → treat like bradycardia (atropine, pacing); may need a permanent pacemaker · More P's than QRS's = block. The atria are talking, but the message isn't getting through to the ventricles. · Agonal rhythm · A dying heart : very slow, wide, irregular complexes from the ventricles; little or no cardiac output · Often seen at the end of life in patients with a DNR /comfort-care order — support the patient and family · Full-code patient → check for a pulse and respond as a lethal rhythm (CPR, epinephrine)

Assess first, cause second, meds and electricity after · The approach · Goal: optimize cardiac output . · Priority: assess, assess, assess. Symptomatic of ↓ CO → treat. Not symptomatic → monitor (some people live with an out-of-range baseline, such as chronic A-fib). · Look for the cause first (hypoxia, electrolytes, pain, fever, bleeding, drugs, thyroid) and treat it; meds are second . · Maintenance: is long-term therapy needed? (for example, rate control and anticoagulation for A-fib). · Treat the patient , not the monitor. A number on the screen alone is never the reason to act. · Bradycardia pathway (HR typically below 50 and symptomatic) · 1. Assess; identify and treat the cause; O₂ if hypoxemic; cardiac monitor, IV access, 12-lead ECG · 2. Atropine 1 mg IV push , repeat every 3–5 minutes, max 3 mg · 3. If atropine doesn't work: transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine drip 5–20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine drip 2–10 mcg/min · 4. Expert consult; transvenous pacing ; permanent pacemaker if needed · Tachycardia pathway (HR typically 150 or more) · 1. Assess; treat the cause; O₂ if needed; monitor, IV, 12-lead ECG · 2. Unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, acute HF, shock) → synchronized cardioversion · 3. Stable, narrow, regular (SVT) → vagal maneuver (bear down) · 4. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push + 20 mL NS flush ; if no conversion, 12 mg · 5. Beta blocker or CCB (diltiazem) for rate control; antiarrhythmic ( amiodarone ; lidocaine for ventricular rhythms only) as ordered; expert consult · Electrical options · Match the electricity to the problem: brady → pacing , tachy with a pulse → synchronized cardioversion , lethal → defibrillation . · Feature | Pacing | Synchronized cardioversion | Defibrillation · Used for | Symptomatic bradycardia / heart block | Tachydysrhythmias WITH a pulse (unstable SVT, A-fib, A-flutter, VT with a pulse) | V-fib, pulseless VT — no cardiac output · Synced? | — | Yes — SYNC button times the shock to the R wave (avoids the T wave) | No — unsynchronized · Patient awake? | Usually; sedate/medicate for pain with transcutaneous | Usually awake → sedated | Unconscious , pulseless · Consent? | Yes when time allows | Yes — elective or urgent | No — emergency · Energy | Low (set rate and output) | Lower | Higher · Energy (reference) | — | 50–200 joules | Begins at 200 joules, up to 360 joules · Synchronized cardioversion — nursing care · Informed consent (unless emergent); NPO if elective · A-fib/flutter: confirm anticoagulation status; TEE to rule out a clot, especially if A-fib has lasted longer than 48 hours · IV access, O₂ and suction ready, crash cart at the bedside; conscious sedation /analgesia · Pads in place; press SYNC and confirm the marker on each R wave (re-press SYNC if another shock is needed) · “I'm clear, you're clear, everyone's clear” — no one touching the patient or bed; O₂ away from the chest · After: monitor rhythm, vitals, airway/LOC until sedation wears off, skin under the pads (burns); continue anticoagulation as ordered · Defibrillation basics · Emergency for pulseless VT/V-fib — no consent, no sync · Minimize interruptions in CPR; resume compressions immediately after the shock · Stand clear and call it out loud; move O₂ away from the chest (fire risk) · Pads placed correctly, not over a permanent pacemaker or medication patch (remove patches) · Beware the look-alike “A” drugs · Drug | Used for | Key nursing points · Atropine | Bradycardia (symptomatic) | 1 mg IV push q3–5 min, max 3 mg; blocks vagal slowing; short-acting · Adenosine | SVT (stable, narrow, regular) | 6 mg rapid IV push + 20 mL flush, then 12 mg; brief asystole expected; AC/central line; crash cart nearby · Amiodarone | Antiarrhythmic — A-fib rhythm control, ventricular rhythms | IV drip then PO; watch for bradycardia/hypotension, QT prolongation; long-term: lung, liver, thyroid toxicity, photosensitivity · Atropine = A-brady-up. Adenosine = A-reboot. Amiodarone = A-antiarrhythmic. Read the label twice — giving the wrong “A” drug can be deadly. · Lethal rhythm response · Check the pulse (and the patient) · Start CPR and call the code · To shock or not to shock: V-fib/pulseless VT → defibrillate; asystole or PEA → no shock · When in doubt, give epinephrine ; torsades → magnesium · Full code management is covered in Medical Emergencies

Plaque, narrowing, and the road from ischemia to infarction · What CAD is · Coronary artery disease (CAD) is narrowing of the coronary arteries , most often from atherosclerosis . The coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself, so when they narrow, the myocardium does not get the oxygen it needs. CAD is a "narrowing" problem — like hypertension and nephrosclerosis — and its treatment centers on diet, exercise, and medications that keep the vessels open. · How the plaque forms · Endothelial injury (high BP, smoking, high blood sugar, high LDL) lets LDL cholesterol move into the artery wall. · Inflammatory cells swallow the LDL; smooth muscle cells grow a fibrous cap over a fatty core → an atheroma (plaque) that bulges into the lumen and narrows it. · Stable plaque has a thick cap. Vulnerable (unstable) plaque has a thin cap and active inflammation — it can rupture . · A ruptured plaque attracts platelets → thrombus → sudden blockage = acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or MI). · Plaques like to form where arteries branch (turbulent flow). Coronary vasospasm or profound hypotension can also cut off flow. · Ischemia → injury → infarction · Stage | What is happening | Reversible? · Ischemia | O₂ supply does not meet O₂ demand; cells switch to anaerobic metabolism → chest pain (angina) | Yes — restore flow or lower demand and the cells recover · Injury | Ischemia is prolonged or severe; cells are damaged but not yet dead | Still salvageable if flow returns quickly · Infarction | Cells die (necrosis) and are replaced by scar tissue that does not contract | No — dead muscle is permanent; troponin is released · Think "supply vs. demand." Every CAD intervention either increases supply (open the vessel: nitroglycerin, stents, antiplatelets) or decreases demand (rest, beta blockers, treat pain and anxiety). · Risk factors · Nonmodifiable (can't change) | Modifiable (can change) · Age (men above 45, women above 55) | Hyperlipidemia (high LDL, low HDL) · Sex/gender (men develop CAD earlier; women's risk rises after menopause) | Tobacco use (including secondhand smoke) · Family history / genetics (first-degree relative with early CVD; inherited high LDL) | Hypertension · Race/ethnicity (higher incidence in African Americans) | Diabetes and metabolic syndrome · History of premature menopause or pregnancy disorders such as preeclampsia | Obesity , physical inactivity , poor diet, stress · — | Chronic inflammatory conditions (RA, lupus, HIV) and chronic kidney disease · The more risk factors a person has, the greater the chance of CAD. Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, carotid artery disease, and abdominal aortic aneurysm are CAD risk equivalents — these patients carry the same risk for a cardiac event as someone who already has CAD. · How common these risks are · Many Americans have risk factors for cardiovascular disease: · Risk factor | Share of Americans · Obesity | 36% · Physical inactivity | 30% · High blood pressure | 29% · Cigarette smoking | 17% · High cholesterol | 12% · Diabetes | 9% · Metabolic syndrome · A cluster that sharply raises cardiovascular risk. It is diagnosed when 3 of these 5 are present: · Large waist (abdominal obesity) · High triglycerides (or on treatment for them) · Low HDL (or on treatment) · High blood pressure (130/80 or higher, or on treatment) · High fasting glucose (100 mg/dL or higher, or on treatment) · Metabolic syndrome = the "big belly + bad numbers" picture: waist, triglycerides, HDL, BP, glucose. Many people with type 2 diabetes fit it. · Complications of CAD · Myocardial infarction (MI) — a clot completely blocks a narrowed artery. · Heart failure — scarred or chronically ischemic muscle can't pump well. · Dysrhythmias — ischemic muscle is electrically irritable (PVCs, V-tach, V-fib); sudden cardiac death is possible. · A stroke is not a complication of CAD — it is a complication of clots or narrowing in the vessels of the brain. · Diagnostics · Test | What it shows / nursing point · 12-lead ECG | Looks at the whole heart at once for ischemia or injury; obtain within 10 minutes of chest pain. A normal ECG does not rule out CAD. · Troponin (with CK-MB) | Gold standard for heart muscle damage; normally ~0. Rises late, so it is drawn on arrival and repeated. · Lipid panel | Total cholesterol below 200; LDL below 100 with CAD (below 130 otherwise); HDL above 40–60 is protective; triglycerides below 150. · Stress test | Treadmill, or medication-based (dipyridamole, adenosine, dobutamine) if the patient can't walk. NPO, hold beta blockers as ordered. Stop for chest pain, dysrhythmia, SOB, pallor, diaphoresis, BP too high/low, or O₂ sat below 90%. · Echocardiogram | Ultrasound of wall motion, valves, wall thickness, and ejection fraction. · Coronary angiogram / cardiac cath | Dye shows exactly where the arteries are blocked and how well the heart is perfused; stents can be placed. Check contrast allergy and kidney function first. · Prevention & lifestyle · Heart-healthy diet — low saturated fat and cholesterol (DASH, AHA, or Mediterranean style): fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish; limit red meat, sweets, sugary drinks, and sodium. Read labels for saturated fat, trans fat, cholesterol, and fiber. · Exercise — about 150 minutes a week of moderate activity plus strengthening 2 days a week. Start small; exercise at a pace where you can still talk. Stop for chest pain, unusual SOB, dizziness, or nausea. · Smoking cessation — nicotine raises HR and BP, constricts coronary arteries, and carbon monoxide steals O₂ from hemoglobin. Risk drops within the first year of quitting. · Control BP (goal below 130/80), diabetes , and lipids . · Statins lower LDL when diet alone isn't enough — teach to report muscle pain or dark urine (rhabdomyolysis). · Weight loss if needed and stress reduction. · HDL = H appy/ H ealthy (higher is better). LDL = L ousy (lower is better).

Stable vs. unstable, NTG rules, MONA, and the Mr. Bob case · What angina is · Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by myocardial ischemia — the heart's O₂ demand is higher than what the narrowed coronary arteries can supply. When demand rises, a blocked artery can't increase its flow, so ischemia results. Patients describe it as pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness, choking, or a viselike feeling rather than sharp pain — usually behind the sternum , poorly localized, and often spreading to the neck, jaw, shoulders, or inner arms (usually the left). · What triggers it · Trigger | Why it causes ischemia · Physical exertion | Raises myocardial O₂ demand · Cold exposure | Vasoconstriction and ↑ BP → ↑ O₂ demand · Heavy meal | Blood shifts to the gut for digestion, leaving less for the heart muscle · Stress or strong emotion | Catecholamines ↑ BP, HR, and the heart's workload · Pain may come with apprehension or a feeling of impending death , weakness or numbness in the arms, wrists, and hands, SOB, pallor, diaphoresis, dizziness, and nausea or vomiting. The hallmark of angina: it subsides with rest or nitroglycerin . Unstable angina is not closely tied to these triggers. · Types of angina · Type | Pattern | Relieved by | What it means · Stable | Predictable and consistent — with exertion, emotional stress, cold, or a heavy meal; short | Rest + NTG | Fixed plaque; manage with meds and risk-factor control · Unstable (preinfarction, crescendo) | At rest , new, or increasing in frequency and severity | Not reliably relieved by rest/NTG | Emergency — needs medical intervention; part of acute coronary syndrome; can progress to MI · Intractable (refractory) | Severe, incapacitating chest pain | Hard to control | Disabling despite treatment · Variant (Prinzmetal) | Pain at rest with reversible ST elevation ; not tied to exertion | Treated with calcium channel blockers (and nitrates) | Coronary artery spasm · Silent ischemia | No pain , but objective evidence of ischemia (e.g., ECG changes on a stress test) | — | Easy to miss — think of it in older adults and diabetics · Stable = predictable. Unstable = un predictable, at rest, or un relieved → treat it like an MI until proven otherwise. · Assessing chest pain — PQRST · Letter | Ask | Typical angina answer · P — Provokes / Palliates | What brings it on? What makes it better? | Exertion, stress, cold, big meal; better with rest or NTG · Q — Quality | What does it feel like? | Pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness · R — Region / Radiation | Where is it? Does it spread? | Substernal or left chest; may spread to the left arm, jaw, neck, back, or epigastric area · S — Severity / Symptoms | Rate it 0–10. Anything else with it? | SOB, nausea, diaphoresis, palpitations, lightheadedness · T — Timing | When did it start? How long does it last? | Angina usually lasts 5–15 minutes ; pain lasting more than 15 minutes suggests ACS (unstable angina or MI) · Questions to ask during an episode · "Where is the pain? Can you point to it?" and "Can you feel it anywhere else?" · "How would you describe the pain?" · "Is it like the pain you had before?" — a change may mean the disease is worsening or there is a different cause. · "Can you rate it from 0 to 10?" · "When did it begin?" and "How long does it last?" · "What brings it on?" and "What helps it go away?" · "Do you have any other symptoms with the pain?" · Atypical presentations · Not everyone has classic crushing chest pain. Ischemia may show up as: · Women — indigestion, nausea, palpitations, numbness, fatigue, SOB; they tend to wait longer to seek care. · Older adults — pain transmission is diminished with aging, so dyspnea is often the presenting symptom ; confusion, weakness, or fainting may replace chest pain, and some have no symptoms at all (silent CAD) . Teach them to treat chest pain–like symptoms such as weakness as a signal to rest or take their prescribed medication . Angina meds are given cautiously (more adverse reactions). · Diabetics — nerve damage (autonomic neuropathy) dulls pain perception; SOB or fatigue may be the only clue. · Anyone — SOB, indigestion or a choking feeling, weakness, numbness or tingling in the upper extremities, a fluttering heartbeat. Lower abdominal pain is not a typical angina symptom. · Angina vs. ACS · Feature | Stable angina (ischemia) | ACS (unstable angina or MI) · Duration | Usually 5–15 minutes | More than 15 minutes · Brought on by | Exertion, emotional upset, a large meal, temperature extremes | Can occur at rest or during sleep · Relief | Rest, NTG, oxygen | Not relieved by rest or 3 NTG · Muscle damage | None — reversible | MI: permanent, troponin rises (unstable angina: troponin stays normal) · Other S/S | May be mild | Often diaphoresis, nausea, SOB, palpitations, unusual fatigue, sense of doom · The ACS spectrum: unstable angina vs NSTEMI vs STEMI · Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) covers three conditions. The 12-lead ECG and troponin tell them apart. ·  | Unstable angina | NSTEMI | STEMI · What's happening | Ischemia — the artery is narrowed or partly blocked; no muscle death | Artery partly blocked → some heart muscle dies (not the full wall thickness) | Artery completely blocked → full-thickness heart muscle death · 12-lead ECG | Normal, or ST depression / T-wave inversion | ST depression and/or T-wave inversion — no ST elevation | ST elevation (the ST segment sits above the baseline) · Troponin | Normal | Elevated | Elevated · Urgency | Emergency — admit, heparin, antiplatelets, angiogram | Emergency — heparin, antiplatelets, cath | Most urgent — open the artery fast: cath/PCI or a thrombolytic ("time is muscle") · Troponin normal → unstable angina. Troponin up + no ST elevation → NSTEMI. Troponin up + ST elevation → STEMI. Because troponin rises late, it's drawn on arrival and repeated. Full MI management is NUR 211 content. · Treating an angina episode · Step | Nursing action | Why · 1 | Stop all activity ; sit or rest in bed in semi-Fowler's | Lowers the O₂ needs of the ischemic heart muscle · 2 | Assess the angina — is it the same as the patient's usual pain? | A change may mean worsening disease or a different cause · 3 | Vital signs ; watch for respiratory distress | Baseline before NTG · 4 | 12-lead ECG (in the hospital) | Looks for ST-segment and T-wave changes · 5 | NTG SL — repeat every 5 minutes if pain is unchanged or still present, up to 3 doses ; check BP and HR each time | Relieves ischemia; watch for hypotension · 6 | Oxygen , usually 2 L/min by nasal cannula , especially if RR is up or SpO₂ is down | Supports O₂ supply · 7 | Pain significant and continuing → evaluate for MI ; may move to a higher level of care | Unrelieved pain = possible ACS · Nitroglycerin (NTG) basics · Sit down and stop the activity, then place 1 tablet under the tongue (or in the cheek pouch) or use 1 spray; relief ideally comes within about 3 minutes. · Let the SL tablet dissolve under the tongue — nothing to drink until it has dissolved. · Repeat every 5 minutes as needed — maximum 3 doses . · Pain not relieved after 3 doses (15 minutes) → call 911. · Expected: throbbing headache , flushing, dizziness, and reflex tachycardia . The danger is hypotension — that's why the patient sits first. · Never take with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — severe hypotension. · Carry it at all times in the original capped dark glass bottle, and take it before an activity known to cause angina. · NTG "1-5-3" : 1 tab, every 5 minutes, max 3 — then 911. And always sit before you take it. · If the pain isn't relieved: acute chest pain priorities · Assess first — PQRST, vital signs, SpO₂; have the patient sit or rest to lower O₂ demand. · 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival or of the complaint. · MONA (not a priority order): M orphine 2–4 mg IV push for pain unrelieved by NTG, O xygen (often 2 L/min by nasal cannula; needed if SpO₂ is low or breathing is labored), N itroglycerin, A spirin 325 mg chewed (faster antiplatelet effect). Metoprolol is also given (beta blocker → ↓ O₂ demand, ↓ dysrhythmia risk). · 2 large-bore IVs ; keep NPO . · Troponin is the priority lab (CK-MB, BMP, CBC also drawn) — on arrival and repeated about every 6 hours, because it rises late. The ECG + troponin are what tell angina apart from an MI. · Continuous cardiac monitoring — ischemic muscle is prone to lethal dysrhythmias. · The CAD case: Mr. Bob · A 40-year-old man reports chest pain, SOB, and a fluttering heartbeat. Follow the flow: · Step | What happens | Why · 1 | Full assessment | Always assess before acting · 2 | 12-lead ECG | Evaluates the fluttering heartbeat and looks for ischemia · 3 | Diagnosed with angina → NTG SL | Vasodilator, first line for chest pain · 4 | Relieved by 2 NTG → stable angina | Rest + NTG relief = stable · 5 | Home with NTG | Teach: always keep it with you · 6 | Later: pain unrelieved after 3 NTG → calls 911 | Another NTG is NOT the answer now · 7 | ED: MONA , 2 large-bore IVs , troponin | Treat pain/ischemia, prepare for meds, detect damage · 8 | ECG and troponin normal → unstable angina → coronary angiogram/cardiac cath | Shows where perfusion is blocked · 9 | Heparin drip | Prevents new clots and clot extension (does not dissolve clots) · 10 | Clopidogrel | Prevents platelet aggregation · 11 | Metoprolol | Every chest-pain patient gets a beta blocker: ↓ O₂ demand, ↓ risk of lethal tachydysrhythmias · If a thrombolytic is ordered, the nurse first reviews the chart and interviews the client for contraindications (bleeding risk). If the patient suddenly becomes unstable with a fast rhythm (for example HR 140, BP 70/20), anticipate synchronized cardioversion . · Mr. Bob's discharge meds · Medication | Reason · Aspirin | Antiplatelet — prevents clots on plaque/stent · Clopidogrel | Antiplatelet — prevents platelet aggregation · Carvedilol (beta blocker) | ↓ HR and O₂ demand; protects against dysrhythmias · Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) | Prevents ventricular remodeling (scar-driven reshaping of the heart) · Statin (lovastatin) | Lowers LDL and stabilizes plaque · Discharge after CAD = "A-C-B-A-S" : A spirin, C lopidogrel, B eta blocker, A CE inhibitor, S tatin.

Lower O₂ demand, ease anxiety, and teach for home · Assessment · Gather information about the patient's symptoms and the activities that come before and bring on angina attacks (where, what it feels like, is it the same as before, severity, onset, duration, triggers, what relieves it, other symptoms). Also assess CAD risk factors , how the patient responds to angina, how well the patient and family understand the diagnosis , and adherence to the current treatment plan. These answers shape the treatment and prevention plan. · Nursing diagnoses & potential complications · Nursing diagnoses | Potential complications · Risk for impaired cardiac function | ACS and MI · Anxiety related to cardiac symptoms and possible death | Dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest · Lack of knowledge about the underlying disease | Heart failure · Able to perform self-care | Cardiogenic shock · Goals for the patient with angina · Immediate and appropriate treatment when angina occurs. · Prevention of angina. · Reduced anxiety. · Awareness of the disease process and understanding of the prescribed care. · Adherence to the self-care program. · Absence of complications. · During an angina episode · Act right away — for chest pain or warning symptoms (indigestion or nausea, choking, heaviness, weakness or numbness in the arms, dyspnea, dizziness). · Stop all activity and have the patient sit or rest in bed in semi-Fowler's — lowers O₂ demand. · Assess the pain — is it the same as usual? — plus vital signs and signs of respiratory distress; obtain a 12-lead ECG (ST-segment and T-wave changes). · Give NTG SL (hold and notify if SBP below 90); repeat every 5 minutes for pain that is unchanged or still present, up to 3 doses , checking BP and HR each time . · Give O₂ , usually 2 L/min by nasal cannula — especially if RR is up or SpO₂ is down. · Stay with the patient; pain that is significant and continues → notify the provider and treat as possible ACS/MI. · Bed rest until stable ; avoid Valsalva (straining). · Reducing anxiety · Patients with angina often fear losing their roles in the family and society, and fear that the pain means an MI or death . Fear raises catecholamines, which raise HR, BP, and O₂ demand — worsening ischemia. Explore what the diagnosis means to the patient, stay calm, and explain the illness, its treatment, and how to slow its progression in simple terms. Involve the family, and offer stress-reduction methods such as guided imagery or music therapy. Addressing spiritual needs can also ease fear. Morphine, when ordered for unrelieved pain, also eases anxiety. · Anxiety is a demand problem. A calm patient is a heart that needs less oxygen. · Preventing pain: balancing activity and rest · Identify the level of activity that brings on the patient's pain or warning symptoms and plan activities around it. If pain comes often or with minimal activity, alternate activities with rest periods . Balancing activity and rest is a core part of teaching for the patient and family. · Daily exercise that does not cause pain ; increase duration first, then intensity. · Alternate activity with rest ; some fatigue during recovery is expected. · Avoid activity right after a large meal ; eat smaller meals. · Avoid extremes of heat and cold and walking into the wind; in cold weather, dress warmly and cover the mouth and nose with a scarf. · Exercise at a level where you can still talk ; check pulse during activity. · Stop any activity that causes chest pain, extreme SOB, dizziness, or undue fatigue. · Limit caffeine (raises HR); avoid smoke-filled places. · Self-care teaching · Teaching is planned with the patient and family so they can understand the illness, recognize the symptoms of ischemia , state what to do when symptoms start, and prevent chest pain and the progression of CAD. The aims: fewer and milder angina attacks, slower disease progression, and no complications. Any pain not relieved within 15 minutes by the usual methods, including NTG, means calling 911 for transport to the closest ED. · Managing angina at home — what the patient should be able to do · Follow a diet low in saturated fat and high in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains (lower in calories if weight loss is needed). · Balance rest with daily activity — stay below the level that causes chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or undue fatigue; follow the prescribed exercise plan. · Avoid temperature extremes, especially cold — don't exercise in very hot or cold weather. · Know the name, dose, side effects, and schedule of every medication; take aspirin and beta blockers as prescribed . · Carry NTG at all times and know when and how to use it. · Avoid OTC products that raise HR and BP (diet pills, nasal decongestants) unless the provider approves. · Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke — smoking raises HR, BP, and carbon monoxide levels. · Keep blood pressure and blood glucose at goal; manage weight and stress; use support resources during stressful times. · Report any increase in symptoms , keep follow-up appointments and testing, and know how to reach the provider. · Teaching NTG self-administration · Moisten the tablet with saliva , place it under the tongue, and let it dissolve completely before swallowing. · NTG is volatile — heat, moisture, air, light, and time inactivate it. Keep it in the original capped dark glass bottle in a cool place; never move tablets into a plastic pillbox or carry them in a pocket close to the body. · Keep it with you at all times and renew the supply every 3–6 months . · Take it before any activity that may cause pain (exercise, climbing stairs, sexual activity) — it raises tolerance for exercise and stress and works best before pain starts. · Note how long it takes to relieve the discomfort. · Sit down for a few minutes when taking it to avoid hypotension and fainting. · 1 tablet every 5 minutes, maximum 3 — pain still there after the third → call 911 . · Side effects: flushing, throbbing headache, hypotension, and tachycardia . · Never take with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, avanafil) — severe hypotension. · NTG storage = "keep it dark, cool, capped, and fresh" — original dark glass bottle, out of the pocket, renewed every 3–6 months. · When to call 911 vs. the provider · Call 911 | Call the provider · Chest pain or pressure (or warning symptoms) not relieved after 3 NTG in 15 minutes | New or more frequent angina, or angina with less activity · Chest pain with fainting, severe SOB, or sweating | SOB, fainting spells, slow or fast heartbeat · Signs of stroke or severe bleeding | Swelling of the feet and ankles · Cardiac rehabilitation · A structured, supervised program after an MI, stent, or bypass surgery, or for chronic angina. It offers monitored exercise , diet and stress-reduction teaching, help with smoking cessation, guidance on returning to work, driving, and sex, and support groups. Encourage every eligible patient to enroll. · Medication teaching overview · Class | Why | Key teaching · Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) | Prevent clots on plaque or a stent | Bleeding precautions; report black stools; never stop without the cardiologist (especially after a stent); clopidogrel held about 5 days before surgery · Statins | Lower LDL | Report muscle pain or dark urine; liver enzymes checked; not in pregnancy · Beta blockers ("-olol") | ↓ HR, BP, and O₂ demand | Check pulse; hold/notify if HR below 60 or SBP below 90; never stop abruptly · Nitrates (NTG) | Dilate vessels, relieve angina | 1 every 5 min, max 3; sit first; original dark glass bottle, renewed every 3–6 months; no PDE5 inhibitors · ACE inhibitors ("-pril") | Prevent remodeling, lower BP | Dry cough, angioedema, potassium, rise slowly · Full details for each class live in the Medications unit. · Home teaching after a cardiac cath · Check the insertion site (groin or wrist) daily for bleeding, swelling, a hard lump (hematoma) , redness, or drainage. · If the site bleeds, lie down and apply firm pressure ; call 911 if bleeding doesn't stop. · Report numbness, tingling, coldness, color change, or pain in the leg or arm used. · Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for the time ordered. · Drink fluids to help flush the contrast dye (protects the kidneys). · After a stent: take aspirin and clopidogrel exactly as prescribed — stopping early risks a clot inside the stent. · A stent or bypass does not cure CAD — lifestyle changes and meds are still needed. · Hematoma at the site? Hold pressure — never massage. Severe one-sided back or flank pain with ↓BP and ↑HR = retroperitoneal bleed → emergency. · Home care checklist · Can name their condition and how it affects daily life · States name, dose, side effects, and schedule of every medication · Knows how to take NTG and when to call 911 · Follows a heart-healthy diet and activity plan · Commits to smoking cessation and BP, glucose, and lipid control · Knows follow-up appointments, cardiac rehab, and support resources

Can't pump vs. can't fill — and why the body makes it worse · What heart failure is · Heart failure (HF) is a syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. Either the ventricle can't contract well (systolic) or it can't fill well (diastolic). Both end in decreased cardiac output and congestion — fluid backing up behind the weak side. HF is a "volume" problem, so fluid balance is at the center of care. · Compensation: the vicious cycle · When cardiac output drops, the body tries to fix it — and in the short term it works. Over time, these same mechanisms make the heart work harder and cause the signs and symptoms of HF. · Mechanism | What it does | Long-term cost · Sympathetic nervous system (epinephrine, norepinephrine) | ↑ HR and contractility; vasoconstriction | Tachycardia and ↑ afterload raise O₂ demand ( a vasoconstrictor makes the heart work harder ); less blood to kidneys, GI tract, skin · RAAS (renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone) | Low kidney perfusion releases renin; angiotensin II constricts vessels; aldosterone holds sodium and water | Fluid volume overload ; ↑ preload and afterload · Hypertrophy (thickening) | Thicker muscle squeezes harder at first | Stiff walls that can't relax and fill · Dilation (stretching) | Chamber stretches to hold more volume | Overstretched muscle loses its "snap back" · Ventricular remodeling | Abnormal structure and early death of heart cells, fibrosis | Progressive, worsening failure · The overstretched chambers release BNP , which promotes diuresis and vasodilation — but it isn't strong enough to win. That's why BNP is the lab marker for HF. · Why ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, and beta blockers are HF drugs: they block the compensation (RAAS and SNS) that is driving the vicious cycle and remodeling. · Systolic vs. diastolic · Feature | Systolic — HFrEF | Diastolic — HFpEF · Name | Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction | Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction · Ejection fraction | EF below 50% | EF preserved (normal range) · The problem | Can't PUMP — weak contraction | Can't FILL — stiff ventricle can't relax · Ventricle walls | Stretched , thin, "big and boggy" | Thick , stiff, smaller chamber · Result | Fills but can't squeeze it out → ↓ stroke volume | Squeezes but too little blood got in → ↓ stroke volume · How it's diagnosed | Echocardiogram (EF, wall thickness) | Echocardiogram (EF, wall thickness) · Normal EF is 50–70% — the percentage of blood in the ventricle that is pumped out with each beat. A patient can have both types at once. · Systolic = Stretched. Diastolic = thick ("Damn she thick"). Both lead to the same place: decreased cardiac output. · Causes · CAD and MI — a leading cause; ischemic or dead muscle can't contract. · Hypertension — ↑ afterload → hypertrophy → stiff, then failing ventricle (the most common cause of HFpEF). · Valve disease — blood can't move forward; pressure and workload rise. · Cardiomyopathy — disease of the heart muscle itself (including from alcohol or some chemotherapy). · Dysrhythmias — A-fib can cause or result from HF; very fast or very slow rates drop cardiac output. · Anemia and thyroid disease — the heart works harder to meet O₂ demand. · Lung disease (COPD, pulmonary hypertension, PE) — a cause of right-sided HF because the right ventricle pumps against high lung pressure. Right-sided HF caused by chronic lung problems is called cor pulmonale . · Kidney failure with volume overload; hypoxia, acidosis, electrolyte imbalances worsen it. · ACC/AHA stages · Stage | Description | Example · At risk (A) | Risk factors but no structural changes or symptoms | HTN, diabetes, obesity, smoking, high cholesterol, inactivity · Pre-HF (B) | Structural heart changes but no symptoms | Old MI, left ventricular hypertrophy, low EF on echo · HF (C) | Structural disease with current or past symptoms such as SOB and fatigue | Dyspnea, fatigue, edema · Advanced HF (D) | End stage; symptoms don't respond to treatment | Repeated hospitalizations, devices, transplant evaluation · Stages only move forward — they describe the natural progression of the disease, and treatment is matched to the stage. · NYHA functional class · Class | Symptoms with activity · I | No limitation — ordinary activity causes no symptoms · II | Slight limitation — comfortable at rest; ordinary activity causes fatigue, dyspnea, or palpitations · III | Marked limitation — less than ordinary activity causes symptoms · IV | Symptoms at rest ; any activity increases discomfort · NYHA class describes how the patient feels today and can go up or down with treatment; ACC/AHA stage describes disease progression . · Acute vs. chronic · HF is a chronic disease with acute exacerbations (acute decompensated HF). The goal of long-term care is to keep the patient managed and out of exacerbation . Common triggers: too much sodium or fluid, missed medications, uncontrolled HTN, new A-fib or other dysrhythmia, infection, ischemia.

Left → Lungs. Right → Rest of the body. · Why the signs differ · Blood backs up behind the ventricle that is failing. · Left ventricle fails → blood can't move forward into the aorta → it backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins → lungs . Fluid is forced into the alveoli = pulmonary congestion/edema. Forward flow to the body also drops (low-output signs). · Right ventricle fails → blood can't move forward into the lungs → it backs up into the venous system → rest of the body : neck veins, liver, abdomen, legs. When chronic lung disease causes it, right-sided HF is called cor pulmonale . · L = Lungs. R = Rest of the body. The most common cause of right-sided HF is left-sided HF — the pressure backs up through the lungs into the right ventricle. · Signs and symptoms · Left-sided HF (Lungs) | Right-sided HF (Rest of body) · Dyspnea , dyspnea on exertion, tachypnea | Jugular venous distention (JVD) · ↑ Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP — pressure backed up in the lungs; measured with an ICU catheter, NUR 211) | Cor pulmonale when chronic lung disease is the cause · Orthopnea (can't breathe lying flat; uses more pillows) | Dependent edema — feet, ankles, legs; sacrum if on bed rest; ↑ peripheral venous pressure · Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) — wakes up gasping | Weight gain (fluid retention) · Crackles that don't clear with coughing; wheezes | Ascites — ↑ abdominal girth · Cough — dry at first, then pink, frothy, or blood-tinged sputum | Hepatomegaly / splenomegaly — RUQ tenderness · Restlessness, confusion , anxiety (low O₂ to the brain) | Anorexia, nausea, GI distress (congested gut) · S3 heart sound; tachycardia | Fatigue, weakness · Low SpO₂, cyanosis, fatigue, ↓ urine output | Nocturia (fluid returns to circulation lying down) · In chronic HF, patients often have both sets of signs at once. · The S3 heart sound · An S3 ("ventricular gallop") is an extra sound just after S2, heard best at the apex with the bell. It comes from blood rushing into an overfilled ventricle and is an early sign of fluid overload in HF. Rhythm: "Ken- tuc -ky." · Assessing JVD · Position the patient with the head of the bed at 45 degrees , head turned slightly away. · Look at the internal jugular area for the top of the venous pulsation. · Distention more than about 4 cm above the sternal angle is abnormal → suggests high venous pressure and right-sided failure. · Hepatojugular reflux: pressing on the right upper abdomen makes the neck veins rise further — another sign of high venous pressure. · Visible neck veins while sitting up at 45° = the right side is backed up . · Pulmonary edema — an emergency · Acute pulmonary edema (acute decompensated HF) happens when the left ventricle suddenly can't handle the volume and fluid floods the alveoli. It can come on fast ("flash"). · Recognize: sudden severe breathlessness and a feeling of suffocation, tachypnea, low SpO₂, pink frothy sputum , crackles throughout the lungs, restlessness/anxiety/confusion, cool clammy pale or cyanotic skin, tachycardia, JVD. · Priority action | Why · High Fowler's , legs dangling if possible | ↓ venous return (preload) and lung congestion; eases breathing · Oxygen (non-rebreather at first as ordered); pulse oximetry | Relieve hypoxemia; prepare for noninvasive ventilation if not improving · IV access , cardiac monitor | For IV meds; watch for dysrhythmias · IV furosemide (loop diuretic) as ordered | Rapid diuresis pulls fluid off the lungs · Morphine or nitrates per provider order | Vasodilation ↓ preload; morphine also eases anxiety and air hunger · Monitor BP, urine output (bedside commode or catheter), I&O, K⁺, kidneys | Diuresis can drop BP and potassium quickly · Stay with the patient ; calm, simple explanations | Anxiety worsens dyspnea and cardiac workload · Pulmonary edema " sit up, O₂, pee it off ": High Fowler's → oxygen → IV furosemide → watch BP and K⁺.

Diagnostics, treatment by stage, daily weights, and the nursing process · Diagnostics · Test | What it tells you · BNP | Released by overstretched ventricles. Below 100 pg/mL normal; above 100 = HF — the higher, the worse. Rising levels suggest an exacerbation. · Echocardiogram | Confirms HF and the type: shows structural changes to the heart — EF (normal 50–70%; HFrEF below 50%), wall thickness, chamber size, valves · Chest X-ray | Enlarged heart, pulmonary congestion/edema, pleural effusion · BMP | K⁺ (3.5–5.5) and Na⁺ — diuretics and ACE/ARB/ARNI shift them; BUN and creatinine — kidney function · 12-lead ECG | Dysrhythmias (A-fib is common), signs of ischemia or old MI · Others | CBC (anemia), thyroid studies, liver tests, troponin if ischemia is suspected · Treatment by stage · Stage | Treatment · At risk (risk factors, no structural changes or symptoms) | Lifestyle modifications + SGLT2 inhibitor (blood sugar control) — continued at every stage · Pre-HF (structural changes, no symptoms) | ACE inhibitor (or ARB), beta blocker , statin · HF (symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue) | ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan, Entresto ) — first-line HF medication (ACE inhibitor or ARB if an ARNI isn't used) + beta blocker and statin; diuretic — potassium-sparing to start · Advanced HF (symptoms don't respond to treatment) | More invasive device management and IV therapy (NUR 211 content) · Entresto (ARNI) is the first-line medication for HF ; an ACE inhibitor or ARB is used if an ARNI isn't. Switching from an ACE inhibitor: wait 36 hours before Entresto, or 6 weeks before an ARB. · Nitrates and digoxin (cardiac glycoside) can be added at any stage, or used when the patient can't tolerate an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI. Always treat the underlying cause too (HTN, CAD, valve disease, A-fib). · Medication overview · Class | Role in HF | Key nursing point · ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan, Entresto) | First-line HF medication : blocks RAAS and boosts natriuretic peptides | Never with an ACE inhibitor — 36-hour washout (angioedema) · ACE inhibitor ("-pril") / ARB ("-sartan") | Used if an ARNI isn't: block RAAS, ↓ afterload, ↓ fluid retention, slow remodeling | Cough (ACE → switch to ARB, started 6 weeks after the ACE inhibitor is stopped), angioedema, ↑ K⁺, first-dose hypotension, kidneys · Beta blocker | Blocks SNS: ↓ HR and workload, slows remodeling | Hold/notify HR below 60 or SBP below 90;
