never stop abruptly · Diuretics | Remove excess fluid | Daily weights, I&O, BP, K⁺; give in the morning · SGLT2 inhibitor | Blood sugar control; started early in HF | Started with lifestyle changes at the first step · Digoxin / nitrates | Add-ons | Low K⁺ raises digoxin toxicity risk · Full details live in the Medications unit. · Lifestyle modifications · Nutrition: low sodium , low cholesterol , omega-3 ; read labels and avoid canned, processed, and restaurant foods; flavor with herbs, lemon, vinegar. · Fluid management — fluid restriction as ordered ; plan fluids across the day. · Exercise — mild and gradual, often through cardiac rehab ; avoid tachycardia . · Rest and sleep-disorder evaluation (sleep apnea worsens HF). · Evaluation of cardiac rhythm — A-fib is common. · Smoking and alcohol cessation. · Vaccines (influenza, pneumonia) — infections trigger exacerbations. · Oxygen PRN. · Daily weights — the most important self-check · Weigh every morning , same time, same scale , same clothing , after voiding and before breakfast. · Report a gain of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week. · Sudden weight gain in HF is fluid, not fat (1 kg ≈ 1 L of fluid). · Keep a written log to bring to appointments. · "2–3 in a day, 5 in a week" — call the provider before the lungs fill up. · Sodium and fluid limits · Follow the sodium and fluid limits as ordered (sodium is commonly limited to about 2 g/day). Teach that many foods contain hidden sodium, salt substitutes are high in potassium (dangerous with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics), and OTC antacids, cough syrups, and laxatives may contain sodium — check with the provider first. · Balancing activity and rest · Avoid prolonged bed rest unless acutely ill — deconditioning, pressure injuries, and clots. · Daily walking, increased gradually: duration first, then frequency, then intensity . · Alternate activity with rest periods ; don't schedule two big tasks back to back. · Small, frequent meals; sit for tasks (chopping vegetables at the table); wait about 2 hours after eating to exercise. · Must be able to talk during activity; stop for severe SOB, pain, or dizziness; avoid extreme heat, cold, and humidity. · In the hospital, check VS and SpO₂ before, during, and after activity; HR should return to baseline within about 3 minutes. · When to call the provider · Weight gain of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week · Unusual SOB with activity or at rest · ↑ swelling of the ankles, feet, or abdomen · Persistent cough · Loss of appetite · Restless sleep or needing more pillows to breathe at night · Profound fatigue, dizziness, or fainting · Nursing process for the patient with HF · Step | Focus · Assess | Dyspnea, number of pillows, PND, fatigue, edema (0–4+), lung sounds (crackles, wheezes), S3, HR/rhythm, BP (incl. orthostatic), JVD, pulses, skin color/temperature, abdomen (ascites, liver), LOC, I&O, daily weight, emotional response/depression, understanding of self-care · Problems | Activity intolerance; fluid volume excess; anxiety; powerlessness; difficulty managing the regimen. Potential complications: pulmonary edema, hypotension/cardiogenic shock, dysrhythmias, thromboembolism · Interventions | Promote activity tolerance (pace and rest); manage fluid volume (diuretics in the morning, I&O, weights, sodium/fluid limits, HOB up or recliner, skin care for edema); control anxiety (O₂, comfort, family presence, avoid restraints ); minimize powerlessness (offer choices); teach with teach-back · Evaluate | Stable weight, clearer lungs, less dyspnea and edema, tolerates activity, follows the plan, no exacerbation · Watch diuretic problems: hypokalemia (dysrhythmias, weakness — dangerous with digoxin), hyperkalemia (ACE/ARB/spironolactone), hyponatremia, dehydration and hypotension, rising creatinine. Also monitor for oliguria — urine output that drops despite diuretics signals kidney trouble. · Acute exacerbation priorities · Airway and breathing first — high Fowler's, O₂, SpO₂, lung sounds. · Cardiac monitor, IV access, VS frequently. · IV diuretic as ordered; strict I&O, daily weight, K⁺ and kidney labs. · Bed rest during the acute phase; bedside commode to save energy. · Stay with the patient, reduce anxiety. · Find the trigger (diet, missed meds, A-fib, infection) and target teaching to it before discharge.

Virchow triad, assessment, prevention, and anticoagulant safety · What VTE is · Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is the umbrella term for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) . A DVT is a clot in a deep vein, usually the thigh or calf (upper-extremity DVT is usually linked to IV access devices — central lines, ports, dialysis catheters, pacing wires). The danger is the clot's “tail” : it can grow in the direction of blood flow, break off, and travel to the lungs as a PE. VTE is often silent — sometimes the first sign of a DVT is a PE. · Virchow triad — why clots form · A clot is a fibrin mesh that traps red blood cells and platelets. · Three factors set the stage for a venous clot. Any one raises risk; stacking them raises it more (think of the post-op, immobile patient with cancer). · Virchow factor | What it means | Risk factors · Endothelial damage | Injury to the vein's inner lining creates a site for a clot | Central venous catheters, dialysis access catheters, pacing wires, local vein damage (IV irritants), repetitive-motion injury, surgery , trauma /fractures · Venous stasis | Slow blood flow — veins dilate and the calf-muscle pump isn't working | Bed rest/immobilization , age over 65, heart failure , obesity , spinal cord injury, varicose veins, long trips · Altered coagulation (hypercoagulability) | Blood clots more easily than normal | Cancer , oral contraceptives /hormones, pregnancy (and about 6 weeks postpartum), polycythemia, septicemia, inherited clotting disorders (factor V Leiden, protein C/S or antithrombin III deficiency), abruptly stopping an anticoagulant · “Damage, Stasis, Thick blood.” When you see a hip-replacement patient on bed rest, you are looking at two sides of the triangle already — prevention starts on day 0. · Signs and symptoms of DVT · Unilateral edema/swelling of the leg (or arm) — compare sides · Pain, heaviness, or cramping; ankle engorgement · Warmth — the affected limb feels warmer than the other · Tenderness on gentle palpation (often appears later, from vein-wall inflammation) · Prominent superficial veins · Often no symptoms at all — and PE may be the first sign · Assess by measuring: measure the circumference of both legs (thigh and calf) at the same marked level with a tape measure and compare. A difference between sides quantifies the swelling. If both legs are swollen, a difference may be hard to detect. · Superficial vs deep ·  | Superficial thrombophlebitis | Deep vein thrombosis · Where | Veins just under the skin (saphenous, cephalic, basilic) | Deep veins of the thigh/calf (or subclavian with lines) · Look/feel | Pain/tenderness, redness , warmth along a cordlike , palpable vein | Unilateral swelling , warmth, heaviness, tenderness; may be silent · Embolus risk | Low — most dissolve on their own | High — can break off → PE · Treatment | Often at home: elevate, analgesics, anti-inflammatories | Anticoagulation ± clot removal; prevent extension and PE · Diagnostics · Test | What it shows / why · Venous duplex ultrasound | Main test for DVT — the vein looks enlarged with clot, or won't compress under the probe · D-dimer | Blood test for clot breakdown products — elevated with an active clot (also with surgery, trauma, infection); a normal result makes VTE unlikely · Coagulation studies — PT/INR, aPTT | Baselines before starting anticoagulants · CBC (Hgb/Hct, platelets) | Baseline for bleeding risk and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) · Hypercoagulability workup | If no obvious cause: factor V Leiden, protein C/S, antithrombin III, CRP · Prevention — the most important nursing job · Early ambulation — the single most effective way to prevent stasis; walking beats standing or sitting · Leg exercises (ankle pumps, calf flexion) every hour while in bed or on long trips; deep breathing also helps venous return · Anti-embolism stockings and intermittent pneumatic compression devices (SCDs) as ordered · Prophylactic anticoagulant : SubQ unfractionated heparin or LMWH (enoxaparin) · Hydration — dehydration thickens the blood · No crossing the legs, no pillows under the knees , no prolonged sitting with hips and knees bent · Never massage the leg — it can dislodge a clot · Lifestyle: weight loss, smoking cessation, regular exercise · Move it, squeeze it, thin it, water it — but never rub it. Ambulation/leg exercises, stockings/SCDs, heparin/LMWH, fluids — and no massage, no crossed legs, no pillow under the knees. · Nursing care of the patient with a DVT · Elevate the feet and lower legs above the level of the heart to empty the veins · Walk once anticoagulation has started — goal at least 10 minutes every 1–2 hours · Graduated compression stockings improve venous return and comfort; teach how to apply them · Warm packs may reduce discomfort; give analgesics as ordered · Measure and compare leg circumference daily; reassess pain, warmth, and color · Watch for PE : sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachypnea, anxiety · Anticoagulants prevent new clots and stop the clot from growing — they do not dissolve a clot that has already formed. The body breaks down the existing clot over time. · Monitoring anticoagulant therapy · Drug | Monitor | Antidote · Heparin (IV drip/SubQ) | aPTT (“two t's make an H”); platelets for HIT | Protamine sulfate · LMWH (enoxaparin) SubQ | Platelets, bleeding; don't expel the air bubble, don't aspirate or rub the site | Protamine (partial) · Warfarin (PO) | PT/INR , goal 2–3 ; takes days to work, so it's bridged with heparin | Vitamin K · DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) | No routine lab monitoring; bleeding | Andexanet alfa (Xa inhibitors); idarucizumab (dabigatran) · For every anticoagulant: get baseline labs, watch Hgb/Hct and platelets, and assess for bleeding. Bleeding is reported immediately ; the drug may be stopped or reversed. · Teaching — taking anticoagulants · Take exactly as prescribed; don't stop unless told to; warfarin at the same time every day · Wear/carry ID stating the anticoagulant; tell every provider and dentist; check before dental work or surgery · Keep all lab appointments (INR for warfarin) · Ask before taking other drugs or supplements — especially aspirin, NSAIDs , antibiotics, cold medicines, vitamins, herbals · Warfarin: avoid alcohol ; keep vitamin K intake consistent (leafy greens) — no big diet changes · Bleeding precautions: electric razor , soft toothbrush , avoid contact sports and sharps · Report: bleeding that won't stop, nosebleeds, extensive bruising, red/brown urine , red or black stools , possible pregnancy · Complications of venous thrombosis · Pulmonary embolism — the deadly one · Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic leg swelling and skin changes) · Chronic venous insufficiency · Edema · Varicosities · Venous ulcers · Venous gangrene · A calf that is swollen, warm, and tender on one side = think DVT. A patient who suddenly can't catch their breath = think the DVT just moved.

Dead space, right-heart strain, stable vs unstable management · What a PE is · A pulmonary embolism is a blockage of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches. Most often it is a DVT that broke off , traveled through the vena cava and right heart, and lodged in the lungs. Other emboli: air, fat (long-bone fractures), amniotic fluid, and septic emboli. · Pathophysiology — follow the clot · 1. Dead space: the blocked area is still ventilated (air moves in and out) but has no blood flow — so no gas exchange happens there → hypoxemia. · 2. Vasoconstriction: substances released from the clot constrict nearby vessels and bronchioles, making the V/Q mismatch worse. · 3. ↑ Pulmonary vascular resistance → ↑ pulmonary artery pressure → the right ventricle has to push harder. · 4. Right ventricular strain/failure → less blood reaches the left side → ↓ cardiac output, ↓ BP, shock . · Small emboli can cause pulmonary infarction (dead lung tissue). · V/Q mismatch — dead space vs shunt · Gas exchange needs both air (ventilation, V) and blood (perfusion, Q) in the same place at the same time. ·  | Ventilation (air) | Perfusion (blood) | Example · Normal | Yes | Yes | Healthy alveolus next to a working capillary · Dead space | Yes | No | Pulmonary embolism — air arrives, but the blood can't get there · Shunt | No | Yes | Pneumonia, atelectasis, pulmonary edema — blood passes alveoli filled with fluid or collapsed · PE = Plenty of air, Empty vessel. Dead space is a clot problem; shunt is an alveoli problem. · Signs and symptoms · Dyspnea — the most common symptom , usually sudden · Tachypnea — the most common sign · Sudden pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with breathing in); Pain often comes before swelling ; repeated bleeds → joint damage, chronic pain, loss of motion · Muscles — hematomas can compress nerves (numbness, weakness) and cause compartment syndrome · GI bleeding , hematuria · Mucous membranes — gums, nose; bleeding after dental work and surgery · Intracranial — the most dangerous; any head injury needs immediate evaluation ; falls are especially dangerous in adults · Treatment — give the missing factor · Replace the clotting factor IV (recombinant factor VIII or IX) — as soon as bleeding starts ; earlier treatment = less damage · Prophylactic factor several times a week to protect the joints, and before any procedure or surgery · Patients and families learn to give factor IV at home at the first sign of a bleed · Desmopressin may raise factor VIII in mild hemophilia A · Some patients develop inhibitors (antibodies) against the factor → it stops working well; watch for bleeding that doesn't respond · Caring for an active bleed · DO | DON'T · Give the clotting factor as ordered — first and fast | No heat — it dilates vessels and increases bleeding · Apply pressure to stop the bleed — but not too much | No compression wraps — too much pressure can cause compartment syndrome · Elevate the limb | Don't use the “RICE” mnemonic — compression is not part of hemophilia bleed care · Rest/immobilize the joint (splint) so the blood can be reabsorbed | No aspirin/NSAIDs for the pain; no IM injections · Cold may be applied if ordered; analgesics such as acetaminophen or opioids | No nasal packing for nosebleeds (bleeding restarts when removed) · Factor, Pressure (gentle), Elevate, Rest — never Heat, never Wrap. · Nursing process · Assess the bleed : location and extent, joint pain/swelling/range of motion, neurovascular checks (pulses, sensation, pain out of proportion → compartment syndrome) · Watch for life-threatening bleeds: altered LOC /headache (intracranial), respiratory distress (bleeding into the airway/neck) · After surgery: frequent vital signs, dressings, and drains for bleeding · Manage pain from hematomas and joint bleeds (no NSAIDs) · Avoid all injections and invasive procedures unless factor is given first · Coping : lifelong disease with limits; support independence while keeping the patient safe; involve the family · Genetic counseling for female carriers · Teaching · How to give factor IV at home and when (first sign of bleeding, before procedures) · No aspirin or NSAIDs ; Metoprolol, carvedilol, atenolol, propranolol, labetalol, esmolol — diltiazem, verapamil, amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine · Both classes lower the heart's workload and oxygen demand . Both can drop the heart rate and the blood pressure — so both share the same check before every dose: pulse and BP . · Metoprolol, Carvedilol, Atenolol, Propranolol, Labetalol, Esmolol — Beta Blockers ("-olol") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily/BID; IV push (metoprolol, labetalol — give slowly ); esmolol is a short-acting IV drip . Hypertension, angina/CAD (every chest-pain patient gets one unless contraindicated), after MI, heart failure (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate — started low and titrated up slowly over weeks), rate control for A-fib, A-flutter, and SVT. Labetalol IV is common for acute BP control (e.g., stroke). Metoprolol and atenolol are cardioselective (mostly beta-1 — selectivity is lost at higher doses); propranolol, carvedilol, and labetalol are nonselective · Mechanism of action | Blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart → ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, slower conduction through the AV node, ↓ BP → ↓ myocardial O₂ demand and ↓ dysrhythmia risk. Nonselective drugs also block beta-2 receptors in the lungs · Adverse reactions | The 4 B's: Bradycardia, BP drop, Bronchoconstriction, Blood-sugar masking ; fatigue, dizziness/orthostatic hypotension, depression, erectile dysfunction; HF symptoms can worsen in the first weeks of therapy; cold extremities · Contraindications | Bradycardia , heart block , cardiogenic shock/acutely decompensated HF; use with caution in asthma/COPD (especially nonselective drugs) and diabetes · Nursing interventions | Check the apical pulse and BP before each dose — hold and notify if HR is below 60 or SBP is below 90 ; give IV pushes slowly with the patient on a monitor; daily weights, edema, and lung sounds (wheezes, crackles); monitor glucose in diabetics; hold before a stress test as ordered · Patient education | Never stop abruptly (boxed warning) — rebound tachycardia, worsening angina, MI, or ventricular dysrhythmias, even if it's taken only for BP; the provider tapers it over 1–2 weeks. Take metoprolol with or right after a meal, at the same time each day. Check your pulse at home; rise slowly; diabetics: tremor and fast heartbeat may be hidden, so check glucose (sweating still occurs); no OTC drugs (e.g., decongestants) without approval; report wheezing, SOB, weight gain, or dizziness · Diltiazem, Verapamil, Amlodipine, Nifedipine, Nicardipine — Calcium Channel Blockers · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Two groups. Diltiazem and verapamil act on the heart: rate control for A-fib, A-flutter, and SVT (diltiazem IV push slowly, then a drip, or PO), angina. Amlodipine and nifedipine act on the vessels: hypertension and angina (including vasospastic angina). PO daily (extended-release forms — swallow whole). Nicardipine is an IV CCB drip for BP control (titrated) · Mechanism of action | Blocks calcium entry into heart and vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation , ↓ afterload, ↓ O₂ demand, more blood flow to the heart muscle. Diltiazem and verapamil also slow the SA node and AV conduction and reduce contractility · Adverse reactions | Hypotension , dizziness, headache, flushing; bradycardia/heart block (diltiazem, verapamil); peripheral edema (ankles — especially amlodipine, nifedipine); constipation (most with verapamil); reflex tachycardia (short-acting nifedipine). Hypotension is most likely when given IV · Contraindications | Heart block , sick sinus syndrome, SBP below 90; diltiazem/verapamil with HFrEF or pulmonary congestion (they weaken contraction); caution when combined with a beta blocker (additive bradycardia) — IV diltiazem isn't given within a few hours of an IV beta blocker; diltiazem raises digoxin and some statin levels · Nursing interventions | Check BP and HR — hold and notify if SBP is below 90 or HR is below 60 ; continuous ECG monitoring with IV diltiazem; assess for edema of the hands and feet, weight gain, and SOB; monitor for constipation · Patient education | No grapefruit or grapefruit juice (raises drug levels); rise slowly; don't stop abruptly (more frequent, longer angina); NTG can still be taken for acute angina; report swelling, SOB, dizziness, or a slow pulse; fiber and fluids for constipation · Same Checks, Different Jobs ·  | Beta blockers | CCBs · Recognize | "-olol" (plus carvedilol, labetalol) | Diltiazem, verapamil, "-dipine" (amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine) · Hold/notify | HR below 60 or SBP below 90 | HR below 60 or SBP below 90 · Signature warning | 4 B's; never stop abruptly | Grapefruit; edema; heart block · Rhythm use | Rate control (metoprolol) | Rate control (diltiazem) · Avoid in | Heart block, asthma (caution) | Heart block, SBP below 90 · DIL-tiazem DILates and slows the rate; amlo-DIP-ine DIPs the pressure. For beta blockers think 4 B's — and the 5th: Bye-bye abruptly? Never. · Heart block on the strip? No beta blockers and no CCBs — both slow AV conduction even more.

Lisinopril, enalapril, captopril, benazepril — losartan, valsartan — sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) · These drugs block the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system — the hormone loop that squeezes vessels and holds onto sodium and water. Blocking it lowers BP, takes fluid off, and prevents remodeling of the heart. They share the same big three to monitor: BP, potassium, kidney function — and none are given in pregnancy. · Lisinopril, Enalapril, Captopril, Benazepril — ACE Inhibitors ("-pril") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily (enalaprilat is IV). Hypertension , heart failure (slows progression, fewer hospitalizations), after MI/at discharge with CAD ( prevents ventricular remodeling ), diabetes with kidney protection · Mechanism of action | Blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II → vasodilation (↓ afterload — less pressure to pump against) and less aldosterone (↓ sodium and water retention — ↓ preload); the kidneys keep potassium · Adverse reactions | Dry, hacking cough (bradykinin builds up); angioedema — swelling of the lips, tongue, face, throat (can occur after the first dose or even after years of use; intestinal angioedema shows up as abdominal pain); hyperkalemia ; first-dose hypotension /orthostatic hypotension and dizziness; rising creatinine (kidney injury) · Contraindications | Pregnancy (black box — fetal injury/death); history of angioedema; bilateral renal artery stenosis; hyperkalemia; never with an ARNI (36-hour washout); not combined with an ARB unless specifically ordered · Nursing interventions | Check BP before each dose (first dose — watch closely for hypotension); monitor potassium, BUN/creatinine ; assess for angioedema — airway emergency: stop the drug, call for help; assess any cough (a wet cough with crackles may mean worsening HF, not the drug). Interactions: potassium supplements/potassium-sparing diuretics (hyperkalemia), diuretics (extra hypotension), NSAIDs (blunt the BP effect, stress the kidneys), lithium (toxicity) · Patient education | Rise slowly (fall risk); avoid salt substitutes (potassium chloride) and potassium supplements unless ordered; report facial/tongue swelling or trouble breathing right away (911); report a cough that won't stop — the provider may switch to an ARB (started 6 weeks after the ACE inhibitor is stopped); use contraception and report pregnancy; take consistently · Losartan, Valsartan — Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs, "-sartan") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily. Same uses as ACE inhibitors — hypertension, heart failure, kidney protection in diabetes, stroke prevention through BP control. The usual switch when an ACE inhibitor causes a cough — wait 6 weeks after stopping the ACE inhibitor before starting the ARB . In HF, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is used if an ARNI (Entresto) isn't · Mechanism of action | Blocks angiotensin II at its receptor → vasodilation and less aldosterone. ARBs don't build up bradykinin, so no cough · Adverse reactions | Hypotension, dizziness, hyperkalemia , kidney impairment; angioedema is possible but less common than with ACE inhibitors · Contraindications | Pregnancy (black box — fetal toxicity; stop immediately); hyperkalemia; bilateral renal artery stenosis; not with an ACE inhibitor unless specifically ordered · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP (watch for hypotension, especially with diuretics or volume depletion), potassium , BUN/creatinine, and I&O; angioedema → stop the drug and treat as an emergency. When switching from an ACE inhibitor, verify that 6 weeks have passed since the last ACE inhibitor dose before the first ARB dose. Same interactions as ACE inhibitors: potassium supplements/potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, lithium · Patient education | Same as ACE inhibitors: rise slowly, no salt substitutes, report swelling of the face/lips; take it every day (adherence) along with lifestyle changes; if switching from an ACE inhibitor, the ARB starts 6 weeks after the last ACE inhibitor dose; contraception · Sacubitril/Valsartan (Entresto) — Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibitor (ARNI) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO twice daily . Heart failure — the first-line medication for HF ; reduces cardiovascular death and hospitalization. Sacubitril/valsartan is the only FDA-approved drug in its class . If an ARNI isn't used (e.g., cost), an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the alternative · Mechanism of action | Two drugs in one tablet: valsartan (an ARB) blocks angiotensin II, and sacubitril blocks neprilysin — the enzyme that breaks down the body's own natriuretic peptides — so more sodium and water are excreted and vessels relax · Adverse reactions | Hypotension , hyperkalemia , kidney impairment , angioedema , dizziness, cough · Contraindications | Never with an ACE inhibitor — stop the ACE inhibitor at least 36 hours before the first dose (together they cause angioedema); history of angioedema; pregnancy · Nursing interventions | Verify the 36-hour washout when switching from an ACE inhibitor; monitor BP, potassium, and kidney function (BUN/creatinine); assess for angioedema · Patient education | Never take it with a "-pril" drug; rise slowly; avoid salt substitutes; report facial/throat swelling (911); contraception — report pregnancy; it's taken twice a day · Telling Them Apart ·  | ACE inhibitor | ARB | ARNI · Ending | -pril | -sartan | sacubitril/valsartan · Cough | Yes (classic) | No | Less common · Angioedema | Yes — any time | Rare | Yes · K⁺/kidneys/BP | Monitor all three | Monitor all three | Monitor all three · Pregnancy | Contraindicated | Contraindicated | Contraindicated · Role in HF | Used if an ARNI isn't | Used if an ARNI isn't | First-line · Switching from an ACE inhibitor | — | Wait 6 weeks after the last ACE inhibitor dose | Wait 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose · Key rule | Switch to ARB if cough | Don't combine with an ACE inhibitor | Never with an ACE inhibitor (angioedema) · "Pril" = the Pill that makes you cough. Swap the pril for a sartan and the cough goes. Entresto + a pril = angioedema — so wait 36 hours between them. Pril → sartan: wait 6 weeks. Pril → Entresto: wait 36 hours. · All three keep potassium . Put that next to a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) and the K⁺ can climb fast — and no salt substitutes.

Speeding up a slow heart — atropine, dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and phentolamine for extravasation · Bradycardia is treated when it is symptomatic (signs of decreased cardiac output) — HR is typically below 50. Look for and treat the cause first. The drug order: atropine first → if it doesn't work, transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine drip → transvenous pacing/expert consult. · Atropine — Anticholinergic · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Symptomatic bradycardia — first-line drug. 1 mg IV push every 3–5 minutes, max 3 mg . Comes in a prefilled syringe; short-acting (wears off in roughly 30–45 minutes) · Mechanism of action | Blocks the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) "brake" on the SA and AV nodes → the heart rate rises · Adverse reactions | Tachycardia, palpitations; anticholinergic effects — dry mouth, blurred vision/dilated pupils, urinary retention, flushed hot dry skin, confusion; can increase O₂ demand/ischemia · Contraindications | Angle-closure glaucoma; urinary obstruction; may not work in a heart-transplant patient (no vagal connection) or in some heart blocks — move to pacing · Nursing interventions | Continuous ECG, HR, and BP; have pacing pads ready if it fails; reassess symptoms (BP, LOC, chest pain) after each dose; monitor urine output · Patient education | Explain the expected racing heart, dry mouth, and blurry vision; report trouble urinating or chest pain · Dopamine, Epinephrine, Norepinephrine — Vasopressors · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Continuous IV drips, titrated — ICU/ER drugs (nobody goes home on them). For bradycardia when atropine fails: dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2–10 mcg/min . Norepinephrine is the go-to for low BP/shock . Epinephrine is also the cardiac-arrest drug (Medical Emergencies) · Mechanism of action | Stimulate adrenergic receptors → ↑ heart rate and contractility (beta-1) and vasoconstriction (alpha) → ↑ BP and perfusion pressure · Adverse reactions | Tachycardia, dysrhythmias (PVCs, SVT, V-tach — palpitations), chest pain/ischemia (↑ O₂ demand), hypertension, headache; poor peripheral perfusion (cool, pale fingers and toes); vesicant — extravasation causes tissue necrosis · Contraindications | Uncorrected hypovolemia (fill the tank first); tachydysrhythmias/V-fib (except epinephrine in arrest); use with caution in CAD · Nursing interventions | Infusion pump ; large vein — central line preferred ; check the IV site often; titrate to orders; BP, HR, and rhythm frequently (e.g., every 5 minutes while titrating), pulses, capillary refill, urine output; protect epinephrine/norepinephrine from light per pharmacy; never stop abruptly — wean · Patient education | Explain the monitor and frequent checks; report pain, burning, or swelling at the IV site, chest pain, or palpitations right away · Phentolamine — Extravasation Antidote · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Extravasation of a vasopressor (norepinephrine, dopamine, epinephrine) — diluted and injected SubQ in several spots around the infiltrated area as soon as possible · Mechanism of action | Alpha-blocker — reverses the intense local vasoconstriction so blood returns to the tissue before it dies · Adverse reactions | Hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness · Contraindications | Caution with CAD (reflex tachycardia, ischemia) · Nursing interventions | At the first sign (pain, swelling, blanching, coolness at the site): stop the infusion , disconnect the tubing, aspirate from the catheter if possible, notify the provider, give phentolamine as ordered, elevate, mark and monitor the site; follow facility extravasation protocol; restart the drip in another (preferably central) line · Patient education | Report any burning, pain, or coolness at the IV site immediately · Brady ladder: A-P-D-E — A tropine 1 mg (max 3), then P acing and/or D opamine or E pinephrine drip. · Vasopressors are vesicants. Blanched, cold, painful site? Stop, aspirate, phentolamine. Norepinephrine "pulls the blood away" — phentolamine "puts it back."

Adenosine, amiodarone, lidocaine, and magnesium sulfate · Antiarrhythmics are the second line — find and treat the cause first (electrolytes, hypoxia, fever, pain, bleeding). Unstable patients get electricity, not a pill. · The Classes at a Glance · Class | Drugs | What it does · IB — sodium channel blocker | Lidocaine | Ventricular dysrhythmias only · II — beta blockers | Metoprolol, esmolol, propranolol | Slow the rate (A-fib, A-flutter, SVT) · III — potassium channel blocker | Amiodarone | Atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias; prolongs repolarization · IV — calcium channel blockers | Diltiazem, verapamil | Slow AV conduction (rate control) · Miscellaneous | Adenosine, atropine, epinephrine (also magnesium sulfate) | Adenosine resets SVT; atropine speeds brady; epinephrine for brady/arrest; magnesium for torsades · Adenosine (Adenocard) — Miscellaneous Antiarrhythmic · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Stable, narrow, regular tachycardia (SVT) after vagal maneuvers fail. 6 mg rapid IV push followed by a 20 mL NS flush ; if no conversion in 1–2 minutes, 12 mg · Mechanism of action | Briefly blocks conduction through the AV node — interrupts the reentry circuit and "reboots" the heart. Half-life under 10 seconds · Adverse reactions | Brief asystole/pause (expected) , flushing, chest pressure, dyspnea, light-headedness, a feeling of doom; transient dysrhythmias. Effects pass within seconds · Contraindications | Heart block or sick sinus without a pacemaker; caution in asthma (bronchospasm); not for irregular or wide-complex rhythms · Nursing interventions | Crash cart and provider at the bedside ; continuous ECG (print the strip); use an antecubital or central line closest to the heart; two-syringe or stopcock technique — push fast, flush fast , raise the arm · Patient education | Warn the patient beforehand: "You may feel your heart stop, chest pressure, or flushing for a few seconds — it passes quickly" · Amiodarone (Cordarone, Pacerone) — Class III · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV bolus/drip in acute settings, then PO for maintenance once stable. A-fib/A-flutter (rate or rhythm control), recurrent or unstable V-tach, V-fib (in arrest it is given IV push — Medical Emergencies). Very long half-life (weeks) · Mechanism of action | Blocks potassium (and sodium) channels → prolongs repolarization, slows electrical impulses, and decreases cardiac excitability; also has beta-blocking effects · Adverse reactions | Black box: pulmonary toxicity (cough, dyspnea — can be fatal) and liver toxicity ; thyroid problems (hypo- or hyper-, it contains iodine); vision changes (corneal deposits); photosensitivity, blue-gray skin ; bradycardia, hypotension , heart block; QT prolongation /proarrhythmia · Contraindications | Severe sinus node disease, marked bradycardia, heart block without a pacemaker; caution with beta blockers/CCBs (additive slowing) · Nursing interventions | Continuous ECG (HR, QT), BP; baseline and periodic chest X-ray/pulmonary function, liver enzymes, thyroid levels, eye exams , electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺); infusion pump; raises warfarin and digoxin levels · Patient education | Sunscreen and protective clothing; avoid grapefruit juice ; keep all lab and eye appointments; report cough/SOB, vision changes, jaundice/dark urine, palpitations, dizziness, or weight change/heat-cold intolerance · Lidocaine — Class IB · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Ventricular dysrhythmias only — V-tach, V-fib, frequent PVCs. IV bolus, then a continuous drip on an infusion pump (1–4 mg/min) · Mechanism of action | Blocks sodium channels in the ventricles → decreases ventricular excitability (" Lido = Lowers ventricular irritability") · Adverse reactions | CNS toxicity — confusion, drowsiness, numbness/tingling around the mouth, tinnitus , slurred speech, tremor, seizures ; bradycardia, hypotension, heart block · Contraindications | Allergy to amide local anesthetics; severe heart block without a pacemaker; not for atrial rhythms · Nursing interventions | Continuous ECG; infusion pump — never exceed the ordered rate ; neuro checks for toxicity; seizure precautions; caution in older adults, liver disease, HF (slower clearance) · Patient education | Report confusion, ringing in the ears, numbness/tingling, or feeling shaky; continued heart monitoring is needed · Magnesium Sulfate — for Torsades de Pointes · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Torsades de pointes (polymorphic V-tach linked to low magnesium/long QT) and hypomagnesemia. 1–2 g IV, diluted, over minutes (faster in arrest) · Mechanism of action | Stabilizes the cardiac cell membrane and shortens the abnormal repolarization that triggers torsades · Adverse reactions | Flushing, sweating, hypotension (if pushed too fast); toxicity — loss of deep tendon reflexes , respiratory depression, bradycardia/heart block · Contraindications | Heart block; caution in kidney failure (magnesium builds up) · Nursing interventions | Continuous ECG; BP, RR, deep tendon reflexes ; serum magnesium level; infusion pump; calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity · Patient education | Expect warmth/flushing; report weakness or trouble breathing · Beware the Look-Alike "A" Drugs · Drug | Use | What it does to the rate · A tropine | Symptomatic bradycardia | Speeds it up · A denosine | Stable narrow-complex SVT | Briefly stops it (reset) · A miodarone | A-fib, V-tach/V-fib | Steadies and slows it · A lteplase (bonus) | Clot-busting thrombolytic — not an antiarrhythmic | None — dissolves clots · Atropine = Accelerate . Adenosine = A pause ("slam and flush"). Amiodarone = A lot of organs to watch — TELLS : T hyroid, E yes, L ungs, L iver, S kin. · Lidocaine lives in the ventricles. Torsades → magnesium.

Heparin, enoxaparin, warfarin, and the DOACs — labs, reversal agents, and bleeding precautions · Anticoagulants prevent new clots and stop existing clots from growing — they do not dissolve clots (that's a thrombolytic). They're used for DVT/PE treatment and prevention and for A-fib/A-flutter (blood pooling in the atria). The big risk for all of them is bleeding . · Heparin (Unfractionated) — Anticoagulant · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV continuous infusion (weight-based, on an electronic pump) for DVT/PE, unstable angina/chest pain (lowers the chance of MI), A-fib — often an IV bolus, then a continuous infusion; SubQ for DVT prevention. IV starts working right away (SubQ in 20–30 min); short half-life (about 0.5–2 hours, longer at high doses). Used to bridge until warfarin is therapeutic · Mechanism of action | Binds antithrombin → inactivates clotting factors (thrombin, Xa) → prevents extension of the thrombus and new clot formation · Adverse reactions | Bleeding ; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — platelets fall and, paradoxically, new clots form (can appear even weeks after heparin is stopped); bruising/hematoma at injection sites; hyperkalemia; osteoporosis with long-term use · Contraindications | Active uncontrolled bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia, history of HIT, recent brain/spine/eye surgery, uncontrolled HTN; some products are pork-derived (pork allergy) · Nursing interventions | Monitor aPTT ("two t's make an H") — dose is adjusted to the aPTT, and therapy is usually considered therapeutic at about 1.5–2.5 times the normal (control) aPTT , per the facility protocol; draw the aPTT from the opposite arm — never from the heparin line or the infused vein (falsely high); monitor the platelet count , Hgb/Hct, and K⁺. Infusion pump; never piggyback other drugs into the heparin line. Watch for external and internal bleeding (↓ BP, ↑ HR, falling Hgb/Hct). Bleeding precautions: hold pressure on needle sites longer than usual, avoid IM injections , avoid trauma and constant use of an automatic BP cuff. If HIT is suspected: stop all heparin (including flushes), notify — a direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban) may be ordered. SubQ: abdomen at least 2 inches from the umbilicus, don't aspirate or rub . Double-check doses with another nurse (high-alert). Antidote: protamine sulfate (watch for hypotension, bradycardia) · Patient education | Report bleeding gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine/stool, red or black vomit, bruising, headache, or a change in mental status; bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, electric razor); no aspirin-containing OTC products or herbal supplements unless approved; tell the dentist and other providers · Enoxaparin (Lovenox), Dalteparin — Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | SubQ once or twice daily . DVT prevention (after surgery, immobility) and treatment of DVT/PE; may replace IV heparin for unstable angina ; bridging to warfarin; can be given at home. Can be used during pregnancy (with close monitoring) · Mechanism of action | Inhibits factor Xa → prevents thrombus extension and new clots · Adverse reactions | Bleeding (fewer complications than unfractionated heparin), injection-site bruising/hematoma, lower risk of HIT · Contraindications | Active major bleeding; history of HIT (recent); pork allergy; caution with kidney impairment. Boxed warning: spinal/epidural hematoma (can cause permanent paralysis) with epidural or spinal anesthesia or a spinal puncture · Nursing interventions | Prefilled syringe: do NOT expel the air bubble (it ensures the full dose); with the patient lying down, inject deep SubQ into the abdomen ("love handles"), rotate sites; don't aspirate, don't rub ; never IM ; monitor platelets, CBC, kidney function — routine aPTT/PT isn't needed (anti-Xa level if bleeding or kidney impairment). With an epidural/spinal: frequent neuro checks of the legs (numbness, weakness). Not interchangeable with heparin. Antidote: protamine sulfate (only partly effective) · Patient education | Self-injection technique; expect small bruises; report bleeding or large bruises; report numbness or weakness of the legs right away (spinal hematoma); avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and herbal supplements unless approved; safe sharps disposal · Warfarin (Coumadin) — Vitamin K Antagonist · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO once daily at the same time . Long-term prevention: A-fib, after DVT/PE (at least 3–6 months), mechanical heart valves. Slow onset — days (full antithrombotic effect in 2–7 days), so heparin or LMWH is given with it at the start ( bridging ) until the INR is therapeutic. Narrow therapeutic window · Mechanism of action | Blocks the liver's use of vitamin K to make clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X · Adverse reactions | Bleeding/hemorrhage (black box — most likely when starting and at higher doses); bruising; reddish/brown urine, red or black stools; purple toe syndrome (dark purple, mottled, painful toes from tiny emboli); skin necrosis · Contraindications | Active bleeding; pregnancy (crosses the placenta — fetal bleeding/defects; use contraception during and for 1 month after); severe uncontrolled HTN; recent or planned brain, eye, or spinal surgery; severe liver disease; patients unable to follow up with labs or at high risk of nonadherence (e.g., unsupervised dementia, alcohol use disorder) · Nursing interventions | Monitor PT/INR — goal 2–3 (daily at the start until stable, then every 1–4 weeks); avoid IM injections; many drug and food interactions (antibiotics, amiodarone, aspirin/NSAIDs, acetaminophen in high doses, herbals such as ginkgo and garlic, cranberry juice ); hold and call the provider for fever or rash; antidote: vitamin K (phytonadione) ; fresh-frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for serious bleeding; periprocedural bridging when held · Patient education | Keep vitamin K intake consistent (leafy greens — don't suddenly add or stop them); avoid alcohol; avoid cranberry juice; no aspirin, NSAIDs, or supplements without approval; keep every INR appointment; carry an ID card; bleeding precautions; report heavier-than-usual periods, sudden cold, painful, purple toes, fever, or severe diarrhea · Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), Apixaban (Eliquis), Dabigatran (Pradaxa) — Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, fixed doses — no routine INR monitoring . Treat and prevent DVT/PE; stroke prevention in A-fib (not for mechanical valves). Rivaroxaban once or twice daily (higher doses with food); apixaban twice daily; dabigatran twice daily · Mechanism of action | Rivaroxaban and apixaban directly inhibit factor Xa ; dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor . Fast onset (hours) · Adverse reactions | Bleeding ; GI upset/dyspepsia (dabigatran); spinal hematoma with epidural/spinal procedures · Contraindications | Active bleeding; mechanical heart valves; severe kidney impairment (low creatinine clearance); pregnancy (generally avoided) · Nursing interventions | Assess kidney function (and liver), CBC; dose by age/weight/kidney function as ordered; may need bridging around procedures. Reversal: andexanet alfa for rivaroxaban/apixaban; idarucizumab (Praxbind) for dabigatran; activated charcoal for a recent overdose · Patient education | Don't skip doses — protection wears off quickly; no known food interactions; dabigatran: swallow capsules whole and keep them in the original bottle (moisture); bleeding precautions; tell every provider/dentist · Monitoring Labs and Reversal Agents · Drug | Lab to monitor | Reversal agent · Heparin (IV) | aPTT , platelets (HIT) | Protamine sulfate · Enoxaparin (LMWH) | Platelets, CBC, kidney function | Protamine sulfate (partial) · Warfarin | PT/INR (goal 2–3) | Vitamin K ; FFP or prothrombin complex concentrate · Rivaroxaban, apixaban | No routine coagulation test; kidney function | Andexanet alfa (or activated charcoal) · Dabigatran | No routine coagulation test; kidney function | Idarucizumab · Argatroban (if HIT) | aPTT, liver function | None specific — stop the drip · Teaching for Anyone on an Anticoagulant · Take it exactly as prescribed — don't stop it unless told to ; warfarin at the same time every day. · Wear or carry medical identification ; tell every provider and dentist; call the managing provider before dental work or surgery. · Keep all lab appointments (INR for warfarin). · Check with the provider before taking vitamins, cold medicines, antihistamines, antibiotics, aspirin , laxatives, or anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) — or herbal supplements. · Warfarin: avoid alcohol , and avoid big changes in diet, especially vitamin K foods (leafy greens). No known food or alcohol interactions with oral factor Xa inhibitors. · Bleeding precautions : electric razor, soft-bristled toothbrush, avoid sharps and contact sports. · Report right away: bleeding, cuts that won't stop bleeding, nosebleeds, extensive bruising, reddish/brown urine , red or black stools , vomiting blood, sudden severe headache. · Tell the provider if you might be pregnant. · Two t's make an H — pT T → H eparin. PT/INR → Warfarin , goal 2–3 . Heparin ↔ Protamine (both have an "in"), Warfarin ↔ Vitamin K . · Lovenox: leave the bubble, don't rub the belly.

Aspirin and clopidogrel prevent clots — alteplase, tenecteplase, and reteplase dissolve them · Three clot drug groups, three jobs: antiplatelets keep platelets from sticking (arterial clots — CAD, stroke prevention), anticoagulants block clotting factors (venous clots, A-fib), and thrombolytics are the only ones that dissolve a clot that's already there. · Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid) — Antiplatelet · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Emergency chest pain: 325 mg chewed (part of MONA). New angina diagnosis: 162–325 mg, then continued at 81–325 mg daily. Prevention: usually 81 mg daily — CAD/angina, after stents, ischemic stroke/TIA prevention · Mechanism of action | Irreversibly blocks platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet (about 7–10 days) · Adverse reactions | GI bleeding /ulcers, bleeding, bruising; tinnitus (toxicity); allergic reactions/bronchospasm (asthma, nasal polyps) · Contraindications | Active bleeding, bleeding disorders (hemophilia), peptic ulcer disease, children/teens with viral illness (Reye syndrome) , aspirin allergy; caution with other NSAIDs and anticoagulants (no aspirin with warfarin unless prescribed) · Nursing interventions | Assess for bleeding (stools, gums, bruising); give with food for daily doses; an H2 blocker (famotidine) or PPI may be ordered to protect the stomach; hold about 5–7 days before elective surgery as ordered (platelets must be replaced); ask about tinnitus; periodic Hgb/Hct and kidney function with long-term use · Patient education | Chew 325 mg if having chest pain and calling 911 (as directed by the provider); take the daily dose with food; keep taking aspirin even when also taking acetaminophen for pain; report black stools, ringing in the ears, or bleeding; avoid ibuprofen/other NSAIDs unless approved (they block aspirin's antiplatelet effect and add GI bleeding risk); limit alcohol (GI bleeding); don't stop daily aspirin without the provider; discard tablets that smell like vinegar; keep out of children's reach · Clopidogrel (Plavix), Prasugrel, Ticagrelor — Antiplatelets (P2Y12 Inhibitors) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily. CAD/angina, after MI, after coronary stents (with aspirin — dual antiplatelet therapy), stroke/TIA prevention, peripheral artery disease. Often added to aspirin for patients at high risk for MI. Unlike aspirin, may take a few days to reach full antiplatelet effect — a loading dose may be given in an emergency. Prasugrel and ticagrelor may be used instead of clopidogrel during coronary events and interventions · Mechanism of action | Blocks the platelet ADP receptor → prevents platelet aggregation . Does not dissolve or break apart clots · Adverse reactions | Bleeding — GI tract or other sites, bruising, GI upset; rare but life-threatening thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP — low platelets, fever, confusion, kidney problems) · Contraindications | Active bleeding (e.g., peptic ulcer, intracranial bleed); caution with other antiplatelets/anticoagulants (aspirin, NSAIDs, warfarin, DOACs), SSRIs, and kidney or liver impairment. Boxed warning: clopidogrel must be activated by a liver enzyme (CYP2C19) — poor metabolizers get less protection (a genetic test is available; another drug may be chosen) · Nursing interventions | Monitor for bleeding, CBC; hold about 5 days before surgery as ordered (unless a recent stent — the cardiologist decides); bleeding precautions; avoid omeprazole/esomeprazole (they block clopidogrel's activation — another stomach protector is chosen) · Patient education | Don't stop it on your own — especially after a stent (the stent can clot → MI); tell the dentist/surgeon and every provider before new drugs; report black stools, blood in urine, or unusual bruising; it may take longer to stop bleeding; soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid grapefruit/grapefruit juice (may weaken the effect) and herbal supplements such as garlic, ginkgo, or turmeric · Alteplase (tPA), Tenecteplase, Reteplase — Thrombolytics ("-ase") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV. Ischemic stroke (alteplase or tenecteplase within 4 hours of symptom onset (last known well) , only after a non-contrast CT rules out bleeding and BP is below 185/110); unstable (massive) PE ; MI; DVT. Tenecteplase is a single IV bolus; reteplase is two boluses; alteplase is a bolus then an infusion. Low-dose alteplase also clears occluded central lines · Mechanism of action | Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin → lyses (dissolves) the existing clot and restores perfusion · Adverse reactions | Bleeding/hemorrhage — including intracranial hemorrhage ; bleeding from IV/puncture sites; hypotension; allergic reactions including angioedema (tongue/lip swelling — higher risk in clients taking an ACE inhibitor); reperfusion dysrhythmias · Contraindications | Active bleeding ; surgery within the last 2 weeks ; stroke within the last 2 weeks ; trauma, especially head trauma ; previous thrombolytic therapy ; history of hemorrhagic stroke ; uncontrolled hypertension ; intracranial tumor/aneurysm; anticoagulant use; severe liver disease. Hemophilia depends on severity (not an automatic no) · Nursing interventions | Review the chart and interview for contraindications first ; baseline CBC, platelets, aPTT, type and crossmatch; two IV lines — don't mix with other IV drugs ; frequent VS and neuro checks ; minimize needle sticks (start lines first; no IM injections; avoid nonessential handling), pressure on puncture sites ≥30 minutes; strict bed rest; any uncontrollable bleeding → stop the infusion and notify; no anticoagulants or antiplatelets for 24 hours after tPA for stroke. Sudden severe headache, ↓ LOC, new deficits, or N/V → stop the infusion and notify (intracranial bleed) · Patient education | Report headache, bleeding, or new weakness right away; bleeding precautions (electric razor, soft toothbrush); teach stroke signs — BE-FAST, call 911, note the time · Stroke Timing at a Glance · Step | Key point · Last known well | Note the exact time of symptom onset — the clock starts here · Blood glucose | Check first — hypoglycemia mimics stroke · Non-contrast head CT | Must rule out bleeding before any thrombolytic · tPA window | Within 4 hours of symptom onset (last known well) · BP | Below 185/110 before tPA · After tPA | No anticoagulant/antiplatelet for 24 hours; neuro checks; bleeding precautions · "-ase" erASEs the clot. Antiplatelets and anticoagulants only prevent — thrombolytics dissolve . Before any "-ase": Is there a bleed, a recent bleed risk, or a sky-high BP? · Aspirin in an emergency: 325, chewed . Aspirin every day: 81 .

Atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin — nitroglycerin and isosorbide · Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Simvastatin, Lovastatin — HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors ("-statin") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily. High LDL/CAD — slows plaque buildup and lowers the risk of MI and stroke; given at discharge with CAD. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin can be taken any time of day; simvastatin and lovastatin in the evening (cholesterol is made at night; lovastatin with the evening meal) · Mechanism of action | Blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the liver enzyme that makes cholesterol → ↓ LDL and triglycerides, slight ↑ HDL; stabilizes plaque · Adverse reactions | Serious: rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown (muscle pain/weakness, dark, tea-colored urine , ↑ CK, kidney injury); liver toxicity (↑ liver enzymes); ↑ blood glucose; GI upset, headache · Contraindications | Pregnancy and breastfeeding ; active liver disease ; caution with heavy alcohol use, age 65 or older, hypothyroidism, kidney impairment, and interacting drugs that raise the risk of rhabdomyolysis (e.g., gemfibrozil , niacin, amiodarone, diltiazem, colchicine) · Nursing interventions | Baseline and periodic liver enzymes and kidney function; lipid panel to track response (about 4–12 weeks after starting or a dose change); glucose/HbA1c; CK if muscle pain; assess for muscle pain and urine color; antacids are separated from the dose by about 2 hours · Patient education | Report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness (especially with fever or feeling unwell) and dark urine ; report jaundice or upper abdominal pain; avoid or limit alcohol (liver); avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin); keep up the low-cholesterol diet (DASH), exercise, and smoking cessation; contraception · Nitroglycerin (SL, Spray, Patch, Ointment, IV), Isosorbide Mononitrate/Dinitrate — Nitrates · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | Angina — SL tablet or spray for acute attacks (and before exertion); patch, ointment, and isosorbide PO for prevention ; IV drip for recurring ischemia or unrelieved chest pain (titrated to pain and BP; usually not given if SBP is below 90 ; switched to PO or topical once symptom-free); heart failure add-on (isosorbide dinitrate + hydralazine) · Mechanism of action | Vasodilator — mainly veins → ↓ preload (less blood returning to the heart); also dilates coronary arteries → ↓ O₂ demand and ↑ O₂ supply to the heart muscle · Adverse reactions | Headache (common — means it's working; treat with acetaminophen), hypotension /orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, flushing, reflex tachycardia ; tolerance with continuous use · Contraindications | PDE5 inhibitors — sildenafil, vardenafil (within 24 h), tadalafil (within 48 h) → severe, possibly fatal hypotension; SBP below 90; head trauma/increased ICP · Nursing interventions | Check BP before each dose ; have the patient sit or lie down; SL: 1 tablet every 5 minutes, max 3 — BP before each; notify the provider if pain isn't relieved after 3; IV: pump, continuous BP; patch/ointment: wear gloves, remove the old one, clean the site, rotate hairless sites; remove patches before defibrillation (burns/arcing) · Patient education | Carry SL NTG at all times; keep it in the original amber glass bottle , tightly closed, away from light, heat, and moisture (not in a pocket against the body or in a hot car); renew the supply every 3–6 months ; moisten the tablet with saliva and let it dissolve completely under the tongue — don't swallow it whole; take it before activities that cause angina; note how long relief takes (ideally within about 3 minutes); a slight sting may mean it's fresh. Take 1 tablet every 5 minutes, max 3; if the pain isn't relieved after 3 tablets (15 minutes), call 911 . Never with sildenafil-type drugs ; rise slowly; don't stop long-acting nitrates abruptly · Nitrate Forms · Form | How it's used | Key point · SL tablet | Under the tongue at the first sign of angina | 1 every 5 min, max 3; amber glass bottle · Translingual spray | Sprayed onto or under the tongue | Don't inhale the spray; same 5-minute rule · Transdermal patch | Once daily — on in the morning, off at bedtime | 10–12-hour patch-free period prevents tolerance; rotate sites; remove before defibrillation · Ointment | Measured on dose paper, spread on hairless skin, covered | Wear gloves; don't rub it in; remove the old dose · IV drip | Titrated for unrelieved chest pain/HF | Continuous BP; infusion pump · Isosorbide (PO) | Daily/BID prevention — not for an acute attack | Swallow extended-release whole · NTG rule: 1 – 5 – 3. 1 tablet every 5 minutes, no more than 3 — pain still there after the third (15 minutes)? Call 911. · Nitrates need a night off — the patch-free period keeps them working. And "Viagra + NTG = BP drops to zero." · Statins: "Sore muscles + cola-colored pee = stop and call."

SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics recap, and digoxin as an add-on · HF drug therapy builds in layers: lifestyle + SGLT2 inhibitor → ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan, Entresto) — the first-line HF medication (an ACE inhibitor or ARB if an ARNI isn't used), plus a beta blocker and statin → a diuretic (potassium-sparing to start) → devices/IV therapy. Nitrates and digoxin can be added, or used when an ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI isn't tolerated. · Dapagliflozin (Farxiga), Empagliflozin (Jardiance) — SGLT2 Inhibitors ("-gliflozin") · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO once daily. Type 2 diabetes — and heart failure (both HFrEF and HFpEF), with or without diabetes ; also CKD. Fewer HF hospitalizations and deaths · Mechanism of action | Blocks glucose and sodium reabsorption in the kidney tubules → glucose and sodium leave in the urine → mild diuresis, ↓ preload and afterload, ↓ BP · Adverse reactions | Genital yeast infections and UTIs (sugar in the urine); volume depletion — dehydration, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension; ketoacidosis (can occur with a near-normal glucose); hypoglycemia if combined with insulin/sulfonylureas · Contraindications | Type 1 diabetes/history of DKA; dialysis/severe kidney failure; caution with volume depletion · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP, I&O, weight, kidney function, and glucose; assess for dehydration; hold before surgery (usually about 3 days, as ordered) and when the client is NPO/not eating or acutely ill ; urine glucose will be positive (expected) · Patient education | Good genital hygiene; report itching, discharge, burning with urination; stay hydrated; sick-day rule — skip it when vomiting or not eating and call the provider; report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, unusual fatigue, or trouble breathing (ketoacidosis) even if the glucose is normal · Furosemide (Lasix) — Loop Diuretic (recap) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO/IV. Fluid overload in HF — pulmonary edema, peripheral edema, weight gain. Give IV slowly. Acts fast and strong · Mechanism of action | Blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle → water follows → ↓ preload; potassium is lost · Adverse reactions | Hypokalemia (→ dysrhythmias, digoxin toxicity), dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, ototoxicity (rapid IV push) · Contraindications | Anuria; sulfa allergy (caution) · Nursing interventions | Monitor K⁺ (3.5–5.5) , BP, daily weight, I&O, lung sounds, edema · Patient education | Take it in the morning; potassium-rich foods; daily weights — report 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week ; rise slowly · Sulfa allergy tip: furosemide and the thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide) are both sulfonamide derivatives . Thiazides are listed as contraindicated with a sulfa allergy; furosemide is listed as a caution . Either way, ask about a sulfa allergy before giving any of these diuretics , and hold and notify the provider if the client reports one. · Spironolactone (Aldactone), Eplerenone — Potassium-Sparing Diuretic / Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist (MRA) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily. HF (HFrEF) — reduces hospitalizations and death; the diuretic to start in the HF layer; often paired with a loop diuretic · Mechanism of action | Blocks aldosterone → sodium and water out, potassium kept ; reduces fibrosis/remodeling of the heart · Adverse reactions | Hyperkalemia ; gynecomastia (spironolactone); kidney impairment · Contraindications | Hyperkalemia; severe kidney failure · Nursing interventions | Monitor K⁺ closely , especially with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or an ARNI (they also raise K⁺); kidney function; ECG changes (peaked T waves) · Patient education | No salt substitutes or potassium supplements; don't overdo high-potassium foods; report muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat · Digoxin (Lanoxin) — Cardiac Glycoside (add-on) · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily (IV available). Add-on for HF symptoms and for rate control in A-fib. Improves symptoms and hospitalizations, not survival. Lower doses in older adults and kidney impairment (renally excreted) · Mechanism of action | Increases contractility (stronger squeeze → ↑ cardiac output) and slows the heart rate /AV conduction · Adverse reactions | Toxicity — anorexia, nausea/vomiting , diarrhea; vision changes (blurred, yellow-green halos ); confusion, fatigue; bradycardia and dysrhythmias · Contraindications | Bradycardia/heart block; V-fib; digoxin toxicity · Nursing interventions | Apical pulse for a full minute before each dose — hold if below 60 and notify; monitor K⁺ ( hypokalemia raises toxicity — watch with loop diuretics), digoxin level (therapeutic about 0.5–2.0 ng/mL), kidney function. Antidote: digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) · Patient education | Take your pulse daily — call if below 60; report nausea, appetite loss, or visual halos; don't switch brands or take antacids at the same time; eat potassium-rich foods if on a loop diuretic · SGLT2 = Sugar Goes Through To the Toilet — so expect yeast/UTIs and dehydration , and hold it when not eating . · Digoxin: pulse below 60 — don't give it. Low K⁺ = high dig toxicity. Toxic clues: N/V + halos + slow/irregular rhythm.

Iron, folic acid, vitamin B12, epoetin alfa, hydroxyurea, and clotting factors VIII and IX · Iron, folic acid, and vitamin B12 all help the body build healthy red blood cells. Clients with anemia are advised to take ALL three supplements — no matter which deficiency they have. Pair them with an RBC-building diet: red meat and organ meat, dark leafy greens, beans, fortified cereals, and citrus with iron. · Ferrous Sulfate (and Other Iron Products) — Iron Supplement · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO (tablet or liquid) — iron deficiency and anemia; may be increased gradually from 1 tablet/day to 2–3 divided doses to reduce GI upset. IV iron when stores are very low or oral iron isn't tolerated; IM iron is given by Z-track . Continue for months — until iron stores are refilled, even after fatigue improves · Mechanism of action | Replaces the iron needed to make hemoglobin · Adverse reactions | Constipation , nausea, cramping, GI upset; dark/black stools (expected) ; liquid iron stains the teeth; IV/IM iron — anaphylaxis risk · Contraindications | Iron overload (e.g., hemochromatosis, repeated transfusions); hemolytic anemia without iron loss · Nursing interventions | Give on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal) if tolerated; with food only if GI upset is severe (less absorbed); not with milk, dairy, or antacids ; separate from other meds as directed; IM by Z-track; watch for anaphylaxis with parenteral iron; monitor Hgb/Hct · Patient education | Take with orange juice/vitamin C (better absorption); stools will be dark or black; eat high-fiber foods and drink fluids (stool softener if needed); liquid iron through a straw or with the spoon at the back of the mouth, then rinse; keep out of reach of children (iron overdose is dangerous) · Folic Acid (Folate) — Vitamin B9 · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, typically 1 mg daily (IM if malabsorption). Folic-acid deficiency anemia, alcohol use (continue as long as drinking continues), pregnancy, sickle cell disease (daily — high RBC turnover) · Mechanism of action | Needed for DNA synthesis and normal RBC maturation · Adverse reactions | Rare — mild GI upset, allergic reaction · Contraindications | Folic acid alone can correct the anemia of B12 deficiency while the nerve damage keeps progressing — one reason to give B12 along with it · Nursing interventions | Monitor CBC; assess diet and alcohol use · Patient education | Foods: dark leafy greens, beans, citrus, fortified cereals/breads; limit alcohol · Cyanocobalamin — Vitamin B12 · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO, IM, or intranasal . Dietary deficiency (e.g., strict vegan diets) → oral supplements/fortified foods. Pernicious anemia (no intrinsic factor, so B12 can't be absorbed from the gut) → typically monthly IM injections for life (very high oral doses or nasal spray/gel are alternatives) · Mechanism of action | Needed for RBC maturation and healthy nerves (myelin) · Adverse reactions | Rare — injection-site pain, mild diarrhea, itching; hypokalemia early in treatment of severe deficiency · Contraindications | Cobalt/B12 allergy · Nursing interventions | Teach self- or family injection; monitor CBC (reticulocytes rise within about a week); assess neuro symptoms (numbness/tingling, balance) — nerve recovery is slower and may be incomplete · Patient education | Pernicious anemia means lifelong B12 — stopping lets the anemia and nerve damage return; foods: meat, eggs, dairy, fortified cereals/soy milk · Epoetin Alfa (Epogen, Procrit) — Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agent · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | SubQ or IV, 1–3 times weekly. Anemia of CKD — replaces the erythropoietin the failing kidneys no longer make; also chemotherapy-related anemia · Mechanism of action | Stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells · Adverse reactions | Hypertension ; blood clots — stroke, MI, DVT (black box); seizures; headache · Contraindications | Uncontrolled hypertension · Nursing interventions | Monitor BP and Hgb ; hold and notify if Hgb is above about 10–11 g/dL (clot/stroke risk); check iron levels — iron is needed for it to work; don't shake the vial · Patient education | Hgb rises gradually over weeks; take iron supplements as ordered; check BP; report headache, chest pain, or a swollen, painful leg · Hydroxyurea (Droxia, Hydrea) — Antimetabolite for Sickle Cell Disease · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | PO daily (capsule — don't open or crush). Sickle cell disease — fewer pain crises, less acute chest syndrome, fewer transfusions; may lower stroke risk. Full benefit takes months · Mechanism of action | Raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF) , which doesn't sickle → fewer sickled cells and less adhesion to vessel walls · Adverse reactions | Bone marrow suppression — immunosuppression → infection risk ; low platelets → bleeding risk ; ↓ RBCs; teratogenic ; possible infertility; risk of later malignancy; mouth sores, hair thinning, skin/nail darkening · Contraindications | Pregnancy /breastfeeding; severe bone marrow suppression ( hold if WBC or platelets are too low ) · Nursing interventions | CBC with WBC and platelets regularly; hazardous drug — wear gloves (chemo precautions); assess for infection and bleeding · Patient education | Report fever, sore throat, unusual bleeding/bruising; reliable contraception (men and women); caregivers wear gloves when handling; regular lab draws; sun protection; no live vaccines without approval; stay hydrated; take exactly as prescribed · Factor VIII and Factor IX Concentrates — Clotting Factor Replacement · Category | Detail · Indications/dosage | IV . Hemophilia A → factor VIII; hemophilia B → factor IX (recombinant products are common). Given at the first sign of a bleed, before procedures/dental work, and prophylactically several times a week (especially children — protects the joints). Patients/families learn to give it at home . Desmopressin may be used for mild hemophilia A · Mechanism of action | Replaces the missing clotting factor so a normal clot can form · Adverse reactions | Allergic/infusion reactions; inhibitors (antibodies) that make the factor stop working; rarely, clots · Contraindications | Known allergy to the product (or its components) · Nursing interventions | Give early in a bleed; IV technique — no IM injections; assess bleeding, joints (pain, swelling, warmth), and response; report if bleeding doesn't respond (possible inhibitor) · Patient education | Home infusion: aseptic technique, correct mixing, safe sharps disposal; infuse at the first sign of a joint bleed (tingling, warmth, stiffness); keep an infusion log; medical ID; no aspirin/NSAIDs; soft toothbrush, electric razor; avoid contact sports · Which Drug for Which Blood Problem? · Problem | Drug | Must-know · Any nutritional anemia | Iron + folic acid + B12 | Take all of them · Pernicious anemia | Cyanocobalamin | Lifelong (monthly IM) · Anemia of CKD | Epoetin alfa | Hold if Hgb above ~10–11; HTN, clots · Sickle cell disease | Hydroxyurea (+ folic acid) | ↑ HbF; CBC; contraception; gloves · Hemophilia A / B | Factor VIII / factor IX | IV, often at home · Iron rules: empty stomach, orange juice, no milk or antacids , dark stools are expected , liquid through a straw . · A comes before B and 8 comes before 9 — hemophilia A = factor VIII , hemophilia B = factor IX .

The building blocks every other calculation relies on · Before any drip rate or weight-based dose can be calculated, you need to be fluent in the basic conversions underneath them — pounds to kilograms, and the metric ladder from kilograms down to micrograms. Almost every calculation error in practice traces back to a mistake at this level, not the fancier formula built on top of it. · Basic Dosage Calculation · Formula: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = Amount to administer · Worked example: Order is 500 mg PO; available as 250 mg tablets. (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets . · Worked example 2: Order is 2 mg lorazepam; available as a 4 mg/mL vial. (2 ÷ 4) × 1 mL = 0.5 mL . · Weight Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Pounds → kilograms | lbs ÷ 2.2 = kg | 154 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg · Kilograms → pounds | kg × 2.2 = lbs | 100 kg × 2.2 = 220 lbs · Almost every weight-based drug calculation in this unit starts with converting the patient's weight to kilograms — if that first conversion is wrong, every step after it is wrong too, even if the rest of the math is done perfectly. This matters directly in this module for weight-based pediatric dosing (ADHD/ASD medications) and for BSA-based chemotherapy dosing. · Metric System Conversions — the 1000 rule · Standard medical units (kg, g, mg, mcg) are each separated from their neighbor by a factor of 1000. · Direction | Rule | Example · Larger → smaller (kg→g, g→mg, mg→mcg) | Multiply by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places right) | 2 g × 1000 = 2000 mg · Smaller → larger (mcg→mg, mg→g, g→kg) | Divide by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places left) | 2500 mcg ÷ 1000 = 2.5 mg · Volume Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Milliliters → liters | mL ÷ 1000 = L | 2500 mL ÷ 1000 = 2.5 L · Liters → milliliters | L × 1000 = mL | 0.5 L × 1000 = 500 mL · Household & Volume Equivalents · Household/Metric | Equivalent · 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL · 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL (or 3 tsp) · 1 ounce (oz) | 30 mL (or 2 tbsp) · 1 cup | 240 mL (8 oz) · 1 quart (approx.) | 1000 mL (1 L)

t: IV Flow Rates, Drip Rates & Concentration
x: Getting fluid and medication into the vein at the right speed · These formulas answer one of two questions: how fast should this infusion pump run (mL/hr), or how many drops per minute should a gravity IV be set to (gtt/min) when there's no pump involved? A third formula, concentration, sets up weight-based drip calculations. · Flow Rate / Infusion Rate (mL/hr) — for infusion pumps · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Total Time (hr) = mL/hr · Worked example: Infuse 1000 mL of Normal Saline over 8 hours. 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr . · Infusion Time — working backward from a known rate · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Flow Rate (mL/hr) = Time (hours) · Worked example: A 1000 mL bag is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How long will it last? 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours . · Drip Rate (gtt/min) — for gravity IV tubing without a pump · There are two equivalent ways to reach the same answer, depending on whether you already know the mL/hr rate or are starting from the total order. · Starting point | Formula · You already know mL/hr | (mL/hr ÷ 60) × Drop Factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min · You're starting from the total order | (Total Volume [mL] × Drop Factor [gtt/mL]) ÷ Time (minutes) = gtt/min · Worked example (method 1): Infuse at 125 mL/hr using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. First, mL/min: 125 ÷ 60 = 2.08 mL/min. Then: 2.08 × 15 = 31.2, rounded to 31 gtt/min . · Worked example (method 2): Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours (480 minutes) with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min — the same answer either way. · IV Push Medication Rate · A common general safety rule for IV push medications is roughly 1 mL per minute unless the drug's specific administration guidelines say otherwise. Worked example: a 10 mL medication is administered over 10 minutes, consistent with the 1 mL/min rule. Pushing too fast is a common cause of adverse drug reactions — relevant here for IV push benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam for agitation/status epilepticus) and IV antihistamines. · Concentration Calculation — the setup step for weight-based drips · Formula: (Total mg in the bag × 1000) ÷ Total mL in the bag = Concentration (mcg/mL) · Worked example: A bag contains 400 mg of a drug in 250 mL of D5W. (400 × 1000) ÷ 250 = 1600 mcg/mL .

Calculations that scale a dose — or a diagnosis — to the patient's size · These two calculations both answer a version of the same question — how big is this patient, in a way that's useful for dosing or risk assessment? BMI is a general screening number used constantly in this module's eating-disorder content; BSA is a more precise scaling factor used specifically for chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · BMI — Body Mass Index · System | Formula · Metric | Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]² · Imperial | [Weight (lbs) × 703] ÷ [Height (in)]² · Worked example (metric): Weight 70 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625. Divide weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86 (normal weight range). · Worked example (imperial): Weight 154 lbs, height 69 inches. 154 × 703 = 108,262. Square the height: 69 × 69 = 4,761. Divide: 108,262 ÷ 4,761 = 22.74 — the same result as the metric calculation, just arrived at with different starting units. · This is exactly the calculation behind the BMI thresholds in the Anorexia Nervosa lesson: a BMI under 17 is a diagnostic marker of the disorder, and under 15 is considered extreme/life-threatening. Knowing how to compute BMI from a height and weight given in a case stem — not just recognize the threshold — is testable on its own. · BSA — Body Surface Area · BSA approximates a patient's total skin surface area in square meters (m²), and it's used specifically for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, chemotherapy agents, pediatric patients, and burn patients — situations where a small dosing error has an outsized effect. This is the calculation behind chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · Formula: BSA = √[(Height in cm × Weight in kg) ÷ 3600] · Fully worked pediatric dosing example · Order: a chemotherapy agent at 2 mg/m². Patient: 37 lb, 97 cm tall. Supply: 1 mg/mL. · Step 1 — convert weight to kg: 37 lb ÷ 2.2 = 16.8 kg · Step 2 — calculate BSA: √[(97 cm × 16.8 kg) ÷ 3600] = √[1629.6 ÷ 3600] = √0.4527 = 0.67 m² · Step 3 — calculate the dose in mg: 2 mg/m² × 0.67 m² = 1.34 mg · Step 4 — calculate the dose in mL: 1.34 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 1.34 mL to administer · Notice this whole calculation depends on the weight-to-kg conversion from the first Med Math lesson — get that first step wrong, and every subsequent step (BSA, mg dose, mL dose) inherits the error.

MAP, CPP, and weight-/unit-based infusions · This lesson groups together the calculations that show up most often in critical care and high-alert medication administration — all of them either measure perfusion pressure directly, or calculate the pump rate for a drug that manipulates that pressure. Relevant here for a client in delirium tremens, an oncology patient in septic shock, or any client on a high-alert IV drip. · MAP — Mean Arterial Pressure · Formula: (Systolic BP + [2 × Diastolic BP]) ÷ 3 = MAP · Worked example: BP is 120/80. (120 + [2 × 80]) ÷ 3 = (120 + 160) ÷ 3 = 93.3 mmHg . · MAP reflects the average pressure driving blood into the organs across the whole cardiac cycle — it's weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more time in diastole than systole. A MAP of roughly 65 mmHg or higher is generally considered necessary to maintain adequate organ perfusion in a critically ill patient. · CPP — Cerebral Perfusion Pressure · Formula: MAP − ICP = CPP · Worked example: MAP is 93, ICP is 15. 93 − 15 = 78 mmHg . · CPP depends directly on MAP — if you already calculated MAP for a patient, you're one subtraction away from CPP. A CPP that drops too low (generally below ~60 mmHg) risks cerebral ischemia, which is why both numbers are tracked together in a patient with a head injury or elevated ICP. · Weight-Based Infusion (mcg/kg/min) · Formula: (Desired mcg × kg × 60 minutes) ÷ Concentration (mcg/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient, with a concentration of 1600 mcg/mL (from the concentration calculation in the previous lesson). (5 × 80 × 60) ÷ 1600 = 15 mL/hr . · Units-Based Infusion (Units/kg/hr) — e.g., Heparin · Formula: (Units × kg) ÷ Concentration (Units/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 12 Units/kg/hr for a 100 kg patient, with a concentration of 100 Units/mL. (12 × 100) ÷ 100 = 12 mL/hr . · Both weight-based and units-based drips are high-alert medications given by infusion pump only — the shared theme across every high-alert drug is a computerized pump, frequent reassessment, and a clear plan for what triggers stopping or adjusting the rate.

Heparin, dopamine, epinephrine, amiodarone, atropine, adenosine · These are high-alert drugs on an infusion pump (or a rapid push). Find the concentration first, then solve for mL/h or mL. The concentrations below are examples — always use the label on the bag or syringe in front of you. · Heparin — units/h and mL/h · Given: heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL; order 1,000 units/h · Concentration: 25,000 ÷ 250 = 100 units/mL · Formula: ordered units/h ÷ units/mL = mL/h · Steps: 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 · Answer: 10 mL/h · Weight-based — Given: 18 units/kg/h for an 80 kg client; same bag (100 units/mL) · Steps: 18 × 80 = 1,440 units/h → 1,440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 · Answer: 14.4 mL/h (1,440 units/h) · Heparin is monitored with the PTT — "two t's make an H." Watch platelets for HIT; the antidote is protamine sulfate. · Dopamine — mcg/kg/min → mL/h · Given: dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL; order 5 mcg/kg/min; client 80 kg · Concentration: 400 mg × 1,000 = 400,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 1,600 mcg/mL · Formula: (mcg × kg × 60 min) ÷ mcg/mL = mL/h · Steps: 5 × 80 = 400 mcg/min → × 60 = 24,000 mcg/h → 24,000 ÷ 1,600 = 15 · Answer: 15 mL/h .
