(At the top of the 5–20 mcg/kg/min brady range, 20 mcg/kg/min for the same client = 96,000 ÷ 1,600 = 60 mL/h.) · Epinephrine — mcg/min → mL/h · Given: epinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL; order 2 mcg/min (brady range 2–10 mcg/min) · Concentration: 4 mg × 1,000 = 4,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 16 mcg/mL · Formula: (mcg/min × 60) ÷ mcg/mL = mL/h (no weight in this one) · Steps: 2 × 60 = 120 mcg/h → 120 ÷ 16 = 7.5 · Answer: 7.5 mL/h . At 10 mcg/min: 600 ÷ 16 = 37.5 mL/h. · Dopamine and epinephrine are vesicants — large vein or central line, check the site often; extravasation antidote is phentolamine. · Amiodarone — mg/min → mL/h · Given: amiodarone 900 mg in 500 mL; maintenance 1 mg/min · Concentration: 900 ÷ 500 = 1.8 mg/mL · Steps: 1 mg/min × 60 = 60 mg/h → 60 ÷ 1.8 = 33.33 · Answer: 33.3 mL/h (33 mL/h to the nearest whole number) · Push doses — atropine and adenosine · Drug | Given | Steps | Answer · Atropine 1 mg IV push | Prefilled syringe 0.1 mg/mL (1 mg/10 mL) | 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10 | 10 mL — repeat q3–5 min, max 3 mg (30 mL total) · Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push | Vial 3 mg/mL | 6 ÷ 3 = 2 | 2 mL , then 20 mL NS flush fast · Adenosine 12 mg (second dose) | Vial 3 mg/mL | 12 ÷ 3 = 4 | 4 mL , then flush · Beware the look-alike, sound-alike "A" drugs : A tropine speeds a slow heart, A denosine briefly stops a fast one, A miodarone is an antiarrhythmic drip. Read the label twice.

CO = HR × SV — and why a racing heart can pump less · Every rhythm, drug, and fluid decision in Perfusion is really about one goal: optimize cardiac output . Two quick formulas let you see how heart rate and stroke volume trade off against each other. · The formulas · Value | Formula | Normal · Cardiac output (CO) | Heart rate × stroke volume (mL) ÷ 1,000 = L/min | 4–8 L/min · Stroke volume (SV) | (CO in L/min × 1,000) ÷ heart rate = mL/beat | 60–100 mL/beat · Stroke volume is measured in mL per beat , but cardiac output is reported in liters per minute — so divide by 1,000 at the end (or multiply by 1,000 to go back). · Worked example 1 — finding CO · Given: HR 72 beats/min, SV 70 mL/beat · Formula: CO = HR × SV · Steps: 72 × 70 = 5,040 mL/min → 5,040 ÷ 1,000 = 5.04 L/min · Answer: CO ≈ 5 L/min — within the normal 4–8 L/min · Worked example 2 — finding SV · Given: CO 5.5 L/min, HR 80 beats/min · Formula: SV = (CO × 1,000) ÷ HR · Steps: 5.5 × 1,000 = 5,500 mL/min → 5,500 ÷ 80 = 68.75 · Answer: SV = 68.75 mL/beat (≈ 69) — within the normal 60–100 mL/beat · Worked example 3 — why tachycardia eventually LOWERS CO · Faster sounds like more output, and at first it is. But the ventricles fill during diastole , and diastole is the part of the cycle that shrinks when the rate climbs. Less filling time → less blood in the ventricle → ↓ stroke volume . · Situation | HR | SV | CO · Resting | 80 | 70 mL | 80 × 70 = 5,600 mL → 5.6 L/min · Sustained tachycardia, poor filling | 160 | 25 mL | 160 × 25 = 4,000 mL → 4.0 L/min · The rate doubled, but stroke volume fell so far that cardiac output dropped . Lose the atrial kick (as in A-fib) and filling drops even more; a fast heart also raises myocardial O₂ demand — which is why a patient in a fast rhythm can show signs of decreased CO (↓BP, dizziness, chest pain). · CO = HR × SV. If one side drops, the other has to rise to keep up. A slow heart lowers CO through HR; a very fast heart lowers CO through SV (no time to fill).

t: Heart Rate from a Strip & Ejection Fraction
x: The 6-second method and the EF percentage · Two numbers you'll calculate constantly: the heart rate off a rhythm strip, and the ejection fraction that classifies heart failure. · Heart rate — the 6-second method · Formula: number of QRS complexes in a 6-second strip × 10 = heart rate (beats/min). Count the QRS complexes (the tall spikes), not the P waves. One big box = 0.20 s, so 30 big boxes = 6 seconds. · Given: 7 QRS complexes in 6 seconds (a 7–8 count is typical for this rate) · Steps: 7 × 10 = 70 · Answer: about 70–75 beats/min → within 60–100 = normal rate · Given: 5 QRS complexes in 6 seconds · Steps: 5 × 10 = 50 · Answer: about 50 beats/min → below 60 = bradycardia. Check whether the client is symptomatic before treating. · The 6-second method is an estimate — great for regular and irregular rhythms alike (it's the go-to for A-fib). A partial complex at the edge makes the count land a little above or below the true rate. · QRS in 6 s | Rate | Interpretation (if sinus) · 3 | 30 | Very slow — brady · 5 | 50 | Brady (below 60) · 6–10 | 60–100 | Normal rate · 12 | 120 | Tachy (above 100) · 18 | 180 | SVT range (150–250) — not sinus tach · Ejection fraction (EF) · Formula: (volume ejected ÷ end-diastolic volume) × 100 = EF %. End-diastolic volume is how much blood is in the ventricle when it's full; volume ejected is what leaves with one squeeze (the stroke volume). · Given: end-diastolic volume 100 mL; 60 mL ejected · Steps: 60 ÷ 100 = 0.60 → × 100 = 60 · Answer: EF = 60% → normal · Given: end-diastolic volume 120 mL; 42 mL ejected · Steps: 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35 → × 100 = 35 · Answer: EF = 35% → below 50% = HFrEF (systolic, can't pump) · EF | Meaning · 50–70% | Normal · Below 50% | HFrEF — reduced EF, systolic HF, stretched/boggy walls that can't pump · Normal EF with HF symptoms | HFpEF — preserved EF, diastolic HF, thick stiff walls that can't fill · An echocardiogram is the go-to test for EF. Remember "Systolic = stretched" (low EF) and "Diastolic = thick" (EF preserved).

Perfusion pressure to the organs and the brain · In stroke and neuro patients you'll often need two steps : calculate MAP from the blood pressure, then subtract ICP to get cerebral perfusion pressure. · The formulas · Value | Formula | Target · MAP | (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 | 65 or higher = adequate organ perfusion · CPP | MAP − ICP | Below ~60 = cerebral ischemia risk · Diastole counts twice in MAP because the heart spends about two-thirds of each cycle in diastole. Always finish MAP before you subtract ICP. · Example 1 — post-stroke client, adequate · Given: BP 150/90, ICP 15 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 90 = 180 → 150 + 180 = 330 → 330 ÷ 3 = 110 · Step 2 (CPP): 110 − 15 = 95 mmHg · Interpret: MAP 65 or higher and CPP well above 60 → brain is being perfused · Example 2 — low BP, rising ICP · Given: BP 84/48, ICP 22 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 48 = 96 → 84 + 96 = 180 → 180 ÷ 3 = 60 · Step 2 (CPP): 60 − 22 = 38 mmHg · Interpret: MAP below 65 AND CPP far below 60 → cerebral ischemia risk. Report immediately; this client needs perfusion support. · Example 3 — normal MAP, but high ICP · Given: BP 120/75, ICP 35 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 75 = 150 → 120 + 150 = 270 → 270 ÷ 3 = 90 · Step 2 (CPP): 90 − 35 = 55 mmHg · Interpret: MAP looks fine, but CPP is below ~60 → the brain is at risk. A "normal" BP doesn't guarantee brain perfusion when ICP is high. · Example 4 — rounding a MAP · Given: BP 118/76, ICP 12 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 76 = 152 → 118 + 152 = 270 → 270 ÷ 3 = 90 · Step 2 (CPP): 90 − 12 = 78 mmHg → adequate · If MAP doesn't divide evenly (e.g., 122/78 → 278 ÷ 3 = 92.67), round only at the end, as the question directs (92.7 or 93). · Quick interpretation table · Result | Meaning | Nursing thought · MAP 65 or higher | Organs perfused | Keep monitoring · MAP below 65 | Organ perfusion at risk | Report; think decreased CO care (SBP goal above 90) · CPP about 60 or higher | Brain perfused | Keep monitoring neuro status · CPP below ~60 | Cerebral ischemia risk | Report; neuro checks; check BP and ICP trends

Cardiac output sized to the body — plus intracardiac pressures · Likely NUR 211 content — kept here for next semester; not on the Module 4 exam. · Why index cardiac output? · A CO of 4 L/min means something different for a small adult than for a very large one. Cardiac index (CI) adjusts cardiac output for body size by dividing by body surface area (BSA). · Formula · Value | Formula | Normal · Cardiac index | CO (L/min) ÷ BSA (m²) | 2.5–4 L/min/m² · Worked example · Given: CO 5.5 L/min, BSA 1.64 m² · Formula: CI = CO ÷ BSA · Steps: 5.5 ÷ 1.64 = 3.354 → rounds to 3.35 · Answer: CI ≈ 3.35 L/min/m² → within the normal 2.5–4 · Bedside monitors usually calculate BSA and CI automatically once height and weight are entered. · Normal intracardiac pressures (likely 211) · Location | Normal (mmHg) · Right atrium | 0–8 · Right ventricle | Systolic 15–25 / diastolic 0–8 · Pulmonary artery | Systolic 15–25 / diastolic 8–15 · Left atrium | 4–12 · Left ventricle | Systolic 110–130 / diastolic 4–12 · Aorta | Systolic 110–130 / diastolic 70–80 · Pattern to notice: the right side is a low-pressure system (pumps only to the lungs); the left side is high pressure (pumps to the whole body) — which is why the left ventricle is the thickest chamber.

Tracking what goes in, what comes out, and what IV fluids do to cells · Intake and output tracking is really just accounting for fluid — but a couple of categories have special rules that are easy to get wrong, and tonicity explains why the choice of IV fluid itself matters beyond just the volume. This is directly relevant to fluid management in cancer/chemotherapy patients, HIV/AIDS patients with diarrhea or wasting, and any client receiving IV psychiatric medications. · What counts as intake · Oral (PO) fluids — water, juice, soda, milk, coffee · Liquid foods — soups, broths, gelatin, sherbet, sorbet, pudding · Ice chips — recorded as half the original volume (200 mL of ice chips = 100 mL intake), since ice chips are mostly air/space between solid pieces · IV fluids — maintenance fluids, boluses, and piggyback medications (like antibiotics) · Tube feedings — formula and water flushes (relevant for a client with anorexia nervosa on enteral nutritional rehabilitation) · What counts as output · Urine — voided, catheterized, or urostomy drainage · Emesis (vomitus) — relevant for a client with bulimia or chemotherapy-induced nausea · Liquid stool — diarrhea or colostomy drainage · Wound drainage — from JP drains, Hemovacs, or chest tubes · Suction — gastric (NG) or respiratory · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake of 3000 mL, output of 800 mL. 3000 − 800 = +2200 mL (a positive balance, meaning the patient is retaining more fluid than they're losing). · Insensible Loss · Fluid lost through the skin and lungs that can't be directly measured. Standard estimate: 600–900 mL/day , or roughly 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Worked example: a 70 kg patient: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/hr, or roughly 840 mL/day. · Fluid Weight Calculation · Rule of thumb: a 1 kg weight change equals roughly 1 L of fluid change. Worked example: a patient's weight rises 2 kg over two days — that's roughly a 2 L fluid gain, not necessarily 2 kg of actual tissue. · An output under 30 mL/hr is always reported as a potential emergency — it signals inadequate perfusion to the kidneys. · Tonicity — what different IV fluids do to cells · Type | Solute concentration vs. inside the cell | Effect on the cell | Examples | Clinical use · Hypertonic | Higher outside the cell | Water leaves the cell — it shrinks (plasmolysis) | 3% or 5% NaCl; 10% Dextrose in Water | Cerebral edema, severe hyponatremia · Hypotonic | Lower outside the cell | Water enters the cell — it swells or bursts (cytolysis) | 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline) | Dehydration — pushes water back into cells · Isotonic | Equal inside and outside | No net water movement — equilibrium maintained | 0.9% Normal Saline, Lactated Ringer's, D5W | Routine IV fluid replacement and hydration · A simple way to remember the direction: hyper tonic pulls water OUT of the cell (think 'hyper' = high solute outside, pulling water toward it), while hypo tonic pushes water IN . Isotonic is the 'do no harm' default fluid.

t: Renal Math: Urine Output, Fluid Restriction & Daily Weights
x: The calculations behind the AKI, CKD, and fluid-balance lessons · Hourly Urine Output (mL/kg/hr) · Formula: Urine output (mL) ÷ Hours ÷ Weight (kg) = mL/kg/hr. The minimum acceptable adult output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (roughly 30 mL/hr). · Minimum for a given client: Weight (kg) × 0.5 = minimum mL/hr. A 70 kg client needs at least 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr . · Worked example: An 80 kg client voids 200 mL over 8 hours. 200 ÷ 8 = 25 mL/hr; 25 ÷ 80 = 0.31 mL/kg/hr — below 0.5, so it's reported as an early warning of AKI. · 24-Hour Output — naming the problem · 24-hour urine output | Term · Less than 400–500 mL | Oliguria (the oliguric phase of AKI: below 400 mL/day) · Less than 50 mL | Anuria · 4–5 L/day | Diuretic phase of AKI — watch for fluid volume deficit · More than 3 L/day after an obstruction is relieved | Postobstructive diuresis · Fluid Restriction · Formula: Previous 24-hour urine output + about 500–600 mL (insensible losses) = Fluid allowance for the next 24 hours. (Some references use 500–800 mL.) · Worked example: A client in the oliguric phase put out 350 mL of urine yesterday. 350 + 500 = 850 mL to 350 + 600 = 950 mL — a fluid allowance of about 850–950 mL for today. · The fluid allowance is spread across all 24 hours — with sips, ice chips, and frequent mouth care for thirst — and it has to include the fluid used to take medications. · Daily Weights — 1 kg = 1 L · Rule: a 1 kg weight change equals about 1 L of fluid (about 2.2 lb per liter). Weigh at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing. · Worked example: Yesterday 72.0 kg; today 74.5 kg. 74.5 − 72.0 = 2.5 kg = about 2.5 L of retained fluid . · Worked example (pounds): A weight gain of 4.4 lb ÷ 2.2 = 2 kg = about 2 L of fluid. · BUN:Creatinine Ratio · Formula: BUN ÷ Creatinine. Normal is about 10:1 to 20:1; above 20:1 points toward a prerenal cause (dehydration, low perfusion). · BUN | Creatinine | Ratio | Points toward · 48 mg/dL | 1.2 mg/dL | 48 ÷ 1.2 = 40:1 | Prerenal — BUN rising out of proportion (dehydration) · 80 mg/dL | 8.0 mg/dL | 80 ÷ 8 = 10:1 | Intrarenal or postrenal — both rising together · Phosphate Binder Dose per Meal (Sevelamer) · Formula: Total daily dose ÷ Number of meals the client actually eats = Dose per meal · Worked example: Sevelamer 4,800 mg/day. Three meals a day: 4,800 ÷ 3 = 1,600 mg with each meal . The same client skips breakfast and eats 2 meals: 4,800 ÷ 2 = 2,400 mg with each meal . · The number of meals comes from the client's eating pattern, not a standard schedule — fewer meals means a bigger dose with each meal. And no meal, no binder. · Maximum-Rate Problems · Formula: Dose (mg) ÷ Maximum rate (mg/min) = Minimum time (minutes) · Worked example: High-dose IV furosemide is infused no faster than 4 mg/min (ototoxicity). For a 120 mg dose: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes minimum . · Rapid IV furosemide is what causes the tinnitus and hearing loss — if the math says 30 minutes, it never goes in faster, even when the client is fluid overloaded. · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake: PO 600 mL + IV 900 mL + ice chips 200 mL (counts as 100 mL) = 1,600 mL. Output: urine 450 mL + emesis 150 mL = 600 mL. 1,600 − 600 = +1,000 mL — a positive balance (fluid retention).

t: Dialysis Fluid Math: Hemodialysis, PD & CRRT
x: How much fluid came off — and how to count it · Hemodialysis — Fluid Removal Goal · Formula: Pre-dialysis weight − Dry (target) weight = Fluid to remove (1 kg = 1 L) · Worked example: Pre-dialysis weight 78.4 kg; dry weight 76.0 kg. 78.4 − 76.0 = 2.4 kg = about 2.4 L to remove. The post-dialysis weight confirms how much actually came off. · Peritoneal Dialysis — Net Ultrafiltration · Formula: Outflow (drained) − Inflow (instilled) = Net fluid removed. A negative result means the client absorbed (retained) dialysate. · Inflow | Outflow | Result | Meaning · 2,000 mL | 2,500 mL | +500 mL | 500 mL removed — recorded as output · 2,000 mL | 1,800 mL | −200 mL | 200 mL retained — counts toward intake; check for kinks, constipation, and position · Multiple exchanges: add the net result of each one. Exchanges of +300, +150, and −100 mL = +350 mL net removed. If drainage is short by 500 mL or more over several exchanges, evaluate for fluid retention and notify the provider. · PD outflow is not urine. Record the client's true urine output separately from the dialysate drained. · CRRT — Hourly Fluid Balance · The nurse totals all intake and output every hour and adjusts to meet the ordered hourly balance goal. · Formula: Hourly net fluid removal needed = Hourly intake (IV fluids, meds, feedings, replacement fluid) + Desired hourly fluid loss · Worked example: The goal is a net loss of 100 mL/hr. This hour the client receives IV fluid 50 mL + tube feeding 60 mL + IV meds 40 mL = 150 mL. To achieve −100 mL, the machine must remove 150 + 100 = 250 mL of fluid from the client this hour.

Boxes, intervals, pacemaker rates, rhythm rates · Graph paper · Item | Value · Little box | 0.04 s · Big box (5 little boxes) | 0.20 s · Standard strip | 6 seconds (30 big boxes) · Heart rate | QRS complexes in 6 s × 10 · Normal intervals · Interval | Normal | Abnormal · PR interval (start of P to start of QRS) | 0.12–0.20 s (no more than one big box) | Longer = think heart block (problem with the PR interval) · QRS complex | 0.06–0.10 s — narrow, fits in a big box | 0.12 s or more = wide (ventricular origin) · Intrinsic (pacemaker) rates · Pacemaker site | Rate · SA node | 60–100 · AV node | 40–60 · Purkinje fibers / ventricles | 20–40 · Each backup pacemaker is slower than the one above it: 60–100 → 40–60 → 20–40 . The lower the source, the slower (and less reliable) the beat. · Rhythm rate ranges · Rhythm | Rate · Normal sinus rhythm | 60–100 · Sinus bradycardia | Below 60 · Sinus tachycardia | Above 100 (usually 100–150) · SVT | 150–250 (P waves typically lost around 160) · A-fib | Varies — can be normal when controlled; fast when uncontrolled; always irregular · A-flutter | Atrial flutter waves very fast; ventricular rate often 75–150 · V-tach | Fast, wide QRS — usually 100–200 (recognize: lethal) · V-fib / asystole | No countable rate — no cardiac output · Treat-threshold numbers (2025 AHA) · Bradyarrhythmia: HR typically below 50 AND symptomatic → treat · Tachyarrhythmia: HR typically 150 or more → tachy algorithm

Cardiac markers, lipids, coagulation, electrolytes · Cardiac markers · Lab | Normal | Key point · Troponin | ~0 (undetectable) | Gold standard for heart damage; drawn on arrival and serially (≈ q6h × 2); delayed rise — one normal value doesn't rule out MI; first lab priority with chest pain · CK-MB | Drawn with troponin | Heart-muscle enzyme; supports troponin · BNP | Below 100 pg/mL | Above 100 = HF; higher = worse · High-sensitivity (HS) BNP | 400 or below | Above 400 = abnormal · Lipids · Lab | Goal · Total cholesterol | Below 200 · LDL | Below 100 with CAD (below 130 otherwise) · HDL | Above 40–60 (higher is better — "H = healthy") · Triglycerides | Below 150 · Coagulation · Lab | Monitors | Goal / antidote · PTT (aPTT) | Heparin — "two t's make an H" | Antidote: protamine sulfate · PT/INR | Warfarin | INR 2–3 ; antidote: vitamin K · Platelets | Heparin therapy | Watch for a falling count = HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia); LMWH has a lower HIT risk · Electrolytes and glucose · Lab | Value / why it matters · Potassium (K⁺) | 3.5–5.5 ; low or high K⁺ triggers dysrhythmias; ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise K⁺ · Magnesium (Mg²⁺) | Low Mg²⁺ is linked to torsades → give magnesium; check with long-term diuretic use · Blood glucose (stroke) | Check first — hypoglycemia mimics stroke; avoid both hypo- and hyperglycemia after stroke · Heparin → PTT (two t's make an H). Warfarin → PT/INR, goal 2–3 . Heparin's antidote is protamine; warfarin's is vitamin K.

below 50% = HFrEF · Medication hold parameters and rules · Drug / rule | Number · Beta blocker | Hold/notify if HR below 60 or SBP below 90 · Calcium channel blocker | Hold if SBP below 90 or HR below 60 · Nitroglycerin SL | 1 tablet every 5 min , max 3 ; not relieved after 3 (15 min) → call 911 · Aspirin (chest pain) | 325 mg chewed ; 81 mg daily for prevention · Morphine (MONA) | 2–4 mg IV push · Heart failure weights | Daily; report 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week · ARNI (Entresto) after ACE inhibitor | 36-hour washout · ARB after ACE inhibitor | Wait 6 weeks after stopping the ACE inhibitor · Emergency rhythm doses (2025 AHA) · Drug | Dose · Atropine (brady) | 1 mg IV q3–5 min, max 3 mg · Dopamine drip (brady) | 5–20 mcg/kg/min · Epinephrine drip (brady) | 2–10 mcg/min · Adenosine (stable narrow regular tachy) | 6 mg rapid IV push + 20 mL NS flush , then 12 mg · Stroke timing · Item | Number · tPA (alteplase, tenecteplase) window | Within 4 hours of symptom onset (last known well) — after CT rules out bleeding · BP before tPA | Must be below 185/110 · After tPA | No anticoagulant/antiplatelet for 24 hours · CT and ischemia | Bleed shows immediately; ischemic damage may not show for ~48 h · Procedures and timing · Item | Number · Post-cath vitals | q15 min × 1 h → q30 min × 1 h → hourly ; site + distal pulses each time · Pressure after sheath removal | Hold ≈ 10 min · Puncture sites during thrombolytics | Pressure at least 30 min · A-fib and cardioversion | A-fib longer than 48 h → anticoagulate first; Recognize only means know it on a strip; treatment comes in a later course. · Exemplar | Scope for 114 | Where · Sinus rhythm, sinus brady, sinus tachy | Recognize and treat | 3.5, 4.1–4.3 · A-fib, A-flutter, SVT | Recognize and treat | 3.5, 4.3 · PVC, V-tach, Torsades, V-fib, asystole | Recognize only — treatment in Medical Emergencies | 3.6 · Pacemaker — atrial, ventricular, dual | Recognize only — care in 211 | 3.8 · Heart block | Basic understanding — types not differentiated in 114 | 3.7 · Pulmonary emboli | Know | 6.1–6.3 · Stroke — ischemic vs. hemorrhagic, CVA & TIA | Know | 6.4–6.8 · Hemophilia | Know | 7.3 · Anemias — iron deficiency, folic acid deficiency (B12) | Know | 7.1–7.2 · Sickle cell disease | Know | 7.4 · Coronary artery disease | Know | Part 2 · Basic heart failure — left vs. right, systolic vs. diastolic | Know | Part 5 · Medication on the list | Card · Beta blockers · calcium channel blockers | 8.2 · ACE inhibitors & ARBs · ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) | 8.1 · Vasopressors (for bradycardia) · atropine | 8.4 · Anticoagulants/antiplatelets · thrombolytics | 8.5 · Lipid-lowering agents (statins) · nitrates (nitroglycerin) | 8.6 · Antiarrhythmics | 8.3 · Supplements for anemia · hydroxyurea · clotting factors for hemophilia | 8.7 · Also on the list: medications from previous content areas and 113 Those are not in these notes, so pull your 113 med list to review alongside Part 8. · Part 1 · Perfusion Foundations & Diagnostics · Perfusion is blood delivery to tissue. Almost every perfusion problem is one of three things — too little volume or pumping (the heart is not moving enough blood), narrowing (a vessel is too small), or clots (something is blocking flow). The diagnostics in this part tell you which one you are dealing with. · 1.1 The Big Picture — Volume, Narrowing, Clots ·  | Volume | Narrowing | Clots · Exemplars | Heart failure, tachy/brady cardia, anemia, hemophilia | Coronary artery disease | Pulmonary emboli, brain attack (stroke) · Builds on | Fluid & electrolytes | Hypertension, nephrosclerosis | DVT · Treatment | Fluid balance, heart rate control | Diet and exercise | Prevention · Medications | Diuretics/fluids, heart rate meds, epoetin, clotting factors | Statins, BP meds, antiplatelets/anticoagulants | Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, thrombolytics · 1.2 Blood Flow Through the Heart · 1. Body → superior/inferior vena cava · 2. Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle · 3. Pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs · 4. Left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle · 5. Aortic valve → aorta → rest of the body · Coronary arteries are perfused in DIASTOLE Every other organ is perfused during systole. The left ventricle pushes blood out the aorta, the valve snaps shut, and the blood that falls back fills the coronary arteries. The heart needs good rest periods to perfuse. The left coronary artery is the "widow maker" — it supplies the entire left side of the heart. · 1.3 Key Terms · Term | Definition | What it tells the nurse · Preload | Volume of blood returning to the right atrium (end of diastole) | Volume. Fluid volume overload = high, dehydration = low. Treat with diuretics · Afterload | Resistance the ventricle pumps against | Pressure. Too much (HTN, vasoconstriction) wears the heart out; too little = no blood left to perfuse the heart. Treat with BP meds · SVR / PVR | Afterload for the left side (systemic) / right side (pulmonary) | Left pumps to the body, right pumps to the lungs · Stroke volume | Volume ejected from the ventricle per beat | Described in volume · Ejection fraction | Percent of blood ejected per beat | Normal 50–70% . Below 50% = heart failure. Never above 70% — some must stay behind. Only an echo gives EF · Cardiac output | Stroke volume × heart rate | Normal 4–8 L/min — say LITERS per MINUTE. Cardiac index adjusts for body size · Contractility | How easily the heart snaps back to its shape | Poor snap-back = big and boggy heart · Compliance | How easily something stretches |  · Arteriosclerosis | Arteries hardened and narrowed | Smoking, HTN, diabetes, drug abuse · Atherosclerosis | Plaque buildup inside the arteries | High cholesterol, genetics · Ischemia | Lack of blood supply to tissue | Reversible — priority is restoring oxygen and perfusion · Necrosis | Tissue death | Not reversible · Heart murmur | Whoosh from a valve not snapping back correctly | A new murmur means something changed — often fluid overload in HF · Worked cardiac output example HR 70 × stroke volume 70 mL = 4,900 mL/min = 4.9 L/min . Convert mL to L before comparing to the 4–8 L/min range. · 1.4 Cardiac Labs · Lab | What it tells you | Key point · Troponin | Breakdown of heart muscle fibers | Normal is 0. Rises slowly — drawn in a series (about q6h). Priority lab with chest pain · CK-MB | CK = any muscle; MB = cardiac muscle | Cardiac-specific breakdown · Myoglobin | Muscle breakdown all over the body | Not cardiac-specific · BNP | Heart is big and boggy, not snapping back | High in HF — the routine HF lab, changes acute and chronic · Electrolytes | K⁺, Mg, Ca, Na reflect cardiac status | Check K⁺ with diuretics. Tall peaked T = hyperkalemia · Lipid panel | Cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, LDL | Evaluates atherosclerosis · PTT | Monitors heparin | "Two T's make an H" · PT/INR | Monitors warfarin | Most HF and A-fib patients are on an anticoagulant · ACT | Blood-thinner level | Checked after cardiac cath · 1.5 Stress Test · Evaluates how well the heart works under pressure. Treadmill, or medication-based for patients who cannot get on the treadmill. · Before · EKG leads and vitals hooked up; baseline vitals and assessment ; heart and lung sounds · NPO about 2 hours, verify consent , crash cart close by · Hold medications that can be held · During · About 20 minutes on the treadmill, compared to the baseline vitals · Stop the test (the patient fails) if HR passes the limit, the rhythm or EKG changes, or the patient has chest pain, SOB, abnormal beats, or looks pale and diaphoretic · 1.6 Echocardiogram · Shows structure, valves opening and closing, blood flow, muscle size, and clots in the ventricles. It is the only way to get ejection fraction , and it tells you systolic vs. diastolic HF. ·  | Transcutaneous | Transesophageal (TEE) · Route | Through the skin | Through the esophagus · Picture | Less clear, less invasive | Much more clear · Before | NPO | NPO since midnight, consent, baseline vitals · After | No post-op care | Vitals; liquids → soft foods → solids; watch respiratory rate (anesthesia) · 1.7 Cardiac Cath (Angiogram) · If the patient fails the stress test, this is next — the only test that shows perfusion of the coronary arteries . Contrast dye shows narrowing and clots. A 100% occlusion may be fixed in the cath; otherwise open heart/CABG. Wrist (radial) is the most common, preferred site with fewer complications; femoral has the most risk and post-op care. · Before · NPO, consent, vitals · Trim and prep the groin if femoral · Evaluate the kidneys — contrast dye is nephrotoxic; fluids/bicarb may be given · Do not keep the patient flat before the procedure · After — the red flag is bleeding · Vitals q15 min × 1 hour, then q30 min × 2, then hourly — check the site every time . Groin site: patient lies flat (length depends on the closure). Check bilateral pulses, temperature, and color of the leg, plus coag studies and ACT. Hematoma → hold pressure . · Watch for | Red flags · Vital signs | BP drops and HR goes up = internal bleeding · Site | Bleeding, bruising, hematoma (hard, enlarged, painful, tight, big bulge) · Back/flank | One-sided back pain = retroperitoneal hemorrhage (seen on CT) · Extremity | Unequal pulses, cool or pale leg = poor perfusion · Not assessed | Gag reflex is NOT part of post-cath care · Part 2 · Decreased Cardiac Output, CAD & Angina · When the heart cannot move enough blood, every organ is short on oxygen. Anemia, heart failure, bradycardia, and tachycardia all present as decreased cardiac output , so the nursing care is the same — assess first, find the cause, support perfusion. CAD is the "narrowing" version: plaque shrinks the coronary arteries and the heart muscle itself is starved. · 2.1 Signs of Decreased Cardiac Output · System | Findings · Skin | Pale, cyanotic, cool and clammy, diaphoresis · Cardiovascular | Low BP, high HR, weak/thready/diminished pulses, poor cap refill, dependent edema, syncope · Respiratory | SOB, high RR, decreased O₂ sat · Neurologic | Dizziness, confusion, fatigue · Renal / GI | Decreased urine output, nausea · Anemia looks like decreased cardiac output The patient is tired, pale, tachycardic, and short of breath because tissues are not getting oxygen. Nursing care is the same — space activities with rest periods , small self-care tasks, hydration. · 2.2 Priority Interventions · Fluid balance — give fluids only if indicated; still low pressure → vasopressors · Monitoring — EKG/telemetry, serum labs, urine output, O₂ PRN · Position — HOB up if BP is okay and MAP > 60; MAP < 60 → lay flat with legs up · Avoid Valsalva (so they do not vagal out) · Bed rest and clustered care with rest periods between activities · 2.3 CAD — Risk Factors · Modifiable | Nonmodifiable · Stress, smoking, diet, exercise, diabetes, hypertension | Age, ethnicity (African American/Hispanic), male gender, genetics/family history · Women and the elderly May complain of indigestion that is actually cardiac. Do not assume it is only GI. · 2.4 Priority Assessments, Labs & Diagnostics · Chest pain and what relieves it (rest and nitro vs. not) · 12-lead EKG ; troponin (priority), CK-MB, BNP; cholesterol and triglycerides · Echo and stress test → coronary angiogram if the EKG and troponin are normal but CAD is still suspected · Poor perfusion of the heart muscle can cause dysrhythmias · 2.5 Stable vs. Unstable Angina ·  | Stable angina | Unstable angina · Relief | Relieved by rest and nitroglycerin | Still has pain after rest and 3 NTG tablets · Meaning | Predictable, demand-related chest pain | Emergency — heart muscle is not getting enough blood · 2.6 Nitroglycerin — the High-Yield Rules · Rule | Detail · Action | Vasodilator — opens the vessels · Dose | 1 tablet every 5 minutes, maximum 3 in 15 minutes . Not better after 3 → 911/ER . A 4th tablet is the wrong answer · Watch | BP drops and HR goes up · Teach | Carry it at all times; amber glass, away from sun and light · 2.7 Chest Pain Priorities · MONA — Morphine, O₂, Nitroglycerin, Aspirin · Start two large-bore IVs (procedures may follow) · Heparin drip prevents new clots — it does NOT break up an existing clot. Plavix prevents platelet aggregation (works differently from heparin) · Metoprolol lowers dysrhythmia risk and workload · Lisinopril is not indicated during acute chest pain · After discharge: statin, possibly aspirin, limit salt, more fruits and vegetables · 2.8 Practice Set — Worked Answers · Question | Answer | Why · Test for a "fluttering" heartbeat? | 12-lead EKG | Could be SVT, A-fib, or flutter · Pain not better after 3 NTG? | Unstable angina | Emergency · Intervention contraindicated now? | A 4th NTG tablet | Max is 3 · What else should be done? | Two large-bore IVs | He may need several procedures · Priority lab? | Troponin | Is the heart being damaged? · Medication NOT indicated now? | Lisinopril | Lowers BP — not an acute chest pain drug · EKG and troponin normal — next test? | Coronary angiogram | Shows whether arteries are narrowed · All before cath EXCEPT? | Keeping flat in bed | Flat bed rest is done AFTER · All after cath EXCEPT? | Gag reflex | Watch back pain, groin, pedal pulses · Purpose of heparin drip? | Prevent a clot from forming | Will not break up the existing one · Purpose of Plavix? | Prevent platelet aggregation | Different from heparin · Purpose of metoprolol? | Decrease risk of dysrhythmias | Beta blocker

x: Strip basics, the 5 questions, sinus/atrial/ventricular rhythms, blocks, pacers · treatment, ACLS, cardioversion · Part 3 · EKG Basics & Rhythm Interpretation · The EKG records the heart's electrical activity. Assess the patient first — if the patient is symptomatic, treat; if not, do not treat. The goal is always optimizing cardiac output. This part identifies the rhythm; Part 4 treats it. · 3.1 Strip Basics · Item | What to know · Big box | 0.20 seconds · Little box | 0.04 seconds · Strip length | 6 seconds · Heart rate | Count the QRS complexes on the 6-second strip × 10 · Electrodes | Change stickers every 24 hours to reduce artifact · Artifact | False readings — if you cannot read the strip, assess the patient · 12-lead EKG | 10 stickers (each arm and leg + 6 on the chest), 12 views at once — shows where perfusion is lacking · 3.2 Electrical Conduction — Who Is the Pacemaker? · Structure | Rate | Job · SA node | 60–100 | The pacemaker — tells the heart to beat · AV node | 40–60 | Takes over if the SA node fails · Bundle of His → R/L bundle branches | — | Carries the impulse into the ventricles · Purkinje fibers | 20–40 | Last backup pacemaker · 3.3 The Waves · Wave | What it means | Normal · P wave | SA node fired — atrial depolarization | Easy to see, facing up. No SA firing = no P · PR interval | Start of P to the Q | Fits in a big box · QRS complex | Ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization) | Narrow, fits in a big box; can point up or down · T wave | Ventricular repolarization (resting) | Rounded. Tall/peaked = hyperkalemia · 3.4 The 5 Questions · Step 1 — HR: count QRS × 10 · Step 2 — Regular? Same gap between each QRS · Step 3 — P wave for every QRS? · Step 4 — QRS within a big box? · Step 5 — PR interval within a big box? · All yes + HR 60–100 = normal sinus rhythm Any NO means do not call it sinus. Atrial = problem with the P wave. Ventricular = problem with the QRS. · 3.5 Sinus & Atrial Rhythms — You Can Live With These · Rhythm | Rate | Regular? | P wave | Key clue · Normal sinus | 60–100 | Yes | Yes | Breaks no rules · Sinus brady | < 60 (ex: 40) | Yes | Yes | Everything normal except the rate · Sinus tachy | > 100 (ex: 110) | Yes | Yes | Everything normal except the rate · SVT | 150+ (ex: 160) | Yes | No | QRS fits in a big box → problem is above the ventricles. PSVT starts/stops suddenly · A-fib | Any (RVR > 100) | No | No | 3 hallmarks: irregular, no P, fibrillating baseline . #1 rhythm people walk around with · A-flutter | Any | Either | No | Sawtooth flutter waves — sister to A-fib, treated the same · A-fib = blood pools = clots = stroke The atria quiver instead of contracting, so blood pools and clots. A-fib is the #1 cause of stroke — A-fib patients take an antiarrhythmic (or rate control) plus a blood thinner every day . · 3.6 Ventricular Rhythms — Recognize Only · Scope for 114: recognize these on a strip Treatment of ventricular rhythms is taught in Medical Emergencies . For this exam, know what each looks like and that V-tach, Torsades, and V-fib are lethal . · Rhythm | Look for | Danger · PVC | Sinus rhythm with a broken (wide) QRS | "Sinus rhythm with PVC" — QRS breaks the big box rule · Unifocal PVC | Same shape every time | Usually not concerning · Multifocal PVC | Different shapes (one up, one down) | More concerning · Couplet | Two PVCs together | Very concerning · Run | 3 or more PVCs in a row | = V-tach · R on T | PVC lands on the T wave | Can trigger V-tach/V-fib · V-tach | Big wide QRS — all you see are ventricles | LETHAL · Torsades de pointes | Twisting V-tach; low magnesium | LETHAL — medical emergency · V-fib | No QRS, no P, quivering baseline | LETHAL · Asystole | Flat line | No electrical activity · Agonal | Slow, wide, dying complexes | Think DNR/dying · PEA | Organized rhythm on monitor, no pulse | Check the patient, not just the monitor · 3.7 Heart Blocks — Basic Understanding · A heart block breaks the PR interval rule — typically more P waves than QRS complexes · Heart blocks only cause bradycardia, never tachycardia · Not always dangerous — look at the heart rate . A block with HR 25 is an emergency · 114 does not differentiate the types (1st, 2nd, 3rd degree) — know what a block is, how to spot it, and that it causes bradycardia · 3.8 Pacemaker Rhythms — Recognize Only · Know atrial, ventricular, and dual (AV) paced rhythms on a strip. Pacemaker care is covered in 211 . · Strip finding | Meaning · Spike before the P wave | Atrial paced · Spike before the QRS | Ventricular paced — the huge, ugly QRS is an expected finding · Spike before both | AV (atrial + ventricular) paced · Spike on the T wave / not firing | Malfunctioning pacemaker — can cause R on T · Demand paced | Only fires when HR drops below the set rate · Pacemaker patients can still get HR-lowering meds Pacemaker set at 60, HR 60 — you can still give a medication that lowers HR because the pacemaker keeps the heart above its set rate . · 3.9 Practice Set — Worked Answers · Description | Answer | Why · HR 40, regular, P before every QRS, narrow QRS | Sinus bradycardia | All rules met, rate too slow · HR 110, regular, P before every QRS, narrow QRS | Sinus tachycardia | All rules met, rate too fast · HR 160, regular, no P wave, narrow QRS | SVT | Narrow QRS = above the ventricles · Irregular, no P, chaotic baseline, narrow QRS | A-fib | 3 hallmarks — antiarrhythmic + blood thinner · No P, sawtooth baseline, narrow QRS | A-flutter | Treated the same as A-fib · Sinus rhythm with a wide beat, same shape each time | Unifocal PVC | Usually not concerning · Wide beats of different shapes | Multifocal PVC | More concerning · 3 or more wide beats in a row | V-tach | Lethal · No QRS, no P, quivering baseline | V-fib | Lethal · Spike right before each P wave | Atrial pacemaker | Spike belongs before P or QRS · PR interval way too long, HR 25 | Heart block | Dangerous because of the rate · 8 QRS complexes on a 6-second strip | HR 80 | 8 × 10 · Part 4 · Treating Dysrhythmias · Same four ideas every time: the goal is optimizing cardiac output, the priority is assessment (symptomatic or not), prevention means looking for the cause, and maintenance asks whether long-term therapy is needed. Most rhythm problems are fixed by treating the cause, not by reaching for a cardiac drug. · 4.1 Bradycardia (Slow) · Cause | Fix the cause first · Opioids/fentanyl/overdose | Naloxone (Narcan) · Hypothermia | Warm the patient · Sleep apnea | Tell them to breathe · Just climbed stairs | Let them rest and breathe · Cardiac meds (CCB, beta blockers, digoxin), anesthesia, SA node failure, ischemia, hypoxia, hyperkalemia | Treat the cause; support ABCs · Atropine is first line — IV push, stimulates the SA node, very fast onset, short half-life. Patient on telemetry (HR, rhythm, O₂, BP). A band aid; can be given up to 3 times · Atropine not working → transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine drip (quick on and off) · Pacemaker = bradycardia only. Temporary (pads on the chest, or invasive) vs. permanent (implanted) · Never give atropine for A-fib · 4.2 Tachycardia (Fast) · Cause | Fix the cause first · Exercise | Sit down and rest · Dehydration | Fluids · Fever | Tylenol · Anxiety, fear, anger | Calm the patient · Pain | Pain medication · Caffeine, cocaine/meth, allergic reaction, infection, blood loss, anemia, FVO, HF, CAD, respiratory disease | Treat the cause · Adenosine is first line for regular tachy rhythms like SVT — it "reboots" the heart, stopping it 6–10 seconds. Half-life ~10 seconds, so SLAM it in a big IV; a slow push can fail. x: HF stages, systolic vs. diastolic, left vs. right · DVT/PE · ischemic vs. hemorrhagic stroke, CVA vs. TIA · Part 5 · Heart Failure · Heart failure is how well the heart pumps blood to the body. It is a chronic condition that can have acute exacerbations , and it is the classic "volume" problem — both types involve fluid volume overload. The goal is to treat the underlying cause and keep the patient out of exacerbation. · 5.1 Stages · Stage | Description · 1 · At risk | Risk factors — obesity, inactivity, high BP, smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes · 2 · Pre-heart failure | Structural changes but no symptoms · 3 · Heart failure | Symptoms present · 4 · Advanced | End stage · 5.2 Systolic vs. Diastolic · An echocardiogram tells you which type. A patient can have both. ·  | Systolic (HFrEF) | Diastolic (HFpEF) · Hook | "SYSTOLIC = STRETCHED OUT" | "DIASTOLIC = DAMN SHE THICK" · Problem | Big and boggy ventricle — fills but cannot snap back and squeeze out | Thick muscle wall, smaller chamber — cannot fill · Ejection fraction | Reduced (< 50%) | Preserved · BNP | High |  · Result | Both → decreased stroke volume and cardiac output. Tachycardia makes it worse |  · 5.3 Left-Sided vs. Right-Sided ·  | Left-sided failure | Right-sided failure · Backs up to | Lungs | Rest of the body · Signs | Pulmonary congestion/edema, wet cough, crackles, wheezes, dyspnea, orthopnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, blood-tinged sputum, confusion, restlessness, cyanosis, fatigue | Dependent edema, weight gain, JVD, ascites, enlarged liver and spleen, anorexia/GI distress, fatigue · Watch the wording The left ventricle pumps TO the body, but when it fails blood backs up into the LUNGS . The right ventricle pumps to the lungs, but when it fails blood backs up into the BODY . Left failure = lungs; right failure = body. · 5.4 Priority Assessments · Lung sounds (crackles, wheezes), cough, orthopnea, SOB, O₂ sat, RR · HR and BP — tachycardia makes HF worse · Edema, JVD, ascites, weight gain — daily weights and I&O · Mental status (confusion, restlessness) and urine output · Heart sounds — a new murmur means something changed · 5.5 Priority Labs & Diagnostics · Echocardiogram — type and ejection fraction · BNP — high = big and boggy heart · Potassium and other electrolytes, especially on diuretics · EKG for rhythm (A-fib is common); digoxin level if on digoxin · 5.6 Priority Interventions · Treat the underlying cause · Limit sodium and possibly fluids (fluid volume overload) · Adequate rest to avoid tachycardia; mild exercise started very low and controlled — cardiac rehab first if needed · Stop smoking and alcohol; keep oxygenation adequate · Diuretics take the fluid off (monitor K⁺); CPAP forces O₂ in when the patient cannot take a deep breath · Medications: diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs/ARNI (Entresto), beta blockers, SGLT2 inhibitors, nitrates, digoxin — nitrates and digoxin can be added if the patient cannot tolerate ACE/ARB/ARNI · Slides by stage: lifestyle + SGLT2 → ACE inhibitor, beta blocker, statin → ARNI + diuretic (potassium-sparing to start) → device and IV management · 5.7 Acute HF Case — Worked Answers · HR 110, O₂ 94%, SOB, wheezes in the upper lungs, crackles in the lower lobes, fluid volume overload. · Question | Answer | Why · Priority medication? | Furosemide | Decreases preload, treats the overload · Why monitor potassium? | He is on a diuretic | Low K⁺ causes more cardiac problems · Potassium chloride? | Replaces K⁺ lost with the diuretic | Keeps K⁺ up · Sodium restriction? | Fluid volume overload | Sodium holds water · Beta blocker? | Lowers workload, BP, and HR |  · Nitroglycerin drip? | Vasodilator — decreases afterload | Worry about a BP drop · CPAP mask? | Forces O₂ into the lungs | He cannot take a deep breath · Why is BNP high? | Heart is big and boggy | Systolic HF · Also in A-fib — which meds? | Amiodarone + a blood thinner | Atria quiver, blood pools · 5.8 Complications, Meds & Teaching · Category | Key points · Complications | Pulmonary edema · dysrhythmias · A-fib with clots/stroke · organ failure · acute exacerbation · Priority meds | Furosemide (monitor K⁺) · ACE/ARB/ARNI · beta blocker · digoxin · nitroglycerin drip in acute HF (see Part 8) · Teaching | Sodium and fluid limits · daily weights · rest to avoid tachycardia · start exercise slowly (cardiac rehab) · stop smoking and alcohol · digoxin toxicity = yellow/green vision changes · Part 6 · Clotting: DVT, Pulmonary Embolism & Stroke · The "clot" exemplars. A clot blocks flow and the tissue past it is starved of oxygen. Goals are prevention first , then restoring perfusion. The two big ones: a clot that travels to the lungs (PE) and a clot or bleed in the brain (stroke). · 6.1 DVT & Pulmonary Embolism · A PE is a DVT that broke off and went to the lungs The #1 cause of PE is a DVT , so the best thing to do is prevent . Risk factors: oral contraceptives/hormones, post-surgery, bedbound. · Prevention | Detail · Movement | Get up and move · Compression | Compression socks and SCDs · Positioning | Elevate legs; do NOT bend the knees or cross the legs — no pillows behind the knees · Medication | Anticoagulants · Do not | Massage the clot · Lifestyle | Healthy lifestyle · 6.2 PE Signs — Symptoms Are Basically the Diagnosis · SOB, rapid breathing, hyperventilation · Chest pain when breathing in, tachycardia · Anxiety, restlessness, panic · Blue from the chest up = lethal PE (worst case) · 6.3 PE Diagnostics & Treatment · Diagnostics | Treatment · V/Q scan (ventilation/perfusion) — the perfusion test | Anticoagulants — heparin drip or Lovenox · CT with contrast | Embolectomy — pull out / break up the clot (angiogram) · Pulmonary angiogram | IVC filter if past history of clots · MRI, chest X-ray | Thrombolytic therapy — see warning below · Your notes disagree on clot busters for PE The 3/19 class notes say no clot busters for PE . Your handwritten notes and the Exam 4 Meds sheet list thrombolytics for PE. Anticoagulants are the consistent answer in all of them — ask your instructor which to use on the exam. · 6.4 Stroke — Ischemic vs. Hemorrhagic ·  | Ischemic stroke | Hemorrhagic stroke · What happens | Blood clot — tissue dies past the clot | A vessel ruptures · Causes | #1 is A-fib (not controlled with an anticoagulant), thrombosis, embolism, unknown, clotting issues | Trauma, aneurysms , massive HTN · Notes | TIA = temporary — a warning sign | Even more of a medical emergency ·  | CVA (stroke) | TIA (transient ischemic attack) · What it is | Brain attack — blood flow is blocked (ischemic) or a vessel bleeds (hemorrhagic) | Temporary ischemia — stroke symptoms that resolve on their own (usually within minutes to hours) · Damage | Brain tissue dies | No lasting damage · Why it matters | Time is brain — thrombolytic window is 3 hours | Warning sign that a stroke may be coming — needs a workup and prevention (antiplatelets, control A-fib and HTN) · 6.5 Stroke Signs · Depends on where in the brain · Hemiparesis/hemiplegia — one-sided paralysis, on the opposite side · Homonymous hemianopsia — loss of half the visual field · Aphasia — cannot speak and/or understand speech · Swallowing issues, seizures; paralysis can affect the airway or diaphragm · Teach the signs — face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, time to call 911 · 6.6 Stroke Diagnostics · Test | Key point · CT without contrast | First — about 5 minutes. A bleed shows immediately; ischemic tissue death takes ~48 hours to show · MRI | Better — shows ischemic stroke on admission, but takes ~45 minutes · Glucose check | Symptoms look like low blood sugar, which is much easier to fix · 6.7 Stroke Treatment · Thrombolytic first line — within 3 hours of symptom start. The earlier, the less brain tissue dies · Cannot have a thrombolytic → anticoagulant (heparin drip) · No thrombolytic with: hemorrhagic stroke (current or history), surgery in the last 2 weeks, head trauma, uncontrolled HTN · Carotid endarterectomy helps prevent stroke · Long term: antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), control A-fib and HTN · 6.8 Practice Set — Worked Answers · Question | Answer | Why · #1 cause of PE? | DVT | A clot that broke off · Wrong pillow position? | Pillows behind the knees | Bent knees promote clots · What do you NOT do to a DVT? | Massage it | It can break off · Perfusion test for PE? | V/Q scan | Ventilation and perfusion · Blue from the chest up | Lethal PE | Worst case · First imaging for stroke? | CT without contrast | Fast; a bleed shows right away · What else right away? | Blood glucose | Similar symptoms, easy fix · Thrombolytic window? | 3 hours from symptom start | Limits tissue death · Cannot have a thrombolytic? | Anticoagulant | Heparin drip · #1 cause of ischemic stroke? | A-fib | Blood pools and clots · Thrombolytic in hemorrhagic stroke? | No | Contraindicated

x: Anemia and its types · hemophilia · sickle cell disease and HOPP · Part 7 · Blood Disorders: Anemia, Hemophilia & Sickle Cell · The blood-side "volume" exemplars: too few red cells ( anemia ), a missing clotting factor ( hemophilia ), or abnormal cells that clump and clot ( sickle cell ). Anemia looks like decreased cardiac output, hemophilia is about bleeding, and sickle cell is about perfusion and pain. · 7.1 Anemia · The body is either not making enough red blood cells or destroying them too fast . Several types exist. Chronic kidney failure patients have anemia. · System | Findings · Skin | Paleness, cold, jaundice (yellow eyes from rapid RBC breakdown) · Respiratory | SOB · Muscle | Weakness, fatigue · Vitals | Low BP, high HR · Other | Spleen enlargement (RBCs destroyed too fast) · Anemia = decreased cardiac output Same nursing care as decreased CO. Tachycardic → sit down and rest . Space activities with rest periods, small self-care tasks, good hydration. · Diet and meds — iron, folic acid, vitamin B (red meat), folate; if diet does not work → epoetin alfa injection · Teach — frequent rest and adequate diet · 7.2 Types of Anemia — Iron Deficiency vs. Folic Acid/B12 · Added from standard nursing content Your class notes do not break anemia into types, so this table comes from standard nursing content. Check it against your textbook chapter. ·  | Iron deficiency | Folic acid / B12 deficiency · Causes | Blood loss (GI bleeding, heavy periods), poor intake, pregnancy, poor absorption | Folic acid: poor diet, alcohol use, pregnancy. B12: strict vegan diet, poor absorption — pernicious anemia (no intrinsic factor), gastric surgery · RBC size | Small, pale cells (microcytic) | Large cells (macrocytic/megaloblastic) · Unique signs | Fatigue, pallor, brittle or spoon-shaped nails, pica (craving ice or dirt), sore tongue | Fatigue, pallor, smooth red tongue. B12 only: neuro signs — numbness, tingling, poor balance, confusion · Foods | Red meat, liver, leafy greens, beans, iron-fortified cereal | Folic acid: leafy greens, citrus, beans, fortified grains. B12: meat, eggs, dairy · Treatment | Oral iron (ferrous sulfate); IV iron if severe | Folic acid tablets. B12 injections — lifelong for pernicious anemia · 7.3 Hemophilia · A genetic, recessive X-linked clotting factor deficiency — males are at higher risk. · Severity | What to expect · Mild | May not know they have it; bleeds more with trauma or after surgery · Moderate | They will probably know · Severe | Spontaneous bleeds into joints, muscles, and the GI tract · Nursing care — give the clotting factor, especially when bleeding · Teach — how to do their own IV; NO heat ; pressure to stop a bleed but not too much (compartment syndrome); elevate the limb and rest so the blood is reabsorbed · Antiplatelets are contraindicated in hemophilia · 7.4 Sickle Cell Disease · Autosomal recessive. Red blood cells are crescent-shaped, so they clump together and form clots. · Risk | Key point · Acute chest syndrome | #1 cause of death. Massive vaso-occlusive crisis in the lungs, triggered by infection — chest pain, cough, fever, low O₂ · Acute respiratory distress | Perfusion and oxygenation problem · Sickle cell crisis | Pain and clotting · HOPP — the management goals H ydrate (avoid triggers) · O xygenate (acute chest syndrome) · P erfuse (HF, stroke, reproductive and wound issues) · P ain (control the crisis).
