t: Sky's Workbook — Perfusion Foundations, Diagnostics & CAD
x: Workbook questions with answer key · foundations, labs, cardiac cath, decreased CO, CAD & angina · Fill it in from memory first, then check the answer under each question. Anything you miss goes on your final-review list. · Perfusion Basics · 1. What is perfusion? · Blood delivery to tissue. · 2. What are the three categories of perfusion problems? Give an exemplar for each. · Volume (too little volume or pumping) — heart failure, tachy/bradycardia, anemia, hemophilia · Narrowing (a vessel is too small) — coronary artery disease · Clots (something is blocking flow) — pulmonary emboli, brain attack (stroke) · 3. Trace the flow of blood through the heart, starting with blood returning from the body. · 1. Body → superior/inferior vena cava · 2. Right atrium · 3. Tricuspid valve · 4. Right ventricle · 5. Pulmonary valve · 6. Pulmonary artery · 7. Lungs · 8. Left atrium · 9. Bicuspid (mitral) valve · 10. Left ventricle · 11. Aortic valve → aorta → rest of the body · 4. When are the coronary arteries perfused? Why does a fast heart rate put the heart muscle at risk? · In diastole (every other organ is perfused during systole). The left ventricle pushes blood out the aorta, the valve snaps shut, and the blood that falls back fills the coronary arteries. The heart needs good rest periods to perfuse — a fast rate shortens that rest time, so the heart muscle gets less blood. · 5. Which coronary artery is called the “widow maker”? Why? · The left coronary artery — it supplies the entire left side of the heart. · 6. Definitions · Term | Definition / what it tells the nurse · Preload | Volume of blood returning to the right atrium (end of diastole). Volume — FVO = high, dehydration = low. Treat with diuretics · Afterload | Resistance the ventricle pumps against. Pressure — too much (HTN, vasoconstriction) wears the heart out; too little = no blood left to perfuse the heart. Treat with BP meds · Stroke volume | Volume ejected from the ventricle per beat · Ejection fraction | Percent of blood ejected per beat — normal 50 to 70% . Below 50% = heart failure. Only an echo gives EF · Cardiac output | Stroke volume × heart rate — normal 4 to 8 L/min · Contractility | How easily the heart snaps back to its shape (poor snap-back = big and boggy heart) · Compliance | How easily something stretches · SVR | Afterload for the left side — the left ventricle pumps to the body · PVR | Afterload for the right side — the right ventricle pumps to the lungs · Arteriosclerosis | Arteries hardened and narrowed — smoking, HTN, diabetes, drug abuse · Atherosclerosis | Plaque buildup inside the arteries — high cholesterol, genetics · Ischemia | Lack of blood supply to tissue — reversible · Necrosis | Tissue death — not reversible · Heart murmur | Whoosh from a valve not snapping back correctly. A new murmur means something changed — often fluid overload in HF · 7. Calculate the cardiac output: HR 80, stroke volume 60 mL. Is this normal? Show your work. · 80 × 60 mL = 4,800 mL/min → ÷ 1,000 = 4.8 L/min . Normal (4–8 L/min). Convert mL to L before comparing. · 8. What is the difference between ischemia and necrosis? Which one can the nurse reverse, and how? · Ischemia = lack of blood supply; necrosis = tissue death. Ischemia is reversible — the priority is restoring oxygen and perfusion. Necrosis is not reversible. · Diagnostic Tests · 9. Diagnostic tests: what does it show, pre-procedure care, post-procedure care · Test | What it shows | Pre-procedure | Post-procedure · 12-lead EKG | 10 stickers (each arm and leg + 6 on the chest), 12 views at once — shows where perfusion is lacking |  |  · Stress test (treadmill) | How well the heart works under pressure (about 20 min on the treadmill, compared to baseline) | EKG leads and vitals; baseline vitals and assessment; heart and lung sounds; NPO about 2 hrs; consent; crash cart close by; hold meds that can be held | Stop the test if HR passes the limit, rhythm/EKG changes, chest pain, SOB, abnormal beats, pale and diaphoretic · Stress test (medication) | Same as treadmill — for patients who cannot get on the treadmill | Same as treadmill | Same as treadmill · Transcutaneous echo | Structure, valves, blood flow, muscle size, clots in the ventricles; ejection fraction; systolic vs. diastolic HF. Less clear, less invasive | NPO | No post-op care · Transesophageal echo (TEE) | Same, through the esophagus — much more clear | NPO since midnight, consent, baseline vitals | Vitals; liquids → soft foods → solids; watch respiratory rate (anesthesia) · Cardiac cath / angiogram | Only test that shows perfusion of the coronary arteries — contrast shows narrowing and clots; 100% occlusion may be fixed in the cath | NPO, consent, vitals; trim/prep groin if femoral; evaluate kidneys (contrast is nephrotoxic); do NOT keep flat before | Vitals q15 min × 1 hr, q30 min × 2, then hourly + site check each time; groin = lie flat; bilateral pulses, temp, color; coags and ACT; hematoma → hold pressure · 10. When should a stress test be stopped? List the findings. · HR passes the limit · Rhythm or EKG changes · Chest pain · SOB · Abnormal beats · Pale and diaphoretic · 11. Which test is the only way to obtain an ejection fraction? · Echocardiogram. · 12. Which test is the only one that shows perfusion of the coronary arteries? When is it ordered? · Cardiac cath (coronary angiogram). Ordered if the patient fails the stress test, or when the EKG and troponin are normal but CAD is still suspected. · 13. Normal lab values · Lab | Normal value | Significance · Troponin | Normal is 0 | Breakdown of heart muscle fibers. Rises slowly — drawn in a series (about q6h). Priority lab with chest pain · CK-MB |  | CK = any muscle; MB = cardiac muscle — cardiac-specific breakdown · Myoglobin |  | Muscle breakdown all over the body — not cardiac-specific · BNP |  | High = heart is big and boggy, not snapping back. The routine HF lab · Potassium |  | Check with diuretics. Tall peaked T = hyperkalemia. Low K⁺ causes more cardiac problems and worsens digoxin toxicity · Magnesium |  | Low magnesium → Torsades de pointes · Cholesterol / LDL / HDL |  | Lipid panel — evaluates atherosclerosis · PTT |  | Monitors heparin (“two T's make an H”) · PT/INR |  | Monitors warfarin · Digoxin level | 0.8–2.0 | Know the toxic level; toxicity worsened by hypokalemia · 14. Why is troponin drawn in a series instead of once? · It rises slowly after heart muscle damage, so one normal result does not rule out damage — drawn about q6h. · Cardiac Cath · 15. Which insertion site is preferred and why? Which site needs the most post-procedure care? · Wrist (radial) — most common, fewer complications. Femoral has the most risk and post-op care. · 16. Why does the nurse evaluate kidney function before a cardiac cath? · Contrast dye is nephrotoxic — fluids/bicarb may be given. · 17. What is the post-procedure vital sign schedule? What else is assessed with every set of vitals? · q15 min × 1 hour, then q30 min × 2, then hourly. Check the site every time (plus pulses, temperature, and color of the extremity). · 18. After a femoral cath, the patient's BP drops and HR rises. What do you suspect? What other symptom would you expect? · Internal bleeding — retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Expect one-sided back/flank pain (seen on CT). · 19. A hard, painful bulge develops at the insertion site. What is it? What is your first nursing intervention? · Hematoma. Hold pressure. · 20. Which is NOT part of the post-cath assessment: pedal pulses, back pain, gag reflex, groin site? Why? · Gag reflex — the cath goes through an artery, not the throat. Watch back pain, groin, and pedal pulses. · Decreased Cardiac Output · 21. List signs and symptoms of decreased cardiac output · Skin: pale, cyanotic, cool and clammy, diaphoresis · Low BP, high HR · Weak/thready/diminished pulses, poor cap refill · Dependent edema, syncope · SOB, high RR, decreased O₂ sat · Dizziness, confusion, fatigue · Decreased urine output · Nausea · 22. List nursing interventions for the patient with decreased cardiac output · Fluid balance — fluids only if indicated; still low pressure → vasopressors · Monitoring — EKG/telemetry, serum labs, urine output · O₂ PRN · Position — HOB up if BP okay and MAP above 60; MAP below 60 → flat with legs up · Avoid Valsalva · Bed rest and clustered care with rest periods between activities · 23. The patient's MAP is 55. How should the nurse position the patient? · Lay flat with the legs up (MAP below 60). · 24. Why should a patient with decreased cardiac output avoid the Valsalva maneuver? · So they do not “vagal out” — bearing down stimulates the vagus nerve and slows the heart. · Coronary Artery Disease · 25. Modifiable vs. nonmodifiable risk factors · Modifiable | Nonmodifiable · Stress | Age · Smoking | Ethnicity (African American/Hispanic) · Diet, exercise | Male gender · Diabetes, hypertension | Genetics/family history · 26. How might chest pain present differently in women and older adults? · They may complain of indigestion that is actually cardiac — do not assume it is only GI. · 27. Stable vs. unstable angina ·  | Stable angina | Unstable angina · Description | Predictable, demand-related chest pain | Emergency — heart muscle is not getting enough blood · Relieved by | Rest and nitroglycerin | Not relieved — still has pain after rest and 3 NTG tablets · Nursing actions | Rest, NTG (1 tab q5 min, max 3) | 911/ER · MONA · two large-bore IVs · 12-lead EKG · troponin · 28. What should the patient be taught about nitroglycerin? · a. How to take it: 1 tablet every 5 minutes · b. Maximum 3 in 15 minutes — not better after 3 → 911/ER (a 4th tablet is the wrong answer) · c. Side effects: BP drops and HR goes up · d. Storage: amber glass, away from sun and light; carry it at all times · 29. What does MONA stand for? · M orphine · O xygen · N itroglycerin · A spirin · 30. A patient is admitted with chest pain not relieved by 3 nitroglycerin tablets · a. Type of angina: unstable angina — emergency · b. Contraindicated now: a 4th NTG tablet (max is 3) · c. Two large-bore IVs: he may need several procedures · d. Priority lab: troponin — is the heart being damaged? · e. NOT indicated now: lisinopril — lowers BP; not an acute chest pain drug · f. EKG and troponin normal → next test: coronary angiogram (shows whether arteries are narrowed) · g. Heparin drip prevents a new clot (does NOT break up the existing one) · Plavix prevents platelet aggregation · Metoprolol decreases dysrhythmia risk and workload · h. Home: statin, possibly aspirin; limit salt; more fruits and vegetables

t: Sky's Workbook — EKG, Rhythms & Treating Dysrhythmias
x: Workbook questions with answer key · EKG basics, sinus/atrial/ventricular rhythms, pacers, blocks, treatment · Fill it in from memory first, then check the answer under each question. · EKG Basics · 1. Strip basics · One big box = 0.20 seconds · One little box = 0.04 seconds · Strip length = 6 seconds · 2. How do you calculate heart rate on a 6-second strip? · Count the QRS complexes × 10 (8 QRS = HR 80). · 3. How often should EKG electrodes be changed? Why? · Every 24 hours — to reduce artifact. · 4. What is artifact? What should the nurse do first? · False readings on the monitor. If you cannot read the strip, assess the patient first. · 5. Electrical conduction: pathway in order and intrinsic rate of each pacemaker site · Structure | Intrinsic rate | Role · SA node | 60–100 | The pacemaker — tells the heart to beat · AV node | 40–60 | Takes over if the SA node fails · Bundle of His | — | Carries the impulse into the ventricles · Right/left bundle branches | — | Carry the impulse into the ventricles · Purkinje fibers | 20–40 | Last backup pacemaker · 6. What does each wave or interval represent? What is normal? · Wave | Represents | Normal · P wave | SA node fired — atrial depolarization | Easy to see, facing up · PR interval | Start of P to the Q | Fits in a big box · QRS complex | Ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization hidden here) | Narrow, fits in a big box; can point up or down · T wave | Ventricular repolarization (resting) | Rounded · Tall, peaked T wave = hyperkalemia . · 7. List the five questions used to interpret a rhythm strip · 1. HR — count QRS × 10 · 2. Regular? Same gap between each QRS · 3. P wave for every QRS? · 4. QRS within a big box? · 5. PR interval within a big box? · 8. If all five answers are “yes” and the HR is 60–100, what is the rhythm? · Normal sinus rhythm. Any NO means do not call it sinus. · 9. Atrial rhythms are a problem with which wave? Ventricular rhythms? · Atrial = P wave . Ventricular = QRS . · 10. A patient's rhythm is abnormal, but he has no symptoms. Should you treat? · No. Assess the patient first — symptomatic → treat; asymptomatic → do not treat. The goal is always optimizing cardiac output. · Sinus & Atrial Dysrhythmias (recognize and treat) · 11. Rhythm table · Rhythm | Rate | Regular? | P wave? | Key feature | Causes / treatment · Normal sinus | 60–100 | Yes | Yes | Breaks no rules | None — keep assessing · Sinus brady | below 60 | Yes | Yes | Everything normal except the rate | Asymptomatic → none. Symptomatic → treat the cause → atropine → pacing and/or dopamine or epi drip · Sinus tachy | above 100 | Yes | Yes | Everything normal except the rate | Treat the cause — rest, fluids, Tylenol, pain meds, calm anxiety · SVT | 150+ | Yes | No | Narrow QRS → problem is above the ventricles; PSVT starts/stops suddenly | Vagal maneuver → adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg → BB or CCB. Unstable → synchronized cardioversion · Atrial fibrillation | Any (RVR above 100) | No | No | Irregular, no P, fibrillating baseline | Rate control (BB/CCB), amiodarone, anticoagulant every day. Never atropine · Atrial flutter | Any | Either | No | Sawtooth flutter waves | Same as A-fib · 12. What are the three hallmark signs of A-fib? · Irregular · No P wave · Fibrillating baseline · 13. Why do A-fib patients take a blood thinner every day? What is A-fib the #1 cause of? · The atria quiver instead of contracting, so blood pools and clots . A-fib is the #1 cause of stroke . · 14. What must be ruled out before cardioverting A-fib? How? · A clot in the atria — TEE to confirm no clots, unless the patient has been therapeutically anticoagulated for at least 2 weeks. · Ventricular Dysrhythmias (recognize only) · 15. Ventricular rhythm table · Rhythm | What it looks like | Lethal? · PVC — unifocal | Sinus rhythm with a wide QRS beat, same shape every time | N — usually not concerning · PVC — multifocal | Wide beats of different shapes (one up, one down) | N — more concerning · PVC — couplet | Two PVCs together | N — very concerning · R on T | PVC lands on the T wave | N — but can trigger V-tach/V-fib · Ventricular tachycardia | Big wide QRS — all you see are ventricles | Y · Torsades de pointes | Twisting V-tach | Y · Ventricular fibrillation | No QRS, no P, quivering baseline | Y · Asystole | Flat line — no electrical activity | Y · 16. How many PVCs in a row make V-tach? · 3 or more. · 17. What electrolyte imbalance is linked to Torsades de pointes? · Low magnesium. · Pacemakers (recognize only) · 18. Where is the pacer spike for each? · Atrial — spike before the P wave · Ventricular — spike before the QRS (the huge, wide QRS is expected) · Dual (AV) — spike before both · 19. What does a pacer spike on the T wave indicate? · A malfunctioning pacemaker — can cause R on T. · 20. Pacemaker set at 60 and HR 60. Can you give metoprolol? Why? · Yes — the pacemaker keeps the heart at its set rate. · Heart Block (basic understanding) · 21. Which EKG rule does a heart block break? · The PR interval rule — typically more P waves than QRS complexes. · 22. Bradycardia or tachycardia? When is a heart block dangerous? · Bradycardia only , never tachycardia. Dangerous depending on the heart rate — a block with HR 25 is an emergency. · Treatment of Dysrhythmias · 23. Five causes of bradycardia and how to treat each · Opioids/fentanyl/overdose → naloxone (Narcan) · Hypothermia → warm the patient · Sleep apnea → tell them to breathe · Just climbed stairs → let them rest and breathe · Cardiac meds (CCB, BB, digoxin), anesthesia, SA node failure, ischemia, hypoxia, hyperkalemia → treat the cause, support ABCs · 24. Five causes of tachycardia and how to treat each · Exercise → sit down and rest · Dehydration → fluids · Fever → Tylenol · Anxiety, fear, anger → calm the patient · Pain → pain medication · Also: caffeine, cocaine/meth, allergic reaction, infection, blood loss, anemia, FVO, HF, CAD, respiratory disease → treat the cause. · 25. Dysrhythmia drugs · Drug | Use | Dose | Key facts · Atropine | Symptomatic bradycardia — first line; blocks vagal slowing | 1 mg IV push, repeat q3–5 min, max 3 mg | Fast onset, short half-life (a band aid). Tachycardia, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion in older adults. Telemetry. Never for A-fib · Adenosine | SVT / regular narrow tachy — first line | 6 mg rapid IV push + NS flush, then 12 mg | “Reboots” the heart (stops it 6–10 sec); half-life ~10 sec — SLAM it in a big IV · Amiodarone | Tachyarrhythmias, V-tach, A-fib | 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min × 6 hrs | Fatal lung/liver toxicity, ↑ QT; no grapefruit; sun sensitivity, blue-gray skin · Lidocaine | Ventricular rhythms ONLY | Drip | Seizure risk · Dopamine drip | Brady after atropine fails | 5–20 mcg/kg/min | Titrate, taper slowly; vesicant (phentolamine) · Epinephrine drip | Brady drip, lethal rhythms | 2–10 mcg/min | “When in doubt, give EPI”; vesicant; photosensitive · 26. How should adenosine be given? Why? · Rapid IV push in a big IV, then flush — its half-life is about 10 seconds, so a slow push can fail. · 27. Atropine is not working for symptomatic bradycardia. Next two options? · Transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine drip . · 28. What makes a tachycardia “unstable”? What is the treatment? · Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute HF → synchronized cardioversion . · 29. Synchronized cardioversion vs. defibrillation ·  | Synchronized cardioversion | Defibrillation · Rhythms used for | Fast rhythm WITH a pulse — SVT, A-fib, unstable tachy | V-fib or pulseless V-tach · Pulse? | Yes | No · Patient | Awake, frequently sedated | Unconscious · Synch | ON — synchronized with the QRS | OFF · Energy | 50–200 J | Begin at 200 J, up to 360 J · Consent? | Yes — consent form | No — emergency; call a code · 30. List the steps for a lethal rhythm · 1. Check the pulse · 2. Start CPR · 3. Shock or not? (V-fib and pulseless V-tach are shockable) · 4. When in doubt, give EPI

t: Sky's Workbook — Heart Failure, PE, Stroke, Blood Disorders & Meds
x: Workbook questions with answer key · HF, PE, stroke, anemia, hemophilia, sickle cell, medications · Fill it in from memory first, then check the answer under each question. · Heart Failure · 1. List the four stages of heart failure · 1. At risk — risk factors (obesity, inactivity, high BP, smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes) · 2. Pre-heart failure — structural changes, no symptoms · 3. Heart failure — symptoms present · 4. Advanced — end stage · 2. Systolic vs. diastolic ·  | Systolic (HFrEF) | Diastolic (HFpEF) · What happens to the ventricle | Big and boggy — fills but cannot snap back and squeeze out | Thick muscle wall, smaller chamber — cannot fill · Ejection fraction | Reduced (below 50%) | Preserved · BNP | High |  · Memory trick | “SYSTOLIC = STRETCHED OUT” | “DIASTOLIC = DAMN SHE THICK” · 3. What test determines the type of heart failure? · Echocardiogram (a patient can have both types). · 4. Left-sided vs. right-sided ·  | Left-sided HF | Right-sided HF · Blood backs up to | Lungs | Rest of the body · Signs and symptoms | Pulmonary congestion/edema, wet cough, crackles, wheezes, dyspnea, orthopnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, blood-tinged sputum, confusion, restlessness, cyanosis, fatigue | Dependent edema, weight gain, JVD, ascites, enlarged liver and spleen, anorexia/GI distress, fatigue · 5. Why does tachycardia make heart failure worse? · Both types already have decreased stroke volume and cardiac output — a fast rate adds workload and leaves less time to fill, so output drops further. Adequate rest avoids tachycardia. · 6. Nursing interventions for the patient with HF · Treat the underlying cause · Limit sodium and possibly fluids · Adequate rest to avoid tachycardia; mild exercise started very low (cardiac rehab) · Stop smoking and alcohol; keep oxygenation adequate · Daily weights and I&O; monitor K⁺ on diuretics · CPAP when the patient cannot take a deep breath · 7. Medications for HF and why · Diuretics (furosemide) — take the fluid off, ↓ preload; monitor K⁺ · ACE inhibitors — ↓ afterload, BP, workload; prevent remodeling · ARBs / ARNI (Entresto) — ↓ BP and afterload; ARNI for HFrEF · Beta blockers — ↓ workload, BP, HR · SGLT2 inhibitors — early-stage therapy with lifestyle changes · Nitrates and digoxin — can be added if ACE/ARB/ARNI not tolerated · 8. HF patient: HR 110, O₂ 94%, wheezes in upper lobes, crackles in lower lobes · a. Priority medication: furosemide — decreases preload, treats the overload · b. Monitor potassium: he is on a diuretic — low K⁺ causes more cardiac problems · c. CPAP: forces O₂ into the lungs — he cannot take a deep breath · d. Nitroglycerin drip: vasodilator — decreases afterload (watch for a BP drop) · e. Also in A-fib: amiodarone + a blood thinner · 9. HF discharge teaching · Sodium and fluid limits · Daily weights · Rest to avoid tachycardia; start exercise slowly (cardiac rehab) · Stop smoking and alcohol · Digoxin toxicity = yellow/green vision changes · Pulmonary Emboli · 10. What is the #1 cause of a pulmonary embolism? · DVT — a clot that broke off and went to the lungs. · 11. Risk factors for DVT/PE · Oral contraceptives/hormones · Post-surgery · Bedbound · 12. DVT/PE prevention teaching · Get up and move · Compression socks and SCDs · Elevate legs; do NOT bend the knees or cross the legs — no pillows behind the knees · Anticoagulants · Do NOT massage the clot; healthy lifestyle · 13. Signs and symptoms of a PE · SOB, rapid breathing, hyperventilation · Chest pain when breathing in · Tachycardia · Anxiety, restlessness, panic · Blue from the chest up = lethal PE · 14. Diagnostic tests for a PE? Which is the perfusion test? · V/Q scan ( the perfusion test ), CT with contrast, pulmonary angiogram, MRI, chest X-ray. · 15. How is a PE treated? When is an IVC filter used? · Anticoagulants (heparin drip or Lovenox); embolectomy. IVC filter if a past history of clots. Thrombolytics for PE: Sky's notes disagree (3/19 class notes say no; handwritten notes and the Exam 4 Meds sheet say yes) — ask the instructor. · Stroke · 16. Ischemic vs. hemorrhagic ·  | Ischemic stroke | Hemorrhagic stroke · What happens | Blood clot — tissue dies past the clot | A vessel ruptures · Causes | #1 A-fib (not on an anticoagulant), thrombosis, embolism, unknown, clotting issues | Trauma, aneurysms, massive HTN · Thrombolytic? | Yes — within 3 hours | No — contraindicated · 17. CVA vs. TIA ·  | CVA | TIA · Definition | Brain attack — blood flow blocked (ischemic) or a vessel bleeds (hemorrhagic) | Temporary ischemia — stroke symptoms that resolve on their own (minutes to hours) · Lasting damage? | Yes — brain tissue dies | No · Nursing significance | Time is brain — thrombolytic window 3 hours | Warning sign a stroke may be coming — workup and prevention (antiplatelets, control A-fib and HTN) · 18. What is the #1 cause of ischemic stroke? · A-fib. · 19. Define · Hemiparesis/hemiplegia — one-sided weakness/paralysis, on the opposite side of the brain injury · Homonymous hemianopsia — loss of half the visual field · Aphasia — cannot speak and/or understand speech · 20. First imaging test for suspected stroke? Why is an MRI not first? · CT without contrast — about 5 minutes; a bleed shows immediately. MRI is better for ischemic stroke but takes about 45 minutes. · 21. Why is blood glucose checked on a patient with stroke symptoms? · Low blood sugar looks like a stroke and is much easier to fix. · 22. Time window for a thrombolytic? What if the patient cannot have one? · Within 3 hours of symptom start. Cannot have one → anticoagulant (heparin drip). · 23. Contraindications to a thrombolytic · Hemorrhagic stroke (current or history) · Surgery in the last 2 weeks · Head trauma · Uncontrolled HTN · Also: active bleeding, severe hypotension, allergy · 24. Signs of stroke to teach the public · Face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, time to call 911. · Anemias · 25. Two main causes of anemia · The body is not making enough red blood cells, or destroying them too fast . · 26. Why does anemia look like decreased cardiac output? Signs and symptoms · Tissues are not getting oxygen. Paleness, cold skin, jaundice (rapid RBC breakdown), SOB, weakness, fatigue, low BP, high HR, enlarged spleen. · 27. Iron deficiency vs. folic acid/B12 deficiency · Sky's guide marks this table as standard nursing content, not class notes. ·  | Iron deficiency | Folic acid / B12 deficiency · Causes | Blood loss (GI bleeding, heavy periods), poor intake, pregnancy, poor absorption | Folic acid: poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy. B12: strict vegan diet, poor absorption — pernicious anemia, gastric surgery · RBC size | Small, pale (microcytic) | Large (macrocytic/megaloblastic) · Unique signs | Brittle or spoon-shaped nails, pica (ice or dirt), sore tongue | Smooth red tongue. B12 only: neuro signs — numbness, tingling, poor balance, confusion · Food sources | Red meat, liver, leafy greens, beans, iron-fortified cereal | Folate: leafy greens, citrus, beans, fortified grains. B12: meat, eggs, dairy · Treatment | Oral iron (ferrous sulfate); IV iron if severe | Folic acid tablets; B12 injections — lifelong for pernicious anemia · 28. What should the patient taking iron be taught? · Best absorbed between meals with vitamin C (orange juice); with food if GI upset · Keep apart from antacids, dairy, and calcium · Liquid iron through a straw (stains teeth) · Dark/black stools are expected · Constipation → fluids and fiber · 29. What is pernicious anemia? How is it treated? · B12 deficiency from no intrinsic factor — cannot absorb B12 from the gut. Lifelong B12 injections. · 30. When is epoetin alfa used? · When diet, iron, folic acid, and B vitamins are not enough (especially chronic kidney failure) — stimulates RBC production. Monitor Hgb and BP. · Hemophilia · 31. How is hemophilia inherited? Who is at higher risk? · Recessive X-linked — males are at higher risk. · 32. Severity · Severity | What to expect · Mild | May not know they have it; bleeds more with trauma or after surgery · Moderate | They will probably know · Severe | Spontaneous bleeds into joints, muscles, and the GI tract · 33. Treatment for a bleed? Teaching about heat and pressure? · Give the clotting factor. NO heat. Pressure to stop the bleed but not too much (compartment syndrome). Elevate and rest so the blood is reabsorbed. · Sickle Cell Disease · 34. How is sickle cell inherited? What happens to the RBCs? · Autosomal recessive. RBCs are crescent-shaped, so they clump together and form clots. · 35. #1 cause of death? Signs and trigger? · Acute chest syndrome — chest pain, cough, fever, low O₂. Triggered by infection . · 36. What does HOPP stand for? · H ydrate (avoid triggers) · O xygenate (acute chest syndrome) · P erfuse (HF, stroke, reproductive and wound issues) · P ain (control the crisis) · 37. Why are fluids important in sickle cell crisis? · Fluids keep the cells apart. · 38. Precautions with ketorolac? A blood transfusion? · Ketorolac (NSAID) — caution with kidneys . Transfusion — watch for a reaction and fluid volume overload ; monitor iron levels. · Medications · 39. Medication summary (full cards in Sky's Study Guide — Medication Cards) · Class | Key points · Beta blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol) | ↓ O₂ demand, BP, HR. 4 B's. Black box: abrupt stop → MI. Call provider if HR below 60 · CCBs (diltiazem, amlodipine) | Vasodilate, slow SA/AV. Hold if SBP below 90 or HR below 60. No grapefruit · ACE inhibitors (lisinopril) | ↓ afterload/BP/workload. Black box: pregnancy, angioedema. Dry cough; no salt substitutes · ARBs (losartan, valsartan) | Black box: fetal toxicity. Rebound HTN if stopped · ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) | HFrEF. Never with an ACE inhibitor — stop ACE 36 hrs before. Hyperkalemia, angioedema · Vasopressors (dopamine, epi, norepi) | Brady/low perfusion; ICU/ER only. Vesicant — phentolamine · Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, enoxaparin) | Bleeding, HIT. Heparin = PTT; warfarin = PT/INR. Keep the Lovenox air bubble · Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) | Long-term clot prevention; do not dissolve clots. No aspirin with warfarin; clopidogrel — no grapefruit · Thrombolytics (alteplase) | Destroy clots — ischemic stroke within 3 hrs. Stop for any bleeding · Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) | Prevent plaque. Rhabdomyolysis — report muscle pain; liver labs · Antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, lidocaine) | Lung/liver toxicity, ↑ QT. Lidocaine = ventricular only · Digoxin | HF. Level 0.8–2.0. Toxicity: yellow/green vision, GI, brady; Digibind; hypokalemia worsens · Atropine | Symptomatic brady first line; 1 mg q3–5 min, max 3 mg · Anemia supplements (iron, folic acid, B12, epoetin) | See anemia section above · Hydroxyurea | Sickle cell; bone marrow suppression — hold if WBC low; gloves; contraception · Clotting factors | VIII (hemophilia A), IX (hemophilia B); IV; self-infusion teaching · Nitroglycerin | Vasodilator; 1 q5 min, max 3 → ER; BP drops, HR rises; amber glass · 40. When should a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker be held? · Beta blocker — HR below 60 (call the provider). CCB — SBP below 90 or HR below 60 . · 41. Which drugs should not be taken with grapefruit? · Calcium channel blockers, clopidogrel, amiodarone. · 42. Signs of digoxin toxicity? Antidote? Electrolyte that makes it worse? · Yellow/green vision changes, GI symptoms (N/V/diarrhea), decreased HR. Antidote Digibind . Hypokalemia worsens toxicity. · 43. Antidote for a vasopressor that leaks into the tissue? · Phentolamine. · 44. Which lab monitors heparin? Warfarin? · Heparin = PTT . Warfarin = PT/INR . · 45. How long must an ACE inhibitor be stopped before starting sacubitril/valsartan? Why? · At least 36 hours — angioedema risk. · 46. Every emergency starts with the ABCs · Every medical emergency in this module is prioritized the same way: airway, breathing, circulation . The three feed each other — an airway that closes stops breathing, poor breathing starves the heart and brain of oxygen, and a failing circulation can't deliver the oxygen that breathing brings in. · Circulation · Circulation depends on three things working together: · Volume — enough blood/fluid in the tank (lost in hemorrhage, burns, dehydration) · Vessel diameter — vessels tight enough to hold pressure (lost when vessels dilate, as in anaphylaxis) · Perfusion — a pump strong enough to move the blood to the tissues · Low BP → lay the client flat (legs elevated if ordered) so blood returns to the heart and brain. High BP → sit the client up so blood pools in the legs and the pressure comes down. Exception: a client with IICP stays at HOB 30–45° with the head midline. · Priority nursing diagnosis | When it fits · Fluid volume deficit | Volume is lost or shifted out of the vessels — hemorrhage, hypovolemic shock, burns, heat exhaustion · Decreased cardiac output | The pump or rhythm fails — lethal dysrhythmias, cardiac arrest, severe hypothermia · Airway & breathing · Priority nursing diagnosis | When it fits · Impaired airway clearance | Something blocks the airway — swelling (anaphylaxis, smoke inhalation), secretions, the tongue in an unconscious client · Impaired breathing pattern | The drive or mechanics to breathe fail — opioid/benzodiazepine overdose, IICP pressing on the brainstem · Impaired gas exchange | Air moves but oxygen doesn't cross into the blood — carbon monoxide, aspirated water after submersion, pulmonary edema · An endotracheal tube secures a threatened airway: the tube passes through the vocal cords into the trachea, and an inflated cuff seals it so air goes to the lungs instead of the esophagus. · Using the frame on each exemplar · For every exemplar, ask: which of these diagnoses is the highest priority for this client right now? · Exemplar | Usual top priority | Why · Increased intracranial pressure | Impaired breathing pattern | Brainstem pressure depresses the respiratory drive; a falling LOC also threatens the airway · Burns with smoke inhalation | Impaired airway clearance | Airway swelling can close the airway within hours · Large burns without inhalation injury | Fluid volume deficit | Massive fluid shifts out of the vessels · Opioid / benzodiazepine overdose | Impaired breathing pattern | Respiratory depression · Hypovolemic shock | Fluid volume deficit | Lost circulating volume · Submersion injury | Impaired gas exchange | Water in the alveoli blocks oxygen exchange · Anaphylaxis | Impaired airway clearance | Laryngeal and airway swelling, bronchospasm · A before B before C. If a client has both a fluid problem and an airway problem, the airway wins — a full tank does no good if no oxygen gets in.

ABCDE, then FGHI · The primary survey finds and treats life threats in the first minutes. If a threat is found at any letter, fix it before moving on. If not — or if GCS is 8 or below — the next step is intubation with an endotracheal tube. · The nurse's role in intubation · Before | After · Continuous monitoring: telemetry, SpO₂, automatic BP | Suction · Suction and crash cart at the bedside | Ventilator settings and alarms · Bag-valve mask plugged into oxygen (not air) , turned all the way up | Secure the tube! · Call respiratory therapy (ventilator) and anesthesia (brings its own drugs) | Chart the tube depth number at the lip · Quick report and handoff | Sedation and pain control · Pull the headboard off and pull the bed out from the wall | Oral care every 2 hours ·  | Confirm placement: end-tidal CO₂ (gold standard) , bilateral breath sounds, symmetrical chest expansion, chest X-ray · End-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) · Reading | Meaning · 35–45 mm Hg | Normal · Below 10 mm Hg during CPR | Poor-quality compressions — push harder and faster · Sudden jump to 35–45 during a code | Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) · After intubation, ETCO₂ confirms the tube is in the trachea ; the chest X-ray confirms how deep it sits.

The skull is a closed box · The Monro-Kellie hypothesis · The skull is a CLOSED BOX . · It CANNOT EXPAND to accommodate changes in volume. · Three things share the space: brain tissue 80% , CSF 10% , blood 10% . · If one of the three grows — a swollen brain, a bleed, a tumor, extra CSF — something else has to leave, or the pressure inside the box rises. That rise is increased intracranial pressure (IICP) . · Cerebral edema · Swelling of the brain tissue itself is one of the most common reasons the box overfills. On a CT scan, an edematous brain looks crowded: the folds (sulci) are squeezed, and the lateral horns of the ventricles — the holders of CSF — are squished or gone. Missing lateral horns are a definitive cue for cerebral edema. · Compensatory mechanisms · Mechanism | How it makes room · Autoregulation | Arterioles of the brain adjust their diameter to keep blood flow steady · CSF production or reabsorption | The brain makes less CSF or reabsorbs more · Shunting | CSF is pushed down into the spinal canal; blood is pushed out into the venous system · These mechanisms buy time, but they are limited. Once they are used up, even a small added volume causes a sharp rise in pressure — and the client deteriorates quickly. · The exception: babies. An infant's skull sutures are still open, so the box can expand (see Hydrocephaly). · 80 / 10 / 10 in a box that can't stretch. Brain, CSF, blood — if one goes up, another must come down, or the pressure climbs.

t: Neuro Assessment: Cranial Nerves, LOC & Posturing
x: The tools for catching IICP early · Cranial nerves · Mnemonic: "Oh Oh Oh To Take A Family Vacation, Go Vagus After Hours." · Cranial nerve | Quick assessment | How to test · I — Olfactory | Smell | Alcohol swab under the nose · II — Optic | Visual acuity | Snellen chart; read a name badge · III — Oculomotor | PERRLA; up/down eye movement | Pupils; cardinal fields of gaze · IV — Trochlear | Inferomedial (down and in) eye movement | Cardinal fields of gaze · V — Trigeminal | Sense of touch on the face; clench the jaw | Touch the face; clench the jaw · VI — Abducens | Lateral eye movement | Cardinal fields of gaze · VII — Facial | Facial expressions; tearing | Make "funny faces" — smile, frown · VIII — Acoustic (vestibulocochlear) | Hearing; equilibrium | Whisper test · IX — Glossopharyngeal | Say "ahh" — uvula rises midline | Say "ahh" · X — Vagus | Gag reflex | Gag reflex (tested with IX) · XI — Spinal accessory | Raise the shoulders | Shoulder shrug against resistance · XII — Hypoglossal | Tongue protrudes midline | Stick out the tongue · III, IV, and VI are tested together with the six cardinal fields of gaze. · V, VII, IX, XI, and XII can be checked together during a functional moment such as oral care or a meal. · Corneal (blink) reflex: CN V is the sensory trigger (feeling the touch) and CN VII is the motor action (closing the lid). No blink means either the client didn't feel it (V) or can't move the eyelid (VII). · CN III controls the pupil. A pupil that dilates on one side is often the first eye sign of IICP, because swelling presses on CN III. · Level of consciousness — the stimulus ladder · Describe the client as alert , lethargic , or unresponsive . When the client doesn't respond, escalate the stimulus from least to most intense, and stop at the first one that gets a response: · Step | Category | Nursing action | Responds here → LOC · 1 | Verbal | State the client's name in a normal voice — drop your pitch for older adults, who hear low voices better | Alert · 2 | Tactile | Touch the arm | Lethargic · 3 | Tactile | Lightly pat the arm | Lethargic · 4 | Tactile | Shake the arm | Lethargic · 5 | Pain | Pinch (trapezius or triceps) | Lethargic — responds only to pain · 6 & 7 together | Pain | Nailbed pressure and sternal rub — watch for a grimace or posturing | Lethargic — responds only to pain · 8, 9 & 10 together | Reflex | Gag reflex; brush the cornea with sterile gauze (corneal reflex); tap the forehead — the eyes should blink to protect | Unresponsive — no response to voice, touch, or pain; only reflexes are left to test · Steps 6 and 7 are done together, and steps 8, 9, and 10 are done together. Steps 8–10 test brainstem reflexes in a client who does not respond to verbal, tactile, or painful stimuli. · AVPU (rapid check) | Meaning · A lert | Awake and oriented · V erbal | Responds only when spoken to · P ain | Responds only to a painful stimulus (sternal rub, nailbed pressure) · U nresponsive | No response to any stimulus · Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) · Category | Best response | Points · Eye opening | Spontaneous · to sound · to pressure · none | 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 · Verbal | Oriented · confused · words (inappropriate) · sounds (incomprehensible) · none | 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 · Motor | Obeys commands · localizes · withdraws · flexion (decorticate) · extension (decerebrate) · none | 6 · 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 · Total ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert and responsive). · A score of 8 or below = coma; the client can't protect the airway — "less than 8, intubate." · A drop of 2 points or more is a significant decline — report it. · Posturing · Posture | What it looks like | Level of damage · Decorticate | Arms flexed in toward the chest ("to the core"), wrists and fingers flexed, legs extended, feet plantar flexed | Above the midbrain · Decerebrate | Arms extended and twisted out by the client's sides (internally rotated), wrists flexed, legs extended, feet plantar flexed | Midbrain — worse than decorticate · Upper extremities extended, lower extremities flexed | Mixed posture | Pons · Flaccid | Little or no motor response | Medulla — the worst sign · Decorticate = arms to the core — the "mummy pose." Decerebrate = arms twisting out by the sides — a deeper, more serious level. · Disorders of consciousness · Term | Meaning · Coma | Unarousable; may show posturing (decorticate or decerebrate) · Persistent vegetative state | An unresponsive person — sleep–wake cycles and eyes may open, but no awareness. Terri Schiavo: at autopsy her brain weighed half of normal and she was blind; her "tracking" movements were brainstem reflexes, not awareness. · Locked-in syndrome | A paralyzed person with the "lights on" — fully aware, but can move only the eyes. Jean-Dominique Bauby wrote The Diving Bell and the Butterfly by blinking his left eye — the diving bell is the paralysis, the butterfly is his mind.

Change in LOC comes first · Signs and symptoms of IICP · CHANGE IN LOC — the earliest and most important sign (restlessness, confusion, lethargy) · Pupillary changes — early: unilateral (one pupil dilates, sluggish); late: fixed and dilated (bilateral) · Reflex impairment · Seizures · Projectile vomiting without nausea — a hallmark LATE sign of IICP · Assess the pupils every hour . A fixed, dilated pupil is called "blown" — pressure on CN III. · Case: Luke Kwon · A golfer hit his head on a steel bridge railing while riding in a golf cart. He never lost consciousness, played seven more holes he can't remember, and drove about 40 minutes to his hotel with a worsening headache and sleepiness. Hours later he vomited repeatedly outside the ER, gave a nonsense answer to an orientation question, then seized and slipped in and out of a coma. That period of seeming "fine" is the lucid interval — pressure keeps building until it overwhelms compensation. His injury was an epidural hemorrhage — an arterial bleed, the classic cause of a lucid interval. (Full case in Worksheets.) · Effects on motor movement · As pressure moves down the brainstem, motor responses worsen: decorticate (above the midbrain) → decerebrate (midbrain) → arms extended with legs flexed (pons) → flaccid (medulla, the vital center). Pressure on the pons changes the breathing pattern; pressure on the medulla produces Cushing's triad and the need for a ventilator. · Effects on the respiratory pattern · Pattern | Level of the brain · Cheyne-Stokes — the "roller coaster": fast and deep, slowing to a stop (apnea), then ramping back up | Cortex or upper brainstem · Central neurogenic hyperventilation — rapid, deep, sustained | Midbrain or upper pons · Cluster or ataxic — irregular, unpredictable | Pons or medulla · Bradypnea | Overall CNS depression · Effects on vital signs · Cushing's triad — a late sign from pressure on the medulla: · Hypertension with a widened pulse pressure (systolic up, diastolic down) · Bradycardia · Bradypnea (irregular) · Temperature | Meaning · Central fever (neuro storm) | Pressure on the hypothalamus disrupts temperature control — acetaminophen won't help; use external cooling and ice · Peripheral fever | From infection — treat the cause · Either kind of fever raises the brain's oxygen demand. · Cushing's triad is the brain fighting to push blood in against rising pressure: BP up and pulse pressure wide, heart rate down, breathing slow. It is a late sign — herniation may be close. · Stages of IICP · Stage | Mental status | Pupils | Breathing | Vital signs · 1 — Compensation | Awake and alert | Equal and reactive | Normal | Normal · 2 — Compensation | Episodes of confusion, restlessness, lethargy | Equal and reactive | Normal | Normal · 3 — Beginning decompensation | Can't stay awake → progressively deeper coma | Small and reactive → sluggish → one side dilates and fixes | May slow → Cheyne-Stokes → central neurogenic hyperventilation | Systolic BP rises, pulse pressure widens , pulse slows and is full and bounding · 4 — Decompensation (herniation) | Deep coma | Both dilated and fixed | Apneustic or ataxic | BP falls; pulse becomes irregular → death · Intervention works best in stages 1–2, is urgently needed in stage 3, and is usually futile in stage 4. · Complications · Complication | What happens | Key findings · Diabetes insipidus (DI) | The body stops producing ADH | A LOT of dilute urine, excessive thirst, dehydration, high serum sodium. Action: give fluids; administer vasopressin · SIADH | Too much ADH | Fluid retention, fluid volume overload, pulmonary edema, low serum sodium (dilutional). Action: restrict fluids; monitor for crackles and hyponatremia · Herniation | Brain tissue shifts from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure | Loss of blood flow — signals impending brain death · DI = D ry (losing water, sodium climbs). SIADH = S oaked (holding water, sodium drops).

CPP = MAP − ICP · Monitoring ICP · Device | Notes · Ventriculostomy (external ventricular drain, EVD) | Surgeons drill through the skull and insert a catheter into a lateral ventricle — it measures ICP and can drain CSF . If the client can't get to the OR, the nurse clips the hair and brings the ventriculostomy cart. · Subarachnoid bolt | Measures ICP; can't drain CSF · Epidural monitor | Measures ICP; can't drain CSF · Ventricular drain care · The transducer MUST be zeroed and level with the tragus of the ear at all times · Drain too low → over-drains CSF and "dries the client out" — the brain can collapse · Drain too high → under-drains; CSF backs up and the pressure keeps building · Clamp the drain per protocol before repositioning or moving the client, and unclamp afterward · Strict sterile technique; watch for fever and other signs of infection · CSF appearance | Meaning · Clear, maybe a hint of yellow, sediment-free | Normal · Bloody or pink (after the initial period) | Brain bleed · Opaque / cloudy | Infection · Cerebral perfusion pressure · Value | Formula / normal · Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) | CPP = MAP − ICP · Normal ICP | 0–15 mm Hg — over 20 = PROBLEM; neuro clients need a higher MAP to keep the CPP at 70–100. · Avoid fast changes in blood pressure — autoregulation is already failing, and rapid swings can cause herniation. · Normal central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO₂) is about 70% ; lower means the tissues are consuming more oxygen under stress. · To raise CPP, either lower the ICP or raise the MAP . · Manipulating CPP · Decrease the ICP | Manipulate the MAP · Diuretics — mannitol, an osmotic diuretic, pulls fluid from the brain into the vascular space (assumes the kidneys work) | Vasopressors — raise a low MAP · Steroids — dexamethasone (Decadron) decreases inflammation when a tumor is the cause | Antihypertensives — nicardipine (calcium channel blocker), the #1 choice in neuro clients · Avoid Valsalva — stool softener (Colace); No consciousness, no reflexes, no respirations · Brain death is the absence of · Absent | How it's tested · Consciousness | No response to any stimulus; caloric test (ice water in the ear — painful) produces no eye movement · Reflexes | Brainstem reflexes absent — doll's eye test abnormal, no corneal, gag, or cough reflex · Respirations | Apnea test: a 2-minute pause from the ventilator; no spontaneous breath confirms brain death, and the client goes back on the vent · A brain-dead client can still have a pulse and perfuse the organs, because the heart has its own pacemaker — but the respiratory center in the medulla is dead. That is why the apnea test decides. · Doll's eye test (oculocephalic reflex) · The head is turned briskly side to side while the eyes are watched. · Normal (brainstem intact): the eyes move opposite to the head turn, staying focused forward. · Abnormal : the eyes stay fixed in the head and move with it. · Never perform it until a cervical spine injury has been ruled out. · Organ donation · A potential organ donor is a VERY BUSY patient. After brain death, the body loses its own control of blood pressure, temperature, and fluid balance, so the nurse works to keep the organs perfused and oxygenated: · Ventilator support and oxygenation · Fluids and vasopressors to maintain BP · Treat diabetes insipidus (large urine output) and electrolyte imbalances · Temperature control · Notify the organ procurement organization per policy; trained requesters talk with the family about donation · One donor can help 75 people — corneas, heart and valves, lungs, liver, pancreas, kidneys, intestines, bone, skin, tendons, ligaments, and veins.

Extra CSF in a closed box · Hydrocephaly is an abnormal buildup of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricles of the brain. The ventricles enlarge and press on the surrounding brain tissue — the CSF part of the Monro-Kellie box grows. · Why CSF builds up · Feature | Communicating (nonobstructive) | Noncommunicating (obstructive) · Pathophysiology | Impaired absorption of CSF | Physical block within the ventricles · Common causes | Subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis | Tumors, aqueductal stenosis, malformations · Shunt assessment focus | Gradual changes in LOC | Acute IICP — projectile vomiting · Signs depend on age · Infant (skull sutures still open) | Older child / adult (skull closed) · Rapidly increasing head circumference | Signs of IICP: headache, vomiting, change in LOC · Bulging, tense anterior fontanel ; widely separated sutures | Papilledema, vision changes · Distended scalp veins; thin, shiny scalp | Gait changes, balance problems · "Sunset eyes" — eyes deviate downward with sclera visible above the iris | Normal pressure hydrocephalus (older adults): gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia · High-pitched cry , irritability, poor feeding, vomiting |  · Because an infant's skull can still expand, the head grows first and the classic IICP signs show up later. Once the sutures close, the skull becomes the closed box, and IICP signs appear sooner. · Normal pressure hydrocephalus in older adults: wet, wobbly, and wacky — incontinence, gait disturbance, confusion. · Diagnosis · Serial head circumference measurements (infants) · CT or MRI shows enlarged ventricles · May be found on prenatal ultrasound · Treatment: the shunt · A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt drains excess CSF from a ventricle through tubing under the skin into the peritoneal cavity , where it is absorbed. Children need revisions as they grow. · Shunt infection vs. shunt malfunction · Feature | Shunt infection | Shunt malfunction (obstruction/kinking) · Cause | Bacterial colonization (often Staphylococcus ), usually within weeks of surgery | Mechanical blockage of CSF flow · Systemic signs | High fever, chills, tachycardia | Usually afebrile · Local signs | Redness, warmth, or swelling along the shunt tract or incision | Minimal skin changes; may have a fluid collection · GI | General nausea and vomiting | Projectile vomiting , often without nausea · Neuro | Stiff neck, photophobia, worsening irritability | IICP signs : headache, sunset eyes, bulging fontanel (infants) · Mental status | Gradual decline in alertness; lethargy | Rapid change in LOC — agitation to somnolence · Labs / imaging | Elevated WBC, CRP/ESR; positive CSF culture | Labs normal; CT/MRI shows larger ventricles than baseline · Both can cause poor feeding, sleepiness, new or more frequent seizures, and irritability. For a suspected malfunction the priority is the rapid rise in ICP — watch for Cushing's triad as a late sign. For an older child, the first sign of a failing shunt is the return of IICP signs (headache, LOC change). · Nursing care · Monitor neuro status and signs of IICP; measure head circumference daily in infants · Position after surgery FLAT on the nonoperative side — prevents rapid CSF drainage (which can cause a subdural hematoma) and keeps pressure off the valve behind the ear · A shunt is not placed while the client has a fever or active infection — it would seed the shunt · Protect the shunt: no contact sports · Monitor the abdomen for distention or tenderness (peritonitis, ileus) · Strictly monitor the incision for purulent drainage or "tracking" (red lines following the shunt path) · Teach the family the signs of shunt malfunction and infection and when to call

Partial or full thickness. · Chemical | Acids or alkalis · Electrical | Lightning or high-voltage wires · Smoke inhalation | Heat and toxic gases breathed in (often with thermal burns) · Burn depth · Depth | Appearance | Pain · Superficial (1st degree) — epidermis only | Red, dry; blanches with pressure; no edema , no blisters (like a sunburn) | Painful · Partial thickness (2nd degree) — involves the dermis | Blistered, moist , weepy, pink/red | Most painful — nerve endings are exposed · Full thickness (3rd degree) | Dry , leathery, waxy; white, discolored, or charred | No pain in the burned area — nerves are destroyed · Deep full thickness (4th degree) | Charred; bone or tendon visible | No pain; high risk for myoglobinuria · Superficial = sunburn. Partial = blister, moist, ouch . Full = dry, discolored, no pain — a painless burn is the deep one, not the mild one. · Full-thickness burns are often surrounded by partial-thickness areas, so a client with a painless center may still have severe pain at the edges. · Scene safety and first steps · Stop the burning process — stop, drop, and roll; remove smoldering clothing and jewelry · Chemical: remove all contaminated clothing immediately · No ice on a burn — it constricts vessels and deepens the injury · Burn center referral · Partial-thickness burns over a large area of the body · Any full-thickness burn, in any age group · Burns of the face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, or major joints · Electrical burns (including lightning), chemical burns, and inhalation injuries · Burns in clients with pre-existing heart or kidney disease · Scope · The rule of nines and body surface area methods, grafting, and long-term burn care are not covered in this module.

The skin barrier is gone — strict asepsis for all wound care. · Eschar as a tourniquet · Taut, burned tissue doesn't stretch. When the naloxone wears off, the client can stop breathing again. · Aspiration is the killer in alcohol and drug overdoses — if not intubated, place the client in the recovery (side-lying) position. · CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) · The gold-standard tool for scoring alcohol withdrawal and titrating benzodiazepines. t: Hypovolemic Shock & the Stages of Shock
x: The most general type — not enough in the tank · Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion — the cells don't get enough oxygen. Hypovolemic shock is the most general type: circulating volume is lost, so there isn't enough in the tank. · Causes · Hemorrhage (trauma, surgery, GI bleeding) · Burns (fluid shifts out of the vessels) · Severe vomiting or diarrhea · Excessive diuresis, dehydration · Hallmark findings · Flat neck veins , low CVP · Tachycardia — the first compensation · Skin cool and clammy · Restlessness and anxiety early · Falling urine output · The stages of shock · Stage | BP / HR | LOC | Urine output · Compensatory | BP normal; HR above 100 | Restless, anxious | Slightly decreased · Progressive | SBP below 90; HR very fast | Lethargic, confused | Below 30 mL/hr (oliguria) · Refractory | BP requires vasopressors | Comatose / unconscious | Anuria · Recovery | Returning to baseline | Improving orientation | Diuresis above 30 mL/hr · A normal BP doesn't mean the client is okay — in compensatory shock the heart rate and restlessness rise first, while BP holds. · Treatment · Two large-bore IVs (18-gauge) · Rapid IV fluid bolus — isotonic crystalloid (LR or NS); replace what was lost, including blood products for hemorrhage · Stop the bleeding : direct pressure; tourniquet for uncontrolled hemorrhage — above the wound, tightened until no pulse is felt; maximum 6 hours (amputation risk after that) · Oxygen; monitor vital signs, urine output, and LOC · Fluid stability decision · Status | Action · MAP 60 or higher — fluid stable | Continue monitoring; organs are being perfused · MAP below 60 — fluid unstable | Fluid challenge with isotonic crystalloid (NS or LR) · Challenge improves MAP to 60 or higher | Continue fluid resuscitation · Challenge fails — MAP stays below 60 | Start vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin, epinephrine) · Is it working? Hemodynamic goals · Parameter | Goal | Meaning · MAP | Above 65 mm Hg | Minimum pressure to keep organs alive · Urine output | Above 0.5 mL/kg/hr | Gold standard for kidney perfusion · Lactate | Below 2 mmol/L | Rising = cells dying (anaerobic metabolism) · CVP | 8–12 mm Hg | The tank is full enough · ScvO₂ | 70% | Lower = tissues using too much oxygen under stress · When shock isn't reversed · SIRS — the body's alarm: fever, tachycardia, tachypnea · MODS — organs fail like dominoes: usually the lungs (ARDS) first, then the kidneys · DIC — clotting and bleeding at the same time; look for oozing from IV sites

Cardiogenic, septic, neurogenic, anaphylactic · Shock types — hemodynamic footprints · Type | Cause | Critical cues | Priority action · Hypovolemic | Lost volume | Flat neck veins, low CVP, tachycardia, cool clammy skin | Rapid IV fluid bolus (LR or NS) · Cardiogenic | Pump failure (e.g., MI, heart failure) | Crackles , JVD , high CVP | NO fluid boluses — "pump" meds (dobutamine, dopamine) · Septic | Infection → widespread vasodilation | Fever, flushed warm skin (early), lactate above 2; mottled, cool skin = cold phase (late, organ failure) | 1-hour sepsis bundle · Neurogenic | Spinal cord injury → loss of sympathetic tone | Bradycardia + hypotension ; skin warm and dry | Vasopressors — the only shock where the HR goes down · Anaphylactic | Severe allergic reaction → vasodilation and airway swelling | Wheezing, stridor, hives, angioedema | Epinephrine IM ; maintain the airway · Cardiogenic = wet and pump-weak (crackles, JVD) — no extra fluid. Neurogenic = the only shock with a slow heart rate and warm, dry skin. · The 1-hour sepsis bundle (in order) · Step | Action · 1. Measure lactate | Normal below 2; critical 4 or higher. Measure first · 2. Blood cultures | Obtain before antibiotics · 3. Antibiotics | Broad-spectrum within 60 minutes · 4. Fluid resuscitation | 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate of 4 or higher · 5. Vasopressors | Norepinephrine if MAP stays below 65 after fluids · Vasopressor safety — norepinephrine (Levophed) · Vasopressors are vesicants ; give through a central line whenever possible. · Infiltration : the site turns cold, hard, and pale — the drug is constricting the vessels so tightly it kills the skin. · Step | Action · 1 | Stop the infusion at that site · 2 | Notify the provider for the antidote order · 3 | Give phentolamine (Regitine) subcutaneously around the infiltrated area — it dilates the vessels and saves the tissue · 4 | Restart the vasopressor in a new site in a different limb — the client still needs it to survive

It's the pulmonary edema, not the type of water · Drowning vs. near-drowning ·  | Drowning | Near-drowning · Definition | Death from suffocation after submersion in water | Survival — at least for a time — after a submersion that could have been fatal · What the nurse does | Resuscitation; if the client is cold, keep going — not dead until warm and dead | Airway, oxygen, C-spine if they dove or fell, and close monitoring · The danger after rescue | — | Secondary drowning / ARDS within 24 hours , even if the client looks fine at first · Watch for | — | Crackles, pink frothy sputum, falling SpO₂ · Freshwater vs. saltwater ·  | Freshwater | Saltwater · What it does to the lungs | Washes away surfactant | Pulls fluid into the alveoli · End result | Alveolar collapse → ARDS | Alveolar collapse → ARDS · Bottom line | The pulmonary edema matters more than the type of water | The pulmonary edema matters more than the type of water · Critical cues and actions · Topic | Cues | Priority action · Airway | Water in the lungs; hypoxia | Maintain the airway; prepare for mechanical ventilation · Trauma rule | The client jumped, dove, or fell into the water | Assume a cervical spine injury — stabilize the neck while managing the airway · Secretions | Frothy, pink-tinged sputum | This is fluid, not mucus — severe alveolar–capillary damage · Ventilation | Collapsed, fluid-filled alveoli | PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) pushes fluid out of the alveoli and back into the vascular space · Safety | High risk for secondary drowning or ARDS within 24 hours | Continuous pulse oximetry; frequent lung sounds for new crackles — even if the client looks fine at first · No expectorants — this is edema fluid, not a productive cough. Suctioning and PEEP clear the airway. · Submersion victims are often hypothermic too — a client is not dead until "warm and dead"; resuscitation continues until the core is rewarmed. · Pink, frothy sputum + crackles after a near-drowning = pulmonary edema . Watch closely for 24 hours, and protect the C-spine if they dove in.

Warm the core first — handle gently · Hypothermia · Topic | Cues | Priorities · Definition | Core temperature below 95°F (35°C). Shivering early → no shivering late | Warm the core first (trunk and chest) to prevent afterdrop and lethal dysrhythmias · Cardiac risk | The cold heart is extremely irritable — V-fib risk | Handle the client gently — rough movement can trigger V-fib · Rewarming | Internal: warm IV fluids, warm humidified O₂. External: heating blankets, radiant lamps |  · Afterdrop | Cold blood from the extremities returns to the core during rewarming | If the hands and feet are warmed first, that cold blood hits the heart and triggers V-fib · Metabolism | Drug clearance is severely slowed when cold | Hold or space out ACLS meds (epinephrine, amiodarone) until the client is warmer (usually above 86°F / 30°C) — otherwise the trapped drugs hit the heart all at once when rewarmed · Hemostasis | Cold blood doesn't clot well (coagulopathy) | High bleeding risk even without obvious trauma · Not dead until warm and dead. Resuscitation continues until the core is rewarmed to about 90–95°F (32–35°C). · Frostbite · Topic | Cues / actions · Appearance | White, waxy, or blue/mottled skin; hard to the touch · Before rewarming | Remove all jewelry and constricting clothing — thawed tissue swells and jewelry becomes a tourniquet · Rewarming | Warm water bath, 104–108°F (40–42°C) · Pain | Rewarming is intensely painful — premedicate with IV analgesics before the bath · Don't | Do not rub or massage — ice crystals in the cells cause more damage · After | Elevate the extremity to heart level to reduce thaw edema · Side by side: hypothermia vs. frostbite ·  | Hypothermia | Frostbite · What it is | Whole-body — core temperature below 95°F (35°C) | Local — tissue freezes (ice crystals in the cells) · Looks like | Shivering early → no shivering late; confusion; slowed metabolism | White, waxy, or blue/mottled skin; hard to the touch · Biggest danger | V-fib from the irritable cold heart and afterdrop | Tissue loss ; thaw swelling that turns jewelry into a tourniquet · How to rewarm | Core first — warm IV fluids, warm humidified O₂, heating blankets | Warm water bath, 104–108°F (40–42°C) · Before rewarming | Handle gently; space out ACLS meds while cold | Remove jewelry; premedicate with IV analgesics · Never | Warm the hands and feet first; rough handling | Rub or massage the tissue · After | Resuscitate until warm — "not dead until warm and dead" | Elevate to heart level to reduce thaw edema

x: No sweat = emergency ·  | Heat exhaustion | Heat stroke · Temperature | Normal to mildly elevated | Above 104°F (40°C) · Skin | Profuse sweating | NO sweating — hot and dry · Neuro | Headache, weakness | Mental status changes, coma — the brain is "cooking" · Action | Move to a cool place; oral or IV fluid replacement | Medical emergency — rapid cooling · Cooling heat stroke · Cool IV fluids, cooling blankets · Ice packs over large vessels : axilla, groin, and neck · Stop cooling at 102°F (38.9°C) to prevent shivering and rebound hypothermia · Shivering is the enemy — it produces heat. Irrigate, tetanus, and know when to give rabies prophylaxis · Animal bites · Wound contamination → infection risk · Copious irrigation with soap and water; debridement if needed · Tetanus toxoid if status is unknown or it has been more than 5 years · Rabies · For a bite from a wild animal or an animal of unknown status: · When | What · Day 0 | HRIG (human rabies immune globulin) — passive immunity, infiltrated around the wound edges if possible — plus the first vaccine dose · Days 3, 7, and 14 | Vaccine doses (active immunity) · Site | Deltoid — never the gluteal area (poor absorption) · A bite from a currently vaccinated dog usually does not need rabies vaccination: wash the wound, have a provider assess the risk, and quarantine and observe the dog for 10 days. · Ticks · Lyme disease: look for the bull's-eye rash (erythema migrans); treated with doxycycline · Removal: grasp the tick at the head with tweezers and pull straight up. Watch for anaphylaxis.

Mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery · The four phases of disaster management · Phase | Definition | Examples · Mitigation | Actions before a disaster that prevent or reduce long-term risk | Hazard mapping (flood zones), building codes, standardized protocols · Preparedness | Building the capacity to respond before a disaster | Mock mass-casualty drills; stocking emergency kits; phone trees and communication plans · Response | Immediate actions during or right after the event | START triage at the scene; opening the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) · Recovery | Long-term return to normal | PTSD counseling; an "after-action report" to evaluate the response · Hospital plans and decontamination · Zone | What happens · Hot zone | The area of contamination — only specialized hazmat teams; no nursing care · Warm zone | Decontamination — patients are scrubbed down; nurses work here in full PPE · Cold zone | Only decontaminated or unexposed patients; standard PPE · Decontaminate before the patient enters the ED — otherwise the whole hospital is contaminated. · Hospitals hold disaster drills twice a year to maintain accreditation. · PPE level | Protection · Level A | Highest — self-contained breathing apparatus plus a vapor-tight suit · Level B | High respiratory protection, less skin protection (splash-resistant) · Level C | Most common in hospitals — air-purifying respirator plus a chemical suit · Level D | Standard uniform — gown, gloves, mask · Personal disaster kit (3-day supply) · Water — about 4 liters per person per day · Non-perishable food · Battery or hand-crank radio, flashlight, batteries, whistle · Copies of important documents (birth certificates, medication lists, pet information) · Biological and chemical agents · Agent | Cues | Priority action · Anthrax | Inhalation (fever, cough, SOB) or cutaneous (black eschar) | Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for 60 days; not contagious person to person — standard precautions · Smallpox | High fever, then a rash all at the same stage (unlike chickenpox) | Strict airborne + contact precautions · Sarin gas | SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, emesis | Antidotes: atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM) · Botulism | Drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing, descending paralysis | Monitor for respiratory failure (ventilator)

Here and now — safety and basic needs first · Phases of a crisis · Phase | What the client feels | Nursing focus · 1 — Impact | Shock, denial, numbness | Safety and basic needs — water, a blanket, shelter · 2 — Recoil | Beginning to feel the pain; looking for someone to blame | Listen — let them vent and cry · 3 — Reorganization | Accepting a "new normal" and moving forward | Referrals — support groups, therapy · In crisis, focus on the here and now . Be direct and calm, and meet basic needs (safety, water). For an older adult with impaired mobility, have them sit — sitting prevents injuries from a fall. · Domestic violence — myths and facts · Myth | Fact · It only happens to women | 1 in 3 women and 1 in 4 men are affected · It's caused by drugs, alcohol, or mental illness | These complicate abuse but do not cause it · Abusers are out of control and need anger management | Abusers use deliberate tactics to maintain control · It's physical abuse only | Emotional, financial, verbal, intimidation, threats, and isolation are all used as tactics · If the victim stays, it must not be that bad | It takes an average of 7 attempts to leave before succeeding · Nursing care · Screen every client privately , away from the partner · Believe the client; don't judge a decision to stay · Document injuries objectively, with the client's own words in quotes · Help develop a safety plan and give resources · Leaving is a process, not one event — and the time of leaving is often the most dangerous. Support, don't pressure.

Medical needs first, then forensic care — and give back control · What is sexual assault? · Any sexual contact or behavior that happens without clear, voluntary, and informed consent — including attempted rape, unwanted touching, forced sexual acts, penetration without consent (legally rape), coercion through threats, lies, guilt, or intimidation, and sexual activity with someone who can't consent because of age, intoxication, disability, or unconsciousness. · The SANE · A Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner is an RN with specialized education and clinical preparation in medical forensic care. · Typically requires 2 years of RN practice (emergency, critical care, or maternal-child preferred), about 40 hours of training, and precepted clinical experience. · Certification (SANE-A for adults and adolescents; SANE-P for pediatrics) is needed mainly to manage a program or teach. · The SANE is an expert witness — their documentation is powerful evidence in court. · Neurobiology of trauma · Brain area / chemical | Effect during trauma · Prefrontal cortex | Rational thinking, planning, decision making — goes offline under fear · Amygdala | Activated at the onset of fear; impairs rational thinking; drives survival reflexes · Hippocampus | Processes information into memories; very sensitive to stress hormones · Catecholamines | Natural adrenaline — fight or flight · Cortisol | Reduces available energy; the body may shut down and freeze · Opioids | Natural morphine — blocks pain, which can cause a flat affect · Oxytocin | Good feelings · Survival reflexes are fight, flight, and freeze — some victims experience tonic immobility (like a rabbit or deer). · Memories may be fragmented, incomplete, inconsistent, or disorganized ; fear onset, central details, and survival reflexes may be recalled accurately. It takes about two sleep cycles to process the event, so the story often becomes clearer later. · Trauma-informed care · Recognize that clients may have many traumas, and avoid re-traumatizing them. Give back control and explain why you ask what you ask. Instead of "What were you wearing?" — which sounds like blame — explain the purpose: "Would you tell me what you were wearing so I can find you on the surveillance video?" · Reporting and the exam · Medical needs come before forensic needs. The client can report to law enforcement (911), go to the emergency department, or contact the SAFE center directly. · Under the Violence Against Women Act , a medical forensic exam is free, and the client does not have to report to law enforcement or cooperate with the justice system to get it. · Reporting options: full disclosure to law enforcement (evidence collection and treatment → possible prosecution); Jane/John Doe report (evidence collected and treated, kit stored by law enforcement but not sent to the crime lab — the client can decide later); no disclosure (medical treatment only); university students may also disclose to the school. · The interview: the goal is for the client to tell the story ONE TIME , privately, only to those who need to hear it. The narrative becomes part of the evidence kit. · The physical exam: head to toe. Bruises may not show yet — palpate for tenderness. Document with written notes, pictograms, and photographs (filters reveal hidden bruising). A speculum exam gives a magnified, illuminated view. Genital injury is often absent — that does not mean an assault didn't happen. · Evidence: photos before collection; evidence collected head to toe; body diagrams; samples for drug testing if drug-facilitated assault is suspected. · Preserve the evidence · Don't let the client wash, shower, brush teeth, urinate, or change clothes until the kit is collected, if possible · Place clothing in paper bags , never plastic (plastic traps moisture and destroys DNA) · Chain of custody: everyone who handles evidence signs for it — a broken chain makes evidence useless in court · Don't leave the client alone · Prophylactic medication · Purpose | Medication · Chlamydia / gonorrhea | Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) , doxycycline · Trichomoniasis | Metronidazole (Flagyl) · Nausea | Ondansetron (Zofran) · Pregnancy prevention | Levonorgestrel (Plan B) — progestin stops the ovary from releasing an egg; will not end an existing pregnancy · Pain | Ibuprofen (Motrin) · Discharge and follow-up · Safety first: does the client have a safe place to go? Help develop a safety plan. · Community resources and counseling; follow-up with a primary care provider or the health department for HIV, syphilis, and HPV testing · A follow-up exam within days reviews injuries (bruises may appear later) and repeats photos; a 1-month phone check asks how the client is coping

monitor I&O, serum osmolality, electrolytes · Dexamethasone (Decadron) | Decreases inflammation when a tumor causes IICP | Monitor glucose; GI protection · Propofol | Induced coma — lowers metabolic demand | Very short half-life allows quick neuro checks;
