silver nitrate stains black · Poisonings · Drug | Use · Activated charcoal | Binds many toxins — not alcohol, lithium, iron, or corrosives; check bowel sounds first · Thiamine (banana bag) | Before or with glucose — prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy · Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam) | Alcohol withdrawal, guided by CIWA-Ar · Sodium bicarbonate | Salicylate and tricyclic overdose · Antidotes: acetylcysteine, deferoxamine, fomepizole, digoxin immune Fab | Acetaminophen, iron, ethylene glycol, digoxin (see Reversal Agents) · Shock and cardiac arrest · Drug | Use · Norepinephrine | First vasopressor for septic shock (MAP below 65 after fluids) · Dobutamine , dopamine | "Pump" meds for cardiogenic shock · Phentolamine | Antidote for vasopressor infiltration — injected around the site · Amiodarone or lidocaine | Shockable arrest after the third shock · Environmental and anaphylaxis · Drug | Use · Chlorpromazine or a benzodiazepine | Shivering during heat-stroke cooling · Doxycycline | Lyme disease · Diphenhydramine , steroids | After epinephrine in anaphylaxis · Glucagon | Anaphylaxis not responding to epinephrine in a client on beta blockers

Anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Anaphylaxis: IM into the anterolateral thigh (auto-injector 0.3 mg adult, 0.15 mg child); may repeat in 5–15 minutes. Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes (ASAP in asystole/PEA; after the second shock in VF/pVT). Racemic epinephrine by nebulizer for airway swelling · Mechanism of action | Alpha and beta agonist: vasoconstriction (raises BP, reduces swelling), bronchodilation , increased heart rate and contractility · Adverse reactions | Tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypertension, chest pain, anxiety, tremor, headache; tissue necrosis if an IV infiltrates · Contraindications | None in a life-threatening emergency such as anaphylaxis or cardiac arrest; caution with heart disease · Nursing interventions | Give first in anaphylaxis, before antihistamines or steroids; monitor HR, BP, and rhythm; IM is preferred for anaphylaxis; clients on beta blockers may need glucagon; monitor 1–72 hours for a biphasic reaction · Patient education | Carry two auto-injectors at all times; inject into the outer thigh (through clothing if needed); call 911 and go to the ED even if symptoms improve — symptoms can return; check the expiration date; wear medical alert ID · IM in the thigh for anaphylaxis. IV/IO 1 mg every 3–5 minutes in a code.

Topical burn antimicrobial · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Topical antimicrobial cream to prevent and treat burn wound infection (partial- and full-thickness burns); applied in a thin layer once or twice daily per orders · Mechanism of action | Silver and sulfa act against a broad range of bacteria and yeast on the wound surface · Adverse reactions | Leukopenia (transient drop in WBC); rash; burning; sulfa crystals in the urine; can stain · Contraindications | Sulfa allergy ; late pregnancy and newborns (risk of kernicterus) · Nursing interventions | Check for a sulfa allergy first; apply with sterile technique ; premedicate for pain before dressing changes; cleanse off old cream before reapplying; monitor the WBC; monitor urine for crystals; not used on the face · Patient education | Report rash or itching; dressing changes will be done with sterile technique; it can stain

Who gets the shot · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Tetanus toxoid (Td or Tdap) IM for any burn , bite (animal, snake, spider), or dirty wound when the status is unknown or the last dose was more than 5 years ago . Tetanus immune globulin (TIG) adds immediate passive protection for a dirty wound when the client never completed the primary series · Mechanism of action | Toxoid stimulates the client's own antibodies (active immunity); TIG supplies ready-made antibodies (passive immunity) · Adverse reactions | Soreness, redness, and swelling at the site; low-grade fever · Contraindications | Previous severe allergic reaction to a tetanus-containing vaccine · Nursing interventions | Ask when the last tetanus dose was; give IM (deltoid); document the date; tetanus is not required for smoke inhalation alone with no break in the skin · Patient education | Keep tetanus up to date — a booster every 10 years, sooner after a dirty wound; keep a record of the date · Burn, bite, or dirty wound + unknown status or more than 5 years → tetanus toxoid .

Snake and spider envenomation · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Envenomation with progressing signs: CroFab for pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads) — most effective within 6 hours ; coral snake antivenin; black widow antivenin. IV, dosed by severity and response · Mechanism of action | Antibodies bind and neutralize the venom · Adverse reactions | Allergic reaction / anaphylaxis during the infusion; serum sickness days to weeks later (fever, rash, joint pain) · Contraindications | Known allergy to the product's source — weigh against the severity of the bite · Nursing interventions | Have epinephrine and resuscitation equipment at the bedside ; monitor vital signs closely during the infusion; mark and measure the swelling to track progression; keep the snake-bitten limb immobilized and dependent; give tetanus · Patient education | Report rash, joint pain, or fever in the following weeks (serum sickness)

Naloxone, flumazenil, and the specific antidotes · Naloxone (Narcan) · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Opioid overdose with respiratory depression; IV, IM, or intranasal; repeat every 2–3 minutes as needed · Mechanism of action | Opioid antagonist — displaces opioids from receptors · Adverse reactions | Acute opioid withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, tachycardia, pain); re-sedation as it wears off · Contraindications | None in a life-threatening overdose · Nursing interventions | Give for pinpoint pupils and RR below 10 without waiting for labs; support ventilation; monitor for re-sedation — naloxone lasts 30–90 minutes, many opioids last 4–6 hours; repeat doses as needed · Patient education | Family and friends of people who use opioids can carry intranasal naloxone; call 911 after giving it · Flumazenil (Romazicon) · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Benzodiazepine overdose or reversal of sedation; IV · Mechanism of action | Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist · Adverse reactions | Seizures , especially in chronic benzodiazepine users reversed too fast; re-sedation · Contraindications | Caution in chronic benzodiazepine users and mixed overdoses (e.g., with tricyclics) · Nursing interventions | Seizure precautions; monitor LOC and respirations for re-sedation · Patient education | — · Other antidotes — quick match · Toxin | Reversal agent · Acetaminophen | Acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) · Digoxin | Digoxin immune Fab (Digibind) · Iron | Deferoxamine · Ethylene glycol | Fomepizole · Salicylates, tricyclics | Sodium bicarbonate · Carbon monoxide | 100% oxygen · Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin · Nerve agents (sarin) | Atropine and pralidoxime · Vasopressor infiltration | Phentolamine · Acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) — acetaminophen · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Acetaminophen overdose; works best when started early, within about 8 hours of the ingestion. PO (mixed in juice or soda) or IV as a loading dose followed by an infusion · Mechanism of action | Restores glutathione, which the liver uses to neutralize the toxic acetaminophen byproduct — protects the liver · Adverse reactions | PO: nausea and vomiting (it smells like rotten eggs ). IV: allergic-type reaction — flushing, rash, bronchospasm — most often during the loading dose · Contraindications | None in a life-threatening overdose; use caution with asthma (bronchospasm) · Nursing interventions | Draw an acetaminophen level and liver labs ( ALT/AST , PT/INR); mix the oral form in chilled juice and give an antiemetic; repeat the dose if the client vomits within 1 hour; slow or pause the IV infusion for a reaction · Patient education | Check OTC labels — many cold and pain products also contain acetaminophen · Digoxin immune Fab (Digibind) — digoxin · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Life-threatening digoxin toxicity: dangerous dysrhythmias, severe bradycardia, hyperkalemia; IV · Mechanism of action | Antibody fragments bind digoxin so it can't act on the heart; the bound drug is excreted by the kidneys · Adverse reactions | Hypokalemia as potassium moves back into the cells; worsening heart failure or a fast ventricular rate once digoxin's effect is gone; allergic reaction · Contraindications | Allergy to sheep (ovine) proteins · Nursing interventions | Continuous ECG; monitor potassium closely; digoxin levels are unreliable after Fab because the test also measures bound drug · Patient education | Report yellow or green halos, nausea, or a slow pulse; take the pulse before each digoxin dose · Deferoxamine — iron · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Serious iron poisoning; IV infusion (or IM) · Mechanism of action | Chelates (binds) iron so it can be excreted in the urine · Adverse reactions | Reddish-pink urine (expected — it shows iron is leaving); hypotension and flushing if infused too fast · Contraindications | Severe kidney disease or anuria — the iron complex leaves through the kidneys · Nursing interventions | Infuse slowly and monitor BP; watch the urine color — it clears as the iron is removed; monitor I&O; remember charcoal does not bind iron · Patient education | Keep iron supplements and children's vitamins with iron locked up · Fomepizole (Antizol) — ethylene glycol · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning; IV · Mechanism of action | Blocks the liver enzyme (alcohol dehydrogenase) that turns ethylene glycol into its toxic acids · Adverse reactions | Headache, nausea, dizziness · Contraindications | Allergy to the drug · Nursing interventions | Monitor ABGs for metabolic acidosis and kidney function; prepare for hemodialysis if ordered · Patient education | Store antifreeze in its original container — its sweet taste attracts children and pets · Sodium bicarbonate — salicylates and tricyclics · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Salicylate (aspirin) overdose and tricyclic antidepressant overdose; IV · Mechanism of action | Salicylates: alkalinizes the urine so the kidneys trap and excrete the acid. Tricyclics: stabilizes the heart and narrows the wide QRS · Adverse reactions | Metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, sodium and fluid overload; tissue damage if it infiltrates · Contraindications | Existing alkalosis · Nursing interventions | Monitor ABGs, potassium, and urine pH; continuous ECG for the QRS width; check IV patency · Patient education | Keep aspirin out of reach; some OTC products, such as bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol), also contain salicylate · 100% oxygen — carbon monoxide · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Carbon monoxide poisoning; nonrebreather mask ; hyperbaric oxygen for severe cases · Mechanism of action | High-concentration oxygen pushes CO off the hemoglobin faster · Adverse reactions | Oxygen toxicity with prolonged high concentrations · Contraindications | None in an emergency · Nursing interventions | Remove the client from the source; don't trust the SpO₂ — it reads falsely normal; follow the carboxyhemoglobin level; keep the oxygen on until it normalizes · Patient education | Install CO detectors; never run generators, grills, or cars in enclosed spaces · Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) — cyanide · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Cyanide poisoning, often from smoke inhalation (burning plastics and synthetics); IV infusion · Mechanism of action | Binds cyanide to form vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin), which is excreted in the urine · Adverse reactions | Red skin and red urine (expected, can last for days); hypertension; allergic reaction · Contraindications | Known allergy — weighed against a life-threatening exposure · Nursing interventions | Draw labs before the dose — the red color interferes with some lab tests; monitor BP; give 100% oxygen · Patient education | The red skin and urine are expected and fade · Atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM) — nerve agents · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Nerve agents (sarin) and organophosphate insecticides — the SLUDGE picture; IM auto-injector or IV · Mechanism of action | Atropine blocks the excess acetylcholine and dries secretions. Pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, reversing muscle weakness — it works best given early · Adverse reactions | Atropine: tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision. Pralidoxime: blurred vision, dizziness, hypertension · Contraindications | None in a life-threatening exposure · Nursing interventions | Decontaminate and wear PPE first; repeat atropine until the secretions dry ; protect the airway · Patient education | — · Phentolamine (Regitine) — vasopressor infiltration · Category | Detail · Indications / dosage | Extravasation of a vasopressor such as norepinephrine or dopamine; injected subcutaneously around the site as soon as possible · Mechanism of action | Alpha blocker — reverses the intense vasoconstriction and restores blood flow so the tissue doesn't die · Adverse reactions | Hypotension, tachycardia, dysrhythmias · Contraindications | Use caution with coronary artery disease · Nursing interventions | Stop the infusion at that site and notify the provider; inject around the area as prescribed; monitor BP; mark and watch the site · Patient education | Report pain, burning, or coolness at an IV site right away · Narcan wears off before the opioid — watch for the client to stop breathing again.

The building blocks every other calculation relies on · Before any drip rate or weight-based dose can be calculated, you need to be fluent in the basic conversions underneath them — pounds to kilograms, and the metric ladder from kilograms down to micrograms. Almost every calculation error in practice traces back to a mistake at this level, not the fancier formula built on top of it. · Basic Dosage Calculation · Formula: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = Amount to administer · Worked example: Order is 500 mg PO; available as 250 mg tablets. (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets . · Worked example 2: Order is 2 mg lorazepam; available as a 4 mg/mL vial. (2 ÷ 4) × 1 mL = 0.5 mL . · Weight Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Pounds → kilograms | lbs ÷ 2.2 = kg | 154 lbs ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg · Kilograms → pounds | kg × 2.2 = lbs | 100 kg × 2.2 = 220 lbs · Almost every weight-based drug calculation in this unit starts with converting the patient's weight to kilograms — if that first conversion is wrong, every step after it is wrong too, even if the rest of the math is done perfectly. This matters directly in this module for weight-based pediatric dosing (ADHD/ASD medications) and for BSA-based chemotherapy dosing. · Metric System Conversions — the 1000 rule · Standard medical units (kg, g, mg, mcg) are each separated from their neighbor by a factor of 1000. · Direction | Rule | Example · Larger → smaller (kg→g, g→mg, mg→mcg) | Multiply by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places right) | 2 g × 1000 = 2000 mg · Smaller → larger (mcg→mg, mg→g, g→kg) | Divide by 1000 (move the decimal 3 places left) | 2500 mcg ÷ 1000 = 2.5 mg · Volume Conversions · Conversion | Formula | Example · Milliliters → liters | mL ÷ 1000 = L | 2500 mL ÷ 1000 = 2.5 L · Liters → milliliters | L × 1000 = mL | 0.5 L × 1000 = 500 mL · Household & Volume Equivalents · Household/Metric | Equivalent · 1 teaspoon (tsp) | 5 mL · 1 tablespoon (tbsp) | 15 mL (or 3 tsp) · 1 ounce (oz) | 30 mL (or 2 tbsp) · 1 cup | 240 mL (8 oz) · 1 quart (approx.) | 1000 mL (1 L)

t: IV Flow Rates, Drip Rates & Concentration
x: Getting fluid and medication into the vein at the right speed · These formulas answer one of two questions: how fast should this infusion pump run (mL/hr), or how many drops per minute should a gravity IV be set to (gtt/min) when there's no pump involved? A third formula, concentration, sets up weight-based drip calculations. · Flow Rate / Infusion Rate (mL/hr) — for infusion pumps · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Total Time (hr) = mL/hr · Worked example: Infuse 1000 mL of Normal Saline over 8 hours. 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr . · Infusion Time — working backward from a known rate · Formula: Total Volume (mL) ÷ Flow Rate (mL/hr) = Time (hours) · Worked example: A 1000 mL bag is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How long will it last? 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 hours . · Drip Rate (gtt/min) — for gravity IV tubing without a pump · There are two equivalent ways to reach the same answer, depending on whether you already know the mL/hr rate or are starting from the total order. · Starting point | Formula · You already know mL/hr | (mL/hr ÷ 60) × Drop Factor (gtt/mL) = gtt/min · You're starting from the total order | (Total Volume [mL] × Drop Factor [gtt/mL]) ÷ Time (minutes) = gtt/min · Worked example (method 1): Infuse at 125 mL/hr using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. First, mL/min: 125 ÷ 60 = 2.08 mL/min. Then: 2.08 × 15 = 31.2, rounded to 31 gtt/min . · Worked example (method 2): Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours (480 minutes) with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25, rounded to 31 gtt/min — the same answer either way. · IV Push Medication Rate · A common general safety rule for IV push medications is roughly 1 mL per minute unless the drug's specific administration guidelines say otherwise. Worked example: a 10 mL medication is administered over 10 minutes, consistent with the 1 mL/min rule. Pushing too fast is a common cause of adverse drug reactions — relevant here for IV push benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam for agitation/status epilepticus) and IV antihistamines. · Concentration Calculation — the setup step for weight-based drips · Formula: (Total mg in the bag × 1000) ÷ Total mL in the bag = Concentration (mcg/mL) · Worked example: A bag contains 400 mg of a drug in 250 mL of D5W. (400 × 1000) ÷ 250 = 1600 mcg/mL .

Calculations that scale a dose — or a diagnosis — to the patient's size · These two calculations both answer a version of the same question — how big is this patient, in a way that's useful for dosing or risk assessment? BMI is a general screening number used constantly in this module's eating-disorder content; BSA is a more precise scaling factor used specifically for chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · BMI — Body Mass Index · System | Formula · Metric | Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]² · Imperial | [Weight (lbs) × 703] ÷ [Height (in)]² · Worked example (metric): Weight 70 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625. Divide weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86 (normal weight range). · Worked example (imperial): Weight 154 lbs, height 69 inches. 154 × 703 = 108,262. Square the height: 69 × 69 = 4,761. Divide: 108,262 ÷ 4,761 = 22.74 — the same result as the metric calculation, just arrived at with different starting units. · This is exactly the calculation behind the BMI thresholds in the Anorexia Nervosa lesson: a BMI under 17 is a diagnostic marker of the disorder, and under 15 is considered extreme/life-threatening. Knowing how to compute BMI from a height and weight given in a case stem — not just recognize the threshold — is testable on its own. · BSA — Body Surface Area · BSA approximates a patient's total skin surface area in square meters (m²), and it's used specifically for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, chemotherapy agents, pediatric patients, and burn patients — situations where a small dosing error has an outsized effect. This is the calculation behind chemotherapy dosing in the Cancer unit. · Formula: BSA = √[(Height in cm × Weight in kg) ÷ 3600] · Fully worked pediatric dosing example · Order: a chemotherapy agent at 2 mg/m². Patient: 37 lb, 97 cm tall. Supply: 1 mg/mL. · Step 1 — convert weight to kg: 37 lb ÷ 2.2 = 16.8 kg · Step 2 — calculate BSA: √[(97 cm × 16.8 kg) ÷ 3600] = √[1629.6 ÷ 3600] = √0.4527 = 0.67 m² · Step 3 — calculate the dose in mg: 2 mg/m² × 0.67 m² = 1.34 mg · Step 4 — calculate the dose in mL: 1.34 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 1.34 mL to administer · Notice this whole calculation depends on the weight-to-kg conversion from the first Med Math lesson — get that first step wrong, and every subsequent step (BSA, mg dose, mL dose) inherits the error.

MAP, CPP, and weight-/unit-based infusions · This lesson groups together the calculations that show up most often in critical care and high-alert medication administration — all of them either measure perfusion pressure directly, or calculate the pump rate for a drug that manipulates that pressure. Relevant here for a client in delirium tremens, an oncology patient in septic shock, or any client on a high-alert IV drip. · MAP — Mean Arterial Pressure · Formula: (Systolic BP + [2 × Diastolic BP]) ÷ 3 = MAP · Worked example: BP is 120/80. (120 + [2 × 80]) ÷ 3 = (120 + 160) ÷ 3 = 93.3 mmHg . · MAP reflects the average pressure driving blood into the organs across the whole cardiac cycle — it's weighted toward diastole because the heart spends more time in diastole than systole. A MAP of roughly 65 mmHg or higher is generally considered necessary to maintain adequate organ perfusion in a critically ill patient. · CPP — Cerebral Perfusion Pressure · Formula: MAP − ICP = CPP · Worked example: MAP is 93, ICP is 15. 93 − 15 = 78 mmHg . · CPP depends directly on MAP — if you already calculated MAP for a patient, you're one subtraction away from CPP. A CPP that drops too low (generally below ~60 mmHg) risks cerebral ischemia, which is why both numbers are tracked together in a patient with a head injury or elevated ICP. · Weight-Based Infusion (mcg/kg/min) · Formula: (Desired mcg × kg × 60 minutes) ÷ Concentration (mcg/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg patient, with a concentration of 1600 mcg/mL (from the concentration calculation in the previous lesson). (5 × 80 × 60) ÷ 1600 = 15 mL/hr . · Units-Based Infusion (Units/kg/hr) — e.g., Heparin · Formula: (Units × kg) ÷ Concentration (Units/mL) = mL/hr · Worked example: Order is 12 Units/kg/hr for a 100 kg patient, with a concentration of 100 Units/mL. (12 × 100) ÷ 100 = 12 mL/hr . · Both weight-based and units-based drips are high-alert medications given by infusion pump only — the shared theme across every high-alert drug is a computerized pump, frequent reassessment, and a clear plan for what triggers stopping or adjusting the rate.

Heparin, dopamine, epinephrine, amiodarone, atropine, adenosine · These are high-alert drugs on an infusion pump (or a rapid push). Find the concentration first, then solve for mL/h or mL. The concentrations below are examples — always use the label on the bag or syringe in front of you. · Heparin — units/h and mL/h · Given: heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL; order 1,000 units/h · Concentration: 25,000 ÷ 250 = 100 units/mL · Formula: ordered units/h ÷ units/mL = mL/h · Steps: 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 · Answer: 10 mL/h · Weight-based — Given: 18 units/kg/h for an 80 kg client; same bag (100 units/mL) · Steps: 18 × 80 = 1,440 units/h → 1,440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 · Answer: 14.4 mL/h (1,440 units/h) · Heparin is monitored with the PTT — "two t's make an H." Watch platelets for HIT; the antidote is protamine sulfate. · Dopamine — mcg/kg/min → mL/h · Given: dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL; order 5 mcg/kg/min; client 80 kg · Concentration: 400 mg × 1,000 = 400,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 1,600 mcg/mL · Formula: (mcg × kg × 60 min) ÷ mcg/mL = mL/h · Steps: 5 × 80 = 400 mcg/min → × 60 = 24,000 mcg/h → 24,000 ÷ 1,600 = 15 · Answer: 15 mL/h . (At the top of the 5–20 mcg/kg/min brady range, 20 mcg/kg/min for the same client = 96,000 ÷ 1,600 = 60 mL/h.) · Epinephrine — mcg/min → mL/h · Given: epinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL; order 2 mcg/min (brady range 2–10 mcg/min) · Concentration: 4 mg × 1,000 = 4,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 16 mcg/mL · Formula: (mcg/min × 60) ÷ mcg/mL = mL/h (no weight in this one) · Steps: 2 × 60 = 120 mcg/h → 120 ÷ 16 = 7.5 · Answer: 7.5 mL/h . At 10 mcg/min: 600 ÷ 16 = 37.5 mL/h. · Dopamine and epinephrine are vesicants — large vein or central line, check the site often; extravasation antidote is phentolamine. · Amiodarone — mg/min → mL/h · Given: amiodarone 900 mg in 500 mL; maintenance 1 mg/min · Concentration: 900 ÷ 500 = 1.8 mg/mL · Steps: 1 mg/min × 60 = 60 mg/h → 60 ÷ 1.8 = 33.33 · Answer: 33.3 mL/h (33 mL/h to the nearest whole number) · Push doses — atropine and adenosine · Drug | Given | Steps | Answer · Atropine 1 mg IV push | Prefilled syringe 0.1 mg/mL (1 mg/10 mL) | 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10 | 10 mL — repeat q3–5 min, max 3 mg (30 mL total) · Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push | Vial 3 mg/mL | 6 ÷ 3 = 2 | 2 mL , then 20 mL NS flush fast · Adenosine 12 mg (second dose) | Vial 3 mg/mL | 12 ÷ 3 = 4 | 4 mL , then flush · Beware the look-alike, sound-alike "A" drugs : A tropine speeds a slow heart, A denosine briefly stops a fast one, A miodarone is an antiarrhythmic drip. Read the label twice.

CO = HR × SV — and why a racing heart can pump less · Every rhythm, drug, and fluid decision in Perfusion is really about one goal: optimize cardiac output . Two quick formulas let you see how heart rate and stroke volume trade off against each other. · The formulas · Value | Formula | Normal · Cardiac output (CO) | Heart rate × stroke volume (mL) ÷ 1,000 = L/min | 4–8 L/min · Stroke volume (SV) | (CO in L/min × 1,000) ÷ heart rate = mL/beat | 60–100 mL/beat · Stroke volume is measured in mL per beat , but cardiac output is reported in liters per minute — so divide by 1,000 at the end (or multiply by 1,000 to go back). · Worked example 1 — finding CO · Given: HR 72 beats/min, SV 70 mL/beat · Formula: CO = HR × SV · Steps: 72 × 70 = 5,040 mL/min → 5,040 ÷ 1,000 = 5.04 L/min · Answer: CO ≈ 5 L/min — within the normal 4–8 L/min · Worked example 2 — finding SV · Given: CO 5.5 L/min, HR 80 beats/min · Formula: SV = (CO × 1,000) ÷ HR · Steps: 5.5 × 1,000 = 5,500 mL/min → 5,500 ÷ 80 = 68.75 · Answer: SV = 68.75 mL/beat (≈ 69) — within the normal 60–100 mL/beat · Worked example 3 — why tachycardia eventually LOWERS CO · Faster sounds like more output, and at first it is. But the ventricles fill during diastole , and diastole is the part of the cycle that shrinks when the rate climbs. Less filling time → less blood in the ventricle → ↓ stroke volume . · Situation | HR | SV | CO · Resting | 80 | 70 mL | 80 × 70 = 5,600 mL → 5.6 L/min · Sustained tachycardia, poor filling | 160 | 25 mL | 160 × 25 = 4,000 mL → 4.0 L/min · The rate doubled, but stroke volume fell so far that cardiac output dropped . Lose the atrial kick (as in A-fib) and filling drops even more; a fast heart also raises myocardial O₂ demand — which is why a patient in a fast rhythm can show signs of decreased CO (↓BP, dizziness, chest pain). · CO = HR × SV. If one side drops, the other has to rise to keep up. A slow heart lowers CO through HR; a very fast heart lowers CO through SV (no time to fill).

t: Heart Rate from a Strip & Ejection Fraction
x: The 6-second method and the EF percentage · Two numbers you'll calculate constantly: the heart rate off a rhythm strip, and the ejection fraction that classifies heart failure. · Heart rate — the 6-second method · Formula: number of QRS complexes in a 6-second strip × 10 = heart rate (beats/min). Count the QRS complexes (the tall spikes), not the P waves. One big box = 0.20 s, so 30 big boxes = 6 seconds. · Given: 7 QRS complexes in 6 seconds (a 7–8 count is typical for this rate) · Steps: 7 × 10 = 70 · Answer: about 70–75 beats/min → within 60–100 = normal rate · Given: 5 QRS complexes in 6 seconds · Steps: 5 × 10 = 50 · Answer: about 50 beats/min → below 60 = bradycardia. Check whether the client is symptomatic before treating. · The 6-second method is an estimate — great for regular and irregular rhythms alike (it's the go-to for A-fib). A partial complex at the edge makes the count land a little above or below the true rate. · QRS in 6 s | Rate | Interpretation (if sinus) · 3 | 30 | Very slow — brady · 5 | 50 | Brady (below 60) · 6–10 | 60–100 | Normal rate · 12 | 120 | Tachy (above 100) · 18 | 180 | SVT range (150–250) — not sinus tach · Ejection fraction (EF) · Formula: (volume ejected ÷ end-diastolic volume) × 100 = EF %. End-diastolic volume is how much blood is in the ventricle when it's full; volume ejected is what leaves with one squeeze (the stroke volume). · Given: end-diastolic volume 100 mL; 60 mL ejected · Steps: 60 ÷ 100 = 0.60 → × 100 = 60 · Answer: EF = 60% → normal · Given: end-diastolic volume 120 mL; 42 mL ejected · Steps: 42 ÷ 120 = 0.35 → × 100 = 35 · Answer: EF = 35% → below 50% = HFrEF (systolic, can't pump) · EF | Meaning · 50–70% | Normal · Below 50% | HFrEF — reduced EF, systolic HF, stretched/boggy walls that can't pump · Normal EF with HF symptoms | HFpEF — preserved EF, diastolic HF, thick stiff walls that can't fill · An echocardiogram is the go-to test for EF. Remember "Systolic = stretched" (low EF) and "Diastolic = thick" (EF preserved).

Perfusion pressure to the organs and the brain · In stroke and neuro patients you'll often need two steps : calculate MAP from the blood pressure, then subtract ICP to get cerebral perfusion pressure. · The formulas · Value | Formula | Target · MAP | (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 | 65 or higher = adequate organ perfusion · CPP | MAP − ICP | Below ~60 = cerebral ischemia risk · Diastole counts twice in MAP because the heart spends about two-thirds of each cycle in diastole. Always finish MAP before you subtract ICP. · Example 1 — post-stroke client, adequate · Given: BP 150/90, ICP 15 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 90 = 180 → 150 + 180 = 330 → 330 ÷ 3 = 110 · Step 2 (CPP): 110 − 15 = 95 mmHg · Interpret: MAP 65 or higher and CPP well above 60 → brain is being perfused · Example 2 — low BP, rising ICP · Given: BP 84/48, ICP 22 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 48 = 96 → 84 + 96 = 180 → 180 ÷ 3 = 60 · Step 2 (CPP): 60 − 22 = 38 mmHg · Interpret: MAP below 65 AND CPP far below 60 → cerebral ischemia risk. Report immediately; this client needs perfusion support. · Example 3 — normal MAP, but high ICP · Given: BP 120/75, ICP 35 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 75 = 150 → 120 + 150 = 270 → 270 ÷ 3 = 90 · Step 2 (CPP): 90 − 35 = 55 mmHg · Interpret: MAP looks fine, but CPP is below ~60 → the brain is at risk. A "normal" BP doesn't guarantee brain perfusion when ICP is high. · Example 4 — rounding a MAP · Given: BP 118/76, ICP 12 mmHg · Step 1 (MAP): 2 × 76 = 152 → 118 + 152 = 270 → 270 ÷ 3 = 90 · Step 2 (CPP): 90 − 12 = 78 mmHg → adequate · If MAP doesn't divide evenly (e.g., 122/78 → 278 ÷ 3 = 92.67), round only at the end, as the question directs (92.7 or 93). · Quick interpretation table · Result | Meaning | Nursing thought · MAP 65 or higher | Organs perfused | Keep monitoring · MAP below 65 | Organ perfusion at risk | Report; think decreased CO care (SBP goal above 90) · CPP about 60 or higher | Brain perfused | Keep monitoring neuro status · CPP below ~60 | Cerebral ischemia risk | Report; neuro checks; check BP and ICP trends

CPP = MAP − ICP with the IICP thresholds · Value | Formula / normal · CPP | MAP − ICP · MAP (when only a BP is given) | (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 · Normal ICP | 0–15 mm Hg · Normal CPP | 70–100 mm Hg · CPP | Meaning · Above 150 | Hyperperfusion — more edema, higher ICP · 70–100 | Normal · Below 50 | Cerebral ischemia · Below 30 | Neuronal death · 0 (ICP = MAP) | No cerebral blood flow — brain death · Example 1 · Given: MAP 88, ICP 12 · CPP = 88 − 12 = 76 mm Hg → normal · Example 2 — start from a BP · Given: BP 130/70, ICP 30 · MAP = (130 + 140) ÷ 3 = 90 · CPP = 90 − 30 = 60 mm Hg → below normal; report and work to lower the ICP or support the MAP · Example 3 · Given: MAP 70, ICP 26 · CPP = 70 − 26 = 44 mm Hg → below 50: cerebral ischemia · Finish the MAP first, then subtract the ICP. A normal BP does not guarantee brain perfusion when the ICP is high.

Cardiac output sized to the body — plus intracardiac pressures · Likely NUR 211 content — kept here for next semester; not on the Module 4 exam. · Why index cardiac output? · A CO of 4 L/min means something different for a small adult than for a very large one. Cardiac index (CI) adjusts cardiac output for body size by dividing by body surface area (BSA). · Formula · Value | Formula | Normal · Cardiac index | CO (L/min) ÷ BSA (m²) | 2.5–4 L/min/m² · Worked example · Given: CO 5.5 L/min, BSA 1.64 m² · Formula: CI = CO ÷ BSA · Steps: 5.5 ÷ 1.64 = 3.354 → rounds to 3.35 · Answer: CI ≈ 3.35 L/min/m² → within the normal 2.5–4 · Bedside monitors usually calculate BSA and CI automatically once height and weight are entered. · Normal intracardiac pressures (likely 211) · Location | Normal (mmHg) · Right atrium | 0–8 · Right ventricle | Systolic 15–25 / diastolic 0–8 · Pulmonary artery | Systolic 15–25 / diastolic 8–15 · Left atrium | 4–12 · Left ventricle | Systolic 110–130 / diastolic 4–12 · Aorta | Systolic 110–130 / diastolic 70–80 · Pattern to notice: the right side is a low-pressure system (pumps only to the lungs); the left side is high pressure (pumps to the whole body) — which is why the left ventricle is the thickest chamber.

Estimating small or scattered burns · For very small or scattered burns, the client's own palm and fingers equal about 1% of their total body surface area (TBSA). · Use the client's hand, not the nurse's — the estimate scales with the client's size. · Count how many of the client's palms would cover the burned areas. · Each palm-sized area ≈ 1% TBSA. · Example · Scattered burns on the forearm and thigh would be covered by about 4 of the client's palms → about 4% TBSA . · One client palm ≈ 1%. Body surface area methods are a reference skill in this module — know what the rule means.

Tracking what goes in, what comes out, and what IV fluids do to cells · Intake and output tracking is really just accounting for fluid — but a couple of categories have special rules that are easy to get wrong, and tonicity explains why the choice of IV fluid itself matters beyond just the volume. This is directly relevant to fluid management in cancer/chemotherapy patients, HIV/AIDS patients with diarrhea or wasting, and any client receiving IV psychiatric medications. · What counts as intake · Oral (PO) fluids — water, juice, soda, milk, coffee · Liquid foods — soups, broths, gelatin, sherbet, sorbet, pudding · Ice chips — recorded as half the original volume (200 mL of ice chips = 100 mL intake), since ice chips are mostly air/space between solid pieces · IV fluids — maintenance fluids, boluses, and piggyback medications (like antibiotics) · Tube feedings — formula and water flushes (relevant for a client with anorexia nervosa on enteral nutritional rehabilitation) · What counts as output · Urine — voided, catheterized, or urostomy drainage · Emesis (vomitus) — relevant for a client with bulimia or chemotherapy-induced nausea · Liquid stool — diarrhea or colostomy drainage · Wound drainage — from JP drains, Hemovacs, or chest tubes · Suction — gastric (NG) or respiratory · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake of 3000 mL, output of 800 mL. 3000 − 800 = +2200 mL (a positive balance, meaning the patient is retaining more fluid than they're losing). · Insensible Loss · Fluid lost through the skin and lungs that can't be directly measured. Standard estimate: 600–900 mL/day , or roughly 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Worked example: a 70 kg patient: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mL/hr, or roughly 840 mL/day. · Fluid Weight Calculation · Rule of thumb: a 1 kg weight change equals roughly 1 L of fluid change. Worked example: a patient's weight rises 2 kg over two days — that's roughly a 2 L fluid gain, not necessarily 2 kg of actual tissue. · An output under 30 mL/hr is always reported as a potential emergency — it signals inadequate perfusion to the kidneys. · Tonicity — what different IV fluids do to cells · Type | Solute concentration vs. inside the cell | Effect on the cell | Examples | Clinical use · Hypertonic | Higher outside the cell | Water leaves the cell — it shrinks (plasmolysis) | 3% or 5% NaCl; 10% Dextrose in Water | Cerebral edema, severe hyponatremia · Hypotonic | Lower outside the cell | Water enters the cell — it swells or bursts (cytolysis) | 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline) | Dehydration — pushes water back into cells · Isotonic | Equal inside and outside | No net water movement — equilibrium maintained | 0.9% Normal Saline, Lactated Ringer's, D5W | Routine IV fluid replacement and hydration · A simple way to remember the direction: hyper tonic pulls water OUT of the cell (think 'hyper' = high solute outside, pulling water toward it), while hypo tonic pushes water IN . Isotonic is the 'do no harm' default fluid.

Normal values, who compensates for whom, and acute (uncompensated) vs. chronic (compensated) · The lungs and the kidneys are the body's two acid–base regulators. When the kidneys fail, they can no longer excrete acid or make bicarbonate, so metabolic acidosis is an expected finding in renal failure — and the lungs will try to make up for it. · Normal values · Value | Normal range | What it represents · pH | 7.35–7.45 (absolute normal is 7.40 ) | Below 7.35 = acidosis; above 7.45 = alkalosis · PaCO 2 | 35–45 mmHg | The acid — controlled by the lungs (respiratory). Because CO 2 is an acid, the ends of its range are reversed: above 45 = acidotic , below 35 = alkalotic · HCO 3 | 22–26 mEq/L | The base — controlled by the kidneys (metabolic). Below 22 = acidotic , above 26 = alkalotic · PaO 2 | 80–100 mmHg | Oxygenation. Low = hypoxemia ; high = usually oxygen therapy · SaO 2 | 95–100% | Oxygen saturation. Low = hypoxemia · The body always tries to compensate to get back to 7.40 . Carbon dioxide and bicarbonate will fluctuate to make this happen. · Who compensates, and how fast · System | Controls | Speed | How it compensates · Lungs (respiratory) | CO 2 (acid) | Fast — within minutes to hours | Breathe fast to blow off CO 2 (raises pH); breathe slow to retain CO 2 (lowers pH) · Kidneys (metabolic) | HCO 3 (base) | Slow — may take days | Make more HCO 3 (raises pH); make less HCO 3 (lowers pH) · Kussmaul respirations — deep, rapid breathing — in a patient with renal failure or DKA are the lungs compensating for metabolic acidosis by blowing off CO 2 . In a renal patient, expect the pH to be low (below 7.35). That breathing pattern is a cue, not the primary problem. · Uncompensated, partially compensated, fully compensated ·  | Uncompensated (acute) | Partially compensated | Fully compensated (chronic) · pH | Abnormal | Still abnormal | Normal (7.35–7.45) · CO 2 and HCO 3 | Only one is abnormal; the other is normal (or close to it) | All three values are abnormal | Both are abnormal · Why | One system is causing the problem, and the other hasn't started fixing it yet | The opposing system has started to help, but hasn't finished | The opposing system has pushed the pH back into range, but is working hard to hold it there · Pattern tables · Uncompensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ Low (acid) | ↑ High (acid) | Normal · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ High (alk) | ↓ Low (alk) | Normal · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ Low (acid) | Normal | ↓ Low (acid) · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ High (alk) | Normal | ↑ High (alk) · Partially compensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ Low | ↑ High (cause) | ↑ High (fixing) · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ High | ↓ Low (cause) | ↓ Low (fixing) · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ Low | ↓ Low (fixing) | ↓ Low (cause) · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ High | ↑ High (fixing) | ↑ High (cause) · Fully compensated | pH | PaCO 2 | HCO 3 · Respiratory acidosis | Normal (low side, 7.35–7.39) | ↑ High | ↑ High · Respiratory alkalosis | Normal (high side, 7.41–7.45) | ↓ Low | ↓ Low · Metabolic acidosis | Normal (low side, 7.35–7.39) | ↓ Low | ↓ Low · Metabolic alkalosis | Normal (high side, 7.41–7.45) | ↑ High | ↑ High · Worked example of partial compensation: pH 7.31 (acid), CO 2 50 (acid), HCO 3 28 (base). The pH is still abnormal, and all three values are abnormal. High CO 2 matches the acidosis, so this is respiratory acidosis — and the kidneys are partially compensating by raising HCO 3 . · Reading a compensated gas — finding the "problem child" · Look at which end of the scale the pH is closer to. Below 7.40 = the underlying problem is acidosis ; above 7.40 = the underlying problem is alkalosis · You will never have a compensated problem with a pH right smack in the middle — it will always lean toward one end or the other · In a compensation situation, HCO 3 and CO 2 will both be high or both be low together · Too much base (high HCO 3 ) or too little acid (low CO 2 ) = alkalosis · Too much acid (high CO 2 ) or too little base (low HCO 3 ) = acidosis · Whichever value matches the direction of the pH is the problem child (the cause); the other value is the compensation · Step-by-step method · Step 1 — pH: acidosis (<7.35), alkalosis (>7.45), or normal? If normal, note whether it leans below or above 7.40 · Step 2 — CO 2 : is it high (acid excess), low (acid deficit), or normal? · Step 3 — HCO 3 : is it high (base excess), low (base deficit), or normal? · Step 4 — match: which value explains the pH direction? That names the disorder — respiratory if CO 2 , metabolic if HCO 3 · Step 5 — compensation: if the other value is normal = uncompensated; if all three are abnormal = partially compensated; if both are abnormal and pH is normal = fully compensated · ROME: R espiratory O pposite (pH and CO 2 move in opposite directions — pH down, CO 2 up in respiratory acidosis), M etabolic E qual (pH and HCO 3 move in the same direction — pH down, HCO 3 down in metabolic acidosis). · Causes and priority treatment for each imbalance · Imbalance | The problem | Common causes | Priority treatment · Respiratory acidosis (CO 2 ↑) | Lungs are retaining CO 2 (hypoventilation) | COPD, asthma, opioid overdose , pneumonia, oversedation | Improve ventilation — oxygen, incentive spirometry, naloxone (Narcan) if opioid-induced, BiPAP or intubation · Respiratory alkalosis (CO 2 ↓) | Lungs are blowing off CO 2 (hyperventilation) | Anxiety/panic attack, pain, fever, high altitude | Slow the breathing — paper bag breathing, treat pain and anxiety · Metabolic acidosis (HCO 3 ↓) | Kidneys losing bicarbonate or retaining acid | Renal failure (AKI/CKD) , severe diarrhea, DKA (ketones) | Fix the cause — dialysis (renal), insulin (DKA), antidiarrheals · Metabolic alkalosis (HCO 3 ↑) | Stomach losing acid | Vomiting, NG suctioning, antacid overuse | Stop the loss — antiemetics, stop suctioning, replace electrolytes (K⁺) · Acidosis and potassium travel together. In acidosis, hydrogen ions move into cells and potassium moves out into the blood — so a patient in renal failure with metabolic acidosis is doubly at risk for hyperkalemia. Correcting the acidosis (for example, with sodium bicarbonate) pushes potassium back into cells.

t: ABG Chart: Uncompensated, Partially & Fully Compensated
x: Normal values and the arrow patterns for all four imbalances · ABG values · Test | Normal | ↓ Value | ↑ Value · pH | 7.35–7.45 | Acidosis | Alkalosis · PaCO₂ | 35–45 mmHg | Alkalosis | Acidosis · HCO₃⁻ | 22–26 mEq/L | Acidosis | Alkalosis · PaO₂ | 80–100 mmHg | Hypoxemia | O₂ therapy · SaO₂ | 95–100% | Hypoxemia | — · PaCO₂ is the one that runs backward: CO₂ is an acid, so a high PaCO₂ means acidosis and a low PaCO₂ means alkalosis . pH and HCO₃⁻ read the same direction as the imbalance. · Uncompensated (acute) — only one system is off · System | ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Lungs | Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | Normal · Lungs | Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | Normal · Kidneys | Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | Normal | ↓ · Kidneys | Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | Normal | ↑ · Partially compensated — pH still abnormal, the other system has started to move · ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | ↑ | ↑ · Fully compensated (chronic) — pH back in range, both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ abnormal · ABG | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃⁻ · Respiratory acidosis | Normal (7.35–7.39, acid side) | ↑ | ↑ · Respiratory alkalosis | Normal (7.41–7.45, alkaline side) | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic acidosis | Normal (7.35–7.39, acid side) | ↓ | ↓ · Metabolic alkalosis | Normal (7.41–7.45, alkaline side) | ↑ | ↑ · Same arrows, different pH. The PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ arrows look identical in partial and full compensation — the pH is what tells them apart. Abnormal pH = partial; normal pH = full. Acute = uncompensated (pH abnormal, only one value off); chronic = compensated (pH normal, both values off). To name the original problem in full compensation, look at which side of 7.40 the pH leans toward. · ROME: R espiratory O pposite — pH and PaCO₂ arrows point in opposite directions. M etabolic E qual — pH and HCO₃⁻ arrows point in the same direction.

Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal — combined with your arrows · ROME = Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal. Compare the arrow on the pH with the arrow on PaCO₂ and HCO₃. The value that matches the ROME rule is the cause. · The four imbalances — arrows · Imbalance | pH | PaCO₂ | HCO₃ | ROME · Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | ↔ (or ↑ if compensating) | pH and CO₂ opposite → Respiratory · Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | ↔ (or ↓ if compensating) | pH and CO₂ opposite → Respiratory · Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | ↔ (or ↓ if compensating) | ↓ | pH and HCO₃ equal → Metabolic · Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | ↔ (or ↑ if compensating) | ↑ | pH and HCO₃ equal → Metabolic · Step by step · 1. pH — below 7.35 = acidosis (↓); above 7.45 = alkalosis (↑). If it is 7.35–7.45, note which side of 7.40 it leans toward. · 2. Draw the arrows for pH, PaCO₂ (35–45), and HCO₃ (22–26). · 3. ROME — PaCO₂ arrow opposite the pH arrow → respiratory. HCO₃ arrow same as the pH arrow → metabolic. · 4. Compensation — the other value normal → uncompensated . The other value abnormal and pH still abnormal → partially compensated . Both abnormal and pH back to normal → fully compensated . · The tic-tac-toe boxes · Put each value in a box — Acid, Normal, or Base. Remember PaCO₂ is reversed: high CO₂ = acid , low CO₂ = base. The value in the same box as the pH is the cause; the value in the opposite box is compensating. · Example: pH 7.31 · PaCO₂ 52 · HCO₃ 29 | Acid | Normal | Base · pH 7.31 | ✓ |  |  · PaCO₂ 52 | ✓ (cause) |  |  · HCO₃ 29 |  |  | ✓ (compensating) · Arrows: pH ↓, PaCO₂ ↑ — opposite → respiratory. Boxes: pH and CO₂ share the acid box → respiratory acidosis. HCO₃ is moving (base) and the pH is still abnormal → partially compensated respiratory acidosis . · Fully compensated — use 7.40 · pH 7.37 · PaCO₂ 30 · HCO₃ 17. The pH is normal but below 7.40, so it leans acid . HCO₃ 17 is acid (same as the lean) → metabolic; CO₂ 30 is base (compensating). Both abnormal, pH normal → fully compensated metabolic acidosis . · Use both: the arrows for ROME and the boxes to see which value matches the pH. For endless practice, see Games → Endless ABGs (classic or ROME boxes).

Which gas goes with which emergency · Use the same steps as the ABG Review: pH first, then match CO₂ (lungs) or HCO₃ (kidneys) to the pH, then check compensation. These are the gases that show up with this module's exemplars. · Emergency | Expected gas | Why · Opioid or benzodiazepine overdose | Respiratory acidosis | Respiratory depression — CO₂ is retained · Alcohol intoxication with slow breathing | Respiratory acidosis | CNS and respiratory depression · IICP — therapeutic hyperventilation | Respiratory alkalosis (on purpose) | Blowing off CO₂ (a vasodilator) constricts cerebral vessels and lowers ICP — brief use only · Salicylate (aspirin) overdose | Respiratory alkalosis first → metabolic acidosis | Aspirin stimulates the respiratory center; then acid builds up in the blood · Shock (any type) | Metabolic acidosis | Poor perfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid (lactate above 2 = cells in trouble) · Burns — emergent phase | Metabolic acidosis | Lost bicarbonate and lactic acid from poor perfusion · Cardiac arrest | Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis | No breathing (CO₂ builds) and no perfusion (lactic acid) — "hydrogen ion (acidosis)" is one of the H's · Anxiety / panic, early sepsis | Respiratory alkalosis | Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ · Carbon monoxide — a special case · Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal (98–100%) with carbon monoxide. An ABG with a carboxyhemoglobin level shows the true picture. Treat with 100% O₂ by nonrebreather. · Slow breathing = CO₂ builds = respiratory acidosis . Poor perfusion = lactic acid = metabolic acidosis . Fast breathing = CO₂ blown off = respiratory alkalosis .

t: Renal Math: Urine Output, Fluid Restriction & Daily Weights
x: The calculations behind the AKI, CKD, and fluid-balance lessons · Hourly Urine Output (mL/kg/hr) · Formula: Urine output (mL) ÷ Hours ÷ Weight (kg) = mL/kg/hr. The minimum acceptable adult output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr (roughly 30 mL/hr). · Minimum for a given client: Weight (kg) × 0.5 = minimum mL/hr. A 70 kg client needs at least 70 × 0.5 = 35 mL/hr . · Worked example: An 80 kg client voids 200 mL over 8 hours. 200 ÷ 8 = 25 mL/hr; 25 ÷ 80 = 0.31 mL/kg/hr — below 0.5, so it's reported as an early warning of AKI. · 24-Hour Output — naming the problem · 24-hour urine output | Term · Less than 400–500 mL | Oliguria (the oliguric phase of AKI: below 400 mL/day) · Less than 50 mL | Anuria · 4–5 L/day | Diuretic phase of AKI — watch for fluid volume deficit · More than 3 L/day after an obstruction is relieved | Postobstructive diuresis · Fluid Restriction · Formula: Previous 24-hour urine output + about 500–600 mL (insensible losses) = Fluid allowance for the next 24 hours. (Some references use 500–800 mL.) · Worked example: A client in the oliguric phase put out 350 mL of urine yesterday. 350 + 500 = 850 mL to 350 + 600 = 950 mL — a fluid allowance of about 850–950 mL for today. · The fluid allowance is spread across all 24 hours — with sips, ice chips, and frequent mouth care for thirst — and it has to include the fluid used to take medications. · Daily Weights — 1 kg = 1 L · Rule: a 1 kg weight change equals about 1 L of fluid (about 2.2 lb per liter). Weigh at the same time, on the same scale, in the same clothing. · Worked example: Yesterday 72.0 kg; today 74.5 kg. 74.5 − 72.0 = 2.5 kg = about 2.5 L of retained fluid . · Worked example (pounds): A weight gain of 4.4 lb ÷ 2.2 = 2 kg = about 2 L of fluid. · BUN:Creatinine Ratio · Formula: BUN ÷ Creatinine. Normal is about 10:1 to 20:1; above 20:1 points toward a prerenal cause (dehydration, low perfusion). · BUN | Creatinine | Ratio | Points toward · 48 mg/dL | 1.2 mg/dL | 48 ÷ 1.2 = 40:1 | Prerenal — BUN rising out of proportion (dehydration) · 80 mg/dL | 8.0 mg/dL | 80 ÷ 8 = 10:1 | Intrarenal or postrenal — both rising together · Phosphate Binder Dose per Meal (Sevelamer) · Formula: Total daily dose ÷ Number of meals the client actually eats = Dose per meal · Worked example: Sevelamer 4,800 mg/day. Three meals a day: 4,800 ÷ 3 = 1,600 mg with each meal . The same client skips breakfast and eats 2 meals: 4,800 ÷ 2 = 2,400 mg with each meal . · The number of meals comes from the client's eating pattern, not a standard schedule — fewer meals means a bigger dose with each meal. And no meal, no binder. · Maximum-Rate Problems · Formula: Dose (mg) ÷ Maximum rate (mg/min) = Minimum time (minutes) · Worked example: High-dose IV furosemide is infused no faster than 4 mg/min (ototoxicity). For a 120 mg dose: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes minimum . · Rapid IV furosemide is what causes the tinnitus and hearing loss — if the math says 30 minutes, it never goes in faster, even when the client is fluid overloaded. · Net Fluid Balance · Formula: Total Intake − Total Output = Net Balance · Worked example: Intake: PO 600 mL + IV 900 mL + ice chips 200 mL (counts as 100 mL) = 1,600 mL. Output: urine 450 mL + emesis 150 mL = 600 mL. 1,600 − 600 = +1,000 mL — a positive balance (fluid retention).

x: How much fluid came off — and how to count it · Hemodialysis — Fluid Removal Goal · Formula: Pre-dialysis weight − Dry (target) weight = Fluid to remove (1 kg = 1 L) · Worked example: Pre-dialysis weight 78.4 kg; dry weight 76.0 kg. 78.4 − 76.0 = 2.4 kg = about 2.4 L to remove. The post-dialysis weight confirms how much actually came off. · Peritoneal Dialysis — Net Ultrafiltration · Formula: Outflow (drained) − Inflow (instilled) = Net fluid removed. A negative result means the client absorbed (retained) dialysate. · Inflow | Outflow | Result | Meaning · 2,000 mL | 2,500 mL | +500 mL | 500 mL removed — recorded as output · 2,000 mL | 1,800 mL | −200 mL | 200 mL retained — counts toward intake; check for kinks, constipation, and position · Multiple exchanges: add the net result of each one. Exchanges of +300, +150, and −100 mL = +350 mL net removed. If drainage is short by 500 mL or more over several exchanges, evaluate for fluid retention and notify the provider. · PD outflow is not urine. Record the client's true urine output separately from the dialysate drained. · CRRT — Hourly Fluid Balance · The nurse totals all intake and output every hour and adjusts to meet the ordered hourly balance goal. · Formula: Hourly net fluid removal needed = Hourly intake (IV fluids, meds, feedings, replacement fluid) + Desired hourly fluid loss · Worked example: The goal is a net loss of 100 mL/hr. This hour the client receives IV fluid 50 mL + tube feeding 60 mL + IV meds 40 mL = 150 mL. To achieve −100 mL, the machine must remove 150 + 100 = 250 mL of fluid from the client this hour.

Check pulse / start CPR → rhythm check: asystole or PEA → epinephrine ASAP → CPR 2 min (find the H's and T's) → rhythm check: NOW SHOCKABLE → shock #1 (the electricity reset) → CPR 2 min → rhythm check: shockable → shock #2 → CPR 2 min + epinephrine → shock #3 → CPR 2 min + amiodarone . · Pathway 4 — The "Reverse" (VF → asystole) · The heart loses all electrical activity after unsuccessful shocks. A head injury, a lucid interval, and a race against herniation · Luke Kwon, a professional golfer and YouTube creator, survived an epidural hemorrhage in September 2022 — and was extremely lucky to live. It is the same type of head injury that killed actress Natasha Richardson in 2009: after a fall on a beginner ski slope she felt fine and declined medical care, then declined hours later. · His video account is a layperson's telling of a complex neurological emergency, pieced together from what he remembers and what others told him. · Case question: which of his symptoms show that his intracranial pressure had risen to a very dangerous level? · What happened · Time | Events | Cues · The injury | Riding in a golf cart with his head out, he struck a steel bridge railing. "Ow — what was that?" He did not pass out. | Mechanism of a head injury; no loss of consciousness does not rule out a bleed · The next hours | Played seven more holes — remembers none of them. Texted that he felt confused. Drove about 40 minutes to his hotel. | Amnesia for the event; confusion — a change in LOC · At the hotel | Excruciating, worsening headache; very sleepy; asked the clerk to wake him and check his orientation. Did not want the ER because of cost. | Worsening headache and lethargy = rising ICP; the lucid interval is ending · Arriving at the ER | Vomited three times outside the entrance. Minutes later, asked where he was, he answered with something unrelated (switching his website payment system). | Vomiting from pressure; disorientation — LOC is falling fast · Emergency CT | Large collection of blood across the top left of the skull; staff called out the amount of blood. | Space-occupying bleed in a closed box · Before transfer | In and out of a coma; seven seizures, two serious. The first hospital had no neurosurgeon, and he was too unstable to transfer — he was sedated more until stable enough. | Seizures and coma = decompensation. Sedation lowers the brain's metabolic demand and protects the airway · Surgery | Transferred to a hospital with a neurosurgeon; the blood was drained in about 2.5 hours. The eight practice gases from the ABG review, worked step by step · Each gas below is worked using the same five steps: pH direction → CO 2 → HCO 3 → which value matches → is the other value normal or abnormal. Normal ranges: pH 7.35–7.45, CO 2 35–45, HCO 3 22–26. · Set 1 — compensated or uncompensated? · # | pH | CO 2 | HCO 3 | Interpretation | Why · 1 | 7.22 | 72 | 23 | Uncompensated respiratory acidosis | pH is acidotic; CO 2 is high (acid excess) and matches; HCO 3 is normal, so the kidneys haven't compensated yet · 2 | 7.30 | 42 | 6 | Uncompensated metabolic acidosis | pH is acidotic; HCO 3 is very low (base deficit) and matches; CO 2 is normal, so the lungs haven't compensated yet · 3 | 7.50 | 25 | 23 | Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis | pH is alkalotic; CO 2 is low (acid deficit) and matches; HCO 3 is normal · 4 | 7.48 | 41 | 35 | Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis | pH is alkalotic; HCO 3 is high (base excess) and matches; CO 2 is normal · Set 2 — compensated or uncompensated, and who is causing the problem? · # | pH | CO 2 | HCO 3 | Interpretation | Why · 5 | 7.37 | 72 | 36 | Compensated respiratory acidosis | pH is normal but leans acid (below 7.40); both values abnormal = compensated. High CO 2 causes acidosis → the lungs are the problem child; the kidneys raised HCO 3 to compensate · 6 | 7.38 | 15 | 6 | Compensated metabolic acidosis | pH is normal but leans acid; both values low together = compensated. Low HCO 3 causes acidosis → the kidneys are the problem child; the lungs blew off CO 2 to compensate (the pattern expected in renal failure) · 7 | 7.42 | 25 | 18 | Compensated respiratory alkalosis | pH is normal but leans alkaline (above 7.40); both values low. Low CO 2 causes alkalosis → the lungs are the problem child; the kidneys dropped HCO 3 to compensate · 8 | 7.43 | 50 | 35 | Compensated metabolic alkalosis | pH is normal but leans alkaline; both values high. High HCO 3 causes alkalosis → the kidneys are the problem child; the lungs retained CO 2 to compensate · In a compensated gas, the two abnormal values always point in the same direction (both high or both low), so they can't tell you the diagnosis by themselves. The pH's lean — even a tiny one like 7.38 vs. 7.42 — is what breaks the tie. · Connecting the practice gases to patients · Gas 1 (7.22 / 72 / 23) fits a patient who was suddenly oversedated with opioids — acute hypoventilation, no time for the kidneys to respond · Gas 5 (7.37 / 72 / 36) fits a patient with long-standing COPD — the CO 2 has been high for so long that the kidneys have fully compensated · Gas 2 (7.30 / 42 / 6) and Gas 6 (7.38 / 15 / 6) both show the severe bicarbonate loss of kidney failure — Gas 6 is what it looks like once the lungs have caught up with Kussmaul breathing · Gas 4 (7.48 / 41 / 35) fits a patient with prolonged vomiting or NG suction — acid lost from the stomach

The nurse's job is to stop the loss, restore volume, and keep MAP ≥ 60 . Priority diagnoses: fluid volume deficit, decreased cardiac output. · MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) ÷ 3 Goal 60 or above (class notes). Elevate HOB if MAP is good; lay flat if MAP is below 60. · Numbers that differ between your sources Your class notes use MAP ≥ 60 . Your textbook (Ch. 11) says MAP must exceed 65 mmHg for cells to get enough oxygen. Go with your instructor's 60 on the exam unless told otherwise — but know 65 is the textbook number. · 2.1 Hemorrhage — Stop the Bleed · Assess | Intervene · HR ↑, RR ↑, BP ↓, change in LOC, poor cap refill, cold, diaphoretic, weak pulses, syncope | Tourniquet on extremities only (~6 hours before permanent damage). Trunk/abdominal wound: pack it, then pressure · Can't feel pulses? Check carotid or femoral , then use a Doppler . · 2.2 Fluids — The Fluid-Responsive Test · Lay the patient flat with legs up. BP rises → they need fluids. BP stays the same → fluids won't help; go to vasopressors. · Step | Fluid | Notes · 1st | Isotonic crystalloids — NS, LR | First line · 2nd | Colloids — albumin, blood products, volume expanders | Stay where you put them · 3rd | Vasopressors | Not fluid-responsive, or nothing else works · 2.3 Vasopressors · Topic | Key point · Action | Constrict vessels → BP ↑ · Titration | MAP < 60 → start lowest dose, titrate up, add another pressor if needed. MAP > 60 → titrate down. Resp acidosis: blow off CO₂. Full-thickness and deeper burns may be painless because nerve fibers are destroyed — the textbook says this often deceives patients about how serious the burn is. · Numbers that differ between your sources Your burns handout says deep full-thickness burns need grafts . Your textbook (Table 58-1) says for 4th-degree burns amputation is likely and grafting is of no benefit . Then phentolamine SubQ infiltrated across the entire area. · 2.8 Complete the shock chart: · Type | Cause | Key signs | Priority treatment · Hypovolemic | Fluid/blood loss (~20%); ↓ preload | Tachycardia, tachypnea → bradypnea, hypotension | Stop bleeding, NS/LR, PRBCs + clotting factors, legs up · Septic | Infection; systemic vasodilation | Tachycardia, late hypotension, hyper/hypothermia, warm flushed skin | Antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors · Cardiogenic | MI (most common), tamponade, myocarditis | Pump failure — massive left HF | Control dysrhythmias, ↑ contractility · Anaphylactic | Drugs, food, venom; histamine ↓ afterload | SOB, stridor, wheezing, rash, swelling | Epinephrine first, O₂, fluids · Neurogenic | Spinal cord injury, spinal anesthesia, TBI | Dysfunction at injury level (bladder) | Support perfusion · 2.9 List early vs. late signs of shock: · Early | Late · Tachycardia, tachypnea, anxiety, restlessness, confusion | Hypotension · Prolonged cap refill, weak pulses, pallor, coolness | Change in LOC · Hypoactive bowel sounds | ↓ urine output, narrowing pulse pressure

x: IICP, Hydrocephalus & Brain Death · 3. IICP, Hydrocephalus & Brain Death · 3.1 Explain the Monro-Kellie hypothesis. What percentage of the skull is brain, CSF and blood? · The skull is a closed box (except in babies) and can't expand — a rise in one component must be offset by another. Brain 80%, CSF 10%, blood 10%. · 3.2 List the three ways the brain compensates for cerebral edema: · Autoregulation — arterioles dilate/constrict · CSF — ↓ production or ↑ reabsorption · Shunting — CSF to the spinal canal; blood to the venous system (keep neck straight) · 3.3 Cranial nerves — fill in the name and how to assess each one: · # | Nerve | How to assess · I | Olfactory | Smell (alcohol swab) · II | Optic | Snellen chart / read name badge · III | Oculomotor | PERRLA, cardinal fields of gaze · IV | Trochlear | Cardinal fields of gaze (down and in) · V | Trigeminal | Clench jaw, touch face · VI | Abducens | Cardinal fields of gaze (lateral) · VII | Facial | Funny faces, smile · VIII | Acoustic | Hearing, balance · IX | Glossopharyngeal | Say "ahh", uvula midline · X | Vagus | Gag reflex · XI | Spinal accessory | Shrug shoulders · XII | Hypoglossal | Tongue out midline · Mnemonic: "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, AH!" · 3.4 Put the LOC assessment in order (1–10) and label where the patient is alert, lethargic or unresponsive: · Step | Stimulus | Responds here = ? · 1 | State their name | Alert · 2 | Touch arm | Lethargic · 3 | Lightly pat arm | Lethargic · 4 | Shake arm | Lethargic · 5 | Pinch arm | No response = unresponsive · 6 | Nailbed pressure | Unresponsive · 7 | Sternal rub | Unresponsive · 8 | Tap forehead | Reflex · 9 | Gag | Reflex · 10 | Brush cornea with sterile gauze | No reflexes → assess brain death · 3.5 Define: · Persistent vegetative state: · Locked-in syndrome: · Persistent vegetative state: awake but unresponsive — "lights on, no one home" · Locked-in syndrome: neurologically intact but fully paralyzed · 3.6 What is the FIRST sign of IICP? Is headache a reliable sign? · Change in LOC (restless, lethargic, confused, any change from baseline). No — headache is not reliable. · 3.7 Label each sign as early or late: · Sign | Early / late · Unequal pupils | Early · Fixed, dilated pupils | Late · Vomiting without nausea | Late · Reflex impairment | Very late · Seizures | Any time · Cushing's triad | Late · 3.8 List the three signs of Cushing's triad: · Bradycardia · Hypertension with widened pulse pressure (SBP ↑, DBP ↓) · Bradypnea · 3.9 Posturing — match each to its brain level. Which is worse? · Posturing | Description | Level · Decorticate | Arms flexed in "to the core" | Above midbrain · Decerebrate (worse) | Arms extended, twisted out | Midbrain · Arms extended, legs flexed | — | Pons · Flaccid | Little or no response | Medulla · 3.10 Respiratory patterns — match each to its brain level: · Pattern | Level · Cheyne-Stokes | Cortex / upper brainstem · Hyperventilation | Midbrain / upper pons · Cluster / ataxic | Pons / medulla · 3.11 Central vs. peripheral fever — what causes each, and how is central fever treated? · Central = pressure on the hypothalamus — erratic ("neuro storm"); cool externally. Peripheral = infection. · 3.12 Complete the complications chart: · Complication | What happens | What you'll see · Diabetes insipidus | Too little ADH | Lots of urine · SIADH | Too much ADH | Fluid retention, swelling · Herniation | Brain shifts from high to low pressure | Loss of blood flow → brain death · 3.13 Ventriculostomy care — list four nursing responsibilities: · Maintain the drain (works by gravity) · Keep the transducer level with the tragus of the ear · Keep the insertion site sterile · Fluid should be clear — never cloudy · 3.14 Write the CPP formula and fill in the values: · CPP = MAP − ICP · Value | Meaning · Normal ICP | 0–15 mmHg · Normal CPP | 70–100 mmHg · CPP > 150 | Cerebral edema · CPP < 50 | Ischemia · CPP < 30 | Irreversible ischemia (necrosis) · CPP = 0 | Brain death (ICP = MAP) · 3.15 Calculate: MAP 80, ICP 25. What is the CPP? Is it normal? · 80 − 25 = 55. Low (normal 70–100) — heading toward ischemia. · 3.16 List interventions to decrease ICP and to manipulate MAP: · Decrease ICP | Manipulate MAP · Mannitol (osmotic diuretic — needs good kidneys) | BP low → vasopressors · Decadron (steroid) | BP low → blood transfusion · Avoid Valsalva — stool softener, loose restraints | BP high → nicardipine (CCB) · HOB up if MAP good; hyperventilation |  · Induced coma (propofol); temperature control |  · 3.17 Why is the patient hyperventilated? Why is HOB raised only if MAP is good? · Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis → vasoconstriction (CO₂ is a vasodilator) → ↓ ICP. Raising the HOB lowers ICP but also lowers cerebral perfusion if MAP is already low. · 3.18 Hydrocephalus — list priority assessments, diagnostics, post-shunt care and teaching: ·  | Answer · Assessment | Neuro checks, head circumference, bulging fontanel, pupils, LOC · Diagnostics | Ultrasound (ventricle size); CT in an emergency · Post-shunt care | HOB 15–30°, head circumference, neuro/pupil checks, seizure watch, dressing, feed as tolerated, prophylactic IV antibiotics · Teaching | Signs of IICP, no contact sports, protect from infection · 3.19 What three things are absent in brain death? Describe the caloric test and the doll's eye test. · No consciousness, no reflexes, no respirations. Caloric test: ice water against the eardrum — no eye response. Doll's eye: turn the head — eyes stay fixed (normal = eyes move). · 3.20 Why is an organ donor a "very busy" patient? · The heart keeps beating and perfusing organs until oxygen runs out — every organ must be checked and supported.

Burns & Smoke Inhalation, Environmental Emergencies · 4. Burns & Smoke Inhalation · 4.1 Complete the burn depth chart: · Depth | Appearance | Pain / sensation | Healing / treatment · 1st (superficial) | Sunburn | Painful | Heals on its own · 2nd (partial thickness) | Blisters, scalds | MOST painful — nerve endings exposed | Wound care · 3rd (full thickness) | Red or waxy white, thick | Decreased | Weeks–months; eschar removal + grafting; contractures · Deep full-thickness | Black, hard inelastic eschar; fascia/muscle/bone | None — nerves destroyed | Months; grafts required · 4.2 A patient with a black, leathery burn says it doesn't hurt. Is this a good sign? Why? · No. No pain means the nerve endings are destroyed — a deep full-thickness burn, the most serious type. · 4.3 List five priority assessments for a burn patient: · VS / ABCs; ABGs · Depth, extent, location · Urine output, HR, BP, MAP > 60 · Frequent temps (hypothermia, infection) · Pulse checks — compartment syndrome · 4.4 Complete the care-by-type chart: · Burn type | Priority care · Chemical | Remove the agent, flush with water, then treat as thermal · Thermal | Silver sulfadiazine (sterile application), dry sterile dressing, debridement, temperature control · Electrical | Cardiac monitoring, entry + exit wounds, electrolytes (K⁺), IV fluids for rhabdo, UOP, compartment syndrome · 4.5 Why is an electrical burn more dangerous than it looks? What is the priority? · Current travels through the heart and muscle — small skin wound, big internal damage. Priority = continuous cardiac monitoring. · 4.6 Why are burn patients at risk for hyperkalemia? · Destroyed cells release potassium into the blood → dysrhythmias. · 4.7 Burn location — what is the risk for each? · Location | Risk · Head, neck, chest | Pulmonary complications · Face | Corneal abrasion · Ears | Auricular chondritis · Hands and joints | Disability — aggressive therapy · Perineum | Contamination from urine/feces · Circumferential limb | Compartment syndrome · Circumferential thorax | Impaired chest expansion and ventilation · 4.8 When is a tetanus shot given? Is it needed for smoke inhalation alone? · Any break in the skin (burns, bites, wounds) if none in 10 years. Not needed for smoke inhalation alone. · 4.9 Smoke inhalation — fill in: · Signs of airway injury: · Carbon monoxide antidote: · Cyanide antidote (and its expected side effect): · When should the patient be intubated? · How long should they be observed? · Airway injury: facial burns, soot in sputum, hoarseness, stridor, wheezing · CO: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather · Cyanide: hydroxocobalamin — turns urine, skin, eyes RED · Intubate: early rather than late — especially with stridor · Observe: 12–24 hours for delayed airway injury · 4.10 List four burn teaching points: · Burns alter fluid balance · May need debridement and skin grafting · Nutrition and hydration for healing · Signs of infection: pain, pus, foul odor, spreading redness · 5. Environmental Emergencies · 5.1 Fill in the rule: Hypothermia → warm ________. Hyperthermia → cool ________. · Hypothermia → warm SLOWLY. Hyperthermia → cool QUICKLY. · 5.2 List five interventions for hypothermia: · Remove wet clothing · Warm blankets · Warm IV fluids and warm O₂ · Cardiac monitoring · Check glucose and electrolytes; assess for frostbite · 5.3 What two things should you NOT do for a hypothermic patient? · Don't massage extremities · Don't give atropine for the bradycardia · 5.4 Frostbite — answer each: · Signs (superficial vs. deep): · How is it rewarmed? · What should be given before rewarming? Why? · List three "don'ts": · Signs: superficial: white/waxy, numb, tingling; deep: hard, gray/mottled, no sensation, blisters after rewarming, black = gangrene · Rewarm: rapidly in warm water (~98.6–102°F) until pink and soft — treat hypothermia first · Before: pain medication — rewarming is very painful · Don'ts: don't rub/massage, no dry heat, don't walk on it, don't rewarm if it could refreeze · 5.5 Heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke: · Heat exhaustion (early) | Heat stroke (late) · Heavy sweating | Core temp > 104°F, NO sweating · Muscle cramps | Seizures, delirium, ataxia · N/V, headache, dizziness, weakness | Hypotension, arrhythmias, tachypnea · Tachycardia | Oliguria, rhabdomyolysis · 5.6 List the cooling measures for heat stroke. Why are antipyretics not used? · Remove clothes; ice packs to groin, neck, armpits; ice bath; evaporative cooling. Plus airway, high-flow O₂, IV fluids, ECG, treat seizures. Antipyretics are ineffective — the hypothalamus set point isn't the problem. · 5.7 Near drowning — list the signs, five interventions, and the key discharge teaching: · Signs: · Interventions: · Discharge teaching: · Signs: coughing, chest pain, dyspnea, cyanosis, crackles, tachy/brady · Interventions: patent airway, 100% O₂, albuterol, high Fowler's, NT suction, remove wet clothes + warm, IV fluids · Teaching: water safety; pulmonary edema up to 24 h later — return for cough, chest pain, dyspnea

Bites, Poisoning & Overdose, Cardiac Arrest (ACLS) · 6. Bites, Poisoning & Overdose · 6.1 Animal bites — what is the first wound care? What is the rabies vaccine schedule? · Rinse, rinse, rinse the wound; tetanus. Rabies vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14. · 6.2 Snake bites — list the signs, the treatment, and two things you must NOT do: · Signs: · Treatment: · Do NOT: · Signs: swelling, SOB, intense pain, metallic/rubbery taste, numbness/tingling · Treatment: antivenin within 4–6 h, IV fluids, morphine, EKG, coag labs, watch compartment syndrome, wound care · Do NOT: use a tourniquet/anything constricting, or elevate — keep limb below the heart · 6.3 What reaction should you watch for with antivenin? Why? · Allergic reaction — antivenin is made from horses. · 6.4 Spider bites — list the signs and interventions: · May be unnoticed; hours later redness, swelling, nausea, necrosis, ulcer. Soap and water, cool compress, elevate, pain meds, antihistamines, possible antibiotics/antivenom, surgery for necrosis. · 6.5 Complete the antidote chart: · Overdose / poison | Antidote | Key point · Opioids | Naloxone | Projectile vomiting, withdrawal · Benzodiazepines | Flumazenil | Withdrawal seizures · Acetaminophen | Acetylcysteine | Protects the liver · Unknown PO | Activated charcoal | Within 1 hour · Carbon monoxide | Oxygen | 100% non-rebreather · Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin | Red urine/skin · Vasopressor infiltration | Phentolamine | New IV first; SubQ · 6.6 Why can reversing an overdose too quickly be dangerous? · Long-term users can go into lethal rhythms with sudden withdrawal; abrupt benzo withdrawal can cause lethal seizures. · 6.7 List the nursing care and discharge teaching for an overdose patient: · Monitor RR and HR, antiemetic, raise HOB, safety, telemetry. Discharge: social worker, education on drug dangers, how to give naloxone at home. · 6.8 Alcohol — complete the chart: ·  | Intoxication / poisoning | Withdrawal · Signs | Slurred speech, ataxia, vomiting, ↓ LOC, slow breathing, hypothermia, hypoglycemia | Tremors, anxiety, tachycardia, HTN, sweating; seizures; DTs (hallucinations, fever) · Timeline | — | Starts 6–24 h; seizures 12–48 h; DTs 48–72 h · Priority care | Airway/aspiration — side-lying, suction, O₂, fluids, glucose, warmth | Benzos per CIWA, seizure precautions, quiet room, VS · Meds | Fluids, dextrose, thiamine | Benzos, thiamine, folic acid, magnesium · 6.9 Why is thiamine given before glucose to a chronic drinker? · Glucose without thiamine can trigger Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, eye problems). · 6.10 Put the general poisoning steps in order: · ABCs — airway, O₂, IV, monitor · Identify the toxin; call Poison Control · Decontaminate by route (flush skin/eyes, fresh air, charcoal) · Give the antidote · Monitor VS, LOC, labs · 6.11 When is activated charcoal NOT given? · Caustics (acids/alkalis), hydrocarbons, alcohol, iron, lithium, or an unprotected airway. · 7. Cardiac Arrest (ACLS) · 7.1 Which rhythms are shockable? Which are not? · Shockable: · Non-shockable: · Shockable: V-fib, pulseless V-tach (torsades — add magnesium) · Non-shockable: asystole, PEA · 7.2 Fill in the algorithm steps: · Step | Shockable (VF / pVT) | Non-shockable (asystole / PEA) · 1 | Shock ASAP | Epinephrine ASAP · 2 | CPR 2 min, IV/IO | CPR 2 min, IV/IO, advanced airway · 3 | Shock → CPR + epi every 3–5 min | Recheck rhythm; switch tracks if shockable · 4 | Shock → CPR + amiodarone/lidocaine | CPR + epi every 3–5 min; treat H's & T's · 7.3 List five elements of high-quality CPR: · Push hard (≥ 2 in) and fast (100–120/min) · Full chest recoil · Minimize interruptions (2-min checks) · Avoid excessive ventilation; swap compressors every 2 min · 30:2 without airway; 1 breath every 6 s with advanced airway · 7.4 Fill in the doses: · Drug / shock | Dose · Epinephrine | 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 min · Amiodarone | 300 mg, then 150 mg · Lidocaine | 1–1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg · Biphasic shock | 120–200 J (or max) · Monophasic shock | 360 J · Magnesium | Torsades · 7.5 What are the signs of ROSC? What does a low ETCO₂ during CPR tell you? · ROSC: pulse and BP return, sudden sustained ETCO₂ rise (≥ 40). Low ETCO₂ during CPR = poor CPR quality — push harder/faster. · 7.6 List the H's and T's: · H's | T's · Hypovolemia | Tension pneumothorax · Hypoxia | Tamponade · Hydrogen ion (acidosis) | Toxins · Hypo/hyperkalemia | Thrombosis — pulmonary · Hypothermia | Thrombosis — coronary · 7.7 PVCs and V-tach with a pulse — what is the treatment? · Rhythm | Treatment · PVCs | Assess patient; treat the cause (hypoxia, low K⁺/Mg²⁺, caffeine, stimulants, MI, pressors) · V-tach with pulse, stable | O₂, IV, 12-lead, amiodarone · V-tach with pulse, unstable | Synchronized cardioversion · V-tach without pulse | CPR + defibrillate
